beginner: Pick a slicing cucumber to match your garden. Marketmore 76 and Straight Eight are dependable all-rounders for fresh eating, Poinsett 76 and Ashley handle hot, humid weather and disease better, and burpless or seedless types like Sweet Slice and Sweet Success are mild and easy to digest. If you only have a pot or a small bed, choose a compact bush type like Spacemaster. Disease-resistant varieties are worth seeking out, and milder, less-bitter kinds also attract fewer pest beetles.
seasoned: Choose a slicing cucumber by climate and space. Marketmore 76 and Straight Eight are the reliable open-pollinated, monoecious standards, while Poinsett 76 and Ashley are bred for the disease pressure of humid Southern heat. Gynoecious hybrids like Dasher II set heavily but usually want a pollenizer plant nearby, and burpless or parthenocarpic types such as Sweet Slice and Sweet Success are mild, thin-skinned, and, in the seedless kinds, fruit without bees, which suits covered and container growing. Compact bush types like Spacemaster fit small beds and pots. Where disease pressure is high, lead with mildew- and wilt-tolerant varieties, and remember that less-bitter varieties also attract fewer cucumber beetles.

beginner: Do not plant slicing cucumbers where you grew squash, melons, pumpkins, or other cucumbers in the last few years. They get the same pests and diseases, which build up in the soil.
seasoned: Avoid planting slicing cucumbers where another cucurbit grew in the last few years, including squash, melon, pumpkin, and other cucumbers. They share cucumber beetle with the bacterial wilt it spreads, squash bug, powdery and downy mildew, angular leaf spot, and anthracnose, all of which build up in the soil and on debris.

beginner: Try not to grow cucumbers or their relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years or so. Moving them around the garden each year helps avoid a buildup of pests and disease. Clean up old vines at the end of the season too.
seasoned: Rotate cucurbits on a 3 year cycle, and a 3 to 4 year break where angular leaf spot or anthracnose has been a problem, since both persist on residue. The point is to break the buildup of cucumber beetle, beetle-vectored wilt, and soilborne and seedborne disease. Clear and remove spent vines at season's end rather than tilling them in, which cuts overwintering pest and disease sites and makes rotation more effective.

beginner: Slicing cucumbers do not keep long at room temperature, just a day or two. Use them soon or put them in the fridge, but not the coldest part.
seasoned: Slicing cucumbers are tender and short-lived off the vine. At room temperature they keep only a day or two before softening, so use them quickly or refrigerate, with the caveat that cucumbers are chilling-sensitive and do not love a very cold fridge either.

beginner: Keep slicing cucumbers in the fridge for about a week, in the warmer crisper drawer rather than the coldest spot, since too-cold storage causes soft, pitted spots. Keep them away from apples and tomatoes, which make them go bad faster.
seasoned: Stored in the warmest part of the refrigerator, ideally around 45 to 50°F at high humidity, slicing cucumbers keep about a week. They are chilling-sensitive below about 50°F, where prolonged cold causes pitting, water-soaked spots, and faster breakdown, so they store neither as long nor as cold as hardy vegetables. Keep them away from apples, tomatoes, and other ethylene producers, which hasten yellowing.

beginner: Slicing cucumbers do not freeze well, since they are mostly water and turn mushy. The best way to keep extra cucumbers is to eat them fresh, share them, or make quick pickles.
seasoned: Slicing cucumbers do not freeze well for fresh use, turning limp and watery because of their high water content. A glut is better kept by quick-pickling; freezing is only worth it for blended uses like soups or smoothies.

beginner: Slicing cucumbers are best used fresh and soon after picking. If you have too many, the best options are to eat them, share them, or make quick pickles. Keep them cool but not too cold, and use them within about a week.
seasoned: Treat slicing cucumbers as a use-it-soon vegetable rather than a keeper. The answer to a glut is not long storage but eating, sharing, and quick-pickling. Keep fruit cool but not cold, around 45 to 50°F at high humidity, and use within a week.

beginner: In warm soil, seeds sprout in about a week. Two seed leaves push up first. If the soil is cold, seeds rot instead of sprouting.
seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 4 to 10 days in warm soil (70 to 95°F is ideal); cold soil below about 50°F rots seed rather than germinating it.

beginner: Plant seeds 1 inch deep once the soil is warm. Keep the soil damp until they sprout. If several come up together, keep the strongest one.
seasoned: Sow 1 inch deep in warm soil, keeping it evenly moist but not soggy. If you sowed several seeds per spot, thin to the strongest seedling once true leaves appear.

beginner: Have your seeds sprouted yet?
seasoned: Did your slicing cucumber seeds germinate, and how many days did it take?

beginner: After the first two rounded leaves, true leaves appear and the plant grows quickly. Watch for striped or spotted beetles chewing the young leaves.
seasoned: Cotyledons followed by the first true leaves; growth is fast once warm. Watch for cucumber beetles, which target young plants and can transmit bacterial wilt, to which slicing cucumbers are very susceptible.

beginner: Keep an eye out for beetles on young plants. Set up a trellis now if your cucumbers climb. Water regularly and keep weeds down. A light row cover protects seedlings, but remove it once flowers form.
seasoned: Protect from cucumber beetles, with row cover if needed (remove it at flowering for pollination). Get a trellis up early for vining types, and keep the plants evenly watered and weed-free.

beginner: How do your young plants look?
seasoned: How are your seedlings developing? Any sign of beetle damage?

beginner: The plant grows fast, sending out vines and curling tendrils that grab onto a trellis. This is when you feed it and make sure it has something to climb.
seasoned: Rapid leafy growth and lengthening vines that throw tendrils and begin to climb. This is the window to side-dress and to get the trellis in place before the long vines sprawl, and to keep scouting for beetles and aphids.

beginner: Give the plant a light feeding of nitrogen now. Guide the vines onto their trellis. Add mulch to keep the soil evenly moist, which keeps the fruit from going bitter.
seasoned: Side-dress lightly with nitrogen as flowering nears. Train vines onto the trellis so the long fruit will hang straight. Mulch to hold even moisture, which prevents bitterness, and keep scouting for cucumber beetles and aphids.

beginner: Are your plants climbing and growing well?
seasoned: Have your cucumbers been side-dressed and trained up? Any pests on the leaves?

beginner: Yellow flowers open. The first flowers are usually male and fall off, which is normal. Female flowers have a tiny cucumber at their base.
seasoned: Yellow flowers open. Most slicing cucumbers are monoecious, so male flowers (on thin stalks) usually open first and drop, which is normal; female flowers carry a tiny cucumber behind the bloom. Gynoecious and parthenocarpic types behave differently.

beginner: Let the bees do their work and do not spray the flowers. If tiny cucumbers turn yellow and shrivel, the flowers were not pollinated, and you can hand-pollinate with a small brush. Keep watering steadily.
seasoned: Encourage pollinators and avoid spraying open blooms, since fruit set depends on repeated bee visits. If small fruit yellow and shrivel, pollination is poor; hand-pollinate in the morning. Keep moisture steady now to avoid bitterness.

beginner: Is your plant flowering? Are any little cucumbers forming?
seasoned: Are you seeing female flowers and fruit set? Any small fruit aborting?

beginner: Shiny, firm cucumbers reaching about 6 to 8 inches. They grow fast, so they are ready before you expect.
seasoned: Glossy, firm, deep-green fruit reaching slicing size, about 6 to 8 inches for most varieties, sizing up fast, often noticeably bigger day to day at peak.

beginner: Check every day or two and pick the cucumbers while they are firm and shiny. Cut the stem rather than pulling. Picking often keeps more coming, and remove any big yellow ones you missed.
seasoned: Pick every 1 to 2 days, cutting or clipping the stem. Harvest young for tenderness and to keep the plant producing; remove any oversized or yellowed fruit you missed, since they shut down new set and turn bitter.

beginner: Have you started picking cucumbers?
seasoned: How much are you harvesting, and how often are you picking?

beginner: The plant slows down and the leaves may get powdery and white or yellow and spotted, or it wilts suddenly from disease. Frost kills it.
seasoned: Declining production, spreading powdery or downy mildew, or sudden wilting from bacterial wilt. The first frost kills the plant outright.

beginner: Pull out finished plants and clear them away at the end of the season. This helps prevent pests and disease next year. A second planting made in summer often keeps producing after the first one is done.
seasoned: Pull and remove spent vines rather than tilling them in, to cut overwintering pest and disease sites. A summer-sown succession often crops cleanly after the first planting fades to mildew or wilt.

beginner: Is your plant finished for the season?
seasoned: Is this planting winding down? Did you remove the spent vines?

beginner: Time to watch for beetles
seasoned: Start scouting for cucumber beetles

beginner: Your young cucumbers are up. Check for small striped or spotted yellow beetles, which spread a wilt disease cucumbers catch easily, and cover the plants until they flower.
seasoned: Your slicing cucumber seedlings are up, which is when cucumber beetles colonize and can infect highly susceptible plants with bacterial wilt. Scout daily and protect young plants with row cover until flowering.

beginner: Wait for warm soil before sowing. Cucumber seeds rot in cold ground but sprout fast once it warms up.
seasoned: Soil temperature, not the calendar, governs cucumber germination. Wait until soil is at least 70°F at 1 inch; seed sown in cold ground below about 50°F rots before it sprouts.

beginner: Protect young plants from beetles. A light cover helps, but take it off once flowers appear so bees can reach them.
seasoned: Cucumber beetles swarm young plants and spread bacterial wilt, which slicing cucumbers catch easily. A floating row cover protects seedlings, but pull it off at flowering so bees can pollinate.

beginner: Give your cucumbers something to climb. Grown up a trellis, the long fruit is straighter and cleaner and the plant gets less disease.
seasoned: Get the trellis in early. Slicing cucumbers grown up a trellis make straighter, cleaner fruit, dry faster, suffer less disease, and are far easier to pick than sprawling vines.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist and mulched. Letting cucumbers dry out, then soaking them, is what makes them taste bitter.
seasoned: Even moisture is the anti-bitterness habit. Mulch and water steadily; the drought and heat swings that stress the plant are exactly what drive the bitter compound into the fruit, worst at the stem end and skin.

beginner: The first flowers often fall off without making cucumbers, that is normal. Real trouble is when tiny cucumbers turn yellow and shrivel, which means poor pollination.
seasoned: Early male flowers opening and dropping with no fruit is normal; females, each with a tiny cucumber behind the bloom, come a little later. Judge pollination by whether small fruit size up or yellow and shrivel.

beginner: If cucumbers are not forming, you can hand-pollinate. In the morning, pick a male flower, peel off the petals, and gently touch it to the center of a female flower.
seasoned: If set is poor in cool or pollinator-scarce conditions, hand-pollinate in the morning: pick a male flower, strip the petals, and dab pollen onto the center of each open female. Parthenocarpic types skip this entirely.

beginner: Pick cucumbers while firm and shiny and check every day or two, they grow fast. Picking often keeps more cucumbers coming.
seasoned: Pick young and pick often. At peak, slicing fruit sizes up fast, so check every 1 to 2 days; harvesting promptly keeps the plant setting new fruit instead of slowing down, and young fruit is the most tender.

beginner: If a cucumber got big and yellow, pick it off anyway. Leaving over-ripe fruit on the plant makes it stop producing.
seasoned: Missed one and it turned yellow and seedy? Cut it off and compost it; leaving mature, seedy fruit on the vine tells the plant to stop setting, and over-ripe slicers turn bitter anyway.

beginner: At the end of the season, pull up old vines and clear them away. This cuts down on pests and disease next year.
seasoned: Pull spent vines and remove them rather than tilling them under, which buries overwintering beetles and disease residue. Clean beds now mean fewer pests and less angular leaf spot and anthracnose next season.

beginner: One slicing cucumber plant produces a lot over the season, often a dozen or more cucumbers. Two or three plants are plenty for fresh eating.
seasoned: A healthy slicing plant yields heavily over its short season, commonly 10 or more full-size cucumbers per vine, often 5 pounds or more in a long, warm climate. A few plants are plenty for fresh salad use; scale up only if you want a steady daily supply.

beginner: At its peak, a cucumber plant makes fruit fast. Pick every day or two, since picking often actually keeps more cucumbers coming.
seasoned: At peak in warm weather a plant sets fruit quickly, and slicers size up so fast that picking every 1 to 2 days is essential. Frequent harvest at this stage actually keeps the plant producing; leaving a mature, seedy fruit on the vine signals it to slow down or stop.

beginner: The slicing cucumber is the classic salad cucumber you eat fresh, long, smooth, and dark green, rather than one you turn into pickles. It is an easy, fast summer vegetable that grows as a long vine or a compact bush and makes a lot of fruit in a short time. Pick the cucumbers while they are young and shiny, around 6 to 8 inches; if you leave one on too long it gets fat, yellow, and seedy, and the plant stops making more. Growing the vines up a trellis keeps the long fruit straight and clean and helps the plant stay healthy.
seasoned: The slicing cucumber is the standard American salad cucumber, a fast warm-season cucurbit (Cucumis sativus) grown for long, smooth, dark-green fruit eaten fresh rather than pickled. Vines are vigorous and tendrilled, running long or forming compact bushes, and they crop heavily over a short summer window once soil and air warm. Slicers are picked young, at about 6 to 8 inches, while the skin is glossy and the seeds soft; a slicer left on the vine goes fat, seedy, and yellow, and new set slows. Most garden slicers are monoecious open-pollinated standards such as Marketmore 76 and Straight Eight, though gynoecious hybrids and seedless parthenocarpic types are widely sold. Grown up a trellis, the long fruit hangs straight and clean and the foliage stays drier against disease.

beginner: Pick slicing cucumbers while they are young, firm, shiny, and deep green, usually around 6 to 8 inches long. The exact size is up to you, but younger cucumbers are more tender. Cut or clip the stem instead of pulling, so you do not tear the vine. Check every day or two, because cucumbers grow fast and one left too long turns yellow, seedy, and bitter while the plant slows down.
seasoned: Pick slicing cucumbers young, while the skin is glossy and firm, the color deep green, and the seeds still soft, generally at about 6 to 8 inches for the variety. Earlier is more tender; a slicer left to over-size dulls, yellows at the tip, turns bitter and seedy, and tells the plant to stop setting. Cut or clip the stem rather than pulling, to spare the brittle vine. At peak in warm weather the fruit sizes up fast, so check every 1 to 2 days and pick often to keep new fruit coming.

beginner: Most slicing cucumber plants have both male and female flowers, so you only need one plant to get fruit. Bees carry the pollen between the flowers, and each cucumber needs several bee visits, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. If your early cucumbers stay small and shrivel, the flowers usually were not pollinated well, often in cool or rainy weather. Some special varieties, called seedless or parthenocarpic, make cucumbers with no bees at all, which is handy for pots and covered beds.
seasoned: Most slicing cucumbers are monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a single plant sets fruit with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and each female needs several bee visits to size a full slicing fruit. Poor pollination, common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions, shows up as small fruit that yellow and shrivel at the tip, and early-season male flowers routinely open and drop before the first females appear, which is normal. Two variety types behave differently: gynoecious (nearly all-female) hybrids set heavily but usually want a pollenizer plant in the mix, and parthenocarpic types set seedless fruit with no pollination at all, which is why they suit greenhouses, row covers, and containers. Plant flowers nearby and avoid spraying open blooms to keep bees working, and hand-pollinate with a small brush in the morning if set stalls.

beginner: Kale likes rich, loose soil that holds moisture but still drains well. Mix in plenty of compost before planting. It is not fussy and grows in most garden soils, but it does best when the soil is fertile and never bone dry or waterlogged.
seasoned: Kale is forgiving about soil and grows in a wide range of textures, but it performs best in a fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter. Work in compost before planting and keep moisture even; the plant is a leafy heavy feeder whose tenderness and color suffer in soil that either ponds water or dries out hard.

beginner: Kale grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, around 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, keeping the soil closer to neutral helps.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0; kale still does fine across a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Holding the soil toward neutral, roughly 6.8 to 7.2, also helps suppress clubroot, a key brassica soil disease, so a grower with clubroot history should lean to the high end.

beginner: Kale needs regular feeding to keep making tender leaves. Give it a feed when you plant it, again about 4 weeks later, and a light feed after each big harvest so it grows fresh leaves. Do not overdo it, since too much fertilizer makes soft growth that bugs love.
seasoned: Kale is a leafy crop that needs steady nitrogen for tender, dark green leaves. Use a starter fertilizer at transplanting, then side-dress with nitrogen about 4 weeks later, and feed again with a light dose of nitrogen after each heavy cutting of leaves to push new growth. Its nutrient demand is moderate rather than extreme, so avoid overdoing nitrogen, which softens growth and draws aphids.

beginner: Time to feed your kale.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your kale with nitrogen.

beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a balanced vegetable fertilizer.
seasoned: High N for leafy growth; e.g. 21-0-0 side-dress or blood meal. Starter feed at transplant, then a light nitrogen feed after each cutting.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer.
seasoned: Side-dress about half a cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row roughly 4 weeks after transplanting, then a lighter feed after heavy cuttings.

beginner: Kale does well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick cool-season crops like lettuce and beets. The main thing is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share its pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most kale companion pairings are traditional rather than research-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents against cabbage pests, and lettuce, spinach, or beets as cool-season interplants that use space and light while kale is small. The well-grounded caution is to separate kale from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for kale; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.
seasoned: Onions are one of the better-supported brassica companions. Their pungent allium scent helps mask the kale from cabbage-family pests, loopers, cabbageworms, and root maggots, that hunt partly by smell, and extension trial work including onion in a mix with cole crops showed reduced caterpillar damage. Alliums are shallow-rooted and undemanding, so they tuck around kale without competing for much.

beginner: Dill is a classic friend for cabbage-family plants. Its strong smell is said to put off pests, and its flowers bring in helpful insects.
seasoned: Dill works for kale mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers attract parasitoid wasps and predators like hoverflies and ladybugs that prey on the aphids and cabbage caterpillars kale draws, and extension work pairing aromatic umbels with brassicas has shown reduced caterpillar damage. Let some dill flower for the benefit, and site it nearby rather than crowding the kale.

beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low, so you can tuck it between young kale plants to use the space while the kale fills in.
seasoned: Lettuce and kale interplant well on structure and timing rather than chemistry. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick, kale taller and slower, so the lettuce uses the open ground and light between young kale plants and is harvested before the kale spreads. Expect an efficient use of the bed, not pest protection.

beginner: Keep kale away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, collards, and cauliflower. They share the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes problems worse.
seasoned: Planting kale cheek-by-jowl with its brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, collards, Brussels sprouts, concentrates the whole family's shared pests (cabbage worms, loopers, flea beetles, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

beginner: You'll see ragged holes eaten in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and little dark droppings. Some caterpillars loop up in the middle as they crawl.
seasoned: Ragged holes chewed through the leaves, with green caterpillars and dark frass on the foliage. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed.

beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants like kale and chew the leaves, which are the part you eat.
seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Because kale is harvested as leaves, even modest feeding damages the crop.

beginner: Spray a product called Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick the caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad, which target caterpillars, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.

beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover right after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs. Clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
seasoned: Use floating row cover from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

beginner: You'll see clusters of tiny soft insects on the new growth and tucked into the curled leaves, often a waxy gray-green kind. Leaves curl and pucker, and there may be a sticky coating.
seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on growing tips and leaf undersides; the waxy gray-green cabbage aphid is especially troublesome because it lodges in the crinkles and curls of kale leaves and is very hard to wash out at harvest.

beginner: Aphids are tiny insects that suck juice from the plant. They breed fast and hide deep in kale's crinkled leaves, where they are hard to wash out.
seasoned: Several aphid species, notably the cabbage aphid, suck sap from kale; they multiply quickly and their feeding distorts growth and contaminates the harvested leaves.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil, making sure to hit under the leaves and into the crinkles where they hide. Repeat every few days.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water, or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides and the leaf crinkles; repeat every few days. Curly-leaf varieties are hardest to clear, so catch infestations early.

beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings that eat aphids, don't overdo the nitrogen fertilizer (lush growth attracts them), and check the new growth often.
seasoned: Encourage natural enemies like ladybugs and lacewings, avoid overfeeding nitrogen (which spurs the soft growth aphids favor), and inspect growing tips early so colonies do not lodge in the leaves.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and scars the leaves of a leaf crop.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; on kale they also leave cosmetic shot-holes in the harvested leaves.

beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle it.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover, and spray spinosad or apply kaolin clay if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.

beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
seasoned: Use row cover from sowing or transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It's worst in cool, wet spring soil.
seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet spring soil.

beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool spring weather.
seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed on the roots below, sometimes killing young plants.

beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.

beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Don't plant into cold, soggy soil, and avoid spots where you grew cabbage-family plants last year.
seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It's mostly a warm-region problem and loves kale.
seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region pest that prefers kale, mustard, and collards over other cole crops.

beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants like kale, mustard, and collards, especially in the South.
seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a brassica-specialist stink bug, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes two to four generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.

beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their eggs (little barrel-shaped eggs in rows), and young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull out badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Pyrethrins are permitted in organic production if pressure is severe.

beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard or an early kale planting to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard, kale, or rapeseed to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.

beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and causes the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years and spreads in contaminated soil and water.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Adding lime to make the soil less acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward 7.0 or above with lime can suppress the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.

beginner: Don't grow kale or its cabbage-family relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years, or longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
seasoned: Rotate brassicas on a cycle of at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is known; keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the leaves you want to eat.
seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot the harvested leaves.

beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the plant's veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.

beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.

beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors and downgrades the leaves.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
seasoned: A fungus-like organism that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it. Kale's cool-season window overlaps the weather it likes.

beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.

beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches with concentric rings, like a tiny target. Bad cases make the leaves yellow and unusable.
seasoned: Small dark lesions enlarge into circular spots with characteristic concentric rings (a target-spot look) and a yellow halo; because the leaves are the crop, even moderate spotting reduces the harvest. Favored by warm, wet conditions.

beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather and infects the leaves, leaving target-like spots. It's worse on stressed plants and in crowded, damp plantings.
seasoned: Fungi in the genus Alternaria (with Cercospora causing a similar leaf spot) infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive it.

beginner: Remove and destroy badly spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and use a copper spray if it spreads. Avoid wetting the leaves when you water.
seasoned: Remove and destroy spotted leaves and debris, improve airflow, avoid overhead watering, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high.

beginner: Start with clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and keep plants healthy so they resist infection.
seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, rotate away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept even through the season.

beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, a little more in hot, dry spells.

beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp, soft growth; kale dislikes waterlogged soil and can rot at the crown.

beginner: Wilting leaves that turn tough and bitter.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and tough, bitter leaves; drought stress hurts leaf quality and invites pests.

beginner: Keep the soil or tray damp while the seeds come up, without letting the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed or tray surface evenly moist through germination; brassica seed is shallow and should not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp as they grow.
seasoned: Grow the seedlings on with steady, even moisture.

beginner: Water evenly as the plant grows its leaves. Steady water makes the leaves tender and mild.
seasoned: Keep even moisture as the plant builds its leafy frame; steady water sets up tender, mild leaves.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while you harvest outer leaves over the weeks. If the plant dries out, the leaves get tough and strong-tasting.
seasoned: Even moisture through the main leaf-production weeks matters most for tender, mild leaves; drought turns them tough and strong-flavored. Pick the outer leaves and keep the plant watered to keep them coming.

beginner: In winter kale needs little watering, and frost makes it sweeter. Do not keep cold soil soggy.
seasoned: In cold weather a hardy kale plant needs little to no supplemental water; frost actually sweetens the leaves. Avoid waterlogging cold soil.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the leaves stay tender, not tough.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps the leaves tender and mild; dry spells make kale tougher and more bitter.

beginner: Water steadily while the plant is making lots of leaves.
seasoned: Even moisture through the main leaf-production weeks matters most for tender, mild leaves.

beginner: You can sow kale seeds right in the garden or start them indoors. For spring, start seeds about a month before planting out, and set plants in the garden a few weeks before your last frost, or just sow seeds once the soil can be worked. For a fall crop, sow in mid to late summer so it is ready before winter. If you grow your own transplants, let them get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.
seasoned: Kale can be direct sown or transplanted. For a spring crop, start seeds indoors about 4 to 5 weeks before set-out and transplant around 4 to 5 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow as soon as the soil is workable; kale tolerates frost. For a fall and overwintering crop, sow in midsummer (often direct in the garden) so plants size up before cold, then harvest through fall and, in milder zones, winter. Harden transplants off over 7 to 10 days.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A light, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Mix in some compost for a steady supply of nutrients.
seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release nitrogen source; container kale still feeds steadily.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries out.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Feed a bit more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.
seasoned: Container kale needs more frequent feeding than in-ground plants because watering leaches nutrients.

beginner: In mild-winter areas, kale in a pot keeps going through winter; just move it to a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, pull the pot against the house or into an unheated garage during hard freezes, or grow a fast variety and enjoy it before deep winter.
seasoned: Kale is cold-hardy enough to overwinter in a container in mild zones, where it keeps producing through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In colder zones the limited root volume of a pot freezes harder than open ground, so move containers against a wall or into an unheated structure during hard freezes, or treat the potted crop as a single fall-into-early-winter planting.

beginner: Kale grows well in a pot of at least 3 gallons that is 10 inches or more deep, one or two plants per pot. Keep it watered and fed, and pick the outer leaves as you need them. In hot areas, give it some afternoon shade.
seasoned: Kale is a good container crop because it is compact and harvested as leaves over a long period. Use a container of at least 3 gallons and 10 inches deep, one or two plants per pot, and keep moisture even since pots dry quickly. Pick outer leaves and leave the growing point, and in warm regions give afternoon shade and avoid heat-absorbing dark pots.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps kale leaves tender.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits kale well, since it smooths out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and mild.

beginner: Kale does not get huge, but it grows for a long time, so give it a pot that holds at least 3 gallons and is about 10 inches deep. A wider pot is better than a tall skinny one because it holds moisture better and gives the roots room.
seasoned: Kale stays relatively compact but builds a substantial root system over a long season, so choose a container at least 3 gallons and 10 inches deep. Width matters more than height: a broad pot gives room to grow one or two plants and buffers the fast drying that narrow pots suffer.

beginner: Winterbor and Dwarf Siberian are easy, very hardy choices, great for a fall or winter crop. Red Russian is tender and fast, nice for salads. Lacinato (Dinosaur kale) is popular for cooking but is the least cold-hardy, so cover it when it gets really cold.
seasoned: Match the variety to the slot and the climate. For fall and overwintering, lean on the hardiest types: Winterbor, Improved Dwarf Siberian, and Red Russian shrug off hard frost, while Lacinato is the least cold-hardy and wants protection. Curly types (Winterbor, Vates, Redbor) hold texture and color in cold; flat types (Lacinato, Red Russian) are more tender for fresh eating. Where clubroot or other brassica diseases are a concern, look for resistant cultivars.

beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, collards, and turnips.
seasoned: Other brassicas (broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, collards, Brussels sprouts, kohlrabi, turnip, radish, mustard), which share clubroot and cabbage-family pests.

beginner: Do not plant kale or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between them, and longer if you have had clubroot, helps avoid soil diseases.
seasoned: Rotate so kale and its brassica relatives do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present, since the clubroot organism persists in soil for years. The University of Minnesota advises not growing cole crops in the same spot for the past four years. Keeping soil pH near neutral also helps suppress clubroot.

beginner: Do not leave kale out on the counter. It wilts and yellows fast in the warmth, so get it into the fridge soon after picking.
seasoned: Kale wilts and toughens at room temperature and its leaves yellow within a day or two, so do not leave it out. Refrigerate as soon as possible after cutting; if it must sit out briefly, stand the stems in water like cut flowers.

beginner: Store kale unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where it stays good for about a week, sometimes up to 2 weeks if very cold. Wait to wash it until you are ready to cook.
seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; kale holds its quality for roughly 1 week, and up to about 2 weeks held near 32°F at high humidity. Washing before storage traps moisture and speeds spoilage.

beginner: Kale freezes well if you blanch it first. Strip the leaves off the stems, boil them for 2 to 3 minutes, cool them right away in ice water, drain, and freeze.
seasoned: Kale freezes well once blanched: strip the leaves from the stems, blanch about 2 to 3 minutes in boiling water, cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that otherwise cause off-flavors and loss of color in storage.

beginner: Kale is best right after you pick it, and the plant is its own best storage: in cool weather the leaves keep on the plant for weeks and even get sweeter after frost. So pick what you need when you need it, and chill it quickly after cutting.
seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden, and a key kale advantage is that the plant itself is the best storage: leaves keep on the plant for weeks in cool weather and sweeten after frost, so harvest close to when you will use it rather than stockpiling. Chilling promptly after cutting keeps the leaves crisp and mild.

beginner: In about 5 to 10 days, your seeds sprout and push up their first two little leaves (the seed leaves).
seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days at soil temperatures of roughly 45 to 85°F, pushing up two seed leaves (cotyledons).

beginner: Your kale stayed small and yellowish, wilted in the afternoon, and when you dug it up the roots were swollen into lumps. That is clubroot, a soil disease that infects cabbage-family roots and lasts for years in the soil. It usually builds up when brassicas are grown in the same spot repeatedly. Next time, rotate so cabbage-family crops do not return to that bed for at least 3 years, keep the soil pH near neutral, and improve drainage.
seasoned: Plants were stunted and chlorotic, wilted by day, and showed galled, clubbed roots, the signature of clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae). The soilborne organism persists for years and builds under repeated brassica cropping and acidic, poorly drained soil. Next time rotate cabbage-family crops out for at least 3 years (longer where known), lime toward a neutral-to-slightly-alkaline pH, and improve drainage; there is no in-season cure.

In zones 3 to 5 deep winter ends the crop, though a low tunnel extends it; in zones 6 to 7 kale frequently overwinters with simple protection and resumes before bolting in spring. beginner: Kale grows twice a year in St. George. Sow outdoors about February 15, USU Extension's St. George date, for tender leaves by mid-April. The spring picking stops by the end of April as the heat builds, so let the bed rest through the worst of summer and sow again from July 1 to August 15, a date USU documents specifically for a fall kale crop, for leaves through early October. Frost returns around November 1.
seasoned: USU Extension's St. George chart sets kale in the Group A (Hardy) band, spring sowing about February 15, leaves ready to cut at about 55 days through late April. Kale toughens and pushes toward bolting once St. George's 100°F June and July stretch arrives, so the spring cutting closes out before then. USU's chart also names kale specifically among its dated fall crops, sown July 1 to August 15, for a fall harvest running into early October ahead of the November 1 average first frost.

beginner: Kale is a leafy cabbage-family plant you grow for its leaves, picking a few at a time over a long season instead of harvesting it all at once. It loves cool weather and is one of the toughest vegetables you can grow: it survives hard frost, and the cold actually makes the leaves taste sweeter. In mild areas it keeps going all winter, and in cold areas it can survive winter with a little cover, so one planting can feed you for months.
seasoned: Kale is a hardy, non-heading cole crop grown for its nutritious leaves, which are harvested continuously rather than as a single head. A cool-season brassica, it produces the best quality in the cool weather of spring and fall and is one of the most cold-hardy vegetables in the garden: mature plants shrug off hard frost, and a touch of cold actually sweetens the leaves as the plant converts starch to sugar. In mild-winter regions it grows right through winter, and in colder zones it overwinters with simple protection, making it one of the longest-cropping plants a gardener can grow.

beginner: Begin picking when the outer leaves are big enough to use, about the length of your hand: small baby leaves in about a month, full leaves in roughly 2 months. Take the lowest, outside leaves first and leave the small center leaves to keep growing, so the same plant feeds you for months. Do not strip the whole plant at once. Keep picking right through fall, and know that the leaves taste sweetest after frost, so you can harvest even when it is cold out.
seasoned: Start picking once the outer leaves reach a usable size, about hand-length: baby leaves in roughly 25 to 30 days, full-size leaves in about 50 to 65 days. Harvest with the cut-and-come-again method, snapping or cutting the lowest, outermost leaves and leaving the central growing point and young inner leaves to keep producing. Avoid stripping more than about a third of the plant at once. Picking continues for months and runs right through fall frosts; the leaves are sweetest after a frost or two, so in cool weather you can harvest straight from the garden even after the leaves have frozen.

beginner: Mix a couple of inches of compost into the bed before planting so the soil is rich and holds moisture but still drains. Loosen it well. Try not to plant kale where you grew other cabbage-family crops (broccoli, cabbage, collards) in the last few years, since that spreads soil diseases.
seasoned: Work in 1 to 2 inches of compost before planting to build a fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained bed; kale is a leafy heavy feeder that rewards organic matter. Loosen the soil well, and aim for a pH near 6.0 to 7.0. Because brassica diseases like clubroot build in the soil, choose a bed where no cabbage-family crop has grown for at least 3 years.

beginner: Spinach likes rich, loose soil that holds moisture but drains well, with lots of compost mixed in. The one thing it really cares about is not-too-acidic soil, so if your ground is very acidic, add a little lime to bring it closer to neutral. A quick soil test tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Spinach does best in a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. Its defining soil need is a near-neutral pH: spinach is notably sensitive to acidic soil and grows poorly below about 6.0, so lime an acid plot up toward 6.5 to 7.5 before sowing. Work in compost to feed the fast leafy growth and hold steady moisture, which delays bolting and keeps the leaves tender.

beginner: Spinach grows best in soil that is close to neutral, about 6.5 to 7.5. It does not like acidic soil, so if a soil test reads below 6.0, mix in some lime before planting.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.5 to 7.5; spinach is one of the more acid-sensitive vegetables and yields drop on soils below roughly 6.0, where manganese can become available enough to injure the plant. Clemson advises a 6.0 to 7.0 minimum and the University of Minnesota up to about 8, so lean to the neutral-to-slightly-alkaline side and lime an acid plot the season before.

beginner: Spinach grows fast and likes nitrogen for big green leaves. Mix some compost or fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it one feeding of a nitrogen fertilizer about 3 to 4 weeks after the seeds come up. Because the crop is quick, you usually do not need to feed it more than that.
seasoned: Spinach is a fast leafy crop that runs on nitrogen, but the season is short, so one or two feedings are usually enough. Work compost or a balanced fertilizer in before sowing, then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after planting (or at thinning) to push tender, dark-green leaves. Utah State suggests about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row; Clemson uses calcium nitrate. Avoid heavy late feeding, since spinach readily takes up nitrate and lush growth draws aphids and leafminers.

beginner: Time to give your spinach a feeding.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your spinach with nitrogen.

beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a 21-0-0 fertilizer once the plants are a few weeks old.
seasoned: High N for leafy growth; e.g. a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 ft of row, or calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0), side-dressed 3 to 4 weeks after sowing. No phosphorus or potassium needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer, one feeding a few weeks after the seeds sprout.
seasoned: About a quarter cup of 21-0-0 (or 1 pound of calcium nitrate per 100 square feet) side-dressed once, 3 to 4 weeks after sowing.

beginner: Spinach is small, fast, and shade-tolerant, so it tucks in well between slower, taller crops. It grows happily next to peas and beans, strawberries, and members of the cabbage family, and it does not get along badly with much. Just keep it away from its close relatives beets and chard, which share its leafminer pest.
seasoned: Most spinach companion pairings rest on space, timing, and tradition rather than measured effects. The practical ones are structural: spinach is shallow-rooted, quick, and tolerates light shade, so it interplants under or beside taller, slower crops (peas, beans, brassicas) and is harvested before they crowd it. The one well-grounded caution is to separate spinach from beets and Swiss chard, its close relatives in the goosefoot family, which share the spinach leafminer and several diseases, a rotation and pest principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

beginner: Peas grow up while spinach stays low, so they share a bed without competing, and both love the same cool weather. Peas also add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy spinach can use.
seasoned: Peas and spinach are a traditional cool-season pairing on structure and timing: peas trellis upward and cast light shade that suits spinach, both thrive in the same early-spring and fall windows, and the legume fixes a little nitrogen the leafy spinach can draw on. Expect efficient use of the bed and season rather than a documented growth boost.

beginner: Strawberries and spinach are a long-standing garden pairing. The low spinach fills space between strawberry plants early in the season and is picked before the berries take over.
seasoned: Strawberries and spinach are a traditional pairing that works mainly on habit and timing: low, quick spinach uses the open ground between young strawberry plants in the cool of spring and is harvested before the berries spread. A space-use tradition, not a measured effect.

beginner: Tall cabbage-family plants give spinach a bit of light shade in warm spells, which helps it last longer before bolting, and the quick spinach is gone before the brassicas need the room.
seasoned: Spinach interplants beneath cabbage-family crops on a space-and-light basis: it tolerates the partial shade taller brassicas cast, which can buy a little time against bolting in warm spells, and it matures and is cleared before the brassicas fill out. Traditional and practical rather than a documented adjacency effect; the two do not share a major pest.

beginner: Keep spinach away from beets and Swiss chard. They are close relatives and share the same leafminer pest and some diseases, so planting them together helps those problems build up.
seasoned: Beets, Swiss chard, and spinach all belong to the goosefoot family and are the favored hosts of the spinach leafminer, whose maggots blister and ruin the leaves; they also share several leaf diseases. Planting them side by side or in succession concentrates the leafminer and disease pressure and lets the soil-overwintering leafminer build. Separate them in space and rotate so goosefoot crops do not follow one another.

beginner: You'll see pale, winding tunnels in the leaves that widen into large tan blisters or blotches. If you hold a leaf up to the light, you can sometimes see the tiny maggot inside. The damaged parts are not good to eat.
seasoned: Slender, winding mines in the foliage enlarge into translucent tan blotches; heavily mined leaves are unmarketable and the crop is the leaf, so even light feeding matters. The pale legless maggots are visible inside the leaf against the light.

beginner: A small fly lays eggs on the underside of the leaves, and the maggots that hatch tunnel inside the leaf between the top and bottom layers, eating as they go. Spinach, beets, and chard are its favorites.
seasoned: The spinach leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami) overwinters as pupae in the soil and emerges around mid-May; females lay rows of white eggs on leaf undersides, and the maggots tunnel between the leaf surfaces. There are three to four overlapping generations a season on spinach, beets, chard, and goosefoot weeds.

beginner: Once a maggot is inside a leaf, sprays do not reach it well, so pick off and destroy mined leaves as soon as you see them, before the maggots drop to the soil. Crushing the maggot inside the leaf works too.
seasoned: Insecticides poorly reach larvae inside the leaf, so rely on cultural control: pick and destroy mined leaves before larvae drop to pupate, and crush maggots in the leaf. Spinosad has some activity on young larvae; abamectin is a conventional option.

beginner: Cover the plants with a light row cover right after sowing so the flies cannot lay eggs, and pull nearby weeds like lambsquarters that host the pest. Rotating where you grow spinach, beets, and chard each year also helps.
seasoned: Exclude the egg-laying flies with floating row cover or insect netting from sowing, control goosefoot weeds (lambsquarters, chickweed, nightshade) that host the pest, rotate away from where spinach, beets, or chard grew, and deep-cultivate in spring to bury overwintering pupae.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, sometimes with curled, puckered leaves and a sticky coating. They are hard to wash out of crinkled savoy leaves.
seasoned: Colonies of green peach or other aphids on leaf undersides and growing tips distort and pucker the foliage; honeydew and sooty mold downgrade the crop, and curly savoy leaves are hard to clean. Aphids also transmit cucumber mosaic and other viruses.

beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck sap from the plant. They breed quickly, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer, and they can spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on spinach; they reproduce rapidly, favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces, and are most damaging as virus vectors.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil, making sure to hit the undersides of the leaves. Repeat every few days until they are gone.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps.

beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen fertilizer, and check the new growth often so you catch them early.
seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and use row cover, which doubles as leafminer exclusion.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes peppering the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump like fleas when you come near. Heavy damage can stunt seedlings.
seasoned: Small round shot-holes pepper the leaves of young plants; the tiny dark beetles jump when disturbed. Damage is mostly cosmetic on a leaf crop but can stunt or kill seedlings at high pressure.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew little holes in young leaves. They hurt small seedlings the most, since a tiny plant cannot outgrow the damage.
seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young spinach and are most damaging at the seedling stage; the holes mar the harvested leaves.

beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are many beetles use a spinosad spray or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to shrug it off.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad or apply kaolin clay if pressure is high; the aim is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.

beginner: Use row cover from sowing, keep seedlings strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and clear weeds nearby.
seasoned: Row cover from sowing, vigorous seedlings kept evenly watered and fed, and clean cultivation of nearby weeds.

beginner: Ragged chewed holes in the leaves, green or striped caterpillars on the plants, and dark droppings. They are mostly a warm-season and southern problem.
seasoned: Ragged feeding holes with green or striped larvae and frass; cabbage loopers, beet armyworms, and corn earworms feed on spinach, mostly in warm-season and southern plantings.

beginner: Several moths lay eggs on the leaves, and the caterpillars that hatch chew the foliage. Because you eat the leaves, even a little chewing is a problem.
seasoned: The larvae of several moths feed on spinach foliage; on a leaf crop even modest defoliation reduces the harvest.

beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick them off by hand. Spray again after rain since it washes off.
seasoned: Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad targeting young larvae, and hand-pick where practical; repeat after rain.

beginner: Use a row cover, clean up old plants and weeds where moths shelter, and check the undersides of leaves for eggs and small caterpillars.
seasoned: Use row cover, clean up crop debris and weed hosts, and scout leaf undersides for eggs and early instars.

beginner: Pale yellow patches on the tops of the leaves with a fuzzy gray-purple mold on the undersides, mostly in cool, damp, crowded conditions. Bad cases yellow and collapse the leaves.
seasoned: Irregular pale-yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface with grayish-purple sporulation beneath (the blue mold), spreading in cool, wet, humid weather; lesions brown and the leaves collapse. It is the most important spinach disease.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves the same cool, wet weather spinach grows in, and spreads through wet leaves and splashing water. Crowded plants and long leaf wetness make it worse.
seasoned: Peronospora effusa, an oomycete favored by cool temperatures, long leaf wetness, and high humidity; it spreads by wind- and splash-borne spores and survives on debris and as oospores, with many physiological races that overcome resistance.

beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the airflow so leaves dry faster, and water at the soil instead of over the plants. It is hard to stop once it gets going, so prevention matters most.
seasoned: Cultural control dominates: improve airflow, avoid overhead irrigation, remove infected leaves and debris; copper has limited efficacy. There is no rescue once it is established in humid weather.

beginner: Grow resistant varieties (this is the main defense), space plants for good airflow, water at the base, and rotate where you plant spinach each year.
seasoned: Plant resistant cultivars (the primary tool, choosing the broadest race resistance available), widen spacing for airflow, use drip rather than overhead water, and rotate away from spinach for several years.

beginner: White, blister-like bumps on the undersides of leaves, with yellow spots on top. Badly spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: White, blister-like pustules on leaf undersides with chlorotic spotting above; severe infection distorts and downgrades the foliage. A serious disease in the southern and south-central states.

beginner: A different mold-like disease, not a true rust, that makes white pustules on the leaves and spreads in cool, moist weather. It can ruin a crop quickly.
seasoned: The oomycete Albugo occidentalis, favored by cool nights, warm days, and leaf wetness; it spreads by splash- and wind-dispersed spores and survives on debris.

beginner: Remove and destroy infected leaves, improve airflow, and water at the soil line. As with downy mildew, prevention works better than trying to cure it.
seasoned: Remove infected leaves and debris, improve airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation; chemical options are limited for the home garden.

beginner: Choose resistant varieties where it is common, space plants out, avoid wetting the leaves, and rotate your planting spot.
seasoned: Grow resistant cultivars where white rust is endemic, space for airflow, use drip irrigation, and rotate away from spinach.

beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where germination is slow.

beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the seeds are slow to come up. Spinach sown in cold wet ground is at risk.
seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium species attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows emergence favors them.

beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention. Pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
seasoned: No cure once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.

beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant at the right depth in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up fast.
seasoned: Sow into well-drained soil when temperatures favor quick emergence, avoid overwatering, use fresh viable seed, and consider treated seed where damping-off is chronic.

beginner: Older leaves yellow and wilt even though the soil is moist, and the wilting spreads up the plant, which is stunted and may die. It is worse in warm soil.
seasoned: Progressive yellowing and wilting from the lower leaves upward despite adequate soil moisture, with stunting and plant death; symptoms intensify as soil warms through the season.

beginner: A soil fungus infects the roots and clogs the plant's water pipes, so it wilts and yellows. It lives in the soil for years and is worse when the soil warms up.
seasoned: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. spinaciae, a soilborne vascular pathogen that persists for years and is favored by warm soil and acidic conditions; once established it limits where spinach can be grown.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant is infected, so pull and destroy wilted plants. Put your effort into rotation and timing for next time.
seasoned: No effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants and manage the soilborne population by rotation and timing.

beginner: Plant spinach in the cooler parts of the season, keep the soil near neutral (not acidic), and do not grow spinach in the same spot year after year. Resistant varieties help where it is a problem.
seasoned: Schedule the crop for the cool side of the season when soils are cooler, maintain a near-neutral pH, use long rotations away from spinach, and choose resistant cultivars where the wilt is established.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, kept even; spinach is shallow-rooted and bolts faster under drought stress.

beginner: Aim for about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, a bit more when it is warm.
seasoned: Roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week (Utah State cites 1 to 2 inches), more in warm, dry spells.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the foliage dry checks downy mildew and white rust.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and leaves get moldy in soggy, crowded beds.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and downy mildew in crowded, constantly wet plantings.

beginner: Wilting leaves and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than it should.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and faster bolting; drought stress is a direct bolt trigger in spinach.

beginner: Keep the soil damp and cool while spinach sprouts. It comes up poorly in warm soil.
seasoned: Spinach germinates best in cool, moist soil; keep the surface damp, since warm soil gives poor, patchy germination.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp. Spinach roots are shallow and dry out fast.
seasoned: Keep the seedlings evenly moist; spinach is shallow-rooted with little drought buffer.

beginner: Water evenly, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, as the leaves grow.
seasoned: Hold even moisture through leaf growth at about 1 to 1.5 inches a week; steady water builds thick, tender leaves.

beginner: Keep the water steady while you pick leaves, and give extra attention in warm weather. If spinach dries out it bolts (flowers) sooner and the harvest ends.
seasoned: Steady moisture through the leaf-bulking weeks, and especially through any warm, lengthening-day spell, delays bolt; spinach bolts faster under drought stress. Cut outer leaves and keep it watered to stretch the harvest.

beginner: When spinach sends up a flower stalk the leaves turn bitter, and watering will not fix it. Pull it and resow when it is cool.
seasoned: Once warmth and long days push it to bolt, the leaves turn bitter and arrow-shaped and watering will not reverse it. Pull and resow in cool weather.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the plants grow fast and tender and do not bolt early.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps spinach growing fast and tender and delays bolting; dry spells push it to flower and turn the leaves bitter.

beginner: Spinach is best planted straight in the garden from seed, because it grows quickly and does not like having its roots disturbed. Sow the seeds about half an inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop. The seeds sprout even in cold soil, but they will not come up well in hot soil, so do not sow in the heat of summer.
seasoned: Spinach is almost always direct-sown, since it grows fast and resents root disturbance. Sow seed about 0.5 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring (it germinates in soil as cool as 40°F), and again in late summer for the main fall crop. Transplanting is possible from cells or soil blocks for an early start or to place an overwintering crop, but handle the roots gently. Germination is poor in soil above about 75 to 85°F, so summer sowings in warm regions wait for cooling soil.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix high in organic matter.

beginner: In mild areas, a pot of fall-sown spinach can keep going through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes, and it will often resume in spring.
seasoned: Spinach is very cold-hardy, so a fall-sown container can overwinter in mild zones, holding through winter in a sheltered spot and resuming growth in spring. In cold zones the limited root volume of a pot freezes harder than open ground, so sink it, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or cover it during hard freezes; an overwintered pot then yields the earliest spring picking.

beginner: Spinach grows well in a wide, shallow pot at least 6 inches deep, sown thickly and thinned for baby leaves or spaced for full plants. Keep it watered and in the cool seasons, and give it some afternoon shade in warm weather.
seasoned: Spinach is a good container crop because it is shallow-rooted, compact, and quick. Use a broad container at least 6 inches deep, one gallon or more, sown densely for cut baby leaves or thinned to 3 to 4 inches for full plants, and keep moisture even since shallow pots dry fast. Grow it in the cool seasons and give afternoon shade in warm spells to slow bolting.

beginner: Do not leave spinach out on the counter. It wilts fast in the warmth, so get it into the fridge soon after picking.
seasoned: Spinach wilts and yellows within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate it promptly after cutting; if it must sit briefly, keep it cool and out of the sun.

beginner: Store spinach unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where it keeps for 1 to 2 weeks if kept very cold. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; spinach holds about 1 to 2 weeks near 32°F at high humidity. Washing before storage traps moisture and speeds breakdown, so wait to wash until use.

beginner: Spinach freezes well if you blanch it first. Boil the leaves for about 2 minutes, cool them right away in ice water, drain, and freeze.
seasoned: Spinach freezes well once blanched: dunk leaves in boiling water about 2 minutes, cool quickly in ice water, drain well, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that otherwise cause off-flavors and color loss.

beginner: Spinach is best right after you pick it and does not keep as long as tougher greens. Chill it quickly, use it within a week or so, and freeze any extra.
seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden. Spinach is more perishable than sturdier greens like kale, so chill it fast and use it within a week or so fresh; freezing is the best way to hold a glut from a fast spring or fall crop.

beginner: Spinach flowers (bolts) when the days get long and warm in late spring, and then the leaves turn bitter. To avoid it, plant as early as you can in spring, pick slow-bolting varieties, water steadily, and harvest before midsummer. The fall crop hardly bolts at all, which is why fall is the best time to grow spinach.
seasoned: Spinach bolts primarily in response to long days, so the spring window is short: sow as early as the soil can be worked, choose slow-bolting (long-standing) varieties, keep moisture and nitrogen steady, and harvest before the longest days of June. The fall crop, grown under shortening days, rarely bolts and is the main season; overwintered plants bolt in spring as days lengthen, so crop them before the flower stalk elongates.

beginner: Spinach bolts (sends up a flower stalk and turns bitter) when days get long and warm. It is a normal part of its life cycle, not something you did wrong. The trick is to grow it in the cool, short-day parts of the year, especially fall.
seasoned: Bolting in spinach is mainly a long-day (photoperiod) response, with heat and drought speeding it; once the plant sends up a seed stalk the leaves turn bitter and tough. This is why spinach is grown as a fall, winter, and very-early-spring crop and the summer is left out across most regions.

beginner: For spring, pick slow-bolting kinds like Bloomsdale Long Standing or Tyee so the plants last longer before flowering. Melody and Space are easy, disease-resistant choices. For a fall or winter crop, grow a hardy type like Giant Winter. Smooth-leaf varieties are easiest to wash; the crinkly savoy types are the most cold-hardy but hold more grit.
seasoned: Match the variety to the slot. For the short spring window and any warm stretch, lean on slow-bolting (long-standing) types like Bloomsdale Long Standing, Tyee, and Olympia. Where downy mildew is a concern, choose resistant cultivars (Tyee, Melody, Space, and newer race-resistant hybrids). For fall and overwintering, the hardiest savoys (Giant Winter, Bloomsdale) take the most cold. Smooth-leaf types (Space, Olympia) wash easily and suit baby-leaf and containers; savoys are hardiest but trap grit; semi-savoys split the difference.

beginner: Spinach is often sown a bit thick, then thinned so plants stand about 3 to 4 inches apart. Do not waste the thinnings, they are tender baby spinach. Thinning gives each plant room to grow full leaves.
seasoned: Sow a little thick and thin to 3 to 4 inches once plants have 3 to 4 true leaves; eat the thinnings as baby spinach. Crowded plants compete, stay small, and bolt sooner, and poor airflow invites downy mildew.
