beginner: Beans like loose, fertile soil that drains well. If water sits on top of your bed for a long time after rain, work in some compost first to help it drain.
seasoned: Fertile, well-drained loam, ideally with compost worked in before planting. The critical trait is steady moisture without waterlogging through pod set and fill.

beginner: Beans do well in slightly acidic to neutral soil. If you have not tested your soil, a pH near 6.5 is a safe target and most garden beds are already close.
seasoned: A soil pH of 5.8 to 6.5 suits snap beans. A soil test is the reliable way to confirm both pH and fertility before the season starts.

beginner: Beans make a lot of their own food from the air, so they do not need much fertilizer. Mix a little balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant, and feed once more right before the plants flower. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy plants but fewer beans.
seasoned: Snap beans are moderate, light feeders. As legumes they fix much of their own nitrogen, so heavy nitrogen pushes leafy growth at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work in a balanced starter before planting, then sidedress once just before the first bloom. Sandy beds or leaching rains can call for a second light sidedress.

beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 works well.
seasoned: Pre-plant 5-10-10 if no soil test is available; sidedress a nitrogen source before bloom.

beginner: About 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet of bed before planting.
seasoned: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, per Clemson HGIC.

beginner: Beans get along with most vegetables. The classic trio is beans with corn and squash. The one pairing to avoid is planting beans right next to onions or garlic.
seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, beans leave the soil better for what follows and pair traditionally with corn and squash in the Three Sisters planting. The long-standing caution is to keep beans away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress them.

beginner: The traditional Three Sisters partner; corn gives a little structure and the planting has been grown together for generations.
seasoned: Corn is the classic bean partner in three-sisters planting. With pole beans the corn is a living trellis; with bush beans the relationship is looser, mostly foliage diversity and efficient use of the same bed. The benefit is structural and space-based rather than a measured pest effect, and since corn is a heavy feeder, the beans' nitrogen fixation helps balance the bed over the season.

beginner: The third Sister; its broad leaves shade the soil and keep weeds down around the beans.
seasoned: Squash rounds out the three-sisters trio. Its broad sprawling leaves shade the soil, hold moisture, and suppress weeds around the beans, while the varied foliage heights of the planting make it harder for pests to lock onto any one crop. This is a soil-and-space benefit; give the squash room so it does not swamp bush beans, which sit lower than pole beans would.

beginner: A common, easy neighbor that shares similar warm-season, full-sun needs.
seasoned: Cucumber and bush beans coexist comfortably: similar warm-season timing and water needs, complementary growth habits, and the beans' nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the cucumber as a moderate feeder. The added foliage diversity is a modest plus for pest disruption. This is a compatibility pairing rather than a strongly protective one, so expect easy cohabitation more than active pest control.

beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from beans, which are said to grow poorly near them.
seasoned: Onions and beans is one of the better-grounded 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds that interfere with the Rhizobium bacteria living on bean roots, the very bacteria the bean depends on to fix nitrogen, so bean growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. A useful corollary: beans or peas grown before onions actually improve the soil for the following allium crop.

beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for beans.
seasoned: Garlic acts on beans the same way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds that disrupt the nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria on bean roots, slowing the beans down. Treat garlic and bush beans as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the bean-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

beginner: Leaves that look skeletonized or lacy, with the tissue chewed away from underneath but the veins left behind. Both the spiny yellow young (larvae) and the round, coppery adult beetles feed on the undersides of the leaves, and when there are a lot of them they also chew stems and pods. The adult is yellow to copper colored with rows of small black spots on its back.
seasoned: Leaves taking on a skeletonized, lacy look as tissue is chewed away from the undersides, leaving the network of veins behind. Both the spiny yellow larvae and the dome-shaped, coppery adults feed on the leaf undersides, and when abundant they move on to stems and pods. The adult is yellow to coppery-brown with eight small black spots on each wing cover.

beginner: The Mexican bean beetle, a leaf-eating cousin of the ladybug. The adults come out of hiding near woods in spring, feed, then lay clusters of yellow eggs under the leaves, and several generations build up over the summer. It is worst in the Mid-Atlantic and southern Appalachian areas and is rarely a problem on the West Coast.
seasoned: The Mexican bean beetle (Epilachna varivestis), a leaf-eating member of the ladybeetle family. Adults emerge from overwintering near woodland edges, feed for a week or two, then lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides; there are about three generations a year, so populations build through the season. It is most damaging in the Mid-Atlantic and southern Appalachian regions and is largely absent from the Pacific Coast states.

beginner: Pick off and destroy the adults, the yellow egg clusters, and the spiny young, looking under the leaves. Done early, this works well in a home garden. Beans can lose a fair amount of leaf without losing beans, so you do not need to spray for light damage. If they get bad, an organic spray such as spinosad is labeled for bean beetles, and a tiny helper wasp is sold to control them.
seasoned: Handpick and destroy adults, the yellow egg clusters, and the spiny larvae, checking leaf undersides; this is effective in a home patch caught early. Beans tolerate real defoliation without yield loss (about 30 percent before bloom, 15 percent during bloom and pod fill), so light feeding needs no spray. Where pressure is heavy, an organic option such as spinosad or a pyrethrin is labeled for bean beetles; the parasitic wasp Pediobius foveolatus is sold for biological control.

beginner: Because most damage happens in July and August, fast-maturing beans planted very early or in late summer can mostly dodge it. The varieties Wade and Black Valentine hold up better. Clear and turn under the old plants right after harvest so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter, and move your beans to a new spot each year.
seasoned: Since most damage falls in July and August, quick-maturing varieties sown very early or in late summer can largely escape it. The varieties Wade and Black Valentine are tolerant. Work crop debris into the soil promptly after harvest to remove overwintering shelter, and rotate beans away from last year's bed.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects, usually green but sometimes black or pink, packed onto the growing tips and the undersides of leaves. Heavy feeding stunts young plants and slows them down, and a sticky residue may appear. Aphids can also spread virus diseases from plant to plant.
seasoned: Colonies of soft-bodied, pinhead-sized insects clustered on growing tips and leaf undersides, usually green but sometimes black, yellow, or pink. Heavy feeding stunts young plants and delays maturity as the insects withdraw large volumes of sap; a sticky honeydew and sooty mold may follow. Aphids also transmit the mosaic viruses of beans.

beginner: Several kinds of aphids, most common in cool, dry weather on small plants. They multiply fast and build up thick colonies before their natural enemies catch up. Warmer weather and helpful bugs like ladybugs usually knock them back.
seasoned: Several aphid species (Aphis and Macrosiphum), most prevalent in cool, dry weather on small plants. They reproduce rapidly, building dense colonies before natural enemies catch up; warm weather and predators such as ladybugs usually bring them down.

beginner: Blast the colonies off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap, which works on contact. Start as soon as you see them. Once it warms up, ladybugs and other helpful insects usually take care of the rest.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water, or treat with insecticidal soap, which gives good control on contact. Begin as soon as colonies are found. Once the weather warms, ladybugs and other natural enemies generally take over.

beginner: Lay down reflective mulch, which confuses aphids and cuts both their feeding and the viruses they spread, and pull nearby weeds that shelter them. Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is exactly what aphids like.
seasoned: Lay reflective mulch, which disorients aphids and reduces both feeding and virus spread, and control nearby weeds that harbor them. Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft, lush growth aphids favor.

beginner: Fine whitish or yellow speckling on the leaves at first, turning to a dried, bronzed look as they multiply. The clue is fine webbing on the undersides of the leaves. The mites themselves are tiny specks, easiest to see by tapping a leaf over white paper. They explode in hot, dry weather.
seasoned: A fine whitish or yellow stippling on the leaves at first, progressing to a bronzed, dried-out look as populations build; fine silken webbing over the leaf undersides is the giveaway. The mites are minute specks on the undersides, easiest to confirm by tapping a leaf over white paper. They build explosively in hot, dry weather, completing a generation in as few as eight days.

beginner: Two-spotted spider mites, tiny eight-legged relatives of spiders that pierce the leaf and suck out the contents. Hot, dry weather lets them build up fast, and dusty, dried-out plants are the most likely to be hit.
seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae), tiny eight-legged relatives of spiders that pierce leaf cells and suck the contents. Hot, dry conditions favor rapid buildup, and dusty, drought-stressed plants are most prone.

beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water to knock off the mites and webbing, and use insecticidal soap before they get too thick. Keeping the plants well watered and unstressed slows them down, and helpful bugs pitch in.
seasoned: Hose the undersides of leaves with a strong spray of water to dislodge mites and webbing, and treat with insecticidal soap before numbers climb too high. Keeping plants well watered and unstressed slows buildup, and ladybugs and other predators help.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist, because dried-out plants are much more likely to get mites, and keep dust down. Check the undersides of the leaves during hot, dry weather so you catch them early.
seasoned: Maintain even soil moisture, since drought-stressed plants are far more mite-prone, and avoid the dusty conditions mites thrive in. Watch the undersides of leaves closely through hot, dry spells so you catch the buildup early.

beginner: Large ragged holes chewed in the leaves, and on young plants, chewing around the stem near the soil that can kill seedlings. The adult is a small beetle, usually reddish or yellowish, with a few black spots running down each wing cover. The color varies a lot. Early-season damage is the worst because it thins out the plants.
seasoned: Large, irregular holes chewed in leaves, and on young plants, girdling of stems near the soil line that can thin the stand. The adult is small and variable in color, usually reddish or yellowish, marked with a handful of black spots set along each wing cover near where the two covers meet. Damage early in the season matters most because it reduces the stand.

beginner: The bean leaf beetle, which is rarely a serious problem in most home gardens. The adults chew leaves and stems, and young seedlings are the most at risk.
seasoned: The bean leaf beetle (Cerotoma trifurcata), rarely a serious pest in most home gardens. Adults feed on foliage and stems, with seedlings the most vulnerable stage.

beginner: Picking them off and the same steps you would use for Mexican bean beetle usually keep them in check. Beans can lose a good bit of leaf without losing beans, so light damage needs nothing. Focus on protecting young seedlings, which are the most at risk.
seasoned: Handpicking and the same measures used against Mexican bean beetle generally keep it in check; beans tolerate considerable leaf loss without yield penalty, so light feeding needs no action. Protect emerging seedlings, the vulnerable stage, where beetles are active.

beginner: Clear away the old plants after harvest and move your beans each year so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter. A lightweight row cover over young seedlings protects them through the risky early weeks if this beetle is a problem where you are.
seasoned: Clear crop debris after harvest and rotate beans to deny overwintering sites. A floating row cover over emerging seedlings protects the stand through the vulnerable early weeks where the beetle is a known problem.

beginner: Rust-colored bumps, mostly on the undersides of the leaves. Badly infected leaves turn yellow, wilt, and fall off. Stems and pods can get it too. It shows up in humid weather and can hit most kinds of beans.
seasoned: Rust-colored, raised spots that form mainly underneath the leaves; badly infected leaves yellow, wilt, and drop. Stems and pods can be infected too. It develops under humid conditions and can affect most types of beans.

beginner: A fungus that survives the winter in the soil, on old plant debris, and even on stakes used the year before. Humid weather is what lets it take hold and spread.
seasoned: The fungus Uromyces appendiculatus. It carries over from one season to the next in the soil and on leftover plant debris, and can persist on stakes or poles reused from a previous crop. Humid conditions drive infection and spread.

beginner: Pick off and throw away (do not compost) infected leaves and give the plants room to breathe. Where rust is bad, a sulfur dust or spray gives good control if you start as the plants begin to flower and repeat every week or two, following the label.
seasoned: Remove and destroy infected leaves and improve airflow. Where rust has been severe, a sulfur dust or spray gives good control when begun as the plants start to bloom and repeated on a 10-to-14-day schedule; follow the label.

beginner: Move your beans to a new spot if rust has been a problem, since the fungus carries over on old plants and stakes, and clean or replace stakes between years. Water at the base instead of overhead, give plants room, and pick a rust-resistant variety if it keeps coming back.
seasoned: Rotate beans where rust has been a problem, since the fungus carries over on debris and stakes; clean or replace stakes between seasons. Avoid overhead watering and space plants for airflow, and choose rust-resistant varieties where it recurs.

beginner: Black, sunken spots about half an inch across on the pods, the clearest sign, sometimes with a pinkish ooze in wet weather. The veins on the undersides of leaves turn black, and spots show up on stems too. It shows up in cool, wet spring and fall weather, not in hot, dry summers.
seasoned: Black, sunken lesions about half an inch across on pods, the most prominent sign, sometimes oozing salmon-colored spores in wet weather; the veins on lower leaf surfaces turn black, and lesions appear on stems and seedling leaves. It develops in cool, wet spring and fall weather, not in hot, dry summers.

beginner: A fungus that rides in on infected seed and survives up to two years on old plant debris in the soil. Splashing water spreads it, and cool, wet weather is when it strikes.
seasoned: The fungus Colletotrichum lindemuthianum, carried on infected seed and surviving up to two years on plant debris in the soil. Splashing water spreads it, and cool, wet conditions favor infection.

beginner: You cannot cure tissue that is already infected; pull and throw away (do not compost) affected plants and debris to slow it down. On snap beans, a copper fungicide can help if you start early, but keeping seed clean and rotating does most of the work.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected plants and debris to limit spread. On snap beans, a copper fungicide or chlorothalonil can suppress it when started early; cultural control is the mainstay for a home crop.

beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Clear away all the old plants after harvest, and do not grow beans in that spot for two to three years. Water at the base and avoid splashing soil up onto the plants.
seasoned: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Remove all plant debris after harvest, and do not plant beans where the disease occurred for two to three years. Avoid overhead watering and splashing soil onto the plants.

beginner: Two related diseases. Halo blight makes pale greenish-yellow rings around brown spots on the leaves and shows up in cool weather. Common blight turns leaves brown so they drop fast, with no ring, and likes warm weather. Both hit stems, leaves, and pods, and both spread in rain and damp conditions.
seasoned: Two related diseases. Halo blight shows light greenish-yellow halos around brown leaf spots and appears in cool weather; common blight turns leaves brown so they drop quickly, with no halo, and favors warm weather. Both infect stems, leaves, and pods, and both are spread by rain and damp conditions.

beginner: Two kinds of bacteria, one causing common blight and one causing halo blight. Both start on infected seed, spread easily when it is wet, and survive up to two years on old plant debris in the soil.
seasoned: Two bacteria, Xanthomonas campestris pv. phaseoli (common blight) and Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola (halo blight). Both start on infected seed, spread readily in moisture, and survive up to two years on plant debris in the soil.

beginner: There is no cure once plants are infected; copper sprays every 10 days can slow it down. Water at the base, not overhead, and do not touch the plants when the leaves are wet, since that carries the bacteria from plant to plant.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; copper fungicides applied on a 10-day schedule can slow spread. Avoid overhead watering and do not handle plants when foliage is wet, which moves the bacteria from plant to plant.

beginner: Buy new, certified seed each year instead of saving your own, since the disease travels on seed. Do not grow beans in the same spot more than once every three years, and keep out of the patch when the leaves are wet.

seasoned: Big leafy plants but few beans

seasoned: The plants grew large and dark and leafy but set few pods, because they were given too much nitrogen. As legumes, beans fix much of their own nitrogen, and extra fertilizer over-stimulates leaf growth, delays flowering, and reduces pod set.

seasoned: Skip the nitrogen feeding. Work in only a little balanced fertilizer or compost before planting, and at most one light side-dressing just before bloom, and only on poor or sandy soil. Let the plant's own nitrogen fixation carry the crop.

beginner: The beans came out small, tough, or crooked, usually because the plants dried out while flowering and filling pods, which is the time they most need water, or because the pods were left on too long, until the swelling seeds made them woody. Both are easy to fix.
seasoned: The pods came out small, fibrous, or misshapen, usually from drought stress during and after flowering, which is the moisture-critical window, or from leaving pods on the plant past their tender stage, when the enlarging seeds make the pod woody. Both are easy to prevent.

seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample from first flower through pod fill, and pick every two to three days, harvesting pods while they are still firm, crisp, and before the seeds bulge. Frequent picking also keeps the plant producing.

seasoned: Bush beans crop heavily over a short two-to-three-week window, then taper. Sow a fresh short row every two weeks from the last spring frost until about two months before your first fall frost, and you will keep fresh beans coming all season instead of facing one big glut.

The earliest sowings begin yielding in roughly 50 days, and harvest carries through until frost.

beginner: Bush beans are one of the easiest vegetables to grow and a great first crop. They are small, tidy plants that do not need staking, and they go from seed to harvest in about two months. You plant the seeds straight in the garden after the last frost, keep them watered, and start picking. Because a patch produces a big batch all at once, planting a new short row every couple of weeks keeps fresh beans on the table all summer.
seasoned: Bush snap beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) are a fast, frost-tender warm-season legume grown for their tender immature pods. Compact and self-supporting, they crop heavily over a concentrated two-to-three-week window, which makes succession sowing the key to a steady supply. Direct-sown into warm soil after the last frost, they fix their own nitrogen, ask little of the gardener, and reach a pickable crop in about 50 to 60 days.

beginner: Beans are ready when the pods are firm and crisp and break with a clean snap, before you can see the seeds bulging inside. Pick every few days to keep more beans coming.
seasoned: Pick when pods are firm, crisp, and snap cleanly, before the enlarging seeds bulge the pod. Harvesting every couple of days keeps plants producing and catches pods at peak tenderness.

beginner: Snap peas like loose, fertile soil that drains well, with some compost mixed in. The main thing they care about is good drainage, because peas planted in cold, soggy soil tend to rot before they sprout. If water sits on your bed for a long time after rain, work in compost or plant on a raised bed first.
seasoned: Sugar snap peas do best in a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam with compost worked in before sowing. The critical trait is drainage: pea seed sown into cold, wet, poorly drained ground rots before it germinates, and the soilborne root rots that follow are the main early-season risk. Steady, even moisture without waterlogging carries the crop through flowering and pod fill, the stage that decides whether the pods plump up. Peas are legumes and fix much of their own nitrogen, so the bed needs fertility and tilth more than heavy feeding.

beginner: Snap peas grow best in soil from about 6.0 to 7.0, which is slightly acidic to neutral. They do poorly in strongly acidic soil below 6.0, so if a soil test reads low, mix in some lime before planting. Most garden beds are already in a good range.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0. Clemson targets 6.0 to 6.5 for peas, and growth is inhibited on acid soils at pH 6.0 and below, so lime an acid plot the season before sowing. Peas tolerate up to roughly 7.5, and a soil test is the reliable way to confirm both pH and fertility before the season starts.

beginner: Peas make much of their own food from the air, so they barely need fertilizer. Mix a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant and that is enough. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy vines but fewer pods. If you like, you can coat the seed with a pea inoculant powder, which helps the roots make nitrogen, but it is optional.
seasoned: Sugar snap peas are light feeders. As legumes they fix much of their own nitrogen through root nodules, so heavy nitrogen drives leafy vine growth at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the bed before sowing; that is usually all peas need. An inoculant of the right Rhizobium bacteria is optional and can help nodulation where peas have not been grown before. Avoid high-nitrogen feeds, which delay flowering and cut pod set.

beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 mixed into the bed before planting is plenty.
seasoned: A balanced 5-10-10 worked in before sowing if no soil test is available; skip extra nitrogen, which peas supply themselves.

beginner: About 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet, mixed into the bed before planting.
seasoned: 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet worked in before sowing, per Clemson, when no soil test is available.

beginner: Snap peas get along with most cool-season vegetables. They grow happily beside carrots, radishes, and lettuce, and because they leave nitrogen in the soil, they are a good crop to grow before a leafy green. The pairing to avoid is planting peas right next to onions or garlic.
seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, sugar snap peas leave the soil richer for what follows and sit comfortably among the other cool-season crops grown in the same early-spring and fall windows: carrots, radishes, and lettuce are classic bed-mates. The long-standing caution is to keep peas away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress legumes through the same root-bacteria interference seen with beans.

beginner: A classic cool-season neighbor that shares snap peas' early-spring and fall timing; the carrots root deep while the peas climb, so they use the bed without crowding.
seasoned: Carrots and peas grow in the same cool windows and use the bed in complementary ways: the carrot works the soil deep while the pea climbs above it, and the peas' nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the carrot. The pairing is traditional and compatibility-based rather than a measured pest defense, so expect easy cohabitation more than active protection.

beginner: Radishes sprout fast and mark the pea rows while the slower peas come up, then are pulled long before the peas need the space.
seasoned: Radishes germinate in days and mark the rows while the peas emerge, and they finish and come out weeks before the vines size up, so they never compete. Both are cool-season crops sown at the same time, which makes them a tidy, low-risk interplant rather than a measured protective pairing.

beginner: Lettuce shares snap peas' cool-season timing and stays low, tucking in along the base of the pea row or trellis.
seasoned: Lettuce slots in below a pea trellis or alongside a bush row, sharing the same cool-season window and water needs while occupying a different layer of the bed. As the peas leaf out they offer the lettuce a little light afternoon shade that delays bolting. It is a compatibility pairing on sound shared-conditions grounds rather than a measured protective one.

beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from peas, which are said to grow poorly near them.
seasoned: Onions next to peas is the better-grounded of the 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds that are widely held to interfere with the Rhizobium bacteria on pea roots, the bacteria the plant relies on to fix nitrogen, so pea growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. The useful corollary is that peas grown before an allium crop leave the soil better for it.

beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for peas.
seasoned: Garlic acts on peas the way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds held to disrupt the nitrogen-fixing bacteria on pea roots, slowing the vines. Treat garlic and peas as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the pea-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

beginner: Clusters of small, soft green insects packed onto the growing tips, flower stems, and undersides of the leaves. They curl and yellow the new growth and stunt the plants, and they leave a sticky residue. The bigger problem is that pea aphids spread virus diseases from plant to plant, so they are worth catching early.
seasoned: Colonies of soft, pinhead-sized green aphids clustered on the growing tips, flower stalks, and leaf undersides. Heavy feeding curls and yellows the new growth, stunts the vines, and can drop blossoms; a sticky honeydew and sooty mold may follow. Most important, pea aphids transmit the virus diseases of peas, including pea enation mosaic, so even modest numbers matter.

beginner: The pea aphid, a large green aphid that multiplies quickly in the cool weather of spring and fall when peas are growing. It builds up fast, before helpful insects like ladybugs catch up.
seasoned: The pea aphid (Acyrthosiphon pisum), a large green aphid that builds up fast in the cool, mild weather of spring and fall, exactly the seasons peas grow. It reproduces rapidly, so colonies form before natural enemies catch up.

beginner: Blast the colonies off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap, which works on contact. Start as soon as you see them, while there are only a few. Ladybugs and other helpful insects usually finish the job. Since aphids spread viruses, it is worth dealing with them early.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water, or treat with insecticidal soap, which controls aphids on contact; begin as soon as colonies are found, while numbers are low. Ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually bring populations down on their own. Because the real risk is virus transmission, act early rather than waiting for visible damage.

beginner: Lay down reflective mulch, which confuses aphids and cuts the viruses they spread, and pull nearby weeds that shelter them. Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is exactly what aphids like. Where pea viruses are common, plant a resistant variety like Cascadia or Sugar Sprint.
seasoned: Lay reflective mulch, which disorients aphids and reduces both feeding and virus spread, and control nearby weeds and clover that harbor them. Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft, lush growth aphids favor, and choose virus-resistant snap varieties such as Cascadia or Sugar Sprint where pea viruses are a known problem.

beginner: Little notches chewed out of the leaf edges of young plants, and beetles on the flowers in spring. The hidden damage is worse: the grubs tunnel into the peas forming inside the pods, leaving tiny round holes in the dried seeds. Since you eat snap peas pod and all, infested pods are especially unwelcome. Holes in saved seed are the tell, and the pea weevil eats only peas.
seasoned: Small notches chewed from the leaf margins of young plants in spring, and adults feeding on the blossoms. The real damage is hidden: larvae bore into the developing seeds inside the pods and feed there, leaving tiny round exit holes in the dried peas. Because snap peas are eaten pod and all, weevil-infested pods are especially unwelcome. Saved seed with holes is the giveaway, and the pea weevil feeds only on peas (Pisum).

beginner: The pea weevil, a small brown beetle that feeds only on peas. The adults spend the winter in garden trash, move in when the peas flower to lay eggs on the young pods, and the grubs grow up inside the seeds. There is one generation each year.
seasoned: The pea weevil (Bruchus pisorum), a small brownish beetle whose host range is peas alone. Adults overwinter in debris and trash, move into the crop at bloom to lay eggs on young pods, and the larvae develop inside the seeds. There is one generation a year.

beginner: Watch for the beetles while the peas are flowering, which is when they lay eggs. Picking them off and covering the plants with a light row cover at flowering both help. At the end of the season, check dried peas for tiny round holes before you save seed, and freezing saved seed for a few days kills any grubs inside.
seasoned: Monitor for adults during bloom, when egg-laying begins. In a home patch, handpicking and floating row cover over the crop at flowering reduce egg-laying. At season's end, inspect dried peas for the small round exit holes before storing seed; freezing saved seed for several days kills any larvae inside.

beginner: Clear away and destroy the old pea plants after harvest so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter, and move your peas to a new spot each year. Do not save seed that has holes in it. Planting early so the pods finish before the beetles get busy also helps.
seasoned: Clean up and destroy pea debris after harvest to remove overwintering shelter, and rotate peas away from last year's bed. Do not save or replant seed showing exit holes. Where the weevil is established, an early sowing that finishes pod fill before peak adult activity escapes the worst.

beginner: Cutworms cut off young pea seedlings right at the soil line overnight, so you find plants toppled over and gaps in the row. Armyworms are smooth caterpillars that chew the leaves and sometimes the pods, and they can show up in numbers. Both feed at night and hide during the day.
seasoned: Cutworms sever young seedlings at or just below the soil line overnight, leaving toppled plants and thinned rows in spring. Armyworms are smooth caterpillars that chew foliage and can move through a planting in numbers, skeletonizing leaves and nicking pods. Both feed mostly at night and hide in the soil or debris by day.

beginner: Several kinds of night-feeding caterpillars: cutworms and armyworms, the young of different moths. They come in from weedy or grassy areas, and young seedlings are the most at risk.
seasoned: Several night-feeding caterpillars, including cutworms (the larvae of various moths) and beet or western yellowstriped armyworms. They overwinter or move in from weedy ground and grassy cover, and seedlings are the most vulnerable stage.

beginner: Pick the caterpillars off in the evening or early morning, and dig a little around fallen seedlings to find the curled-up cutworm. A collar of cardboard or foil around a seedling blocks cutworms, and a Bt spray controls young armyworms on the leaves. A light row cover keeps the moths from laying eggs.
seasoned: Handpick caterpillars in the evening or early morning, and check the soil around toppled seedlings for the curled cutworm. A cardboard or foil collar around a seedling stops cutworms; Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) controls young armyworms on the foliage. A floating row cover keeps egg-laying moths off the planting.

beginner: Clear weeds and tall grass before planting so the moths have fewer places to lay eggs, and turn the soil a couple of weeks before sowing to expose the grubs. Keep the edges of the bed weeded, and cover young seedlings with a row cover if these caterpillars are a problem where you are.
seasoned: Clear weeds and grassy cover before sowing to remove egg-laying sites, and turn the bed a couple of weeks ahead of planting to expose and dry out resident larvae. Keep row edges weed-free through the season, and protect emerging seedlings, the vulnerable stage, with a row cover where these caterpillars are a known problem.

beginner: Fine silvery streaks and pale flecks on the leaves and pods, with tiny dark specks, where the slender insects scrape the surface and feed. Bad infestations twist the new growth and leave scars on the pods. Thrips can also spread some viruses.
seasoned: Fine silvery or whitish scarring and flecking on leaves and pods, with tiny dark specks of excrement, as the slender insects rasp the surface and feed on the released sap. Heavy feeding distorts new growth and can scar pods cosmetically. Thrips also vector some plant viruses.

beginner: Thrips, slender insects much smaller than an aphid that build up in warm, dry weather toward the end of the pea season. They scrape the surface of the plant and feed on the sap.
seasoned: Several thrips species, slender insects a fraction the size of an aphid that build up in warm, dry stretches late in the pea season. They rasp the plant surface and feed on the sap that wells up.

beginner: Peas usually shrug off a little thrips damage. If they build up, a strong spray of water and insecticidal soap knock them back, and helpful insects pitch in. Keep the plants watered and unstressed, since dried-out peas are more likely to be hit.
seasoned: Peas usually outgrow light thrips feeding without treatment. Where numbers climb, a strong spray of water and insecticidal soap reduce them, and natural enemies such as minute pirate bugs and lacewings help. Keep plants unstressed and well watered, since drought-stressed peas are more prone.

beginner: Pull nearby weeds that shelter thrips, lay reflective mulch to confuse them, and keep the soil evenly moist so the plants are not stressed. Most home pea crops are done before thrips become a real problem.
seasoned: Control weeds that harbor thrips, lay reflective mulch to disorient them and reduce virus spread, and keep moisture even so plants are not drought-stressed. Most home pea crops finish before thrips become a real problem.

beginner: A white to gray powdery dust that starts as spots on top of the leaves and spreads over the leaves, stems, and pods. The leaves yellow and dry out, the vines weaken, and the pods get spotted, which matters more when you eat the whole pod. It is the classic late-season pea problem, showing up as the weather warms and dries toward the end of the spring crop.
seasoned: A white to grayish powdery coating that starts as small spots on the upper leaf surfaces and spreads to cover leaves, stems, and pods. Affected leaves yellow and dry, vines lose vigor, and pods are spotted and off-flavored, which matters more for a snap pea eaten pod and all. It is the classic late-season pea disease, arriving as the spring crop runs into warmer, drier weather.

beginner: A fungus (Erysiphe pisi) that thrives in warm days, cool nights, and dry leaves, which is exactly the weather at the end of the pea season. It spreads on the wind and moves fast once it starts, so catching it early and planting resistant varieties matter most.
seasoned: The fungus Erysiphe pisi, favored by warm days, cool nights, and dry foliage, the conditions that arrive late in the pea season. Spores spread on the wind, and the disease moves fast once established, which is why early control and resistant varieties matter most.

beginner: Powdery mildew is easiest to handle the moment you first see it; once it covers the leaves, it is hard to stop. Pick off the worst leaves and open up the planting for airflow. A sulfur spray started early and repeated per the label helps. If the spring crop is nearly finished, the simplest move is to pick what is ready and pull the plants.
seasoned: Powdery mildew is best managed at the very first signs; once it covers the leaves and yellowing sets in, control is difficult. Remove the worst-affected leaves and improve airflow. Sulfur or a labeled biofungicide, begun early and repeated per the label, suppresses it. On a spring crop that is nearly done, harvesting promptly and pulling the planting is often the practical choice.

beginner: Plant a resistant variety, which is the best defense: Super Sugar Snap, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint resist powdery mildew. Plant early so the crop finishes before the mildew weather arrives, give the plants room and a trellis so air moves through them, and stay out of the patch when the vines are wet.
seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, the single most effective step: Super Sugar Snap, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint all carry powdery mildew resistance. Sow early so the crop finishes pod fill before the late-season mildew weather, give plants room and a trellis for airflow, and avoid working among wet vines.

beginner: The lower leaves turn yellow and the yellowing creeps up the plant, which becomes stunted, curls, and wilts. If you cut the lower stem, the tissue inside is stained reddish or orange. Affected plants often die before making a crop. It shows up in patches and gets worse as the soil warms.
seasoned: A yellowing of the lower leaves that progresses up the plant, with downward curling, stunting, and wilting; a cut through the lower stem shows a reddish or orange discoloration of the water-conducting tissue. Plants often die before pod fill. Symptoms appear in patches and worsen as the soil warms.

beginner: A fungus that lives in the soil and enters through the roots, clogging the plant's plumbing. It survives in the soil for years and likes warm soil. Once it is in a bed you cannot get rid of it, so the answer is resistant varieties and moving your peas around.
seasoned: The soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. pisi, which enters through the roots, plugs the vascular system, and persists in the soil for years. Several races exist. Warm soil favors it, and once a bed is infested the fungus cannot be eradicated, so resistant varieties and rotation are the management.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant is infected; pull and throw away (do not compost) the affected plants. You manage this one by preventing it, with resistant varieties and rotation, not by spraying.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected plants; remove and destroy them to limit buildup. Management is preventive: the disease is handled through resistant varieties and rotation, not treatment.

beginner: Plant a wilt-resistant snap variety such as Sugar Snap or Cascadia. Move your peas to a new spot on a three-to-four-year cycle, improve drainage, and avoid carrying infected soil from bed to bed.
seasoned: Plant Fusarium-resistant varieties, which are widely available among snap peas: Sugar Snap and Cascadia both carry wilt resistance. Rotate peas on a three-to-four-year cycle away from infested ground, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil between beds.

beginner: Seeds that rot before they come up, and seedlings that flop over at a pinched, water-soaked spot near the soil. On bigger plants the roots rot, the vines stunt, and the lower leaves yellow and die. It is worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil that makes the seed sit too long before sprouting.
seasoned: Seed that rots before emerging, and seedlings that damp off, collapsing at a water-soaked, pinched stem base. On older plants the root rot complex stunts the vines, yellows and kills the lower leaves, and rots the roots and lower stem brown. Damage is worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil that slows germination and keeps seedlings vulnerable.

beginner: A group of soil fungi and water molds (including Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Aphanomyces) that attack seeds, roots, and seedlings. Cold, soggy soil and damaged roots at planting let them in, and they build up where peas are grown too often in the same spot.
seasoned: A complex of soilborne fungi and water molds, chiefly Pythium, Rhizoctonia, Fusarium solani, and Aphanomyces euteiches. Cold, saturated soil and root injury at planting set the stage; Aphanomyces in particular builds up in beds cropped to peas too often and severe infections kill plants outright.

beginner: There is no saving seed or seedlings that have rotted; replant once the soil is warmer and drains better. Pulling affected plants and improving drainage help, but the main thing is preventing it, since these organisms live in the soil.
seasoned: There is no rescue for rotted seed or collapsed seedlings; replant into warmer, better-drained conditions once the soil has dried. Removing affected plants and improving drainage limits further loss, but prevention is the real lever since the organisms are already in the soil.

beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of cold, wet, low spots, and never sow peas into soggy ground. Avoid damaging the roots when planting, move your peas around the garden on a three-to-four-year cycle, and clear away the old plants after harvest.
seasoned: Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than cold, low, wet spots, and do not sow peas into waterlogged soil. Avoid root injury at planting, rotate peas on a three-to-four-year cycle to keep Aphanomyces down, and clear crop debris after harvest. Some varieties offer partial root-rot tolerance.

beginner: Brown to purple-black spots and streaks on the leaves, stems, and pods, sometimes with a blackened stem base. Sunken spots on the pods can carry the disease into the seed. It shows up in cool, wet spring and fall weather and rides in on infected seed and old plant debris.
seasoned: Brown to purplish-black spots and streaks on leaves, stems, and pods, often with darker margins; a blackening at the base of the stem (foot rot) in one form, and sunken lesions on the pods that can carry the fungus into the seed. It develops in cool, wet spring and fall weather and is carried on infected seed and debris.

beginner: A group of related fungi that survive on infected seed and on old pea plants left in the soil. Cool, wet weather and splashing water spread them. Once they are on the seed, they travel with it to the next planting.
seasoned: A complex of related fungi (the Ascochyta blight complex). The fungi survive on infected seed and on pea debris in the soil, and cool, wet conditions with splashing water drive infection and spread.

beginner: You cannot cure tissue that is already infected; pull and throw away (do not compost) affected plants and all the old debris to slow it down. For a home garden, prevention does most of the work, since the disease travels on seed and old plants.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected plants and all debris to limit spread. Cultural control is the mainstay for a home crop, since the disease is seed- and debris-borne.

beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Clear away all the old pea plants after harvest, and do not grow peas in that spot for at least three to four years. Water at the base, not overhead, and stay out of the patch when the vines are wet.
seasoned: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Remove all pea debris after harvest and rotate peas off the ground for a minimum of three to four years before returning. Avoid overhead watering and working among wet vines, which splash and carry the fungus.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist but not soggy. Pay closest attention while the plants are flowering and the pods are filling out.
seasoned: Regular and even through the season, keeping the soil moist but never waterlogged. The need peaks during flowering and pod fill; before that, established vines in cool weather ask relatively little.

beginner: Water deeply enough to wet the soil about 6 inches down. Deep, less frequent watering beats a daily light sprinkle.
seasoned: Enough to wet the root zone roughly 6 inches down; watering deeply and less often builds deeper roots than frequent light sprinkles. Clemson advises watering to moisten the soil to a depth of 6 inches.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and do it in the morning so the plants dry off during the day. Wet leaves, especially overnight, help spread disease.
seasoned: Water at the soil level in the morning so the foliage dries before evening; this limits the powdery mildew and Ascochyta the crop is prone to. Avoid overhead watering on a trellised crop in particular.

beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt or the lower leaves turn yellow, you may be overwatering. Soggy soil rots pea roots.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and stunted vines point to waterlogged roots and the onset of the root rots peas are prone to in cold, wet ground.

beginner: If plants dry out while flowering, they drop their flowers and the pods stay small and never fill out. Keep the water steady at that stage.
seasoned: Drought stress during and after flowering aborts blossoms and leaves the pods small and poorly filled, so they never plump up into a proper snap pod; it also hastens the late-season decline as heat arrives.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, not soggy, until the seedlings come up. Pea seeds rot in cold, wet ground.
seasoned: Direct-sown into cool soil, sugar snap peas want an evenly moist seedbed until emergence, but not soggy: pea seed rots in cold, waterlogged ground.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered as they get going and start to climb.
seasoned: Grow the young vines on with steady, even moisture as they root out and start to climb.

beginner: In cool weather the growing vines need fairly little water. Soak the soil about 6 inches down, in the morning at the soil so the leaves dry off. Do not overwater peas before they flower.
seasoned: Established vines in cool weather ask relatively little: water deeply enough to wet the root zone about 6 inches down (Clemson advises moistening to 6 inches), at soil level in the morning so foliage dries and powdery mildew and Ascochyta stay down. Do not overwater a cool-season crop before it flowers.

beginner: Keep the water steady once the peas flower. Drought now drops the blossoms and you get fewer pods.
seasoned: Flowering is moisture-critical: stress here aborts blossoms and directly cuts the crop. Keep the soil evenly moist and water at the base, avoiding overhead wetting on the trellised vines.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the pods fill. Sugar snap peas need steady water to plump up into fat, crisp snap pods; if they dry out now the pods stay thin and flat.
seasoned: Pod fill is the peak, and on a snap pea it is what makes the pod: drought here leaves the pods thin and poorly filled so they never plump up into a proper, crisp snap pod. Keep moisture steady right through filling.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while you pick the plump pods. Steady water keeps them crisp, though the vines naturally fade as the weather warms up.
seasoned: Keep even moisture through the picking run so the pods stay plump and crisp; the crop naturally winds down as heat arrives and hastens the late-season decline.

beginner: Try not to spray the whole plant from above. The most important time to keep water steady is when the plants are flowering and forming pods.
seasoned: Avoid overhead watering where practical; the critical moisture window is flowering through pod fill.

beginner: Flowering and pod-filling are the times peas most need steady water.
seasoned: Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages; stress here directly cuts the crop and leaves the pods thin instead of plump.

beginner: You do not need to harden off peas. They are planted straight into the garden from seed.
seasoned: Not applicable. Peas are direct-sown in place and are not started indoors or hardened off.

beginner: Plant snap pea seeds right where they will grow, as soon as the soil can be worked in spring and again in late summer for fall. Peas do not like their roots disturbed, so skip starting them indoors. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep and 1 to 2 inches apart.
seasoned: Direct-sow into cool, workable soil as early as the ground can be prepared in spring, and again for a fall crop. Peas resent root disturbance and germinate readily in cool soil, so transplanting offers no advantage. Sow about 1 to 1.5 inches deep and 1 to 2 inches apart in rows roughly 18 to 24 inches apart; some growers presoak seed overnight to speed emergence.

beginner: Use a good potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in pots.
seasoned: A well-draining potting mix; avoid native garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in containers and worsens root rot.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Mix in a little compost for fertility.
seasoned: Blend in compost for baseline fertility and tilth; peas need little added nitrogen.

beginner: Pots dry out faster than garden beds, so check the soil daily in warm weather and water when the top inch is dry.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; monitor daily in warm spells and water when the top inch dries.

beginner: Container peas still need little feeding; a little compost in the mix is usually enough.
seasoned: Feeding needs stay low in containers; compost blended into the mix usually suffices.

beginner: Not applicable. Peas are a cool-season annual; they finish in one season and are not overwintered as a plant.
seasoned: Not applicable. As a single-season annual, peas complete their cycle and are pulled; in mild regions a fall sowing is grown over winter in the ground, but a container crop is grown and finished within a season.

beginner: Bush and short snap peas like Sugar Ann grow well in a pot at least 5 gallons and 8 inches deep. Push a few short twiggy branches or a small trellis into the pot for the tendrils to climb, plant several seeds, and keep the mix evenly moist.
seasoned: Bush and semi-dwarf snap pea types suit containers well; tall climbing varieties like Sugar Snap are awkward in pots because of their trellis height. A pot of at least 5 gallons and 8 inches deep, planted with several seeds and given a few twiggy branches or a small trellis for support, performs well with even moisture. Sugar Ann, a compact bush type, is the easiest container choice.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match for peas because it keeps the water steady, which is what they like, without leaving the roots soggy.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits peas well, smoothing out the steady moisture they want through pod fill while avoiding the soggy roots they dislike.

beginner: Pick the pot to fit the variety. Low bush peas like Sugar Ann do well in a wide pot with several plants together; tall climbing peas need a deep, heavy pot that will not tip over once the trellis is loaded with vines. For a pot, a short bush variety is usually the easier pick.
seasoned: Match the container to the variety: a wide, shallow pot suits low bush types like Sugar Ann grown several together, while a tall climbing Sugar Snap needs a deep, stable pot that will not tip under a loaded trellis. For most container growers a bush snap pea in a broad pot is the easier choice.

beginner: Do not plant snap peas where peas or beans grew last year. Diseases build up in the soil and hit the next crop. If you have had root rot or blight, wait even longer, up to four years, before peas return.
seasoned: Avoid following peas with peas or other legumes in the same bed; rotate to break the soilborne disease cycle (root rots, Fusarium, Ascochyta) that peas are prone to. Where Ascochyta or Aphanomyces root rot have appeared, extend the rotation toward four years.

beginner: Move your peas to a new spot each year, on about a three-year rotation, and longer if you have had disease trouble. Because peas feed the soil with nitrogen, whatever you plant there next will benefit.
seasoned: Rotate peas on a roughly three-year cycle, longer where Ascochyta blight or root rot have shown up. Their nitrogen-fixing habit makes them a good predecessor for nitrogen-hungry crops.

beginner: Do not leave snap peas out on the counter. They go limp and lose their sweetness quickly, so cool them soon after picking.
seasoned: Not recommended. Sugar snap peas lose sweetness and crispness fast at room temperature and should be cooled promptly after picking rather than held on the counter.

beginner: Cool the pods right after picking, then keep them in the fridge in a loosely closed bag. They stay best for only about two to three days; the longer they sit, the less sweet and crisp they get.
seasoned: Cool sugar snap peas immediately after harvest to shed field heat, then refrigerate in a perforated bag. They hold good quality for only about two to three days kept cold and humid, near 32 to 40°F at high humidity; the sugars convert to starch quickly, so use them sooner rather than later.

beginner: Snap peas freeze well for keeping longer. Give them a quick dip in boiling water (blanch), cool them, and freeze within a few hours of picking for the best result.
seasoned: Sugar snap peas freeze well for longer storage. Blanch briefly to set the color and texture, cool, and freeze within a few hours of picking for the best quality.

beginner: Snap peas taste best soon after picking. To keep them, cool them fast, store them cold and slightly damp for two to three days at most, and freeze (after a quick blanch) within a few hours if you want them to last longer.
seasoned: Sugar snap peas are at their sweetest and crispest within hours of picking and are best used promptly. To hold them, cool them fast to remove field heat, keep them cold and humid for two to three days at most, and blanch and freeze within a few hours if you want to store them longer.

beginner: These are snap peas, the plump, sweet kind you eat whole once the pods fill out, different from flat snow peas and from shelling peas you pop open for the seeds. Pick a type to fit your space: tall kinds like Sugar Snap need a trellis, while short bush kinds like Sugar Ann hold themselves up and do well in pots. If powdery mildew or wilt is common where you garden, choose a resistant variety like Super Sugar Snap, Cascadia, or Sugar Sprint. Older kinds have a stringy seam you peel off; Sugar Ann, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint are stringless.
seasoned: These are snap (sugar snap) peas, bred for plump, rounded, edible pods eaten whole once the peas have filled out; do not confuse them with flat snow peas, which are picked young and flat, or with shelling peas grown only for the seed. Match the variety to your support: tall climbers like Sugar Snap and Super Sugar Snap reach several feet and need a sturdy trellis, while bush types like Sugar Ann stand on their own and suit containers and small beds. Where powdery mildew or wilt recur, lean on the resistant varieties: Super Sugar Snap, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint carry powdery mildew resistance, and Cascadia adds Fusarium wilt and pea enation mosaic virus resistance. Older varieties carry a string along the pod seam that is pulled before eating; Sugar Ann, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint are stringless.

beginner: Bare soil for a week or so, then the little plants push up. Peas come up in cool soil and can go in very early, but seed planted in cold, soggy ground rots instead of sprouting. They come up fastest when the soil is around 55 to 65°F.
seasoned: Bare soil for about a week to ten days, then the seedling pushes up through the surface. Peas germinate in cool soil and can be sown as soon as the ground is workable, but seed sown into cold, saturated ground rots before it emerges. Emergence is quickest in soil around 55 to 65°F and slows below that; the lower limit for germination is about 40°F.

beginner: Plant as soon as you can work the soil, about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, in moist but well-drained ground. Do not keep the bed soggy after planting, since that rots the seed. Soaking the seeds overnight before planting can speed things up.
seasoned: Sow as early as the soil can be worked, about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, into a moist but well-drained bed; do not sow into waterlogged ground. There is no benefit to soaking the bed afterward, which suffocates the seed and feeds root rot. An optional overnight presoak of the seed speeds emergence, and a pea inoculant helps nodulation where peas are new to the bed.

beginner: Have your peas come up yet? Write down the date you first saw them break the soil.
seasoned: Have your peas emerged? Note the date to track days to maturity from a real sowing rather than the seed packet.

beginner: Small plants a few inches tall with their first leaves and the little curling tendrils that peas use to climb. Young peas handle light frost fine, but this is when cutworms can cut them off at the ground and slugs can chew them in wet weather.
seasoned: Young plants a few inches tall putting out their first leaves and, soon, the curling tendrils that mark a climbing crop. Pea seedlings are cold-hardy and shrug off light spring frost, but they are the stage most vulnerable to cutworms, which sever them at the soil line, and to slugs in wet weather.

beginner: Put up the support now, before the vines sprawl: a trellis, netting, or twiggy branches alongside the row, even for short types. Keep the soil evenly moist, pull weeds early, and weed shallowly so you do not damage the roots. Check for plants cut off at the ground, which means cutworms.
seasoned: Set up support now, before the vines flop: push twiggy branches or a trellis or netting in alongside even bush types, which crop better held up. Keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free, cultivate shallowly since pea roots run near the surface, and watch for toppled seedlings that signal cutworms.

beginner: How do your young pea plants look? Note any chewed or toppled plants and whether the tendrils are reaching for the trellis.
seasoned: How is your pea stand looking? Note any gaps, cutworm damage, or the first tendrils reaching for support.

beginner: The vines climb and fill in, their tendrils grabbing the support as they go. Short bush types reach about two feet, tall types five to six. Peas make much of their own food (nitrogen) at this stage, so you want healthy green growth, not huge dark leafy vines, which usually mean too much fertilizer and fewer pods.
seasoned: Steady growth as the vines climb and fill their support, tendrils gripping as they go. Bush types like Sugar Ann reach about two feet and stand together; tall types like Sugar Snap climb to five or six feet. The plants are fixing much of their own nitrogen now through root nodules, so vigorous green growth, not dark, overfed lushness, is the goal.

beginner: Keep the watering steady and do not add fertilizer now. Peas need very little, and extra just gives you big leafy vines with fewer pods. Help the first tendrils find the trellis, and keep the plants from getting crowded so air moves through them.
seasoned: Keep moisture steady and resist the urge to feed; peas need little nitrogen and extra now pushes foliage at the expense of pods. Guide the first tendrils onto the support, and keep the rows open for airflow to hold off powdery mildew as the weather warms.

beginner: How tall are your pea vines getting? Note how well they are climbing the trellis.
seasoned: How are your pea vines filling in? Note their height and whether they are climbing the support cleanly.

beginner: Small white (sometimes pink or purple) flowers open along the vines. This is an important time for water: if the plants dry out or it stays hotter than about 80 to 85°F, the flowers drop without making pods. The flowers and tiny pods are much more sensitive to frost than the young plants were.
seasoned: Small white (sometimes pink or purple) pea flowers open along the vines. This is a moisture-critical stage: water stress now aborts blossoms, and sustained heat above about 80 to 85°F causes the plant to drop flowers instead of setting pods. The flowers and tiny pods are far more frost-tender than the hardy seedlings were.

beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants flower, because dry soil now means fewer peas. Water the soil, not the leaves. Cover the plants overnight if a frost threatens the open flowers, and water deeply before a heat wave. The plants set pods again once it cools, but the spring crop is running out of cool weather by now.
seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom; this is where water stress directly cuts the crop. Avoid overhead watering on the dense canopy. If a late frost threatens open flowers, cover the planting overnight, and in a heat wave water deeply ahead of time; the plant will set again when it cools, but the spring crop is racing the heat at this point.

beginner: Are your peas flowering yet? Note when the flowers opened and whether any dropped in hot weather.
seasoned: Are your peas flowering? Note the date bloom started and any blossom drop in heat.

beginner: Pods form where the flowers were and then fatten up as the peas inside fill them, unlike flat snow peas. With snap peas you want a plump, rounded pod that is still bright green, crisp, and sweet, ready about 5 to 8 days after the flowers open. If you wait too long the pod gets dull and tough and the peas turn starchy, so the window is short.
seasoned: Pods form where the flowers were and then swell and round out as the peas inside fill them, unlike a snow pea, which is picked flat. For snap peas the aim is a plump, rounded, full pod that is still bright green, crisp, and tender, reached about 5 to 8 days after flowering. Left too long the seeds bulge, the pod dulls and toughens, and the sugars turn starchy, so the pickable window is short.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the pods fill, which is what lets them plump up. Start checking the vines every day once the first pods start to round out, because snap peas go from sweet and crisp to tough and starchy in just a few days.
seasoned: Maintain even moisture right through pod fill, the payoff stage for steady watering and the stage that decides whether pods plump up properly. Begin checking the vines daily as the first pods start to round out, since the snap-pea window from full-and-sweet to tough-and-starchy is only a few days.

beginner: Are pods filling out? Note when you first saw them start to fatten and how quickly they are plumping.
seasoned: Are pods filling? Note the date you first saw pods start to round out and how fast they are plumping.

beginner: Plump, rounded, crisp pods picked while the peas inside are full but the pod is still bright and sweet, about 5 to 8 days after flowering. Pick every one to three days: regular picking keeps more pods coming, while pods left to get starchy tell the plant to quit. Snap peas crop for a few weeks, longer than snow peas, then fade as it warms up.
seasoned: Plump, rounded, crisp pods snapped from the vine while the peas inside are full but the pod is still bright and tender, about 5 to 8 days after flowering. Picking every one to three days is essential: regular harvest keeps the vines flowering and producing, while pods left to go starchy signal the plant to stop. Snap types crop over a longer window than snow peas, often three to four weeks, then decline as the heat builds.

beginner: Pick in the cool morning, holding the vine with one hand and pulling the pod with the other so you do not tear the stem, and peel the string off older kinds before eating. Pick every one to three days, because old pods left on the plant make it stop producing. When the vines fade in the heat, pull them up and compost them.
seasoned: Pick in the cool of the morning, holding the vine with one hand and the pod with the other so you do not tear the brittle stems, and pull the string off older, stringed varieties before eating. Harvest every one to three days; leaving overmature pods on the vine ends the crop early. Pull the planting once it declines in the heat and add the vines to the compost, roots left to return their nitrogen.

beginner: Have you picked your first snap peas? Note the date and how they turned out.
seasoned: Have you made your first picking? Log the date and how plump and sweet the pods came in.

beginner: Plant peas as early as you can work the soil, but make sure it drains well and is not soggy. Pea seeds sprout in cool soil but rot in cold, wet mud, which is the usual reason for gaps in the row. Good drainage matters more than planting on an exact date.
seasoned: Sow peas as soon as the soil can be worked, but into moist, well-drained ground, not cold mud. Pea seed germinates from about 40°F up and fastest at 55 to 65°F, yet it rots in cold, saturated soil, the most common cause of a thin stand. Raised beds and good drainage matter more than calendar date.

beginner: Peas make their own nitrogen with the help of tiny bacteria on their roots. If peas or beans have grown in your bed before, the bacteria are already there. In a brand-new bed you can coat the seed with a pea inoculant powder to help, but it is optional.
seasoned: Peas fix their own nitrogen with Rhizobium bacteria on their roots. Where peas or beans have grown before, those bacteria are already present; in a new bed, an inexpensive seed inoculant can improve nodulation. It is optional, not required, and no substitute for good drainage and tilth.

beginner: Put up the trellis or netting early, when you plant or right after. Even short peas do better held up off the ground, and tall ones need support before they start to flop. If you wait too long you can tear the vines or hurt the roots putting it in.
seasoned: Put the support in early, at or just after sowing. Even bush peas crop better and stay cleaner held up off the ground, and tall types must have a trellis or netting before the vines start to sprawl. Setting it up later risks tearing the brittle vines and damaging shallow roots.

beginner: Do not add nitrogen fertilizer now. Peas make much of their own from the air, and extra fertilizer just gives you big leafy vines with fewer peas. A little compost mixed into the bed before planting is all they need.
seasoned: Hold off on nitrogen. As legumes, peas fix much of their own through root nodules, and extra nitrogen now drives leafy vine growth at the expense of flowers and pods. A little compost or balanced fertilizer worked in before sowing is all peas need.

beginner: Keep the water steady and generous while the plants flower. Flowering and pod-filling are when peas most need water, and letting them dry out now means fewer peas. Water the soil in the morning, not the leaves, to keep disease down.
seasoned: Keep moisture steady and ample through bloom. Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages, and water stress now aborts blossoms and shrinks the crop. Water at the soil in the morning, not overhead, to keep the canopy dry and slow powdery mildew.

beginner: The spring crop is in a race with the heat. Once it stays above about 80°F, peas drop their flowers instead of making pods, so a planting that flowers as summer arrives makes few peas. Plant early, and where summer comes fast, pick the earliest, quickest snow peas.
seasoned: The spring crop is racing the heat. Once sustained temperatures pass about 80°F, peas drop blossoms instead of setting pods, so a planting that flowers into early summer heat sets poorly. Sow early, and where summers come on fast, lean to the earliest, shortest-season snow peas.

beginner: Pick snap peas when the pods are plump and rounded and the peas have filled out, but the pod is still crisp and sweet, about a week after flowering. Snow peas are picked flat, but snap peas you let fill; just catch them before they get dull and tough. Start checking early, because the window is short.
seasoned: Pick sugar snap peas when the pods are plump and rounded, with the peas inside full but the pod still bright, crisp, and tender, about 5 to 8 days after flowering. Unlike a snow pea, which is picked flat, a snap pea is left to fill out; but pick before the seeds bulge and the pod dulls and toughens, when it turns starchy. Start checking early, because the window is short.

beginner: Pick every one to three days. Snap peas crop for a few weeks, and leaving old pods on the vine tells the plant to quit. Picking often keeps more pods coming and catches them while they are plump, sweet, and crisp.
seasoned: Pick every one to three days. Snap peas crop over a few weeks, and leaving overmature pods on the vine signals the plant to stop flowering and ends the crop early. Frequent picking keeps the vines producing and catches the pods at their plump, sweet, crisp best.

beginner: Each pea plant gives only a modest amount, so peas are grown in rows, not one at a time. A 10-foot row of snap peas gives about 3 to 4 pounds of pods over its picking weeks.
seasoned: Sugar snap peas yield modestly per plant, so they are grown in rows or blocks rather than singly. Utah State puts a snap or snow pea crop at about 3 to 4 pounds of pods per 10 feet of row over its cropping window; a trellised double row in a small bed gives a steady picking for several weeks.

beginner: Snap peas crop for three to four weeks, then slow down as it heats up. Because one planting keeps going for a while, you often need only one or two sowings, plus a fall crop where it works.
seasoned: Snap peas come on over three to four weeks, a longer window than snow peas, and then decline as the weather warms. Because a single sowing crops for a while, one or two sowings usually suffice, with a separate fall crop where summers allow.

beginner: Snap peas are a great first-year crop. You plant the seed straight into cool spring soil, and in about two months you are picking plump, sweet pods. The main things that affect your harvest are planting early before the heat, giving tall vines a trellis, and picking often once the pods fill out.
seasoned: Sugar snap peas are a rewarding first-year crop: cold-hardy seed sown straight into early-spring soil, quick to a plump, sweet pod in about 58 to 70 days, and forgiving of cool weather. The main levers on yield are sowing early enough to beat the heat, giving climbing types a trellis, and picking often once the pods plump up.

beginner: Flowers fell off without making pods
seasoned: Flowers dropped or no pods set

beginner: The plants flowered but made few or no pods, or the pods never filled out, because it got too hot. Once it stays above about 80 to 85°F, peas drop their flowers instead of making pods, and the few that form stay thin and tough. This usually happens to a spring crop planted too late that runs into summer heat. It is a weather problem, not a disease.
seasoned: The vines flowered but set few or no pods, or set pods that never plumped up, because the weather turned too warm. Once sustained temperatures pass about 80 to 85°F, peas abort their blossoms instead of setting pods, and any pods that form stay thin and tough. It is the classic fate of a spring crop sown too late, caught by early-summer heat, and it is a weather problem, not a disease.

beginner: Plant as early as you can work the soil so the peas flower and fill in cool weather, before the heat. Where summer comes fast, pick the quickest snow peas, and try a fall planting timed to finish as it cools down.
seasoned: Sow as early as the soil can be worked so the crop flowers and fills pods in cool weather, well before summer heat. Where summers come on fast, choose the earliest short-season snow peas, and add a fall sowing timed so the crop matures in cooling weather.

beginner: Seeds rotted or did not come up
seasoned: Seed rotted or came up poorly

beginner: The seed went into cold, soggy soil and rotted instead of sprouting, or came up thin and patchy. Peas like cool soil, but wet, poorly drained ground rots the seed and lets soil fungi get to it. Planting too early into a wet bed is the usual reason for gaps.
seasoned: The seed was sown into cold, saturated soil and rotted before emerging, or came up as a thin, patchy stand. Peas tolerate cool soil, but waterlogged ground starves the seed of oxygen and feeds the soilborne root rots, so a too-early sowing into a wet, poorly drained bed is the usual cause of gaps.

beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds instead of cold, wet, low spots, and wait until the soil is workable, not muddy. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, do not keep the bed soggy, and soaking the seeds overnight helps them come up faster.
seasoned: Sow into well-drained ground or raised beds rather than cold, low, wet spots, and wait for the surface to be workable rather than muddy. Plant about 1 to 1.5 inches deep, do not keep the bed soggy, and an overnight presoak helps the seed get up and out of harm's way faster.

beginner: White powdery dust on the leaves and pods
seasoned: White powdery coating late in the crop

beginner: A white to gray powdery dust spread over the leaves and pods as the weather warmed up and the nights stayed cool. This is powdery mildew, the classic late-season pea disease. It weakens the plants and spoils the pods, and it is hard to stop once it has spread.
seasoned: A white to gray powdery film spread over the leaves, stems, and pods as the crop ran into warm days and cool nights, the conditions that favor powdery mildew. It is the classic end-of-season pea disease; it weakens the vines, taints the pods, and is hard to stop once it has covered the foliage.

beginner: Plant a resistant variety, which works best (Super Sugar Snap, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint resist mildew), and plant early so the crop finishes before mildew weather arrives. Give the vines a trellis and room to breathe, water at the soil, and pull the old plants once the spring crop is done.
seasoned: Plant powdery-mildew-resistant varieties, the most effective step (Super Sugar Snap, Cascadia, and Sugar Sprint all resist it), and sow early so the crop finishes before the mildew weather. Give the vines a trellis and room for airflow, water at the soil, and pull a spent spring planting promptly.

beginner: Pods came out tough and starchy
seasoned: Pods tough, overmature, or starchy

beginner: The pods came out tough and starchy instead of plump, crisp, and sweet, usually because they were left on the vine too long, until the peas overfilled, or because heat and dry soil hit while the pods were filling. Snap peas are best picked at the plump-but-tender stage and go from sweet to starchy in just a few days.
seasoned: The snap pods came out tough and starchy rather than plump, crisp, and sweet, usually because they were left on the vine past their short pickable window, when the over-full seeds toughen the pod and the sugars turn to starch, or because heat and drought stress hit during pod fill. Snap peas are best caught at the plump-but-tender stage and go from sweet to starchy in a few days.

beginner: Pick every one to three days while the pods are plump and still crisp, before the peas overfill, starting about 5 to 8 days after the flowers open. Keep the water steady while the pods fill, and plant early so they grow in cool weather, not heat.
seasoned: Pick every one to three days while the pods are plump, rounded, and still bright and crisp, before the seeds overfill and the pod dulls, starting about 5 to 8 days after flowering. Keep moisture steady through pod fill, and sow early so the pods size up in cool rather than hot weather.

beginner: Snap peas crop for a few weeks from one planting, so you may not need many sowings. Plant a second short row a week or two after the first to stretch the supply, and again in late summer for fall where it works. In hot areas, skip summer and sow through the cool months.
seasoned: Sugar snap peas, especially the tall indeterminate types, crop over a longer window than snow peas, so one sowing often carries the spring crop; add a second sowing a week or two later only to stretch the supply, and a separate fall crop where summers allow. beginner: In cold regions, grow snap peas in spring, and again in fall where you can. Plant as soon as you can work the soil in spring, even before the last frost, because young peas handle cold.
