seasoned: Across the cold northern tier sugar snap peas are a spring crop, with a second fall crop where the season allows. Sow as soon as the ground can be worked, even weeks before the last frost, since pea seedlings are cold-hardy; the spring crop is picked in late spring to early summer and then ends as midsummer heat stops the vines from filling pods and brings on powdery mildew. The hot weeks are left out, and a late-summer sowing gives a fall crop the frost-tolerant plants carry into autumn. From the milder end of the region (zone 7) a fall sowing can be grown through the cool months for a winter-into-spring harvest. The summer gap here is a true heat exclusion for peas, backed at each cell.

beginner: Sugar snap peas are the plump, sweet peas you eat whole, pod and all. Unlike flat snow peas, which you pick while the pod is still flat, you let snap peas fill out until the peas inside are round and the pod is fat, crisp, and sweet. They are a cool-weather crop: plant the seeds straight in the garden as soon as you can work the soil in spring, and again in late summer for fall. Some kinds grow into tall vines that need a trellis, like Sugar Snap; others, like Sugar Ann, stay short and bushy and hold themselves up. Older kinds have a stringy seam you peel off before eating; newer kinds are stringless.
seasoned: Sugar snap peas are an edible-pod pea grown for plump, rounded pods eaten whole, pod and peas together, while the pod is still crisp, bright, and sweet. They are the plump-podded cousin of the flat snow pea: where a snow pea is picked young and flat before its seeds develop, a snap pea is left until the peas inside have swelled and nearly filled the pod, giving the crunchy, sugary pod that names the type. Like all peas they are a cool-season legume, sown as early as the ground can be worked in spring and again for a fall crop, and they fix much of their own nitrogen. Types range from tall climbing vines that need a trellis, such as the original Sugar Snap, to compact bush types like Sugar Ann that stand on their own; older varieties carry a string along the pod that is pulled off before eating, while newer ones are stringless.

beginner: Start your seeds indoors where it's about 60 to 75°F. They sprout quickly, in 5 to 10 days, and need bright light right away or they'll get leggy.

beginner: Plant the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep in damp seed-starting mix, and keep it evenly moist while they sprout.
seasoned: Sow about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep into a moist seed-starting mix; broccoli germinates reliably across a wide soil-temperature range as long as moisture stays even.

beginner: Move seedlings outside when they have 4 to 6 real leaves, around 5 to 7 weeks old. Planting ones that are too old or pot-bound can cause tiny premature heads.
seasoned: Transplant at 4 to 6 true leaves, about 5 to 7 weeks old; older, root-bound starts are the classic trigger for buttoning.

beginner: Toughen up your seedlings over about a week before planting them out, and pick a stretch of cool, steady weather rather than just before a hot spell.

beginner: Water steadily, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, while the plant builds its leaves. Letting it dry out or get stressed now leads to poor heads later.

beginner: Up north, grow broccoli twice a year in the cooler weather at each end of the season. Plant your spring crop a couple of weeks before your last frost date so it makes heads before summer heat, and harvest starting in early summer. Then plant a second crop in mid-July for a fall harvest. The fall crop often tastes better and lasts longer because broccoli likes cool weather, and in the milder cold zones it can give you more than the spring crop. Pick fast-maturing varieties in the coldest areas, and keep a row cover handy to protect young plants from a late spring frost or an early fall one.
seasoned: In the cold zones broccoli runs as two frost-bracketed crops. Set spring transplants out about 2 to 4 weeks before the last frost (roughly late April into May in zone 3) so heads form during the cool, lengthening days before summer heat arrives, then harvest from late June. A second crop goes out in mid-July, timed to head as nights cool in September and October; fall broccoli often eats sweeter and holds longer in the field because cool weather suits it, and in zone 6 to 7 it frequently out-yields the spring sowing. Midsummer is the gap, not a heat exclusion you plant around: nights stay short enough that the limit on both ends is frost, not the day-and-night heat that stalls heading farther south. Lean on fast, short-cycle varieties in the coldest zones, and use row cover at both shoulders to buffer late and early frosts.

beginner: After you plant the cloves in fall, they grow roots underground and may send up a small green shoot before winter. This is normal. The garlic is settling in and starting to feel the cold it needs, not making big leaves yet.

beginner: Plant the cloves at the right time for your area and water them in. In cold regions, once the ground begins to freeze, cover the bed with a few inches of straw or chopped leaves to protect the cloves over winter.

beginner: Write down when you planted, which kind of garlic, and how big the cloves were. It helps you do better next year.

beginner: In cold areas the garlic mostly rests under its mulch all winter. In mild areas it keeps growing slowly. When spring arrives, green shoots come up and the plant starts making leaves.

beginner: Write down when the green shoots came up in spring and when you first fed the plants.
seasoned: Note when shoots emerged or resumed and your first spring feeding; emergence timing tracks how your winter ran.

beginner: The garlic grows lots of upright leaves in spring. This stage matters most for bulb size, because the leaves now turn into the layers of the bulb later. The more healthy leaves it grows, the bigger the bulb can be.

seasoned: Push leaf growth: keep moisture even, finish nitrogen feeding by early May, and stay on top of weeds. Front-load feeding so the canopy is built before bulbing; nitrogen applied late delays bulbing and worsens storage.

beginner: Count the leaves and note when you fed. More leaves now usually means bigger bulbs later.
seasoned: Track leaf count and feeding dates; leaf count going into bulbing is the best in-season predictor of final bulb size.

beginner: If you grow hardneck garlic, cut off the curly scape when it appears so the plant puts its energy into the bulb, and cook with the scape. Keep watering evenly while the bulb sizes up, and do not add more fertilizer now.
seasoned: On hardnecks, snip the scape off once it curls to redirect energy into the bulb (and eat it, it is a delicacy). Hold even moisture through sizing and keep nitrogen off; do not bend or knock down the tops to force maturity.

beginner: Write down when the scapes appeared and any times the bed dried out while bulbs were sizing.
seasoned: Note the scape date (hardnecks) and any dry spells during sizing; matching these to final size tunes your timing.

beginner: The lower leaves turn brown and die back while the top leaves are still green. Garlic is ready when about a third to a half of the leaves have browned. Dig one bulb to check: if the cloves fill out the skins, it is time.
seasoned: The lower leaves brown and die back while several upper leaves stay green; the cue is when about a third to half of the leaves have turned, with roughly the lower half browning and five or so green leaves remaining (each green leaf is an intact wrapper). beginner: Stop watering about two weeks before, then loosen the bulbs out of the ground with a fork on a dry day, handling them gently. Do not wait until all the leaves are brown, or the bulbs split open and store poorly.
seasoned: Stop watering about two weeks ahead, then lift, do not pull, the bulbs gently with a fork on a dry day to avoid bruising. Do not wait for all the leaves to brown, which over-matures the bulbs and splits the wrappers and storage.

beginner: Write down when you harvested and how many green leaves were left. It helps you judge timing next year.
seasoned: Record the harvest date and how many green leaves remained; green-leaf count at harvest is the cleanest maturity gauge to repeat.

beginner: Just-dug garlic needs to dry before storing. Keep the bulbs with their tops on in a warm, dry, airy, shady spot for two to four weeks until the necks dry shut and the skins go papery.

beginner: Dry the garlic in a shady, breezy place out of the sun, leaving the tops and roots on until it is fully dry. Then trim the tops and roots, brush off the dirt (do not wash it), and store it cool and dry. Keep your biggest bulbs to replant.
seasoned: Cure with good airflow out of direct sun, keeping tops and roots on until dry. Then trim tops to about an inch and roots close, brush off loose dirt (do not wash), and store cool and dry; save the biggest bulbs as next year's seed.

beginner: Write down how long you dried the garlic and how well it kept, so you know how long to cure next time.
seasoned: Log the curing length and how the bulbs stored; curing time versus storage life is the feedback that pays off all season.

Dig the bulbs in early-to-mid summer once the lower leaves have turned brown, and let them cure in a warm, airy spot before storing.
seasoned: Garlic in the Mid-Atlantic is a single fall-planted, overwintering crop, no spring planting: Virginia Cooperative Extension's 426-331 tables carry only a fall window for this crop (Oct 15 to Nov 15 in zone 8, Oct 1 to Oct 30 in zone 7), the belt's real winter cold serving as the vernalization hardneck garlic needs. Set cloves so they root before the ground cools, mulch once true cold sets in, and let the planting go dormant. Growth resumes in spring and bulbs mature in early-to-mid summer as the lower leaves brown, the warmer Coastal Plain finishing a little ahead of the cooler Piedmont; lift, cure, and store before the wrappers split from over-maturity.

beginner: In the Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands, plant garlic in fall, October into mid-November, not in spring. The cloves grow roots, then rest through winter under a layer of straw or leaves, and finish the following summer. Dig the bulbs in early-to-mid summer once the lower leaves have turned brown, and let them cure in a warm, airy spot before storing.
seasoned: Garlic in the Mid-South is a single fall-planted, overwintering crop with no spring planting. It goes in during mid to late fall, roughly mid October into mid November in zone 8 and about two weeks earlier in the cooler zone 7 uplands; the University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension recommends fall planting for hardneck garlic, and the belt's real winter cold supplies the vernalization it needs. Set cloves so they root before the ground cools, mulch once true cold sets in, and let the planting go dormant. Growth resumes in spring and bulbs mature in early-to-mid summer as the lower leaves brown, the warmer lowland South (zone 8, harvest late May into late June) finishing a little ahead of the cooler Ozark uplands (zone 7, harvest early June into early July); lift, cure, and store before the wrappers split from over-maturity.

beginner: Plant garlic cloves in the ground from early September through mid-October, a narrower fall window than the neighboring desert regions use. The cloves root through fall and winter and the bulbs are ready to dig the following late spring or early summer. Break a head into cloves and plant each one pointy end up, a couple of inches deep.
seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley plants garlic cloves in a tight fall window, early September through about mid-October per the UNLV Master Gardener Southern Nevada chart, earlier and narrower than the Arizona low desert or the interior high desert, which run into November. Cloves establish roots through the mild desert fall and winter, size up as days lengthen in spring, and are lifted in late spring at Laughlin through early summer in the cooler zone 8 pockets.

beginner: Plant garlic cloves in the ground from about Sep 20 through Oct 25, within USU Extension's late-September-to-November fall window. The cloves root through fall and keep growing over the mild St. George winter, then size up as spring days lengthen. Lift the bulbs from early June once the tops begin to yellow. Break a head into cloves and plant each one pointy end up, a couple of inches deep.
seasoned: St. George plants garlic cloves in fall, per USU Extension's "Garlic in the Garden," which gives a late-September-to-November window; this cell uses a defined late-September-to-late-October slice so cloves establish before the coldest nights. Garlic is genuinely frost-hardy and keeps growing through the mild winter rather than truly pausing, sizes up as spring days lengthen, and is lifted from about Jun 5 through mid-July once the tops begin to yellow. The bed then rests through August, the hottest stretch of the year, before the next fall planting.

beginner: Garlic is one of the easiest crops to grow, but it works on an unusual schedule. You plant the cloves in fall, they rest through winter (under a mulch blanket where it is cold), and they finish growing the next summer, so a single planting takes most of a year. Garlic needs that winter cold to form a proper bulb, which is why you plant in fall rather than spring. Grow hardneck garlic where winters are cold and softneck garlic where they are mild.
seasoned: Garlic (Allium sativum) is a hardy allium grown from individual cloves planted in fall. It roots before winter, overwinters in the ground (mulched in cold regions), then resumes growth in spring and matures the following summer, an eight to nine month crop that spans the year. Winter cold is essential: cloves must be vernalized to divide and bulb properly, which is why fall planting beats spring. Hardneck types suit cold winters, produce edible scapes, and store a few months; softneck types suit mild climates, braid well, and store the longest.

beginner: Garlic is ready in early summer (or late spring in warm areas) when the lower leaves have turned brown but the top leaves are still green, about a third to half of them browned. Do not wait for all the leaves to die. Dig one bulb to check: if the cloves fill out the skins, it is time to harvest.
seasoned: Garlic is ready in early to mid summer (late spring in warm regions) when the lower leaves have browned and died back while several upper leaves stay green, about a third to half the foliage turned. Each green leaf is an intact wrapper, so do not wait for all the leaves to brown. Confirm by lifting a test bulb: ready bulbs have cloves that fill the skins.

beginner: Peach likes a deep soil that drains well and lets air reach the roots. Good drainage is the one rule you cannot bend with stone fruit, because peach roots will not stand being wet. A sandy loam (a loose soil that drains easily) is a great fit, and a lighter sandy soil works if you stay on top of watering and feeding. Heavy clay that holds water is the trouble spot, since it can bring on crown and root rot; on clay, plant the tree on a raised mound so the roots sit above the soggy soil. A soil of average richness with some compost worked in suits it well.
seasoned: Peach wants a deep, well-drained loam with good aeration; drainage is the non-negotiable for stone fruit, which will not tolerate wet feet. A sandy loam is well suited and a lighter sandy soil is workable with attention to water and feeding. Heavy clay that holds water is the problem texture, raising the risk of crown and root rot; on such ground, plant on a raised mound or berm to lift the roots above standing water. Moderate fertility and a modest amount of organic matter suit it well.

beginner: Peach grows best in slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and is fine up to about 7.0 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if you need to: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if the soil is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is much easier to fix before the permanent tree goes in.
seasoned: Peach does best in a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerates up to about 7.0. Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, while elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground.

beginner: Scatter the fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. On sandy soil it helps to split it, most in spring and a little after harvest. Never feed late in the year, because late feeding keeps the tree growing when it should be going dormant and makes winter damage more likely.
seasoned: Broadcast the fertilizer evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, keeping it off the trunk, and water it in. Split timing (the bulk in spring, a lighter touch after harvest) suits sandy soils; never feed late in the season, since late nitrogen delays dormancy and invites winter injury and short-life problems.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works well for backyard peaches. Do not overdo nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth and more disease instead of fruit.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits backyard peaches; mature trees draw most heavily on nitrogen (N) and potassium (K). Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which pushes soft, disease-prone growth at the expense of fruit.

beginner: A simple rule is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, spread in spring as the tree blooms, up to about 10 cups for a full-grown tree. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing. If a late frost kills the flowers and you get no fruit that year, skip any summer or fall feeding.
seasoned: A common home-garden rate is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 per year of tree age, applied in spring from bloom to petal fall, up to roughly 10 cups for a mature tree (about 1/2 to 1 pound of fertilizer per year of age, to a maximum near 10 pounds). Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins. If a late frost takes the crop, skip the postharvest feeding that year.

beginner: Peach is self-fertile, which means one tree makes fruit on its own and you do not need a second tree to pollinate it (one well-known variety, J.H. Hale, is the exception and does need another peach blooming nearby). For a tree, the things that matter are not the usual vegetable-garden pairings but what grows around the roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, because lawn competes hard with a young tree for water and food, and a mulched, weed-free area around the trunk helps the tree settle in faster. The one site rule to follow is replant disease: do not plant a peach where another peach or stone fruit was recently growing, because something left behind in that soil holds the new tree back.
seasoned: Peach is self-fertile, so a single tree fruits on its own and there is no need to pair it with a pollinizer (the standout exception is J.H. Hale, which does need another peach blooming at the same time). The interactions that matter for a tree are about the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep grass and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since turf competes hard with a young tree for water and nitrogen, and a mulched, competition-free root area establishes the tree faster. The one site rule to respect is replant disease: do not plant a peach where another peach or stone fruit recently grew, because soilborne carryover stunts the replacement.

beginner: Look at the very bottom of the trunk where it meets the soil. Peachtree borers leave a sticky, gummy ooze mixed with what looks like wet sawdust (called frass, the droppings and chewed wood the larvae push out). You may see a small mound of this gum and frass at the base. A young tree with several borers can be killed in one season, so this is one to catch early.
seasoned: Gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass at the base of the trunk, right around the soil line, often with a mounded look where the bark meets the ground. Bark in that zone may be cracked or sunken. A heavily infested young tree loses vigor as the larvae girdle the inner bark; several borers in one trunk can kill a newly planted tree in a single season.

beginner: The larvae (young, grub-like stage) of the peachtree borer, a moth whose adults look like wasps and fly during the day. The adults lay eggs on the lower trunk in summer, and the larvae burrow into the bark at and below the soil line. Trees with existing wounds are hit hardest, but a healthy tree can be attacked too.
seasoned: Larvae of the peachtree borer (Synanthedon exitiosa), a clearwing moth whose adults are day-flying and wasp-like. Eggs are laid on the lower trunk in summer; the larvae tunnel in the inner bark at and just below the soil line. Trees already stressed by winter injury, mechanical wounds, or canker are attacked first, but healthy bark can also be entered.

beginner: Once the larvae are tunneling inside, no spray reaches them. The backyard fix is to scrape soil away from the base in late summer or fall, find the holes marked by gum and frass, and kill the larvae with a thin, stiff wire pushed into each hole. Then smooth the soil back. Avoid nicking the trunk base with mowers or trimmers, since wounds invite the moths.
seasoned: There is no rescue spray once larvae are tunneling inside the trunk. The practical home control is to expose the crown in late summer or fall, find the entry holes by the gum and frass, and kill larvae by hand with a thin wire (worming). Keep the trunk base free of wounds. Pheromone mating-disruption is used commercially but is not practical for a single backyard tree.

beginner: Keep mowers and string trimmers away from the trunk; the wounds they leave attract the egg-laying moths. Keep grass and weeds cleared from the base so you can see the soil line, and check it every late summer for fresh gummy ooze so you catch borers early.
seasoned: Protect the lower trunk from mechanical injury (the wounds that draw egg-laying females), keep the tree vigorous, and clear weeds and tall grass from the base so the crown stays open and easy to inspect. Inspect the soil line each late summer for fresh gum so an infestation is caught in its first year.

beginner: Sticky gum and sawdust-like frass on the upper trunk and main branches (the scaffolds), not down at the soil line. It almost always shows up on an existing wound, pruning cut, or canker. Over time the affected branches weaken.
seasoned: Gum and frass higher up than the peachtree borer, on the upper trunk and scaffold limbs rather than at the soil line, almost always centered on existing wounds, pruning cuts, or canker margins. Repeated attacks weaken scaffolds and can girdle limbs.

beginner: The larvae of the lesser peachtree borer, a close relative of the peachtree borer. This one attacks wounded bark up in the branches instead of at the base, so it tends to follow canker (a sunken, dead patch of bark) and pruning cuts.
seasoned: Larvae of the lesser peachtree borer (Synanthedon pictipes), a clearwing moth closely related to the peachtree borer. Unlike its relative, it targets wounded bark up in the canopy, so its damage is tightly linked to Cytospora canker and pruning injuries.

beginner: No spray reaches the larvae once they are inside. Where you can reach them, dig them out with a wire as for the peachtree borer. The better fix is to stop giving them wounds to enter: prune cleanly, cut out dead cankered bark, and keep the tree vigorous.
seasoned: As with the peachtree borer, no spray reaches established larvae; worm them out by hand where accessible. The durable control is to minimize the wounds it colonizes: prune cleanly in late dormancy, remove cankered wood, and keep the tree healthy.

beginner: Make clean pruning cuts in late winter, cut away any dead or cankered bark, and do not leave torn bark or branch stubs. Fewer wounds means fewer places for this borer to get in.
seasoned: Prune at the right time (late dormant season) with clean cuts, remove canker promptly, and avoid leaving stubs or torn bark. A tree kept free of open wounds gives this borer few places to establish.

beginner: On small developing peaches, look for a curved, crescent-shaped scar, the mark the beetle leaves when it lays an egg. Damaged fruit often drops early, and some that stays on the tree ends up misshapen or has a grub inside. You see this soon after the petals fall.
seasoned: Small young fruit carries a distinctive crescent-shaped scar where the female cut a slit to lay an egg. Infested fruit often drops early; fruit that hangs on may be gnarled or have a grub tunneling inside. Damage appears shortly after petal fall.

beginner: A small beetle with a long snout called the plum curculio. The adults show up around bloom and start damaging the little fruits right after the petals drop, laying eggs inside them. The larvae then feed within the fruit.
seasoned: The plum curculio (Conotrachelus nenuphar), a small snout beetle. Adults emerge around bloom and attack fruit from petal fall onward, laying eggs in the developing fruit; the larvae feed inside.

beginner: Early in the morning the beetles are slow. Spread a sheet under the tree, tap the branches so the beetles fall, and destroy them. Pick up and throw away any dropped fruit promptly so the larvae inside do not mature. A kaolin clay spray (a fine white mineral coating) starting at petal fall helps keep them off.
seasoned: For a backyard tree, jarring the limbs over a sheet in the early morning when the beetles are sluggish, then destroying what drops, reduces the population. Promptly gather and dispose of dropped infested fruit to break the cycle. Kaolin clay applied from petal fall is an organic deterrent.

beginner: The main thing is cleanup. Pick up fallen fruit all season so the larvae inside cannot finish growing in the soil under the tree. Keeping the ground clear lowers the number of beetles the next year.
seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: remove dropped fruit through the season so larvae cannot complete development in the soil beneath the tree. A clean orchard floor and prompt fruit pickup steadily lower pressure year over year.

beginner: Early on, the tips of new shoots wilt and die as larvae tunnel into them, which looks like small flags of dead growth. Later in the season the larvae bore into the fruit, often near the stem, with a little gum at the entry hole and tunneling inside.
seasoned: Early in the season, new shoot tips wilt and die back (flagging) as larvae bore into tender growth. Later generations tunnel into fruit, often entering near the stem, leaving a gummy entry point and internal feeding near the pit.

beginner: A small moth called the Oriental fruit moth. It has several rounds of larvae through the summer. The first rounds attack shoots and the later rounds attack fruit, so the damage moves from twigs to peaches as the season goes on.
seasoned: The Oriental fruit moth (Grapholita molesta). It produces several overlapping generations a season; early broods attack shoots, later broods attack fruit, which is why damage shifts from twigs to fruit as summer progresses.

beginner: Clip off and destroy the wilted shoot tips early, before the later larvae move to the fruit. Remove any tunneled fruit you find. For one backyard tree, this cleanup is the main organic control.
seasoned: Prune out and destroy wilted shoot tips early to remove larvae before they reach the fruit-feeding generations. Remove infested fruit. Pheromone mating disruption is the commercial tool; for a single tree, shoot sanitation plus prompt fruit removal is the practical organic approach.

beginner: Watch for wilted shoot tips early and clip them off as they appear, and clean up fallen fruit. Knocking back the early larvae means fewer of them reach your peaches.
seasoned: Keep on top of early shoot flagging so each generation is knocked back before it builds, and clear dropped fruit. Lower early pressure means less fruit damage later.

beginner: Ripe peaches have sunken, puckered, dimpled patches, a look growers call catfacing. It comes from insects feeding on the fruit when it was small. The fruit is still usable; the damage is mostly on the surface and does not spread.
seasoned: Mature fruit shows sunken, dimpled, corky distortions, the puckered 'catfaced' look, where feeding occurred on young fruit. The damage is cosmetic on the surface but can run into the flesh; it does not spread or rot on its own.

beginner: A group of insects, mainly stink bugs and a small one called the tarnished plant bug, that pierce the young fruit to feed. The spots they feed on stop growing while the rest of the fruit keeps swelling, so the peach ends up dimpled.
seasoned: A group of true bugs, chiefly stink bugs and tarnished plant bug, that pierce young fruit to feed. The cells around each feeding site stop expanding, so the fruit grows in around them and ends up distorted at maturity.

beginner: These bugs come in from nearby weeds and brush, so spraying one tree does little. The better approach is to keep the area around the tree mowed and clear of weedy growth where the bugs gather.
seasoned: These bugs move in from surrounding weeds and brush, so control is mostly habitat management rather than spraying a single tree. Keep the area around the tree mowed and free of broadleaf weeds where the bugs build up.

beginner: Keep a mowed, weed-free zone around the tree. Removing the weedy plants the bugs live in means fewer of them move onto your fruit.
seasoned: Manage the surrounding vegetation: a mowed, weed-free zone around the tree removes the broadleaf hosts these bugs breed in and reduces how many move onto the fruit.

beginner: In spring, new leaves come out thick, puckered, and curled, with a red or purple tint that fades to yellow before the leaves drop. The tree usually grows a fresh set of leaves afterward, but losing the first set early weakens it and cuts the peach crop.
seasoned: In spring, newly emerging leaves are thickened, puckered, and curled, flushed red to purple before fading to yellow, then dropping. Severely infected shoots may be stunted. The tree pushes a second flush of leaves after the infected ones fall, but the early defoliation saps vigor and reduces the crop.

beginner: A fungus called Taphrina deformans. Its spores spend the winter on the bark and buds, then infect the brand-new leaves as the buds swell in cool, wet spring weather. It only infects once each spring, so the timing of control matters.
seasoned: The fungus Taphrina deformans. Spores overwinter on the bark and around the buds and infect the tiny leaves as the buds swell in cool, wet spring weather. It infects only once each spring; once leaves are out and the weather warms, new growth is no longer susceptible.

beginner: Once you see the curled leaves, it is too late to fix them for that year. The one thing that works is a single, well-timed spray of fixed copper (an organic-approved copper fungicide) while the tree is leafless and dormant, either in fall after about 90 percent of the leaves have fallen, or in late winter just before the buds swell. Spraying after the leaves are out does nothing. Keep the tree watered and fed so it bounces back from a bad year.
seasoned: There is no cure once the curled leaves appear; the damage is already done for that season. The single effective measure is a dormant fungicide, and the timing is what matters: one thorough application of fixed copper either in autumn after about 90 percent of the leaves have dropped, or in late winter just before the buds swell. Support the tree through a bad year with steady watering and balanced feeding so it recovers from the second leaf flush.

beginner: In areas where leaf curl shows up, put on the dormant copper spray on schedule every year. It is easy to prevent with the right timing but impossible to stop once the leaves curl. Cool, wet springs make it worse, so do not skip the spray in those years.
seasoned: Apply the dormant copper spray on schedule every year in regions where leaf curl is common; the disease is easy to control with correct timing but unstoppable once missed. Cool, wet springs raise the risk, so do not skip the spray in mild, damp years.

beginner: At bloom, infected flowers go limp and brown, and small gummy dead patches form on the nearby twigs. As the peaches ripen, brown spots appear and spread quickly, sometimes rotting a whole fruit in a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan fuzz on the surface. Rotted fruit shrivels into a hard, dried 'mummy' that hangs on the tree.
seasoned: At bloom, infected blossoms wilt and turn brown, and the infection runs back into the twig to form a small gummy canker. As fruit ripens, brown circular spots appear and spread fast, sometimes rotting the whole peach within a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan spore mass on the surface. Rotted fruit dries into a 'mummy' that clings to the tree.

beginner: A fungus called Monilinia fructicola. It survives the winter in dried mummy fruit and in dead twig patches, then releases spores at bloom that infect the flowers. Those flower infections later cause the fruit to rot. Warm, humid, wet weather makes it spread fast.
seasoned: The fungus Monilinia fructicola. It overwinters in mummified fruit, whether still hanging in the canopy or fallen below, and in twig cankers; spores released at bloom infect flowers, and those infections later seed the fruit rot. Warm, humid, wet conditions drive rapid spread.

beginner: The main control is cleanup: take off and destroy every dried mummy from the tree and the ground, and prune out the gummy dead twig patches, since these hold the spores. If the weather is wet during bloom, an organic-approved spray at bloom helps protect the flowers. As soon as you see a peach rotting, pick it and throw it away so it does not spread.
seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: remove and destroy every mummy from the tree and the ground, and prune out gummy twig cankers, because these are the spore sources. During a wet bloom, an organic-approved bloom-time fungicide reduces blossom blight. Once fruit is rotting, pick and dispose of it promptly so it does not seed more infections.

beginner: Cleanup all year prevents most of the damage: never leave dried mummies on the tree over winter, pick up dropped fruit, and prune so the tree is open and the peaches dry fast after rain. Pick fruit on time, handle it gently so it does not bruise, and chill it soon after picking.
seasoned: Year-round sanitation prevents most loss: never leave mummies on the tree over winter, remove dropped and thinned fruit, and keep the canopy open with good pruning so fruit dries quickly after rain. Harvest promptly and handle fruit gently, since wounds let the rot in, and cool fruit soon after picking.

beginner: Leaves get small angular water-soaked spots that turn brown and fall out, leaving little holes, called a shot-hole look. Bad cases turn leaves yellow and thin out the tree. On the fruit, small sunken spots and skin cracks form. How badly a tree is hit depends a lot on the variety.
seasoned: Small angular, water-soaked spots on leaves turn brown and drop out, leaving a shot-hole look; heavy infection yellows and thins the canopy. On fruit, small sunken spots and cracks develop on the skin. Susceptibility varies sharply by cultivar.

beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism, not a fungus) called Xanthomonas. It spreads in warm, wet weather and builds up when there are other susceptible peach or plum trees close by. The spots can look like spray damage.
seasoned: The bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It spreads in warm, wet weather and builds up where susceptible peach and related trees grow nearby. Symptoms are sometimes mistaken for spray injury.

beginner: There is no good home cure once it shows up. Copper sprays help a little as prevention but can hurt the tree if overused, so they are not a dependable fix. The best you can do is keep the tree healthy so it shrugs off the damage.
seasoned: Home options are limited once symptoms appear: copper sprays help more as prevention than cure and can injure the tree if overused, so they are not a reliable home fix. Keeping the tree vigorous helps it tolerate the disease.

beginner: The best prevention is the variety you pick. Choosing a peach known to resist or tolerate bacterial spot avoids most of the trouble, so it is a decision to make before planting. Good airflow and a healthy tree also help.
seasoned: The most effective measure is choosing a resistant or tolerant cultivar at planting; this is largely a variety decision made before the tree goes in. Good airflow and tree vigor reduce severity.

beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Plan on about once or twice a week while a young tree is getting established, easing to about once a week for a fruiting tree in summer heat, adjusting for rain and your soil. Sandy soil dries out faster and needs watering more often; heavier soil stays wet longer. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs very little and rain usually covers it.
seasoned: Water on a deep-and-infrequent rhythm rather than a little every day: about once or twice a week while a young tree establishes, easing to roughly weekly for a bearing tree in the heat of summer, always adjusted for rain and soil type. A sandy soil dries faster and needs more frequent soaks; a heavier soil holds longer. Through winter dormancy, water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.

beginner: Each time you water, give the tree a deep soak that reaches all the way down to the roots, not just a quick splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak. An older, fruiting tree wants roughly an inch of water a week through the growing season, and more when it is hot. Deep soaks help the tree grow deep roots that handle dry spells.
seasoned: Water deeply each time so the moisture reaches the full depth of the root zone, rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing tree, that is on the order of 5 gallons per soak; for a bearing tree, aim for roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week through the growing season, more in heat. Deep, thorough soaks drive the deep rooting that carries the tree through dry spells.

beginner: Water at the ground around the roots using a drip line or a soaker hose, and keep the leaves and fruit dry. Spraying water over the top wets the leaves and fruit and helps diseases like brown rot take hold, so put the water on the soil, not on the tree. Spread it across the root area out to the edge of the branches, not just right at the trunk.
seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose, and keep the canopy and fruit dry. Overhead watering that wets the leaves and fruit prolongs leaf wetness and feeds brown rot and leaf diseases, so deliver water to the soil, not the tree. Apply it across the root area out toward the drip line rather than only at the trunk.

beginner: Too much water, or soil that drains poorly, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that slowly goes downhill. That is because waterlogged roots cannot breathe and start to rot. In peach, soil that stays wet can also bring on crown and root rot, which often kills the tree and usually cannot be undone once it sets in. Soil that never dries out between waterings is your warning to back off.
seasoned: Overwatering and poor drainage show as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists even in wet soil, and a generally declining tree, since waterlogged roots suffocate and rot. In stone fruit, chronically wet soil also invites crown and root rot, which is often fatal and rarely reversible once advanced. Soggy soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign to act on.

beginner: Too little water shows as wilting and dull, curling leaves, slower growth, and leaves dropping early in a long dry spell. The clearest sign is in the fruit: a tree that runs short of water while the peaches are sizing up makes small, less sweet fruit, even though the tree itself lives through it. Try to catch the dry stress before the fruit suffers for it.
seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting and dull, curling leaves, slowed shoot growth, and early leaf drop in a prolonged dry spell. The most telling symptom is on the fruit: a tree short of water during the final swell sizes its peaches poorly, leaving them small and less sweet even though the tree itself survives. Catch the dry stress before the fruit pays for it.

beginner: While the tree is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps the tree grow the deep roots it needs.
seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the deep root system the tree relies on later.

beginner: While the peaches are sizing up, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch of water a week, more when it is hot, given as deep soaks. This is exactly when steady watering pays off in bigger, better peaches.
seasoned: During fruit sizing, do not let the tree dry out. Aim for the equivalent of about an inch of water per week, more in heat, delivered as deep soaks. This is the window where consistent moisture translates directly into larger, better fruit.

beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during long dry stretches so the roots do not dry out. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.
seasoned: Once the tree is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only during prolonged dry spells to keep roots from desiccating. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.

beginner: Give the tree a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) instead of spraying the leaves, since wet leaves and fruit lead to disease. beginner: Pick off all the flowers the first year. If a brand-new tree fruits, it spends energy it needs for roots and branches, and it cannot make that up.

beginner: The cold of winter is what sets up next spring's flowers. Pick a variety whose chill needs match your winters. A high-chill variety in a mild-winter area will barely bloom.

beginner: Peaches get pruned harder than most fruit trees, and they fruit on wood that grew last year. So pruning every year is a must, not a maybe, if you want a crop.

beginner: Make clean cuts and remove any dead, sunken cankered bark. Ragged wounds and cankers are just what attract the borers.

beginner: Sticky gum mixed with what looks like wet sawdust (frass) has shown up where the trunk meets the soil, sometimes in a little mound. This is the sign of peachtree borer, whose larvae tunnel in the bark at the base. Peaches ooze gum for many reasons, so it is easy to shrug off as ordinary sap, but the sawdusty frass means larvae are inside, and they can kill a young tree. The fix is to scrape away the soil, find the holes, and kill the larvae with a wire, then keep the trunk base free of the wounds that draw the moths.
seasoned: Gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass has appeared at the soil line, sometimes with a mounded look. This is the signature of peachtree borer, whose larvae tunnel in the inner bark at the crown. Peaches gum in response to many stresses, so the ooze alone is sometimes dismissed as harmless sap; the frass is the tell that larvae are inside, and a young tree can be girdled and killed. The corrective action is to expose the crown, locate the entry holes, and kill the larvae by hand, then protect the trunk base from the wounds that attract egg-laying.

beginner: A peach is a fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and gives you fruit you can let ripen right on the branch, which is where peaches taste their best. One tree fruits on its own, so you do not need a second one to get peaches. A peach also needs enough winter chill to break dormancy evenly, so variety choice is matched to your winters. Given that care, a backyard tree rewards you with fruit grocery shelves cannot match.

seasoned: Peach trees survive winters across zones 4 to 9, but surviving is not the same as fruiting. The tree itself is hardy to roughly -20°F; below that the wood is damaged, and around -25°F the tree can be killed. The fruit buds are the weak link: they begin to die between -13°F and -18°F, so the reliable-fruit band is narrower than the survival band. Peaches fruit most dependably in zones 6 to 8. Zone 5 is a marginal lower edge where only the hardiest late-blooming cultivars (Reliance, Contender) crop in good years, and then only on sites that escape the coldest air. The warm edge near zone 9 is limited not by cold but by winter chill: where winters no longer bank enough chill hours, even a thriving tree blooms poorly and sets little fruit.

The main exception is the variety J.H. Hale, which is not self-fertile and needs another peach blooming nearby at the same time. Bees do the pollinating, so anything that helps bees be active during bloom helps your tree set fruit, even a single self-fertile one.
seasoned: Most peaches are self-fertile, so a single tree sets a full crop on its own without a pollinizer partner; this is the inverse of many apples, which require cross-pollination. The notable exception among recommended varieties is J.H. Hale, which is not self-fertile and needs a second peach blooming at the same time nearby. Peaches are insect-pollinated, mainly by bees, so supporting pollinator activity at bloom helps fruit set even on a lone self-fertile tree.

beginner: The first year is about helping the tree settle in, not getting fruit. Plant a bare-root tree in late winter while it is still dormant, cut it back at planting to start the open vase shape, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk, and water it steadily through the first couple of seasons. Pull off any fruit that forms. Wait to fertilize until the tree starts growing, and never feed late in the year.
seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment over fruit. Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter, head it back at planting to begin the open-center scaffold, keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk, and water consistently through the first two seasons. Remove any fruit that sets. Hold fertilizer until growth begins, and never feed late in the season.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Self-fertile means one tree fruits on its own, no second tree required. The one common exception is J.H. Hale, which needs another peach blooming nearby at the same time. Bees do the work, so good bee activity during bloom helps the tree set a full crop.
seasoned: Self-fertile: a single tree fruits without a pollinizer. Exception: J.H. Hale requires a compatible second peach blooming concurrently. Bees are the primary pollinators; ensure bloom-time pollinator activity for reliable set.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: A full-size, traditional rootstock that does well in heavier soils and resists a problem called peach tree short life, but it is not the best where soil-dwelling nematode pests are present. A good standard choice if your soil does not have nematode trouble.
seasoned: Standard-size seedling rootstock and the long-time benchmark. Tolerant of peach tree short life and suited to heavier, well-drained soils, but susceptible to root-knot nematode and weaker on replant sites. A solid default where nematode pressure is low.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: A full-size rootstock much like Lovell, good for heavier soils as long as nematodes are not a problem in your ground. It is not the one to pick where those soil pests are present.
seasoned: Standard seedling rootstock similar in stature to Lovell, well-suited to heavier soils where ring nematodes are not a concern. Like Lovell, it lacks strong nematode resistance, so it is best matched to sites without that pressure.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: A full-size rootstock developed for the Southeast that resists both a deadly problem called peach tree short life and soil nematode pests, so trees on it survive much better on sandy southern sites. This is the one to ask for where those soil problems exist.
seasoned: Standard-size rootstock released by USDA-ARS and Clemson, bred for the Southeast. Its standout trait is a combination of peach tree short life resistance and root-knot nematode resistance, giving excellent survival on sandy southeastern sites where older rootstocks fail. The preferred choice where ring nematodes and short-life are present.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: A full-size rootstock that strongly resists soil nematode pests and grows well in sandy, well-drained soil. Its downside is that it is prone to peach tree short life, so it fits best where nematodes are the worry rather than that disease.
seasoned: Standard-size rootstock valued for strong root-knot nematode resistance and vigor on sandy, well-drained soils. Its weakness is susceptibility to peach tree short life, so it is best where nematodes are the main concern and short-life pressure is low; it also dislikes high-pH or saline soils.
