beginner: Acorn squash grows well in a container if you choose a bush type like Table King or Honey Bear, since full-size vining kinds are too big for a pot. Use a large container, at least 10 gallons and 12 inches deep, put it in full sun, keep it well watered (pots dry out fast), and feed it regularly. Water the soil, not the leaves, to help avoid mildew.
seasoned: Acorn squash is one of the more container-friendly winter squashes, because true bush and semi-bush varieties are widely available. Choose a compact type (Table King, Honey Bear, or Table Ace) and give it a big pot: at least 10 gallons and 12 inches deep, larger is better. Give it full sun, let any vines trail out over the rim or up a sturdy support, water at the base daily in heat, and feed regularly, since a small soil volume dries and depletes fast. The container figures here follow general container-vegetable guidance; acorn-squash-specific container numbers are modeled.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which acorn squash likes. Keep the reservoir filled, especially in hot weather, and use a big pot.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits a potted acorn squash well, smoothing the moisture swings this thirsty, mildew-prone plant dislikes. Keep the reservoir topped up in heat, still water from below to keep foliage dry, and use a large enough planter that the roots are not constantly waterlogged.

beginner: Give a container acorn squash a large, deep, heavy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 10 gallons or more, and let any vines trail out of it or climb a small trellis. A wide, sturdy pot is better than a tall, narrow one. Only grow small or bush varieties in pots, such as Table King or Honey Bear, not the big vining kinds.
seasoned: A container acorn squash needs a wide, deep, heavy pot, at least 12 inches deep and 10 gallons or more, with room for any vines to trail out over the edge or up a trellis. Wide and sturdy beats tall and narrow, since a plant in a small pot dries out and tips. Choose bush or semi-bush types such as Table King or Honey Bear for containers, never a full-size vining acorn squash.

beginner: Do not plant acorn squash where you grew cucumbers, melons, or other squash in the last few years. They get the same pests and diseases, which build up in the soil.

beginner: Acorn squash does not keep as long as other winter squash, only about 1 to 2 months, so plan to eat it within a month or two rather than storing it all winter. You can eat it straight from the vine. Do not cure it the way you would a butternut: for acorn squash, curing actually makes it worse and does not help it keep. Just store it somewhere cool but not cold, about 50 to 55°F, with some air movement, and check it often, since it softens sooner than long-keeping squash.
seasoned: Acorn squash is the shortest keeper of the common winter squashes, storing only about 1 to 2 months, well short of a spaghetti squash and far short of a butternut's 4 to 6. Because it is a Cucurbita pepo, it is fully edible right off the vine and needs no curing. In fact, unlike other winter squash, acorn squash should not be cured at all: the high heat and humidity of a cure reduce its quality, shorten its already brief storage, and can leave the flesh dry and stringy. Instead, once harvested, store it directly, cool but not cold, ideally 50 to 55°F with 50 to 70 percent humidity and good airflow. Store only blemish-free fruit with the stem intact, and check often, since acorn squash softens faster than the long-keeping squashes; eat it within a month or two rather than saving it for late winter.

Acorn squash comes in both true bush and vining forms, so it suits small gardens as readily as large ones, with vining types running roughly 4 to 8 feet and compact bush types like Table King and Honey Bear staying tidy. It is monoecious, carrying separate male and female flowers on one plant, and fruit set is strongly pollinator-dependent. As a pepo, it is susceptible to the squash vine borer, so managing that pest is part of growing it. The season's shape is set by three things: a warm runway of 80 to 100 frost-free days to mature the crop, moderate pest and disease pressure (squash bug, squash vine borer, cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it spreads, plus powdery and downy mildew), and the single fall harvest, timed at a hard rind with an orange ground spot, before frost.

seasoned: Acorn squash is the most forgiving winter squash for the maritime Pacific Northwest's cool, marine-tempered summer: at 80 to 100 days to maturity it is short enough to size up and cure before the wet fall closes in. Vines size up through June and July, and the crop ripens from mid to late summer into October. Favor a fast, often bush-habit variety such as Table Ace, especially in the cooler, foggier coastal pockets, and cure fruit a week or two in a warm, dry spot before storage, since the region's autumn rain can undercut curing on the vine (OSU / WSU).

beginner: Plant spaghetti squash in rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in. It is a large, long-season plant, so give it a generous, fertile bed. Many gardeners plant on low hills or mounds, which warm up faster and drain better. If your soil is heavy or stays wet, build up mounds or use raised beds so the roots and developing fruit do not sit in water.
seasoned: Spaghetti squash wants deep, fertile, well-drained loam rich in organic matter, with steady moisture but no waterlogging. It is a big, long-season vine with hungry roots, so work several inches of compost or rotted manure into the bed before planting. Many growers set plants in low hills or mounds, which warm faster in spring, improve drainage, and give the sprawling vines a clear starting point. Sandy loams warm early and suit the earliest sowings, while heavy clay holds water and invites crown and fruit rot, so amend it generously or build raised mounds.

beginner: Spaghetti squash likes soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and most garden soil is already close. An inexpensive soil test tells you where you stand and whether you need to adjust it before planting.
seasoned: Spaghetti squash does best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.8, with a sweet spot near 6.0 to 6.5. It still grows across a wider band, roughly 5.8 to 7.5, but uptake of some nutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline. Test before planting and lime or add sulfur only on the test's advice rather than by guess.

beginner: Spaghetti squash grows for a long time and likes steady feeding. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a little extra nitrogen about three to four weeks later as the vines start to run, and again when flowers appear. Once the squash begin to form, go easy on the nitrogen, because too much makes leafy vines instead of fruit.
seasoned: Spaghetti squash is a moderate feeder over a long season. Work a complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting, then side-dress with nitrogen about three to four weeks after planting as the vines begin to run, and again as flowering starts. Ease off heavy nitrogen once fruit has set, since late, lush vine growth comes at the expense of fruit and draws pests. Pair feeding with even moisture, because the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.

beginner: Your spaghetti squash vines are spreading. Give them a feeding of nitrogen now.
seasoned: Your spaghetti squash vines are running, time to side-dress with nitrogen. Keep feeding moderate once fruit sets so the plant builds squash, not just leaves.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a little nitrogen as the vines spread. Do not overdo the nitrogen once fruit forms.
seasoned: A complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress while vines run, easing off once fruit sets. Avoid pushing high nitrogen late, which gives vine at the expense of fruit.

beginner: Mix a balanced fertilizer or a few inches of compost into the soil before planting. Then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer about three to four weeks later, scratched into the soil a few inches away from the plants, and once more when flowers appear.
seasoned: A common rate is a complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked into the bed before planting (roughly 1.5 pounds per 100 square feet, or a balanced scoop per hill), then a nitrogen side-dress about three to four weeks after planting placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in, repeated lightly at flowering.

beginner: The most useful spaghetti squash companions are flowers that bring in bees, since spaghetti squash needs lots of bee visits to set fruit, and the traditional Three Sisters partners, corn and beans. Nasturtiums can lure pests away. The one rule that really matters is to keep spaghetti squash away from other squash, cucumbers, and melons, which all share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most spaghetti squash companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on serve two practical ends: pollination and pest pressure. Because cucurbit fruit set is pollinator-limited, with each female flower needing many bee visits, flowering insectary plants like borage near the patch are a genuine help. The Three Sisters partners, corn and beans, give the sprawling vines structure and a nitrogen boost while sharing none of spaghetti squash's pests, and a trap planting of nasturtium can divert squash bugs and beetles. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep spaghetti squash away from other cucurbits, which share the full squash pest and disease complex, including the squash vine borer this pepo squash is prone to.

beginner: Corn and spaghetti squash are the traditional Three Sisters pairing. The corn stands tall while the squash vines spread along the ground, and the big leaves shade out weeds. It is a time-tested combination more than a proven boost.
seasoned: The classic Three Sisters partner: tall corn gives sprawling spaghetti squash vines structure and light shade in high heat, while the broad squash leaves shade the soil and suppress weeds beneath the corn. A long-standing intercropping tradition with a sound space-and-shade rationale, not a measured yield effect for this exact pair.

beginner: Beans are the third Three Sisters plant. They pull nitrogen from the air into the soil, which the hungry squash appreciates, and they do not share spaghetti squash's pests. A good, traditional neighbor.
seasoned: The third of the Three Sisters: pole or bush beans fix nitrogen that benefits the long-feeding spaghetti squash, and they share none of the cucurbit pests. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near squash to lure squash bugs and beetles away, and their flowers bring in bees, which spaghetti squash needs to set fruit. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
seasoned: Often planted near cucurbits as a trap and deterrent for squash bugs and cucumber beetles, and its flowers also draw the bees spaghetti squash depends on for fruit set. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-spaghetti squash effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

beginner: Borage flowers are loved by bees, and spaghetti squash needs lots of bee visits to set fruit, so a few borage plants nearby can help with pollination. Mainly grown to bring in bees.
seasoned: A strong bee magnet whose flowers recruit the pollinators that spaghetti squash fruit set depends on, since each female flower needs many bee visits to size a fruit. Pollinator-habitat value is well grounded; the specific borage-spaghetti squash pairing is traditional rather than trial-tested.

beginner: Keep spaghetti squash away from other squash, cucumbers, and melons. They share most of the same pests and diseases, including the squash vine borer, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
seasoned: Cucumber, melon, summer squash, and other winter squash share spaghetti squash's pest and disease complex, including squash bug, the squash vine borer that readily attacks this pepo squash, cucumber beetle with the bacterial wilt it spreads, and powdery and downy mildew. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread cucurbits out and rotate them.

beginner: Some gardeners keep potatoes and squash apart, since both are big, hungry plants and potatoes can bring their own diseases. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
seasoned: A traditional caution that potatoes and cucurbits compete heavily and that potatoes can harbor disease and attract pests near squash. There is no strong T1 mechanism for the specific pairing, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

beginner: Leaves get yellow spots, then brown and wilt, and you find clusters of shield-shaped gray-brown bugs and their bronze eggs on the undersides of leaves near the base of the plant.
seasoned: Leaves develop yellow specks that brown and wilt, and heavily fed vines wilt rapidly and turn brittle, a damage pattern sometimes called anasa wilt. Flat bronze egg clusters appear on leaf undersides along the veins, and gray-brown adults and pale nymphs cluster near the crown and under debris.

beginner: Squash bugs pierce the leaves and stems and suck out the juices, which makes the vines wilt. They breed through the summer and hide in plant debris over winter.
seasoned: The squash bug, a true bug that feeds with piercing-sucking mouthparts on cucurbit foliage and stems, injecting saliva that wilts and browns the vines. Populations build through the season and are hardest to control once nymphs are large; the bugs overwinter as adults in garden debris.

beginner: Pick the bugs off by hand and scrape off the egg clusters under the leaves. A board laid on the ground overnight draws them underneath, then lift it in the morning and destroy them. Treat the young bugs with insecticidal soap.
seasoned: Hand-pick adults, crush the egg masses on leaf undersides, and trap bugs by laying a board near the plants overnight, then lifting it in the morning and destroying the cluster underneath. Target young nymphs with insecticidal soap, since large nymphs and adults are tough to kill.

beginner: Cover young plants until they flower, check under the leaves for eggs early in the season, and clean up old vines after harvest so the bugs have nowhere to overwinter.
seasoned: Use row cover on young plants until flowering, clean up vines and debris at season's end to cut overwintering sites, and rotate cucurbits. Scout leaf undersides for the bronze egg clusters from early in the season and act before nymphs mature.

beginner: Small yellow beetles with stripes or spots chew on the leaves and flowers, especially of young plants. Worse, they can spread a disease called bacterial wilt that makes the vines collapse later.
seasoned: Small yellow beetles, striped or spotted, chew young leaves, stems, and flowers, and can scar developing fruit. The bigger threat is indirect: striped and spotted cucumber beetles transmit bacterial wilt, so beetle feeding on seedlings can be followed weeks later by sudden vine wilt.

beginner: Cucumber beetles feed on spaghetti squash plants and carry the germ that causes bacterial wilt, infecting the plant as they chew. Young seedlings are most at risk.
seasoned: Striped and spotted cucumber beetles feed on cucurbits and carry the bacterium that causes bacterial wilt in their gut, infecting plants as they feed. Seedlings are most vulnerable; once plants have several leaves they tolerate some feeding, and bacterial wilt is generally less severe in winter squash like spaghetti squash than in cucumber and melon.

beginner: Cover young plants with row cover (remove it when flowers open), pick the beetles off, and use yellow sticky traps. Keeping the beetles down is the best way to avoid the wilt disease they spread.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover removed at flowering, hand-pick beetles, and use yellow sticky traps to monitor and reduce numbers. Where bacterial wilt is a known problem, controlling the beetles is the most effective control of the disease, since there is no cure once a plant is infected.

beginner: Cover seedlings until they flower, keep them growing strong, clear away weeds and old plants, and do not plant where squash-family crops grew last year.
seasoned: Exclude beetles from seedlings with row cover, keep young plants vigorous so they grow past the vulnerable stage, clear weeds and debris, and rotate away from where cucurbits grew. Aim control at the early-season colonizers that vector wilt.

beginner: A healthy plant wilts all at once in summer, with what looks like wet sawdust at a hole near the base of the stem and a fat white grub inside. Spaghetti squash is one of the squashes borers love, so watch for this.
seasoned: A vigorous vine wilts suddenly in mid to late summer, often one runner at a time, with sawdust-like frass oozing from a small hole low on the stem and a fat white caterpillar tunneling inside. As a Cucurbita pepo, spaghetti squash is a preferred, susceptible host, so a healthy plant can collapse within days once a borer is inside.

beginner: A moth lays eggs at the base of the stem in early summer, and the grubs tunnel inside and kill the vine. The moth likes thin-stemmed squash such as spaghetti squash and zucchini, so this squash is a common target.
seasoned: The larva of the squash vine borer moth, which lays eggs at the stem base in early summer; the hatching larvae bore into the stem and cut off the plant's water. The moth strongly prefers thin-stemmed Cucurbita pepo squash, which includes spaghetti squash along with zucchini, acorn, and summer squash, so this is a pest to plan for rather than hope to avoid.

beginner: Check the base of the stems often in summer. If you find a borer, slit the stem with a knife, dig out the grub, and cover the spot with damp soil so the vine can re-root. Pull and destroy badly damaged vines so the pest does not come back next year.
seasoned: Catch it early: scout the stem base for frass from early summer. If a borer has entered, slit the stem lengthwise with a knife, remove the larva, and mound moist soil over that node to encourage re-rooting. Burying vine joints as they run so a damaged plant can survive on secondary roots, and removing and destroying infested vines at season's end, both reduce next year's brood.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they flower, then take it off so bees can reach the blooms. Check the base of the stems for the sawdust-like frass starting in early summer, and clean up old vines after harvest so borers cannot overwinter.
seasoned: Row cover from planting until flowering excludes the egg-laying moths and is the most reliable defense; remove it at bloom so bees can pollinate. Time a planting to dodge the main moth flight where its timing is known, wrap or mound soil over the lower stem, and choose semi-bush types, which some growers find recover better. Scout the stem base for frass from early summer and act at the first sign.

beginner: Tiny soft insects gather on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, making leaves curl and turn yellow, often with a sticky film. They can also spread viruses.
seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often melon aphids, cluster on leaf undersides and growing tips, causing leaves to curl, pucker, and yellow, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, aphids transmit mosaic viruses that mottle and distort the foliage.

beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck the plant's juices and multiply fast, especially on soft, over-fed growth. The sticky honeydew they leave behind grows black mold.
seasoned: Melon and other aphids suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up quickly on stressed or over-fertilized plants. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold, and several aphid species spread cucurbit mosaic viruses.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants.

beginner: A white, powdery coating spreads over the leaves until they turn yellow and brown and die. The plant fades early, and the squash may not size up or sweeten well.
seasoned: White, powdery patches appear first on the upper and lower leaf surfaces and stems, spreading until leaves yellow, brown, and die back ahead of schedule. Early defoliation cuts the season short, reduces fruit size and the sugars that make spaghetti squash sweet, and exposes fruit to sunscald.

beginner: A fungus that spreads on warm, humid days, especially where plants are crowded and air does not move well. It does not need wet leaves to take hold.
seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi that thrive in warm conditions with high humidity but do not need leaf wetness, spreading by wind-blown spores. Crowded plantings, poor airflow, and shade worsen it, and it is one of the most common late-season winter-squash diseases.

beginner: Treat early, at the first white spots, with a labeled fungicide like sulfur or horticultural oil, and remove badly affected leaves. Water the soil, not the leaves. Once it covers the plant it is hard to stop.
seasoned: Treat at the first spots, before it spreads, with a labeled fungicide such as sulfur or a horticultural oil or biofungicide, covering both leaf surfaces, and remove the worst leaves. Avoid overhead watering. Once it is widespread, control is mostly damage limitation.

beginner: Pick mildew-tolerant varieties if you can, give plants plenty of room so air moves between them, plant in full sun, and water at the base. Start checking in midsummer and act at the first white spots.
seasoned: Choose mildew-tolerant varieties where available (some spaghetti squash hybrids such as Stripetti hold up better), space plants generously for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering. Scout from midsummer and treat at the first sign, since prevention and early action beat rescue.

beginner: Yellow patches show on top of the leaves with fuzzy gray growth underneath, mostly in damp, humid weather. The spots brown and spread until the leaves die.
seasoned: Angular yellow blotches, bounded by the leaf veins, appear on the upper leaf surface, with a grayish or purplish fuzzy growth on the underside in humid weather. Spots brown and coalesce, and severe infection rapidly defoliates the vines.

beginner: A mold-like disease that spreads in wet, humid weather and needs wet leaves to infect. It can move through a planting quickly.
seasoned: A fungus-like water mold that spreads on wind-borne spores and needs leaf wetness and humidity to infect, so it flares in wet, humid spells and dewy conditions. It moves fast once established and is favored by crowding and prolonged leaf wetness.

beginner: Open up the planting so leaves dry faster, remove the worst leaves, and use a labeled fungicide when wet weather sets in. Do not water over the leaves.
seasoned: Improve airflow, let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a labeled fungicide, covering leaf undersides, when conditions favor the disease. Avoid overhead irrigation, which keeps leaves wet and feeds the infection.

beginner: Give plants room so air moves between them, water at the base, and watch closely in humid weather. Choose resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space for airflow, water at the soil line rather than overhead, choose resistant varieties where available, and avoid working among wet vines. Scout closely in humid weather, when the disease can appear and spread quickly.

beginner: Vines wilt and die even though the soil is wet. If you cut a wilted stem and pull the two ends apart slowly, infected sap stretches into sticky white strings.
seasoned: Individual leaves, then whole vines, wilt and collapse even though the soil is moist, often spreading until the plant dies. A field test helps confirm it: cut a wilted stem and slowly draw the cut ends apart, and infected sap pulls into thin, sticky white strands.

beginner: A germ spread by cucumber beetles as they feed. It blocks the plant's water pipes, so the vine wilts even when watered. Spaghetti squash is somewhat less prone than cucumbers or melons.
seasoned: A bacterium spread by striped and spotted cucumber beetles, which carry it in their gut and infect plants as they feed. It clogs the water-conducting tissue, so the plant wilts despite adequate water. Winter squash like spaghetti squash are generally less susceptible than cucumber and melon, but losses still occur.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real fix is keeping cucumber beetles down, since they spread it.
seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy wilting plants to limit spread. Control is really beetle control, so management aims at keeping cucumber beetle numbers down, especially early in the season.

beginner: Keep cucumber beetles under control, since they spread the disease. Cover young plants until they flower, and pull any plant that wilts and tests positive.
seasoned: Manage cucumber beetles from seedling stage with row cover removed at flowering, keep young plants vigorous, and remove infected plants promptly. Controlling the beetle vector is the most effective control of the disease.

beginner: Give spaghetti squash about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day.
seasoned: Aim for at least 1 inch of water per week, leaning to 1.5 inches in heat or sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. The long-season, big-leaved vine transpires heavily through summer.

beginner: About 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week is a good target, more while the plant is flowering and the squash are growing.

beginner: Unlike summer squash, you pick spaghetti squash once, when it is fully ripe. Look for a deep, even yellow color with no green, a hard rind you cannot dent with a thumbnail, and a dry, woody stem. The skin also goes from shiny to dull when ready, and the pale spot where it sits on the ground turns yellow. A ripe squash is what makes those nice spaghetti-like strands; picked too early it comes out mushy instead. Cut the squash off the vine with a knife, leaving a short piece of stem attached. Bring them in before a hard frost. You can eat it right away, or let it cure in a warm, dry place for about 10 days so the skin toughens for storage.
seasoned: Harvest spaghetti squash once at full maturity, not young: wait for a deep, even golden-yellow rind with no green or cream tint, a hard rind a thumbnail cannot dent, and a dried, corky stem. The skin turns from glossy to dull at ripeness, and the ground spot where the fruit rests turns from white to a deep yellow. A mature spaghetti squash is what strands well when cooked; picked immature it stays pale and cooks up mushy rather than into distinct strands. Cut the fruit from the vine with shears or a knife, leaving a 1 to 2 inch handle of stem, and avoid carrying it by the stem. Get the crop in before a hard frost, which damages the rind and shortens storage. A short cure of about 10 days in a warm, dry spot hardens the skin, though as a Cucurbita pepo it is also fine to eat straight from the vine.

beginner: If you started seedlings indoors, set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they get used to sun and wind. Be gentle with the roots when you plant, since squash do not like having their roots disturbed.
seasoned: Harden off indoor-started spaghetti squash over 7 to 10 days, easing the plants into direct sun and wind before transplanting. Handle the rootball gently, because cucurbits resent root disturbance and a checked seedling sulks for weeks; use larger cells and set plants out young, before the roots circle the pot.

beginner: The easiest way to grow spaghetti squash is to sow seeds right where they will grow, once the soil is warm (about 70°F). Plant a few seeds 1 inch deep in each hill and keep the strongest. Start seeds indoors only if your season is short, about three weeks before planting out, and move them outside while they are still small. In cold areas, use transplants and a fast-maturing variety like Small Wonder so the fruit ripens before frost.
seasoned: Because cucurbits resent root disturbance, direct sowing once the soil is reliably warm (at least 65°F, ideally 70°F, at 2 inches) is the simplest, most reliable method, and direct-sown plants quickly catch up. Sow several seeds about 1 inch deep per hill and thin to the strongest. Start seeds indoors only to gain two to three weeks in a short season, sowing in large cells and setting plants out before they outgrow the pot. In the coldest zones, transplants and an early-maturing variety such as Small Wonder are what make a fall crop possible.

beginner: Plant three or four seeds in each hill, then keep the one or two strongest seedlings once they grow their first real leaves. Cut the extra ones off at the ground instead of pulling them, so you do not hurt the roots of the ones you keep.
seasoned: Sow three to four seeds per hill and thin to the one or two strongest once they have a true leaf or two. Snip the extras off at soil line rather than pulling, so you do not disturb the roots of the keepers. In rows, thin to one plant every 24 to 36 inches.

beginner: Do not plant spaghetti squash where you grew cucumbers, melons, or other squash in the last few years. They get the same pests and diseases, which build up in the soil.
seasoned: Avoid planting spaghetti squash where another cucurbit grew in the last few years, including cucumber, melon, summer squash, and other winter squash. They share squash bug, cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, the mildews, and soilborne rots, all of which build up in the soil and on debris.

beginner: Try not to grow spaghetti squash or its relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years or so. Moving them around the garden each year helps avoid a buildup of pests and disease. Clean up old vines at the end of the season too.
seasoned: Rotate cucurbits on a 3 year cycle, returning spaghetti squash to a given bed no sooner than the third or fourth year, to break the buildup of squash bug, beetle-vectored wilt, and soilborne disease. Clear and remove spent vines at season's end rather than tilling them in, which removes overwintering pest and disease sites and makes rotation more effective.

beginner: A spaghetti squash keeps well at room temperature, often for a couple of months in a cool spot out of the sun, much longer than summer squash but not as long as a butternut. Keep it off cold, damp floors so the bottom does not rot.
seasoned: A sound spaghetti squash is a good keeper at room temperature, the opposite of tender summer squash, though a moderate one: figure a couple of months in a cool room out of direct sun, not the half-year a butternut manages. Warm indoor heat shortens that. It keeps best sitting on a shelf with airflow rather than on a cold or damp floor.

beginner: Do not put a whole spaghetti squash in the fridge, it is too cold and makes it break down faster. Once it is cut, wrap the pieces and keep them in the fridge for a few days, or freeze them.
seasoned: Whole spaghetti squash is not refrigerated; cold storage below about 50°F causes chilling injury and faster breakdown. Cut squash and cooked or pureed flesh, however, should be refrigerated and used within a few days, or frozen.

beginner: Spaghetti squash freezes well once cooked. Roast or steam it, scrape the flesh into strands with a fork, cool it, and freeze it in portions. It keeps about a year; drain off any extra water when you reheat it.
seasoned: Spaghetti squash freezes well as cooked strands: roast or steam the halves, fork the flesh into strands, cool, and freeze in measured portions, draining off excess water when you reheat. Frozen cooked spaghetti squash keeps about a year.

beginner: Spaghetti squash keeps for a couple of months, which is why you pick it once when fully ripe. You can eat it straight from the vine, or toughen the skin for storage with a short cure of about 10 days in a warm spot (around 80 to 85°F). Then keep it somewhere cool but not cold, about 50 to 60°F, with some air movement, where good squash last about 1 to 3 months. Store only perfect squash with the stem still on, and check now and then for any starting to go soft.
seasoned: Spaghetti squash is a moderate keeper, which is why it is harvested once at full maturity: as a Cucurbita pepo it stores about 1 to 3 months, longer than acorn but well short of a butternut's 4 to 6. Being a pepo, it is edible right off the vine and does not strictly need curing; a short cure of about 10 days at 80 to 85°F with good airflow hardens the rind and heals small wounds for longer storage, though holding it too warm too long can shorten its keeping. Then store cool but not cold, ideally 50 to 60°F with 50 to 70 percent humidity and good airflow. Store only blemish-free fruit with the stem intact, and check periodically, removing any that begin to soften.

beginner: Pick a spaghetti squash variety by your season and space. For a full-size, reliable squash, grow Vegetable Spaghetti. If your garden or season is small or short, grow the compact Tivoli or Small Wonder. Orangetti has sweeter, orange flesh on a smaller plant, and Stripetti stores the longest and stands up to mildew better if those are problems where you live.
seasoned: Choose by season length and space. Where there is room, the open-pollinated Vegetable Spaghetti is the dependable full-size standard. For small beds or containers, the bush Tivoli and the compact semi-bush Small Wonder stay tidy, and Small Wonder ripens earliest for short seasons. Orangetti offers sweeter, orange flesh on a semi-bush plant, and where powdery mildew or a long storage life matters, the striped Stripetti keeps best and holds up better to mildew.

beginner: A spaghetti squash plant usually gives you several squash, often 4 to 5, each 2 to 4 pounds. Bush types like Tivoli make fewer but take much less room. Plan on one or two plants going a long way, since each one spreads widely.
seasoned: A healthy spaghetti squash vine typically yields 4 to 5 oblong fruit of 2 to 4 pounds each; compact and bush types set fewer, smaller fruit on far less space. Vining types need plenty of room per plant, and even moisture and feeding through sizing build full, well-formed squash that strand cleanly.

beginner: Unlike summer squash, spaghetti squash does not keep producing all season. The plant sets its fruit over the summer and they all ripen together in fall, when you harvest once. Removing the latest tiny fruit helps the rest grow bigger before frost.
seasoned: Spaghetti squash does not produce continuously; the plant sets fruit through summer and then the crop matures together in fall for a single harvest. Once several fruit have set, removing the latest small fruit and pinching vine tips channels energy into sizing and ripening the keepers before frost.

beginner: The big first-year surprise is how far spaghetti squash vines spread, often 6 to 8 feet. Give them more room than you think, and grow flowers nearby to bring in bees, since the plant needs lots of bee visits to set fruit.

beginner: You plant spaghetti squash once for the season. It grows all summer and ripens together in the fall for a single harvest, so there is no need to replant every few weeks. In most places a later planting would be caught by frost before the squash could ripen. Only in very warm, nearly frost-free areas can you fit a second planting, and that is really a separate season.
seasoned: Spaghetti squash is not a succession crop. It is a single, long-season planting that sets fruit through summer and matures together for one fall harvest, so you sow once per season rather than at intervals. In most zones a second sowing would be killed by frost before its 90 to 100 day crop could ripen. Only in the warmest, frost-free or near-frost-free zones, or the low desert where a summer sowing is the fall crop, is a second seasonal window viable, and that is a separate season, not a succession.

beginner: Each spaghetti squash plant has both male and female flowers, so you only need one plant to get fruit. Bees move the pollen between the flowers, and the plant needs a lot of bee visits to set each fruit, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. The first flowers are usually male and fall off, which is normal. If your little squash stay small and rot at the tip, the flowers were not pollinated well, so hand-pollinate in the morning and grow some flowers nearby for the bees.
seasoned: Spaghetti squash is monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a single plant sets fruit with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and pollen must move from the male to the female blooms. Spaghetti squash is strongly pollinator-dependent: each female flower needs several bee visits to set a full fruit, and poor pollination shows up as young fruit that yellow and rot at the blossom end, or as small, misshapen squash. Early-season male flowers often open and drop for a week or more before the first females appear, which is normal. Plant flowers nearby, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate with a male flower or small brush in the morning if set stalls.

beginner: Spaghetti squash is a warm-season squash grown for its unusual flesh: once cooked, it pulls apart into long strands like spaghetti. You harvest it once in the fall, when the oblong fruit turns a deep, even yellow and the skin is too hard to dent with a thumbnail, unlike summer squash that you pick young all season. It grows on vines that spread about 6 to 8 feet, so it needs a good amount of room, though compact bush types like Tivoli and Small Wonder fit smaller gardens and pots. Each plant has both male and female flowers and needs plenty of bee visits to set fruit. The main things to know: give it a warm season of about 90 to 100 days and space to run, water steadily while the fruit grows, watch for squash bugs, squash vine borers, beetles, and mildew, and harvest when the squash are fully yellow with hard, dull skin and a dry stem, before frost. Stored in a cool, dry spot it keeps for a couple of months, much longer than summer squash.
seasoned: Spaghetti squash is a warm-season winter squash (Cucurbita pepo, the same species as zucchini and acorn) grown for its mature, hard-rind fruit, whose cooked flesh separates into long, pale strands like spaghetti, which is the whole point of growing it. Unlike its summer-squash cousin zucchini, it is harvested once, at full maturity in fall, when the oblong rind turns a deep, even yellow and a thumbnail cannot dent it. It is a moderate keeper: after an optional short cure it stores about 1 to 3 months, not as long as a butternut but far longer than any summer squash. Plants are moderately vigorous vines that run roughly 6 to 8 feet, so they need real room, though compact bush and semi-bush types like Tivoli and Small Wonder suit small gardens and containers. Spaghetti squash is monoecious, carrying separate male and female flowers on one plant, and fruit set is strongly pollinator-dependent. As a pepo, it is susceptible to the squash vine borer, so managing that pest is part of growing it. The season's shape is set by three things: a warm runway of 90 to 100 frost-free days to mature the crop, moderate pest and disease pressure (squash bug, squash vine borer, cucumber beetle and the bacterial wilt it spreads, plus powdery and downy mildew), and the single fall harvest, timed at a hard, fully yellow rind, before frost.

beginner: Pick a sunny spot with rich, well-drained soil and mix in plenty of compost before planting, since spaghetti squash is a large, hungry plant. Plant it on low hills or mounds, which warm up and drain better. Give it room: space plants about 2 to 3 feet apart in rows 3 to 5 feet apart, since the vines can spread 6 to 8 feet (bush types like Tivoli need less). If your soil is heavy or wet, build the mounds up higher so water drains away from the roots and fruit.
seasoned: Prepare a fertile, well-drained bed in full sun, working several inches of compost or rotted manure into the soil before planting, since spaghetti squash is a hungry, long-season plant. Many growers set plants in low hills or mounds about a foot across, which warm faster in spring, drain better, and give the vines a clear starting point. Space generously: roughly 24 to 36 inches between plants in the row with 3 to 5 feet between rows for vining types (closer for bush types like Tivoli), because the vines can run 6 to 8 feet. On heavy or wet ground, build the mounds up for drainage to head off crown and fruit rot.

beginner: Pole beans grow best in rich, loose soil that drains well. Loam, a balanced soil that holds some moisture but never stays soggy, is ideal. Pole beans set the heaviest pods in soil that holds moisture through their long pod-fill season yet never stays waterlogged, since soggy ground invites the root rots beans are prone to. Work in compost before planting and set the trellis or poles in place at the same time so you do not disturb the roots later.

beginner: Pole beans make a lot of their own food from the air, so they need little fertilizer. Mix a little balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant, and feed once more lightly right before the plants flower. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy vines climbing the trellis but fewer beans, and it delays flowering.
seasoned: Pole beans are light feeders. As legumes they fix much of their own nitrogen through root nodules, and excess nitrogen delays flowering and pushes leafy vine growth up the trellis at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work a balanced starter into the bed before planting, then sidedress lightly just before the first bloom. Sandy beds or leaching rains can call for a second light feeding across the long bearing season.

beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 works well.
seasoned: Pre-plant 5-10-10 if no soil test is available; sidedress a nitrogen source lightly before bloom.

beginner: Pole beans get along with most vegetables. The classic combination is beans, corn, and squash grown together, with the beans climbing the corn. The one pairing to avoid is planting beans right next to onions or garlic.
seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, pole beans leave the soil better for what follows and are the classic climbing partner in the Three Sisters planting, where the beans scramble up the corn while squash covers the ground. The long-standing caution is to keep beans away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress them.

beginner: The traditional Three Sisters partner; with pole beans the corn works as a living pole for the vines to climb.
seasoned: Corn is the classic pole bean partner in Three Sisters planting, where the corn stalk serves as a living trellis for the climbing vines. Let the corn get a good head start and use sturdy, well-rooted stalks, since vigorous pole beans can overload thin sweet corn. The beans' nitrogen fixation helps balance the bed for the heavy-feeding corn; the benefit is structural and traditional rather than a measured pest effect.

beginner: The third Sister; its broad leaves shade the soil and keep weeds down around the beans.
seasoned: Squash rounds out the Three Sisters trio. Its broad sprawling leaves shade the soil, hold moisture, and suppress weeds around the base of the bean supports, while the mix of heights makes it harder for pests to lock onto any one crop. This is a soil-and-space benefit; give the squash room so it does not swamp the young bean vines before they climb.

beginner: An easy neighbor that shares similar warm-season, full-sun needs.
seasoned: Cucumber and pole beans coexist comfortably: similar warm-season timing and water needs, and the beans' nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the cucumber as a moderate feeder. Trellised cucumbers can even share the vertical structure. This is a compatibility pairing rather than a strongly protective one.

beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from beans, which are said to grow poorly near them.
seasoned: Onions and beans is one of the better-grounded 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds that are held to interfere with the Rhizobium bacteria on bean roots, the very bacteria the bean depends on to fix nitrogen, so bean growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. A useful corollary: beans grown before onions actually improve the soil for the following allium crop.

beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for beans.
seasoned: Garlic acts on beans the same way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds held to disrupt the nitrogen-fixing Rhizobium bacteria on bean roots, slowing the beans down. Treat garlic and pole beans as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the bean-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

beginner: Leaves that look skeletonized or lacy, with the tissue chewed away from underneath but the veins left behind. Both the spiny yellow young and the round, coppery adult beetles feed on the undersides of the leaves, and on a tall pole vine they work their way up high where they are easy to overlook. The adult is yellow to copper colored with rows of small black spots on its back.
seasoned: Leaves taking on a skeletonized, lacy look as tissue is chewed from the undersides, leaving the vein network behind. Both the spiny yellow larvae and the dome-shaped, coppery adults feed on leaf undersides, and on tall pole vines the damage runs high into the canopy where it is easy to miss. The adult is yellow to coppery-brown, one-quarter to one-third inch long, with eight small black spots on each wing cover.

beginner: The Mexican bean beetle, a leaf-eating cousin of the ladybug. The adults come out of hiding near woods in spring, feed, then lay clusters of yellow eggs under the leaves, and several generations build up over the summer.
seasoned: The Mexican bean beetle (Epilachna varivestis), a leaf-eating member of the ladybeetle family. Adults emerge from overwintering near woodland edges, feed, then lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides, and several generations build through the season.

beginner: Pick off and destroy the adults, the yellow egg clusters, and the spiny young, looking under the leaves and up the vine. Done early, this works well in a home garden. Beans can lose a fair amount of leaf without losing beans, so you do not need to spray for light damage. If they get bad, an organic spray such as spinosad is labeled for bean beetles.
seasoned: Handpick and destroy adults, the yellow egg clusters, and the spiny larvae, checking leaf undersides up the trellis. Beans tolerate real defoliation without yield loss, about 30 percent before bloom and 15 percent during bloom and pod fill, so light feeding needs no spray. Where pressure is heavy, an organic option such as spinosad is labeled for bean beetles.

beginner: Because most damage happens in July and August, planting early or making a late-summer sowing can mostly dodge it. Clear and turn under the old vines right after harvest so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter, and move your beans to a new spot each year.
seasoned: Since most damage falls in July and August, an early or a late-summer sowing can escape the worst of it; the varieties Wade and Black Valentine are noted as tolerant. Work crop debris into the soil promptly after harvest to remove overwintering shelter, and rotate beans away from last year's bed.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft-bodied insects, usually green but sometimes black or pink, packed onto the growing tips and the undersides of leaves. Heavy feeding stunts young plants and slows them down, and a sticky residue may appear. Aphids can also spread virus diseases from plant to plant.
seasoned: Colonies of soft-bodied, pinhead-sized insects clustered on growing tips and leaf undersides, usually green but sometimes black, yellow, or pink. Heavy feeding stunts young plants and delays maturity as the insects withdraw sap; sticky honeydew and sooty mold may follow.

beginner: Several kinds of aphids, most common in cool, dry weather on small plants. They multiply fast and build up thick colonies before their natural enemies catch up. Warmer weather and helpful bugs like ladybugs usually knock them back.
seasoned: Several aphid species (Aphis and Macrosiphum euphorbiae), most prevalent in cool, dry weather on small plants. They reproduce rapidly, building dense colonies before natural enemies catch up; warm weather and predators such as ladybugs usually bring them down.

beginner: Blast the colonies off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap, which works on contact. Start as soon as you see them. Once it warms up, ladybugs and other helpful insects usually take care of the rest.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water, or treat with insecticidal soap, which gives good control on contact. Begin as soon as colonies are found. Once the weather warms, ladybugs and other natural enemies generally take over.

beginner: Lay down reflective mulch, which confuses aphids and cuts both their feeding and the viruses they spread, and pull nearby weeds that shelter them. Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is exactly what aphids like.
seasoned: Lay reflective mulch, which disorients aphids and reduces both feeding and virus spread, and control nearby weeds that harbor them. Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft, lush growth aphids favor.

beginner: Fine whitish or yellow speckling on the leaves at first, turning to a dried, bronzed look as they multiply. The clue is fine webbing on the undersides of the leaves. The mites themselves are tiny specks, easiest to see by tapping a leaf over white paper. They explode in hot, dry weather.
seasoned: A fine whitish or yellow stippling on the leaves at first, progressing to a bronzed, dried-out look as populations build; fine silken webbing over the leaf undersides is the giveaway. The mites are minute specks, easiest to confirm by tapping a leaf over white paper. They build explosively in hot, dry weather.

beginner: Two-spotted spider mites, tiny eight-legged relatives of spiders that pierce the leaf and suck out the contents. Hot, dry weather lets them build up fast, and dusty, dried-out plants are the most likely to be hit.
seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae), tiny eight-legged relatives of spiders that pierce leaf cells and suck the contents. Hot, dry conditions favor rapid buildup, and dusty, drought-stressed plants are most prone.

beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water to knock off the mites and webbing, and use insecticidal soap before they get too thick. Keeping the plants well watered and unstressed slows them down.
seasoned: Hose the undersides of leaves with a strong spray of water to dislodge mites and webbing, and treat with insecticidal soap before numbers climb too high. Keeping plants well watered and unstressed slows buildup, and ladybugs and other predators help.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist, because dried-out plants are much more likely to get mites, and keep dust down. Check the undersides of the leaves during hot, dry weather so you catch them early.
seasoned: Maintain even soil moisture, since drought-stressed plants are far more mite-prone, and avoid the dusty conditions mites thrive in. Watch the undersides of leaves closely through hot, dry spells so you catch the buildup early.

beginner: Large ragged holes chewed in the leaves, and on young plants, chewing around the stem near the soil that can kill seedlings. The adult is a small beetle, usually reddish or yellowish, with a few black spots down each wing cover. Early-season damage is the worst because it thins out the plants.
seasoned: Large, irregular holes chewed in leaves, and on young plants, girdling of stems near the soil line that can thin the stand. The adult is one-fifth to one-quarter inch long and variable in color, usually red to yellow, marked with three or four black spots along each wing cover. Damage early in the season matters most because it reduces the stand.

beginner: The bean leaf beetle, which is rarely a serious problem in most home gardens. The adults chew leaves and stems, and young seedlings are the most at risk.
seasoned: The bean leaf beetle (Cerotoma trifurcata), rarely a serious pest in most home gardens. Adults feed on foliage and stems, with seedlings the most vulnerable stage.

beginner: Picking them off and the same steps you would use for Mexican bean beetle usually keep them in check. Beans can lose a good bit of leaf without losing beans, so light damage needs nothing. Focus on protecting young seedlings, which are the most at risk.
seasoned: Handpicking and the same measures used against Mexican bean beetle generally keep it in check; beans tolerate considerable leaf loss without yield penalty, so light feeding needs no action. Protect emerging seedlings, the vulnerable stage, where beetles are active.

beginner: Clear away the old vines after harvest and move your beans each year so the beetles have nowhere to overwinter. A lightweight row cover over young seedlings protects them through the risky early weeks if this beetle is a problem where you are.
seasoned: Clear crop debris after harvest and rotate beans to deny overwintering sites. A floating row cover over emerging seedlings protects the stand through the vulnerable early weeks where the beetle is a known problem.

beginner: Rust-colored bumps, mostly on the undersides of the leaves. Badly infected leaves turn yellow, wilt, and fall off. Stems and pods can get it too. It shows up in humid weather and can hit most kinds of beans.
seasoned: Rust-colored, raised spots that form mainly on the lower leaf surfaces; badly infected leaves yellow, wilt, and drop. Stems and pods can be infected too. It develops under humid conditions and can affect most types of beans.

beginner: A fungus that survives the winter in the soil, on old plant debris, and, importantly for pole beans, on the poles and trellis used the year before. Humid weather is what lets it take hold and spread.
seasoned: The fungus Uromyces appendiculatus. It survives the winter in the soil, on plant debris, and, importantly for pole beans, on the poles and trellis used the previous year, a direct route back to a new crop. Humid conditions drive infection and spread.

beginner: Pick off and throw away, do not compost, infected leaves, and give the vines room to breathe. Where rust is bad, a sulfur dust or spray gives good control if you start as the plants begin to flower and repeat every week or two, following the label.
seasoned: Remove and destroy infected leaves and improve airflow. Where rust has been severe, a sulfur dust or spray gives good control when begun as the plants start to bloom and repeated on a 10-to-14-day schedule; follow the label.

beginner: Move your beans to a new spot if rust has been a problem, and clean or replace your poles and trellis between years, since the fungus rides over on them. Water at the base instead of overhead, keep airflow up, and pick a rust-resistant variety if it keeps coming back.
seasoned: Rotate beans where rust has been a problem, and because the fungus carries over on poles and trellis, clean or replace supports between seasons rather than reusing them unwashed. Grow on a support with good airflow, avoid overhead watering, and choose rust-resistant varieties where it recurs.

beginner: Black, sunken spots about half an inch across on the pods, the clearest sign, sometimes with a pinkish ooze in wet weather. The veins on the undersides of leaves turn black, and spots show up on stems too. It shows up in cool, wet spring and fall weather, not in hot, dry summers.
seasoned: Black, sunken lesions about half an inch across on pods, the most prominent sign, sometimes oozing salmon-colored spores in wet weather; the veins on lower leaf surfaces turn black, and lesions appear on stems and seedling leaves. It develops in cool, wet spring and fall weather, not in hot, dry summers.

beginner: A fungus that rides in on infected seed and survives up to two years on old plant debris in the soil. Splashing water spreads it, and cool, wet weather is when it strikes.
seasoned: The fungus Colletotrichum lindemuthianum, carried on infected seed and surviving up to two years on plant debris in the soil. Splashing water spreads it, and cool, wet conditions favor infection.

beginner: You cannot cure tissue that is already infected; pull and throw away, do not compost, affected plants and debris to slow it down. On snap beans a copper fungicide can help if you start early, but keeping seed clean and rotating does most of the work.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected plants and debris to limit spread. On snap beans a copper fungicide or chlorothalonil can suppress it when started early, but clean seed and rotation do most of the work.

beginner: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Clear away all the old plants after harvest, and do not grow beans in that spot for two to three years. Water at the base and avoid splashing soil up onto the plants.
seasoned: Plant certified disease-free seed and do not save seed from an infected crop. Remove all plant debris after harvest, and do not plant beans where the disease occurred for two to three years. Avoid overhead watering and splashing soil onto the plants.

beginner: Two related diseases. Halo blight makes pale greenish-yellow rings around brown spots on the leaves and shows up in cool weather. Common blight turns leaves brown so they drop fast, with no ring, and likes warm weather. Both hit stems, leaves, and pods, and both spread in rain and damp conditions.
seasoned: Two related diseases. Halo blight shows light greenish-yellow halos around brown leaf spots and appears in cool weather; common blight turns leaves brown so they drop quickly, with no halo, and favors warm weather. Both infect stems, leaves, and pods, and both are spread by rain and damp conditions.

beginner: Two kinds of bacteria, one causing common blight and one causing halo blight. Both start on infected seed, spread easily when it is wet, and survive up to two years on old plant debris in the soil.
seasoned: Two bacteria, Xanthomonas campestris pv. phaseoli (common blight) and Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola (halo blight). Both start on infected seed, spread readily in moisture, and survive up to two years on plant debris in the soil.

beginner: There is no cure once plants are infected; copper sprays every 10 days can slow it down. Water at the base, not overhead, and do not touch the vines when the leaves are wet, since that carries the bacteria from plant to plant.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; copper fungicides applied on a 10-day schedule can slow spread. Avoid overhead watering and do not handle the vines when foliage is wet, which moves the bacteria from plant to plant.

beginner: Buy new, certified seed each year instead of saving your own, since the disease travels on seed. Do not grow beans in the same spot more than once every three years, and keep out of the patch when the leaves are wet.
seasoned: Buy new, certified seed each year rather than saving it, since the disease is seedborne. Do not plant beans in the same spot more often than every third year, and stay out of the planting when the foliage is wet.

beginner: Seeds that rot before they come up, or young seedlings that come up stunted, with a soft, watery rot at the soil line. The roots die and the leaves turn yellow. It is worst in cool, wet soil that makes the seeds sit too long before sprouting.
seasoned: Seeds that rot before emerging, or young seedlings that come up stunted, with a watery soft rot just above or below the soil line; roots die and leaves yellow. The damage shows up most in cool, wet soils that slow germination and keep seedlings vulnerable.

beginner: Several fungi that live in the soil and infect seeds and young seedlings, usually Rhizoctonia, Pythium, and Fusarium. Cool, wet, poorly drained soil and damage to the roots at planting are what let them in.
seasoned: Several soilborne fungi that infect seeds and young seedlings, usually Rhizoctonia solani, Pythium species, and Fusarium solani. Cool, wet, poorly drained soil and root injury at planting set the stage for them.

beginner: There is no saving seedlings that have rotted; replant once the soil is warmer and drains better. Pulling affected plants and improving drainage limits the loss. The main thing is prevention, since these fungi are already in the soil.
seasoned: There is no rescue for rotted seedlings; replant into warmer, better-drained conditions. Removing affected plants and improving drainage limits further loss. The real lever is prevention, since the fungi are already in the soil.

beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to about 69°F before planting, and use raised beds in well-drained ground instead of low, wet spots. Avoid damaging the roots when planting, move your beans around the garden each year, and clear away old plants after harvest.
seasoned: Wait until the soil has warmed to about 69°F at a 4-inch depth before sowing, and plant on raised beds in well-drained ground rather than low, wet spots. Avoid root injury at planting, rotate beans with other vegetables, and clear crop debris after harvest.

beginner: Small, soft, watery spots on stems, leaves, and pods that grow fast in cool, damp weather, join together, and choke off the stem. Affected pods collapse into a brown, watery mush, soon covered in white cottony mold. Crowded, overfed vines with poor airflow are the most at risk.
seasoned: Small, soft, watery spots on stems, leaves, and pods that enlarge fast under cool, moist conditions, run together, and girdle the stem. Affected pods collapse into a brown, watery mush, soon covered by a white cottony fungal growth. Dense, overfed vines with poor airflow are most at risk.

beginner: A fungus that thrives in cool, damp weather and heavy, crowded growth. Too much fertilizer makes the lush, dense vines that trap the still, humid air the mold needs.
seasoned: The fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, favored by cool, moist conditions and heavy, dense growth. Too much fertilizer drives the lush vine growth that creates the still, humid canopy the disease needs.

beginner: There is no home-garden spray for this one; you manage it by how you grow. Pull and throw away, do not compost, infected plants, and open up the airflow. Training the vines up their support and thinning crowded growth helps the leaves dry out faster.
seasoned: There is no recommended chemical control for the home garden; management is cultural. Remove and destroy infected plants, and improve air circulation. Training vines up a support and thinning crowded growth helps the canopy dry.

beginner: Give the vines room for air to move instead of crowding them, and go easy on fertilizer, since too much makes the heavy growth the mold likes. Growing up a trellis actually helps, keeping the leaves off the wet ground. Water at the base and avoid keeping the plants wet and packed together.
seasoned: Give plants good airflow rather than crowding, and go easy on fertilizer, since excess nitrogen feeds the heavy vine growth that favors the disease. Vertical growth on a trellis is an advantage here, keeping the canopy off the ground; avoid overhead watering and the wet, still conditions the fungus needs.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist but never soggy. Pole beans flower and fill pods for a long time, so keep the water steady all the way through the season.
seasoned: Regular and even through the long season, keeping soil moisture near field capacity. The need is greatest during the extended flowering and pod-fill period, which on pole beans runs for many weeks.

beginner: Water deeply enough to wet the soil about 6 inches down. Deep, less frequent watering beats a daily light sprinkle.
seasoned: Enough to wet the root zone roughly 6 inches down; watering deeply and less often builds a deeper root system than frequent light sprinkles.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and do it in the morning. Because pole beans grow up in the air, the leaves dry off faster than on a low bush, which helps keep disease down.
seasoned: Water at the soil level in the morning so foliage dries quickly; trained up a trellis, the canopy dries faster than a sprawling bush, which helps limit the foliar diseases beans are prone to.

beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt or the lower leaves turn yellow, you may be overwatering. Soggy soil rots the roots.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and stunted growth point to waterlogged roots and the onset of root rot.

beginner: If plants dry out while flowering and filling pods, they drop their flowers and the beans come out small and tough. Keep the water steady to keep new pods coming.
seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and pod fill aborts blossoms and produces small, stringy pods, and it can stall the plant's ongoing pod set for the rest of the season.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, not soggy, until the seedlings come up. Bean seeds rot in cold, wet ground.
seasoned: Direct-sown into warm soil, pole beans want an evenly moist seedbed until emergence, but not soggy: bean seed rots in cold, waterlogged ground.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered as they get going and start to climb.
seasoned: Grow the young plants on with steady, even moisture as they root out and start to climb.

beginner: Water deeply to soak about 6 inches down, in the morning at the soil. Because pole beans climb, the leaves dry off faster than on a low bush, which keeps disease down.
seasoned: Keep soil moisture near field capacity, watering deeply to wet the root zone about 6 inches down, at soil level in the morning. Trained up a trellis the canopy dries fast, which helps limit foliar disease.

beginner: Keep the water steady once the beans flower. On pole beans this is the start of a long season, and drought now can stall pod-setting for weeks.
seasoned: Flowering is moisture-critical, and on pole beans it starts a long run: stress here aborts blossoms and can stall the plant's ongoing pod set for the rest of the season.

beginner: Pole beans flower and fill pods for most of the season, so keep the water steady the whole time, not just once. A dry spell in the middle stalls the running crop.
seasoned: The moisture-critical pod-set-through-pod-fill period on pole beans runs for many weeks of continuous cropping, so keep the water steady all season, not just for one flush. A dry spell mid-run both strings the current pods and stalls the next set.

beginner: Keep watering evenly through the long harvest. Pole beans keep making new pods for weeks, so steady water keeps them coming.
seasoned: Keep even moisture right through the long picking run: pole beans keep setting and filling new pods for weeks as you harvest, and steady water sustains that running yield.

beginner: Try not to spray the whole plant from above. The most important time to keep water steady is the long stretch when pods are forming and filling.
seasoned: Avoid overhead watering where practical; the moisture-critical window is the long pod-set-through-pod-fill period.

beginner: Flowering and pod-filling are when beans most need steady water, and on pole beans that lasts most of the season.
seasoned: Flowering and pod fill are the moisture-critical stages, and on pole beans they run for weeks; stress here directly cuts the running yield.

beginner: You do not need to harden off pole beans. They are planted straight into the garden from seed.
seasoned: Not applicable. Pole beans are direct-sown in place and are not started indoors or hardened off.

beginner: Plant pole bean seeds right where they will grow, once the soil has warmed and frost is past, and put up the trellis or poles at the same time. Beans do not like having their roots disturbed, so skip starting them indoors.
seasoned: Sow directly into warm soil after the last spring frost, and set the trellis, poles, or netting in place at planting so you do not disturb the roots later. Beans resent root disturbance and germinate quickly in place, so transplanting offers no advantage.

beginner: Use a good potting mix, not garden soil, which packs down too hard in pots.
seasoned: A well-draining potting mix; avoid native garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in containers.

beginner: Mix in a little compost for fertility.
seasoned: Blend in compost for baseline fertility; beans need little added nitrogen.

beginner: Pots dry out faster than garden beds, especially once the vine is large, so check the soil daily in hot weather and water when the top inch is dry.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds, and a full pole vine transpires heavily, so monitor daily in heat and water when the top inch dries.

beginner: Container pole beans still need little feeding; a light dose before flowering, and maybe one more later in the season, is plenty.
seasoned: Feeding needs stay low; a single light pre-bloom feed suffices, though a long-bearing potted vine may want one more light feeding mid-season.

beginner: Not applicable. Pole beans are a warm-season annual; they finish in one season and are not overwintered.
seasoned: Not applicable. As a frost-tender annual, pole beans complete their cycle in a single season and are not overwintered.

beginner: Pole beans can grow in a big pot, but they need a tall, sturdy support they will not tip over. Use a pot at least 5 gallons, ideally 10 or more and 12 inches deep, set up a 6-foot teepee or trellis in it, plant a few seeds around the base, and keep the mix evenly moist.
seasoned: Pole beans grow in a large container, but they need both room and a sturdy tall support. Use a pot of at least 5 gallons, ideally 10 or more and 12 inches deep, anchored so a 6-foot teepee or trellis will not topple in wind. Plant several seeds around the support and keep the mix evenly moist.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match for pole beans because it keeps the water steady, which is exactly what they like over their long season.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits pole beans well, smoothing out the steady moisture they want across their long bearing season.

beginner: For pole beans, a deep, heavy pot works better than a wide, shallow one. The pot has to hold up a tall support without tipping in the wind and carry a big vine all season, so depth and weight matter more than width.
seasoned: A deep, heavy, stable container is what matters for pole beans, unlike the wide, shallow pot that suits bush types. The pot has to anchor a 6-foot support against wind and hold enough soil to carry a large vine through a long season, so depth and weight beat surface area here.
