beginner: Leafy crops run on nitrogen, the nutrient that drives the leaf growth you are harvesting, so feed a balanced or nitrogen-forward liquid fertilizer every 2 to 3 weeks. Keep it steady rather than heavy: a sudden big dose of nitrogen pushes fast, soft growth that can make tipburn worse (brown, dried edges on the inner leaves). And no amount of feeding stops bolting once heat and long days arrive, because that is driven by the plant's hormones, not by nutrients.
seasoned: Leafy crops run on nitrogen, which directly drives the tender leaf growth you're harvesting, so feed a balanced or nitrogen-forward liquid fertilizer every 2 to 3 weeks. Keep it steady rather than heavy: a sudden surge of nitrogen pushes fast, lush growth that can worsen tipburn by outrunning calcium delivery to the inner leaves. No amount of feeding prevents bolting once heat and long days arrive, since that is hormonal, not nutritional.

beginner: Time to feed your lettuce. A balanced liquid feed keeps the leaves tender.
seasoned: Time to feed your lettuce, a balanced liquid feed keeps leaves tender

beginner: Use a fertilizer with more nitrogen (the first number), such as 10-5-5, or a balanced 10-10-10. Those three numbers on the label are the amounts of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium.
seasoned: higher N, e.g. 10-5-5 or a balanced 10-10-10

beginner: Lettuce likes a bit more nitrogen for quick, tender leaves. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the bed before planting at the label rate, then feed once more when the plants are a few inches tall. A small side-dressing of a nitrogen fertilizer, following the package rate for your row length, is plenty. Keep the fertilizer off the leaves and water it in.
seasoned: Lettuce responds to nitrogen for fast, tender growth. Work in a complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 at about 2 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress nitrogen once plants are 3 to 4 inches tall, about 1 pound per 25 feet of row of 10-10-10 (UMN), or roughly a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row (USU). For tipburn-prone conditions favor a calcium-nitrate source over an ammonium-based one.

beginner: For lettuce, companion planting is mostly about sharing space well, not about one plant protecting another. Its best neighbors are crops that do not compete with it for the same room: fast radishes and deep-rooted carrots, plus chives, whose oniony smell helps hide lettuce from aphids. A lot of the popular "never plant these together" pairings for lettuce are old garden lore with mixed or no real evidence, so we keep those out of the way in the seasoned view. Get sun, water, and spacing right first. Companions are a small bonus on top.
seasoned: Lettuce companions are mostly about sharing space, not chemistry. Its best partners are fast or deep-rooted crops it does not compete with (radishes, carrots) and scent plants that help mask it from aphids (chives). Many popular 'avoid' pairings for lettuce are traditional lore with conflicting evidence rather than documented harm, so we keep those in the seasoned view with honest framing. Get sun, water, and spacing right first, companions are a small bonus on top.

beginner: Radishes grow fast and come out of the bed before the lettuce needs the room, so the two share space well. Their roots also loosen the soil a little for the lettuce. This is about saving space, not keeping pests away.
seasoned: Fast-maturing relay crop: radishes are harvested before lettuce fills the bed, and their taproots loosen surface compaction for lettuce's shallow roots. A space-saving pairing, not a pest control one.

beginner: Lettuce roots stay near the surface and carrots root deep, so the two do not fight for the same space underground and can grow side by side.
seasoned: Different root zones: lettuce is a shallow-rooted light feeder and carrots send a taproot deep, so the two share a bed without competing underground.

beginner: The oniony smell of chives can help hide lettuce from aphids, which find plants by scent. It helps a little rather than solving the problem on its own, so plant chives as a border around the bed.
seasoned: Allium scent compounds help mask lettuce from aphids that locate hosts by smell. A supporting deterrent, not a standalone fix, plant chives as a border row.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and the undersides of leaves. The leaves may curl, yellow, or turn sticky with a substance called honeydew. A black, sooty mold sometimes grows on that stickiness.
seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.

beginner: First knock the colonies off with a strong jet of water, which dislodges most of them, and they rarely find their way back. For any that remain, spray insecticidal soap or neem oil directly onto the aphids, covering the leaf undersides, since both only work when they hit the insect, not by being eaten. Encourage helpful insects like ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps, which keep small infestations in check on their own.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water first, which dislodges most of them and they rarely find their way back. For what remains, spray insecticidal soap or neem oil directly onto the aphids, covering leaf undersides, since both work only on contact and kill by disrupting the insect's outer membrane rather than by being eaten. Encourage ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which keep light infestations in check on their own.

beginner: Go easy on nitrogen fertilizer. The fast, soft growth that lots of nitrogen produces is exactly what aphids feed on, so an over-fed plant attracts far more of them. Plant flowers like marigolds and nasturtiums nearby, and grow some dill or cilantro too, whose flowers feed the helpful wasps and predators that do most of the real control.
seasoned: Go easy on nitrogen fertilizer. The fast, soft growth that high nitrogen pushes is exactly what aphids feed on, so a lush over-fed plant attracts far more of them. Interplant flowers such as marigolds and nasturtiums, and grow some umbellifers like dill or cilantro nearby, whose flowers feed the parasitic wasps and predators that do most of the real control.

beginner: Several kinds of aphid feed on leafy greens, most often the green peach aphid. During the growing season they reproduce without mating, so a few can become a dense colony within days once it warms up and the growth is soft and lush.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on leafy greens, most commonly the green peach aphid. Through the growing season they reproduce asexually, so a few founders become dense colonies within days once temperatures warm and growth is soft and lush.

beginner: Ragged holes appearing in leaves overnight, with shiny slime trails visible in the morning. Seedlings may be cut off right at the soil line.
seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.

beginner: Set beer traps with the rim level with the soil so the slugs fall in and cannot climb out, and refresh them every couple of days. Sprinkle diatomaceous earth in a ring around vulnerable plants, but remember it stops working once it gets wet and needs reapplying after rain or watering. Hand-pick them after dark with a flashlight, when they are out feeding. An iron-phosphate bait (sold as Sluggo and similar) is approved for organic gardens and safe around pets and wildlife; it stops the slugs feeding so they die within a few days. Scatter it in the evening after watering, when slugs are most active, for the best results.
seasoned: Set beer traps with the rim at soil level so they fall in and cannot climb back out, and refresh them every couple of days. Ring vulnerable plants with diatomaceous earth, remembering it stops working once wet and needs reapplying after rain or irrigation. Hand-pick after dark with a flashlight, when they are out feeding. Iron phosphate bait (sold as Sluggo and similar) is approved for organic use and safe around pets and wildlife; it disrupts their gut so they stop feeding and die within a few days. Scatter it in the evening after watering, when slugs are most active, for the best effect.

beginner: Pull mulch back from around seedlings and clear away the boards, pots, and leaf litter near the bed that give slugs a daytime hiding spot. A bare, raked strip around the planting slows them down on their way in. Encourage ground beetles, and hedgehogs if you have them, since both hunt slugs through the night.
seasoned: Pull mulch back from around seedlings and clear the boards, pots, and leaf litter that give slugs a daytime hiding place close to the bed. A bare, cultivated strip around the planting slows their approach. Encourage ground beetles and, if you have them, hedgehogs, which prey on slugs through the night.

beginner: Slugs and snails feed mostly at night and in cool, damp weather, rasping ragged holes in tender leaves and shearing off young seedlings completely. The damage is worst in wet spells and in beds with damp mulch or debris that give them somewhere to hide during the day.
seasoned: Slugs and snails feed mostly at night and in the cool, damp hours, rasping irregular holes through tender leaves and shearing off young seedlings entirely. Damage is heaviest in wet spells and in beds with damp mulch or debris that give them daytime shelter.

beginner: Plants wilt in the heat of the day and just fail to thrive even though you are watering steadily, then slowly decline with no obvious cause above ground. Lift a struggling plant and you find clusters of aphids on the roots under a mass of white, woolly wax. It is easy to mistake for drought or a root disease until you look below the soil.
seasoned: Plants wilt during the heat of the day and fail to thrive despite steady watering, then decline with no obvious cause above ground. Lift a suspect plant and you find clusters of the aphids on the roots under masses of white, woolly wax. The damage is easy to mistake for drought or root disease until you look below the soil.

beginner: Once the aphids are on the roots, no spray will rescue the crop, so the fix is about how you manage the planting rather than treating it. Pull up and remove badly affected plants. Where it has happened, dig the soil over deeply and let it dry out thoroughly before planting lettuce there again, and keep your plants unstressed and well watered so a fast-growing crop can often still finish acceptably.
seasoned: There is no spray that rescues an infested crop once the aphids are on the roots, so control is cultural. Pull and remove badly affected plants. Where the problem has occurred, work the soil deeply and let it dry thoroughly before replanting lettuce there, and keep plants unstressed and well watered so a fast-growing crop can often still finish acceptably.

beginner: Move lettuce around so it does not come back to the same ground each season, and avoid planting it close to Lombardy poplar trees, which are where the aphid spends the winter. Some lettuce varieties are bred to resist root aphid and are worth looking for if this pest keeps showing up in your garden.
seasoned: Rotate lettuce so it does not return to the same ground each season, and avoid planting it close to Lombardy poplars, the aphid's overwintering host. Some lettuce varieties carry resistance to root aphid and are worth seeking out if the pest is a recurring problem in your garden.

beginner: The lettuce root aphid feeds on lettuce roots out of sight. It spends winter as eggs on Lombardy poplar trees, then winged ones fly to lettuce in early summer, which is why the problem is worst where lettuce grows near those trees.
seasoned: The lettuce root aphid, Pemphigus bursarius, feeds on lettuce roots out of sight. It spends winter as eggs on Lombardy poplar, then winged forms migrate to lettuce in early summer, which is why infestations are worst where lettuce grows near those trees.

beginner: Pale yellow patches show up on the upper side of the older leaves first, with a downy gray-purple mold underneath them. In cool, wet weather it spreads fast, and the affected areas turn brown and die as it moves up the plant.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches appear on the upper surface of older leaves first, matched underneath by a downy gray-purple mold. In cool, wet weather it spreads fast, and affected areas brown and die as the infection moves up the plant.

beginner: Remove and throw away affected leaves right away, and open the planting up so air moves through and the leaves dry faster. A copper-based spray can help if you use it before the disease takes hold, as a preventive, rather than trying to cure it once it has spread.
seasoned: Remove and dispose of affected leaves promptly, and open the planting up to improve airflow so leaves dry faster. A copper-based fungicide can help when used preventively, before the disease takes hold, rather than as a cure once it has spread.

beginner: Water at the soil and early in the day so the leaves are not wet overnight, since wet leaves are what this disease needs. Space plants well apart for airflow, and choose resistant varieties, which extension programs rate as the single most effective control. Avoid growing lettuce under cover through fall and winter without good airflow, where the cool, still, humid air is just what the disease likes.
seasoned: Water at soil level and early in the day so leaves are not wet overnight, since leaf wetness is what the pathogen needs. Space plants generously for airflow, and choose resistant varieties, which extension programs rate as the single most effective control. Avoid growing under cover through autumn and winter without good ventilation, where the cool, still, humid air is ideal for it.

beginner: Downy mildew is caused by an organism called Bremia lactucae, a water mold rather than a true fungus. It needs cool, damp conditions and water sitting on the leaves to take hold, and its spores blow on the wind and spread quickly during wet spells. It does not survive in the soil, and because it is not a true fungus, ordinary fungus sprays may not work against it.
seasoned: Downy mildew is caused by Bremia lactucae, an oomycete (a water mold, not a true fungus). It needs cool, damp conditions and water sitting on the leaves to take hold, and its wind-borne spores spread quickly during moist spells. It does not survive in the soil, and because it is not a true fungus, ordinary fungicides aimed at fungi may not touch it.

beginner: Brown, papery scorch appears along the edges of the inner leaves, down in the heart of the plant rather than on the outer leaves. It does not spread from plant to plant, and it shows up most in romaine types and in hot weather.
seasoned: Brown, papery scorch appears along the edges of the inner leaves, down in the heart of the plant rather than the outer leaves. It does not spread from plant to plant, and it shows up most in cos and romaine types and in hot weather.

beginner: There is no fix for leaves that are already scorched. Keep your watering consistent to steady the plant's calcium uptake, and improve airflow around the planting so the inner leaves can release a little more water.
seasoned: There is no fix for leaves already scorched. Keep watering consistent to steady the plant's calcium uptake, and improve air movement around the planting so the inner leaves can transpire a little more.

beginner: Avoid forcing soft, fast growth with heavy nitrogen, which outruns the plant's ability to move calcium into the new leaves. Keep moisture even, harvest before heads are fully tight and mature in hot weather, and choose heat-tolerant varieties if summer tipburn keeps being a problem for you.
seasoned: Avoid pushing soft, rapid growth with heavy nitrogen, which outruns the plant's ability to move calcium into the new leaves. Keep moisture even, harvest before heads are fully tight and mature in hot weather, and choose heat-tolerant varieties where summer tipburn is a recurring problem.

beginner: Tipburn is a growing problem rather than a disease, and it is rarely about a lack of calcium in the soil. Calcium moves through the plant in the stream of water it pulls up and releases through its leaves, so it ends up in the outer leaves that release the most water. The young inner leaves are tucked inside the head where the air is still and humid, so they release very little water and, during fast growth, cannot pull in enough calcium, and their edges collapse. Heat and lush, fast growth make it worse.
seasoned: Tipburn is a physiological disorder, not a disease, and it is rarely about low calcium in the soil. Calcium travels through the plant in the stream of water it pulls up and transpires, so it collects in the fast-transpiring outer leaves. The young inner leaves are enclosed in the head where the air is still and humid and they transpire very little, so during rapid growth they cannot draw enough calcium and their edges collapse. Heat and lush, fast growth make it worse.

beginner: Every 2 to 3 days in mild weather, and more often in heat or in containers. The shallow roots dry out faster than those of deeper-rooted crops, so the topsoil they rely on loses moisture quickly. Uneven watering is the real risk: letting the soil go dry and then soaking it stresses the plant, which both causes tipburn (brown inner-leaf edges) and pushes the plant to bolt.
seasoned: Every 2 to 3 days in mild weather, more often in heat or in containers. The shallow root mass dries out faster than deeper-rooted crops, so the topsoil it depends on loses moisture quickly. Irregular watering is the real risk: a dry-then-flooded cycle stresses the plant, and water stress both reduces calcium transport to the leaf tips, which drives tipburn, and pushes the plant toward bolting.

beginner: About 1 inch of water per week, but for lettuce being consistent matters more than the exact amount. Because the roots are shallow and sit in just the top few inches of soil, lettuce dries out easily, and even short dry spells stress it quickly. Steady, even moisture also helps the plant move calcium to the fast-growing inner leaves, which prevents tipburn (the brown, dried leaf edges).
seasoned: 1 inch of water per week, but consistency matters more than volume for lettuce. Because the root system is shallow and concentrated in the top few inches of soil, lettuce has little buffer against drying out, and brief dry spells translate quickly into stress. Even, frequent moisture also supports the steady calcium uptake that prevents tipburn in fast-growing inner leaves.

beginner: Water at the soil rather than over the top of the plants where you can. Lettuce sits low with its leaves close to the ground, so overhead watering leaves moisture trapped in the center and on the leaves, where it invites diseases like downy mildew and rot. If you do water from above, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off before the cool, damp evening, when leaf diseases are most likely to take hold.
seasoned: Water at soil level rather than overhead where practical. Lettuce sits low with leaves close to the soil, so overhead watering leaves moisture trapped in the crown and on leaf surfaces, where it invites downy mildew, bottom rot, and gray mold. If you do water overhead, do it in the morning so the foliage dries before the cool, damp evening hours when fungal infection is most likely.

beginner: Slimy or rotting leaf bases, yellowing outer leaves, and soil that stays wet. The slime at the base is rot taking hold in a crown that is too wet, and the yellowing lower leaves mean the roots are sitting in soggy, airless soil. Because lettuce roots are shallow, soil that drains poorly keeps them waterlogged longer than it would a deeper-rooted plant.
seasoned: Slimy or rotting leaf bases, yellowing outer leaves, and persistently wet soil. The slime at the base is bottom rot or gray mold taking hold in a crown that stays too wet, and yellowing lower leaves signal roots sitting in oxygen-starved, waterlogged soil. Because lettuce roots are shallow, soil that drains poorly keeps them waterlogged longer than it would a deeper-rooted plant.

beginner: Wilting in the afternoon heat, brown crisping along the edges of the inner leaves (this is called tipburn), and a bitter taste. Tipburn is the clearest sign: when the plant grows fast but cannot move enough calcium to the quickly expanding inner leaves, often because dry conditions have slowed the plant down, the leaf edges die back. Dry stress also makes the plant bolt sooner, and once it bolts the leaves turn bitter.
seasoned: Wilting in the afternoon heat, brown crisping along the edges of the inner leaves (tipburn), and bitterness. Tipburn is the diagnostic one: when the plant grows fast but cannot move enough calcium to the rapidly expanding inner leaves, often because water stress has slowed the transpiration that carries calcium upward, the leaf margins die back. Drought stress also accelerates bolting, after which leaves turn bitter as the plant floods them with defensive compounds.

beginner: Lettuce seeds are tiny and sit right at the surface, so keep the top of the soil damp and cool while they sprout. Warm, dry soil makes them come up poorly.
seasoned: Lettuce seed is tiny and shallow, sown barely covered, and germinates best in light; keep the surface moist and cool for a good stand. Warm, dry soil both slows germination and can induce dormancy.

beginner: Keep the little plants evenly damp. Their roots are shallow and dry out fast.
seasoned: Keep the seedlings evenly moist; the shallow root mass dries faster than deeper-rooted crops and has little buffer.

beginner: Water often and evenly, about every 2 to 3 days in mild weather and more in heat or pots. Lettuce roots are shallow, so it does best with steady, frequent watering.
seasoned: Lettuce has a shallow root mass with little drought buffer, so it wants consistent moisture across its whole short cycle rather than one big soak. Water every 2 to 3 days in mild weather, more often in heat or containers.

beginner: Right before harvest the leaves grow fastest, and this is when watering matters most. If the plant dries out now it turns bitter and the leaf edges brown, so keep it well watered and pick in the cool morning.
seasoned: The final rapid leaf expansion before harvest is the highest-stakes window. Water stress here cuts calcium movement to the inner leaves (tipburn) and turns the plant bitter, and heat plus stress pushes it to bolt. Keep it evenly, generously moist and cut in the cool of the morning.

beginner: Once lettuce shoots up a flower stalk and turns bitter, extra water will not fix it. Pull it and plant a fresh batch.
seasoned: Once heat or long days push it to bolt and turn bitter, watering will not reverse it; a shaded, evenly watered plant simply bolts later. Pull and resow for a fresh cutting.

beginner: Water the soil rather than the leaves where you can. Lettuce grows low to the ground, so water sitting on the leaves can lead to mildew and rot. If you do water from above, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off before evening. Keeping the water even and steady also helps prevent the brown, crispy leaf edges called tipburn.

If overhead is unavoidable, water in the morning so foliage dries before the cool, damp evening. Even, frequent moisture also supports the steady calcium uptake that prevents tipburn.

beginner: You do not need to harden off leaf lettuce when you direct sow it. Seeds go straight into the garden. If you instead buy or raise transplants, give them a few days to adjust to outdoor conditions before planting out.

Sow seed straight into the garden about 3 to 4 weeks before your last spring frost, as soon as you can work the soil, since lettuce handles light frost and sprouts in cool ground. For an earlier harvest, start seeds indoors about 4 weeks ahead and set out the young plants when they are 3 to 4 weeks old, which also lets you skip thinning. Lettuce moves outdoors easily because its shallow roots settle in fast, just harden the plants off first (let them get used to outdoor conditions over several days before planting them out).

To get an earlier harvest, start seeds indoors roughly 4 weeks ahead and set out 3 to 4 week old transplants, which also skips the thinning step. Lettuce transplants easily because its shallow roots re-establish quickly, just harden plants off before moving them outside.

beginner: For lettuce, depth matters far less than you might think and width matters more. The roots are shallow, so about 6 to 8 inches of soil depth is plenty, which is why window boxes, grow bags, shallow troughs, and salad planters all work well. Width mainly decides how many plants you can fit, not whether they will do well: give leaf types a few inches apart and head types more room. A wide, shallow container usually produces more than a tall narrow pot holding the same amount of soil, because it gives you more surface for cut-and-come-again leaves.

beginner: Drainage holes are a must, and the roots must never sit in standing water: waterlogged soil leaves no air for the roots and invites root rot, which lettuce rarely recovers from. If you use a saucer under the pot, empty it after each watering and after rain, or raise the pot up on feet, bricks, or slats so it is not sitting in a puddle or flat on concrete. A removable saucer is much safer than a built-in one you cannot drain. There is a real trade-off, since a saucer does help hold moisture in hot, dry weather, but the risk of standing water outweighs that, so the rule is empty it or raise it rather than skipping drainage.

beginner: Start with a good container or potting mix rather than garden soil, which packs down in a pot and drains poorly; if you do reuse garden soil, keep it to no more than a third of the total. A good blend balances drainage with holding moisture: a peat or coir base to hold water, perlite (the little white specks) for air and drainage, and compost for richness. beginner: Containers dry out much faster than garden beds because they hold less soil and the sides and top are exposed to sun and air, so there is little moisture to fall back on. In summer heat, especially on a sunny patio or balcony, you will often need to water daily, and sometimes twice a day during hot, dry spells. Water until it runs out the drainage holes so the whole root zone gets wet, and do not let the mix dry out completely: once a peat or coir potting mix fully dries it pulls away from the pot wall, and water then runs straight down that gap and leaves the middle dry. Even moisture is the real goal, because the dry-then-wet swings of a small pot stress lettuce's shallow roots and push it toward bitterness and bolting.

Even moisture is the real goal, since the swings that come with under-watering a small pot stress shallow lettuce roots and push the plant toward bitterness and bolting.

beginner: Lettuce in a container needs feeding more often, and more lightly, than lettuce in the ground. A pot holds only a small amount of nutrients, the plant uses them up quickly, and every watering washes a little out the drainage holes, so the supply does not last the way garden soil does. A good rhythm is a balanced liquid feed every 1 to 3 weeks during the growing season, or a slow-release granular fertilizer mixed in at planting with a top-up check mid-season. Lettuce is a leafy crop that likes nitrogen but grows fast and finishes quickly, so steady light feeding works better than heavy doses, which can force soft growth and, in warm weather, speed up bolting.

The limiting factor is heat: once the central stem begins to elongate (bolting), the plant shifts to flowering, and the leaves turn bitter and tough, so take your fullest harvests before sustained warm weather sets in.

beginner: Swiss chard likes loose, fertile, well-drained soil with plenty of compost worked in. Unlike its cousin the beet, chard is grown for its leaves and stalks rather than a round root, so it is not as fussy about deep, stone-free soil, but a loose bed that does not crust still gives the best start. The seed is slow to come up, so keep the top of the soil moist and crumbly so the seedlings can push through. Mix in compost, aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, and chard is happy in most garden soils that drain well.
seasoned: Chard does best in a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. As a leaf-and-stalk crop rather than a root crop, it is less demanding of stone-free depth than beet or carrot, but a loose, non-crusting seedbed still matters because the multigerm seedball is slow to germinate and the seedlings cannot break a hard surface crust. Work in well-finished compost to feed the long cut-and-come-again harvest. Chard tolerates a slightly acidic to neutral pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 and, like its relative the beet, handles mildly alkaline soil better than most greens; it is notably more acid-tolerant than spinach, growing well down to about pH 6.0.

beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Swiss chard does best from about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral, and it is more forgiving of soil type than many greens. It handles a touch of alkalinity better than spinach and is happy in most garden soils. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number and whether you need to add lime.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral. The University of Minnesota notes chard tolerates soil somewhat more acidic than spinach, as low as about pH 6.0, and Clemson cites a 6.0 to 6.5 range; like the beet it is the same species as, chard also handles mildly alkaline soil (to about 7.5) better than most leafy greens. Acidity well below 6.0 is the main risk, where germination and micronutrient uptake suffer. A standard soil test removes the guesswork before sowing.

beginner: Swiss chard grows lots of leaves and likes nitrogen to keep making them. Mix some compost and a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed it with a nitrogen fertilizer about a month after the seedlings come up, and again every 4 to 6 weeks while you are picking. Because you cut from the same plant for months, a steady supply of food keeps the leaves big and tender.
seasoned: Chard is a leafy crop that runs on nitrogen, and because it is cut over a long season it benefits from periodic feeding rather than a single dose. Work compost and a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing, then side-dress with nitrogen about 4 weeks after emergence and again every 4 to 6 weeks while you keep cutting. Utah State suggests about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row. Steady nitrogen and even moisture keep the leaves large, tender, and dark; repeated harvesting pulls a lot out of the plant, so do not let it run hungry.

beginner: Swiss chard is an easygoing neighbor that shares a bed nicely with many crops. It grows well next to beans, the cabbage family (broccoli, cabbage, kale), onions and other alliums, and low herbs. The main plants to keep apart from chard are its close relatives beets and spinach, which share the same leafminer pest, so do not crowd them together. As always, do not trust every companion chart online, since many of their claims have never been tested.
seasoned: Chard fits easily into mixed beds and its companion list mirrors the beet's, since they are the same species. West Virginia University's companion guide lists beans, the cabbage family, and onions among the good neighbors for the chard and beet group, all reasonable on space-and-timing grounds. The one well-grounded caution is to separate chard from its goosefoot-family relatives beets and spinach, which share the leafminer and several leaf diseases, a rotation and pest principle more than a tested adjacency effect. Treat the rest as sensible defaults: as the University of Minnesota stresses, most companion claims are tradition rather than tested science, so use them as a starting point and watch your own results.

beginner: Bush beans and chard make easy bedfellows, and the beans add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy chard can use. Keep tall pole beans out of the way, though, since they shade the low chard.
seasoned: Beans interplant well with chard on structure and soil: bush beans share the bed without crowding the chard rosette and fix a little nitrogen the leafy crop draws on. WVU lists beans among the good companions for the beet and chard group. A space-and-soil benefit rather than a pest one; keep climbing pole beans away, as they shade the low, sun-loving chard.

beginner: Chard and the cabbage-family crops both like the same cool-to-mild weather and do not compete much, with the low chard sitting under the taller brassicas. A productive way to fill a bed.
seasoned: Chard and brassicas share a long cool-to-mild season and a complementary structure, the low chard rosette under the taller cabbage-family canopy, so they coexist without much competition. WVU lists the cabbage family among the good companions for the beet and chard group. A sensible structural pairing rather than a measured effect.

beginner: Onions, leeks, and garlic grow tall and narrow with shallow roots, so they tuck between chard plants without crowding them, and their strong smell is widely used to help keep some leaf-eating pests away.
seasoned: Alliums are a classic interplant for the beet and chard group: shallow-rooted and upright, they share the bed without competing, and their sulfur volatiles are widely credited with masking the crop from some leaf-feeding pests. The space benefit is solid; the pest deterrence is plausible but not proven for chard specifically.

beginner: Keep chard away from beets and spinach. They are close relatives in the same plant family and share the same leafminer pest and some leaf diseases, so planting them together helps those problems build up.
seasoned: Chard, beet, and spinach all belong to the goosefoot family and are the favored hosts of the beet and spinach leafminer, whose maggots blister and ruin the leaves; they also share Cercospora leaf spot and downy mildew. Planting them side by side or in succession concentrates the leafminer and disease pressure and feeds the soil-overwintering pupae. Separate them in space and rotate so goosefoot crops do not follow one another.

beginner: You will see pale, winding tunnels in the leaves that widen into large tan blisters or blotches, with the green skin of the leaf intact above and below. Hold a leaf to the light and you can see the tiny maggot working inside. Since you eat chard leaves, this ruins the damaged parts.
seasoned: Slender, winding mines enlarge into translucent tan blotches; because the crop is the leaf, even light feeding downgrades it, and heavily mined chard is unusable. The pale legless maggots are visible inside the leaf against the light.

beginner: A small fly lays eggs on the underside of the leaves, and the maggots that hatch tunnel inside, eating between the top and bottom layers. Chard, beets, and spinach are its favorites, which is why it helps not to plant them together.
seasoned: The beet and spinach leafminer (Pegomya species) overwinters as pupae in the soil; females lay rows of white eggs on leaf undersides, and the maggots tunnel between the leaf surfaces. There are several overlapping generations a season on chard, beets, spinach, and goosefoot weeds, the reason these relatives are rotated and spaced apart.

beginner: Once a maggot is inside a leaf, sprays do not reach it well, so pick off and destroy mined leaves as soon as you see them, before the maggots drop to the soil. Crushing the maggot inside the leaf works too. Keep the plant healthy and it will outgrow light damage.
seasoned: Insecticides reach larvae inside the leaf poorly, so rely on cultural control: pick and destroy mined leaves before larvae drop to pupate, and crush maggots in the leaf. Vigorous, evenly watered plants outgrow light damage, and naturally occurring parasitic wasps usually keep numbers in check.

beginner: Cover the plants with a light row cover right after sowing so the flies cannot lay eggs, pull nearby weeds like lambsquarters that host the pest, and move chard away from where you grew chard, beets, or spinach last year.
seasoned: Exclude the egg-laying flies with floating row cover from sowing, control goosefoot weeds (lambsquarters, chickweed) that host the pest, rotate away from where chard, beets, or spinach grew, and remove the first mined leaves promptly to break the cycle.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or black insects collect on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, leaving leaves curled, yellowed, and sticky. They can hide down in the crinkled leaves and along the stalks, and they can spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Colonies of soft-bodied aphids on leaf undersides, new growth, and along the petioles distort and yellow the foliage; honeydew and sooty mold downgrade the crop, and the crinkled leaves of savoyed types shelter colonies. Aphids also transmit virus diseases.

beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck sap from the plant. They breed quickly, especially on soft growth from too much nitrogen, and fly in from weeds and other plants.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on chard sap; populations build fastest in mild weather and on the soft, lush growth that excess nitrogen produces, with winged forms moving in from weeds and other crops.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, which often does the trick, or use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on the undersides of the leaves. Ladybugs and other helpers usually take care of the rest. Do not over-feed with nitrogen.
seasoned: A strong water jet dislodges colonies and is often enough; where needed, insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on leaf undersides is effective. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps, and avoid pushing growth with nitrogen.

beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings by not spraying broadly, go easy on nitrogen, keep weeds down, and check the new growth and leaf undersides now and then so you catch them early.
seasoned: Scout new growth and petioles early, avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and control nearby weed hosts. Row cover used against the leafminer also excludes aphids.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes peppering the leaves of young plants, like buckshot, made by small dark beetles that hop away like fleas when you come near. On big plants it is mostly a looks problem, but on tiny seedlings heavy damage can stunt or kill them.
seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes and pits riddle the leaves, heaviest on young seedlings, giving the foliage a sandblasted look; the small dark beetles jump when disturbed. Damage is mostly cosmetic on established plants but can stunt or kill seedlings at high pressure and it disfigures leaves grown for greens.

beginner: Small jumping beetles called flea beetles chew the holes. They spend winter in garden debris and come out in spring, hitting tender young plants hardest in warm, dry weather. They feed on chard, beets, and spinach.
seasoned: Several species of small flea beetles whose adults chew the pits and holes; they overwinter in garden debris and become active in spring, with the heaviest pressure on tender new growth in warm, dry weather. Chard, beet, and spinach are all hosts.

beginner: Keep seedlings well watered and growing fast and they will usually outgrow the damage. If beetles are swarming young plants, dust the leaves with kaolin clay or use a vegetable-labeled product, and clear out weeds nearby. Grown chard rarely needs anything.
seasoned: Healthy, fast-growing plants outgrow flea beetle feeding, so keep seedlings well watered and unstressed. Where pressure is high, treat with kaolin clay or a vegetable-labeled product and clear weedy hosts; mature chard seldom needs treatment.

beginner: A row cover over the seedbed during the early weeks is the best protection, keeping the beetles off while the plants are small. Clean up old plant debris where the beetles spend winter.
seasoned: A floating row cover over the seedbed is the most reliable defense, excluding the beetles during the vulnerable seedling stage. Clean up debris where adults overwinter and keep seedlings vigorous.

beginner: Ragged holes chewed in the leaves, especially the big lower leaves near the ground, with slimy trails that glisten in the morning. They feed at night and in damp, shady spots.
seasoned: Irregular ragged holes with smooth edges in the foliage, concentrated on the large lower leaves and any leaf resting on damp soil, accompanied by silvery slime trails. Feeding is nocturnal and worst in cool, wet, shaded conditions and under dense canopy.

beginner: Slugs and snails are soft, slimy pests that come out at night and in wet weather to chew on tender leaves. Chard's large, low leaves and the moist, shady ground under them are exactly what they like.
seasoned: Slugs and land snails that shelter in moist debris by day and feed on tender foliage at night; chard's broad, low leaves and the humid microclimate beneath a full stand favor them, particularly in wet weather and irrigated beds.

beginner: Pick them off after dark by flashlight, set out shallow dishes of beer to trap them, or scatter an iron-phosphate slug bait, which is safe around pets and wildlife. Remove hiding spots like boards and dense debris near the plants.
seasoned: Hand-pick after dark, trap with shallow beer dishes or boards used as daytime refuges to collect under, and apply an iron-phosphate bait where pressure is high. Reduce the moist daytime harborage that sustains them.

beginner: Water in the morning so the surface dries by night, give plants room for airflow, and clear leaf litter, boards, and weeds where slugs hide during the day. A ring of coarse, scratchy material around plants can slow them down.
seasoned: Irrigate in the morning so surfaces dry by nightfall, space plants for airflow, and clear boards, litter, and weeds that harbor slugs. Remove the lowest leaves resting on soil to cut humidity at the crown.

beginner: The leaves get many small round spots, about an eighth of an inch wide, with a pale tan or gray center and a darker reddish-purple or brown ring around each one. They start on the older outer leaves and spread inward, and when there are lots of them the leaves brown and die. It spoils the leaves you want to eat.
seasoned: Numerous small round spots about an eighth of an inch across, each with a tan to gray center and a darker reddish-purple to brown margin, appear first on the older outer leaves and spread inward; when numerous they merge and the leaf withers. Because the crop is the leaf, even moderate spotting downgrades the harvest, and severe leaf loss reduces overall yield.

beginner: A fungus that lives on old chard and beet debris and on related weeds, and gets splashed onto the plant by rain or overhead watering. It loves warm, humid weather and wet leaves, so it is worst in warm, wet areas and rainy spells.
seasoned: The fungus Cercospora beticola, which survives on infected chard and beet debris and on related weeds and is splashed onto the leaves by rain and overhead irrigation. It is favored by warm, humid weather and prolonged leaf wetness, so it is most damaging in warm, wet regions and seasons, including the long southern harvest.

beginner: You cannot cure leaves that are already spotted, only slow it down. Pick off and throw away the worst leaves, water at the soil in the morning so the leaves dry fast, and give plants room so air moves through. In a very wet year a copper fungicide labeled for vegetables can help if you start early.
seasoned: There is no cure for spotted tissue; management slows spread. Remove and destroy badly infected leaves, water at the base in the morning so foliage dries quickly, and thin or space plants for airflow. In a wet season a copper-based fungicide labeled for vegetables can suppress spread if started early, but cultural control carries most of the load.

beginner: Do not grow chard (or beets and spinach) in the same spot two or three years running, clean up old leaves and debris where the fungus lives, water at the base instead of overhead, and give plants room so the leaves dry quickly.
seasoned: Rotate chard and its relatives (beet, spinach) out of the bed for two to three years, clear and destroy crop debris, avoid overhead watering, and space and thin for airflow. Choose tolerant varieties where the disease recurs.

beginner: Pale yellow patches show on top of the leaves, with a grayish or purplish fuzzy growth underneath in damp weather. The young leaves in the center can be twisted, thick, and curled. It is worst in cool, wet weather and mainly hurts the leaves.
seasoned: Pale yellow, indistinct blotches on the upper leaf surface with a grayish to purplish downy growth on the corresponding undersides in damp weather; young central leaves are often distorted, thickened, and curled. It is most damaging in cool, wet conditions and chiefly disfigures the foliage.

beginner: A fungus-like water mold that infects in cool, wet weather and spreads in damp air and splashing water. It survives on old plant debris and on chard's relatives beets and spinach.
seasoned: The water mold Peronospora farinosa (P. betae), which infects in cool, moist conditions and survives on crop debris and related goosefoot hosts, spreading in moist air and splashing water. Chard shares it with beet and spinach.

beginner: You cannot cure infected leaves, so pick off and throw away the worst ones and help the plants dry out by giving them room. Keeping the leaves dry does most of the work; a copper fungicide is a last resort in a very wet stretch.
seasoned: No cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected leaves to reduce spread and improve airflow and drying. Cultural control is the mainstay, with copper fungicides a last resort in a persistently wet season.

beginner: Water at the soil instead of overhead, give plants room so air moves through, and stay out of the bed when the leaves are wet. Move chard away from where you grew chard, beets, or spinach, and pick a tolerant variety if it keeps showing up.
seasoned: Water at the base, space and thin for airflow, and avoid working among wet plants. Rotate away from chard, beet, and spinach, clear crop debris, and choose tolerant varieties where it recurs.

beginner: Seeds that never come up, or tiny seedlings that flop over and die just after sprouting, with a dark, pinched, wet-looking spot on the stem right at the soil line. You see it as bare gaps in the row. Cool, soggy soil and the slow-sprouting chard seedball make it more likely.
seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with a dark, water-soaked, pinched lesion at the stem base at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where the slow chard seedball prolongs the vulnerable window. Losses show as bare gaps in the row.

beginner: Soil organisms attack sprouting seeds and baby seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the seeds are slow to come up. Chard sown in cold, wet ground is at risk.
seasoned: Soilborne Pythium and Rhizoctonia species that attack germinating seed and young seedlings, favored by cool, wet, poorly drained soil and overwatering; old or weak seed and a crusted seedbed increase losses.

beginner: Seedlings that have flopped will not recover. If it shows up, stop watering for a bit and let the soil surface dry out some, and clear away the fallen seedlings. There is no good home cure once it starts, so this one is mostly about prevention.
seasoned: Affected seedlings cannot be saved. Stop watering and let the surface dry to slow the pathogens, and clear collapsed seedlings; there is no effective home cure once it takes hold, so prevention is the lever.

beginner: Wait until the soil is warm enough and not cold and soggy, keep the seedbed damp without keeping it soaking, plant at the right depth in well-drained soil, and use fresh seed. Soaking the seedballs for a day before sowing helps them come up faster.
seasoned: Sow into warm-enough, well-drained soil rather than cold, wet ground, keep the seedbed evenly moist without saturating it, use fresh seed, and do not sow too deep. Soaking the seedball for a day speeds emergence and shortens the risk window.

beginner: The plants grow slowly and wilt in the heat of the day even when the soil is moist, and the leaves yellow and stay stunted. If you dig up a plant, the roots have small knots or swellings (galls) on them. It is worst in warm, sandy soils, which is why it matters most in places like Florida.
seasoned: Stunting, midday wilting despite adequate soil moisture, chlorosis, and reduced vigor aboveground, with characteristic root galls (knots) belowground. UF/IFAS notes chard is very susceptible. Damage is heaviest in warm, sandy soils and where host crops are grown repeatedly, so it is chiefly a southern and warm-region concern.

beginner: Tiny worms in the soil, too small to see, invade the roots and make the galls that block the plant from taking up water and food. They build up where chard or other host crops are grown over and over in warm soil.
seasoned: Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne species), microscopic soilborne roundworms that invade roots and induce galls that impair water and nutrient uptake; populations build under warm soil and continuous host cropping.

beginner: There is no spray that cures an infected plant, so pull and destroy badly affected plants at the end of the season. The fix is for next time: rotate to a different bed, add lots of compost, and keep plants well watered to help them cope.
seasoned: No rescue for an infected plant; remove and destroy heavily galled plants. Management is preventive and cultural: build organic matter, keep plants watered to tolerate the stress, and break the host cycle for future crops.

beginner: Rotate chard to a fresh spot, add plenty of organic matter, and avoid following other host crops in warm, sandy beds. In bad spots, plant in containers with fresh mix, or grow chard in the cooler months when nematodes are less active.
seasoned: Rotate with non-host or resistant crops, incorporate ample organic matter, avoid following susceptible hosts in warm sandy beds, and consider container culture with fresh mix or cool-season scheduling where nematodes are established.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, paying closest attention while the seeds are sprouting and while you are harvesting. Once the plants are growing, give about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, counting rain, in fewer but deeper waterings.
seasoned: Even, consistent moisture is the rule, most critical during the slow germination window and through the long cutting season. Aim for about 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week including rain once established, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings; chard is shallow-rooted and steady moisture keeps the leaves and stalks tender.

beginner: About 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, including rain, once the plants are growing. Give more in hot, dry weather and less in cool weather. While the seeds are sprouting, just keep the top of the soil damp.
seasoned: Roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week including rainfall once established, more in heat or sandy soil and less in cool or heavy soil. During germination the seedbed needs only enough to stay evenly moist near the surface.

beginner: Water gently at soil level, using a soaker hose or drip line. A hard blast from the hose can wash out the shallow seeds or pack the soil into a crust the sprouts cannot push through, and wet leaves invite disease, so keep it gentle and low.
seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line to keep the surface evenly moist without crusting the bed or washing out the shallow-sown seedballs, and to keep the foliage dry, which checks Cercospora and downy mildew. Avoid hard overhead bursts on a fresh seedbed.

beginner: If the soil stays soaking wet, seedlings can damp off and the leaves can get moldy. Watch for yellow lower leaves and a constantly wet, sour-smelling bed. If you see these, water less and make sure the soil drains well.
seasoned: Constantly saturated soil invites damping-off in seedlings and the leaf diseases, and yellowing lower leaves, soft growth, and a sour, waterlogged bed are signs to back off. Poor drainage is the usual cause.

beginner: Droopy, dull leaves, slow growth, and tough, stringy stems mean the chard needs more water. Chard handles heat well, but only if you keep it watered, so do not let the bed dry out in summer.
seasoned: Dull, wilting leaves, slowed growth, and toughened, stringy stalks signal too little water. Chard is heat-tolerant but only with steady moisture; drought in heat is what stalls it, so keep water even through warm spells.

beginner: Chard is slow to sprout, so keep the top of the soil damp and uncrusted until it does. Each seed is a little cluster, so thin the seedlings after they come up.
seasoned: Chard germination is slow, and the surface must stay continuously moist and uncrusted or the stand comes up thin. The seed is a cluster, so thin the seedlings once they are up.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp as the young plants get growing.
seasoned: Keep even moisture as the seedlings establish after thinning.

beginner: Water deeply about 1 to 1.5 inches a week rather than light daily sprinkles.
seasoned: Settle into deeper, less frequent soakings of about 1 to 1.5 inches a week; chard is shallow-rooted but responds to steady moisture that reaches down.

beginner: Chard keeps producing for months. Keep watering evenly, and give extra in summer heat, so the leaves stay tender instead of tough. Pick outer stalks and keep it watered for more.
seasoned: Chard crops for a long cutting season. Keep even moisture through the weeks, and especially through sustained summer heat: the crop tolerates heat but stalls into tough leaves if it dries out. Cut outer stalks and keep it watered to keep tender leaves coming.

beginner: Chard usually flowers in its second year or in a long hot spell. Once it does the leaves get tough, so start a fresh planting.
seasoned: Chard usually bolts in its second year or under prolonged heat and stress; once it sends up a seed stalk the leaves toughen, and watering only slows the decline. Resow for fresh leaves.

beginner: While the seeds are sprouting, water gently so you do not wash them out or make a hard crust. Once the chard is growing, water more deeply but less often. Keeping the water steady is the secret to harvesting chard right through the summer.
seasoned: On a fresh seedbed, keep the surface evenly moist without crusting or dislodging the shallow seedballs. After establishment, shift to deeper, less frequent soakings; steady moisture is what lets chard keep producing through summer heat that would bolt or scorch lettuce and spinach.

beginner: The two most important times to keep the soil moist are while the seeds are sprouting and during hot summer weather. Steady water in the heat is what lets chard keep going when other greens give up.
seasoned: Two windows matter most: germination through emergence, when the surface must stay continuously moist and uncrusted or the slow stand fails, and any sustained summer heat, when even moisture is what keeps the heat-tolerant crop growing tender leaves instead of stalling.

beginner: You do not need to harden off chard when you direct-sow it. If you start a few plants indoors to transplant, harden them off over about a week before setting them out.

Plant chard seeds right in the garden where they will grow. Sow them about half an inch deep once the soil is no longer frozen or soggy, about 2 to 3 weeks before your last spring frost. Here is the chard surprise: each seed is really a little dried fruit holding several seeds, so one seed grows a small clump of seedlings, which is why you have to thin them later. You can also start a few indoors and transplant them. Do not plant too early into cold soil, which can make young plants flower (bolt) prematurely. Keep the soil surface damp until the sprouts appear, often 1 to 2 weeks.
seasoned: Chard is usually direct-sown, since it grows quickly and, like its relative the beet, transplants best when young; it can be started indoors for an early plant or set out as transplants spaced 4 to 6 inches apart (UMN), but most gardeners sow in place. Sow about half an inch deep once the soil is workable and at least 50°F, from about 2 to 3 weeks before the last spring frost. The key chard-specific point is that each chard seed is a multigerm seedball, a dried fruit containing several embryos, so a single seed sprouts a small cluster of seedlings and the stand must be thinned. Avoid sowing into cold soil, which can vernalize young plants and trigger premature bolting. Keep the surface moist and uncrusted until emergence, often 1 to 2 weeks.

beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of water. Chard likes steady moisture, but soil that stays soggy will rot the plant, so empty the saucer within an hour of watering.
seasoned: Do not let the pot stand in a saucer of water. Chard needs even moisture, but a waterlogged mix rots the crown and invites disease; empty the saucer within an hour of watering.

beginner: Mix in some compost so the soil holds water evenly and feeds the long harvest.
seasoned: Use a light, loose potting mix high in organic matter; blend in compost and a starter nitrogen source for the sustained leafy harvest. Avoid garden soil, which compacts in a pot.

beginner: Pots dry out much faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather. Chard needs steady moisture to keep making tender leaves, so do not let the mix dry out, especially in summer heat.
seasoned: Containers dry far faster than beds, and chard stalls and toughens under drought stress, so check the top inch or two daily in warm weather and water before the mix dries. Aim for consistently moist but never soggy.

beginner: Feed a little more often than in the ground, since watering washes nutrients out of pots. A light liquid feed every couple of weeks keeps the leaves coming.
seasoned: Chard is a sustained leafy feeder. Mix a balanced slow-release fertilizer into the potting mix at sowing and supplement with a half-strength liquid nitrogen feed every couple of weeks through the cutting season, since frequent watering leaches pots.

beginner: In mild areas, a pot of chard can keep producing through winter in a sheltered, sunny spot. In cold areas, move the pot against the house or into a cold frame, or cover it during hard freezes, and it will often resume in spring.
seasoned: Chard is frost-tolerant, so a container can overwinter in mild zones, holding through winter in a sheltered spot and resuming growth in spring. In cold zones the limited root volume of a pot freezes harder than open ground, so sink it, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or cover it during hard freezes. Note that an overwintered plant has been vernalized and will bolt as spring warms, so plan to crop it before the stalk forms.

beginner: Chard is a great container crop and a pretty one, especially the rainbow-stemmed types. Use a pot at least 10 inches deep with drainage holes and loose potting mix, give one plant a 5-gallon pot or space several in a larger one, keep the soil evenly moist, and pick the outer leaves so it keeps regrowing all season.
seasoned: Chard suits containers well and the colorful-stemmed cultivars double as ornamentals. Use a container at least 10 inches deep with drainage holes and a loose, organic potting mix; a single plant fills a 5-gallon pot, or space several in a larger trough. Keep moisture even to keep leaves and stalks tender, feed regularly for the long harvest, and crop the outer leaves cut-and-come-again. It carries well from a sunny patio through much of the year.

beginner: A self-watering pot works well for chard once it is growing, because it keeps the water steady, and steady water means tender leaves through summer. It will not keep the seeds moist while they sprout, though, so water the surface gently by hand until the seedlings come up.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits chard well once it is growing, because steady sub-irrigation delivers the even moisture that keeps the leaves and stalks tender through heat. It does not help germination, though: the seedball sits at the dry surface above the wicking zone, so keep the top inch moist by hand until the stand is up.

beginner: Chard grows into a good-sized plant, so use a roomy pot at least 10 inches deep. One plant is happy in a 5-gallon bucket, or space a few out in a wider container.
seasoned: Chard makes a substantial leafy plant, so give it depth and room: a container at least 10 inches deep with enough width to space plants 6 inches or more apart. A 5-gallon pot suits one full plant; wider troughs hold several for a steady cut-and-come-again supply.

beginner: Do not leave chard out on the counter. The leaves wilt fast in the warmth, so get it into the fridge soon after picking.
seasoned: Poor for more than a day or two. At room temperature chard leaves wilt and yellow quickly; cut leaves should be refrigerated promptly. The sturdy stalks hold a little better than the blades but are still best chilled.

beginner: Store chard unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge's crisper drawer, where it keeps for 1 to 2 weeks if kept very cold. Wash it only when you are ready to cook it.
seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; chard holds about 1 to 2 weeks near 32°F at high humidity, a bit longer than spinach thanks to the sturdier leaves and stalks. Washing before storage traps moisture and speeds breakdown, so wait to wash until use.

beginner: Chard freezes well if you blanch it first. Cut the leaves from the stalks, boil the leaves about 2 minutes (the stalks a little longer), cool them right away in ice water, drain, and freeze.
seasoned: Chard freezes well once blanched: separate the stalks from the leaves (the stalks need a minute or two longer), blanch about 2 minutes, cool quickly in ice water, drain well, and freeze. Blanching halts the enzymes that otherwise cause off-flavors and color loss.

beginner: Chard is best right after you pick it, and since you cut it leaf by leaf you can pick just what you need and let the plant keep growing. Save the colorful stalks to cook on their own. Chill it quickly, use it within a week or so, and freeze any extra after blanching.
seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden, which is one of the joys of a cut-and-come-again crop: pick what you need and the plant keeps making more. The colorful stalks can be stored and cooked separately from the leaves, like a vegetable in their own right. Chill promptly and use fresh within a week or so, or blanch and freeze a glut.

beginner: Good news: chard does not bolt (run to flower) in summer heat the way lettuce and spinach do. It is a biennial, which means it only flowers after living through a winter, so a plant you set out in spring keeps making leaves all season. The one thing to avoid is planting too early into cold soil, which can trick a young plant into flowering. If a plant lives through winter, it will flower in spring, so harvest it and plant a new one.
seasoned: Chard is a biennial and, unlike spinach and lettuce, does not bolt from summer heat or long days; it flowers only after it has lived through a winter, so a spring planting crops cleanly into fall without running to seed. The two ways to trigger premature bolting in the first year are sowing too early into cold soil, which can vernalize the young plants, and an unusually cold spring snap; avoid both by sowing once the soil has warmed past about 50°F. Overwintered plants will bolt as spring warms, so crop them before the stalk elongates and start a fresh sowing.

beginner: Chard bolts (sends up a flower stalk and turns bitter) only after it has gone through a winter, not because of summer heat. That is why one spring planting can feed you for months. If you plant too early into cold soil, a young plant can be fooled into flowering, so wait until the soil warms a little.
seasoned: Bolting resistance is a defining chard advantage. As a biennial it requires vernalization (a winter, or a sustained cold snap on a young plant) to flower, so first-year plants set out after the soil warms run straight through summer and fall, the basis for chard's long single-planting harvest. The failure mode is premature vernalization from a too-early cold-soil sowing, the same mechanism that bolts beets.

beginner: Chard varieties are mostly about color. Fordhook Giant is the reliable white-stemmed classic and takes heat well. For a rainbow of stems, grow Bright Lights; for deep red, Ruby Red; for yellow, Bright Yellow or El Dorado. If you garden somewhere hot, Lucullus and Perpetual Spinach hold up especially well. They all grow the same way and are ready in about 50 to 60 days, with small leaves sooner.
seasoned: Chard varieties differ mainly in stalk color and leaf texture rather than growing needs. Fordhook Giant is the dependable white-stemmed standard and one of the most heat-tolerant; Lucullus and the leaf-beet type Perpetual Spinach are the choices for the hottest regions and the longest harvest. Chard is a cut-and-come-again crop rather than a succession crop, so a single stand from each sowing is harvested leaf by leaf over an extended period.

Cut leaves as the plants size up; once daytime highs push past 90°F, leaves toughen and turn bitter, so let that stand go and sow again from about mid-August to mid-September for a fall and early-winter stand that tolerates a light frost.
