beginner: Swiss chard is ready to pick when the outer leaves are about 8 to 12 inches long (or smaller for baby leaves), around 50 to 60 days after planting. Cut or snap off the outer leaves and leave the middle of the plant to keep growing, and it will produce for months from the same plant. Pick a few leaves from each plant regularly, and save the bright stalks to cook on their own, since they take a little longer than the leaves.
seasoned: Swiss chard is ready to start cutting when the outer leaves reach a usable size, roughly 8 to 12 inches long (or smaller for tender baby leaves), usually about 50 to 60 days from sowing. Harvest cut-and-come-again: snap or cut the outer leaves an inch or two above the crown and leave the central growing point, and the plant keeps generating new leaves for months. Crop regularly to keep new growth tender, and cook the colorful stalks as a separate vegetable, giving them a head start over the quicker leaves.

beginner: Swiss chard is a leafy green grown for both its big, tender leaves and its colorful, edible stalks, which come in white, gold, pink, orange, and red. It is actually the same plant species as the beet, just grown for the leaves and stems instead of a root. What makes chard special is that it handles both heat and cold better than most greens: it does not flower and turn bitter in summer the way lettuce and spinach do, so one spring planting keeps producing right through summer and fall, and in mild-winter areas it lives nearly all year. You harvest it cut-and-come-again, picking the outer leaves while the center keeps growing, so a few plants feed you for months. The rainbow-stemmed kinds are pretty enough for a flower bed, and you can cook the bright stalks like a vegetable on their own.
seasoned: Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris) is a leafy member of the goosefoot family grown for its large, tender leaves and its broad, often vividly colored edible stalks. It is the same species as the beet, selected for leaf and stem rather than root, and it shares the beet's pests, diseases, and multigerm seedball. Its defining trait is an unusual tolerance of both heat and cold: unlike lettuce and spinach, chard does not bolt in summer heat or long days (as a biennial it flowers only after a winter), so a single spring planting crops straight through the summer and well into fall, and in mild zones it overwinters for a harvest that spans much of the year. Harvested cut-and-come-again, the outer leaves picked while the crown keeps producing, one chard plant yields for months. The colorful-stemmed types such as Bright Lights are as ornamental as they are useful, and the stalks cook as a vegetable in their own right.

beginner: Arugula likes loose, rich soil with plenty of compost that holds moisture but still drains well. It is not fussy and grows in most garden soils, but steady moisture keeps the leaves mild and tender; dry, hard soil makes them hot and tough and pushes the plant to flower.
seasoned: Arugula grows in a wide range of soils but does best in a fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. As a fast leafy brassica it responds to compost worked in before sowing, which feeds quick growth and buffers the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and mild. It tolerates a fairly broad pH but leans toward 6.0 to 7.0, and keeping the soil out of the strongly acidic range also helps hold down clubroot, the brassica-family soil disease.

beginner: Arugula grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. Keeping the soil from getting too acidic also helps prevent clubroot, a cabbage-family soil disease.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0; arugula is forgiving and still does fine across roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Clemson lists 6.0 to 6.5 for the leafy greens in its arugula fact sheet. As with other brassicas, holding the soil toward neutral rather than strongly acidic also helps suppress clubroot, so a grower with clubroot history should lean to the high end.

beginner: Arugula grows fast and likes a little nitrogen for tender green leaves. Mix some compost or fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it one light feeding a couple of weeks after the seeds come up. Because the crop is so quick, you usually do not need to feed it again.
seasoned: Arugula is a fast leafy brassica that runs on nitrogen, but the crop is so quick that one light feeding is usually plenty. Work compost or a balanced fertilizer in before sowing, then side-dress lightly with nitrogen about 2 to 3 weeks after the seedlings emerge to push tender, mild leaves. Avoid heavy nitrogen late, since lush growth draws aphids and flea beetles and does not improve a crop you will cut within a few weeks.

beginner: Time to give your arugula a light feeding.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your arugula with a little nitrogen.

beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a 21-0-0 fertilizer once, when the plants are a couple of weeks old.
seasoned: High N for fast leafy growth; a light side-dress of 21-0-0 or blood meal 2 to 3 weeks after emergence. No phosphorus or potassium needed beyond a soil-test baseline; do not overfeed a 3-to-4-week crop.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer, one light feeding a few weeks after the seeds sprout.
seasoned: About a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row, side-dressed once a few weeks after emergence; for baby-leaf patches a single compost-rich bed often needs no extra feed at all.

beginner: Lots of tiny round shot holes peppering the leaves, made by tiny dark beetles that jump like fleas when you come near. Arugula is one of their favorites, and heavy damage can riddle or kill young seedlings.
seasoned: Small round shot-holes pepper the foliage and the tiny dark beetles jump when disturbed. Arugula and other mustards are highly preferred hosts, so pressure is often intense; seedlings can be stunted or killed and the holes mar the harvested leaves of a crop eaten raw.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew little pits and holes in cabbage-family leaves. They are drawn strongly to arugula and mustard and hit small seedlings hardest, since a tiny plant cannot outgrow the damage.
seasoned: Crucifer and striped flea beetles (Phyllotreta species) chew the foliage of brassicas and strongly prefer arugula and mustard; adults overwinter in debris and emerge to attack the earliest, smallest plants. Multiple generations occur through the season.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover from the day you sow, and if beetles are heavy use a spinosad spray or a kaolin clay coating. The main goal is to get the seedlings up and big fast, before the beetles riddle them.
seasoned: Floating row cover from sowing is the most effective tool; spinosad or kaolin clay help under heavy pressure. The aim is rapid establishment past the vulnerable seedling stage, so push fast growth.

beginner: Use row cover from sowing (the single best defense), keep seedlings growing fast with steady water, sow when beetles are less active, and clear nearby cabbage-family weeds. Some growers plant a sacrificial arugula patch as a trap crop.
seasoned: Exclude beetles with row cover from sowing, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and a light feed, clean up crucifer weeds and crop debris, and consider an early trap planting of arugula or mustard to divert beetles from the main crop.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, sometimes with curled, sticky leaves. The waxy gray-green cabbage aphid hides deep in the crinkles and is hard to wash out.
seasoned: Colonies of green peach aphids and the waxy gray-green cabbage aphid (Brevicoryne brassicae) on leaf undersides and tips distort the foliage; honeydew and the aphids lodged in the leaves contaminate a raw-eaten crop, and several aphids vector viruses.

beginner: Aphids are small insects that suck sap from the plant. They breed quickly, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer, and they can spread plant viruses; the cabbage aphid in particular loves brassicas like arugula.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on arugula; they reproduce rapidly, favor the soft growth excess nitrogen produces, and the cabbage aphid is especially hard to dislodge from sheltered leaf folds.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil, hitting the undersides of the leaves. Repeat every few days until they are gone, and pick before a colony lodges in the leaves.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps.

beginner: Welcome helpful bugs like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, check new growth often, and use row cover, which also keeps out flea beetles.
seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and exclude with row cover; harvest the quick crop before colonies build.

beginner: Ragged chewed holes in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plants, and dark droppings. Because you eat the leaves, even a little chewing is a problem.
seasoned: Ragged feeding holes with green or striped larvae and frass; imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth larvae feed on arugula, and on a fast leaf crop even light feeding downgrades the harvest.

beginner: Several moths and white butterflies lay eggs on cabbage-family leaves, and the caterpillars that hatch (imported cabbageworms, loopers, and small wriggling diamondback larvae) chew the foliage.
seasoned: The larvae of several brassica moths and butterflies feed on the foliage; the adults lay eggs on the leaves, and warm-region plantings see the most pressure.

beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick them and their eggs off by hand from the undersides of leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
seasoned: Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) or spinosad targeting young larvae and hand-pick where practical; repeat after rain.

beginner: Use a row cover to keep the adults from laying eggs, clean up old cabbage-family plants and weeds, and check leaf undersides for eggs and small caterpillars.
seasoned: Exclude egg-laying adults with row cover, clean up brassica debris and weed hosts, and scout leaf undersides for eggs and early instars.

beginner: Ragged holes with smooth edges chewed in low leaves, slimy trails on the leaves and soil, and worst damage in cool, damp, shady spots and after rain.
seasoned: Smooth-edged holes in low foliage with silvery slime trails, worst in cool, wet, densely planted or heavily mulched beds; a tender low salad green like arugula is highly susceptible.

beginner: Slugs and snails are soft, moisture-loving mollusks that feed at night and rasp holes in tender low greens like arugula. They thrive in damp mulch and dense, shaded plantings.
seasoned: Several slug and snail species feed nocturnally, rasping the foliage; they shelter in moist debris and mulch by day and build up in cool, wet conditions.

beginner: Hand-pick at night or after rain, set out shallow traps, and use an iron-phosphate slug bait, which is pet-safe. Reduce damp hiding places and water in the morning so the surface dries by night.
seasoned: Hand-pick after dark or rain, use shallow traps and iron-phosphate baits (pet-safe), and remove daytime shelter; morning watering lets the surface dry before they feed.

beginner: Thin and space plants for airflow, keep mulch light near the plants, clear damp debris, and water early in the day rather than at dusk.
seasoned: Reduce moisture and shelter near the plants: thin for airflow, keep mulch off the crowns, clear debris, and irrigate in the morning rather than the evening.

beginner: Pale yellow or angular patches on the tops of the leaves with a fuzzy grayish-white mold on the undersides, mostly in cool, damp, crowded conditions. Bad cases discolor and collapse the leaves.
seasoned: Angular yellow-to-brown lesions on the upper leaf surface with grayish-white sporulation beneath, spreading in cool, wet, humid weather; lesions brown and the leaves collapse. It is a leading arugula disease.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves the same cool, wet weather arugula grows in, spreading through wet leaves and splashing water. Crowded plants and long leaf wetness make it worse.
seasoned: Hyaloperonospora parasitica (the brassica downy mildew oomycete), favored by cool temperatures, long leaf wetness, and high humidity; it spreads by wind- and splash-borne spores and survives on debris.

beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the airflow so leaves dry faster, and water at the soil instead of over the plants. It is hard to stop once it gets going, so prevention matters most.
seasoned: Cultural control dominates: improve airflow, avoid overhead irrigation, and remove infected leaves and debris; there is no rescue once it is established in humid weather.

beginner: Space plants for good airflow, water at the base, choose resistant varieties where available, and rotate where you plant arugula and other brassicas.
seasoned: Widen spacing for airflow, use drip rather than overhead water, choose resistant cultivars where offered, and rotate away from brassicas for several years.

beginner: White, blister-like bumps on the undersides of the leaves, with yellow spots on top. Badly spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: White, blister-like pustules on leaf undersides with chlorotic spotting above; severe infection distorts and downgrades the foliage. A common brassica-greens disease, worse in the South.

beginner: A different mold-like disease, not a true rust, that makes white pustules on cabbage-family leaves and spreads in cool, moist weather. It can ruin a leafy crop quickly.
seasoned: The oomycete Albugo candida, favored by cool nights, mild days, and leaf wetness; it spreads by splash- and wind-dispersed spores and survives on debris and as oospores.

beginner: Remove and destroy infected leaves, improve airflow, and water at the soil line. As with downy mildew, prevention works better than trying to cure it.
seasoned: Remove infected leaves and debris, improve airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation; chemical options are limited for the home garden.

beginner: Space plants out, avoid wetting the leaves, choose resistant varieties where it is common, and rotate your planting spot.
seasoned: Grow resistant cultivars where white rust is endemic, space for airflow, use drip irrigation, and rotate away from brassicas.

beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where germination is slow.

beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the seeds are slow to come up.
seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium species attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows emergence favors them.

beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention. Pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
seasoned: No cure once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.

beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant shallowly in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up fast.
seasoned: Sow shallowly into well-drained soil when temperatures favor quick emergence, avoid overwatering, and use fresh viable seed.

beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches, sometimes with rings like a tiny target or a pale halo. Spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: Small dark lesions enlarge into circular spots, Alternaria often with concentric rings (a target look) and Cercospora as gray-brown spots with a halo; on a leaf crop even moderate spotting reduces the harvest. Favored by warm, wet conditions.

beginner: Fungi that spread in warm, wet weather and infect the leaves, leaving spots. They are worse on stressed plants and in crowded, damp plantings.
seasoned: Alternaria (A. brassicae, A. brassicicola) and Cercospora fungi infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive them.

beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and avoid wetting the leaves when you water. Start with clean seed.
seasoned: Remove spotted leaves and debris, improve airflow, and avoid overhead watering; a copper-based fungicide can help under heavy pressure.

beginner: Use clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris.
seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, rotate away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week, kept even; arugula is shallow-rooted and bolts faster and turns hotter under drought stress.

beginner: Aim for about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, a bit more when it is warm.
seasoned: Roughly 1 to 1.5 inches per week, more in warm, dry spells.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the foliage dry checks downy mildew and white rust on a crop you eat raw.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and leaves get moldy in soggy, crowded beds.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and downy mildew in crowded, constantly wet stands.

beginner: Wilting leaves that turn extra spicy and tough, and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than it should.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, hotter and tougher leaves, and faster bolting; drought stress both sharpens the flavor and triggers the seedstalk.

beginner: Arugula sprouts quickly. Keep the top of the soil damp until it comes up.
seasoned: Arugula germinates fast; keep the shallow-sown seedbed evenly moist and uncrusted through emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp, since the roots are shallow.
seasoned: Keep the seedlings evenly moist; arugula is shallow-rooted with little drought buffer.

beginner: Water evenly, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week, as the leaves grow.
seasoned: Keep even moisture through the few weeks of leaf growth at about 1 to 1.5 inches a week.

beginner: Keep the water steady while you pick leaves. If arugula dries out or the weather warms, it bolts and the leaves get much hotter and sharper, so steady watering keeps them mild.
seasoned: Steady moisture through leaf growth, and during any warm or lengthening-day spell, delays bolt and keeps the peppery bite mild; arugula turns hotter and harsher under drought stress. Cut young leaves and keep it watered for a milder, longer harvest.

beginner: Once arugula flowers the leaves get sharp and tough, and watering will not fix it (the flowers are edible, though). Resow when it is cooler for mild leaves.
seasoned: Once it bolts, the leaves sharpen and toughen and watering will not reverse it, though the flowers are edible. Resow in cooler conditions for mild leaves.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the leaves stay mild and tender and the plant does not bolt early.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps arugula growing fast, tender, and mild; dry, hot spells push it to flower and make the leaves harshly pungent.

beginner: Arugula is best planted straight in the garden from seed, because it grows so fast and does not like having its roots disturbed. Sow the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since they sprout even in cold soil and the plants handle frost. Sow again every couple of weeks, and in hot areas plant in fall through spring instead of summer, because heat keeps the seeds from sprouting well and makes the plants bolt.
seasoned: Arugula is almost always direct-sown, since it grows fast and resents root disturbance. Sow seed about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; it germinates readily even in cool soil, often in 5 to 7 days, and tolerates frost, so it can go in several weeks before the last frost. Sow a little more thickly than the final stand and thin to taste, eating the thinnings. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through spring, since warm soil above about 80°F cuts germination and lengthening warm days bolt the crop.

beginner: Other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, kale, mustard, radishes, and arugula itself, because they share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Other brassicas: cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, collards, mustard, radish, turnip, and arugula itself. They share the cabbage-family pests (flea beetles, cabbage caterpillars, aphids) and the soilborne clubroot, so following one brassica with another concentrates and builds that pressure.

beginner: Try not to grow arugula or other cabbage-family plants (broccoli, kale, cabbage, mustard, radishes) in the same spot more than about once every 3 years. They share pests like flea beetles and a soil disease called clubroot that build up when these crops keep coming back. Plant arugula after peas, beans, onions, squash, or tomatoes instead.
seasoned: Rotate arugula and its brassica relatives so they do not return to the same ground for about 3 years. The cabbage-family pest complex (flea beetles above all, plus cabbage caterpillars and aphids) and the soilborne clubroot organism build up where brassicas repeat, and arugula's quick succession plantings make it easy to keep flea beetles cycling in one bed. Follow brassicas with legumes, alliums, cucurbits, or nightshades, and keep the soil near neutral to help suppress clubroot.

beginner: Arugula flowers (bolts) quickly when it gets warm and the days get long, and the leaves turn harshly spicy and bitter. To avoid it, grow arugula in the cool parts of the year, especially fall, sow a fresh little batch every 2 to 3 weeks, water steadily, and give it some afternoon shade when it is warm. Pick it promptly, and as soon as you see a flower stalk in the middle, harvest the whole plant.
seasoned: Arugula bolts fast once it is warm and the days lengthen, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter as it does. Keep the productive window in the cool shoulders of the year: sow early in spring and crop quickly, lean on the fall crop, choose slower-bolting types or wild (Diplotaxis) rocket where heat is a problem, give light afternoon shade in warm spells, and keep moisture steady. Succession sow every 2 to 3 weeks so a bolted batch is quickly replaced, and harvest promptly at the first sign of a central stalk.

beginner: Arugula bolts (sends up a flower stalk and turns very sharp and bitter) when it gets warm and the days are long. It happens fast and is just the plant's natural cycle, not a mistake. Grow it in cool weather, pick it young, and enjoy the flowers too, which are edible and peppery. Left alone, arugula often drops seed and comes up again on its own.
seasoned: Bolting in arugula is driven by heat and lengthening days, sped by drought and crowding, and it comes on fast because the plant is so quick. Once a central seedstalk rises the leaves narrow and flood with the mustard-oil compounds that make a sharp, almost acrid pungency, so the eating window closes quickly. The flowers are edible and peppery, and one plant left to bloom feeds pollinators and self-sows readily.

beginner: Do not leave arugula out on the counter. It wilts fast in the warmth, so get it into the fridge soon after picking.
seasoned: Arugula wilts and yellows within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate it promptly after cutting; if it must sit briefly, keep it cool and out of the sun.

beginner: Store arugula unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge crisper drawer, where it keeps about a week if kept very cold. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in a loose or perforated bag in the crisper; arugula holds about 5 to 10 days near 32°F at high humidity. It is more perishable than sturdy greens like kale, so use it promptly, and wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.

beginner: Arugula is best fresh and does not freeze well for salads. If you have extra, turn it into pesto and freeze that, or blanch it briefly and freeze it to cook later.
seasoned: Arugula is a salad green and does not freeze well for raw use, losing its texture; if you have a glut, blanch briefly and freeze for cooking, or make pesto and freeze that, where its peppery bite holds up.

beginner: Arugula is best right after you pick it and does not keep long. Chill it quickly and use it within a week or so, and remember the flavor gets stronger the longer it sits.
seasoned: Quality is highest straight from the garden. Arugula is delicate and short-lived once cut, so chill it fast and use it within a week or so fresh; its peppery flavor also turns stronger and harsher in storage, another reason to eat it young and soon.

beginner: For a quick, peppery salad green, grow standard salad arugula like Roquette or the milder Astro, which are fast but flower quickly in heat. For hot weather or a longer-lasting patch, try wild arugula (sold as Sylvetta), which is slower to bolt, more intense in flavor, and can come back year after year in mild areas. Cut-leaf kinds like Surrey are great for snipping baby leaves again and again.
seasoned: Match the type to the slot. Standard salad rocket (Eruca sativa, Roquette and the like) is fastest and most pungent but bolts quickly in heat, so it suits the cool shoulders and baby-leaf cutting. Milder, broad-leaf selections like Astro give a gentler bite and quick baby leaf. For warm weather and a longer stand, wild or perennial rocket (Diplotaxis tenuifolia, sold as Sylvetta or wild arugula) is slower-growing, far slower to bolt, and more intensely flavored, and it can persist as a short-lived perennial in mild climates. Cut-leaf types like Surrey and Esmee are bred for tidy, regrowing baby-leaf patches.

beginner: Arugula is small, fast, and easygoing, so it tucks in between slower crops. It grows well next to lettuce and other quick greens, bush beans, and aromatic herbs like dill, and alliums such as onions. The main thing is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share its pests and diseases, and to watch for flea beetles, which love it.
seasoned: Most arugula companion pairings rest on space, timing, and tradition rather than measured effects. The practical ones are structural: arugula is quick and shallow-rooted, so it interplants with lettuce and other fast greens and tucks beside legumes and aromatic herbs. Aromatic herbs and alliums are the traditional scent-based deterrents for the cabbage-family pests arugula shares. The well-grounded caution is to separate arugula from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cole-crop pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect; arugula is also a flea-beetle magnet, sometimes deliberately used as a trap crop near choicer brassicas.

beginner: Beans add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy arugula can use, and the two share a cool-to-mild season without competing much.
seasoned: A legume interplant on nitrogen and structure: beans fix a little nitrogen the leafy arugula draws on, and the quick arugula uses the ground between young bean plants. Sound space and timing logic rather than a measured arugula effect.

beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low like arugula, so you can sow them together to fill a salad bed, and both like the same cool weather.
seasoned: Arugula and lettuce share a cool season, a shallow root zone, and a salad bed, so they interplant efficiently and are cut young together. A space-and-timing pairing, not a documented growth boost; the two share no major pest.

beginner: Strong-smelling herbs like dill are a classic neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their scent is said to confuse pests, and their flowers bring in helpful insects.
seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill draw the parasitoid wasps and predators that attack brassica aphids and caterpillars, and extension work pairing umbels with cole crops has shown reduced damage. Let some flower nearby; a partial-mechanism aid, not a measured arugula-specific effect.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their strong smell is thought to help put off the pests that hunt by scent.
seasoned: Alliums are the classic scent-based brassica companion, their pungency thought to mask the crop from cabbage pests that locate hosts partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, they tuck around arugula without competing. Traditional with partial mechanistic support, not an arugula-specific measured effect.

beginner: Keep arugula away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, kale, mustard, and radishes. They share the same pests and diseases, so planting them together makes flea beetles and clubroot worse.
seasoned: Planting arugula shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, kale, mustard, radish, concentrates the shared cabbage-family pests, flea beetles above all, plus cabbage caterpillars and aphids, and repeated same-family planting builds soilborne clubroot. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow. Because arugula is a strong flea-beetle draw, some growers exploit this and use it as a sacrificial trap crop away from choicer brassicas.

beginner: The first pair of little rounded leaves poking up. Arugula sprouts fast, often in under a week, even in cool soil.
seasoned: The first pair of rounded seed leaves pushing up through the soil. Arugula comes up fast, often in 3 to 7 days, even in cool soil, and germination is usually even if the surface has not dried out.

beginner: Keep the soil surface evenly moist but not soggy until the seedlings are up. Arugula sprouts well in cool soil but badly in hot soil, so sow in spring or fall, not the heat of summer.
seasoned: Keep the soil surface consistently moist but never waterlogged until seedlings are up. Arugula germinates well in cool soil but poorly in warm soil above about 80°F, so early-spring and fall sowings come up best.

seasoned: Any sprouts yet?

beginner: The first true leaves, which look like tiny versions of the grown arugula leaf. Now you can thin them.
seasoned: The first true leaves, lobed little versions of the grown leaf. Now you can tell seedlings from weeds and start thinning.

beginner: Thin the seedlings, leaving them close for baby leaves or farther apart for bigger plants, and eat the ones you pull. Watch for tiny holes from flea beetles, and use a row cover if they are bad.
seasoned: Thin to taste, dense at 1 to 3 inches for baby leaf or 4 to 6 inches for full plants, and eat the thinnings. Watch for flea beetles, which hit small seedlings hardest; row cover from sowing is the best defense.

beginner: Leaves big enough to use and the patch looking full, before any flower stalk appears. This is the productive stretch.
seasoned: Leaves reaching a useful size and the patch looking full, well before any central stalk rises. This is the short, productive window for a fast leaf crop.

beginner: Start picking the outer leaves or snipping baby leaves now. Picking often keeps new leaves coming. Keep the water steady so it does not bolt, and pick faster when it warms up.
seasoned: Start cutting outer leaves or shearing baby leaf now rather than waiting; regular light cutting keeps new growth coming. Keep moisture even to hold off bolt, and crop faster as the weather warms.

beginner: Full, tender leaves and no flower stalk in the middle yet. Once a stalk appears the good window is closing fast.
seasoned: Full, tender leaves with no central flower stalk forming. Once a stalk appears the eating window is closing fast, since arugula bolts quickly.

beginner: Take the outer leaves, or cut the whole patch about an inch above the soil so it regrows. Pick young and in the cool morning, and clear it as soon as you see a flower stalk.
seasoned: Cut-and-come-again: take outer leaves or shear the patch an inch above the crown for a second or third cutting. Pick young and in the cool morning, and clear a patch as soon as it shows a stalk.

beginner: A stalk shooting up from the middle, with the new leaves turning very sharp and bitter. This is bolting, and in arugula it happens fast.
seasoned: A central stalk shooting up, the newer leaves narrowing and turning sharply hot and bitter. This is bolting, the plant shifting to flower and seed; it comes on fast in arugula.

beginner: Pick everything good right away, since the leaves get sharper by the day. The flowers are edible and peppery, so you can enjoy them, and arugula often drops seed and comes back on its own.
seasoned: Harvest everything worth eating at once, since the flavor turns quickly. The flowers are edible and peppery; leave one plant to bloom for pollinators or to self-sow, then pull the rest and resow or give the space to a warm-season crop.

beginner: Arugula sprouts quickly, even in cold soil, but not in hot soil, so do not sow in the heat of summer. Sow it shallow and a bit thick, then thin the seedlings out, eating the ones you pull.
seasoned: Arugula germinates fast and in cool soil, but germination drops off sharply above about 80°F, which is why midsummer sowings fail. Sow shallowly, a little thicker than your final stand, and thin to taste.

beginner: Flea beetles love young arugula and chew tiny holes all over it. Covering the bed with a light row cover from the day you sow is the best way to stop them, and keeping the plants growing fast helps too.
seasoned: Flea beetles target young arugula hard, riddling seedlings with shot-holes. A floating row cover from the day you sow is the single most effective defense; keep seedlings growing fast so they outrun the damage.

beginner: Pick arugula young for the mildest taste. Bigger or heat-stressed leaves get a lot spicier. Keep the water steady so the leaves stay mild and the plants do not bolt as fast.
seasoned: Cut arugula young for the mildest flavor: leaves picked small are nutty and gentle, while older leaves and any heat stress turn them sharply pungent. Steady moisture keeps the bite mild and delays bolt.

beginner: Cut a baby-leaf patch about an inch above the soil and it grows back for another cutting or two. Pick in the cool morning and get it in the fridge right away, because it wilts quickly.
seasoned: Shear a baby-leaf patch about an inch above the crown and it will regrow for a second and often third cutting; pick in the cool morning and refrigerate at once, since arugula wilts fast.

beginner: Arugula bolts fast and the leaves get very sharp, so just pick the patch when you see a flower stalk. The flowers are edible and peppery, and the plant often reseeds itself. A fall crop bolts much less than a spring one.
seasoned: Bolting arrives fast in arugula and the leaves turn harshly hot, so do not fight it: harvest the patch at the first stalk, enjoy the edible peppery flowers, and let one plant self-sow. A fall sowing bolts far less than spring.

beginner: Each arugula plant gives a small bunch of leaves, so it is grown in patches or rows rather than as one big plant. A patch gives a few cuttings before it bolts, so sow more every couple of weeks.
seasoned: A single arugula plant yields a small rosette of leaves over a few weeks, so the crop is grown in dense patches or rows rather than per plant. Cut as baby leaf or cut-and-come-again, a bed gives two or three cuttings before heat or bolt ends it; the productive window is bounded by temperature, not a fixed calendar.

beginner: Arugula produces the most in the cool weather of fall and early spring. A spring patch gives a couple of good weeks and then bolts, but a fall crop lasts longer and can carry into winter under a cover.
seasoned: Production peaks in the cool weeks of fall and early spring. A spring patch produces hard for a couple of weeks and then ends abruptly at bolt, while the fall crop, under cooling weather and shortening days, holds longer and, with cover, into winter.

beginner: Arugula is one of the easiest, fastest crops for a beginner, with baby leaves in about 3 weeks. The trick is to sow a little every couple of weeks, pick it young, and grow it in cool weather, especially fall, so it does not bolt before you get to eat it.
seasoned: Arugula is one of the fastest, most forgiving crops for a first season: baby leaves in about 3 weeks from sowing and almost nothing to go wrong if you sow into cool weather. The key to total yield is frequent succession sowing and picking young, and leaning on the fall crop, since a spring patch sown too late bolts before it produces much.

Sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool windows, spring until heat and long days set in, and again from late summer through fall, which is the longer, more reliable run. In hot regions skip summer and succession-sow through the cool fall, winter, and spring.

beginner: Up North (zones 3 through 7), arugula is a quick spring-and-fall crop. Start sowing in early spring as soon as you can work the soil, since arugula shrugs off frost, and sow a little every 2 to 3 weeks. In the coldest zones the cool summer lets it keep going, but in the milder zones 6 and 7 the hottest weeks make it bolt and turn harsh, so take a break in midsummer and sow again for fall, which is the best crop. A last sowing under a row cover can live through winter for super-early spring greens.
seasoned: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), arugula is a fast spring-and-fall succession green built around frost. Sow as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since arugula tolerates frost and even germinates in cool soil, and sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks for a steady supply. In the coolest zones the cool summer often carries a continuous crop straight through, while in the warmer end of this band (zones 6 and 7) midsummer heat and long days bolt it, so the calendar pauses through the hottest weeks and resumes for the main fall crop. A late-summer sowing run into fall is the most reliable, and a final sowing under a row cover can overwinter for the earliest spring picking.

Arugula bolts and turns hot-flavored above about 75°F, consistent with the gap Mustard's own spring/fall split shows; sow every 2 to 3 weeks through each window and skip midsummer entirely.

beginner: In St. George you get two arugula crops. Sow seed directly outdoors from mid-February, USU Extension's earliest planting date for the area, and cut peppery baby leaves by mid-March. The spring picking stops in mid-April because arugula turns hot and bitter once the heat builds, so let the bed rest through the summer wall and sow again from mid-July through mid-August for a second, milder fall crop you can pick into September. Frost returns around November 1.
seasoned: USU Extension's St. George vegetable chart puts arugula in the earliest, hardiest planting band, February 15, just before the March 30 average last frost. At 30 days to a cut the spring sowing is ready by mid-March and finished by mid-April, since the leaves turn sharply bitter and the plants bolt once summer heat arrives; St. George reaches 100°F in June, July, and August. USU's fall-gardening guidance for the St. George area groups arugula with the other quick greens re-sown mid-July through mid-August, once the worst heat has broken, for a second cutting that runs into September ahead of the November 1 average first frost.

beginner: Arugula is a fast-growing, cool-season salad green with a peppery, mustardy flavor. It is one of the quickest things you can grow, giving baby leaves in about 3 weeks, and it handles frost and even grows through winter in mild areas. Its main quirk is that it bolts (sends up a flower stalk) very fast in heat and long days, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter when it does. So it grows best in the cool parts of the year, especially fall, and in hot places it is a fall-to-spring crop. Sow a little every couple of weeks for a steady supply. It is easy and beginner-friendly; the main pest to watch is the flea beetle, which chews tiny holes in the leaves. There is also a wild kind of arugula that is slower to bolt and even more peppery.
seasoned: Arugula (Eruca sativa), also called salad rocket or roquette, is a fast, cool-season leafy green in the mustard family (Brassicaceae), grown for its tender, peppery leaves. It is one of the quickest crops in the garden, giving baby leaves in about 3 weeks and full leaves in around a month, and it germinates readily even in cool soil and tolerates frost, so it can be sown very early and overwinters in mild zones. Its defining habit is how fast it bolts: heat above about 75°F and lengthening days send it to seed quickly, and the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter as it does, so the spring window is short, fall is the main crop, and in hot regions it is grown through the cool fall, winter, and spring. A separate wild or perennial rocket (Diplotaxis tenuifolia, sold as Sylvetta) is slower, more pungent, and far slower to bolt. Arugula is easy, succession-sown every 2 to 3 weeks, and a strong first-season choice, though flea beetles are its signature pest.

beginner: Arugula is ready to pick as soon as the leaves are big enough, often baby leaves in about 3 weeks and full leaves in around a month. Take the outer leaves a few at a time, or cut the whole patch about an inch above the soil so it grows back. Pick young and in the cool morning, and harvest it all before it flowers (bolts), because the leaves get very sharp and bitter then.
seasoned: Arugula is ready as soon as the leaves are big enough to use, often baby leaf at 2 to 3 weeks and full leaf around 30 to 40 days. Cut the outer leaves cut-and-come-again, or shear the whole patch about an inch above the crown and let it regrow for a second or third cutting. Pick young and in the cool morning, and crop fast as the weather warms, since the leaves turn sharply hot and bitter once the plant bolts.

beginner: Arugula is usually sown a bit thick, then thinned. For baby leaves you can leave it dense, about an inch or two apart; for bigger plants, thin to 4 to 6 inches. Do not waste the thinnings, they are tender baby arugula.
seasoned: Sow a little thick and thin in stages: for baby-leaf cutting, leave plants dense at 1 to 3 inches; for larger, full plants, thin to 4 to 6 inches. Eat every thinning as tender baby arugula, so thinning is just an early harvest. Crowded plants compete, stay small, and bolt sooner.

beginner: Bok choy likes loose, rich soil with plenty of compost that holds moisture but still drains well. Steady, even moisture keeps the leaf-stalks crisp and mild and keeps the plant from bolting; dry, hard soil stresses it and pushes it to flower.
seasoned: Bok choy grows best in a fertile, well-drained yet moisture-retentive loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, held at even moisture (UMN). As a fast, shallow-rooted leafy brassica it responds to compost worked in before sowing, which feeds quick growth and buffers the steady moisture that keeps the leaf-stalks crisp and tender. Uneven moisture both stresses the plant toward bolting and contributes to tipburn of the inner leaves, and keeping the soil out of the strongly acidic range also helps hold down clubroot, the brassica-family soil disease.

beginner: Bok choy grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. Keeping the soil from getting too acidic also helps prevent clubroot, a cabbage-family soil disease.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0. Bok choy is forgiving and grows well across roughly 5.5 to 7.5: UMN and NCSU both give 6.0 to 7.5 for Chinese cabbage and bok choy, while Clemson lists 5.8 to 6.5. As with other brassicas, holding the soil toward neutral rather than strongly acidic also helps suppress clubroot, so a grower with clubroot history should lean to the high end.

beginner: Bok choy grows fast and likes steady nitrogen for tender leaves and stalks. Mix some compost or a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it one light feeding a couple of weeks after the seedlings come up. Because the crop is so quick, you usually do not need to feed it much more.
seasoned: Bok choy is a fast leafy brassica that runs on nitrogen for quick, tender growth, but the crop is so quick that one or two light feedings are plenty. Work compost or a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing, then side-dress lightly with nitrogen about 2 to 3 weeks after emergence to push crisp, mild leaf-stalks. Clemson gives the cole-crop rate of 5-10-10 worked in before planting, then about 34-0-0 side-dressed; for a 30-to-50-day crop, keep it light, since lush late growth draws aphids and does little for a plant you will cut soon.

beginner: Time to give your bok choy a light feeding.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your bok choy with a little nitrogen.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then one light nitrogen feed a couple of weeks after the seedlings come up.
seasoned: High N for fast, tender leafy growth: a balanced 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 worked in before planting, then a light nitrogen side-dress such as 21-0-0, calcium nitrate, or blood meal 2 to 3 weeks after emergence. Do not overfeed a quick crop.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then one light nitrogen feed beside the plants a couple of weeks later.
seasoned: Work in 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting (Clemson), then side-dress about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 (or 1 pound per 100 feet of row) once a few weeks after emergence; a compost-rich bed of baby bok choy often needs no extra feed.

beginner: Bok choy is small, fast, and easygoing, so it tucks in between slower crops. It grows well next to lettuce and other quick greens, bush beans, and aromatic herbs like dill, and alliums such as onions. The main thing is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share its pests and diseases, and to watch for flea beetles, which love it.
seasoned: Most bok choy companion pairings rest on space, timing, and tradition rather than measured effects. The practical ones are structural: bok choy is quick and shallow-rooted, so it interplants with lettuce and other fast greens and tucks beside legumes and aromatic herbs. Aromatic herbs and alliums are the traditional scent-based deterrents for the cabbage-family pests bok choy shares. The well-grounded caution is to separate bok choy from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cole-crop pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect; bok choy is also a flea-beetle magnet, sometimes deliberately used as a trap crop near choicer brassicas.

beginner: Beans add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy bok choy can use, and the two share a cool-to-mild season without crowding each other.
seasoned: A legume interplant on nitrogen and structure: beans fix a little nitrogen the leafy bok choy draws on, and the quick bok choy uses the open ground between young bean plants. Sound space and timing logic rather than a measured bok choy effect.

beginner: Lettuce grows fast and low like bok choy, so you can sow them together to fill a salad bed, and both like the same cool weather.
seasoned: Bok choy and lettuce share a cool season, a shallow root zone, and a bed, so they interplant efficiently and are harvested young together. A space-and-timing pairing, not a documented growth boost; the two share no major pest.

beginner: Strong-smelling herbs like dill are a classic neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their scent is said to confuse pests, and their flowers bring in helpful insects.
seasoned: Aromatic umbels like dill are a traditional brassica companion, their flowers drawing the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack brassica aphids and caterpillars. Let some flower nearby; treat it as a partial-mechanism aid rather than a measured bok-choy-specific effect.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cabbage-family plants; their strong smell is thought to help put off the pests that hunt by scent.
seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage-family pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, they tuck around young bok choy without competing for much. A low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

beginner: Keep bok choy away from other cabbage-family plants like cabbage, broccoli, kale, mustard, turnips, and radishes. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them makes flea beetles, caterpillars, and clubroot worse.
seasoned: Planting bok choy shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, cabbage, broccoli, kale, mustard, turnip, radish, concentrates the family's shared pests (flea beetles above all, plus cabbage aphids, cabbageworms, loopers, diamondback moths, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

beginner: Lots of tiny round shot holes peppering the leaves, made by tiny dark beetles that jump like fleas when you come near. Bok choy is one of their very favorite plants, and heavy damage can riddle or kill young seedlings.
seasoned: Small round shotholes pepper the foliage and the tiny dark beetles jump when disturbed. Bok choy and other mustards are highly preferred hosts, so pressure is often intense; seedlings can be stunted or killed and the holes mar the leaf-stalks of a crop eaten raw or lightly cooked.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew little pits and holes in cabbage-family leaves. They are drawn strongly to bok choy and mustards and hit small seedlings hardest, since a tiny plant cannot outgrow the damage.
seasoned: Crucifer flea beetles (Phyllotreta species) chew the foliage of brassicas and strongly prefer bok choy and mustard; adults overwinter in debris and emerge to attack the earliest, smallest plants, with multiple generations through the season.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover from the day you sow, and if beetles are heavy use a spinosad spray. The main goal is to get the seedlings up and growing fast, before the beetles riddle them.
seasoned: Floating row cover from sowing is the most effective tool; spinosad helps under heavy pressure. The aim is rapid establishment past the vulnerable seedling stage, so push fast growth.

beginner: Use row cover from sowing, the single best defense, keep seedlings growing fast with steady water, and clear nearby cabbage-family weeds. Some growers plant a sacrificial mustard patch as a trap crop.
seasoned: Exclude beetles with row cover from sowing, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and a light feed, clean up crucifer weeds and crop debris, and consider an early trap planting of mustard to divert beetles from the main crop.

beginner: Clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked deep into the folds where the leaf-stalks meet, where they are very hard to wash out. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and lodges deep in the leaf-stalk folds, where it contaminates the harvested plant with insects and honeydew and is very hard to clean. Clemson notes aphid feeding yellows, stunts, curls, and wrinkles the foliage and brings sooty mold, with pressure heaviest on the fall crop.

beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage-family plants and hide down in the stalk crevices, which is the part you eat.
seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid (with green peach aphid also present), sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; contamination of the harvested stalks with aphids and sticky honeydew is usually the real problem rather than plant stunting.

beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves and the crevices with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, which eat aphids.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides and the stalk crevices; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (parasitoid wasps, hoverflies, ladybugs).

beginner: Check the growing center and the stalk crevices often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen, since soft growth draws them, use row cover, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
seasoned: Scout growing tips and the stalk crevices weekly and catch infestations before aphids lodge in the plant. Avoid excess nitrogen, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

beginner: Ragged chewed holes in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plants, and dark droppings. Because you eat the leaves and stalks, even a little chewing and mess is a problem.
seasoned: Ragged feeding holes with green or striped larvae and frass; the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth larvae feed on bok choy (UMN lists all three), and on a fast leaf-and-stalk crop even light feeding and contamination downgrade the harvest.

beginner: Several white butterflies and moths lay eggs on cabbage-family leaves, and the caterpillars that hatch (imported cabbageworms, loopers, and small wriggling diamondback larvae) chew the foliage.
seasoned: The larvae of several brassica moths and butterflies feed on the foliage; the adults lay eggs on the leaves, and warm-region plantings see the most pressure. The diamondback moth is often the most numerous in the South.

beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or pick them and their eggs off by hand from the undersides of leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
seasoned: Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad targeting young larvae and hand-pick where practical; repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down.

beginner: Use a row cover to keep the adults from laying eggs, clean up old cabbage-family plants and weeds, and check leaf undersides for eggs and small caterpillars.
seasoned: Exclude egg-laying adults with row cover, clean up brassica debris and weed hosts, and scout leaf undersides for eggs and early instars.

beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet spring soil.
seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment (UMN lists cabbage maggots among bok choy's pests).

beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp weather, so spring transplants are most at risk.
seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.

beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.

beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop pale spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs brightly marked black-and-orange or black-and-red feed with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave pale stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region brassica specialist (Clemson).

beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.

beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped eggs laid in rows, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap or neem helps where pressure is severe.

beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

beginner: Ragged holes with smooth edges chewed in the low leaves and stalks, slimy trails on the plant and soil, and worst damage in cool, damp, shady spots and after rain.
seasoned: Smooth-edged holes in low foliage and tender stalks with silvery slime trails, worst in cool, wet, densely planted or heavily mulched beds; a succulent low green like bok choy is highly susceptible (NCSU lists slugs and snails).

beginner: Slugs and snails are soft, moisture-loving mollusks that feed at night and rasp holes in tender low greens like bok choy. They thrive in damp mulch and dense, shaded plantings.
seasoned: Several slug and snail species feed nocturnally, rasping the foliage; they shelter in moist debris and mulch by day and build up in cool, wet conditions.

beginner: Hand-pick at night or after rain, set out shallow traps, and use an iron-phosphate slug bait, which is pet-safe. Reduce damp hiding places and water in the morning so the surface dries by night.
seasoned: Hand-pick after dark or rain, use shallow traps and iron-phosphate baits (pet-safe), and remove daytime shelter; morning watering lets the surface dry before they feed.

beginner: Thin and space plants for airflow, keep mulch light near the plants, clear damp debris, and water early in the day rather than at dusk.
seasoned: Reduce moisture and shelter near the plants: thin for airflow, keep mulch off the crowns, clear debris, and irrigate in the morning rather than the evening.

beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.

beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and infects most readily in acidic soils below about pH 6.5.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil from being too acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.

beginner: Don't grow bok choy or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (UMN advises up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor and spot the leaves and stalks.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors and spots the leaves and stalks. Bok choy's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves the cool, wet weather bok choy grows in, spreading through wet leaves and splashing water. Crowded plants and long leaf wetness make it worse.
seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora brassicae) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it (Clemson).

beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and water at the soil instead of from above. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp, so prevention matters most.
seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.

beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil line, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot it.
seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black (Clemson); the disease moves through the vascular system and can rot the plant. Often the most serious brassica disease in warm, wet weather, and UMN lists it among bok choy's diseases.

beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.

beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.

beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants (a hot-water seed treatment helps), rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

beginner: Small dark spots on the leaves that grow into round patches, often with rings like a tiny target. Bok choy is especially prone to it, and spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: Brown circular leaf spots with characteristic concentric rings (target spots) that enlarge and coalesce (Clemson); on a leaf crop even moderate spotting downgrades the harvest. Clemson notes Chinese cabbage and bok choy are more susceptible to Alternaria than common cabbage, and UMN lists it among bok choy's diseases.

beginner: A fungus that spreads in warm, wet weather and infects the leaves, leaving spots. It is worse on crowded, damp plantings and comes in on infected seed.
seasoned: Alternaria fungi (A. brassicicola, A. brassicae) infect brassica foliage, spreading by spores in wind and splashing water; infected seed, crop debris, and long leaf wetness drive them.

beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves and old plant debris, improve airflow so leaves dry quickly, and avoid wetting the leaves when you water. Start with clean seed.
seasoned: Remove spotted leaves and crop debris immediately, improve airflow, and avoid overhead watering; a copper-based fungicide can help under heavy pressure.

beginner: Use clean seed, rotate away from brassicas, space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris after harvest.
seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, rotate away from brassicas, space for airflow, water at the soil line, and clear crop debris that harbors spores after harvest.

beginner: White, blister-like bumps on the undersides of the leaves, with yellow spots on top. Badly spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: White, blister-like pustules on leaf undersides with chlorotic spotting above; severe infection distorts and downgrades the foliage. A common brassica-greens disease, listed among bok choy's problems by NCSU and worse in mild, moist conditions.

beginner: A mold-like disease, not a true rust, that makes white pustules on cabbage-family leaves and spreads in cool, moist weather. It can ruin a leafy crop quickly.
seasoned: The oomycete Albugo candida, favored by cool nights, mild days, and leaf wetness; it spreads by splash- and wind-dispersed spores and survives on debris and as oospores.

beginner: Remove and destroy infected leaves, improve airflow, and water at the soil line. As with downy mildew, prevention works better than trying to cure it.
seasoned: Remove infected leaves and debris, improve airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation; chemical options are limited for the home garden.

beginner: Space plants out, avoid wetting the leaves, choose resistant varieties where it is common, and rotate your planting spot.
seasoned: Grow resistant cultivars where white rust is endemic, space for airflow, use drip irrigation, and rotate away from brassicas.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week.
seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept as even as possible; bok choy is shallow-rooted and bolts faster and turns bitter under drought stress (UMN).

beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is warm.
seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week (UMN: about 1 inch of rainfall a week is good), more in warm, dry spells while the plants are sizing up.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible to keep foliage dry and discourage leaf disease.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp, and seedlings may rot at the base.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; bok choy dislikes waterlogged soil, which invites damping-off in seedlings and crown and bacterial soft rot in cold, wet ground.

beginner: Wilting leaves that turn tougher and stronger-tasting, and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than it should.
seasoned: Wilting and stalled growth, then tougher, more pungent leaf-stalks and faster bolting; drought stress is a direct bolting trigger and also worsens tipburn of the inner leaves.

beginner: Keep the soil or tray damp while the seeds come up, without letting the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed or tray surface evenly moist through germination; brassica seed is shallow and should not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp as they grow. Bok choy has shallow roots, so keep the top of the soil damp.
