beginner: Sweet potatoes want loose, well-drained, sandy or loamy soil that the swelling storage roots can push through easily. Light soil on raised ridges or mounds is ideal, because it drains well and gives the roots room to grow smooth and long. Heavy, wet clay is the thing to avoid: it stays soggy, rots the roots, and forces them into short, knobby shapes. If your soil is heavy, build up a ridge or a raised bed of loose mix, which also warms up faster in spring. Keep the soil slightly acidic, about pH 5.8 to 6.5. Go easy on nitrogen and fresh manure, which grow lots of leafy vine and few roots.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes yield best in loose, friable, well-drained sandy loam worked into raised ridges or mounds, which give the developing storage roots room to expand and keep them out of standing water. A light, warm soil produces the longest, smoothest roots; cold, heavy, poorly drained clay stays wet, rots roots, and produces short and misshapen ones, and is best improved with organic matter or replaced with a built-up ridge or raised bed. Hold the soil slightly acidic, roughly pH 5.8 to 6.5. Keep nitrogen modest and avoid fresh manure: rich, high-nitrogen ground drives rampant vine growth at the expense of roots. Even, moderate moisture in free-draining soil is the goal, never waterlogged ground.

beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Sweet potatoes like it slightly acidic, about 5.8 to 6.5, which is close to what most vegetables want. They are not fussy and will grow from about 5.0 up to nearly neutral, so you rarely need to change your soil much. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number, and if your soil is very alkaline, mixing in compost helps. Do not overdo lime.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes grow best in slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 5.8 to 6.5 (University of Georgia gives 6.0 to 6.5). They are adaptable and will crop from about 5.0 up toward neutral, so pH is rarely the limiting factor. Where soil pox and Streptomyces soil rot are a problem on susceptible varieties, growers avoid pushing the pH high and lean on resistant cultivars rather than heavy liming. Amend very alkaline ground with organic matter and confirm your starting point with a soil test before planting.

beginner: Sweet potatoes do not need much feeding, and too much of the wrong kind backfires. Mix a low-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 into the ridge before you plant, then feed once more about a month after setting the slips. Do not pile on high-nitrogen fertilizer or fresh manure: that grows a jungle of leafy vine and hardly any sweet potatoes underneath. A little compost worked into the bed is the safe way to enrich it.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes are light feeders and specifically want restrained nitrogen. University of Georgia suggests working in about 30 pounds of 5-10-10 per 1,000 square feet before planting, then side-dressing roughly 4 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 feet of row about 4 to 6 weeks after transplanting. Favor a low-nitrogen, higher-potassium ratio: too much nitrogen (and fresh manure) grows lush, sprawling vine and few storage roots, while adequate potassium supports root sizing and quality.

beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Sweet potatoes do best with a low first number, like 5-10-10, not a high-nitrogen feed. Too much nitrogen grows leaves and vines instead of sweet potatoes, so use a low-nitrogen fertilizer and some compost.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes are light feeders that want low nitrogen and good potassium. A blend such as 5-10-10 worked into the ridge before planting covers most home soils. Excess nitrogen drives vine at the expense of roots, and fresh manure has the same effect, so lean on a low-nitrogen fertilizer and compost rather than a balanced or high-nitrogen feed.

beginner: Mix in about 30 pounds of 5-10-10 per 1,000 square feet before planting, then side-dress lightly about a month later. Go easy: more fertilizer, especially nitrogen, grows more leaves, not more sweet potatoes.
seasoned: Work about 30 pounds of 5-10-10 per 1,000 square feet into the ridge before planting (UGA), then side-dress about 4 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 feet of row roughly 4 to 6 weeks after transplanting. Keep nitrogen low; excess nitrogen grows vine at the expense of storage roots.

beginner: Sweet potatoes are easygoing and take up a lot of ground with their sprawling vines, so companions are mostly about using the edges of the bed. Bush beans and other legumes are a sensible neighbor because they add nitrogen to the soil. The main thing to avoid is crowding them next to other sprawling vine crops like squash and pumpkins, which fight for the same space and sunlight. Do not trust every companion chart online; many of their claims have never been tested.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes are undemanding neighbors but greedy for space, since a single plant can run vines many feet in every direction. The best-grounded pairing is with legumes (bush beans, southern peas), which fix nitrogen and share the bed without heavy competition. Aromatic herbs are a traditional edge planting. The clearest practical avoids are other rampant vine crops, squash, pumpkins, and melons, which compete for the same ground and light. Most companion-chart claims for sweet potato are folklore; treat them with healthy skepticism, since university reviews find little evidence behind most of them.

beginner: Beans are legumes that pull nitrogen from the air and leave some in the soil, which suits sweet potatoes since they want only modest nitrogen. Bush beans stay compact and can share the edge of the bed without fighting the vines for space.
seasoned: Bush beans and other legumes are a sensible sweet potato neighbor: they fix nitrogen and, being compact and upright, do not compete hard with the ground-running vines. The nitrogen contribution is a real mechanism; treat the pairing as a grounded tradition rather than a measured yield effect.

beginner: Some gardeners plant strong-smelling herbs around the edge of the sweet potato patch in the hope of confusing pests. It is a traditional idea rather than a proven one, but the herbs use the border space the vines do not need early on.
seasoned: Aromatic herbs at the border are a traditional pest-confusion planting with no controlled evidence behind it for sweet potato. Recorded as hedged tradition; the concrete value is filling edge space the vines reach only later in the season.

beginner: These are all big, sprawling vine crops, just like sweet potatoes. Grown side by side they smother each other and fight for the same sunlight and ground, so give each its own space in the garden.
seasoned: Cucurbits (squash, pumpkins, melons) are rampant ground-running vines like sweet potato, so interplanting them means two sprawling crops competing for the same ground and light. This is a habit-based space conflict, not a shared-disease risk, and the fix is simply separate beds.

beginner: Small holes and dark, spongy tunnels inside the sweet potatoes, which you usually find only when you dig or slice them. Even a little feeding makes the roots taste bitter and smell off, so they are no longer good to eat. The beetle itself is a slim, ant-like weevil with a long snout, reddish legs, and a shiny blue-black body. It is the worst sweet potato pest, especially in the Deep South.
seasoned: Small holes and dark, spongy tunnels running through the storage roots, found when you dig or cut them. Even light feeding triggers a chemical reaction that gives the roots a bitter taste and an off, turpentine-like odor, ruining them for eating. The adult is a slender, ant-like weevil, about a quarter inch long, with a dark head and snout, reddish legs, and a metallic blue-black body; you may see chewing on stems and leaves. This is the single most serious pest of sweet potato, worst in the Deep South and Gulf.

beginner: A small weevil called the sweet potato weevil. Its grubs tunnel through the sweet potatoes and stems, and the plant reacts by turning bitter, so even lightly damaged roots are ruined. It rides in on infested slips and survives in leftover sweet potatoes in the ground, and it keeps damaging the crop even after harvest in storage.
seasoned: The sweet potato weevil (Cylas formicarius, family Brentidae). Larvae do the principal damage by mining tunnels through the storage roots (and stems), leaving them riddled with cavities, spongy, and darkened; the feeding induces bitter terpenes even at low levels. It breeds continuously in warm climates, spreads mainly on infested slips and in leftover roots, and continues to damage the crop in storage.

beginner: You cannot fix sweet potatoes that are already tunneled, so throw them out. The whole game is prevention: plant only certified weevil-free slips, and clean up every leftover or volunteer sweet potato in the ground after harvest, because the weevil lives on in them. Dig your crop on time instead of leaving it in the soil, and do not plant next to last year's bed.
seasoned: There is no rescue for tunneled roots; discard them. Control is prevention: start only with certified weevil-free slips, and practice strict sanitation, removing and destroying every leftover, cull, and volunteer root that can harbor the weevil between crops. Harvest promptly once the crop matures rather than leaving roots in infested soil, and keep new plantings away from last year's beds and from stored roots.

beginner: Start with certified weevil-free slips, not saved sweet potatoes. Move the patch to a new spot each year, well away from where sweet potatoes grew before and away from where you store them. After you dig, clean up every leftover and volunteer root, because the weevil survives in them. Harvest on time rather than leaving the crop in the ground.
seasoned: Buy certified, weevil-free slips rather than saving your own or using field-run roots. Rotate sweet potatoes well away from last year's beds and from any sweet potato storage, since the weevil moves only short distances. Remove all volunteer and cull roots after harvest, harvest promptly, and in badly infested areas grow on a strict rotation with a fallow break. Certified slips plus sanitation carry nearly all of the control.

beginner: Narrow holes and shallow tracks drilled into the sweet potatoes, found when you dig them. They are made by hard, shiny soil worms (wireworms) and the grubs of cucumber and flea beetles. You do not see anything above ground; you find the little tunnels and pits at harvest, and damaged roots do not store as well.
seasoned: Narrow holes and shallow, winding grooves bored straight into the storage roots, leaving pinhole punctures and tracks that downgrade quality and open the door to storage rots. The culprits are slender, shiny, hard-bodied wireworms (click beetle larvae) plus the larvae of cucumber beetles and flea beetles (the wireworm, Diabrotica, Systena complex). There are no useful aboveground signs; the damage is found at harvest.

beginner: Wireworms are the larvae of click beetles; they live in the soil for years and are worst in beds that were lawn, grass, or corn not long ago. The larvae of cucumber beetles and flea beetles do similar damage, moving into the soil to nibble the sweet potatoes as they grow.
seasoned: Wireworms are click beetle larvae that live in the soil for several years and are most numerous in ground recently in sod, grass, or corn. The same root-scarring complex includes larvae of spotted and banded cucumber beetles (Diabrotica) and flea beetles (Systena), which move into the soil to feed on the developing roots through the season.

beginner: You cannot fix roots that are already tunneled, so cut out the bad spots and eat those first instead of storing them. Dig the crop on time rather than leaving it in the ground, where the worms keep boring, and keep grassy weeds down.
seasoned: There is no rescue for scarred roots; trim damaged areas and use those roots first rather than storing them. Harvest promptly once the crop matures rather than leaving roots in infested soil, where feeding accumulates. Keeping the ground worked and free of grassy weeds reduces the habitat these larvae favor.

beginner: Do not plant sweet potatoes in a bed that was grass, lawn, or corn in the last year or two, where wireworms are worst. Rotate your crops, work the soil, pull grassy weeds, and dig on time. If wireworms keep ruining a bed, use a raised bed with clean soil.
seasoned: Avoid planting sweet potatoes in ground that was recently pasture, lawn, or corn, where wireworm numbers peak; extend the interval between grass and a root crop. Rotate, keep the soil well worked, control grassy weeds, and harvest on time. Where wireworm history is bad, grow elsewhere or in clean raised-bed soil.

beginner: Lots of tiny holes in the leaves, as if peppered with shot, made by little dark beetles that hop away when you come near. Young slips are hurt most; big, healthy vines shrug it off. The grubs in the soil can also scar the sweet potatoes.
seasoned: Tiny dark beetles that jump when disturbed and chew many small round shot-holes in the leaves. Heavy early feeding on young transplants stunts growth; the soil-dwelling larvae also scar the developing storage roots. Established, vigorously running plants usually outgrow light foliage feeding.

beginner: Small beetles called flea beetles that spend winter nearby and jump onto young sweet potato plants. They do the most harm to freshly set slips and in warm, dry spells, and their grubs can scar the roots underground.
seasoned: Several species of small flea beetles that overwinter nearby and move onto young sweet potato foliage in spring and early summer. They are worst on small, slow transplants and in warm, dry weather; their larvae contribute to the root-scarring complex below ground.

beginner: Keep young slips growing strong with steady water and they usually outgrow the damage as the vines take off. A row cover protects them early on, and clearing weeds and old plant debris takes away their winter hiding spots.
seasoned: Healthy, well-watered transplants usually outgrow flea beetle feeding once the vines run. Floating row cover protects young plants during the vulnerable first weeks; remove it as the vines begin to sprawl. Clearing weeds and old crop debris reduces the shelter they overwinter in.

beginner: Move the patch to a new spot, pull weeds, and cover the young slips until they are established and the vines start to run. Plants that are well watered handle flea beetles much better than struggling ones.
seasoned: Rotate away from last year's beds, keep the area weed-free, and protect freshly set slips with row cover until they are established and running. Vigorous, evenly watered transplants tolerate feeding far better than stressed ones.

beginner: Tiny white flying insects that scatter in a cloud when you brush the leaves, clustered underneath with a sticky film. Their feeding is minor, but they can pass on plant viruses that mottle and curl the leaves and cut your harvest. A plant that catches a virus will not get better.
seasoned: Clouds of tiny white, moth-like insects that lift off the foliage when disturbed, clustered on leaf undersides with sticky honeydew and sooty mold. The bigger problem is not their feeding but the viruses they transmit (such as sweet potato feathery mottle virus and sweet potato leaf curl virus), which mottle, curl, and stunt the foliage and erode yield over time; virus-infected plants do not recover.

beginner: Whiteflies are tiny sap-sucking insects, and as they move from plant to plant they carry sweet potato viruses. The viruses, more than the bugs, are the real concern, which is why it is best to plant certified, disease-tested slips instead of saving your own.
seasoned: Whiteflies colonize sweet potato foliage and, as they move plant to plant, transmit sweet potato viruses. Virus pressure, not the feeding itself, is the main reason to manage them, and it is the reason growers are advised to start from certified, virus-tested slips rather than saved or field-run material.

beginner: Plant certified, disease-tested slips so the patch starts clean. A few whiteflies are fine, because helpful bugs usually keep them in check; for heavy clusters, spray them off with water or use insecticidal soap. Pull and throw away any plant that clearly has a virus.
seasoned: Start with certified, virus-tested slips to keep virus out of the patch. Tolerate light whitefly numbers, since beneficial insects often control them; a strong spray of water or insecticidal soap knocks down heavy colonies on the leaf undersides. Remove and destroy any plant showing clear virus symptoms.

beginner: Buy certified slips, avoid harsh sprays that kill the helpful bugs, keep weeds down, and pull out any virus-looking plant right away. Do not save slips from a patch that had virus, because it comes back with them.
seasoned: Use certified slips, encourage beneficial insects by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays, control nearby weeds that host whiteflies and virus, and rogue out virus-symptomatic plants promptly. Do not save and replant slips from a patch that showed virus, since it carries over.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and wilt, often on one side of the plant, and the vine is stunted; if you slit a stem near the base you see brown streaks inside. Badly affected plants wilt and die before making sweet potatoes. It usually comes in on infected slips or from the soil.
seasoned: Yellowing and wilting that starts on the lower leaves and progresses up the vine, often on one side, with stunting; a lengthwise cut of the stem near the base shows a brown, discolored streak in the water-conducting tissue. Plants may collapse before making a crop. It moves up from infected slips or through the soil.

beginner: A soil fungus (Fusarium oxysporum) that gets into the roots and stem and clogs the plant's plumbing. It lives in the soil for years and rides in on infected slips, and it builds up if you grow sweet potatoes in the same spot again and again.
seasoned: The soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum, which enters through the roots and stem base and plugs the vascular tissue. It survives for years in the soil and is carried on infected slips, so it builds up where sweet potatoes are grown repeatedly in the same ground.

beginner: You cannot cure an infected plant, so pull it and throw it away (do not compost it). There is no spray fix; you prevent it with clean slips, resistant varieties, and rotating the bed.
seasoned: There is no cure for an infected plant; remove and destroy it. Management is preventive and variety-based: it is controlled by clean slips, resistant cultivars, and rotation, not by a spray.

beginner: Plant certified, disease-free slips and choose a wilt-resistant variety if this has been a problem. Do not grow sweet potatoes in the same bed year after year, and never save slips from a patch that wilted.
seasoned: Start with certified, disease-free slips and grow Fusarium-resistant varieties (such as Sumor or other wilt-resistant releases) where the disease occurs. Rotate sweet potatoes out of an infected bed for several years, and do not save slips from a patch that showed wilt.

beginner: Plants that are stunted and wilt easily even with water, and sweet potatoes that come up cracked, bumpy, and rough-skinned with little knots on them. The damage is worst in sandy soil and hot regions. You usually see it clearly only when you dig the roots.
seasoned: Stunted, off-color, wilt-prone vines above ground, and below ground storage roots that are cracked, bumpy, and galled, with small knots and rough, split skin that downgrade quality and storage. The southern root-knot nematode is the main species, and damage is worst in sandy soils and warm regions.

beginner: A microscopic soil roundworm (the southern root-knot nematode) that attacks the roots and makes them crack and knot. It lives in the soil and feeds on many crops, so it builds up when you grow the same kinds of plants in one spot over and over.
seasoned: The southern root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne incognita), a microscopic soil roundworm that invades the roots, causing galling and the cracked, bumpy roots that grade out. It persists in the soil and on many hosts, so it builds up where susceptible crops are grown repeatedly.

beginner: You cannot fix roots that are already cracked and knotted. Instead, prevent it: grow a nematode-resistant variety, rotate the bed to different crops, and build up the soil with compost. In hot climates, covering moist soil with clear plastic through the summer can knock the numbers down.
seasoned: There is no rescue for galled, cracked roots. Management is preventive: grow nematode-resistant varieties, rotate to non-host or less-susceptible crops, and keep the soil high in organic matter. Solarizing the bed in the hot months and cover cropping can lower populations over time.

beginner: Grow a nematode-resistant variety like Centennial or Covington, rotate your crops so sweet potatoes and their susceptible cousins are not in the same bed each year, and add plenty of compost. Start with certified, clean slips.
seasoned: Choose root-knot-resistant varieties (such as Centennial, Covington, or other resistant releases), rotate away from susceptible hosts on a multi-year cycle, and raise soil organic matter. Start with certified, clean slips so you do not introduce new populations.

beginner: Dark, sunken, round spots on the sweet potatoes, firm and greenish-black to brown, and the affected part can taste bitter. It also shows as dark patches on the lower stems. It gets worse in storage and comes in on infected slips or from the soil.
seasoned: Round, dark, sunken lesions on the storage roots that are firm and greenish-black to dark brown, sometimes with a bitter taste in the affected tissue; on the lower stems it shows as dark cankers. It spreads in storage and in the field from infected slips and contaminated soil, and it is a major cause of cull and storage loss.

beginner: A fungus (Ceratocystis fimbriata) that gets into the roots and stems through cuts and bruises, lives in the soil and on old plant debris, and rides in on infected slips. It likes warm, damp conditions and keeps spreading on stored sweet potatoes.
seasoned: The fungus Ceratocystis fimbriata, which infects roots and stems through wounds, survives in soil and crop debris, and is spread on infected slips and by handling. Warmth and moisture favor it, and it continues to develop on stored roots.

beginner: You cannot cure an infected sweet potato, so throw out affected ones and never store damaged roots. The fix is prevention: clean slips, gentle handling, curing right after harvest, and keeping tools and bins clean.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected roots; discard them and do not store blemished ones. Management is preventive: clean slips, careful handling to avoid wounds, prompt curing, and sanitation.

beginner: Use certified, disease-free slips, rotate the bed, and handle the sweet potatoes gently so you do not bruise them, since the fungus enters through cuts. Cure the crop right after digging and clean up leftover roots.
seasoned: Start with certified, disease-free slips from clean stock, rotate out of infected beds, handle roots gently to avoid the wounds the fungus enters through, and cure the crop promptly after harvest. Discard cull and volunteer roots that carry the fungus over.

beginner: Scurf is dark brown to black blotches on the skin of the sweet potato; it does not rot the inside, but it makes the roots look poor and dry out faster in storage. Soft rot turns bruised or too-cold roots into a soft, wet, smelly mush in the bin. Both are worst on damaged roots that were not cured or were stored wrong.
seasoned: Scurf shows as brown to blackish blotches on the skin surface that do not penetrate the flesh; it is a cosmetic, skin-quality problem that also increases moisture loss and shrinkage in storage. Bacterial and fungal soft rots turn wounded or chilled roots into a soft, wet, sometimes foul mush in storage. Both are worst on bruised, poorly cured, or improperly stored roots.

beginner: Scurf is a skin fungus that comes in on infected slips and lives in the soil. Soft rot is caused by bacteria and fungi that get into bruised roots, especially when the sweet potatoes were not cured or were stored too cold or too wet.
seasoned: Scurf is caused by the fungus Monilochaetes infuscans, carried on infected slips and in soil, and confined to the skin. Storage soft rots are caused by bacteria and fungi (including Rhizopus) that enter through wounds and are favored by bruising, poor curing, and cold or damp storage.

beginner: You cannot fix scurf or soft rot. Scurfy sweet potatoes are still fine to eat once peeled, but soft, rotting ones should be thrown out. Prevent both with clean slips, gentle handling, curing, and proper warm storage.
seasoned: There is no rescue for scurfed or rotting roots; scurfed ones are safe to eat after peeling, but soft-rotted ones are discarded. Management is preventive: clean slips, careful handling, prompt curing, and correct warm storage.

beginner: Plant certified, clean slips, rotate the bed, and be gentle with the sweet potatoes so you do not bruise them. Cure them warm and humid right after digging so the skins heal, then store them warm (not in the fridge), and never store damaged roots.
seasoned: Use certified, scurf-free slips, rotate out of infected beds, and handle roots gently to avoid wounds. Cure the crop warm and humid right after harvest to heal skins, then store warm (never cold or wet), and do not store bruised or diseased roots.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly, moderately damp, especially right after planting the slips and later while the sweet potatoes are sizing up. Give about 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, in fewer but deeper waterings. Once the vines are growing well the plants handle dry spells fairly well, but letting the soil go dry and then soaking it while the roots form makes them crack. Cut back on water in the last few weeks before you dig.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes want even, moderate moisture, especially while the slips establish and again while the storage roots are sizing. Aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings. Ease off water in the last few weeks before harvest so the roots do not split and the skins firm up.

beginner: Grow sweet potatoes from slips, which are rooted sprouts. beginner: Pick a variety for your area and how long your season is. In cooler, shorter-season gardens, choose the fastest kinds (Georgia Jet, Beauregard, Centennial) and warm the soil with black plastic. Where summers are long, bigger keepers like Jewel and Covington do well and store for months. If nematodes are a problem, pick a resistant variety like Covington or Centennial. For a pot or a small bed, the compact bush type Vardaman is ideal. There are also white, purple-skinned Japanese, and purple-fleshed types to try. Always buy certified disease-free slips, not sprouts off a grocery-store sweet potato.
seasoned: Choose by maturity and your climate. In short-season and northern gardens, lean on the fastest orange types (Georgia Jet, Beauregard, Centennial) and warm the soil with black plastic. Where the season is long, higher-yielding keepers like Jewel and Covington size up and store well. Covington and Centennial carry useful root-knot nematode resistance, and Sumor is a Fusarium-wilt-resistant option where that disease occurs. For containers or tight beds, the compact bush type Vardaman saves space. Beyond the standard orange types, there are pale-fleshed heirlooms, purple-skinned Japanese types (Murasaki), and deep-purple-fleshed varieties. Always start from certified disease-free and weevil-free slips.

beginner: Do not grow sweet potatoes where you grew sweet potatoes in the last few years, because soil diseases and the sweet potato weevil pile up. Also avoid beds that were lawn, grass, or corn recently, where wireworms live and damage the roots, and skip beds with fresh manure or lots of nitrogen, which grow leaves instead of roots. Wait about 3 to 4 years before sweet potatoes go back in a bed.
seasoned: Do not plant sweet potatoes where sweet potatoes grew recently, which builds up soilborne Fusarium wilt, black rot, scurf, and the sweet potato weevil. Also avoid following ground recently in pasture, lawn, or corn, where wireworms are numerous and scar the roots, and avoid heavily manured or high-nitrogen beds, which grow vine over roots. Where root-knot nematode is present, keep sweet potatoes out of beds that grew other susceptible hosts. The standard guideline is a 3 to 4 year gap before sweet potatoes return to a bed.

beginner: Move your sweet potatoes to a different spot each year and do not put them back in the same bed for about 3 to 4 years. This keeps soil diseases, nematodes, and the sweet potato weevil from building up. Planting after beans or peas is great, since those add nitrogen. Avoid beds that were just lawn, grass, or corn, where wireworms live.
seasoned: Rotate sweet potatoes on a 3 to 4 year cycle, keeping them out of a bed for several seasons to break the buildup of Fusarium wilt, black rot, scurf, root-knot nematode, and the sweet potato weevil. Following a legume (which adds nitrogen) or a clean, non-host crop is ideal. Avoid planting into ground recently in sod, grass, or corn, which harbors wireworms, and avoid heavily manured beds, which favor rampant vine and soft rots.

beginner: After curing, keep sweet potatoes in a cool but not cold spot, ideally around 55 to 60°F, in the dark with some airflow, where they last for months. A normal warm room is fine for a couple of weeks but shortens their life, so keep a few on the counter and store the rest somewhere cooler like a pantry or cellar.
seasoned: Once cured, sweet potatoes are best kept at warm room-to-cellar temperatures, roughly 55 to 60°F in a dark, well-ventilated spot, where they hold for months. Ordinary heated-room temperatures (68 to 75°F) are fine for a few weeks but shorten storage and can encourage sprouting; keep only what you will use soon on the counter and store the rest in a cooler pantry or cellar.

beginner: Keep sweet potatoes out of the fridge. When they get colder than about 50 to 55°F they get damaged: they taste off, stay hard in the middle even after cooking, and rot faster. This is different from most vegetables. Store them in a cool pantry or cellar around 55 to 60°F instead, never the refrigerator.
seasoned: Do not refrigerate sweet potatoes. Below about 50 to 55°F they suffer chilling injury: the flesh develops off-flavors, hard cores that will not soften when cooked, internal browning, and a greater tendency to rot. This is the opposite of many vegetables. A cool pantry or cellar near 55 to 60°F, never the refrigerator, is the right place for raw sweet potatoes.

beginner: Do not freeze raw sweet potatoes. Freeze them only after cooking, like baked or mashed, and they keep for several months.
seasoned: Raw sweet potatoes do not freeze well. Freeze only after cooking (baked, mashed, or as prepared dishes), where they keep for several months.

beginner: Sweet potatoes must be cured before storing, and this is opposite to how you store regular potatoes. Right after digging, keep them somewhere warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F and quite damp, for 1 to 2 weeks. Curing heals the skins and turns the starch to sugar, which is what makes them sweet. A warm room with the roots in a loosely covered box works at home. Then store them in the dark around 55 to 60°F with some airflow, where they keep for 6 months or more. Never put them in the fridge or anywhere below about 50 to 55°F, because the cold ruins them. Do not wash them until you use them.
seasoned: Curing is essential and is the opposite of potato storage. Right after digging, cure the roots warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F at 85 to 90 percent humidity for roughly 1 to 2 weeks (5 to 7 days minimum), which heals skin nicks, sets a protective skin, and converts starch to sugar so the flesh turns sweet. A simple home method is a warm room with the roots in a container loosely covered to hold humidity. After curing, store in the dark at about 55 to 60°F with high humidity and good ventilation, where a well-cured crop keeps 6 months or more. Never store below about 50 to 55°F or refrigerate (chilling injury), and do not wash until use or store bruised or diseased roots.

beginner: The slips you planted will droop for the first few days, which is normal, then perk up and start growing new leaves once they have rooted. Not much happens above ground yet while they get established.
seasoned: Freshly set slips that often wilt for the first several days, then recover, green up, and put out new leaves as they root in. Little top growth happens yet; the plant is building roots. Warm soil speeds this along.

beginner: Keep the soil damp while the slips root, and water them in the afternoon if they wilt badly. Cover them if a late frost threatens, since frost kills the leaves. If a slip does not perk up after a week or so, replace it.
seasoned: Keep the soil evenly moist while slips root in, and shade or water in the heat of the day if they wilt hard. Protect from any late frost, which kills the tender foliage. Replace any slips that fail to take within the first week or two.

beginner: Sweet potatoes are a warm-weather crop grown for the sweet, starchy roots that form underground. Despite the name, they are not related to regular potatoes; they belong to the morning glory family. You do not grow them from seed or from tubers. Instead you plant slips, which are rooted sprouts, set out only after all frost is past and the soil is warm. The plants send out long, trailing vines that cover the ground, so they are grown on ridges or mounds with plenty of room. Sweet potatoes need a long, hot summer (about 3 to 4 months of warm, frost-free weather) and they love heat, so the warm South, Gulf, Florida, and the desert Southwest are the best places to grow them, while cooler northern gardens are a stretch and use black plastic and fast varieties. Go easy on fertilizer, especially nitrogen, or you get lots of vine and few sweet potatoes. Dig the crop before the first frost, which kills the vines, then cure the roots somewhere warm and humid for a week or two, which heals the skins and makes them sweet, and store them warm, around 55 to 60°F. Never put sweet potatoes in the fridge or anywhere cold, which ruins them. This is the opposite of how you store regular potatoes. The young leaves are also good to eat as a cooked green.
seasoned: Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is a warm-season, frost-tender member of the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae), not a nightshade and unrelated to the ordinary potato despite the shared name. It is grown for its swollen storage roots and planted not from seed or tubers but from slips: rooted sprouts pulled from a bedded seed root and set out only after all frost danger has passed and the soil is warm, above about 65°F. The plant is a vigorous, sprawling groundcover, running long vines that root at the nodes, and it is grown on raised ridges or mounds that drain well and give the roots room to expand. The crop needs a long, hot season, roughly 90 to 120 frost-free days, and it relishes the summer heat that stalls many other vegetables, so the warm South, Gulf, Florida, and the low deserts are its stronghold while short-season northern gardens are marginal and lean on black plastic and fast varieties. Feed sparingly and keep nitrogen low, since rich ground grows rampant vine and few roots. The crop is dug before the first frost, which kills the vines, then cured warm and humid (about 80 to 85°F at high humidity for one to two weeks) to heal the skins and turn starch to sugar, and stored warm, near 55 to 60°F. Sweet potatoes are damaged by cold and must never be refrigerated or stored below about 50 to 55°F, the opposite of white potato storage. The young leaves and shoots are also edible as a cooked green.

beginner: You harvest sweet potatoes by the calendar and, most importantly, before frost, not by watching the tops die back. They are usually ready about 3 to 4 months after planting, when the roots are full size; the older leaves may yellow, but unlike regular potatoes the vines do not obviously die down. Dig before the first fall frost, because frost kills the vines and cold soil hurts the roots. Loosen the soil with a fork well away from the plant so you do not stab the sweet potatoes, lift them gently, and handle them carefully because they bruise easily and the skins are thin at first. Let them dry off out of the sun, do not wash them, then cure them somewhere warm and humid for a week or two before storing. If frost hits the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two.
seasoned: Sweet potatoes are harvested by days-to-maturity and, above all, before frost, not by a die-back signal. The crop is usually ready about 90 to 120 days from transplanting slips, when the roots have reached full size; the oldest leaves may yellow, but the vines do not clearly die back the way potato tops do. Dig before the first fall frost, since frost kills the vines and cold soil damages the roots and shortens storage. Loosen the soil with a fork well outside the plant so you do not spear or bruise the roots, lift them gently, and handle them carefully, since sweet potatoes bruise easily and skins are thin at harvest. Let them dry briefly out of direct sun, do not wash them, then cure warm and humid, about 80 to 85°F for one to two weeks, before storing. If a frost catches the vines, cut them off and dig within a day or two so rot does not travel down into the roots.

beginner: Getting the soil right matters for sweet potatoes. Loosen the bed deep, mix in compost, and mound the soil up into ridges about 8 to 10 inches high, which drain well, warm up faster, and give the roots room to grow long and smooth. Heavy, cold, soggy clay rots the roots and makes them lumpy, so use ridges or a raised bed if your soil is clay. Keep the soil slightly acidic (pH about 5.8 to 6.5). Go easy on fertilizer and skip fresh manure, which grow leaves instead of roots; use a low-nitrogen fertilizer like 5-10-10 and a little compost. Plant the slips 3 to 4 inches deep and 12 to 18 inches apart along the ridge, in rows about 3 to 4 feet apart, once all frost is past and the soil has warmed to about 65°F. In cooler areas, lay down black plastic to warm the soil and buy extra time.
seasoned: Sweet potato quality starts with loose, warm, well-drained soil built up into ridges or mounds. Work the bed deep, incorporate compost, and form ridges 8 to 10 inches high, which drain well, warm quickly, and give the storage roots room to expand smoothly; heavy clay stays cold and wet, rots roots, and forces short, knobby shapes, and is best improved with organic matter or grown in raised ridges. Aim for a slightly acidic pH, roughly 5.8 to 6.5. Keep nitrogen low and avoid fresh manure, which drive rampant vine at the expense of roots; use a low-nitrogen fertilizer such as 5-10-10 and modest compost. Set slips 3 to 4 inches deep, 12 to 18 inches apart along the ridge in rows 3 to 4 feet apart, once all frost is past and the soil is above about 65°F. In short-season areas, lay black plastic to warm the soil and add growing days.

beginner: Cauliflower grows best in rich, well-drained soil with lots of compost worked in, and it needs steady, even moisture the whole way. More than most vegetables, cauliflower hates being stressed: if it dries out or runs short on food even briefly, it can quit growing and form a tiny, useless head early (called buttoning). Soil that holds moisture but still drains well is ideal.
seasoned: Cauliflower is a heavy feeder that demands a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter held at steady, even moisture. It is the fussiest of the cole crops: any check to growth from drought, low fertility, or a stalled transplant can trigger buttoning (premature, undersized curds), so the goal is uninterrupted, vigorous growth from set-out to harvest. Work in compost before planting and aim for a moisture-retentive but well-draining bed, since waterlogging invites root maggots and rots while drought stress ruins the curd. Clubroot, the key brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic, poorly drained ground.

beginner: Cauliflower grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, a soil disease, keeping the soil closer to neutral (up toward 7.0) helps hold it back.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (UMN and Iowa State both give 6 to 7; Clemson lists 5.8 to 6.5). Cauliflower tolerates a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Clubroot, the major brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic soil below about 6.5, so where it is a concern lime acidic ground well ahead of planting and hold the pH toward neutral.

beginner: Cauliflower needs rich soil and regular feeding to grow a good head. The big rule is to never let it get hungry or stressed: a plant that runs short on food or water stops growing and makes a tiny, useless head early. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer about 3 to 4 weeks after planting out. Keep it growing steadily the whole way.
seasoned: Cauliflower is a heavy feeder, and steady fertility matters even more than with other cole crops because a hungry plant buttons, forming a tiny premature curd instead of a full one. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting, using roughly 33-0-0 or calcium nitrate. Keep the plant growing vigorously and without interruption right up to curd formation; the most common cause of failed curds is any stall in growth from low fertility or uneven water. On acid or sandy soils, a boron and molybdenum deficiency can cause hollow stem and whiptail, so a soil rich in organic matter at a near-neutral pH is the best insurance.

beginner: Time to feed your cauliflower.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your cauliflower with nitrogen to keep it growing without a stall.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed a few weeks after planting out to keep it growing strong.
seasoned: High N to drive steady, uninterrupted growth to a full curd: a 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 starter worked in before planting, then a nitrogen side-dress such as 33-0-0 or calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then a nitrogen feed beside the plants a few weeks after they go out.
seasoned: Work in 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress with about 1 pound of 33-0-0 (or roughly a half cup of 21-0-0 per 10 feet of row) about 3 to 4 weeks after transplanting, watered in alongside the plants.

beginner: Cauliflower does well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick crops you can tuck in while the plants are small. The most important rule is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most cauliflower companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents for cabbage-family pests, small flowering plants such as sweet alyssum and dill to draw the parasitic wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and caterpillars (a habitat tactic Clemson recommends for cole crops), and quick crops like lettuce that use the open ground while the cauliflower fills in. The well-grounded caution is to separate cauliflower from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

beginner: Sweet alyssum makes lots of tiny flowers that bring in helpful insects which eat aphids and caterpillars, two major cauliflower pests.
seasoned: Sweet alyssum is one of the better-supported cole-crop companions. Its low mats of tiny flowers are a classic insectary plant, drawing the hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that prey on cabbage aphids and the cabbage-family caterpillars, and Clemson specifically advises small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control. Let it self-sow along the bed edge.

beginner: Dill's flowers attract helpful insects that hunt the aphids and caterpillars that bother cauliflower.
seasoned: Dill works for cauliflower mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers draw the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and cabbageworms, and Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops for natural control. Let some flower, and keep it off to the side so it does not shade the plants.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cole crops; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.
seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, onions tuck around young cauliflower without competing for much. Treat it as a low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

beginner: Keep cauliflower away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, and kale. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them makes problems worse.
seasoned: Planting cauliflower shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, collards, concentrates the family's shared pests (cabbage aphids, cabbageworms, loopers, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings, and worst of all, caterpillars and their mess tucked down into the curd, where they are very hard to wash out.
seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; as the curd forms, larvae crawl into it and foul it, the costly damage that is very hard to clean from a tight white curd. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed (Clemson rates the diamondback the most numerous cole-crop caterpillar in home gardens).

beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants, chew the leaves, and crawl into the head you want to eat.
seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage and contaminate the curd; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Cauliflower is a primary host for all three.

beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or spinosad, and pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down. Tighten control as the curd forms, when contamination of the head is the expensive kind.

beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

beginner: You'll see clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked into the curd, where they are very hard to wash out. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and then lodges in the curd, where it contaminates the marketable product with insects and honeydew and is nearly impossible to clean from the tight florets. Curling and distortion of young leaves is common.

beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage-family plants and hide down in the curd, which is the part you eat.
seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid, sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; contamination of the harvested curd with aphids and sticky honeydew is usually the real problem rather than plant stunting. Pressure is heaviest on the long-season fall crop.

beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, which eat aphids.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (the parasitoid Diaeretiella rapae, hoverflies, ladybugs) that suppress this aphid.

beginner: Check the growing tips and the developing curd often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen once the curd forms, since soft growth draws them, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
seasoned: Scout growing tips and the curd weekly and catch infestations before aphids colonize the head. Avoid excess nitrogen once the curd sets, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet soil.
seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment, and a root-checked plant is also far likelier to button.

beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp weather, so spring transplants are most at risk.
seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.

beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.

beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region brassica specialist.

beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a true bug that specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.

beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped eggs laid in rows, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap, pyrethrum, or neem help where pressure is severe.

beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and slows establishment, and a checked cauliflower seedling is prone to buttoning.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover, and a stunted cauliflower seedling often heads early and badly.
seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; a vigorous transplant generally outgrows them, but a stalled seedling can be set back badly.

beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle the damage.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage without a growth check.

beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots. A clubroot-checked plant rarely makes a usable curd.

beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and infects most readily in acidic soils below pH 6.5.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil from being too acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.

beginner: Don't grow cauliflower or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (UMN advises up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the curd.
seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot the curd. Often the most serious cole-crop disease in warm, wet weather.

beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.

beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.

beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants (a hot-water seed treatment helps), rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

beginner: Small dark spots with rings like a target appear on the leaves and can spread onto the curd as brown, fuzzy patches that ruin it. It is worse in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: Small dark leaf spots with concentric target-like rings and a yellow halo; in wet weather the spots enlarge, and on cauliflower the fungus can spread onto the curd as a brown, sometimes fuzzy discoloration that ruins its market quality. Clemson lists Alternaria brown spot among the main cauliflower diseases.

beginner: A fungus that spreads by spores in wet weather and on infected seed. It spots the leaves and, on cauliflower, can blemish the white curd, which makes it unsellable.
seasoned: Alternaria species (A. brassicae / A. brassicicola), fungi that spread by airborne and splashed spores and on infected seed; long leaf wetness and warm, humid weather favor them, and they survive in crop debris and on seed.

beginner: Remove badly spotted leaves, improve airflow so leaves dry, and use a copper spray if it is spreading onto the curd. Keep water off the leaves.
seasoned: Remove affected leaves, improve airflow and let foliage dry, and apply a copper-based fungicide if the disease threatens the curd; control is largely preventive.

beginner: Start with clean seed, space plants for airflow, water at the soil rather than overhead, rotate away from cabbage-family crops, and clear away old plants where the fungus survives.
seasoned: Use clean, certified, hot-water-treated seed, space for airflow, water at the soil line, rotate away from brassicas, and bury or remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves and can spot the curd.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors the leaves and can spot and darken the curd. Cauliflower's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora parasitica) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.

beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.

beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

beginner: The curd develops soft, watery, brown or black mushy patches that quickly turn slimy and smell bad. It usually shows up in warm, wet weather on a curd that stayed wet.
seasoned: Soft, water-soaked brown to black lesions on the curd that rapidly become slimy and foul-smelling, the bacterial head rot Clemson lists for cauliflower; it spreads fastest in warm, wet weather and where water sits in a tied (blanched) head.

beginner: Bacteria get into the curd through small wounds or where water sits in the head, then rot it from the inside, especially in warm, humid weather.
seasoned: Soft-rot bacteria (Pectobacterium / Pseudomonas species) enter through wounds and natural openings and macerate the curd tissue; free moisture in the head and warm, humid conditions drive it, and a tightly tied blanch that traps water raises the risk.

beginner: There's no cure for a rotting curd, so remove affected heads. The fix is prevention: keep the curd dry and harvest promptly.
seasoned: There is no cure for a rotting curd; remove and discard affected heads. Management is cultural and preventive.

beginner: Keep water off the curd, give plants room so heads dry quickly after rain, blanch (tie the leaves) loosely so water doesn't pool, harvest promptly, and avoid bruising the heads.
seasoned: Keep the curd dry: space for airflow, blanch loosely so water drains rather than pools, avoid overhead watering and handling wet heads, harvest promptly once the curd is full, and do not bruise the heads.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week. Never let it dry out and wilt, since stress makes it head early and badly.
seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept as even as possible; cauliflower must never go through a dry check, which triggers buttoning.

beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week (UMN: roughly 1 inch a week; USU: 1 to 2 inches, deep and infrequent), more in warm, dry spells while the plant is sizing up.

beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible to keep foliage dry and discourage leaf disease.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; cauliflower dislikes waterlogged soil, which invites root maggots, clubroot, and crown rot in cold, wet ground.

beginner: Wilting leaves and stalled growth, and worst of all, a tiny head forms way too early (buttoning) because the dry spell stressed the plant.
seasoned: Wilting and stalled growth, then the classic failure: a stressed plant buttons, forming a tiny, premature curd instead of a full head. Drought stress is the single most common cause of a ruined cauliflower crop.

beginner: Keep the soil or tray damp while the seeds come up, without letting the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed or tray surface evenly moist through germination; brassica seed is shallow and should not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Cauliflower is fussy. If it dries out even once while young, it can make a tiny useless head instead of a full one. Keep it evenly damp from the beginning.
seasoned: Cauliflower is the least forgiving brassica: a single drought check, even on a young plant, can trigger buttoning, a tiny premature curd that never sizes up. Keep it evenly moist and unstressed from the start.

beginner: Keep the soil steadily damp as the plant grows. Letting it dry out at any point can ruin the head later.
seasoned: Hold unbroken even moisture as the frame builds; any drought stress along the way, not just at heading, sets up buttoning and a poor curd.

beginner: Keep the water steady while the white head forms. Any dry spell now makes it loose, grainy, or bitter.
seasoned: Even moisture from transplant all the way through curd formation drives a smooth, dense, white head. A single check here gives a loose, ricey, or bitter curd.

beginner: Keep watering evenly and cut the head while it is full but still tight and smooth.
seasoned: Keep even moisture and cut the head while the curd is full but still tight and smooth.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the plant never gets stressed. A cauliflower that dries out even once can make a tiny, premature head, so do not let it wilt.
seasoned: Even, uninterrupted moisture is the whole game with cauliflower: more than any other cole crop it punishes a dry check by buttoning, so the goal is steady, vigorous growth with no stress from transplant to harvest.

beginner: Keep the water steady the whole time, especially when the plant is young, so it never gets stressed into heading early.
seasoned: Even moisture matters from transplanting all the way through curd formation; a single drought stress at any point, but especially on a young plant, can trigger buttoning.

beginner: Cauliflower is best grown from transplants, since timing and a smooth, unstressed start are so important. For spring, start seeds indoors about a month before planting out and set the plants out around 2 weeks before your last frost; do not rush them into hard cold, since young cauliflower is touchier than cabbage. For fall, start them in early-to-mid summer. The key is to never let the seedlings get old, root-bound, or chilled, because that stress makes them head early. Let homegrown seedlings get used to the outdoors over a week before planting.
seasoned: Cauliflower is almost always transplanted, since precise timing and an unstressed start matter so much. For spring, start seeds indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before set-out and transplant sturdy young plants out around 2 weeks before the last frost; cauliflower transplants are less cold-hardy than cabbage or broccoli, so do not rush them into hard cold. For fall, start indoors or direct sow in early-to-mid summer and set out so the curd matures in cool fall weather. The single biggest transplant mistake is setting out an old, root-bound, or cold-checked plant: that stress triggers buttoning, where the plant forms a tiny premature curd. Set out stocky plants with 4 to 6 true leaves, harden them off over 7 to 10 days, and keep them growing without a stall.

beginner: Other cabbage-family crops like broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, and turnips.
seasoned: Other brassicas (broccoli, cabbage, brussels sprouts, kale, collards, kohlrabi, turnip, radish, mustard), which share clubroot and the cabbage-family pests.

beginner: Don't plant cauliflower or other cabbage-family crops in the same spot year after year. Waiting at least 3 years between them, and longer if you have had clubroot, helps avoid soil diseases.
seasoned: Rotate so cauliflower and its brassica relatives do not return to the same ground for at least 3 years, and longer where clubroot is present (UMN advises up to a 7-year break where clubroot is known). Repeated same-family cropping builds soil-borne clubroot, and holding soil pH near neutral also helps suppress it.

beginner: Cauliflower does not keep well at room temperature, only a day or two. It is best eaten soon after cutting or frozen.
seasoned: Cauliflower is a poor keeper at room temperature, holding only a day or two before the curd softens and discolors. Unlike cabbage, it is not a storage vegetable: plan to use it fresh or freeze it.

beginner: Store the head unwashed in the fridge crisper, where it keeps about a week (up to 2 to 3 weeks if very cold). Use it soon, since the curd yellows and starts to smell as it sits.
seasoned: Refrigerate the head unwashed, with a few wrapper leaves on, stem side down. It holds about a week in the crisper, and no more than 2 to 3 weeks even at an ideal 32°F and high humidity (Clemson; USU). The curd yellows and develops off odors as it ages, so use it promptly.

beginner: You can freeze cauliflower if you boil the florets briefly first (about 3 minutes), cool them in ice water, drain, and freeze; use them cooked. This freezer step is a different thing from the leaf-tying also called blanching out in the garden.
seasoned: Cauliflower freezes well after blanching: cut into florets, blanch about 3 minutes, cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. Blanching (the boiling step) halts the enzymes that cause off-flavors; frozen cauliflower is best used cooked. Note this freezer blanch is unrelated to the in-garden leaf-tying also called blanching.

beginner: Cauliflower is not a keeper like cabbage. Cut it with a few leaves around the head to protect it, keep it cold, and use it within about a week, or freeze it for longer.
seasoned: Cauliflower is for fresh use or the freezer, not long storage; this is a real difference from cabbage, which keeps for months. Cut the head with a few wrapper leaves to protect the curd, keep it cold, and use it within a week or so. The curd discolors fastest in light and warmth, so refrigerate promptly.

beginner: Pick the type that fits your patience. For a first try, choose an easy self-blanching or self-wrapping kind like Snow Crown, Amazing, or Self Blanche, which need little or no leaf-tying. The colored kinds are fun and skip blanching completely: orange (Cheddar) and purple (Graffiti) just need full sun, and green Romanesco makes a beautiful spiraled head but takes a long, cool fall to do well.
seasoned: Match the variety to the season and your tolerance for fuss. For a first try, the early self-wrapping or self-blanching hybrids (Snow Crown, Amazing, Self Blanche) are the most forgiving and need the least leaf-tying. Open-pollinated whites (Early Snowball, Snowball Y Improved) are seed-saveable but want blanching. The colored types are the fun ones and skip blanching entirely: orange (Cheddar) and purple (Graffiti, Purple of Sicily) are grown in full sun for their color, and lime-green Romanesco (Veronica) brings a spiraled curd but wants a long, steady cool fall. Days-to-maturity figures are approximate and run from transplanting.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A rich, well-drained commercial potting mix high in organic matter.

beginner: Mix in compost and a slow-release fertilizer for steady feeding.
seasoned: Blend in compost and a slow-release balanced fertilizer; a single cauliflower in a pot is a heavy feeder in a small soil volume, and starving it is the fast track to buttoning.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check daily in warm weather and keep the water steady. Cauliflower buttons (heads early) if it ever dries out, so this matters more than for most pot crops.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture daily in heat and water before the mix dries, since any dry check can trigger buttoning.

Transplant Oct 1 through Nov 15 and harvest from Dec 30 into spring; it rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold. Cauliflower follows broccoli's calendar here too: start seed indoors in late summer, transplant October into mid-November, and keep it cool and steady, since heat stress ruins curd quality. Skip planting cauliflower from spring through summer: the Valley heat keeps it from growing well here.
seasoned: Cauliflower in the RGV runs on the winter-garden calendar: transplant Oct 1 through Nov 15, with harvest running Dec 30 through Mar 15. Transplanted on broccoli's schedule per TAMU's RGV Homeowner Guide; 90 to 120 days to harvest (Bilingual LRGV table). Less heat-tolerant than cabbage, so timing matters more. Frost is essentially absent here, so timing is heat-bounded rather than cold-bounded. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: the TAMU AgriLife sources describe a single Valley-wide planting calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

beginner: In the Willamette Valley and around Puget Sound, start cauliflower seeds indoors in February and set plants out from April through early July, staggering plantings a couple of weeks apart for a steady supply of curds from early summer into fall. Right on the coast, OSU's guidance is more specific: plant in January, exploiting the coast's very mild winter, and again in June for a fall curd; there is no long continuous window there like the valley has. Keep cauliflower growing steadily with even water; a cold check or a dry spell can cause tiny, useless button curds instead of a full head.
seasoned: Cauliflower in the Willamette Valley gets a genuinely continuous window: start transplants indoors in February and set them out anywhere from April into mid-July, which supports staggered sowings for a spring curd and a fall one without needing a separate second planting. The immediate coast, per OSU's own numbers, is narrower and more specific: only January and June are marked as viable set-out times there, not a range. The January planting leans on the coast's exceptionally mild, marine-buffered winter, well ahead of the coast's own average last frost in late March; cauliflower transplants tolerate the coast's typically light frosts once hardened off. Neither zone needs a summer heat pause, but cauliflower is fussier than cabbage about steady growth: a cold check or moisture stress causes small, premature button curds rather than one good head, so keep it growing without a stall in either zone.

beginner: Cauliflower is a little fussier than its cousins about heat, so the mid-Atlantic fall is really its season: cool, settled weather lets the curd form clean and white without the heat stress that causes ricing or premature button heads. Grow a spring crop for an earlier harvest, then set out fall transplants in late summer for the belt's better cauliflower.
seasoned: Cauliflower's narrow curd-formation window makes it the most heat-sensitive of the region's cole crops: Virginia Cooperative Extension documents a short spring transplant window that must finish before summer heat arrives, and a fall window set in late summer that matures as the weather cools, generally the belt's more reliable curd. Zone 7's later, cooler spring shortens the spring window further relative to zone 8's.

beginner: Cauliflower is a little fussier than its cousins about heat, so the Mid-South fall is really its season: cool, settled weather lets the curd form clean and white without the heat stress that causes ricing or premature button heads. Grow a spring crop for an earlier harvest, then set out fall transplants in late summer for the belt's better cauliflower.
seasoned: Cauliflower's narrow curd-formation window makes it the most heat-sensitive of the region's cole crops. University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension lists cauliflower in both its spring window (February through April) and its fall table (transplants Aug 10 to Sep 1); this cell holds the spring set-out short, zone 8 late February to mid-March, so curds finish ahead of the belt's heat, while the fall crop, maturing as the weather cools, is generally the more reliable curd. Zone 7 runs the spring window about two weeks later and the fall window about a week earlier.

beginner: Cauliflower gets two chances in St. George. Set plants out about March 1, USU Extension's St. George date, for curds by mid-May; it is the most heat-sensitive of the region's cole crops, so cutting wraps up by the end of May. Set a second round of transplants from mid-July into early August, once the worst heat has broken, for a fall harvest into mid-October. Frost returns around November 1.
seasoned: USU Extension's St. George chart sets cauliflower in the Group B (Semi-Hardy) band, spring set-out about March 1, curds firming up at about 70 days for a harvest through May. Cauliflower is the most heat-sensitive of the region's cole crops, so the spring window closes at month's end, well ahead of St. George's 100°F June stretch. USU's fall-gardening guidance for the St. George area sets cole-crop transplants out from mid-July into early August, the same window used for cabbage and broccoli, for a fall harvest running into mid-October ahead of the November 1 average first frost.
