beginner: Cauliflower grows one dense, round head (the curd) in the center of the plant. There are white kinds plus fun orange, purple, and spiraled green Romanesco types, taking about 2 to 3 months to mature. It likes steady cool weather, so it is grown in spring and fall, not summer heat. Cauliflower is the trickiest of the cabbage family: it needs to grow without any stress, or it makes a tiny head early (buttoning) or a loose, discolored one. Many white types need blanching, where you tie the outer leaves over the head to keep it white. There are no side shoots like broccoli, so it is one head per plant, and it does not store like cabbage, so use it fresh or freeze it.
seasoned: Cauliflower is a cool-season brassica grown for the single dense white curd, the immature flower head, that forms at the center of the plant. It comes in white types plus orange, purple, and lime-green spiraled Romanesco forms, maturing from about 50 to 100 days, and is grown as a spring crop and a fall crop, timed to mature in cool weather. It is the fussiest of the common cole crops and less cold-hardy than cabbage or broccoli: the curd forms well only in steady cool weather around 60°F to 65°F, and almost any stress (heat, cold, drought, or a checked transplant) causes buttoning (a tiny premature curd) or ricing and discoloration of the head. Many white varieties need blanching, tying the outer leaves over the curd to keep it white, while self-blanching and colored types skip that step. Unlike broccoli it forms no side shoots, so it is a single harvest per plant, and unlike cabbage it does not store, so it is used fresh or frozen.

beginner: Your cauliflower is ready when the head is full-sized (about 6 to 8 inches), firm, and still tight, smooth, and white, usually a week or two after you tied the leaves over it. Cut the whole head off with a few leaves attached. Don't wait, because the head quickly goes loose and grainy and yellows. Use it within about a week, since it does not keep like cabbage.
seasoned: Cut the curd when it is full-sized (about 6 to 8 inches across), firm, compact, and still smooth and white, usually 1 to 2 weeks after blanching and roughly 50 to 100 days from transplanting depending on the variety. Slice the whole head off at the base with a few wrapper leaves to protect it. Harvest promptly: a curd left too long rices (separates into a loose, grainy surface), discolors, and starts to open toward flower, and that window is only a few days, shorter in warm weather. Refrigerate soon, since cauliflower does not hold in the garden the way cabbage does.

beginner: Before planting, mix plenty of compost into a rich, well-drained bed and check that the soil is not too acidic. Try not to plant where you grew other cabbage-family crops in the last few years, since that spreads soil diseases. Plan to water evenly and feed steadily, because cauliflower needs to grow without any stress or it heads early and badly.
seasoned: Work plenty of compost into a fertile, well-drained but moisture-retentive bed before planting and confirm pH is near 6.0 to 7.0, liming acidic ground well ahead where clubroot is a concern. Because clubroot builds in the soil, choose a bed where no cole crop has grown for at least 3 years. Set up to water evenly and plan for steady feeding, since the whole secret to cauliflower is uninterrupted growth with no stress, which is what prevents buttoning.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Cabbage grows best in rich, well-drained soil with plenty of compost mixed in, and it likes steady, even moisture. Keep the water consistent: a big swing from dry to soaking wet near harvest makes the heads split. Soil that holds moisture but drains well is ideal.
seasoned: Cabbage is a heavy feeder that rewards a fertile, well-drained loam high in organic matter held at even moisture. Work in compost before planting, and aim for a moisture-retentive but well-draining bed, since both waterlogging (which invites root maggot and rots) and drought stress hurt heading. The signature cabbage soil issue is uneven water near maturity: a sudden flush of water into a firm head bursts it, so steady moisture matters most as the heads fill. Clubroot, the key brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic, poorly drained ground.

beginner: Cabbage grows best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test tells you where you stand. If you have had clubroot, a soil disease, keeping the soil closer to neutral (up toward 7.0 or a bit above) helps hold it back.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (UMN and Iowa State both give 6 to 7; Clemson lists 5.8 to 6.5). Cabbage tolerates a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band. Clubroot, the major brassica soil disease, is far more likely in acidic soil below about 6.5, so where it is a concern lime acidic ground well ahead of planting and hold the pH toward neutral or slightly above.

beginner: Cabbage needs rich soil and regular feeding to grow a big, solid head. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer once the plants take off and again as the heads start to form. Keep the watering even, because a lot of fertilizer plus a sudden soaking can crack the heads.
seasoned: Cabbage is a heavy feeder that needs steady nitrogen to build a large, solid head. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson: 5-10-10 at 3 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress with nitrogen once the plants are established and again as heads begin to cup, using about 34-0-0 or calcium nitrate. Keep nitrogen steady through heading, but pair it with even moisture: a late surge of growth from heavy feeding plus a sudden drink of water is what splits heads.

beginner: Time to feed your cabbage.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your cabbage with nitrogen as the heads begin to form.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed once the plants take off and again as heads form.
seasoned: High N to build a large, solid head: a 5-10-10 or 10-10-10 starter worked in before planting, then a nitrogen side-dress such as 34-0-0 or calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) as the plants establish and begin to head.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer at planting, then a nitrogen feed beside the plants as heads start.
seasoned: Work in 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet before planting, then side-dress with about 1 pound of 34-0-0 (or 2 pounds of calcium nitrate) per 100 feet of row as heads begin to form, watered in alongside the plants.

beginner: Cabbage does well next to aromatic herbs, onions, and quick crops you can tuck in while the plants are small. The most important rule is to keep it away from other cabbage-family plants, which share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Most cabbage companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The ones worth acting on are practical: aromatic herbs and alliums as scent-based deterrents for cabbage pests, small flowering plants such as sweet alyssum and dill to draw the parasitic wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and caterpillars (a habitat tactic Clemson recommends for cole crops), and quick crops like lettuce that use the open ground while the cabbage fills in. The well-grounded caution is to separate cabbage from other brassicas, which share clubroot and the whole cabbage-family pest complex, a rotation and disease principle more than a tested adjacency effect.

beginner: Sweet alyssum makes lots of tiny flowers that bring in helpful insects which eat aphids and caterpillars, two major cabbage pests.
seasoned: Sweet alyssum is one of the better-supported cabbage companions. Its low mats of tiny flowers are a classic insectary plant, drawing the hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that prey on cabbage aphids and the cabbage-family caterpillars, and Clemson specifically advises small flowers like alyssum near cole crops for biological control. Let it self-sow along the bed edge.

beginner: Dill's flowers attract helpful insects that hunt the aphids and caterpillars that bother cabbage.
seasoned: Dill works for cabbage mainly through beneficial insects. Its umbel flowers draw the parasitoid wasps and hoverflies that attack cabbage aphids and cabbageworms, and Clemson lists dill among the flowers to plant near cole crops for natural control. Let some flower, and keep it off to the side so it does not shade the heads.

beginner: Onions are a traditional neighbor for cabbage; their strong smell is said to help confuse and deter cabbage pests.
seasoned: Alliums are a traditional brassica companion, their pungent scent thought to mask the crop from the cabbage pests that hunt partly by smell. Shallow-rooted and undemanding, onions tuck around young cabbage without competing for much. Treat it as a low-risk, scent-based aid rather than a proven control.

beginner: Keep cabbage away from other cabbage-family plants like broccoli, brussels sprouts, kale, and cauliflower. They share the same pests and diseases, so grouping them makes problems worse.
seasoned: Planting cabbage shoulder to shoulder with its brassica relatives, broccoli, brussels sprouts, cauliflower, kale, collards, concentrates the family's shared pests (cabbage aphids, cabbageworms, loopers, harlequin bugs, root maggots) and shared diseases in one spot, and repeated same-family planting lets soil-borne clubroot and Fusarium yellows build up. Spread brassicas out and rotate where they grow each year.

beginner: You'll see ragged holes chewed in the leaves, green caterpillars on the plant, and dark droppings, and worst of all, caterpillars and their mess tunneled down inside the head where they are hard to wash out.
seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in the wrapper leaves with green caterpillars and dark frass; as heads form, larvae bore inside and foul them, the costly damage. Imported cabbageworms are velvety green; cabbage loopers move in a looping arch; diamondback larvae are small and wriggle when disturbed (Clemson rates the diamondback the most numerous cole-crop caterpillar in home gardens).

beginner: These are caterpillars that hatch from eggs laid by white butterflies and small moths. They love cabbage-family plants, chew the leaves, and bore into the head you want to eat.
seasoned: The larvae of the imported cabbageworm, cabbage looper, and diamondback moth feed on brassica foliage and penetrate the head; the adults are white or brownish butterflies and moths that lay eggs on the leaves. Cabbage is a primary host for all three.

beginner: Spray Bt, which is safe and targets only caterpillars, or spinosad, and pick caterpillars and eggs off by hand from under the leaves. Spray again after rain, since it washes off.
seasoned: Spray Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki) or spinosad, which target caterpillars and spare beneficials, and hand-pick larvae and eggs from leaf undersides. Repeat after rain, since Bt breaks down. Tighten control as heads cup, when damage to the head is the expensive kind.

beginner: Cover plants with a light fabric row cover after planting to keep the butterflies and moths from laying eggs, clear away old cabbage-family plants, and watch for the first white butterflies as your signal to act.
seasoned: Use floating row cover or fine mesh from transplanting to exclude the egg-laying adults, clean up brassica debris that shelters pupae, and scout for the first white butterflies as a spray cue.

beginner: You'll see clusters of small gray-green insects with a dusty, waxy coating on the new growth and tucked into the folds of the head, where they are very hard to wash out. Leaves may curl and there can be a sticky film.
seasoned: The gray-green, waxy-coated cabbage aphid forms dense colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides and then lodges in the folds of the developing head, where it contaminates the marketable product with insects and honeydew and is very hard to clean at harvest. Curling and distortion of young leaves is common.

beginner: Cabbage aphids are tiny insects that suck the plant's juices and breed fast. They love cabbage and hide down in the head, which is the part you eat.
seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae, a brassica-specialist aphid, sucks sap and reproduces rapidly; contamination of the harvested head with aphids and sticky honeydew is usually the real problem rather than plant stunting. Pressure is heaviest on the long-season fall crop.

beginner: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water and hit the undersides of leaves with insecticidal soap or neem oil, repeating every few days. Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, which eat aphids.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap, neem, or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides; repeat every few days. Conserve natural enemies (the parasitoid Diaeretiella rapae, hoverflies, ladybugs) that suppress this aphid.

beginner: Check the growing tips and the developing head often and act early. Go easy on nitrogen once heads form, since soft growth draws them, and clear away old cabbage-family plants after harvest.
seasoned: Scout growing tips and the head weekly and catch infestations before aphids colonize the head. Avoid excess nitrogen once heads set, use row cover on young plants, and destroy crop debris that carries them over.

beginner: New transplants wilt and grow badly or fall over. If you pull one up, you'll find small white maggots eating the roots. It is worst in cool, wet soil.
seasoned: Transplants wilt, grow poorly, and may collapse; pulling a plant reveals small white maggots tunneling in the roots and lower stem. Damage is worst in cool, wet soil at spring establishment.

beginner: A small fly lays eggs at the base of the plant, and the maggots that hatch burrow down and eat the roots. The fly is most active in cool, damp weather, so spring transplants are most at risk.
seasoned: The larvae of the cabbage root fly (Delia radicum) tunnel into brassica roots; the adult lays eggs at the stem base, and the maggots feed below, sometimes killing young plants and opening the door to rots.

beginner: Once the maggots are in the roots you can't save that plant, so pull and throw away the badly damaged ones. Put your effort into protecting the rest from new eggs.
seasoned: There is no effective rescue once maggots are in the roots; remove and destroy badly affected plants and protect the rest from further egg-laying.

beginner: Put a small collar or disk around the base of each transplant to stop the fly from laying eggs there, or use a row cover. Avoid planting into cold, soggy soil, and rotate away from where cabbage-family plants grew.
seasoned: Place a collar or disk around the stem base at transplanting to block egg-laying, or use row cover; avoid planting into cold, wet soil and rotate away from where brassicas grew.

beginner: Shield-shaped black-and-orange (or black-and-red) bugs on the leaves, which develop white or yellow spots, then brown and look tattered. It is mostly a warm-region problem and loves cabbage-family plants.
seasoned: Shield-shaped bugs up to about 3/8 inch, brightly black-and-yellow or black-and-red, feeding with piercing-sucking mouthparts that leave white stipples; affected leaves brown and look tattered, and heavy feeding wilts and deforms plants. A warm-region brassica specialist.

beginner: The harlequin bug is a colorful stink-bug relative that pierces the leaves and sucks the juices, leaving pale blotches. It strongly prefers cabbage-family plants, especially in the South.
seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica) is a true bug that specializes on cole crops, most damaging in the southern United States, where it completes several generations a year and overwinters as an adult in debris and weeds.

beginner: Search out and crush the bugs, their barrel-shaped eggs laid in rows, and the young ones by hand. Use a row cover to keep them off, pull badly infested plants, and clear away weeds and old plants where they hide over winter.
seasoned: Hand-pick and crush adults, nymphs, and the barrel-shaped egg rows; exclude with floating row cover; remove heavily infested plants. Insecticidal soap, pyrethrum, or neem help where pressure is severe.

beginner: Clean up garden debris and cabbage-family weeds where the adults overwinter, use row cover, and consider a trap crop of mustard to lure them away from the main crop, then destroy it.
seasoned: Eliminate overwintering sites by removing crop debris and crucifer weeds, use row cover, and deploy an early trap crop of mustard to divert overwintering adults, then destroy it before the main crop is set out.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes in the leaves of young plants, made by small dark beetles that jump away like fleas when you get close. Bad damage can stunt seedlings.
seasoned: Tiny round shot-hole pits chewed in the leaves of young plants; the small dark beetles jump like fleas when disturbed. Heavy feeding stunts or kills seedlings and slows establishment.

beginner: Flea beetles are small jumping beetles that chew on young cabbage-family leaves. They hurt seedlings most, because a tiny plant can't grow fast enough to recover.
seasoned: Flea beetles chew the foliage of young brassicas and are most damaging at the seedling stage; a vigorous transplant generally outgrows them, but a stalled seedling can be set back badly.

beginner: Cover young plants with a row cover, and if there are a lot of beetles, use a spray such as spinosad. The main goal is to get the seedlings big enough to handle the damage.
seasoned: Protect seedlings with row cover and spray spinosad if pressure is high; the goal is getting plants past the vulnerable seedling stage.

beginner: Cover seedlings with row cover from the start, keep them strong with steady water and food so they grow past the damage, and pull nearby weeds in the cabbage family.
seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, keep seedlings vigorous with even water and feeding so they grow through the damage, and clean up weedy brassica relatives nearby.

beginner: Plants wilt in the afternoon, stay small and yellowish, and don't bounce back. If you dig one up, the roots are swollen into lumpy, club-shaped knobs.
seasoned: Plants wilt in the heat of the day, grow stunted and yellowed, and recover poorly; roots are swollen into distorted clubs and galls instead of normal fine roots.

beginner: A germ that lives in the soil infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and makes them swell, which stops the plant from taking up water and food. It stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: A soilborne organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) infects brassica roots and forms the galls, which block water and nutrient uptake. It persists in soil for many years, spreads in contaminated soil and water, and infects most readily in acidic soils below pH 6.5.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. Keeping the soil from being too acidic (closer to neutral) helps hold it back, and growing cabbage-family plants only rarely in that spot starves the germ out.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove and destroy them. Raising soil pH toward neutral with lime suppresses the disease, and long rotations starve it out over time.

beginner: Don't grow cabbage or other cabbage-family plants in the same spot more than once every few years, longer if you've had clubroot. Keep the soil from being too acidic, improve drainage, and clean soil off your tools.
seasoned: Rotate brassicas out of affected ground on a long cycle (UMN advises up to 7 years where clubroot is known), keep soil pH up, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil on tools and boots.

beginner: Yellow patches shaped like the letter V appear at the leaf edges, pointing inward, with black veins inside them. It can spread through the plant and rot the head.
seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions spread inward from the leaf margins, with the veins inside the V turning black; the disease moves through the vascular system and can blacken and rot the head. Often the most serious cabbage disease in warm, wet weather.

beginner: A bacteria that often comes in on infected seeds or transplants. It gets into the leaves and travels through the plant's veins, spreading fastest in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: A seedborne bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris) that enters through leaf pores and wounds and moves through the veins; it spreads in warm, wet conditions and on infected seed or transplants.

beginner: There's no real cure, so remove and destroy infected plants to keep it from spreading. Don't handle or brush against the plants while they're wet, because that spreads the bacteria.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Avoid working among plants when foliage is wet, since that moves the bacteria.

beginner: Begin with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, don't plant where cabbage-family crops grew recently, space plants for good airflow, and avoid overhead watering.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants (a hot-water seed treatment helps), rotate 2 to 3 years away from brassicas, give plants room for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and handling wet foliage.

beginner: Pale, sunken spots dotted with tiny black specks appear on the stem and leaves, and the base of the stem darkens and rots, so the plant may girdle and topple. It often arrives on infected seed.
seasoned: Pale, sunken lesions peppered with small black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) form on stems and leaves, and a dark, girdling canker at the stem base can rot the crown and lodge the plant; cankers may extend into the head.

beginner: A fungus that comes in on infected seed or plants and attacks the stem and leaves of cabbage-family crops. It spreads in wet weather and lingers in old plant debris.
seasoned: The fungus Phoma lingam (Leptosphaeria maculans) is chiefly seedborne and also survives in brassica debris; it spreads in cool, wet weather by splashing water and infects through wounds and pores.

beginner: There's no cure, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real fix is prevention: clean seed, rotation, and clearing away old cabbage-family debris.
seasoned: There is no effective cure; remove and destroy infected plants. Management is preventive, since the pathogen is carried on seed and in residue.

beginner: Start with clean, certified seed and healthy transplants, rotate away from cabbage-family crops for a few years, and clear away old brassica plants where the fungus survives.
seasoned: Use clean, certified, hot-water-treated seed and disease-free transplants, rotate 3 years away from brassicas, and bury or remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

beginner: Whole plants turn a dull yellow-green, often more on one side, with leaves curling and dropping from the bottom up. Cut a stem and the water-carrying tissue inside is browned. It is worst in warm soil.
seasoned: A warm-season wilt: plants turn dull yellow-green (often one-sided), leaves curl, cup, and drop from the base up, and the vascular tissue in the stem browns. Stunting and death follow in susceptible varieties; symptoms resemble black rot but without the V-shaped marginal lesions.

beginner: A soil fungus that gets into the roots and plugs the plant's plumbing, so it yellows and wilts. It lives in the soil for years and is most active when the soil is warm, so it hits summer-grown cabbage hardest.
seasoned: The soilborne fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. conglutinans invades the roots and vascular system; it persists in soil for years and is most active in warm soil (roughly 80°F and up), so it most damages spring cabbage maturing into summer heat.

beginner: There's no cure once a plant is infected, so pull and destroy it. The reliable answer is to plant resistant (yellows-resistant) varieties.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected plants; remove and destroy them. Resistant varieties are the practical control, since the fungus is long-lived in soil.

beginner: Plant yellows-resistant varieties, which are widely available and the main control. Rotate away from cabbage-family crops, and avoid planting cabbage to mature in the hottest soil.
seasoned: Grow yellows-resistant (YR) varieties, which provide durable, effective resistance and are the standard control; rotate away from brassicas and avoid timing the crop to mature in the hottest soil.

beginner: Pale yellow blotches on top of the leaves, with fuzzy grayish growth on the underside, mostly in cool, damp weather. Bad cases discolor the leaves and can spot the head.
seasoned: Pale yellow patches form on the upper leaf surface with a fuzzy gray-white growth underneath, mainly in cool, damp weather; severe infection discolors the wrapper leaves and can blemish the head. Cabbage's cool, humid season overlaps the weather it likes.

beginner: A mold-like disease that loves cool, wet, humid weather and spreads through the air and water. Wet leaves and crowded plants make it worse.
seasoned: A fungus-like organism (Hyaloperonospora parasitica) that thrives in cool, wet, humid conditions and spreads by spores in water and air; long leaf wetness and crowded plantings favor it.

beginner: Open up the airflow so leaves can dry, remove the worst leaves, and use a copper spray if it's spreading. It's hard to stop once the weather stays damp.
seasoned: Improve airflow and let foliage dry, remove badly affected leaves, and apply a copper-based fungicide if pressure is high; the disease is hard to stop once humidity stays high.

beginner: Space plants so air moves between them, water at the soil instead of from above, and pick resistant varieties if downy mildew is common where you live.
seasoned: Space plants for good air movement, water at the soil line rather than overhead, and choose resistant varieties where downy mildew is common.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 to 1.5 inches a week. Try to keep it steady, not dry-then-soaked.
seasoned: Give about 1 to 1.5 inches weekly, kept as even as possible, and ease off slightly right at maturity to avoid splitting.

beginner: Aim for roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches per week (UMN: roughly 1 inch of rainfall a week is enough), more in hot, dry spells while heads are sizing up.

beginner: Water at the base of the plant rather than over the leaves.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose where possible to keep foliage dry and discourage leaf disease.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant looks soggy and limp.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and limp growth; cabbage dislikes waterlogged soil, which invites root maggots, clubroot, and crown rot in cold, wet ground.

For fall, sow indoors or direct seed in early-to-mid summer and set out in mid-to-late summer to mature in cool fall weather. beginner: Store whole, unwashed heads in the fridge crisper, where a firm head keeps for several weeks. In a very cold, humid spot (right around freezing) late storage cabbage keeps for months. Keep it away from apples and other ripening fruit, which make it go off sooner.
seasoned: Refrigerate whole, unwashed heads with the wrapper leaves on; a solid head holds for several weeks to a couple of months in the crisper. beginner: You can freeze cabbage if you blanch it first. Cut it up, boil it briefly (1 to 3 minutes), cool it in ice water, drain, and freeze; use it cooked. Cabbage is also great for making sauerkraut or kimchi, which keep a long time.
seasoned: Cabbage freezes after blanching: cut into wedges or shred, blanch about 1.5 minutes (shreds) to 3 minutes (wedges), cool quickly in ice water, drain, and freeze. beginner: Pick the type that fits your season. Early kinds like Golden Acre and Stonehead grow quickly for spring; later, denser kinds like Danish Ballhead are made to store for months in fall and winter. beginner: Cabbage grows one big, round, solid head of tightly wrapped leaves at the center of the plant. There are green, red, and crinkly savoy types, some quick (about 2 months) and some late storage kinds (about 4 months). It likes cool weather, so it is grown in spring and again in fall, not in summer heat. Cabbage handles frost well, and late storage types keep for months somewhere cold. seasoned: Cabbage is a cool-season brassica grown for the large, solid head of tightly wrapped leaves that forms at the center of the plant. It comes in early, mid, and late types maturing from about 60 to 120 days, in green, red, and crinkled savoy forms, and is grown as a spring crop and again as a fall crop in most regions, timed to head up in cool weather since heat gives loose heads and bolting. It is very cold-hardy, with mature heads tolerating frost down to about 20°F, and dense late storage types are among the best-keeping garden vegetables, holding for months in cold, humid storage. The crop's signature challenge is splitting: a solid head bursts if it takes up water too fast near maturity or is left standing too long.

beginner: Your cabbage is ready when the head is full-sized and firm and solid when you squeeze it. Cut it off at the base with a sharp knife. seasoned: Cut the head when it is full-sized, firm, and solid to a squeeze, about 60 to 120 days from transplanting depending on the type. Slice it off at the base with a sharp knife, leaving a few wrapper leaves for protection. Harvest promptly, since a mature head left in the ground will split, especially after rain; to hold a ripe head, give the plant a quarter turn or a slight lift to shear roots and slow water uptake.

seasoned: Whole cured onions do not need refrigeration and can sweat in the crisper; sweet short-day types, which store poorly, are the exception and keep longer chilled.

beginner: You can chop onions and freeze them for cooking. They go soft after thawing, so use frozen onions in cooked food, not in salads.
seasoned: Onions freeze well chopped for cooking; texture softens, so use frozen onion in cooked dishes rather than raw.

beginner: How long an onion keeps depends on its type. Strong-flavored storage onions last for months; sweet onions do not last long and should be eaten first. Drying (curing) them well is the most important thing for good storage.
seasoned: Storage life tracks type: pungent long-day storage onions hold for months, while sweet short-day types are thin-skinned and best used fresh. Good curing is the single biggest lever on how long any onion keeps.

beginner: The Pacific Northwest sweet onion: very mild, thin-skinned, and a poor keeper, so eat it fresh. It is a long-day type for northern gardens, and in mild-winter areas it is often set out in fall and carried over for an early-summer harvest, about 90 days after transplanting.
seasoned: Long-day, about 90 to 100 days from transplant (Oregon State). Thin-skinned and does not store; often fall-set and overwintered in mild-winter regions. Its overwintering habit is a planting practice, not a break from its long-day response.

beginner: A large, dependable long-day yellow for northern gardens, ready about 110 days after transplanting. It is more pungent than the sweet types, which makes it a better keeper for winter storage.
seasoned: Long-day (Texas A&M lists it by name), about 110 days from transplant. More pungent than the sweet whites and a solid storage onion; matures after Walla Walla and before the short-day types.

beginner: A widely adaptable intermediate-day white that bulbs across most of the country, which is why it is a safe pick if you are unsure of your latitude. It is mild and sweet, ready about 95 days after transplanting, and like most whites it is not for long storage.
seasoned: Intermediate-day (Michigan State names it directly), the safe default when latitude is uncertain. About 95 days from transplant per the seed trade; sold in some catalogs as Sierra Blanca, under which name New Mexico State reports a longer season in cooler conditions, so treat the day count as climate-dependent. Mild white, short storage.

beginner: An intermediate-day storage onion for the central latitudes, between the long-day North and the short-day South. It is a later, firm-bulbing yellow, ready around 115 days after transplanting.
seasoned: Intermediate-day yellow (NC State), a later-maturing storage type for the central band. About 115 days from transplant, derived from New Mexico State's transplant-to-harvest calendar rather than a stated day count, so treat it as approximate.

beginner: A large, very sweet short-day onion for the South, bred by Texas A&M and named for its ideal Rio Grande Valley seeding date, October 15. Set transplants out in fall to winter for a spring harvest, about 110 days after transplanting. It is sweet, so it stores only a couple of months.
seasoned: Short-day (Texas A&M), about 110 days from transplant. Fall-to-winter set for a spring bulb in the South; very sweet, so storage is short. Named for its October 15 Rio Grande Valley seeding date.

beginner: The classic flat sweet short-day onion, the Vidalia type, for southern gardens. It is mild and juicy, ready about 100 days after transplanting, with a short storage life.
seasoned: Short-day (University of Georgia; the Vidalia standard), about 100 days from transplant. Flat, mild, and juicy; a fresh-eating sweet onion with a short storage life.

beginner: Pick the type that matches where you live first, then pick a flavor. Northern gardeners want long-day onions like Walla Walla or Yellow Sweet Spanish. Southern gardeners want short-day onions like Texas 1015Y or Yellow Granex. In the middle of the country, or if you are not sure, choose an intermediate one like Super Star. Remember that sweet onions do not keep long, and stronger onions store for months. The day-length type is the part we are most sure of, and it decides where a bulb will form. The days-to-maturity numbers are counted from when you set out transplants and shift with the variety and your weather, so treat them as a guide and check each onion's confidence tier.
seasoned: Choose by day-length class first, then by use. The set below spans all three classes so a grower at any latitude has a fit: long-day (Walla Walla, Yellow Sweet Spanish) for the North, intermediate-day (Super Star, Cimarron) for the central band, and short-day (Texas 1015Y, Yellow Granex) for the South. As a rule, sweet onions store poorly and pungent storage onions keep for months. When in doubt about your latitude, an intermediate type is the safest bet. One note on the numbers: day-length class is the reliable, well-sourced axis and decides where each onion will bulb. Days to maturity is measured from transplant and is inherently variety- and climate-dependent, and several figures here come from the seed trade rather than university extension, so read each variety's confidence tier as the honest measure of its day count.

beginner: Plant onions a bit close together, then pull out the extras so the ones you keep stand 4 to 6 inches apart. Do this early. The little plants you pull are perfectly good green onions for the kitchen.
seasoned: Sow or set on the close side, then thin to 4 to 6 inches in the row before plants compete or begin to bulb. Thin early; crowding after bulb initiation costs size. Eat the thinnings as green onions.

beginner: Onions are good neighbors for carrots, beets, lettuce, and cabbage-family plants, mostly because their strong smell is thought to keep some pests away. The main thing to avoid is planting onions next to beans or peas, since onions can slow those down. These are helpful traditions, not sure things, so do not worry if your garden does a little differently.
seasoned: Onions earn their companion reputation mostly through their scent, which is traditionally credited with deterring aphids and the carrot rust fly, so they pair well with carrots, beets, lettuce, and brassicas. The one firm caution is the legume conflict: alliums are widely held to inhibit beans and peas, so keep onions away from them. Most of these claims are traditional rather than trial-proven; treat them as low-risk suggestions, not guarantees.

beginner: Onions and carrots are a classic garden pair. Their strong smell is said to help hide carrots from the carrot rust fly, and the two plants do not crowd each other's roots.
seasoned: Carrots and onions are the textbook reciprocal pairing. Your onions' sulfur scent helps mask the carrots from the carrot rust fly, and in return carrots interplanted with onions tend to carry less onion thrips damage, so each crop disrupts the other's main pest. Intercropping trials have measured real reductions in carrot fly where the two grow together. Plant in alternating rows with enough onion density for the scent-masking to register, and note the strongest results come from small mixed plantings rather than large solid blocks.

beginner: Beets and onions grow well side by side. They like the same cool weather and stay out of each other's way.
seasoned: Beets and onions share a bed comfortably. The onion's pungency helps deter pests that bother beets, and because onions bulb shallowly with sparse upright foliage while beets put their energy into a single root, the two do not crowd each other above or below ground. This is mostly a good-neighbor, efficient-space pairing with a modest pest-repel bonus.

beginner: Fast little lettuce plants fit nicely in the gaps between onions and like the same cool season, so you get two crops from one spot.
seasoned: Lettuce and onions interplant efficiently. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick while onions send a narrow bulb down with little leafy spread, so they occupy different space and the lettuce fills in between onion rows. The onion scent offers a little aphid deterrence over the lettuce as a bonus. Treat it as a space-and-timing pairing first, mild pest help second.

beginner: Cabbage and broccoli like the same cool weather as onions, and the strong onion smell is thought to bother some of their pests.
seasoned: Onions are a well-supported brassica companion. Their sulfur scent helps mask the cabbage family and deter its signature pests, cabbage loopers, worms, and root maggots, and extension trial work including onion in a mix with broccoli showed reduced caterpillar damage. Alliums are shallow and undemanding, so they tuck between brassicas without competing for the heavy feeding those crops want.

beginner: Look for thin grass-like shoots coming up. Each one starts bent over in a little loop, like a hairpin, then stands up straight. Onions sprout slowly and not all at once, so do not worry if they come up over a week or two rather than all together.
seasoned: A single looped seed leaf pushes up bent like a hairpin, then straightens into the first slender tube. Stands are sparse and uneven at first; onion germinates slowly and unevenly over a wide soil range (about 48 to 90°F), fastest in the middle of that band.

beginner: Keep the top of the soil damp so the tiny seeds do not dry out while sprouting, and pull weeds early, because young onions lose out to weeds easily. If you planted young plants or sets instead of seeds, you can skip this stage.
seasoned: Keep the surface evenly moist so the fine seed never dries mid-germination, and keep the bed weed-free from the start; onion seedlings are weak competitors. If you set transplants or sets instead of sowing seed, this stage is already behind you.

beginner: Write down when you planted and when the first shoots appeared. That tells you how fast your soil sprouts onions next time.
seasoned: Note your sowing or set-out date and the first emergence; the gap tells you your soil's germination pace for next season.

beginner: The plant grows more and more upright leaves. This stage matters most for how big your onions get, because each leaf turns into a layer of the bulb later. The more healthy leaves the plant grows now, the bigger the onion can be, so you want steady, unbroken growth.
seasoned: The plant adds upright tubular leaves one after another. This is the stage that decides bulb size: each leaf becomes a bulb ring, so the number of leaves a plant builds before bulbing sets its size ceiling. You want vigorous, uninterrupted leaf growth, not a check from drought, weeds, or cold.

beginner: Help the plant grow lots of leaves now. Feed it with a nitrogen fertilizer, keep the soil evenly moist, and keep weeds out. Do most of the feeding early, while it is making leaves, because feeding too late leads to soft necks that do not store well.
seasoned: Push leaf growth: side-dress nitrogen, hold moisture steady, and stay ruthless about weeds. Front-load the feeding so the canopy is built before day length triggers bulbing; nitrogen applied late goes to soft necks instead of rings.

beginner: Count the leaves and note when you fed the plants. The number of leaves when bulbs start forming is a good clue to how big they will be.
seasoned: Track leaf count and feeding dates; counting leaves at bulbing start is the best in-season predictor of final bulb size.

beginner: Day length is how long the daylight lasts. When the days reach the right length for your kind of onion, the plant stops making new leaves and the bottom starts to swell into a bulb. This switch is set by how long the days are where you live, not by the calendar, so you cannot speed it up. The bulb forms using however many leaves the plant already grew.
seasoned: Once day length crosses your cultivar's threshold (long, intermediate, or short day per the variety you planted), the plant stops adding leaves and the base begins to thicken. This is the photoperiod switch: the trigger is day length, set by your latitude and the season, not the calendar date or anything you do. Bulbing starts on whatever leaf count the plant reached, which is why the leaf stage mattered.

beginner: You cannot make this happen faster, so just keep watering steadily as the bulb starts to form. If nothing swells, or it swells when the plants are still tiny, you probably planted the wrong type of onion for your area, which is the thing to fix next year.
seasoned: There is no action that moves this trigger; the work was done in the leaf stage. Keep moisture steady so the swell starts without a check, and confirm you planted the right day-length class for your latitude (a mismatch shows up now as no bulbing or premature bulbing).

beginner: Write down when the bulbs started to swell and how many leaves the plants had. Over time this shows whether your onion type suits where you live.
seasoned: Note the date bulbing visibly began and the leaf count at that point; over seasons this confirms whether your variety's day-length class fits your site.

beginner: The leaves stay green and standing up while the bulb gets bigger below them, and you start to see the tops of the bulbs at the soil surface. This is when onions put on most of their size, so keep the watering steady; letting them dry out now makes smaller onions.
seasoned: Tops stay green and upright while the bulb swells underneath and shoulders begin to show at the soil surface. This is the fast-fill window; steady, even moisture now translates directly into size, while any drought check costs you final bulb weight.

beginner: Keep watering evenly and stop adding nitrogen fertilizer, because feeding now leads to thick necks that do not store. Do not pile soil over the bulbs or bend the green tops down to hurry them, an old trick that actually makes onions smaller, since those leaves are still feeding the bulb.
seasoned: Hold even moisture through the swell and taper nitrogen off; late nitrogen now thickens necks and works against storage. Do not pull soil up over the bulbs or bend the tops to force them, an old trick that backfires because the standing leaves are still feeding the bulb.

beginner: Note when you stopped feeding and any times the bed dried out. Comparing that to your harvest size shows how steady the watering needs to be.
seasoned: Log when you stopped feeding and any dry spells; matching those against final size tells you how tight your moisture needs to be.

beginner: The necks get soft and the green tops flop over by themselves. When about half of them have fallen, it is time to harvest. After you pull the onions, they still are not ready to store until they have dried out: the outer skin turns papery and the neck dries shut, which keeps them from rotting.
seasoned: The neck softens and the tops fall over on their own; about half the tops down is the harvest cue. After lifting, the bulb is not storage-ready until it is cured: outer scales turn papery and the neck dries tight, which seals the bulb against rot.

beginner: On a dry day, loosen the soil and lift the onions, handling them carefully so they do not get bruised (bruised spots tend to rot). Then dry, or cure, them for two to four weeks somewhere warm, shaded, and breezy until the skins go papery and the necks dry shut. Snip the tops to leave about an inch of stem, and keep them somewhere cool and dry.
seasoned: Loosen and lift on a dry day, handling gently to avoid the bruises that seed storage rot. Cure two to four weeks in a warm, airy, shaded spot until scales rustle and necks are tight, then cut tops to leave roughly an inch of stem before storing cool and dry.

beginner: Write down when you harvested, how long you dried the onions, and how well they kept. That tells you next year how long to dry them.
seasoned: Record the lift date, curing length, and how the bulbs stored; curing time versus storage life is the feedback that pays off all season.

beginner: Time to start onion seeds inside
seasoned: Start onion seed indoors

beginner: If you are growing onions from seed, plant them in trays indoors now, about 10 to 12 weeks before they go outside. Onions need this long head start to grow lots of leaves first. If you are using sets or young plants from a store, you can ignore this reminder.
seasoned: If you are growing from seed, sow indoors now, roughly 10 to 12 weeks before set-out. The long lead lets plants build a full leaf canopy before day length triggers bulbing. Growing from sets or bought transplants instead? Skip this one.

beginner: Time to plant onions outside
seasoned: Set out onions

beginner: Plant your sets or young onions outside now, once the soil is workable and not ice-cold. Set them shallow and use small, thin ones. Big sets, or a cold snap right after planting, can make onions bolt (shoot up a flower stalk instead of making a bulb).
seasoned: Plant sets or transplants once soil is workable and has warmed past the cold-snap window. Set them shallow, pencil-thick or smaller, and use small sets; oversized sets and a hard cold spell after planting drive bolting.

beginner: Feed your onions now
seasoned: Feed nitrogen while leaves build

beginner: Give your onions a nitrogen fertilizer now, while they are growing leaves, and again every few weeks until the bulbs start forming. Feeding early builds the leaves that decide bulb size. Once bulbs start to swell, stop feeding, because it does more harm than good then.
seasoned: Side-dress nitrogen during leaf building and repeat every few weeks until bulbing starts. Front-loaded feeding grows the canopy that sets bulb size; feeding is wasted, even harmful, once bulbs begin to swell.

beginner: Onions are starting to make bulbs
seasoned: Your onions are switching to bulbs

beginner: About now, the days have gotten long enough that your onions stop growing new leaves and start growing a bulb instead. You cannot make this go faster. Just keep watering steadily and stop feeding, so the bulbs can swell without interruption.
seasoned: Around now, lengthening days cross your variety's threshold and plants shift from making leaves to filling a bulb. You cannot speed this; just hold moisture steady and stop adding nitrogen so the swell runs uninterrupted.

beginner: Stop watering as tops flop over
seasoned: Ease off water as tops fall

beginner: When the necks get soft and the tops start to flop over, stop watering. Letting the soil and the onions dry out now helps the bulbs firm up and keeps them from rotting later.
seasoned: As necks soften and tops begin to fall, taper off watering so the bulbs firm up and the necks start to dry. Lifting into dry soil and dry weather sets up clean curing and better storage.

beginner: Time to harvest and dry onions
seasoned: Harvest and cure onions

beginner: Once roughly half the tops have fallen on their own, pull the onions on a dry day, handling them carefully to avoid bruising. Cure them for two to four weeks in a warm, shaded, breezy spot until the skins are papery and the necks dry shut. Trim the tops and store the bulbs somewhere cool and dry.
seasoned: When about half the tops have fallen, lift on a dry day and handle gently. Cure two to four weeks in a warm, airy, shaded spot until scales are papery and necks are tight, then trim and store cool and dry.

Cover young plants through an unseasonable cold spell, especially oversized sets or transplants, which are already primed to bolt.

beginner: Plant small sets or thin transplants once the soil has warmed up a bit, so they do not bolt. Set them shallow and do not pile soil over the bulbs, because the roots are shallow and that hurts them.
seasoned: Set out at the right size and time: small sets and pencil-thick transplants into soil that has warmed past the cold-snap window resist bolting. Plant shallow; deep planting and hilling soil over the bulb damage shallow roots and shrink bulbs.

beginner: Focus on growing lots of healthy leaves now, because each leaf becomes a layer in the bulb later. Feed with nitrogen, keep the soil moist, and pull weeds, since onions do not compete with weeds well.
seasoned: Push leaf growth now: this is a leaf crop until day length flips it to a bulb crop, and every leaf becomes a ring. Side-dress nitrogen, keep moisture steady, and stay ruthless about weeds, which onions compete with poorly.

beginner: Keep weeding and watering steadily while the leaves fill in. The more uninterrupted growth the plants get now, the bigger the bulbs can be.
seasoned: Keep the bed weed-free and evenly watered through canopy build; uninterrupted growth before bulbing sets your maximum bulb size.

beginner: When the bulbs start to swell, stop adding nitrogen. Do not bend over the green tops to try to hurry things along, an old trick that actually backfires, because the leaves are still feeding the bulb and breaking them makes the onion smaller.
seasoned: As bulbs swell, taper off nitrogen and let the necks mature; do not bend or break the green tops to force bulbing, since the leaves are still feeding the bulb and knocking them down reduces final size.

beginner: Harvest when about half the tops have flopped over on their own and the necks feel soft. Lift the bulbs gently on a dry day, and try not to bruise them, since bruises lead to rot in storage.
seasoned: Harvest when about half the tops have naturally fallen and necks have softened. Loosen and lift on a dry day; careful handling avoids the bruises that seed storage rot.

beginner: Dry (cure) the onions in a warm, airy, shaded place for two to four weeks until the outer skins are papery and the neck is tight and dry. Then cut the tops about an inch above the bulb. Onions that are not dried well are the ones that rot in storage.
seasoned: Cure in a warm, airy, shaded spot (about 75 to 90°F) for two to four weeks until outer scales are papery and the neck is tight and dry, then trim tops about an inch above the bulb. Poor curing is the main cause of storage loss.

beginner: When the days reach the right length for your kind of onion, the plant stops making leaves and the bottom starts to swell. If nothing swells, or it swells while the plants are still tiny, you likely planted the wrong onion type for your area, which is the thing to fix next year.
seasoned: Bulbing is triggered by day length crossing your cultivar's threshold, not by anything you do, so there is no action that moves it; the leaf count the plant reaches before the switch sets the bulb size. Keep moisture and nitrogen steady so the swell starts without a check, and confirm you planted the right day-length class for your latitude, since a mismatch shows up now as no bulbing or premature bulbing.

beginner: Each onion plant makes one bulb. A 10-foot row can give you about 20 to 25 pounds of onions in a good year.
seasoned: One bulb per plant. A 10-foot row at 4-inch spacing yields roughly 20 to 25 pounds of bulbs in a good season.

beginner: Onions of the same kind all finish around the same time, so you harvest most of them together rather than a few at a time.
seasoned: All bulbs of a variety size up and mature together as day length triggers bulbing, so the harvest comes in one main flush rather than over a long window.

beginner: The most important thing for a good first harvest is picking the right type for where you live. The wrong type will make tiny bulbs or no bulbs.
seasoned: Matching variety day-length type to your latitude is the biggest first-year yield lever; a mismatched type bulbs too early (small) or never bulbs at all.

beginner: Choose long-day onions here. They only start a bulb when days get very long (14 to 16 hours), which your summer delivers. A southern short-day onion would form its bulb too early and end up small.

beginner: In the Piedmont and Coastal Plain, onions are a one-time spring crop. The cooler Piedmont (zone 7) is long-day onion country. Set sets or seedlings out as soon as the ground can be worked; onions shrug off a light frost. seasoned: Onion in the Mid-Atlantic is a single spring-planted crop with no fall crop. Day-length suitability splits by zone: the cooler Piedmont north (zone 7) is long-day onion country, while the Coastal Plain south (zone 8, at or below the 36°N line) is intermediate-day country, where NC State recommends short-day types for eastern North Carolina and calls long-day onions not recommended there. Virginia Cooperative Extension's 426-331 tables carry only a spring window and no fall column; for the intermediate-day Coastal Plain we close the planting window by the end of March, about Feb 20 to Mar 31 in zone 8, rather than running to the table's April date, since intermediate-day onions size up best when set early, while the long-day Piedmont keeps the fuller spring window, about Mar 1 to May 1 in zone 7. Bulbing is triggered by day length rather than by planting date, so bulbs mature on roughly the same midsummer calendar regardless of exactly when they went in; lift and cure two to four weeks before storage.

beginner: An onion is the swollen base of the plant's leaves, packed into the layered bulb you cook with. Here is the part that surprises most first-time growers: an onion decides to start forming its bulb based on how long the days are, not on a date. Because of that, onions are sold by "day length" instead of by the usual hardiness zone. Long-day kinds like Walla Walla need very long summer days and suit the North, short-day kinds like Texas 1015Y need only short days and suit the South, and intermediate kinds like Super Star sit in the middle and grow well across much of the country. Pick the type that matches where you live, give the plants rich loose soil, water them steadily, and they are not hard to grow.
seasoned: Onion (Allium cepa) is a cool-season biennial grown as an annual for its bulb, which is a stack of swollen leaf bases rather than a root. Each green leaf builds one bulb scale, so leaf count at the moment bulbing starts sets the ceiling on bulb size. What triggers bulbing is day length, not the calendar: a cultivar switches from making leaves to filling a bulb only once daylight crosses its threshold. That threshold is what splits onions into long-day (14 to 16 hours, such as Walla Walla), intermediate-day (12 to 14 hours, such as Super Star), and short-day (10 to 12 hours, such as Texas 1015Y) types, and it is why the right variety depends on your latitude. Grow a heavy-feeding, shallow-rooted plant in loose fertile soil, keep moisture steady so growth never stalls, then ease off water as the tops fall to begin curing.

beginner: Your onions are ready to dig when about half the tops have flopped over on their own and the necks feel soft. A simple test: gently pinch the neck just above the bulb. If it is stiff, wait; if it is soft and floppy, it is time. Pull them on a dry day, then dry (cure) them.
seasoned: Bulb onions are ready when about half the tops have naturally fallen over and the necks have begun to soften and dry. Pinch a neck to judge maturity: a stiff neck is immature, a soft, limber neck is ripe, and a collapsed neck means over-mature. Lift on a dry day, then cure.

beginner: Onions are unusual: they start making a bulb based on how long the days are, not on the calendar. Each kind of onion needs a certain number of daylight hours before it will switch from growing leaves to growing a bulb. That is why onions are sold by "day length" instead of by hardiness zone. There are three kinds. Long-day onions need very long summer days (14 to 16 hours) and grow best in the North. Short-day onions need only short days (10 to 12 hours) and grow best in the South, where they are planted in fall or winter. Intermediate onions need about 12 to 14 hours and grow well across the middle of the country. Pick the kind that matches where you live: a northern onion planted in the South may never make a bulb, and a southern onion planted in the North makes only a tiny one. Day length decides when the bulb forms, but it does not change when you plant, which still depends on frost and soil temperature.
seasoned: Onion is photoperiodic: a bulb forms only once day length crosses a cultivar-specific threshold, at which point the plant stops adding leaves and starts filling a bulb. Cultivars fall into three classes by that threshold, long-day at 14 to 16 hours, intermediate-day at 12 to 14 hours, and short-day at 10 to 12 hours, so the suitable class depends on your latitude. Long-day types fit northern latitudes (roughly above 38 to 39°N), where summer days run long enough that plants build a large leaf canopy before the trigger; short-day types fit southern latitudes (roughly below 35°N), where they are planted in fall or winter and bulb as days lengthen; intermediate types span the middle (roughly 32 to 42°N) and grow well across much of the country. Plant the wrong class and a long-day onion in the South may never bulb, while a short-day onion in the North bulbs too early on few leaves and stays small. Day length triggers bulbing only; it never moves your planting date, which stays anchored to frost and soil temperature.

beginner: There are three easy ways. The simplest is to sow seed right in the garden, a quarter to a half inch deep, then thin the seedlings to about one per inch. Or start seeds indoors about four weeks before planting out for an earlier harvest, then set the little plants an inch apart. The tidiest way is to multisow: drop a small pinch of about six to ten seeds into each cell, let them grow as a little clump, and plant the whole clump out without splitting it, about four to six inches from the next one. Because you eat scallions in bunches anyway, there is nothing to thin, and you just pull the biggest few from each clump and let the rest keep growing. In the cooler Piedmont (zone 7), the spring harvest bridges naturally into the fall sowing with no real idle gap, so no heat exclusion is declared there. Sow a short row every two to three weeks through each window for a continuous supply.

Spring sowing runs roughly Feb 21 to Mar 23, with young stems ready about 60 days later; once daytime highs push past 90°F, per UNR Fact Sheet FS-02-61's growth ceiling for the region, seed germinates poorly and stands turn tough and quickly bolt, so sowing pauses through the hottest months. The chart's fall window, about Aug 1 to Sep 10, restarts the crop as the heat breaks, cropping into cooler weather and picked up to the valley's first frost, which this crop tolerates lightly. St. George warms up fast each spring and daytime highs push into the 100s by June, July, and August, so sowing pauses from May; sow again from about Aug 1 to Aug 20 for a fall crop, harvested from late September up to the first frost around Nov 1.

The spring sowing runs from about Feb 15, USU's St. George Group A date for onions, with a quick harvest by late April. beginner: A spring onion, also called a scallion or green onion, is a young onion you eat whole: the long white base and the green tops. You harvest it before it makes a round bulb, so it grows fast and is easy. Some kinds (called bunching onions) never make a bulb at all, and you can also just sow regular onions close together and pull them young as scallions. Plant the seeds shallow, thin the seedlings to about an inch apart, keep the soil damp, and they are usually ready in about 50 to 70 days, when the green tops are 6 to 8 inches tall. They handle cold well, so plant a short row every couple of weeks through the cool season for a steady supply, and nearly year-round where winters are mild.
seasoned: Spring onion, or scallion, is a fast cool-season allium grown for its slender white shank and green tops rather than a mature bulb. It is harvested young, before bulbing, so the day-length trigger that governs bulb onions is irrelevant here: you pull the plant while it is still a straight stem. Two routes give the same kitchen result, true bunching types (Allium fistulosum) that never form a bulb, or regular bulb onions (Allium cepa) sown thickly and pulled at the green stage. Sow seed shallowly, thin to about an inch, keep the soil evenly moist, and harvest in roughly 50 to 70 days when the tops stand 6 to 8 inches. Because the crop is quick and very cold hardy, sow a short row every two to three weeks through the cool season for a steady supply, year-round in mild regions.

beginner: Your scallions are ready when the green tops are about 6 to 8 inches tall and the white bottom is roughly as thick as a pencil. Do not wait for a round bulb to form, pull them while the base is still straight. Lift the whole plant, or with bunching types snip the tops about an inch above the soil and let them grow back. Smaller ones taste milder, bigger ones are a little stronger.
seasoned: Pull scallions once the green tops reach about 6 to 8 inches and the white shank is roughly pencil thick. There is no need to wait for a bulb: harvest at the straight-stem stage, before the base swells. Lift the whole plant, or cut bunching types about an inch above the crown and let them regrow. Younger is milder, so harvest on the small side for salads and a bit larger for cooking.

beginner: Corn grows best in deep, rich, well-drained soil like loam. Because it grows tall and feeds heavily, mixing in compost before planting helps the soil hold the steady moisture the plants need when the ears are forming.
seasoned: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam suits corn best. Its roots run deep and it feeds heavily, so a soil rich in organic matter that holds moisture through the tasseling and silking window without waterlogging gives the fullest ears.

beginner: Both sandy and clay-based soils can grow corn as long as they drain well. Sandy soil warms up early but dries out and loses fertilizer faster, so water and feed a little more often. Heavier soil holds food longer but should be loosened so it does not form a hard crust over the seeds.
seasoned: Sandy and clay loams both grow good corn if drainage is sound. Sandy beds warm faster and suit early sowings but dry out and leach nitrogen quicker, so they need more frequent water and sidedressing; heavier soils hold feeding longer but must be worked so they do not crust over the seed.

beginner: Stay away from cold, soggy, poorly drained soil. Corn seed sits and rots in cold, wet ground instead of sprouting, and standing water keeps the roots from feeding, which corn needs to do a lot of.
seasoned: Avoid cold, wet, poorly drained ground. Corn seed, especially supersweet sh2, rots or suffers chilling injury when sown into soil below 60°F, and standing water stunts the shallow feeder roots and starves the plant of the nitrogen it needs.
