beginner: Corn likes deep, rich, well-drained soil. If water pools on your bed after rain, work in compost and consider a raised bed so the roots never sit wet.
seasoned: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam with compost worked in before planting. The load-bearing traits are warmth at sowing and steady moisture with high fertility through tasseling and silking.

beginner: Corn does best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, around a pH of 6.0 to 6.8. Most garden beds are already close; a soil test is the only way to know for sure and to catch soil that is too acidic.
seasoned: A soil pH of 6.0 to 6.8 suits sweet corn. Lime an acidic bed to reach that range the season before, and confirm both pH and fertility with a soil test, since corn's heavy feeding rewards a well-limed, well-fed bed.

beginner: Corn is hungry, especially for nitrogen. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil at planting, then feed again when the plants are about knee-high and once more when the tassels appear at the top. Those are the times corn needs the most food. In sandy soil or after heavy rain, feed a little more often, since the nitrogen washes away.
seasoned: Corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder. Work a balanced starter into the bed at planting, then sidedress nitrogen twice: once when plants are knee-high and again as the tassels form, the two windows when demand peaks. Sandy soils and heavy rain leach nitrogen, so split the sidedressing further where that applies.

beginner: Time to feed your corn. It is about knee-high now, which is when it needs a nitrogen boost.
seasoned: Sidedress nitrogen now: your corn is at the knee-high stage where demand climbs steeply.

beginner: Corn wants plenty of nitrogen. Use a balanced fertilizer at planting, then feed nitrogen again as it grows.
seasoned: Nitrogen-forward feeding: a balanced starter, then nitrogen sidedressings at knee-high and tasseling.

beginner: Use the amount on the fertilizer label for a hungry vegetable, then two lighter nitrogen feedings as it grows.
seasoned: Follow the label rate for a heavy-feeding vegetable; a common approach is a balanced starter plus two nitrogen sidedressings.

beginner: Corn is the tall centerpiece of the classic Three Sisters planting with beans and squash. The beans feed the soil the corn is so hungry for, and the squash shades the ground below. Keep corn away from tomatoes, since the two share the same ear-and-fruit worm.
seasoned: Corn anchors the traditional Three Sisters trio: beans climb it and fix nitrogen for its heavy demand, and squash sprawls below as a living mulch. The main caution is tomatoes, which share the pest Helicoverpa zea (corn earworm / tomato fruitworm), so a shared planting can concentrate it.

beginner: The Three Sisters partner: beans pull nitrogen from the air and enrich the soil for hungry corn, and can climb the stalks.
seasoned: Pole beans use the cornstalk as a living trellis and fix nitrogen that offsets corn's heavy demand; the pairing is the well-documented Three Sisters polyculture. The benefit is soil-and-structure rather than a measured pest effect.

beginner: The third Sister: its big sprawling leaves shade the soil around the corn, holding moisture and smothering weeds.
seasoned: Squash rounds out the trio as a ground-covering living mulch that shades soil, conserves moisture, and suppresses weeds around the corn. A soil-and-space benefit; give it room so it does not swamp young corn.

beginner: Corn and tomatoes are hit by the same worm, called the corn earworm on corn and the tomato fruitworm on tomatoes, so growing them together can build it up.
seasoned: Corn and tomato share Helicoverpa zea (corn earworm on corn, tomato fruitworm on tomato). Interplanting gives the pest two sequential hosts in one spot, so separating them limits the buildup.

beginner: A fat, striped caterpillar tunneling into the tip of the ear under the husk, leaving chewed kernels and dark droppings. It usually stays near the tip, but the damage can let mold in.
seasoned: Chewed, frass-fouled kernels at the ear tip where a fat, striped caterpillar has fed under the husk; silks may be clipped, and tip damage opens the door to mold.

beginner: The corn earworm, a caterpillar whose moth lays eggs on the silks. The young caterpillars crawl down the silks into the ear. It is the same pest as the tomato fruitworm.
seasoned: The corn earworm (Helicoverpa zea), whose moths lay eggs on fresh silks; the hatching larvae follow the silks down into the ear tip. It is the same species as the tomato fruitworm.

beginner: The good news is the worm usually stays at the very tip, so you can just cut that part off. A classic trick is a few drops of vegetable or mineral oil on the silks after they have been pollinated, and an organic spray such as Bt or spinosad works if you time it to fresh silks.
seasoned: Because most feeding is confined to the ear tip, the loss is often cosmetic: cut off the damaged tip at the kitchen. A few drops of mineral oil applied to the silk channel after pollination is a traditional home tactic; a spinosad or Bt product timed to fresh silks is the labeled organic option.

beginner: Pick varieties with long, tight husks that make it harder for the worm to get in, and plant early so the ears silk before the moths are at their worst in late summer.
seasoned: Choose varieties with tight, long husk cover, which slows the larvae, and plant early so the crop silks before peak moth flights in late summer.

beginner: Tiny holes in the young leaves, then sawdust-like droppings where the leaves meet the stalk, and small holes bored into the stalk itself. Badly tunneled stalks can break.
seasoned: Small shot-hole feeding in the whorl leaves, then sawdust-like frass at leaf axils and pin-sized entry holes in the stalk and ear shank; tunneled stalks weaken and can snap.

beginner: The European corn borer, a caterpillar that starts by chewing the young leaves, then tunnels into the stalks, hollowing them out.
seasoned: The European corn borer (Ostrinia nubilalis), a caterpillar that first feeds in the leaf whorl, then bores into stalks and ear shanks, weakening the plant from inside.

beginner: Check the young leaf whorls and rub out the egg patches and small caterpillars before they tunnel in. An organic Bt spray only works while they are still out on the leaves; once inside the stalk you cannot reach them.
seasoned: Scout the whorls and pick off egg masses and young larvae before they bore in; a Bt product reaches them only while they are still feeding in the open whorl. Once inside the stalk they are protected.

beginner: Chop up and dig in the old cornstalks after harvest, because the borer spends the winter inside them, and move your corn to a new spot each year.
seasoned: Shred and turn under cornstalks after harvest, since the borer overwinters in old stalks; rotating away from last year's patch helps too.

beginner: Young corn plants cut off right at the ground overnight, as if with scissors. If you dig near a cut plant, you often find a fat gray caterpillar curled up in the soil.
seasoned: Young seedlings clipped off at or just above the soil line overnight, often toppled and left; a gray, greasy-looking caterpillar curls up just below the surface nearby.

beginner: Cutworms, fat caterpillars that live in the soil and come out at night to chew through young stems at the base.
seasoned: Cutworms, the soil-dwelling larvae of several night-flying moths, which sever tender seedling stems at the base as they feed after dark.

beginner: Go out at night with a flashlight and pick them off, or dig around a freshly cut plant to find the culprit. A little collar of cardboard or foil pushed into the soil around each stem keeps them out.
seasoned: Handpick at night or just under the soil around fresh damage; a cardboard or foil collar pushed an inch into the soil around each seedling blocks them.

beginner: Clear weeds from the bed before you plant, because the moths lay their eggs in weedy soil, and plant into warm soil so the seedlings grow quickly past the tender stage.
seasoned: Keep the bed weed-free before planting, since cutworm moths lay in weedy ground, and delay sowing until the soil is warm and seedlings grow fast through the vulnerable stage.

beginner: Tiny dark beetles that hop away when you get close, leaving the young leaves peppered with little pinholes. Bad early damage stunts small plants and can spread a corn disease.
seasoned: Tiny dark beetles that jump when disturbed, leaving fine pinholes and shot-hole pitting in the leaves of young plants; heavy early feeding stunts seedlings and can transmit Stewart's wilt.

beginner: Small beetles called flea beetles that chew young corn leaves. One kind also carries the germ that causes Stewart's wilt, a corn disease, spreading it as it feeds.
seasoned: Several flea beetle species that feed on corn seedlings; the corn flea beetle also carries the bacterium that causes Stewart's wilt from plant to plant.

beginner: Small plants usually grow past light damage. If the beetles are thick, cover the young plants with a lightweight row cover, taking it off when the tassels form so the wind can pollinate, and use an organic spinosad spray only if you must.
seasoned: Seedlings usually outgrow light feeding; where beetles are thick, a floating row cover over young plants (removed at tasseling for pollination) protects them, and spinosad is labeled if needed.

beginner: Pull weeds that shelter the beetles, plant into warm soil so the corn grows quickly, and pick varieties that resist Stewart's wilt if it is a problem where you live.
seasoned: Control weeds that harbor the beetles, plant after the soil warms so seedlings grow fast, and choose Stewart's-wilt-tolerant varieties where the disease occurs.

beginner: Ears torn open and eaten, and stalks knocked over, appearing overnight right when the corn is ready. Raccoons seem to know the exact night before you plan to harvest.
seasoned: Ears pulled down, husked, and half-eaten overnight just as they reach the milk stage, with stalks knocked flat; damage arrives suddenly the night before you meant to pick.

beginner: Raccoons, which raid ripe sweet corn at night and can clear a small patch in a night or two. They are one of the most common reasons a home corn crop is lost.
seasoned: Raccoons, which raid sweet corn at the milk stage and can strip a patch in a night or two; they are one of the most common causes of a lost home crop.

beginner: You cannot spray for raccoons; you have to keep them out. A short two-wire electric fence, switched on as the ears get close to ready, is the surest way to protect the patch.
seasoned: There is no spray; exclusion is the answer. A two-wire electric fence (about 4 and 8 inches high) turned on as ears near maturity is the most reliable home defense.

beginner: Set up and turn on the fence before the corn is ripe, not after the first raid. Once raccoons find your corn, they come back every night.
seasoned: Put the fence up and energize it before the ears reach the milk stage, not after the first raid, since once they find the patch they return nightly.

beginner: Puffy silver-white growths on the ears or stalks that later burst into a cloud of black powder. On the ear, these galls take the place of kernels. They show up most on stressed or damaged plants.
seasoned: Silvery-white galls on ears, tassels, or stalks that swell, then rupture to release a mass of powdery black spores; ear galls replace kernels and are most common on stressed or injured plants.

beginner: A fungus that gets in through wounds and silks, especially in hot, dry spells, and forms the galls. Its spores can survive in the soil for years.
seasoned: The fungus Ustilago maydis, which enters through wounds and silks and is favored by hot, dry weather punctuated by injury; its spores survive years in the soil.

beginner: There is no home spray. Cut off and throw away (do not compost) the galls before they burst, so their spores do not spread into your soil.
seasoned: There is no spray for the home garden; cut off and bag the galls before they rupture and blacken, to keep spores out of the soil. Do not compost them.

beginner: Try not to injure the plants while weeding, keep water and feeding steady so the corn is not stressed, move your corn each year, and pick more resistant varieties if smut keeps coming back.
seasoned: Avoid wounding plants during cultivation, keep moisture and fertility steady to reduce stress, rotate away from infected beds, and choose more tolerant varieties where smut recurs.

beginner: Small rusty-brown, powdery spots on both sides of the leaves that darken later in the season. A bad case yellows the leaves and can leave the ears less full.
seasoned: Small cinnamon-brown, powdery pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces, darkening toward the season's end; heavy infection yellows and kills leaf tissue and can cut ear fill.

beginner: A fungus whose spores blow in on the wind and take hold in cool, damp weather. In most gardens it arrives fresh each year rather than surviving the winter in place.
seasoned: The fungus Puccinia sorghi, whose spores blow in on the wind and infect under cool, moist, humid conditions; it does not overwinter in most northern gardens but arrives each year on wind currents.

beginner: Most gardens can live with a little rust. Pull off the worst lower leaves to slow it and give the plants air. You rarely need to spray in a home garden.
seasoned: Most home crops tolerate rust without treatment; remove badly infected lower leaves to slow spread and improve airflow. A labeled fungicide is rarely needed in a garden.

beginner: Pick rust-resistant varieties, which are easy to find, and plant early so the corn is nearly done before rust gets bad late in summer. Water at the base when you can.
seasoned: Choose rust-resistant hybrids, which are widely available, and plant early so the crop matures before rust builds late in the season; avoid overhead watering where practical.

beginner: Long yellow streaks with wavy edges running down the leaves, appearing after flea beetles have been feeding. A bad early case wilts and stunts young plants and can kill them.
seasoned: Long, pale-green to yellow streaks with wavy margins running along the leaves, following flea-beetle feeding scars; severe early infection wilts and stunts seedlings, sometimes killing them.

beginner: A bacterium spread by the corn flea beetle as it feeds. After a mild winter more beetles survive, so the disease tends to be worse the next year.
seasoned: The bacterium Pantoea stewartii, carried and introduced by the corn flea beetle; mild winters that let more beetles survive drive worse outbreaks the following year.

beginner: You cannot cure an infected plant; pull and throw away badly affected seedlings. The real control is keeping the flea beetles that spread it in check.
seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy severely affected seedlings. Management is aimed at the flea-beetle vector, not the bacterium itself.

beginner: Grow resistant varieties, which is the main defense, and keep flea beetles off young plants with a row cover or an organic treatment so they cannot pass the disease along.
seasoned: Grow resistant or tolerant hybrids, the primary defense, and manage flea beetles on young plants with row cover or a labeled treatment to break the transmission cycle.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist. Pay the closest attention from the time the tassels appear through when the ears are filling out, which is when corn needs water the most.
seasoned: Water regularly to keep the root zone evenly moist through the season, with the highest demand from tasseling through silking and ear fill.

beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, and closer to 1.5 inches while the corn is pollinating and filling ears. Water deeply so it soaks down to the roots rather than just wetting the surface.
seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week from rain and irrigation, rising toward 1.5 inches per week across the pollination and ear-fill window; water deeply to wet the full root zone.

beginner: Give corn a deep soak rather than frequent light sprinkles. Corn handles overhead watering better than many crops, but watering at the base wastes less and keeps the leaves drier.
seasoned: Deep soaking at intervals suits corn. Overhead watering is tolerated far better than on disease-prone crops, but soaker or furrow watering conserves water and keeps the canopy from staying wet.

beginner: If the soil stays soggy and the lower leaves yellow while the plant stalls, the roots are drowning. Ease off and let it drain.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and stunted, stalled growth in ground that stays wet point to waterlogged, oxygen-starved roots.

beginner: Leaves that roll up like tubes in the afternoon mean the corn is too dry. If this happens while the tassels and silks are out, you get ears with missing kernels, so keep the water steady then.
seasoned: Leaves that roll or curl at midday, especially near tasseling, signal drought stress; stress in the silking window desiccates silks and pollen and leaves gappy, poorly filled ears.

beginner: Keep the seedbed evenly damp, not soggy, until the seedlings come up. Cold, wet soil rots the seed before it sprouts.
seasoned: Sown into warm soil, corn wants an evenly moist seedbed until emergence, but not saturated: cold, waterlogged soil rots seed and chills supersweet sh2 kernels.

beginner: Water the young plants evenly as they get their roots down.
seasoned: Grow young plants on with steady, even moisture while the root system establishes.

beginner: Give about 1 inch of water a week as the plants shoot up, and water deeply so it reaches the growing roots.
seasoned: Water use climbs steadily as the plants gain height; keep about 1 inch per week and water deeply to follow the deepening roots.

beginner: When the tassels are shedding pollen, the corn must not dry out. Dry soil now means poorly filled ears later, so keep the water steady and generous.
seasoned: Tasseling opens the critical-moisture window: water stress now, as pollen sheds, cuts pollen viability and the eventual kernel set. Keep moisture high and steady.

beginner: Silking is the most important time of all for water. If the plants get dry now, the silks cannot do their job and the ears come out with gaps, so water deeply and keep it up.
seasoned: Silking is the single most moisture-sensitive stage: drought desiccates the silks and drops pollination, giving blank tips and gappy ears. This is where steady water pays off most.

beginner: Keep watering steadily while the kernels plump up. Letting it dry now costs you kernels at the tip of the ear.
seasoned: Demand stays high as kernels fill; stress here aborts kernels at the ear tip rather than causing outright pollination failure. Hold steady moisture until the milk stage.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist through picking. The ears in a block ripen around the same few days, so steady water finishes them well.
seasoned: Keep even moisture through the short milk-stage picking window so the ears finish plump; the block ripens close together.

beginner: The most important time to keep water steady is when the tassels and silks are out and the ears are filling.
seasoned: The critical moisture window is tasseling through silking and into ear fill; do not let the bed dry out then.

seasoned: Tasseling, silking, and ear fill are the moisture-critical stages; drought at silking is the single most damaging, giving gappy, poorly filled ears.

beginner: You do not need to harden off corn. It is planted straight into the garden from seed.
seasoned: Not applicable. Sweet corn is direct-sown in place and is not started indoors or hardened off.

beginner: Plant corn seeds right where they will grow, once the soil has warmed to at least 60°F and frost is past. Corn does not like having its roots disturbed and comes up fast anyway, so there is little reason to start it indoors.
seasoned: Direct-sow into warm soil (at least 60°F, warmer for sh2) after the last spring frost. Corn resents root disturbance and germinates quickly in place, so transplanting offers little gain and risks setting plants back.

beginner: Do not leave corn out on the counter. It loses its sweetness quickest when warm, so get it into the fridge.
seasoned: Not recommended. Sweet corn converts sugar to starch fastest at room temperature, so hold it cold rather than on the counter.

beginner: Cool the ears fast, leaving the husks on, and keep them cold. Old-style sweet (su) corn is best within a day or two, sugary-enhanced (se) holds a little longer, and supersweet (sh2) can keep up to about a week in the fridge.
seasoned: Chill immediately after picking, husks on, to slow the sugar-to-starch conversion. Standard sugary (su) types hold good quality only 1 to 2 days, sugary-enhanced (se) a day or two longer, and supersweet (sh2) up to about a week refrigerated.

beginner: Corn freezes well if you want to keep it. For the best flavor, blanch and freeze it within a few hours of picking, while it is still sweet.
seasoned: Corn freezes well for longer storage. For best quality, blanch and freeze (or can) within a few hours of picking, before the sugars turn.

beginner: Corn is best the day you pick it. Its sugar slowly turns to starch after harvest, fastest in old-style sweet types, so cool it right away, keep it cold, and freeze it within a few hours if you want to store it.
seasoned: Sweet corn is best eaten as soon after picking as possible. The clock is the sugar-to-starch conversion, fastest in su types and slowest in sh2: cool the ears immediately, keep them cold, and process for the freezer within hours for top quality.

beginner: Sweet corn comes in three sugar types. Standard sweet (su) tastes classic but must be eaten quickly. Sugary-enhanced (se) is sweeter and tender and holds a bit longer, and is the easiest all-around choice. Supersweet (sh2) stays sweetest the longest, but its seed needs warmer soil to sprout and it has to be kept apart from the other types so their pollen does not make it starchy.
seasoned: Choose by sugar genetics. Standard sugary (su) gives classic corn flavor but the shortest quality window; sugary-enhanced (se) is sweeter and more tender and holds a little longer; supersweet (sh2) holds sweetness longest and stores best, but its seed needs warmer soil to germinate and it must be isolated from su and se types by distance or planting date, or the cross turns the kernels starchy.

beginner: If you plant the seeds close together to be sure they come up, thin them to about 8 to 12 inches apart within the block when they are a few inches tall. Cut the extra seedlings off at the ground instead of pulling them, so you do not disturb the roots of the ones you are keeping.
seasoned: If you sow thickly to insure a stand, thin within the block to a final in-row spacing of 8 to 12 inches once seedlings are a few inches tall. Snip the extras at the soil line rather than pulling, to spare the shallow roots of the plants you keep.

beginner: How tall is your corn getting? Note its height and when you fed it.
seasoned: How is your corn filling in? Note the height, leaf count, and any sidedressing you did.

beginner: Plant corn in a square block of short rows, not one long row. Corn is pollinated by wind, so the pollen from the tassels has to drift down onto the silks. seasoned: Plant corn in a BLOCK, not a long single row. Corn is wind-pollinated: the tassel sheds pollen that must fall on the silks, and a block of at least four short rows (a 4 by 4 grid) fills the ears far better than one long row where pollen blows off to the side.

beginner: Wait until the soil has warmed to at least 60°F before planting, and a little warmer for supersweet types, whose seeds rot in cold, wet soil. Planting early just gives you missing plants, so there is nothing to gain by rushing.
seasoned: Wait for soil at least 60°F before sowing, warmer for supersweet sh2, whose tougher seed rots or takes imbibitional chilling injury in cold, wet ground. There is no head start in early planting.

beginner: Keep your sweet corn away from popcorn and field corn, and keep supersweet types apart from the others by distance or by planting them two weeks apart. If their pollen mixes, the kernels turn starchy instead of sweet.
seasoned: Keep sweet corn away from popcorn and field corn, and isolate supersweet sh2 from su and se types by about 250 feet or two weeks' difference in tasseling. Stray pollen crosses the kernels and turns them starchy.

beginner: Feed corn with nitrogen when it is about knee-high and again when the tassels appear. Corn is a hungry crop, and those are the two times it needs the most food. In sandy soil, feed a little more often, since the nitrogen washes away.
seasoned: Sidedress nitrogen at knee-high and again as tassels form. Corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder, and the two demand peaks are rapid stalk growth and the run-up to pollination; sandy soils call for splitting it further.

beginner: Keep the soil moist while the tassels are shedding pollen. Hot weather over 95°F or dry soil now ruins the pollen, so the ears end up with missing kernels. Water deeply and keep it steady through this stretch.
seasoned: Do not let the bed dry out at tasseling. Heat over 95°F or drought as pollen sheds kills pollen viability and thins the kernel set. Keep moisture high and steady through the pollination window.

beginner: Silking is the most important time of all for water. If the corn dries out now, the silks cannot catch and hold pollen, and that costs you more than dry weather at any other time. Water deeply through any hot spell while the silks are out.
seasoned: Silking is the single most drought-sensitive stage: stress here desiccates silks and pollen and gives the greatest yield loss of any timing. Water deeply through any heat wave while the silks are receptive.

beginner: Keep watering steadily while the ears fill. After the corn has been pollinated, dry soil shows up as missing kernels at the tip of the ear, so do not let it dry out until the ears are ready.
seasoned: Hold steady moisture through ear fill. Once pollination has succeeded, dry conditions show up as aborted kernels at the ear tip rather than outright failure, so keep water even until the milk stage.

beginner: Pick when the silks have browned and a squeezed kernel runs a milky juice. This peak lasts only a few days and the whole block comes ready together, so check every day. Cool the ears right after picking to keep them sweet.

seasoned: Each stalk typically yields one to two ears, which is why corn is grown in a block of many plants rather than a few; a 10-foot row returns roughly a dozen to two dozen ears over its short window.

beginner: A block of corn comes ready all within a few days, then quickly goes past its best. Planting blocks a couple of weeks apart, or mixing early and late varieties, spreads out the harvest instead of getting it all at once.
seasoned: A block ripens close together over a short 4-to-5-day milk-stage window, then the sugars turn. Staggered blocks (or su, se, and sh2 types of differing maturity) spread the harvest instead of one glut.

beginner: Sweet corn is a fun first-year crop, but it needs room: plant a block of several rows, not just a few plants, keep it watered when the silks are out, and guard the ripe ears from raccoons. Do that and a small block gives a real harvest in 60 to 90 days.

You can keep sowing every couple of weeks into midsummer for a longer harvest instead of one big batch. Always plant corn in a block of several short rows rather than one long row; the wind carries pollen from plant to plant, and a block pollinates far better than a line.
seasoned: Virginia Cooperative Extension Pub. 426-331 gives sweet corn a single spring window with no fall column: zone 8 April 1 to August 10, zone 7 April 10 to July 20. Direct sow into soil that has warmed past 60°F after the last frost, then stagger a few blocks through early summer for a steady supply of ears rather than one glut. Plant in a block of at least four short rows, never a single long row: corn is wind pollinated, and a block lets pollen reach every ear. A 75 day crop like sweet corn easily finishes even from a late sowing, well ahead of the belt's fall frost.

beginner: In the Ozark Uplands and Delta Lowlands, sow sweet corn straight into the garden after your last frost, once the soil feels warm, and keep sowing every couple of weeks for a longer harvest instead of one big batch. University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension also documents a dedicated fall planting here: sow in the first half of July, or the last week of June into early July in zone 7, for a fresh run of ears in September and October. Always plant corn in a block of several short rows rather than one long row; the wind carries pollen from plant to plant, and a block pollinates far better than a line.
seasoned: Sweet corn gets two documented cycles in this belt. The spring runway is long: direct sow into soil that has warmed past 60°F, from late March to mid-August in zone 8 and early April to mid-July in zone 7, staggering blocks every couple of weeks for a steady supply of ears. University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension's fall table then lists sweet corn outright: a dedicated fall planting July 1 to 15 in zone 8, and June 24 to July 8 in zone 7's cooler uplands, brings ears at the milk stage from early September into October. Plant in a block of at least four short rows, never a single long row: corn is wind pollinated, and a block lets pollen reach every ear. (University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension spring and fall planting-date tables)

beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, direct-sow sweet corn outdoors in spring once the last frost has passed, from about Mar 10 through Apr 20, for a harvest before the worst heat hits. Once daytime highs push past 90°F in summer, pollen is killed and the silks dry out before they can catch it, and ears set poorly, so the plants take a long break. Sow again from about Aug 1 to Aug 25 for a fall crop that ripens as the weather cools, picked before the first frost.
seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) grows sweet corn on two direct-sown cycles, per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart. Spring sowing runs roughly Mar 10 to Apr 20, with harvest beginning about 75 days later; the crop is picked before summer's real heat wall. Once daytime highs run past 90°F, pollen is killed and the silks dry out before they can catch it, and ears set poorly, so the chart calls for a real gap through the hottest weeks rather than a continuous summer run. The chart's late-summer window (about Aug 1 to Aug 25) restarts the crop as the heat breaks, timed to finish picking a few days ahead of the valley's first fall frost. Zone 8's cooler pockets compress both ends: a later spring set-out and an earlier fall sowing to beat that zone's earlier frost; zone 10 at Laughlin runs the opposite, earlier spring and a later fall sowing, with its later frost.

beginner: In St. George, direct-sow sweet corn once, at the front of the spring window from about March 15 to April 5 per USU Extension, once the last frost has passed. Ears are ready to pick from late May, over about a five-week window as the different sowing dates catch up; corn does best planted in blocks of at least four short rows so the wind pollinates every ear. There is no fall corn crop here; this is a single spring planting.
seasoned: Sweet corn follows USU Extension's Group C (Tender) St. George date, about March 15, sown as one full-season block rather than a spring-plus-fall succession: USU documents no fall corn planting for St. George. Ears reach the fresh-eating milk stage about 75 days after the earliest sowing, and the picking window closes as the last-sown rows finish about a week and a half behind that, since ears held too long in St. George's summer heat quickly turn starchy. Plant a block of at least four short rows rather than one long row for reliable wind pollination, and keep sweet corn isolated from field corn, flint corn, and popcorn plantings, since their pollen makes sweet corn starchy.

beginner: Sweet corn is a tall summer grass grown for its ears, which you pick young and sweet at the milk stage. Corn is pollinated by wind, not by bees: the feathery tassel at the top drops pollen that has to reach the silks below, and each silk that catches pollen becomes one kernel. That is why you plant corn in a square block of short rows instead of a single long row, so the pollen has plenty of neighbors to land on. It likes warm soil, rich feeding, and steady water while the ears are forming.
seasoned: Sweet corn (Zea mays var. saccharata) is a tall, frost-tender warm-season grass grown for its immature ears, picked green at the milk stage. It is wind-pollinated: the tassel sheds pollen that must land on the silks, so it is planted in a block of short rows rather than one long row. Variety choice turns on sugar genetics (su, se, sh2), which set both sweetness and how long the ears hold quality after picking. Direct-sown into warm soil, it is a heavy feeder with a critical moisture window at tasseling and silking.

beginner: Corn is ready when the silks at the top of the ear have turned brown and dry and the ear feels plump and firm. To be sure, peek at a few kernels and press one with a thumbnail: ready corn runs a milky juice, watery juice means wait, and thick paste means you are late. This peak lasts only a few days, so check daily once the silks brown.
seasoned: Pick at the milk stage: the silks have browned and dried at the ear tip, the ear feels full and firm, and a punctured kernel runs a milky (not clear, not doughy) juice. This is roughly 18 to 20 days after the first silks show, and the window lasts only about 4 to 5 days.

beginner: Pick a sunny spot and mix in compost before planting, because corn is a hungry crop that grows tall. Plant it in a block of at least four short rows rather than one long row: a small square (say four rows of four plants) lets the wind carry pollen from the tassels onto the silks, so the ears fill out with full kernels instead of gappy ones. Keep sweet corn well away from popcorn or field corn so their pollen does not drift in and make your kernels starchy.
seasoned: Work compost or aged manure into a full-sun bed before planting; corn is a heavy feeder and roots deeply. Lay the planting out as a BLOCK of at least four short rows (a 4 by 4 grid beats one long row) so wind pollination fills the ears evenly. Keep sweet corn away from popcorn or field corn, and isolate sh2 supersweets from su or se types, since stray pollen crosses the kernels and turns them starchy.

beginner: Edamame likes loose, fertile soil that drains well, with some compost worked in. It grows best in full sun and warm soil. Like other beans, edamame seed rots in cold, soggy ground, so good drainage matters and you wait for the soil to warm before planting. If water sits on your bed a long time after rain, mix in compost or plant on a raised bed first.
seasoned: Edamame does best in a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam with compost worked in before sowing. As a warm-season soybean it wants full sun and warm soil; the seed is large and rots readily in cold, wet ground, so drainage and soil warmth carry the crop through a clean stand. Steady, even moisture without waterlogging matters most through flowering and pod fill. Edamame is a legume that fixes much of its own nitrogen, so the bed needs fertility and tilth more than heavy feeding.

beginner: Edamame grows best in soil from about 6.0 to 6.8, which is slightly acidic to neutral. It does poorly in strongly acidic soil, so if a soil test reads low, mix in some lime before planting. Most garden beds are already in a good range.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8, the band where soybean nodulates and yields best. Rutgers gives an ideal of 6.0 to 6.5 for edamame; below about 6.0 nitrogen fixation falls off, and above roughly 7.0 the crop is more prone to iron and manganese problems. A soil test is the reliable way to confirm pH and fertility before the season starts, and lime an acid plot the season before sowing.

beginner: Edamame makes much of its own food from the air, so it barely needs fertilizer. Mix a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the bed before you plant and that is enough. The useful step is to coat the seed with an inoculant, but it must be the soybean kind (Bradyrhizobium japonicum), not the regular bean and pea inoculant, since soybeans use a different bacteria. Too much fertilizer gives you big leafy plants but fewer pods.
seasoned: Edamame is a light feeder. As a legume it fixes much of its own nitrogen through root nodules, so heavy nitrogen drives leafy growth at the expense of pods. Without a soil test, work a little balanced fertilizer or compost into the bed before sowing; that is usually all edamame needs. The one feeding step that matters is the inoculant: edamame needs the SOYBEAN-specific bacterium Bradyrhizobium japonicum, not the all-purpose bean and pea inoculant, to nodulate and fix nitrogen, and it helps most where soybeans have not grown before. Avoid high-nitrogen feeds, which delay flowering and cut pod set.

beginner: A balanced vegetable fertilizer like 5-10-10 mixed into the bed before planting is plenty.
seasoned: A balanced 5-10-10 worked in before sowing if no soil test is available; skip extra nitrogen, which edamame supplies itself, and inoculate the seed with a soybean-type inoculant.

beginner: About 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet, mixed into the bed before planting.
seasoned: 5-10-10 at about 3 pounds per 100 square feet worked in before sowing when no soil test is available; the priority input is a soybean inoculant on the seed, not nitrogen.

beginner: Edamame gets along with most warm-season vegetables and, like other beans, leaves nitrogen in the soil for the next crop. It is a classic Three Sisters partner with corn and squash, and a good neighbor to cucumbers and potatoes. The pairing to avoid is planting edamame right next to onions or garlic.
seasoned: As a nitrogen-fixing legume, edamame leaves the soil richer for what follows and sits comfortably among the warm-season crops grown in the same window. It is a traditional Three Sisters partner with corn and squash and a compatible neighbor for cucumbers and potatoes. The long-standing caution is to keep edamame away from the alliums (onion, garlic), which are widely held to suppress legumes by interfering with the root bacteria they depend on to fix nitrogen.

beginner: The traditional Three Sisters partner; the planting has been grown together for generations and the edamame's nitrogen helps the hungry corn.
seasoned: Corn is the classic Three Sisters partner for a bushy soybean like edamame. Edamame does not climb the corn the way pole beans do, so the benefit is mostly foliage diversity and the legume nitrogen helping the heavy-feeding corn over the season. Give the corn room so it does not shade the lower edamame, which needs full sun to fill its pods.

beginner: The third Sister; its broad leaves shade the soil and keep weeds down around the edamame.
seasoned: Squash rounds out the Three Sisters trio. Its sprawling leaves shade the soil, hold moisture, and suppress weeds around the edamame, while the varied foliage heights make it harder for pests to lock onto one crop. This is a soil-and-space benefit; give the squash room so it does not swamp the lower edamame.

beginner: An easy warm-season neighbor that shares edamame's sun, warmth, and water needs.
seasoned: Cucumber and edamame coexist comfortably: similar warm-season timing, sun, and water needs, with complementary growth habits, and the edamame's nitrogen fixation lightly benefits the cucumber as a moderate feeder. It is a compatibility pairing rather than a strongly protective one, so expect easy cohabitation more than active pest control.

beginner: Onions and other alliums are traditionally kept away from beans and soybeans, which are said to grow poorly near them.
seasoned: Onions next to edamame is the better-grounded of the 'bad' pairings. Alliums release antibacterial sulfur compounds widely held to interfere with the nitrogen-fixing bacteria on legume roots, the bacteria edamame relies on, so growth tends to stall near onions. Keep them in separate parts of the bed. The useful corollary is that a legume grown before an allium crop leaves the soil better for it.

beginner: Like onions, garlic is a traditional bad neighbor for beans and soybeans.
seasoned: Garlic acts on edamame the way onions do. As an allium it gives off antibacterial sulfur compounds held to disrupt the nitrogen-fixing bacteria on legume roots, slowing the plants. Treat garlic and edamame as bed-mates to keep apart, and use the legume-then-allium rotation to your advantage instead.

beginner: Round holes chewed in the leaves, and worse, chewing on the pods themselves and even pods clipped off at the stem late in the season. The adult is a small reddish or yellowish beetle with a little black triangle behind its head and rows of black spots on its back.
seasoned: Round to irregular holes chewed through the leaves, and on the pods the more damaging sign: chewing on the pod wall and, late in the season, clipping at the base of the pod that drops it entirely. The adult is a small reddish to yellowish beetle with a black triangle behind the head and usually a row of black spots along each wing cover.

beginner: The bean leaf beetle, the main leaf-eating beetle of soybeans. The adults move into young plants in spring, and a summer generation feeds on the pods, which is the worst damage. It can also spread a virus from plant to plant.
seasoned: The bean leaf beetle (Cerotoma trifurcata), the most important leaf-feeding beetle of soybeans. Overwintered adults move into seedlings in spring, and a later summer generation feeds on the pods, which is the costly stage. It also transmits bean pod mottle virus.

beginner: Edamame can lose a fair amount of leaf early without losing beans, so light leaf damage needs nothing. Pick beetles off in a small patch, and focus on protecting the pods later in the season, when the beetles do the real harm. A light row cover keeps them off, and an organic spray such as spinosad helps if they get bad.
seasoned: Edamame tolerates a lot of early leaf feeding without losing yield, so light damage on the foliage needs nothing. Handpick adults in a small patch, and protect the pods later in the season, when pod feeding and clipping matter; a floating row cover keeps beetles off, and an organic option such as spinosad or pyrethrin is labeled where pressure is heavy.

beginner: Because the pod damage is the worst part, planting early so the pods finish before the summer beetles build up helps. Clear away the old plants after harvest and move your edamame each year, and cover young seedlings with a row cover if this beetle is a problem where you are.
seasoned: Since pod feeding is the costly damage, an early sowing that fills pods before the summer beetle generation peaks helps. Clear crop debris after harvest and rotate edamame away from last year's bed to remove overwintering shelter; a row cover protects emerging seedlings where the beetle is a known problem.

beginner: Pods that look fine on the outside but hold flat, shrunken, or stained beans inside, because the bugs poke through the pod and feed on the seeds. Stink bugs are shield-shaped insects about half an inch long, green or brown.
seasoned: Pods that look intact from outside but hold flat, shriveled, or discolored beans, because the bugs pierce the pod wall and feed on the developing seeds. Green and brown stink bugs are shield-shaped insects about half an inch long; their feeding scars the seed and can stop it filling.

beginner: Several kinds of stink bugs, including the green, brown, and brown marmorated stink bugs. They matter because they feed straight on the beans inside the pods while the pods are filling, which is the part you eat.
seasoned: The stink bug complex (green stink bug, brown stink bug, and the invasive brown marmorated stink bug). They are among the most damaging soybean pests because they feed directly on the seed during pod fill, exactly the part of edamame you eat.

beginner: Pick the shield-shaped bugs and their barrel-shaped egg clusters off by hand, checking while the pods fill. Keep weeds down around the bed, since the bugs come in from weedy edges, and use an organic spray only if they are really feeding on the pods.
seasoned: Handpick the shield-shaped adults and the barrel-shaped egg clusters in a home patch, checking through pod fill. Keep weeds down around the bed, since stink bugs move in from weedy edges, and treat with an organic option such as spinosad or pyrethrin only where feeding on the pods is heavy.

beginner: Check the pods from the time they set through filling, which is when stink bugs do harm. Clear weedy edges that shelter them before the season, move your edamame each year, and clean up old plants after harvest. An early variety can finish before the bugs peak in late summer.
seasoned: Watch the pods closely from pod set through fill, the window stink bugs damage. Mow or clear weedy borders that harbor them ahead of the season, rotate the bed, and clean up debris after harvest. An early-maturing crop can finish before peak late-summer pressure.

beginner: Clusters of tiny, soft, pale-yellow insects on the growing tips and undersides of the upper leaves, sometimes with ants around them. Heavy feeding curls and yellows the leaves and leaves a sticky residue, and the aphids can spread viruses.
seasoned: Colonies of small, soft, pale-yellow aphids on the growing tips, undersides of upper leaves, and stems, often tended by ants. Heavy feeding puckers and yellows the leaves, stunts the plant, and leaves a sticky honeydew that blackens with sooty mold; the aphids also transmit several plant viruses.

beginner: The soybean aphid, an invasive aphid that feeds only on soybeans and can multiply fast in midsummer. Mild weather lets it build up quickly, and ladybugs and other helpers usually bring it down.
seasoned: The soybean aphid (Aphis glycines), an invasive aphid specific to soybeans that can build explosively in midsummer. Cool to warm, calm weather favors rapid buildup; ladybugs and other natural enemies usually catch up.

beginner: Spray the colonies off with a strong jet of water or use insecticidal soap, starting while there are only a few. Ladybugs and other helpful insects usually finish the job, so avoid sprays that kill them too. Deal with aphids early since they can spread viruses.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong spray of water or treat with insecticidal soap, beginning while numbers are low. Ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually control soybean aphid in a garden, so avoid broad sprays that kill those helpers. Act early, since the aphids also move viruses.

beginner: Do not overfeed with fertilizer, since the soft new growth is what aphids like, and keep weeds down nearby. Reflective mulch confuses them and cuts the viruses they spread, and helpful insects do most of the work in a home garden.
seasoned: Avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, which produces the soft growth aphids favor, and keep nearby weeds and buckthorn (the aphid's overwintering host) in check. Reflective mulch disorients them and reduces virus spread, and natural enemies do most of the work in a home garden.

beginner: Leaves chewed down to a lacy skeleton of veins, the classic Japanese beetle damage, as the shiny green-and-copper beetles feed in groups on top of the plants in midsummer. They can strip a lot of leaf, but edamame handles a fair amount of leaf loss.
seasoned: Leaves skeletonized to a lacy network of veins, the classic Japanese beetle signature, as the metallic green-and-copper adults feed in groups on the upper canopy in midsummer. Heavy feeding can strip the foliage, though edamame tolerates a good deal of leaf loss before yield suffers.

beginner: The Japanese beetle, a shiny green beetle with copper wings whose grubs live in lawns and whose adults feed on many plants, including soybeans, in midsummer.
seasoned: The Japanese beetle (Popillia japonica), a metallic green beetle with coppery wing covers whose grubs develop in lawns and whose adults feed on many garden plants, soybeans included, through midsummer.

beginner: Pick the beetles off in the early morning when they are slow, dropping them into soapy water; this works well in a garden. Skip the beetle traps, which often attract more beetles than they catch. Since edamame handles a lot of leaf loss, light damage needs no spray.
seasoned: Handpick the beetles in the early morning when they are sluggish, knocking them into soapy water; this is effective in a home patch and avoids the traps, which draw in more beetles than they catch. Because edamame tolerates real defoliation, light to moderate feeding on the leaves needs no spray.

beginner: Watch through midsummer, when the adults feed, and cover plants with a row cover during a heavy beetle flight if needed. Keeping the lawn a bit drier in midsummer means fewer grubs, and light leaf damage is better tolerated than sprayed.
seasoned: Watch through midsummer, the adult-feeding window, and protect plants with a floating row cover during a heavy flight if needed. Healthy lawns kept on the dry side in midsummer support fewer grubs; tolerate light leaf feeding rather than spraying.

beginner: Fine whitish or yellow speckling on the leaves, turning to a dried, bronzed look, with fine webbing on the undersides. The mites are tiny specks, easiest to see by tapping a leaf over white paper. They explode in hot, dry weather.
seasoned: Fine whitish or yellow stippling on the leaves that progresses to a bronzed, dried-out look, with fine silken webbing on the undersides; the mites are minute specks, easiest to confirm by tapping a leaf over white paper. They build explosively in hot, dry weather.

beginner: Two-spotted spider mites, tiny relatives of spiders that pierce the leaf and suck out the contents. Hot, dry, dusty weather and dried-out plants let them build up fast, so they flare in dry midsummer.
seasoned: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae), tiny relatives of spiders that pierce leaf cells and suck the contents. Hot, dry, dusty conditions and drought-stressed plants favor rapid buildup, so they flare in dry midsummer spells.

beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water to knock off the mites and webbing, and use insecticidal soap before they get thick. Keeping the plants well watered and unstressed slows them down, and helpful bugs pitch in.
seasoned: Hose the undersides of leaves with a strong spray of water to dislodge mites and webbing, and treat with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil before numbers climb. Keeping plants well watered and unstressed slows buildup, and natural predators help.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist, because dried-out plants are much more likely to get mites, and keep dust down. Check the undersides of the leaves during hot, dry weather so you catch them early.
seasoned: Maintain even soil moisture, since drought-stressed plants are far more mite-prone, and keep dust down around the bed. Watch the undersides of leaves through hot, dry spells so you catch the buildup early.

beginner: Stems with a white, cottony mold at the joints, sometimes with hard black lumps in them; the stem above bleaches, wilts, and dies. It shows up in cool, wet weather where the plants are crowded and the air does not move.
seasoned: Water-soaked lesions on the stems at the nodes that turn into a white, cottony fungal growth, often with hard black resting bodies (sclerotia) inside or on the stems; affected stems bleach, wilt, and die above the lesion. It develops in cool, wet weather in dense, lush canopies with poor airflow.

beginner: A fungus, the same white mold that hits beans. Hard black survival bodies live for years in the soil and sprout in cool, damp weather to infect the plants, especially where crowded, overfed growth keeps the leaves humid.
seasoned: The fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, the same white mold that hits beans. Its hard black sclerotia survive years in the soil and germinate in cool, moist conditions to infect flowering plants, especially where dense, overfed growth keeps the canopy humid.

beginner: There is no home spray that cures it; you manage it by how you grow. Pull and throw away (do not compost) infected plants, since the black lumps survive, and space the plants out so the leaves dry faster.
seasoned: There is no home-garden cure once plants are infected; management is cultural. Remove and destroy infected plants (do not compost them, since the sclerotia survive), and open up spacing and airflow to dry the canopy.

beginner: Give plants room so air moves through them, and go easy on fertilizer, since heavy growth feeds the mold. Move edamame away from beans on a long rotation, water at the base instead of overhead, and avoid spots where white mold has been bad.
seasoned: Space plants and rows for good airflow rather than crowding, and go easy on nitrogen, since excess feeding drives the dense growth the mold needs. Rotate away from beans and other susceptible crops on a long cycle, avoid overhead watering, and do not plant where white mold has been severe.

beginner: Small angular spots on the leaves that turn brown to black with a yellowish ring, often falling out to leave the leaves looking torn. It likes cool, wet weather and spreads in blowing rain. It is the most common leaf disease of soybeans.
seasoned: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on the leaves that turn brown to black with a yellow-green halo, the spots often dropping out to leave a ragged, tattered look; it favors cool, wet weather and spreads in wind-driven rain. The most common foliar disease of soybeans.

beginner: A bacterium that survives the winter on old plant debris and seed. Splashing rain and touching wet plants carry it from leaf to leaf, and cool, wet weather is when it strikes.
seasoned: The bacterium Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. glycinea. It overwinters on infected residue and seed, and splashing rain and handling wet plants move it from leaf to leaf; cool, wet conditions favor infection.

beginner: There is no cure once plants are infected, but it rarely costs much in a garden. Water at the base, not overhead, and stay out of the patch when the leaves are wet, since that spreads the bacteria.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; the disease rarely causes real yield loss in a garden. Avoid overhead watering and do not handle plants when the foliage is wet, which moves the bacteria from plant to plant.

beginner: Plant clean seed and do not save seed from infected plants, since the disease travels on seed. Move your edamame each year, clear away old plants after harvest, give the plants room, and keep out of the patch when the leaves are wet.
seasoned: Plant clean seed and do not save seed from an infected crop, since the disease is seedborne. Rotate away from soybeans and beans, clear residue after harvest, give plants room for airflow, and keep out of the bed when the foliage is wet.

beginner: Pale green to yellow blotches on top of the leaves with a grayish, fuzzy growth underneath in humid weather; the spots grow and turn brown. It is common but usually mild, and infected seed can have a white coating.
seasoned: Pale green to yellow spots on the upper leaf surface with a matching grayish, downy fungal growth on the underside in humid weather; spots enlarge and brown. It is common but usually minor, and seed from infected plants can carry a white crust.

beginner: A fungus-like organism that likes warm, humid weather and wet leaves. It survives on old plant debris and seed and spreads in damp, humid spells.
seasoned: The fungus-like organism Peronospora manshurica, favored by warm, humid weather and frequent leaf wetness. It survives on residue and seed and spreads on wind and splashing in humid spells.

beginner: Downy mildew rarely needs treatment in a garden; the plants usually grow through it. Give the plants room and avoid wetting the leaves to slow it, and pull badly spotted leaves if you like.
seasoned: Downy mildew seldom needs treatment in a home garden; edamame outgrows light infection. Improve airflow and avoid wetting the foliage to slow it, and remove badly spotted leaves where practical.

beginner: Give plants room so the leaves dry, water at the base, and move your edamame each year. Clear away old plants after harvest and use clean seed, since it carries over on debris and seed.
seasoned: Space plants for airflow, water at the soil rather than overhead, and rotate away from soybeans. Clean up residue after harvest and use clean seed, since the organism carries over on debris and seed.

beginner: Patches of stunted, yellow, slow plants, usually in spots rather than all over, with very few of the normal root nodules. The clue is tiny lemon-shaped white or yellow specks (cysts) on the roots in summer.
seasoned: Patches of stunted, yellowed, slow-growing plants, often in spots rather than uniformly, with few nodules and tiny lemon-shaped white to yellow females (cysts) just visible on the roots in summer. Above-ground symptoms are easy to miss, but the cysts on the roots are the giveaway.

beginner: The soybean cyst nematode, a microscopic worm that is the most damaging soybean pest in much of the country. Its egg-filled cysts survive in the soil for years and build up where soybeans grow in the same spot again and again.
seasoned: The soybean cyst nematode (Heterodera glycines), a microscopic roundworm that is the most damaging soybean pest in much of the country. Its cysts hold eggs that survive in the soil for years, and they build up where soybeans are grown repeatedly.

beginner: There is no home treatment once it is established; you manage it by prevention. If plants are stunted in patches, check the roots for the tiny cysts in summer, and avoid carrying soil from that bed to clean ground on tools or shoes.
seasoned: There is no rescue treatment in a home garden; management is preventive. Where plants are stunted in patches, check the roots for cysts in summer and avoid moving soil from that bed to clean ground on tools or shoes.

beginner: Rotate edamame with crops other than soybeans and dry beans on a long cycle, which is the main control, and never grow soybeans in the same spot every year. Where it is a known problem, plant resistant varieties and keep weeds down.
seasoned: Rotate edamame with non-host crops (anything but soybeans and dry beans) on a long cycle, the main control, and do not grow soybeans in the same bed year after year. Where the nematode is established, grow resistant soybean varieties and keep the soil clean of weed hosts.

beginner: Water regularly, about an inch a week, so the soil stays evenly moist but not soggy. Pay closest attention while the plants are flowering and the pods are filling out.
seasoned: Regular and even through the season, about an inch of water a week from rain or irrigation, keeping the soil moist but never waterlogged. The need peaks during flowering and pod fill, when moisture stress directly cuts the set.

beginner: Water deeply enough to wet the soil about 6 inches down. Deep, less frequent watering beats a daily light sprinkle.
seasoned: Enough to wet the root zone roughly 6 inches down; watering deeply and less often builds deeper roots than frequent light sprinkles.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and do it in the morning so the plants dry off during the day. Wet leaves, especially overnight, help spread disease.
seasoned: Water at the soil level in the morning so the foliage dries before evening; this limits the foliar diseases edamame is prone to in humid weather.

beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt or the lower leaves turn yellow, you may be overwatering. Soggy soil rots the roots.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and stunted growth point to waterlogged roots and the root rots edamame is prone to in cold, wet ground.

beginner: If plants dry out while flowering, they drop their flowers and the pods fill poorly. Keep the water steady at that stage.

beginner: Edamame is a soybean you eat as plump green pods, boiled or steamed in the pod and popped straight into your mouth. It grows like a bush bean: you plant the seeds in the garden after the last frost once the soil is warm, and the sturdy plants need no trellis. But edamame takes longer than green beans, about 75 to 100 days, and the big difference is that the whole plant ripens at once. Instead of picking for weeks, you harvest the whole plant in one go when the pods are plump and green, and the best window is only a few days. Soybeans flower by day length, so pick a variety suited to your area, and use a soybean inoculant on the seed, not the regular bean kind. Always cook edamame before eating it.
seasoned: Edamame (Glycine max) is a warm-season vegetable soybean grown for its plump, immature green pods, boiled or steamed in the pod and popped out to eat. Like snap beans it is a frost-tender bush legume direct-sown after the last frost into warm soil, but it takes longer to mature (about 75 to 100 days) and, unlike beans, the whole plant ripens together: the crop comes ready in one concentrated harvest at the plump green R6 stage, over a narrow window of only a few days before the beans turn starchy. Soybean is a short-day plant, so the variety's maturity group must match your latitude. As a legume it fixes much of its own nitrogen, but only with the soybean-specific inoculant Bradyrhizobium japonicum, not the general bean and pea kind. Edamame must be cooked before eating; raw soybeans are not eaten.

beginner: Edamame is ready when the pods are plump and bright green and the beans nearly touch inside but are still tender, before they get hard or turn yellow. The whole plant ripens at the same time, so harvest it all at once: pull up the plant and strip off the pods. The best window is only about four to ten days, so check every day as the pods fill and cook or freeze them the same day.
seasoned: Harvest edamame at the R6 stage, when the pods are plump and bright green with the beans filling about 80 to 90 percent of the pod and nearly touching inside, still tender and sweet rather than hard or yellowing. Because the whole plant ripens together, harvest it all in one or two passes, pulling or cutting the plant and stripping the pods. The prime window is short, only about four to ten days, so check daily as the pods plump and cook or freeze the same day.

beginner: Parsley likes loose, fertile soil with plenty of compost worked in, kept evenly moist but never soggy. It is forgiving, but rich, steady soil keeps the leaves tender and green and feeds a plant you cut from all season. It has a deeper root than most salad greens, so loosen the bed well; hard, compacted, or waterlogged ground holds it back and invites root rot.
seasoned: Parsley grows in most soils but does best in a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. The University of Minnesota recommends a soil rich in organic matter and steady moisture for the long cut-and-come-again season. Work compost into the top several inches before sowing to feed the plant through the months you harvest from it, and loosen the bed deeply because parsley sends down a slender taproot. It dislikes compacted or waterlogged ground, which checks growth and invites crown and root rot.

beginner: Parsley grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 7.0. Most garden soil is fine, and a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral, the range the University of Minnesota lists as best for parsley; it still does fine across roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Parsley is not a pH-sensitive plant, so in most gardens no adjustment is needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

beginner: Parsley does not need much feeding. Mix some compost or a little balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it a light feeding once or twice over the season, since you cut from the same plants for a long time. If you grow it in a pot, feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every few weeks because watering washes nutrients out.
seasoned: Parsley is a light to moderate feeder grown for steady leafy growth over a long season. The University of Minnesota suggests a 5-10-5 fertilizer at about 3 ounces per 10 feet of row, once or twice during the season, on top of compost worked in before planting. Because you cut from the same plants for months, a light midseason side-dress of nitrogen keeps fresh green leaves coming; in containers a dilute liquid feed every 3 to 4 weeks replaces what frequent watering leaches out. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which draws aphids and softens the flavor.

beginner: Time to give your parsley a light feeding.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your parsley with a light feeding.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-5 worked into the soil before planting, then feed lightly once or twice during the season.
seasoned: Moderate, balanced feeding for steady leaf growth: a 5-10-5 or balanced vegetable fertilizer worked in before sowing, then a light side-dress once or twice through the season. Go easy on nitrogen, which softens flavor and draws aphids on a crop eaten fresh.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a balanced vegetable fertilizer, one light feeding partway through the season; in a pot, a diluted liquid feed every 3 to 4 weeks.
seasoned: About 3 ounces of 5-10-5 per 10 feet of row, once or twice during the season; a compost-rich bed often needs no more than a single light midseason feeding.

beginner: Plump green caterpillars banded with black and dotted yellow-orange, chewing the leaves and stems, sometimes stripping a stalk. They are the larvae of the black swallowtail butterfly, and many gardeners leave them be.
seasoned: Larvae of the black swallowtail (Papilio polyxenes) feeding on the foliage, banded green and black with yellow spots; on parsley they are seldom numerous enough to do real damage, and parsley is one of their host plants, so most growers tolerate or relocate them rather than spray.

beginner: Big green-and-black striped caterpillars that eat the leaves. They turn into beautiful black swallowtail butterflies, so they are usually welcome guests rather than a real problem.
seasoned: The caterpillar stage of the black swallowtail butterfly, which lays eggs on parsley and other carrot-family plants; populations on a home planting are normally small.

beginner: If you want every leaf, just pick the caterpillars off by hand and move them to a spare plant. They are easy to see and there are rarely many. Planting a little extra parsley lets you share with the butterflies.
seasoned: Hand-pick where leaf loss matters and relocate the larvae to a sacrificial plant; Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) controls them if needed, but on parsley they rarely warrant it. Many gardeners deliberately grow extra parsley as a swallowtail host.

beginner: Pick them off by hand, grow a few extra plants to share, and enjoy the butterflies they become.
seasoned: Scout occasionally and hand-pick if leaf loss matters; tolerate the small numbers a home planting usually sees, and plant extra parsley as a host plant for the butterflies.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on new growth and the undersides of leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
seasoned: Colonies of aphids on growing tips and leaf undersides, the most common parsley pest; honeydew and the lodged insects contaminate a crop eaten fresh, and aphids can vector viruses. Parsley's lacy foliage hides them, so scout closely.

beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. They can spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on parsley; they reproduce rapidly and favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Rinse picked leaves well before use.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days and conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps, which the parsley umbels attract when allowed to flower.

beginner: Welcome helpful insects like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check new growth often.
seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, and conserve natural enemies; letting a second-year plant flower draws in aphid predators.

beginner: Tunnels and rusty-brown trails in the roots and lower stems, stunted or off-color plants, and grubs at the crown. These carrot-family root pests hit parsley too.
seasoned: Larvae of the carrot rust fly (Psila rosae) and the carrot weevil mining the taproot and crown of parsley, a carrot-family host; damage shows as rust-colored tunneling, stunting, and secondary rot, worst where Apiaceae are grown in the same ground year after year.

beginner: Small root maggots from carrot-family pests that tunnel into the parsley root and crown, leaving rusty trails and weak plants.
seasoned: The carrot rust fly and carrot weevil lay eggs near carrot-family plants; their larvae bore into the roots and crowns. They build up where carrots, parsley, and their relatives repeat in the same bed.

beginner: Cover the bed with floating row cover to keep the flies off, rotate parsley away from where carrots or parsley grew, and clean up crop debris in fall.
seasoned: Exclude the adults with floating row cover from emergence, rotate out of Apiaceae ground on a multi-year cycle, delay sowing past the first fly generation where it is severe, and remove crop residue that harbors overwintering stages.

beginner: Use a row cover, move parsley to a fresh spot each year, and clear away old plants in fall.
seasoned: Manage by exclusion (row cover) and rotation: keep parsley out of recent carrot-family ground, time sowings around the fly's generations, and sanitize residue.

beginner: Small tan to brown spots with darker edges scattered across the leaves, sometimes with tiny dark specks in the centers, worst in wet weather. Heavily spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: Numerous small circular tan-to-brown leaf lesions, often with dark pycnidia in the centers, the most commonly reported parsley disease; it spreads in cool, wet, splashy conditions and can arrive on infected seed, and on a leaf crop even moderate spotting ruins the cutting.

beginner: A fungal leaf-spot disease, the most common one on parsley, that spreads through wet leaves and splashing water and can come in on the seed.
seasoned: Septoria petroselini, a seed-borne and splash-spread fungus favored by cool, wet weather and overhead watering.

beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, avoid wetting the foliage, improve airflow, and start with clean seed. Pick and use the clean leaves promptly.
seasoned: Use clean or treated seed, water at the soil line, space for airflow, rotate away from parsley and its relatives, and remove infected debris; the home garden has no reliable spray cure once it is established.

beginner: Use clean seed, water at the soil line rather than over the leaves, space plants for airflow, and clear infected debris.
seasoned: Plant clean seed, switch to drip or soil-line watering, widen spacing, rotate, and remove crop debris that carries the fungus over.

beginner: Wilting, yellowing plants whose crown or roots have turned brown, soft, and mushy, usually in wet, poorly drained soil. Affected plants collapse and do not recover.
seasoned: Soilborne crown and root rots (Pythium, Phytophthora, Rhizoctonia, and related fungi) attacking parsley's taproot and crown in saturated, poorly drained ground; symptoms are wilting, stunting, and a browned, decayed crown, often on plants held over a wet winter.

beginner: Soil fungi rot the parsley root and crown when the soil stays too wet, especially over a soggy winter.
seasoned: Soilborne water-mold and fungal rots (Pythium, Phytophthora, Rhizoctonia) favored by waterlogged, poorly drained soil and overwatering.

beginner: There is no cure for a rotting plant, so remove it. Improve drainage, plant in raised or loosened beds, and do not overwater, especially in winter.
seasoned: Remove affected plants; manage by prevention: well-drained or raised beds, loosened soil for the taproot, moderate winter watering, and rotation out of ground where Apiaceae rotted before.

beginner: Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater, and pull any plant whose crown has gone soft and brown.
seasoned: Site in well-drained, loosened soil, avoid waterlogging (especially overwinter), and rotate away from beds with a rot history.

beginner: Good news: parsley does not bolt in hot weather like cilantro does. It is a biennial, which means it grows leaves the first year and only sends up a flower stalk in its second spring, after a winter, when the leaves turn bitter. You cannot stop that second-year flowering, so the simple plan is to plant fresh parsley each year for the best leaves. Take a few early leaves from an overwintered plant, then let it bloom for the bees and butterflies or pull it out.
seasoned: Unlike fast cool-season herbs, parsley does NOT bolt from first-year summer heat; it is a biennial that flowers in its SECOND year, triggered by the cold of winter (vernalization). The practical consequence is the opposite of cilantro: a first-year plant gives leaves right through summer, but an overwintered plant sends up a flower stalk in its second spring and the leaves coarsen and turn bitter. There is no preventing the second-year bolt, so the standard practice is to grow parsley fresh each year for the best leaves, enjoy a short early-spring cutting from an overwintered plant, then let it flower (the umbels feed pollinators and host swallowtails) or pull it. Flat-leaf types tend to overwinter and hold a little better than curly types.

beginner: Parsley flowers on a two-year cycle: leaves the first year, then a tall flower stalk the second spring after it has been through a winter. That is normal, not a mistake, and it is very different from cilantro, which flowers fast in summer heat. The flowers are great for bees and are food for black swallowtail caterpillars. Grow new parsley each year for the best leaves, and let a second-year plant bloom if you want to feed the pollinators.
seasoned: Bolting in parsley is a biennial life-cycle event, not a heat response: the plant banks energy in a taproot the first year, overwinters, and flowers the second spring after vernalization. This is the defining contrast with cilantro, which bolts within weeks of warm weather. So summer heat does not end the parsley leaf crop, winter does (indirectly), by setting up the second-year bloom. The white umbel flowers are excellent insectary plants and a black swallowtail host, and second-year plants self-sow readily, so a few are worth leaving for pollinators even as you start fresh plants for leaves.

beginner: The best way to store parsley is to leave it growing and cut what you need. Picked parsley keeps 1 to 2 weeks in the fridge. To save extra, freeze it chopped into ice-cube trays rather than drying it, since drying loses most of the flavor.
seasoned: Parsley is best fresh from the garden and, because the plant keeps producing, the easiest storage is simply to cut it as needed. Cut parsley keeps 1 to 2 weeks refrigerated, longer than most herbs.
