beginner: Pick the type for how you cook. Flat-leaf (Italian) parsley like Italian Flat Leaf or Giant of Italy has the most flavor and is best for cooking. Curly parsley like Forest Green or Moss Curled is the frilly kind used for garnish and looks nice in pots. There is also Hamburg or root parsley, grown for an edible root. They all grow the same way, so just keep the soil moist and plant fresh each year.
seasoned: Choose by use. Flat-leaf (Italian) parsley, including Italian Flat Leaf and Giant of Italy, has the strongest, sweetest flavor, taller open plants, and slightly better heat and overwintering tolerance, and is the cook's choice. Curly (French) parsley, such as Forest Green and the Moss Curled and Triple Curled strains, gives the dense, frilly leaves used for garnish and edging, with a milder flavor. Hamburg or root parsley is a distinct type grown for an edible parsnip-like root as well as leaves and wants deep, loose soil. All are grown the same way; variety matters less than steady moisture and fresh annual sowing, since any parsley bolts in its second year.

beginner: Parsley is small, leafy, and easygoing, and its biggest garden gift comes in its second year: if you let it flower, the blooms pull in hoverflies, ladybugs, and tiny parasitic wasps that hunt aphids on nearby crops, and they feed black swallowtail butterflies. It interplants well with tomatoes and peppers, with asparagus, and with brassicas and onions. Keep it away from other carrot-family plants like carrots and celery, which share its pests, and from fennel, a poor herb neighbor.
seasoned: Much of parsley's companion value is real but indirect: a second-year plant allowed to flower is a strong insectary umbel, recruiting hoverflies, ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps that suppress aphids on neighboring crops, and it hosts the black swallowtail. Practically it interplants with tomatoes and peppers (which gain from those beneficials), with asparagus (a long-standing traditional pairing), and with brassicas and alliums that share its cool-tolerant culture. The well-grounded cautions are its own family, the Apiaceae (carrot, celery, dill, parsnip), which share parsley's pests and diseases and should be rotated apart, and fennel, a broad allelopath and poor herb neighbor.

beginner: Let a second-year parsley plant flower near tomatoes and peppers and its blooms bring in helpful insects that eat aphids and other pests. Parsley tucks neatly around the base of taller plants.
seasoned: A beneficial-insect and space pairing: parsley allowed to flower recruits hoverflies and parasitoid wasps that attack aphids on tomatoes and peppers, and the low parsley fills the ground around the taller crops. Sound by mechanism and traditional practice, not a measured parsley-tomato effect.

beginner: Parsley and asparagus are a classic old-time pairing: parsley grows happily in the same long-lived bed and is said to help asparagus, and the asparagus ferns give parsley a little light shade.
seasoned: A traditional perennial-bed pairing: parsley is long associated with asparagus in companion lore, and practically the two share a permanent bed where parsley uses the ground between asparagus crowns and gets light shade from the ferns. Widely taught tradition, not a measured effect.

beginner: Cabbage-family plants and onions grow in the same cool weather as parsley and share a bed well, and parsley's flowers (in year two) help bring in insects that eat cabbage pests.
seasoned: A cool-season interplant on shared culture: brassicas and alliums share parsley's cool-tolerant season and bed, and a flowering parsley adds beneficial-insect pressure against aphids and caterpillars. Traditional and structural rather than a documented pairwise effect.

beginner: Keep parsley away from carrots, celery, dill, and parsnips. They are all in the same family and share the same pests and diseases, like the carrot rust fly and leaf spots, so growing them together builds up trouble.

seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley grows parsley on two direct-sown cycles, matched to the University of Nevada, Reno Extension's cool-season framework (Fact Sheet FS-02-61), which runs mid-February through April and again from mid-August through the end of October. Spring sowing runs roughly Feb 14 to Mar 7; the slow seed takes 2 to 5 weeks to germinate, and leaves are ready roughly 80 days after sowing. Parsley is more heat-tolerant than cilantro or dill and does not first-year bolt, but once daytime highs push past the region's roughly 90°F growth ceiling the plant slows and toughens, so the stand is cut hard and rested rather than sown fresh through summer. The fall window, roughly Aug 15 to Sep 20, opens a second stand that is frost-hardy and, unlike this crop's tender cool-season neighbors, carries a slow cut-and-come-again harvest on into winter. Zone 8's cooler pockets run both windows later than zone 9; zone 10 at Laughlin runs them earlier and its later first frost lets the fall stand carry furthest into winter.

beginner: Parsley is a hardy herb in the carrot family, grown for its tasty, healthy leaves. It is easygoing once it gets started, and very different from both basil and cilantro: it handles frost and cool weather, but it also takes summer heat without flooding into flower the way cilantro does, so one planting gives you leaves from spring all the way through fall. The one tricky part is the beginning: parsley seed is slow, often taking 2 to 5 weeks to sprout, so soak it in warm water first and be patient. You harvest it by cutting the outer stems near the base, and the middle keeps growing new leaves for months. There are two main kinds, flat-leaf (Italian), which has the best flavor for cooking, and curly, the frilly kind used for garnish. One thing to know: parsley lives two years, and in its second spring it sends up a flower stalk and the leaves turn bitter, so plant fresh parsley each year for the best leaves. It has few pests, mainly the big green-and-black parsleyworm caterpillar, which turns into a black swallowtail butterfly and is usually welcome.
seasoned: Parsley (Petroselinum crispum) is a hardy biennial herb in the carrot family (Apiaceae), grown for its flavorful, vitamin-rich leaves. Its biology is the mirror image of warm-season herbs like basil and the opposite of fast cool-season herbs like cilantro. Parsley is COOL-TOLERANT and FROST-HARDY, taking light freezes and overwintering in mild zones, yet it is also genuinely HEAT-TOLERANT: because it is a biennial that does not flower until its second year, it does NOT bolt from first-year summer heat the way cilantro does, so a single planting yields leaves spring through fall, and only the most extreme desert and subtropical summers slow it. That long, flexible season is the headline. The signature challenge is at the start: parsley seed germinates slowly and erratically, often 2 to 5 weeks, so growers soak it and wait. It is harvested cut-and-come-again from the OUTER stems, leaving the center to regrow for months. It comes in flat-leaf (Italian) types, with the stronger, sweeter flavor cooks prefer, and curly (French) types grown for garnish, plus Hamburg root parsley grown for an edible root. The one catch is the biennial cycle: an overwintered plant bolts in its second spring and the leaves turn bitter, so parsley is sown fresh each year for the best leaves. Pests are few, chiefly the parsleyworm (the handsome black swallowtail caterpillar, often left for the butterflies) and aphids, and disease is minimal.

beginner: Start picking parsley when the plants are full and about 6 inches tall, a couple of months after sowing. Cut the OUTER stems near the base, no more than a third at a time, and the middle keeps growing new leaves for months, even through summer heat. Pick in the cool morning for the best flavor and put it in the fridge, where it keeps 1 to 2 weeks. In mild areas a mulched plant can live through winter and give you a few early leaves, but it will flower and turn bitter that second spring, so plant new parsley each year for the best leaves.
seasoned: Begin cutting parsley once plants are full and about 6 inches tall, roughly 70 to 90 days from sowing. Harvest by cutting the OUTER stems at the base, taking no more than about a third at a time, and the plant keeps producing fresh leaves from the center for months, right through summer heat that would bolt cilantro or lettuce, and into fall. Pick in the cool morning for the best flavor and refrigerate at once; cut parsley keeps 1 to 2 weeks. In mild zones a mulched plant overwinters for an early-spring cutting, but take that as a bonus: an overwintered plant bolts in its second spring and the leaves turn bitter, so sow fresh plants each year for the main leaf crop.

beginner: Cilantro likes loose, fertile soil with plenty of compost mixed in that holds moisture but still drains well. It is not fussy, but steady moisture and rich soil keep the leaves tender and mild and put off bolting a little; hot, dry, hard soil makes it rush to flower and turn the foliage bitter.
seasoned: Cilantro grows in most soils but does best in a fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam high in organic matter, kept evenly moist. Utah State University suggests working 2 to 4 inches of well-rotted compost into the top 4 to 6 inches before sowing, which feeds the fast leaf growth and buffers the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender and slow to bolt. It dislikes damp, humid, poorly drained ground, which invites damping-off and leaf disease. The plant has a slender taproot and resents transplanting, so it is best direct-sown into loosened soil.

beginner: Cilantro grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.2 to 6.8. Most garden soil is fine, and a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.2 to 6.8, slightly acidic to neutral; cilantro is forgiving and still does fine across roughly 6.0 to 7.5. Clemson lists a working range of 6 to 7 for the crop. It is not a pH-sensitive plant, so in most gardens no adjustment is needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

beginner: Cilantro grows fast and likes a little nitrogen for tender green leaves. Mix some compost or fertilizer into the soil before planting, then give it one light feeding once the seedlings are up and growing. Because the crop is so quick, you usually do not need to feed it again, and a plant left to make coriander seed needs nothing more.
seasoned: Cilantro is a fast leafy herb that runs on nitrogen, but the crop is so quick that a modest charge is plenty. Utah State University suggests about a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 25 square feet, one to two times during the season. Work compost or a balanced fertilizer in before sowing, then side-dress lightly with nitrogen once the seedlings are established to push tender, mild leaves. Avoid heavy late nitrogen, which draws aphids and does little for a crop you cut within a few weeks; a plant grown on for coriander seed needs no extra feeding once it bolts.

beginner: Time to give your cilantro a light feeding.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your cilantro with a little nitrogen.

beginner: Use a nitrogen-rich feed such as blood meal or a 21-0-0 fertilizer once or twice while the plants are young.
seasoned: High N for fast leafy growth; a light side-dress of 21-0-0 or blood meal once or twice during the crop. No extra phosphorus or potassium needed beyond a soil-test baseline; do not overfeed a 4-to-6-week leaf crop.

beginner: Follow the label rate for a nitrogen-rich vegetable fertilizer, one light feeding while the plants are young.
seasoned: About a quarter cup of 21-0-0 per 25 square feet, side-dressed once or twice during the crop; a compost-rich bed often needs no extra feed at all.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on new growth and the undersides of leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
seasoned: Colonies of green peach and other aphids gather on growing tips and leaf undersides; honeydew and the lodged insects contaminate a crop eaten fresh, and aphids can vector viruses. Cilantro's lacy foliage hides them, so scout closely.

beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. They can spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on cilantro; they reproduce rapidly and favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Pick the leaves before a colony settles in.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days and conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps, which cilantro's own flowers attract.

beginner: Welcome helpful insects like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, check new growth often, and pick the quick crop young.
seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and harvest the fast crop before colonies build; letting a few plants flower draws in aphid predators.

beginner: Small wedge-shaped insects that hop or fly up when disturbed, plus yellowed, twisted, or stunted plants. The leafhoppers themselves do little chewing damage, but they can carry diseases that deform the plant.
seasoned: The beet leafhopper and aster leafhoppers feed on cilantro and, more importantly, transmit aster yellows and beet curly top virus, which yellow, distort, and stunt the plants. Infected plants do not recover and should be removed.

beginner: Tiny jumping insects that suck sap and, more seriously, spread diseases (aster yellows and curly top) that twist and yellow the plants.
seasoned: Leafhoppers (including the beet leafhopper, Circulifer tenellus) feed on the foliage and vector aster yellows and beet curly top virus; the disease damage far outweighs the feeding.

beginner: Cover plants with a light row cover to keep leafhoppers off, pull and discard any yellowed, distorted plants right away, and clear nearby weeds that harbor the insects and the diseases.
seasoned: Exclude leafhoppers with floating row cover, rogue out symptomatic plants promptly since there is no cure for the viral diseases, and control weed reservoirs; insecticides give poor control of a mobile vector.

beginner: Use row cover, clear weedy hosts around the garden, and remove infected plants early so they do not seed disease into the planting.
seasoned: Manage leafhoppers mainly by exclusion (row cover) and sanitation: remove weed reservoirs and rogue symptomatic plants, since spraying rarely stops a mobile virus vector.

beginner: Small dark, angular, water-soaked spots on the leaves that run along the veins and can merge into larger blotches, worst in cool, wet weather. Spotted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: Angular, vein-limited dark lesions on the foliage, sometimes with a yellow halo, spreading in cool, wet, splashy conditions; on a leaf crop even moderate spotting ruins the harvest. It is the most-reported cilantro disease.

beginner: A bacterial disease, the most common one reported on cilantro, that spreads through wet leaves and splashing water and often arrives on infected seed.
seasoned: Pseudomonas syringae pv. coriandricola, a seed-borne and splash-spread bacterium favored by cool, wet weather and overhead watering.

beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, avoid wetting the foliage, improve airflow, and start with clean seed. There is no spray cure in the home garden, so prevention matters most.
seasoned: Use clean, disease-free or hot-water-treated seed, avoid overhead irrigation, space for airflow, rotate away from cilantro and its relatives, and remove infected debris; copper has limited effect once it is established.

beginner: Use clean seed, water at the soil line rather than over the leaves, space plants for airflow, and clear infected debris.
seasoned: Plant clean seed, switch to drip or soil-line watering, widen spacing, rotate, and remove crop debris that carries the bacterium over.

beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where cilantro's slow germination leaves seed sitting.

beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the slow-sprouting cilantro seed sits a long time before emerging.
seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium fungi attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows cilantro's already slow germination favors them.

beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention: pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
seasoned: No rescue once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.

beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant shallowly in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up faster.
seasoned: Sow shallowly into well-drained soil under conditions that favor reasonably quick emergence, avoid overwatering, and use fresh, viable seed; some growers soak the dry seed to speed emergence past the vulnerable window.

beginner: A white, powdery coating on the leaves and stems, usually later in the crop and in warm, dry-day weather. Heavily coated leaves yellow and are unpleasant to eat.
seasoned: A white, talc-like fungal growth on the foliage and stems, the most common fungal disease of cilantro, that builds in warm days with cool nights and crowded plantings; coated leaves lose quality.

beginner: A fungal disease (Erysiphe heraclei) that coats the leaves in white powder, favored by warm days, cool nights, and crowding.
seasoned: The fungus Erysiphe heraclei, favored by warm days and cool humid nights and by dense stands with poor airflow.

beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the planting for airflow, and avoid crowding. Most home crops are harvested before it does much harm.
seasoned: Improve airflow with wider spacing, remove affected leaves, and avoid excess nitrogen; the fast leaf crop is usually cut before mildew matters, but a plant grown on for seed is more exposed.

beginner: Space plants for airflow, avoid crowding and overfeeding, and pick the leaf crop young before mildew builds.
seasoned: Widen spacing for airflow, avoid heavy nitrogen, and harvest the leaf crop promptly; remove infected foliage on plants held for coriander seed.

beginner: Mushy, slimy, foul-smelling collapse of the crown or stems, usually in warm, wet conditions or after the foliage has been damaged. Affected plants rot quickly.
seasoned: Wet, mushy breakdown of the crown and stems with a bad smell, caused by soft-rot bacteria entering through wounds in warm, wet, poorly drained conditions; the plant collapses fast.

beginner: Bacterial soft rot that enters through wounds and rots the tissue in warm, wet, poorly drained soil.
seasoned: Soft-rot bacteria (such as Pectobacterium species) invade through wounds and bruises and dissolve the tissue, favored by warm temperatures, wet soil, and poor drainage.

beginner: Remove and discard rotted plants, improve drainage, avoid injuring the plants, and do not overwater. There is no cure once a plant is rotting.
seasoned: Remove and destroy affected plants, improve drainage and airflow, avoid wounding and overwatering, and do not work the bed when wet; no rescue once rot sets in.

beginner: Plant in well-drained soil, avoid overwatering and injury, and keep the planting open so foliage dries.
seasoned: Site in well-drained soil, avoid waterlogging and mechanical injury, space for drying airflow, and clear infected debris.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week.
seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept even; cilantro is shallow-rooted and bolts faster and turns harsher under drought stress.

beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is warm and dry.
seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week, more in warm, dry spells; Texas A&M notes an inch a week suffices once established unless it turns very hot.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the lacy foliage dry checks bacterial leaf spot and other leaf diseases on a crop eaten fresh.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and plants get mushy or diseased in soggy soil.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and soft rot or leaf disease in constantly wet, poorly drained ground.

beginner: Wilting leaves that taste sharper, and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than you want.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, harsher-tasting leaves, and faster bolting; drought stress hurries the plant toward its coriander seedstalk.

beginner: Cilantro is slow to sprout, so keep the soil evenly damp until the seedlings come up.
seasoned: Cilantro germinates slowly, so keep the seedbed evenly moist through emergence; steady moisture here is the first step in delaying the eventual bolt.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered. Cilantro has shallow roots and dries out quickly.
seasoned: Grow the shallow-rooted seedlings on with steady, even moisture; they show stress fast.

beginner: Keep the water steady, about an inch a week and more when warm. Even moisture keeps cilantro mild and tender and holds off bolting; letting it get dry and hot sends it straight to flower and coarsens the leaves. Water at the base to keep the leaves dry.
seasoned: Cilantro is shallow-rooted and bolts faster and turns harsher under drought, so keep an even inch a week, more in warm spells (TAMU notes an inch a week suffices unless it turns very hot). Even moisture keeps it growing fast, tender, and mild and delays the bolt; water at the soil line to keep the lacy foliage dry against bacterial leaf spot.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while you cut. A dry, hot spell now makes cilantro bolt and turn bitter fast, so steady water keeps the leaves coming a little longer.
seasoned: Keep even moisture right through the cutting weeks: any dry, hot check hurries the plant to flower and makes the leaves harsh, so steady water buys more tender leaf before it bolts.

seasoned: Once cilantro bolts and heads to coriander seed the leaf crop is over; ease off watering, and if you want the coriander seed, a drier finish helps it ripen and dry down on the plant.

beginner: Keep the water steady so the leaves stay mild and tender and the plant does not bolt early.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps cilantro growing fast, tender, and mild; dry, hot spells push it straight to flower and coriander seed and coarsen the leaves.

beginner: Plant cilantro straight in the garden from seed, because it has a deep little root and does not like being moved. Sow the seeds about a quarter to half an inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since the plants handle frost. The seeds are slow, often taking one to three weeks, so keep the soil moist. Sow again every couple of weeks, and in hot areas plant in fall through spring instead of summer, because heat makes it bolt almost right away. A summer crop is really for the coriander seed.
seasoned: Cilantro is almost always direct-sown, since it has a slender taproot and resents transplanting. Sow seed about 0.25 to 0.5 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; it tolerates frost, so it can go in several weeks before the last frost, and it germinates slowly, often 7 to 21 days. The round seed is actually two seeds fused, so growers sometimes gently crack it to speed and even out germination. Sow a little thicker than the final stand and thin to taste. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through spring, since heat both slows germination and bolts the crop almost at once; midsummer sowings are grown for coriander seed rather than leaves.

beginner: Other carrot-family plants like carrots, parsley, dill, fennel, and celery, because they share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Other Apiaceae: carrot, parsley, dill, fennel, celery, parsnip, and cilantro itself. They share carrot-family pests and diseases (leafhopper-vectored aster yellows, the carrot motley dwarf complex, and soilborne rots), so following one with another concentrates that pressure.

beginner: Try not to grow cilantro or other carrot-family plants (carrots, parsley, dill, fennel, celery) in the same spot more than about once every 3 years, since they share pests and diseases. Plant cilantro after peas, beans, cabbage, onions, or tomatoes instead. Cilantro often self-sows, so pull up stray seedlings that pop up where you do not want them.
seasoned: Rotate cilantro and its carrot-family relatives so they do not return to the same ground for about 3 years. The Apiaceae share aster yellows (spread by leafhoppers), the carrot motley dwarf complex, and soilborne rots, which build up where the family repeats. Follow cilantro with legumes, brassicas, alliums, or nightshades. Because cilantro readily self-sows from bolted plants, volunteers can blur a rotation, so pull seedlings that come up out of place.

beginner: Cilantro flowers (bolts) quickly when it gets warm and the days get long, and the leaves turn bitter. To keep the leaves coming, grow it in the cool parts of the year, especially fall, sow a fresh little batch every 2 to 3 weeks, water steadily, give afternoon shade when it is warm, and try slow-bolting types like Santo or Calypso. When it does bolt, do not fight it: let the plant flower and make coriander seed, which is the spice.
seasoned: Cilantro bolts fast once it is warm and the days lengthen, and the leaves coarsen and turn bitter as it shifts to its coriander seedstalk. Keep the leaf window in the cool shoulders of the year: sow early in spring and crop quickly, lean on the fall crop, which is the longer and more reliable leaf season, choose slow-bolting types (Santo, Calypso, Leisure, Slow Bolting) where heat is a problem, give light afternoon shade in warm spells, and keep moisture steady. Succession-sow every 2 to 3 weeks so a bolted batch is quickly replaced. There is no real fix once it bolts, so the productive answer in heat is to stop fighting it and grow the plant on for coriander seed.

beginner: Cilantro bolts (sends up a flower stalk) when it gets warm and the days are long. It happens fast, but it is not a mistake: the very same flowering that ends the leafy cilantro gives you coriander seed, the spice. The flowers are great for bees and helpful insects, and the plant often drops seed and comes up again on its own. Grow it in cool weather for leaves, and let it bloom in summer for seed.
seasoned: Bolting in cilantro is driven by heat above roughly 75°F and lengthening days, sped by drought and crowding, and it comes on fast because the plant is so quick. This is the defining fact of the crop: the same bolt that ends the cilantro leaf harvest begins the coriander seed crop, so the plant is not failing, it is changing product. The white flowers feed pollinators and beneficial insects strongly, and bolted plants self-sow readily. In hot regions the leaf window is short and growers deliberately let summer plantings run to coriander seed.

beginner: Do not leave cut cilantro out on the counter, where it wilts fast; either chill it or stand the stems in a glass of water. Dried coriander seed keeps for months at room temperature.
seasoned: Fresh cilantro leaves wilt within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate promptly after cutting; standing the cut stems in a glass of water on the counter holds them a few days. Coriander seed, by contrast, is shelf-stable for months once dried.

beginner: Store fresh cilantro unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge, where it keeps about a week. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
seasoned: Refrigerate fresh leaves unwashed in a loose or perforated bag, or stems standing in a little water under a loose bag, in the crisper; cilantro holds about a week. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.

beginner: Cilantro does not freeze well for salads, but you can chop it into an ice-cube tray with a little water or oil and freeze that for cooking. For coriander, let the seeds dry on the plant, then store them in a jar.
seasoned: Fresh cilantro loses its texture frozen for raw use, but freezes well chopped into ice-cube trays with water or oil, or blended into sauces, where the flavor holds for cooking. Coriander seed is dried, not frozen: cut seed heads as they brown, dry them, then thresh and store the seed airtight.

beginner: Use fresh cilantro within a week or so of picking, since it does not keep long. Coriander seed is the opposite: dry the brown seed heads, shake out the seeds, and store them in a sealed jar for many months.
seasoned: Cilantro is best straight from the garden, delicate and short-lived once cut, so chill it fast and use it within a week; its flavor is also strongest fresh. The seed is the keeper: harvest coriander when the seed heads turn tan but before they shatter, dry them in a paper bag, and the threshed seed stores airtight for months to a year.

beginner: If you want leaves, pick a slow-bolting cilantro like Santo, Calypso, Leisure, or one labeled Slow Bolting or Long Standing, which take a bit longer to flower. None of them stop flowering in heat, so sow a fresh batch every couple of weeks too. If you want coriander seed, just let any cilantro flower and go to seed.
seasoned: Match the type to the goal. For leaves, choose slow-bolting selections, Santo, Calypso, Leisure, Caribe, and the various Slow Bolting and Long Standing strains, which hold in leaf longer before the seedstalk rises; none truly resist heat and long days, but they buy time. Specialty leaf types include Delfino, a feathery cut-leaf cilantro, and Lemon. For coriander seed, any standard cilantro left to bolt sets seed readily, and large-seeded types like Moroccan are grown specifically for the spice. Because the bolt is inevitable, succession sowing matters more than variety for a steady leaf supply.

beginner: Cilantro is small, fast, and easygoing, and its biggest garden gift comes when it flowers: the blooms pull in hoverflies, ladybugs, and tiny parasitic wasps that hunt aphids and caterpillars on nearby crops. It interplants well with tomatoes and peppers, with quick cool-season greens like lettuce and spinach, and with legumes. Keep it away from fennel, a poor neighbor for most herbs that can also cross-pollinate carrot-family plants.
seasoned: Most cilantro companion value is real but indirect: allowed to flower, cilantro (an Apiaceae umbel) is a strong insectary plant, recruiting hoverflies, ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps that suppress aphids and caterpillars on neighboring crops, an effect extension IPM guidance leans on. Practically it interplants with tomatoes and peppers (which benefit from those beneficials and lend the cool-season cilantro a little afternoon shade), with quick cool greens that share its season, and with legumes. The well-grounded caution is fennel, a broad allelopath and poor herb neighbor that also crosses with carrot-family plants. Avoid clustering cilantro with its Apiaceae relatives (carrot, dill, parsley) on rotation and shared-pest grounds.

beginner: Let some cilantro flower near tomatoes and peppers and its blooms bring in helpful insects that eat aphids and caterpillars. The taller plants also give cilantro a little cooling shade in warm weather.
seasoned: A beneficial-insect pairing: cilantro left to flower recruits hoverflies and parasitoid wasps that attack aphids and hornworms on tomatoes and peppers, and the taller crops shade the cool-season cilantro to slow its bolt. Sound by mechanism and shared culture, not a measured cilantro-tomato effect.

beginner: Lettuce and spinach grow fast and low in the same cool weather as cilantro, so you can sow them together to fill a salad bed.
seasoned: A cool-season interplant on space and timing: cilantro, lettuce, and spinach share a cool window and a salad bed and are cut young together, with no shared major pest. Traditional and structural rather than a documented effect.

beginner: Legumes add a little nitrogen to the soil that the leafy cilantro can use, and they share a cool-to-mild season without crowding it.
seasoned: A legume interplant on nitrogen and structure: beans and peas fix a little nitrogen the leafy cilantro draws on, and the quick cilantro uses the open ground between them. Sound space-and-timing logic, not a measured cilantro effect.

beginner: Keep cilantro away from fennel. Fennel is a poor neighbor for most herbs and vegetables, said to release substances that hold back nearby plants, and it can also cross-pollinate carrot-family plants like cilantro if both flower.
seasoned: Fennel is a broad allelopath and the classic bad herb neighbor, releasing compounds that suppress many plants, and as a fellow Apiaceae it can cross-pollinate cilantro where both flower for seed. Give fennel its own corner. A traditional rule with a real mechanism, not a measured cilantro-fennel trial.

beginner: Cilantro seeds are slow, often one to three weeks. Keep the soil moist the whole time. The round seed is really two seeds, so cracking it gently can help it sprout faster. Sow in cool weather, not summer heat.
seasoned: Cilantro germinates slowly, often 7 to 21 days, partly because each round fruit holds two seeds; some growers gently crack the seed to speed and even out emergence. Sow shallowly into cool, moist soil, since warm soil above about 75°F slows germination and pushes early bolting.

beginner: Watch young cilantro for tiny jumping leafhoppers. They can spread diseases that twist and yellow the plants, so cover the bed with a light row cover and pull out any seedlings that look distorted.
seasoned: Watch for leafhoppers on young plants: their feeding matters less than the aster yellows and curly top viruses they carry, which yellow and twist the plants. A light row cover excludes them; pull any distorted seedlings, since the viral diseases have no cure.

beginner: Pick cilantro young and often for the best flavor. Cut the outer leaves or shear the patch a couple of inches above the soil and it grows back. Keep the water steady so the leaves stay mild and it does not bolt as fast.
seasoned: Cut cilantro young for the mildest flavor and cut often: shearing outer leaves or the whole patch a couple of inches above the crown keeps tender new growth coming. Steady moisture keeps the leaves mild and delays the bolt.

beginner: Cut a cilantro patch a couple of inches above the soil and it grows back for another cutting. Pick in the cool morning and get it in the fridge right away, because it wilts quickly. The broad lower leaves are the best cilantro.
seasoned: Shear a cilantro patch a couple of inches above the crown and it regrows for a second cutting; pick in the cool morning and refrigerate at once, since cut cilantro wilts fast. Use the lower, broad leaves for cilantro and let the upper feathery growth signal the coming bolt.

beginner: Cilantro bolts fast, and that is how you get coriander. When you see the flower stalk, pick the last good leaves, then let it bloom and make seed. Cut the seed heads when they turn tan, dry them, and shake out the coriander. A plant left alone often reseeds itself.
seasoned: Bolting arrives fast and is the whole point of the plant's second act: once the feathery stalk rises, stop fighting it. Harvest the last good leaves, then let the umbels flower for pollinators and set seed. Cut the seed heads as they turn tan but before they shatter, dry them, and thresh out coriander. One plant left to drop seed reliably self-sows.

beginner: Each cilantro plant gives a small bunch of leaves before it flowers, so it is grown in patches rather than as one big plant. A patch gives a couple of cuttings, then bolts, so sow more every couple of weeks. A bolted plant gives you coriander seed.
seasoned: A single cilantro plant yields a small rosette of leaves over a few weeks before bolting, so the crop is grown in dense patches or rows rather than per plant. Cut young or cut-and-come-again, a bed gives one to three cuttings before heat or bolt ends the leaf phase; a plant then left to flower yields a head of coriander seed.

beginner: Cilantro makes the most leaves in the cool weather of fall and early spring. A spring patch gives a couple of good weeks and then bolts, but a fall crop lasts much longer. Summer plants are best left to make coriander seed.
seasoned: Leaf production peaks in the cool weeks of fall and early spring. beginner: Cilantro is one of the easier, faster herbs for a beginner, with leaves in about a month from a cool-weather sowing. seasoned: Cilantro is a fast, forgiving first-season crop: leaves in about 4 to 6 weeks from a cool-weather sowing and almost nothing to go wrong if you do not sow into heat. The key to total yield is frequent succession sowing, picking young, and leaning on the fall crop, since a spring patch sown too late bolts before it produces much. The bonus is that even a bolted crop is not wasted, it becomes coriander.

seasoned: Cilantro is a classic succession crop: it matures fast and bolts faster, so one sowing is gone in a few weeks. Sow a short row every 2 to 3 weeks through the cool windows, spring until heat and long days set in, and again from late summer through fall, which is the longer, more reliable leaf run. seasoned: In the cold-winter North (zones 3 through 7), cilantro is a fast spring-and-fall succession herb built around frost. In the coolest zones the cool summer often carries leaf production through, while in the warmer end of the band midsummer heat and long days bolt it, so the leaf calendar pauses through the hottest weeks and resumes for the main fall crop. A late sowing under a row cover can overwinter for the earliest spring picking, and bolted summer plants are left for coriander seed.

The long days around midsummer, not heat, are still the trigger for bolting here, so ease off new sowings for a few weeks around then and resume in late summer for a fall crop that runs right up to the first frost, z8's in mid-November and z9's just a few days earlier. beginner: Cilantro and coriander come from the very same plant: the leaves are cilantro and the dried seeds are the spice coriander. Unlike warm-season herbs such as basil, cilantro is a cool-weather plant that handles frost but bolts (flowers) very fast once it gets warm, above about 75°F, and the leaves turn bitter. So the trick is to grow it in the cool parts of the year: a short spring window, a longer and better fall crop, and overwintering in mild areas. Sow a little every 2 to 3 weeks, since each plant bolts after a few weeks, and plant the seeds right in the garden because cilantro does not like being moved. It is fast and easy, with baby leaves in about 3 to 4 weeks. And when summer heat finally makes it bolt, do not be discouraged: let it flower and you get coriander seed.
seasoned: Cilantro and coriander are one plant, Coriandrum sativum, an annual herb in the carrot family (Apiaceae) grown for two products: the leaf is the herb cilantro and the dried seed is the spice coriander. Its defining biology is the mirror image of warm-season herbs like basil: cilantro is a COOL-season, frost-tolerant crop that bolts almost the moment the weather warms, sending up a flower stalk above roughly 75°F and with lengthening days. That single fact shapes everything. The spring leaf window is short, fall is the main and most reliable leaf season, and in mild zones a fall sowing overwinters for the earliest, longest spring run; in hot regions and the heat of summer the leaf crop is brief and growers instead let the plant bolt and harvest coriander seed. Because the bolt is fast and inevitable, cilantro is a succession crop above all, sown in small batches every 2 to 3 weeks so a fresh, pre-bolt cohort is always coming on. It is direct-sown (a slender taproot resents transplanting), fast (baby leaf in about 3 to 4 weeks, bolting by 45 to 60 days), and easy, with few serious pests. The grower's real skill is timing the crop into the cool shoulders of the year and accepting the bolt as the start of the coriander harvest rather than a failure.

beginner: Start picking cilantro when the plants are about 4 to 6 inches tall, a few weeks after sowing and before you see a flower stalk. Take the outer leaves or cut the whole patch a couple of inches above the soil so it regrows, and pick in the cool morning for the best flavor. Pick often, because once it bolts the leaves turn bitter fast. To get coriander, let the plant flower and form seeds, then cut the seed heads when they turn tan, dry them, and shake out the round seeds to store.
seasoned: Begin cutting cilantro leaves once plants are about 4 to 6 inches tall, roughly 3 to 6 weeks from sowing, well before any central stalk rises. Cut the broad lower leaves, or shear the whole patch a couple of inches above the crown for a second cutting, taking no more than a third at a time and picking in the cool morning for the mildest flavor. Pick promptly and often as the weather warms, since the leaf window closes fast at bolt. For coriander, stop cutting and let the plant flower and set seed; harvest the seed heads as they turn from green to tan but before they shatter, dry them in a paper bag, then thresh and store the seed airtight.

beginner: Chives are not fussy about soil and grow in almost any kind, but they do best in loose, fertile ground with some compost mixed in, kept evenly moist but never soggy. Good drainage matters most: an established clump handles a short dry spell, but ground that stays wet through winter can rot the roots and crown.
seasoned: Chives tolerate a wide range of soils but grow best in a well-drained loam rich in organic matter, kept evenly moist. The University of Minnesota recommends well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and Michigan State notes chives grow best in soils high in organic matter while adapting to most soil types. Work compost into the bed before planting to feed a clump you cut from for years, and site it where water does not stand, since a waterlogged crown, especially over winter, invites rot on this otherwise trouble-free perennial.

beginner: Chives grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 7.0. Most garden soil is fine, and a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral, the range the University of Minnesota and Michigan State both list as best for chives; they still do fine across roughly 5.5 to 7.5. Chives are not pH-sensitive, so in most gardens no adjustment is needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

beginner: Chives do not need much feeding. Mix some compost into the soil before planting, and that is often enough. If a clump looks weak or you cut it hard, give it a light feeding to bring back fresh green leaves. In a pot, feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every few weeks, since watering washes nutrients out.
seasoned: Chives are light feeders with low nutrient needs and rarely need regular fertilizer. The University of Minnesota suggests only a very light application of a 5-10-5 fertilizer once each spring if a clump looks weak, on top of compost worked in before planting. A clump you cut from repeatedly benefits from a light feeding after a hard shearing to push fresh tender regrowth; in containers, where frequent watering leaches nutrients, a dilute liquid feed every four to six weeks keeps leaves green. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which softens the flavor.

beginner: Time to give your chives a light feeding.
seasoned: Time to give your chives a light feeding if they look weak.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-5, a little worked into the soil before planting, then feed lightly only if the plant looks weak or after you cut it hard.
seasoned: Light, balanced feeding for a low-demand perennial: a little 5-10-5 or balanced fertilizer worked in before planting, then an optional light feed in spring or after a hard cutting. Go easy on nitrogen, which softens flavor on a crop eaten fresh.

beginner: One light feeding in spring is plenty, or none at all if your soil is good; in a pot, a diluted liquid feed every four to six weeks.
seasoned: A very light application of 5-10-5 once in spring is plenty for an established clump; a compost-rich bed often needs no feeding at all, with a light feed only after a hard shearing.

beginner: Tiny, slender pale-yellow to brown insects hiding down in the leaf folds, leaving silvery or whitish streaks and flecks on the green blades. Bad infestations make the foliage look bleached and papery.
seasoned: Onion thrips (Thrips tabaci) feeding in the leaf axils and folds, producing silvery-white stippling, streaking, and a bleached, papery look on heavy pressure; they favor hot, dry weather. On chives the damage is usually cosmetic, but a severe year degrades a leaf crop.

beginner: Thrips are minute sap-sucking insects, common on onion-family plants, that rasp the leaves and are worst in hot, dry weather. Chives usually shrug them off, but a heavy year can mark the leaves.
seasoned: Thrips tabaci, the principal allium thrips, rasps leaf surfaces and feeds on the sap; populations build fast in hot, dry conditions and on stressed plants.

beginner: Hose the plants down to knock thrips off, shear a badly streaked clump to the base so it regrows clean, and use insecticidal soap on the leaves if needed. Rinse cut leaves before use.
seasoned: Dislodge with a strong water jet, shear a heavily infested clump to the base to remove the population and force clean regrowth, and spray insecticidal soap or spinosad if warranted; conserve natural enemies (minute pirate bugs, lacewings). Keeping plants unstressed and watered blunts outbreaks.

beginner: Keep plants watered in hot spells, welcome helpful insects like lacewings and pirate bugs, and cut a marked-up clump back to force fresh leaves.
seasoned: Avoid drought stress, conserve natural enemies, cut back streaked foliage to reset the clump, and avoid siting chives beside heavily thrips-pressured onion or garlic plantings.

beginner: Rows of white dots punched down a leaf where the adult fly fed, then wavy pale mines inside the leaves, with small maggots or brown seed-like pupae tucked into the leaf bases. It shows up in spring and again in fall.
seasoned: Allium leafminer (Phytomyza gymnostoma): lines of white oviposition punctures down the distal leaf, followed by larval mines and brown puparia lodged in leaf sheaths and bulbs. The University of Maryland lists chive (A. schoenoprasum) among its hosts; wounds open the door to secondary bacterial and fungal rots.

beginner: The allium leafminer is a small fly whose larvae tunnel inside onion-family leaves, including chives, and burrow toward the base. It is a newer pest in parts of the eastern United States.
seasoned: Phytomyza gymnostoma, an invasive allium-specific fly with a spring flight (roughly March into May) and a fall flight (September into October); larvae mine toward the leaf base and bulb, with up to dozens of pupae per plant in severe cases.

beginner: Cover plants with floating row cover in early spring and again in fall to keep the flies off, cut off and destroy mined leaves, and clean up plant debris.
seasoned: Exclude the adults with floating row cover timed to the spring and fall flights, remove and destroy mined foliage, and sanitize crop debris; spinosad or azadirachtin can help where pressure is high. Rotation away from recently infested allium ground reduces carryover.

beginner: Use row cover during the spring and fall flights, remove mined leaves, and keep the bed clean.
seasoned: Row-cover through both flight periods, remove infested leaves, sanitize residue, and separate new plantings from pressured allium beds.

beginner: Yellowing, wilting, and stunted growth as small white maggots tunnel into the base of the plant and the bulbs below the soil, sometimes rotting the crown. Worst in cool, wet springs.
seasoned: Onion maggot (Delia antiqua) larvae mining into the basal plate, roots, and bulbs, causing wilting, yellowing, stunting, and crown rot; damage is worst in cool, moist springs and where allium debris accumulates. Established chive clumps are seldom destroyed but can be set back.

beginner: Onion maggots are the larvae of a fly that lays eggs at the base of onion-family plants; the maggots eat into the roots and bulbs. Chives are rarely hit hard, but a clump can be damaged.
seasoned: Delia antiqua overwinters as pupae in the soil; spring flies lay eggs at plant bases and successive generations attack roots and bulbs, favored by cool wet weather and by cull and debris that lure egg-laying.

beginner: There is no rescue for a maggot-riddled crown, so remove badly affected plants. Use row cover to keep the flies off, and clean up debris and culls that attract them.
seasoned: Remove and destroy infested plants, exclude flies with floating row cover, and sanitize debris and culls; rotation and avoiding dense allium plantings limit buildup. No effective organic rescue exists once larvae are in the crown.

beginner: Cover plants with row cover in spring, avoid leaving old bulbs and debris around, and do not crowd alliums together.
seasoned: Row-cover early, sanitize allium residue, rotate, and avoid clustering chives with other alliums that concentrate the fly.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the leaves and flower stalks, sometimes with sticky residue. Chives rarely get them badly, and their scent even helps keep aphids off nearby plants.
seasoned: Occasional aphid colonies on foliage and scapes; chives are among the most aphid-free herbs (their odor is credited with repelling aphids from neighbors), so infestations are minor and sporadic rather than a standing threat.

beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast on soft growth. They are an occasional, minor visitor on chives.
seasoned: Several aphid species may alight on chives in flushes of soft growth, but the plant's sulfur compounds make it an inhospitable host, so colonies rarely persist.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water or use insecticidal soap, and rinse cut leaves before use. It is seldom needed.
seasoned: A water jet or insecticidal soap handles the rare colony; conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and hoverflies, which the chive umbels also feed when in bloom.

beginner: Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check flower stalks now and then.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, conserve natural enemies, and monitor scapes; control is seldom warranted on chives.

beginner: Pale, fuzzy gray-violet patches on the leaves in cool, damp weather, with the blades yellowing and collapsing. It spreads fastest in wet, crowded, poorly drained plantings.
seasoned: Downy mildew (Peronospora destructor) producing pale oval patches that turn violet-gray with sporulation under moisture, with leaves paling, yellowing, and collapsing; it is favored by cool (below about 75°F), humid, wet conditions and affects chives among many alliums.

beginner: A fungus-like disease of the onion family, favored by cool, humid, wet conditions, that can affect chives along with onions, garlic, and leeks.
seasoned: Peronospora destructor, an oomycete spread by wind and splashing water and favored by cool, moist weather and long leaf-wetness periods; crowded, poorly drained plantings hold it.

beginner: Remove affected leaves, improve airflow by dividing crowded clumps, water at the base rather than over the leaves, and cut a badly hit clump back so it regrows in drier weather.
seasoned: Manage culturally: divide crowded clumps and space for airflow, irrigate at the soil line, remove infected foliage, and shear a heavily affected clump to regrow under drier conditions. The home garden has no reliable cure once it is established.

beginner: Space and divide plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and avoid soggy, shaded, crowded spots.
seasoned: Open the canopy by dividing, water at the base, site in well-drained sun, and avoid the cool, wet, crowded conditions the pathogen needs.

beginner: Bright orange raised spots or streaks (pustules) scattered on the leaves. Heavily rusted blades yellow and dry up. It is more common in wet seasons and on crowded, over-fed plants.
seasoned: Allium rust (Puccinia species) forming bright orange to rusty raised pustules on leaves and scapes, with chlorosis and dieback of heavily infected foliage; it is favored by moist conditions, crowding, and lush high-nitrogen growth, and affects chives along with garlic, leeks, and onions.

beginner: Rust is a fungal disease of the onion family, including chives, that shows as orange pustules on the leaves and spreads by airborne spores in damp weather.
seasoned: Puccinia rust fungi spread by airborne urediniospores in humid weather; dense stands and excess nitrogen worsen it.

beginner: Cut off and destroy rusty leaves or shear the clump to the base to regrow clean, thin crowded plantings for airflow, and avoid overhead watering and heavy nitrogen.
seasoned: Shear infected foliage (a hard cut to the base removes the pustules and regrows clean), divide to open crowded clumps, avoid overhead irrigation and heavy nitrogen, and remove debris. Fungicides are rarely warranted in a home planting.

beginner: Give plants room and airflow, water at the base, go easy on nitrogen, and remove rusty foliage promptly.
seasoned: Divide for airflow, moderate nitrogen, irrigate at the soil line, and cut out rust early before it spreads.

beginner: Yellowing, wilting plants whose roots and crown rot, with a fluffy white mold and tiny black specks (like poppy seeds) at the base. Affected plants do not recover, and the disease stays in the soil for many years.
seasoned: White rot (Sclerotium cepivorum) causing yellowing, wilting, and a soft rot of roots and crown, with a fluffy white mycelium and abundant tiny black sclerotia at the base; the sclerotia persist in soil for many years, and the disease affects chives with onions, garlic, and leeks.

beginner: White rot is a serious soil fungus of the onion family that rots the roots and crown. Once it is in the soil it lasts a very long time, so keeping it out is the whole game.
seasoned: Sclerotium cepivorum, a soilborne fungus favored by cool, moist soil; its long-lived sclerotia make an infested site unusable for alliums for a decade or more, so exclusion and sanitation are the only real controls.

beginner: There is no cure. Remove and destroy affected plants along with the soil around the roots, and do not plant chives, onions, or garlic in that spot again. Never move infected soil or plants to a clean bed.
seasoned: No rescue: rogue out affected plants with surrounding soil, avoid spreading infested soil on tools or transplants, and do not replant alliums in the site. Long rotation is the standing management.

beginner: Start with clean plants, do not bring in soil from an infected garden, and rotate onion-family plants to fresh ground.
seasoned: Plant clean, sclerotia-free stock, quarantine infested ground from alliums, sanitize tools, and never import garden soil of unknown history.

beginner: Small whitish sunken spots on the leaves in cool, wet weather that can run together and brown out the tops, sometimes with a gray fuzzy mold. It is worst in humid, crowded plantings.
seasoned: Botrytis leaf blight and neck rot (Botrytis species) producing small white sunken leaf spots that coalesce into blast and tip dieback under cool, moist conditions, sometimes with gray sporulation; humid, crowded stands favor it, and it affects chives among the alliums.

beginner: Botrytis is a gray-mold fungus of the onion family that spots and blights the leaves in cool, damp, crowded conditions.
seasoned: Botrytis fungi favored by cool, wet, humid weather and dense canopies; splashing water and leaf wetness spread the spores.

beginner: Remove spotted leaves or shear the clump to regrow, open up crowded plantings for airflow, and water at the base instead of over the leaves.
seasoned: Cull spotted foliage or shear the clump to regrow, divide to open the stand, irrigate at the soil line, and remove senescing debris. Fungicides are seldom needed on a home chive planting.

beginner: Space and divide for airflow, water at the soil line, and clean up dead foliage.
seasoned: Divide for airflow, water low and early, and sanitize dead foliage to cut inoculum.

beginner: Water about once a week so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week. Established chives handle a dry spell, but even water keeps the leaves tender.
seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept even; chives are drought tolerant once the clump is established, but steady moisture keeps the leaves tender and green over the long cutting season. Do not let established plants sit in constantly wet soil.

beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is hot and dry. Mulch helps keep the soil evenly moist.
seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week, more in hot, dry spells; the University of Minnesota advises watering deeply when rainfall is sparse so the soil does not dry out around the roots. A mulch helps hold even moisture for a clump you cut from for years.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the foliage dry checks the leaf diseases (downy mildew, rust, botrytis) chives can catch in cool, wet, crowded conditions.

beginner: Leaves go yellow and floppy and the base can rot in soggy soil, especially over winter.
seasoned: Yellowing, floppy foliage and crown or root rot in constantly wet, poorly drained ground, especially over winter; downy mildew and botrytis also flare in cool, saturated, crowded conditions.

beginner: Wilting leaves that taste sharper and tougher, and slowed growth when the soil dries out for too long.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and tougher, sharper foliage in prolonged drought; established clumps recover quickly once watered, but a dry, hot spell can push them toward summer dormancy.

beginner: Chive seeds take 2 to 3 weeks to come up, so keep the soil surface evenly damp the whole time. Do not let it dry out while they are sprouting.
seasoned: Chive seed is slow, 2 to 3 weeks, so keep the surface evenly moist through the whole germination; letting it dry mid-sprout stalls an already slow stand.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while a new plant gets going. Water deeply in dry spells, and mulch to hold the moisture.
seasoned: Steady moisture matters most while a new clump puts its root system down; UMN advises watering deeply when rainfall is sparse so the soil does not dry around the roots. Mulch helps hold it for a clump you will cut from for years.

beginner: Established chives handle a dry spell, but even water, about an inch a week, keeps the leaves tender for cutting. Water at the base to keep the leaves dry, and know that a long hot drought makes them tough and can send them dormant early.
seasoned: Once the clump is established chives are drought tolerant, but steady moisture, about an inch a week, keeps the leaves tender and green over the long cutting season. Water at the soil line to keep the foliage dry against downy mildew, rust, and botrytis in crowded conditions. Prolonged drought toughens the leaves and can push the plant into early summer dormancy in hot regions.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while chives bloom. The flowers are edible, and steady water keeps the leaves tender if you keep snipping.
seasoned: Keep even moisture through the bloom; the flowers are edible, and steady water holds leaf quality if you keep cutting alongside the blossoms.

beginner: Water little or none while chives are dormant. The main danger now is rot from soggy winter soil, so do not let the resting clump sit wet.
seasoned: Cut back watering as the clump goes dormant; the biggest risk now is crown and root rot from constantly wet, poorly drained ground over winter, so do not let a dormant clump sit in wet soil.

beginner: Keep the water fairly steady so the leaves stay tender; chives handle a short dry spell once established, but long droughts make them tough.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps chives growing tender and green; an established clump tolerates short dry spells, but prolonged drought toughens the leaves and can trigger early summer dormancy in hot regions.

seasoned: Steady moisture matters most through the slow germination (2 to 3 weeks) and while a new clump establishes; once the root system is down the plant is forgiving.

beginner: The easiest way to start chives is to buy a small pot or split a clump from a friend, which is ready to cut almost right away. You can also grow them from seed, but the seed is slow, taking a couple of weeks or more, so start it indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, sowing a small pinch of seeds in each cell and growing them on as a little clump that you plant out whole without separating, or sow it outside once the soil is warm. Plant outside in spring in cold areas, or in fall through winter where summers are hot. Space plants about 8 to 12 inches apart, and remember one clump can be split into many.
seasoned: Chives are easiest to establish from a division or a nursery clump, which gives a cuttable plant in weeks, but they also grow readily from seed. The seed is slow, germinating over about 2 to 3 weeks (up to 4 to 6 in cool soil), so start it indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost, sowing a pinch of about 8 to 10 seeds per cell and growing them on as an undivided clump that transplants out whole after hardening off, with no thinning (RHS), or direct-sow once the soil warms. Plant outdoors in spring after hard-frost danger passes in cold regions, or in fall through late winter in mild and hot regions. Set clumps 8 to 12 inches apart; they widen over the years and are the easiest herb to propagate by simply lifting and splitting an established clump.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A light, well-drained potting mix with some organic matter.

beginner: Mix in a little compost for steady nutrients.
seasoned: Blend in compost; chives are light feeders, so no heavy starter fertilizer is needed.

beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check every day or two in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist.
seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds; check moisture every day or two in warmth and water deeply before the mix dries out.

beginner: Feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every four to six weeks, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.
seasoned: Container chives need only a light feed, a dilute liquid fertilizer every four to six weeks, because frequent watering leaches the limited mix.

beginner: Chives are very hardy, so a pot can stay outside through fall and winter in most areas; the leaves die back and the plant regrows in spring. In the coldest zones the small amount of soil in a pot freezes harder than the ground, so sink the pot in the garden, move it against the house, or mulch it heavily. You can also dig up a small clump in fall, pot it, and grow it on a bright windowsill for winter snipping.
seasoned: Chives are frost-hardy to roughly zone 3 and go dormant over winter, so an outdoor pot simply dies back and returns in spring. Container root volume freezes harder than open ground, so in cold zones sink the pot, cluster pots against a wall, or mulch to buffer the roots. A classic trick is to lift a small divided clump in fall, pot it, give it a few weeks of cold to satisfy dormancy, then bring it to a sunny window for fresh winter leaves.

beginner: Chives are one of the best herbs for a pot. Use a container at least 6 inches deep with drainage holes, keep it watered, and snip leaves as you need them. A pot does well on a sunny windowsill or step, and because chives are so hardy it can carry on outdoors long after tender herbs are done.
seasoned: Chives grow very well in a container at least 6 inches deep, harvested cut-and-come-again. Keep moisture even, since pots dry fast, and feed only lightly. A pot is the easiest way to keep chives by the kitchen door, to move a small clump indoors for winter cutting, and to contain a plant that self-sows in the open garden.

beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps the water steady, which keeps chives tender and productive.
seasoned: A self-watering container suits chives well, smoothing out the steady moisture that keeps the leaves tender over a long cutting season.

beginner: Chives have shallow roots, so a pot at least 6 inches deep is fine. Extra width lets the clump spread and gives you more to cut.
seasoned: Chives have a shallow, fibrous root system and do not need depth; a pot 6 inches or deeper is plenty, and extra width lets the clump widen and lets you grow more to cut from.

beginner: Do not plant chives where you recently grew onions, garlic, or leeks, since onion-family plants share soil diseases and pests that build up. Because chives stay put for years, this mainly matters when you first choose the spot.
seasoned: Avoid establishing chives where onions, garlic, leeks, shallots, or other chives grew recently: the alliums share soilborne troubles, above all white rot (whose sclerotia persist for years), plus pink root, onion maggot, and thrips. Because chives are a long-lived perennial planted once and left in place, rotation matters mainly when you first site a clump or replace an old one; keep new plantings out of recently cropped allium ground.

beginner: Chives are in the onion family, so they can pick up the same soil diseases as onions and garlic. Since a chive clump stays in one place for years, just choose a spot where you have not grown onion-family plants recently, ideally after leafy greens or beans. Chives that flower drop seed, so pull up stray seedlings where you do not want them.
seasoned: Chives are an allium, so they share the onion family's soilborne diseases (white rot, pink root) and pests (onion maggot, thrips, allium leafminer). Standard allium guidance keeps the family off the same ground for several years, but chives are a permanent perennial, so the practical rule is to establish a new clump in ground that has not recently grown onions, garlic, or leeks, and to follow a leafy or legume crop rather than another allium. A clump left to flower self-sows freely, so pull stray seedlings that come up out of place.

beginner: Chives are not like cilantro; flowering is normal and the flowers are pretty and edible. But two things happen when they bloom: the leaves get tougher, and if the flowers go to seed you get lots of surprise seedlings. So enjoy some flowers, then cut the whole clump back to about 1 to 2 inches. That takes off the old flower stalks before they seed and brings back fresh, tender leaves.
seasoned: Chives do not bolt-and-quit the way lettuce or cilantro do; flowering is a normal, even desirable, part of a perennial allium's year. In late spring to early summer the clump sends up round pink to pale purple flower scapes above the leaves, and the flowers are edible and good for pollinators. The catch is twofold: the foliage around the scapes turns tougher and more hollow, and a clump left to set seed self-sows prolifically (garlic chives especially). The standard practice is to enjoy some flowers, then shear the whole clump down to about 1 to 2 inches after bloom, which removes the spent scapes before they seed and forces a fresh flush of tender leaves. Removing flower stalks at the soil line as they fade also prevents unwanted volunteer seedlings.

beginner: Chives flower in late spring or early summer with round pink-purple blooms, and that is normal, not a mistake. The flowers taste good and feed the bees. Just know the leaves get tougher around the flowers, and the seeds can sprout all over, so cutting the clump back after it blooms keeps the leaves tender and the plant tidy.
seasoned: Flowering in chives is a perennial life-cycle event in late spring to early summer, not a heat response, and it is partly a feature: the pink-purple umbels are edible and strong insectary plants. Its practical downside is coarsened, hollow foliage and prolific self-seeding, both fixed by shearing the clump hard after bloom to renew tender leaves and cut off seed set. Garlic chives (Allium tuberosum) flower later, in late summer, are white, and self-sow so freely they can become weedy if the scapes are not removed.

beginner: Do not leave cut chives out on the counter, where they wilt fast. Chill them and use them soon after cutting.
seasoned: Fresh chives wilt quickly at room temperature, so refrigerate promptly after cutting; the leaves lose their delicate onion aroma fast once cut, so use them soon.

beginner: Store fresh chives unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge, where they keep about a week. Wash them only when you are ready to use them.
seasoned: Refrigerate fresh chives unwashed in a loose or perforated bag, or wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel, in the crisper; they hold about 1 week. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown.

beginner: Chives are best frozen rather than dried. Chop the clean leaves and freeze them loose or in an ice-cube tray with a little water, then use them straight from the freezer without thawing. Drying works but loses most of the flavor.
seasoned: Chives freeze better than they dry: snip the washed leaves and freeze them loose or in ice-cube trays with a little water; the University of Minnesota notes you can use the frozen pieces straight from the freezer without thawing. Drying is the weakest option, since dried chives lose most of their delicate flavor, so freezing is preferred for keeping.

beginner: The best way to store chives is to leave them growing and cut what you need. Picked chives keep about a week in the fridge. To save extra, freeze them chopped rather than drying them, since drying loses most of the flavor.
seasoned: Chives are best fresh, and because the clump keeps producing, the easiest storage is to cut what you need as you need it. Cut chives keep about a week refrigerated. For longer keeping, freeze them chopped (loose or in cubes) rather than drying, which sacrifices most of the flavor; frozen chives go straight into cooking without thawing.

beginner: There are really two kinds. Common chives have thin, hollow leaves and pink-purple flowers and taste mildly of onion; the named types just vary in how fine or sturdy the leaves are. Garlic chives are a different plant with flat leaves, a mild garlic taste, and white flowers in late summer, and they take heat well but spread by seed a lot. They all grow the same way, so pick by flavor and looks, and cut off the flowers if you do not want seedlings everywhere.
seasoned: Chives come in two distinct plants. Common chives (Allium schoenoprasum) are the familiar fine, hollow-leaved clump with pink-purple spring flowers and a mild onion taste; named selections differ mostly in leaf fineness and vigor, from the slender Fine Leaf and Grolau strains favored for pots and forcing, to the thick, easy-cutting Staro, to taller showy-flowered Forescate. Garlic chives (Allium tuberosum) are a separate species with flat leaves, a garlic flavor, and white late-summer flowers; they are tougher in heat and drought but self-sow aggressively. All are grown much the same way, so choice comes down to flavor (onion versus garlic), leaf form, and how much you value the flowers, while any chive self-seeds if you let the blooms set seed.

beginner: Chives are a classic companion herb: their oniony scent is said to help keep aphids and some other pests off nearby plants, and their early flowers feed pollinators and helpful insects. Gardeners traditionally tuck them at the base of roses (for black spot and aphids) and apple trees (for scab), and near carrots and tomatoes. The one plant to keep them away from is beans and peas, which onion-family plants can slow down.
seasoned: Much of the chive companion tradition rests on two real mechanisms: allium sulfur compounds that deter aphids and some fungal problems, and the flowering umbels' pull on hoverflies, ladybugs, and parasitoid wasps. Michigan State, citing Penn State, passes along the traditional pairings of chives at the base of apple trees (to help suppress apple scab) and roses (black spot), plus a reputed boost to carrots. These are hedged tradition with a plausible mechanism, not measured trials. The one well-grounded caution is the allium-legume antagonism: onions and their relatives are widely documented to inhibit beans and peas, so keep chives away from legumes.

beginner: Chives planted around roses are a traditional pairing said to help keep aphids away and reduce black spot, and their early flowers bring in helpful insects.
seasoned: A traditional aromatic-companion pairing: chives are long grown at the base of roses to deter aphids and reduce black spot, with allium sulfur volatiles the plausible mechanism. MSU relays it from Penn State as tradition, not a measured effect.

beginner: Chives grown at the base of an apple tree are traditionally said to help prevent apple scab.
seasoned: A traditional orchard pairing relayed by MSU (citing Penn State): chives ringing an apple trunk are said to help suppress apple scab. Folklore with an antifungal-allium rationale, not a documented trial.

beginner: Chives are a traditional good neighbor for carrots and tomatoes; their scent is said to help keep pests down, and they take up little room.
seasoned: A traditional aromatic interplant: chives are said to improve carrots and to help repel pests around tomatoes, tucking neatly into small gaps. Widely taught tradition with an aromatic-deterrent rationale, not a measured pairwise effect.

beginner: Keep chives away from beans and peas. Onion-family plants tend to slow the growth of legumes when grown close together.
seasoned: A well-grounded antagonism: alliums, chives included, inhibit the growth of beans and peas, so they should not be interplanted. Documented extension guidance for onions and their relatives, not folklore.

beginner: If you sowed seed, the first thin little green blades. Chive seed is slow, often a couple of weeks or more, so be patient. A bought or divided clump skips this step.
seasoned: From seed, the first thin, grassy blades pushing up. Chive seed is slow and can take 2 to 3 weeks, up to 4 to 6 in cool soil, and emergence is uneven. A division or nursery clump skips this stage entirely.

beginner: Keep the soil damp but not soggy until the seedlings appear, which can take a few weeks. For a quicker start, plant a small pot or a split clump instead of seed.
seasoned: Keep the surface evenly moist through the long germination and do not let it crust or dry. If you want a faster start, set out a division or nursery clump instead of sowing seed.

seasoned: Any sprouts yet?

beginner: A small clump of grassy leaves getting fuller. In its first year the plant is putting energy into its roots so it comes back next spring.
seasoned: A young clump filling out with several upright blades. In the first year it is building the root and bulblet reserves it needs to overwinter and return.

beginner: Go easy on cutting the first year and keep the soil moist so the plant gets strong for winter. Space plants about 8 to 12 inches apart.
seasoned: Harvest sparingly the first year and keep moisture steady so the clump can bank strength for winter; a light feeding helps a weak plant. Thin or space seedlings to about 8 to 12 inches.

beginner: How is it filling in?
seasoned: How is the clump filling in?

beginner: Full clumps about 6 inches tall you can keep cutting from. Snip the leaves to about 1 to 2 inches above the soil and they grow back again and again.
seasoned: Full clumps 6 inches or more tall that you cut from repeatedly: shear the outer blades to about 1 to 2 inches and the clump regrows for months, spring through fall in cold regions and through the cool season where summers are hot.

beginner: Cut the leaves to about 1 to 2 inches, leaving some green behind, and they grow back. Cutting often keeps them tender. After the flowers fade, cut the whole clump back to freshen it.
seasoned: Cut blades near the base, leaving some green so the clump keeps feeding itself, and never shear it fully bare. Regular cutting keeps tender new growth coming; shear the whole clump hard after flowering to renew it.

beginner: Harvesting regularly?
seasoned: Harvesting regularly?

beginner: Round pink-purple flowers on stalks above the leaves in late spring or early summer. They are pretty and edible, but the leaves near them get tougher.
seasoned: Round pink to pale purple flower globes rising above the leaves in late spring to early summer (white in late summer for garlic chives). The blooms are edible, but foliage near the scapes coarsens.

beginner: Pick a few flowers to eat, then cut the whole clump back to about 1 to 2 inches. This stops it from seeding everywhere and brings back fresh, tender leaves.
seasoned: Enjoy or harvest some flowers just as they open, then shear the clump to about 1 to 2 inches to remove spent scapes before they seed and to force a fresh flush of tender leaves. Deadhead to prevent prolific self-seeding.

beginner: Any flowers yet?
seasoned: Flowering yet?

beginner: In cold areas the leaves die back and the plant rests over winter, then greens up again very early in spring. In mild areas it may stay green most of the year.
seasoned: In cold regions the foliage yellows and dies back to the ground with hard frost, and the clump rests dormant over winter, pushing up fresh blades as one of the first herbs of spring. In mild regions it may stay semi-evergreen.

beginner: Leave the plant alone as it dies back; clean up the old leaves in late winter. It will come back on its own in spring. Split crowded clumps in early spring.
seasoned: Let the clump die back naturally; tidy old remains in late winter and mulch in the coldest zones. Do nothing to force it; it returns on its own. Divide overgrown clumps in early spring as growth resumes.

beginner: Resting or coming back up?
seasoned: Died back or greening up?

seasoned: Go easy on first-year chives

beginner: Your chives are young. Cut only a little this first year so the plant gets strong for winter.
seasoned: Your chive clump is establishing. Harvest only lightly this first year and keep moisture steady so it banks strength to overwinter and return.

beginner: Time to start snipping chives

seasoned: Important safety note: chives are in the onion (allium) family, and all alliums are toxic to cats, dogs, and horses.
