beginner: Chives are one of the easiest and hardiest herbs you can grow. They are a perennial in the onion family, so you plant them once and they come back every year on their own. The plant dies back over winter, then sends up fresh, thin, grassy green leaves very early in spring, and it carries pretty pink-purple flowers in early summer that you can eat too. Chives like full sun to a little shade, decent soil, and regular water, but they forgive a lot. The clump gets bigger each year, so dig it up and split it every few years. They have a mild oniony taste and hardly any pests. There is also a relative called garlic chives, with flat leaves and a mild garlic flavor.
seasoned: Chives (Allium schoenoprasum) are a hardy, clump-forming perennial in the onion family (Amaryllidaceae), grown for their slender, hollow, grass-like leaves and their edible pink to pale purple pom-pom flowers. Unlike the annual and biennial kitchen herbs, chives are planted once and come back on their own year after year: the clump dies back to the ground over winter, rests dormant, and pushes up fresh green blades as one of the very first herbs of spring. They are among the hardiest herbs grown, reliable to roughly USDA zone 3, and among the easiest, with a mild onion flavor and few real pests. Give them full sun to light shade, average to rich well-drained soil, and steady moisture, though an established clump tolerates short dry spells. The clumps slowly widen from year to year and are best lifted and divided every 2 to 3 years to keep them vigorous. Chives are cool-preferring: in cold regions they run right through the northern summer, while in the hot South and desert they are a cool-season herb that slows or rests in the worst summer heat and revives as it cools. A close relative, garlic chives (Allium tuberosum), is a distinct species with flat leaves, a mild garlic flavor, and white late-summer flowers.

beginner: You can start cutting chives once the clump is about 6 inches tall. From seed that takes a couple of months, but a bought or divided plant is ready much sooner. Snip the leaves down to about 1 to 2 inches above the soil, taking some from each clump, and they grow right back so you can keep cutting all season. Always leave some green behind so the plant stays healthy, and go easy the first year. Cut in the cool morning and use the leaves fresh. The flowers are edible too.
seasoned: Start cutting chives once an established clump is 6 inches or more tall, which from seed is roughly 60 to 90 days but from a division or nursery clump can be just a few weeks. Harvest by shearing the outer leaves down to about 1 to 2 inches above the soil with scissors, taking some blades from each clump rather than shearing it bare; the leaves regrow and you can cut the same plant again and again through the season. Leave enough green so the plant keeps feeding itself, and in the first year cut sparingly so the young clump can build strength to overwinter. Pick in the cool morning, and use the leaves fresh for the best flavor. The pink-purple flowers are edible too and are best picked just as they open.

beginner: Mint likes rich, moist soil and, unlike most kitchen herbs, it loves damp ground. Give it soil with some compost worked in and keep it evenly moist; it will even grow in part shade and in a low, wet spot where other herbs sulk. What it does not like is dry, sandy ground that dries out fast. Because mint spreads so fast underground, most gardeners plant it in a pot or a buried barrier so it cannot take over the bed.
seasoned: Mint grows in most soils but does best in rich, moist to even damp ground high in organic matter, the opposite of the sharp-drained, lean sites the Mediterranean herbs want. Clemson notes mints prefer rich, moist or even damp soil in part shade, and NC State lists it as unsuited to dry soils, tolerating clay, loam, or sand and both occasionally wet and occasionally dry conditions. Utah State recommends rich, moist, slightly acidic soil with no more than about 1 inch of well-composted organic matter per 100 square feet; do not overfeed, since rich soil and heavy nitrogen make the growth floppy and dilute the flavor. Keep the bed evenly moist but not permanently saturated, and remember mint runs by rhizomes and stolons, so grow it in a sunken bottomless container or a lined bed to keep it in bounds.

beginner: Mint grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 7.0, and it is not fussy. Most garden soil is fine; a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral. Utah State describes mint as preferring slightly acidic soil, NC State lists it as tolerant across roughly 6.0 to 8.0, and the University of Minnesota's general herb guidance is a well-drained soil near 6.0 to 7.5, so mint is forgiving and rarely needs any pH adjustment beyond a soil-test baseline.

beginner: Mint does not need much feeding, and too much makes it flop and lose flavor. Mix a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the soil in spring, then leave it alone. If you grow it in a pot, feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every few weeks, since watering washes nutrients out.
seasoned: Mint is a light feeder and is easily overfed. Utah State suggests about one teaspoon of a balanced 16-16-16 fertilizer per plant in early spring as growth resumes; a compost-rich bed often needs no more than a light topdressing. Go easy, because rich soil and heavy nitrogen push soft, floppy stems and thin the essential oils that carry mint's flavor and aroma, a point Wisconsin Horticulture makes for mints grown in lean ground. In a container, where frequent watering leaches nutrients, a dilute liquid feed every few weeks through the growing season keeps the leaves green.

beginner: Time to give your mint a light feeding.
seasoned: Time to give your mint a light spring feeding as it regrows.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer such as 16-16-16, just a light feeding in spring. Do not overdo it; too much makes mint floppy and bland.
seasoned: A light, balanced feed is all mint wants: about a teaspoon of 16-16-16 per plant in early spring, or a compost topdressing. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which makes the stems floppy and waters down the flavor.

beginner: A teaspoon of balanced fertilizer per plant in spring, or a thin layer of compost; in a pot, a diluted liquid feed every few weeks.
seasoned: About one teaspoon of 16-16-16 per plant in early spring (Utah State); a compost-rich or container bed often needs only a light topdressing or a dilute liquid feed every 3 to 4 weeks.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the growing tips and undersides of leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
seasoned: Colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides, one of the pests UC IPM lists for mint; honeydew and the insects themselves contaminate a crop eaten fresh, and soft, overfed growth is the most susceptible.

beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer, and they can spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on mint; they reproduce rapidly and favor the lush growth that excess nitrogen and rich soil produce.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Rinse cut sprigs well before use.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides, and repeat every few days; conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps.

beginner: Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check new growth often.
seasoned: Scout the tips early, avoid overfeeding, and conserve natural enemies; because you eat the leaves, lean toward a strong water spray before anything else.

beginner: A fine stippling or speckling on the leaves, sometimes with faint webbing on the undersides, worst in hot, dry weather. Leaves look dull, sandy, or bronzed.
seasoned: Twospotted and related spider mites, which UC IPM lists for mint, stipple the foliage with pale flecks and spin fine webbing on the undersides; they flare in hot, dry, dusty conditions and on drought-stressed plants, which is why mint's moisture love is also its best mite defense.

beginner: Tiny sap-sucking mites, not true insects, that explode in hot, dry, dusty conditions and are easy to miss until the leaves are speckled.
seasoned: Spider mites feeding with piercing mouthparts; populations build fastest in heat and drought and on dusty, water-stressed plants.

beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water to knock them off, keep the plant well watered, and use insecticidal soap or neem if they persist.
seasoned: Hose the undersides forcefully and repeat, maintain steady soil moisture, and apply insecticidal soap or a miticidal oil to the leaf undersides; conserve predatory mites and minute pirate bugs.

beginner: Keep mint evenly moist and mulched, since drought stress invites mites, and rinse dusty foliage in hot spells.
seasoned: Do not let mint dry out or get dusty, mulch to hold moisture, and scout the undersides in hot weather when mites move fastest.

beginner: Young shoots cut off at the soil line, notched or shot-holed leaves, or plants that weaken and thin out from grubs feeding on the roots and rhizomes.
seasoned: Utah State lists flea beetles and cutworms among mint's insect pests; cutworms sever young shoots at the soil line and mint flea beetles chew small holes, while soil and rhizome feeders thin an established patch from below. On a home planting numbers are usually modest.

beginner: A mix of chewing pests, cutworms and mint flea beetles above ground and root-feeding larvae below, that damage leaves, stems, and the underground runners.
seasoned: A complex of foliage feeders (cutworms, mint flea beetle) and root/rhizome feeders (root and rhizome larvae); the perennial, spreading root mass is what harbors the below-ground stages.

beginner: Handpick cutworms at dusk and use cardboard collars on new transplants, hose or handpick flea beetles, and keep the bed clean; dividing and resetting a tired patch in fresh ground breaks root-pest cycles.
seasoned: Handpick and use collars against cutworms, dislodge flea beetles with water or row cover on new plantings, and manage root pests culturally by dividing and resetting the patch in clean soil; reserve any spray for the labeled edible-herb products.

beginner: Clear plant debris where cutworms shelter, rotate a heavily infested patch to fresh ground, and keep plants vigorous so they outgrow light feeding.
seasoned: Sanitize debris, keep plants vigorous, and reset an infested patch into fresh ground on a multi-year cycle, the same renewal that keeps mint from getting woody.

beginner: Small orange, yellow, or rust-brown powdery pustules on the undersides of the leaves and on the stems, with pale spots on the upper surface. Badly affected leaves curl, brown, and drop, and rusty leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: Puccinia menthae, the classic mint rust: orange to brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides, stems, and petioles, with defoliation in a bad year (NC State lists rust among the main mint diseases). It overwinters in the rhizomes, so an infected patch reinfects itself, and warm humid crowding drives it.

beginner: A rust fungus, the signature mint disease, that thrives in warm, humid, crowded conditions and lives over on the roots and rhizomes from year to year.
seasoned: The rust fungus Puccinia menthae, favored by warm, humid, crowded conditions and carried over in the root and rhizome mass.

beginner: Pick off and destroy rusted leaves as soon as you see them, thin and space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and cut a badly infected patch to the ground; in a severe case, start a fresh planting from clean, rust-free cuttings in a new spot.
seasoned: Remove and destroy infected leaves, open up the planting for airflow, switch to soil-line watering, and mow or cut a heavily infected patch to the ground and clear the debris; renew from clean cuttings in fresh ground where it recurs. There is no reliable home cure once it is established.

beginner: Space plants for good airflow, avoid wetting the foliage, keep the patch from getting congested, and start new plantings from clean stock.
seasoned: Airflow, dry foliage, and uncongested spacing are the defenses; propagate only from rust-free plants and reset a chronically infected patch elsewhere.

beginner: Stunted, off-color plants whose lower leaves yellow and wilt, often on just one side of a stem, with whole shoots or plants dying back in warm weather. It does not wash off and there is no spray cure.
seasoned: Verticillium wilt (a soilborne Verticillium), the disease that most limits mint's longevity: slow, bronze-cast spring growth, one-sided branch development, lower-leaf yellowing and wilt in warm or dry weather, and dieback. The Connecticut Experiment Station and Utah State both flag it for mint. The fungus persists in soil for years and has a wide host range, so it is managed by site selection and renewal, not treatment.

beginner: A soil-borne fungus that clogs the plant's water-conducting tissue; it builds up in the ground and is the disease that shortens the life of a mint patch.
seasoned: A soilborne Verticillium fungus that invades the vascular system; it survives for years in soil and infects many crops (tomato, potato, strawberry, other mints).

beginner: There is no cure for an infected plant, so remove it. Start fresh plantings from clean cuttings in a new bed, and do not follow tomatoes, potatoes, or strawberries, which host the same fungus.
seasoned: Rogue out affected plants and manage by prevention: propagate disease-free cuttings, establish new patches in clean ground away from prior verticillium hosts, and rotate the mint bed on a multi-year cycle where the disease appears.

beginner: Plant clean stock in ground with no recent history of the disease, avoid siting mint after verticillium-susceptible crops, and move the patch to fresh ground every few years.
seasoned: Use clean stock, avoid ground that grew tomatoes, potatoes, eggplant, or strawberries, and reset the patch in fresh soil periodically, since there is no rescue for an infected plant.

beginner: A white, powdery dust on the leaves and stems (powdery mildew), or dark sunken spots and blotches on leaves and stems (anthracnose leaf spot). Heavily spotted or coated leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: Powdery mildew (white powdery patches that brown and shrivel heavy foliage, listed for mint by UC IPM) and anthracnose or leaf spot (Utah State and NC State list leaf-spotting fungi for mint), both favored by crowded, humid conditions and wet leaves.

beginner: Fungal leaf diseases that spread in crowded, humid plantings and on wet foliage, worse where air does not move.
seasoned: Foliar fungi (powdery mildew; anthracnose and other leaf-spot fungi) driven by high humidity, crowding, and prolonged leaf wetness.

beginner: Remove affected leaves, thin the planting and water at the soil line to keep the leaves dry, and cut a badly hit patch back to encourage clean new growth.
seasoned: Improve airflow by thinning and dividing, water at the soil line, remove infected foliage, and shear a badly affected patch to force clean regrowth; drip irrigation and avoiding overnight leaf wetness are the practical controls Utah State recommends.

beginner: Space for airflow, water at the base rather than overhead, and avoid crowding.
seasoned: Open the canopy, keep the foliage dry, and do not let the patch get congested; renew a chronically diseased stand from clean cuttings.

beginner: Water often enough to keep the soil evenly moist, about 1 to 2 inches a week. Mint likes damp soil, so do not let it dry out.
seasoned: Roughly 1 to 2 inches of water per week, kept even; mint is a moisture lover that must not dry out, and Utah State advises 1 to 2 inches per week while cautioning against overwatering, which invites disease.

beginner: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches a week, more when it is hot or in a pot. Keep the soil damp but not swampy.
seasoned: About 1 to 2 inches per week, more in heat and in containers, which dry fast; the goal is steady, even moisture rather than a soak-and-dry cycle. Mulch helps hold it.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent the leaf diseases mint is prone to.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the foliage dry checks mint rust, powdery mildew, and leaf spot on a crop eaten fresh, which Utah State reinforces with its drip-irrigation and no-overnight-wet-leaves advice.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant can rot at the base if the soil stays soggy, and wet leaves bring on leaf diseases.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and root or crown rot in ground that stays waterlogged, plus more rust and mildew where the foliage stays wet; mint tolerates damp soil but not standing water.

beginner: Wilting, dull leaves and more spider mites when the soil dries out. Mint does not handle drought well, so keep it watered.
seasoned: Wilting, dull or bronzed leaves, and a spike in spider mites; sustained drought stress checks growth and, in hot dry regions, scorches the foliage, since mint has little drought tolerance.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while a new mint plant gets rooted. Mint loves damp soil, so do not let it dry out now.
seasoned: Steady moisture matters most while a new division or cutting roots in; mint is a moisture lover and must not dry out as it establishes. Water at the soil line and mulch to hold even moisture.

beginner: Mint likes damp soil, unlike most herbs. Keep it evenly and generously watered, about 1 to 2 inches a week and more in heat or in a pot, but never swampy. Water the soil, not the leaves, to avoid the diseases mint gets.
seasoned: Mint is the rare kitchen herb that thrives in damp ground and part shade, the opposite of rosemary or thyme: give an even, generous 1 to 2 inches a week (USU's figure), more in heat or in fast-drying containers, aiming for steady moisture rather than a soak-and-dry cycle. The one caution is disease, so water the soil, not the leaves, against mint rust, powdery mildew, and leaf spot.

beginner: Keep mint evenly and generously watered while you cut it. If it dries out the leaves go dull and bronzed and spider mites move in, so keep the soil damp.
seasoned: Keep the same even, generous moisture through the cutting season; mint has little drought tolerance, and a dry spell checks growth, dulls or bronzes the leaves, and can bring on spider mites.

beginner: Water little while mint is dormant over winter. Soggy winter ground can rot the roots, so ease right off.
seasoned: Cut back watering as the patch dies back for winter; a dormant patch needs little, and constantly waterlogged winter ground invites root and crown rot.

beginner: As new shoots come up in spring, start watering evenly again to push tender new growth.
seasoned: As shoots push up in spring, resume even, generous watering to drive the tender new growth; an established patch is tougher but still resents drought.

beginner: Keep mint's soil steadily moist; it loves damp ground, unlike most herbs. Just water the soil and not the leaves to avoid disease.
seasoned: Even, generous moisture is the whole trick with mint: it is the rare kitchen herb that thrives in damp ground and part shade, so treat it the opposite of rosemary or thyme. The one caution is disease, so water the soil, not the leaves.

beginner: The easy way to start mint is from a small plant, a cutting, or a piece dug from a friend's patch, not from seed (seed-grown mint is a gamble and often tastes of nothing in particular). If you do want to try seed anyway, press the tiny seed onto the surface and do not cover it, since it needs light to sprout, and start it indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost. Just root a sprig in a glass of water or plant a division in spring. Because mint spreads fast, plant it in a pot or a buried, bottomless container so it cannot run through your whole garden.
seasoned: Start mint from a division, a rooted cutting, or a nursery transplant, not from seed: named mints such as peppermint are hybrids and, as Clemson notes, mint seed does not come true to type, so seedlings are variable. Divide and reset established clumps in early spring (Utah State, Minnesota), or root stem or stolon cuttings in water or moist mix at almost any time in the growing season (Wisconsin, Maryland). Set plants out around the last spring frost; mint is very hardy, so timing is forgiving. Whatever you plant, put it in a sunken bottomless pot or a lined bed, because mint spreads aggressively by runners. If you do start from seed, surface-sow it because the seed needs light to germinate, keep it around 60 to 70°F, and start indoors 6 to 8 weeks before setting out; expect the variable, off-type seedlings noted above.

beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
seasoned: A moisture-retentive potting mix with plenty of organic matter, since mint likes to stay damp.

seasoned: Blend in compost for water-holding and a little balanced starter fertilizer; do not overdo the nitrogen or the plant flops.

beginner: Mint is very hardy and comes back every spring, but a pot freezes harder than the open ground because the roots are exposed on all sides. In cold areas, sink the pot in the ground for winter, move it against the house or into an unheated shed, or mulch over it. Cut the top back after frost; it will resprout from the roots in spring.
seasoned: Mint is a hardy herbaceous perennial (Utah State rates it hardy to about -20°F), so a container overwinters readily, but the confined root ball is more exposed to freezing than in-ground crowns. In cold zones sink the pot, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or heap mulch over it; the top dies back and regrows from the roots and rhizomes in spring. This is also the moment to lift, divide, and refresh a potbound clump.

beginner: A pot is the best way to grow mint, because it keeps the roots from running all over the garden. Use a container at least 8 inches deep, keep it watered, and snip sprigs often. It is happy on a partly shaded step or windowsill and comes back year after year.
seasoned: Containers are the standard way to grow mint, because they cage the aggressive rhizomes that otherwise colonize a bed; Maryland, UF/IFAS, and Wisconsin all recommend potting mint or using a bottomless sunken container to confine it. Use a pot at least 8 inches deep and keep the mix steadily moist, since pots dry fast and mint has little drought tolerance. Divide and repot every year or two when the clump crowds itself, and cut back after frost for a clean flush in spring.

beginner: Use a pot at least 8 inches deep with solid sides. The main point of the pot is to stop the roots from spreading, so a solid container works better than a cloth bag if you bury it in the garden.

beginner: Do not plant mint where tomatoes, potatoes, or strawberries just grew, because they share a soil disease (verticillium wilt) that also attacks mint.
seasoned: Avoid establishing a new mint patch where tomatoes, potatoes, eggplant, peppers, or strawberries recently grew: those crops host Verticillium, the soilborne wilt that most limits mint's longevity. Following one mint patch immediately with another in the same ground also concentrates mint rust and verticillium, which carry over in soil and rhizomes.

beginner: You plant mint once and it stays for years, so there is no yearly rotation. Just start it in clean ground that did not just grow tomatoes, potatoes, or strawberries, and if a patch gets diseased, start fresh plants in a new spot.
seasoned: Mint is a permanent perennial planting rather than a rotated annual, so rotation here is mostly about where you establish or renew a patch. Because verticillium wilt and mint rust persist in soil and rhizomes, site a new planting in clean ground with no recent history of Verticillium hosts (tomato, potato, eggplant, pepper, strawberry) or of a diseased mint stand, and plan to reset the patch in fresh soil every few years if disease or root pests build up. Utah State and commercial mint guidance both treat multi-year renewal as the core disease defense.

beginner: Mint is not like cilantro; it will not bolt and quit in the heat. It just tries to flower in mid to late summer. The flowers are fine for bees, but the leaves get a bit tougher, so pinch off the flower buds and keep cutting the plant to keep the best leaves coming.
seasoned: Mint does not bolt the way a cool-season annual does; as a perennial it simply sends up flower spikes in mid to late summer. Flowering is not a disaster, the bees love it, but once mint blooms the leaves turn a little tougher and less aromatic and the plant puts energy into seed. To keep tender, flavorful leaves, pinch or shear off the flower buds as they form and harvest regularly, which Clemson notes is exactly how frequent cutting keeps mint from flowering. A hard shear to a few inches after a bloom flush brings a clean new crop of leaves.

beginner: Mint flowering in summer is normal. If you want the best leaves, snip the flower buds off and cut the plant back now and then. If you would rather feed the bees, let some of it bloom; it will not hurt the plant.
seasoned: The flower spikes are a normal part of a perennial mint's year, not a failure. Left to bloom, mint feeds pollinators and can self-sow (seedlings come untrue and may be weak), and the foliage coarsens; sheared before or during bloom, the plant resets into fresh leafy growth. Many growers let part of a patch flower for the pollinators and keep another part cut for the kitchen.

beginner: Do not leave cut mint out on the counter, where it wilts. Chill it, or stand the stems in a glass of water like a little bouquet.
seasoned: Fresh-cut mint wilts within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate promptly; standing the cut stems in a glass of water on the counter holds them a few days, like cut flowers.

beginner: Store fresh mint unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge, where it keeps about a week. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
seasoned: Refrigerate fresh mint unwashed in a loose or perforated bag, or with the stems in a little water under a loose bag, in the crisper; it holds about a week. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown and blackening.

beginner: Freeze chopped mint in an ice-cube tray with a little water for drinks and cooking. You can also dry it, but dry it somewhere dark and dry or the leaves go dark and moldy.
seasoned: Mint freezes well chopped into ice-cube trays with water for drinks and cooking, or blended into sauces; frozen sprigs lose their crispness for garnish but keep their flavor. It also dries, but as UF/IFAS warns, dry it in darkness and low humidity or the leaves turn dark and moldy.

beginner: The best way to store mint is to leave it growing and cut what you need. Picked mint keeps about a week in the fridge. To save extra, freeze it in ice-cube trays or dry it in a dark, dry spot.
seasoned: Because a mint patch keeps producing, the easiest storage is to cut sprigs as needed. Cut mint keeps about a week refrigerated. For longer keeping, freeze it (chopped in cubes or in sauces) or dry it; Maryland notes leaves for drying are best cut just as the flowers begin to open, when the oils peak, and UF/IFAS stresses drying in darkness and low humidity to keep the color and avoid mold.

beginner: Pick mint by how it tastes, since they all grow the same. Spearmint is the mild, sweet everyday mint and the easiest; peppermint is stronger and cooler. There are fun flavored kinds too, like chocolate, apple, orange, and mojito mint. Grow any of them from a cutting or a division, not from seed, because seed-grown mint is unpredictable. And whatever you pick, give it a pot so it does not take over.
seasoned: Choose mint by flavor, since culture is nearly identical across the genus. Spearmint (Mentha spicata) is the mild, sweet all-purpose culinary mint and among the hardiest; peppermint (Mentha x piperita) is the stronger, cooler, menthol type and, as a hybrid, must be grown from cuttings or division rather than seed. Flavored selections such as chocolate, orange or bergamot, apple or woolly (and its variegated pineapple mint form), and mojito mint (Mentha x villosa) all grow the same way. Because named mints are hybrids or selections, Clemson notes mint seed does not come true to type, so propagate every one of these from cuttings, divisions, or transplants. Keep different mints apart if you want to preserve distinct flavors, and contain every one of them.

beginner: Mint has a real gift and a real hazard as a companion. Its strong scent is said to confuse pests like cabbage moths, aphids, and flea beetles, and when it flowers it draws in bees and helpful insects. The hazard is that mint spreads so aggressively it will smother its neighbors, so the golden rule is to grow it in a pot, even when it is near the plants it helps. Keep it away from chamomile and other quiet herbs it would overrun, and away from your other mints so the flavors stay distinct.
seasoned: Mint's companion value is mostly aromatic and pollinator-based: its volatile oils are traditionally credited with deterring cabbage moths, aphids, ants, and flea beetles, and a flowering patch is a strong nectar source for bees and predatory insects. The overriding practical fact, though, is its aggression, so any interplanting benefit is realized by sinking mint in a container next to the crop rather than letting it loose in the bed. The well-grounded cautions are structural: keep mint out of the open ground near less vigorous herbs (chamomile, and slower perennials) that it will overrun, and keep different mints separated to preserve their distinct flavors and to slow shared rust.

beginner: Mint's strong smell is traditionally said to put off the cabbage moths and flea beetles that attack cabbage-family plants. Grow the mint in a sunken pot nearby so it helps without taking over.
seasoned: A traditional aromatic pairing: mint's essential oils are long credited with masking or deterring cabbage moths and flea beetles on brassicas. Sound by mechanism and tradition rather than a measured trial, and only safe if the mint is contained.

beginner: Mint is often planted near tomatoes and peppers to help repel aphids and other pests with its scent, and its flowers bring in helpful insects. Keep it in a pot so its roots do not invade.
seasoned: A traditional aromatic and beneficial-insect pairing; the caution is that tomatoes, peppers, and mint share Verticillium, so a contained mint next to them must not later be planted into that soil.

beginner: If you let some mint bloom, the flowers feed bees, hoverflies, and other good bugs that also eat garden pests. Let one contained clump flower for them.
seasoned: A genuine insectary function: a flowering mint patch recruits bees and aphid-eating hoverflies and parasitoids, the same mechanism extension services cite for flowering herbs. Realized best by letting one contained clump bloom while others stay cut.

beginner: Do not plant mint loose in a bed next to gentler herbs like chamomile or marjoram, because mint will run over them. And keep different mints apart, or their flavors blur together and they trade diseases.
seasoned: The signature caution: mint's rhizomes overrun less vigorous neighbors, so keep it out of open ground beside chamomile, marjoram, and slower perennials. Separate different mints to preserve distinct flavors and to slow the rust that congestion spreads. Extension-supported (contain mint) rather than folklore.

beginner: Your new mint plant starting to root in and push new leaves.
seasoned: A newly set division, cutting, or transplant putting out fresh roots and the first new shoots. Early growth is upright before the plant begins to run.

beginner: Water regularly so it does not dry out, and get it into a pot or a buried barrier now, before it runs.
seasoned: Keep the soil evenly moist while roots take hold, and make sure the plant is in its container or barrier before it starts to spread.

beginner: Is it settling in?
seasoned: Is the new mint rooting in?

beginner: Lots of new leafy stems and runners spreading out.
seasoned: Fast leafy growth as the plant sends out runners (stolons and rhizomes) and fills its space; this is when containment earns its keep.

beginner: Keep it moist, pinch the tips to make it bushy, and watch that it does not creep out of its pot.
seasoned: Keep it watered and, in part shade or hot regions, watch for scorch; pinch tips to encourage bushy growth and check that runners are not escaping the container.

beginner: Spreading out?
seasoned: Filling in and running?

beginner: Full, leafy plants you can keep cutting from.

beginner: Mint is one of the easiest herbs to grow, and it comes back every year on its own. Unlike most herbs, it loves moist soil and even grows in part shade, so it is happy in a cool, damp spot. The one thing to know about mint is that it spreads like crazy, running underground and popping up everywhere, so almost everyone grows it in a pot or a buried, bottomless container to keep it from taking over the garden. Grow it from a small plant or a cutting, not from seed, keep it watered, and snip sprigs whenever you want; the more you cut it, the better it grows. Spearmint is the mild, sweet everyday mint and peppermint is the stronger, cooler one, and there are fun flavors like chocolate and apple mint too.
seasoned: Mint (Mentha) is a hardy herbaceous perennial grown for its aromatic leaves, and it breaks nearly every rule the Mediterranean kitchen herbs follow. Where rosemary and thyme want lean, dry, sun-baked ground, mint wants rich, moist to damp soil and happily takes part shade, thriving in low, cool spots that defeat other herbs. It is very cold hardy (Utah State rates it to about -20°F, roughly USDA zones 3 to 9 and beyond), planted once from a division, cutting, or transplant and returning every spring from its roots. Its defining trait is aggression: mint spreads fast by underground rhizomes and above-ground stolons, and every extension source says the same thing, contain it in a sunken bottomless pot or a lined bed or it will take over. Spearmint (Mentha spicata) is the mild, sweet all-purpose culinary type; peppermint (Mentha x piperita) is the stronger, cooler, menthol one; and named mints, being hybrids and selections, come untrue from seed, so they are grown from cuttings and divisions. Harvest is cut-and-come-again all season, and frequent shearing keeps the leaves tender and heads off flowering.

beginner: Mint is ready to pick once the plants are a few inches tall and leafy, which happens fast. Snip sprigs whenever you need them, or cut the whole plant back by a third and it grows again. Creeping thyme (Thymus serpyllum, mother-of-thyme) is a flat, hardy groundcover used between pavers and as a lawn substitute, and is ornamental more than culinary. beginner: Thyme does best in poor, dry soil, so do not add fertilizer or rich compost. Give it your sunniest spot, and if your soil is heavy clay, plant on a little mound or raised bed so water drains away.
seasoned: Plant thyme lean and dry, not rich. Skip the compost-and-fertilizer routine, set it in the sunniest, sharpest-draining spot, and on clay build a mound or raised bed. Rich, wet soil weakens flavor and rots the roots.

beginner: Leave about 8 to 12 inches between plants. That space lets air move around each one, which helps prevent the leaf fungus thyme can get when it stays damp.
seasoned: Space plants 8 to 12 inches apart for airflow. Good air movement between plants is one of the simplest ways to head off the foliar fungus thyme can get in damp or humid conditions.

beginner: The first year is about growing roots. Water fairly often until it takes hold, then water less. Only pick a little this year. Thyme fills out by about year two.
seasoned: Year one is about roots, not harvest. Water until the plant is settled, then taper toward infrequent. Harvest only lightly this season; thyme reaches full size by about the second year.

beginner: Try not to feed it. Thyme needs very little, and too much fertilizer gives soft leaves with less flavor. The same is true for water, where more is not better.
seasoned: Resist the urge to feed. Thyme has low fertility needs, and over-fertilizing produces soft growth with weaker flavor. The same goes for water: more is not better.

beginner: Once it is established, snip thyme often. Regular cutting keeps it bushy and slows it turning woody, and you can pick leaves anytime to cook with.
seasoned: Harvest little and often once the plant is established. Snipping sprigs regularly keeps thyme bushy and productive and slows it going woody; you can take leaves anytime for cooking.

beginner: If you want to tidy the plant, do it in early spring once new growth shows and frost is over. Cut only into the leafy parts, not the hard woody stems.
seasoned: Do any shaping cut in early spring once growth resumes and frost has passed. Cut into leafy growth, not the bare woody stems, which resprout poorly.

beginner: For the best flavor, cut thyme to dry just before or as it starts to flower, when the oils are strongest. Cut in the morning after the dew dries.
seasoned: For the strongest flavor, cut thyme for drying just before or as the first flowers open, when the leaf oils peak. Harvest in the morning once the dew has dried.

beginner: You can leave some flowers for the bees, which love thyme blooms. To dry thyme, hang small bunches somewhere warm and airy, then store the leaves in a sealed jar.
seasoned: Let some flowers open for the bees if you like; thyme blooms are a strong pollinator draw. To dry thyme, hang small bundles in a warm, airy place, then store the stripped leaves sealed.

beginner: After it flowers, trim off the old flower stems and neaten the plant, cutting only into the leafy parts, never the hard wood. Snipping often plus this trim keeps thyme bushy, but it still gets woody, so replace or divide it every few years.
seasoned: Shear off the spent flower stems after bloom and lightly reduce the plant, cutting into leafy growth and never into bare wood. Frequent harvest plus this shear keeps thyme compact, but it still goes woody with age, so divide or replace it every few years.

beginner: Do the main trim after it flowers, not in late fall. A hard trim just before winter can leave the plant weak, so wait until after bloom or early spring for heavy trimming.
seasoned: Time the main shaping after flowering rather than in fall. A late-fall hard cut can leave the plant vulnerable going into winter, so save heavy shaping for after bloom or early spring.

beginner: In winter, do almost nothing. Stop watering and feeding, and save the trim for spring. Thyme sitting in wet winter soil rots, so do not keep watering it.
seasoned: Over winter, do almost nothing: stop watering and feeding, and leave hard shaping for spring. A plant in wet winter soil rots, so the worst thing you can do is keep it watered.

beginner: Shelter the less hardy plants. English and creeping thyme are the toughest and can stay outside in cold areas if drainage is good and the spot is sheltered; grow tender types in pots you can bring under cover.
seasoned: Protect the less hardy plants. English and creeping thymes are the hardiest and overwinter outdoors through the cold zones with sharp drainage and a sheltered spot; grow tender types or cold-edge plants in pots you can move under cover.

beginner: A grown thyme plant gives you plenty of sprigs all season, enough to cook with fresh and to dry, especially once it is a couple of years old.
seasoned: A mature plant yields a steady supply of sprigs through the growing season, easily enough to keep a kitchen stocked with fresh thyme plus bundles to dry; productivity is best once the plant reaches full size at about the second year.

beginner: Do not expect much the first year. Picking lightly while the plant settles in gives you bigger harvests from year two.
seasoned: Expect only light harvests the first year; harvesting sparingly while the plant establishes pays off in fuller production from the second season on.

beginner: Leaves turning yellow or the plant dying back
seasoned: Yellowing leaves or dieback

beginner: For thyme, yellow leaves and dieback usually mean too much water, not too little. Overwatering and soggy soil are the biggest killer. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.
seasoned: With thyme, yellowing and dieback almost always mean too wet, not too dry. Overwatering and poor drainage are the number one killer, leading to root and crown rot. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.

beginner: Water much less and improve drainage. Use poor, well-draining soil in full sun, keep it on the dry side, and on heavy or humid ground plant on a mound. Never let it sit in soggy ground.
seasoned: Cut back on watering hard and fix drainage. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, keep it on the dry side, and on clay or in humid areas use a mound or raised bed. Never let thyme sit in wet ground.

beginner: Woody and bare in the middle
seasoned: Leggy, woody, split-open center

beginner: When thyme gets woody and bare in the middle, it is mostly just getting old. All thyme goes woody eventually; snipping often and trimming after bloom slows it down, but plants are best replaced or divided every few years.
seasoned: A thyme plant that has gone woody and bare or split open in the center is simply aging. Thyme goes woody with time even with good care; frequent harvest and a post-bloom shear slow it, but plants are best divided or replaced every few years.

beginner: Snip thyme often and trim it after it flowers, cutting only into the leafy parts. Every few years, split a healthy older plant or start a new one from a cutting so you always have a fresh, bushy plant.
seasoned: Harvest regularly and shear after bloom to keep growth soft, cutting into leafy growth only, never into bare wood. Divide a healthy older clump or start a fresh plant from a cutting every few years to keep a vigorous supply.

beginner: Not much flavor or soft, floppy growth
seasoned: Weak flavor or soft, floppy growth

beginner: Thyme with little flavor and soft, floppy leaves usually has too much fertilizer or water, or too little sun. Thyme tastes strongest when it is grown lean, dry, and sunny.
seasoned: Bland thyme with soft, lush growth usually means too much feed, too much water, or too little sun. The concentrated oils that give thyme its flavor build up in lean, dry, sunny conditions and thin out in rich, wet, shady ones.

beginner: Stop feeding it, water less, and make sure it gets full sun. Poor, dry, sunny conditions give the best flavor, and picking just before it flowers captures the strongest taste.
seasoned: Stop fertilizing, water less, and give the plant full sun. Lean, dry, sunny conditions concentrate the oils and give the strongest flavor; harvesting just before bloom captures the peak.

beginner: In the northern part of the country, thyme is a tough, low, spreading plant. In zones 5, 6, and 7 the hardy English and creeping types come back year after year in the ground: they leaf out in spring, you harvest them all season, they flower in summer, and you trim them after they bloom. Zone 4 works only with a very hardy type and great drainage, and zone 3 is too cold, so grow thyme there for one season or in a pot you bring inside. The biggest thing to get right is drainage: thyme hates sitting in cold, wet soil and will rot, so give it a high, gritty, fast-draining spot.
seasoned: Across the northern tier, thyme is a hardy, low, spreading perennial in most zones. English (common) and creeping thymes are the toughest: in zones 5, 6, and 7 they overwinter in the ground as low woody sub-shrubs, leaf out in spring, are harvested through the season, flower in summer, and get a tidy-up shear after bloom. Zone 4 is the cold edge, workable in the ground only with a hardy type (German Winter, creeping thyme) and excellent drainage, and zone 3 is too cold to overwinter reliably, so grow thyme there as an annual or a bring-in container plant. Wherever you grow it, the real winter risk is wet feet, not cold alone: thyme rots in soggy, frozen-then-thawing soil, so plant it high and lean with sharp drainage.

beginner: Thyme is a low, spreading herb with tiny fragrant leaves you cook with. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor dry soil, and very little water, and it actually does worse if you pamper it. It grows only about 6 to 12 inches tall and spreads into a low mat. Snip it often and give it a light trim after it flowers to keep it bushy; it gets woody as it ages, so replace or divide it every few years. It is tough and rarely bothered by pests, and bees love its little flowers.
seasoned: Thyme is a low, woody Mediterranean perennial in the mint family, grown for its tiny aromatic leaves that flavor soups, stews, sauces, meats, and fish. It forms a low, spreading, mat-like mound only about 6 to 12 inches tall and thrives on neglect in full sun and lean, sharply drained soil; wet, rich soil rots it and dulls its flavor. Frequent harvesting and a light shear after its summer bloom keep it bushy, though it goes woody with age and is best divided or replaced every few years. It is hardy and pest-resistant, and its small pink, lavender, or white flowers are a strong bee draw.

beginner: You can snip thyme anytime once it is established: cut the top few inches of leafy stems, taking no more than about a third at once. The flavor is strongest just before and as it flowers, so that is the best time to cut thyme to dry. Cut in the morning after the dew dries. Snipping it often also keeps it from getting woody.
seasoned: Harvest thyme sprigs anytime once the plant is established: snip the top few inches of leafy growth, taking no more than about a third of the plant at once. Flavor is most concentrated just before and as the plant flowers, so cut for drying then, on a dry morning after the dew has lifted. Regular harvesting also keeps the plant from going woody.

beginner: Thyme is tough and comes back year after year in most of the country (about zones 5 to 9, and zone 4 for the hardiest types like creeping and German Winter thyme if drainage is good). In the very coldest areas (zone 3), grow it for one season or in a pot you bring inside. Just as important as cold: thyme hates wet feet and will rot in soggy soil, and it also struggles in hot, humid places.
seasoned: Thyme is a hardy perennial. Common, English, French, German Winter, and lemon thymes are reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9, and creeping thyme is hardier still, to about zone 4. With sharp drainage and a sheltered spot, hardy types push into zone 4, while zone 3 usually calls for growing thyme as an annual or a bring-in container plant. Good drainage matters as much as cold: thyme rots in wet winter soil before cold alone kills it, and it also struggles in hot, humid climates.

beginner: Once the summer flowers fade, trim off the old flower stems and neaten the plant, cutting only into the leafy parts and not into the hard woody stems, which do not grow back well. Snipping thyme often plus this trim keeps it bushy, but it still gets woody with age, so replace or divide it every few years.
seasoned: After the summer flowers fade, shear off the spent flower stems and lightly reduce the plant, cutting into leafy growth only and never into the bare woody base, which resprouts poorly. Frequent harvesting through the season plus this post-bloom shear keeps thyme compact; even so, plants go woody with age and are best divided or replaced every few years.

beginner: Dill likes loose, well-drained soil and is not fussy about richness; it actually does fine in lean ground. Mix in a little compost so the soil holds some moisture but still drains freely. Heavy, soggy, or compacted soil is the main thing to avoid, since it rots the slow-sprouting seed and the deep little taproot. Steady moisture keeps the feathery leaves tender.
seasoned: Dill grows in most soils but does best in a loose, well-drained loam or sandy loam, and it tolerates poorer, leaner ground than most herbs. Utah State University describes it as a plant for well-drained, low-fertility to moderately fertile soil, so heavy feeding and very rich beds are unnecessary and can leave it lank. Work a little compost into the top few inches before sowing to hold even moisture, but do not overdo richness. It dislikes damp, poorly drained ground, which invites damping-off of the slow-germinating seed and leaf disease. Dill forms a slender taproot and resents transplanting, so it is best direct-sown into loosened soil.

beginner: Dill grows best in slightly acidic soil, about 5.5 to 6.5. Most garden soil is fine, and a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 5.5 to 6.5, slightly acidic; Utah State University gives this as dill's ideal range. It is forgiving and still does fine up to neutral, roughly 5.5 to 7.0. Dill is not a pH-sensitive plant, so in most gardens no adjustment is needed beyond a soil-test baseline.

beginner: Dill does not need much fertilizer and even grows well in poor soil. Mix a little compost into the bed before planting, and that is usually all it needs. If the soil is poor, you can give one light feeding while the plants are young. Too much fertilizer makes dill floppy and weakens the flavor, so go easy.
seasoned: Dill is a light feeder and one of the few herbs that prefers lean soil; Utah State University notes that no additional nutrients are needed if the soil is amended at planting. Work a little compost in before sowing and, in poor ground, give one light feeding once the plants are growing. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which makes dill lank and floppy and can dull the aromatic oils that give the leaves and seed their flavor. A plant grown on for seed or pickling heads needs no extra feeding once it bolts.

beginner: Your dill can take one light feeding now if the soil is poor.
seasoned: If your dill is in poor soil, you can give it one light feeding now.

beginner: Dill needs very little feeding. Mix compost into the soil at planting, and only feed lightly if the soil is poor.
seasoned: Dill is a light feeder that prefers lean soil; compost worked in at planting usually covers it, with at most one light, balanced feeding in poor ground. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which makes the plant floppy and weakens the aromatic oils.

beginner: Usually just compost at planting. If you feed, use a light all-purpose fertilizer once, at the label rate.
seasoned: Compost worked in at planting is usually enough; in poor soil, one light side-dress of a balanced fertilizer at the label rate while the plants are young.

beginner: Plump green caterpillars banded with black and yellow-orange dots, chewing the feathery leaves. They can strip a young plant, but on an established dill they usually do only light damage.
seasoned: Larvae of the black swallowtail (Papilio polyxenes), banded green, black, and yellow, feed on the foliage. On an established dill the defoliation is usually light and cosmetic; a heavy load can strip a seedling.

beginner: These are the caterpillars of the black swallowtail butterfly, which lays eggs on dill and other carrot-family plants. They are also a welcome garden visitor, since they turn into a beautiful butterfly.
seasoned: Dill is a larval host plant for the black swallowtail butterfly. The caterpillars are a feature as much as a pest, so dill is often planted deliberately to support them.

beginner: On a big plant, just leave them; the damage is minor and you get butterflies. If they threaten a small planting, pick them off by hand and move them to a spare dill plant.
seasoned: On established plants, tolerate them, the feeding is minor and the butterflies are a benefit; on small plantings, handpick and relocate to a sacrificial dill. Bt is effective if control is truly needed, but is rarely warranted on a host plant grown partly for the butterflies.

beginner: Grow a little extra dill so there is enough to share with the caterpillars, and simply relocate them rather than spraying.
seasoned: Manage by tolerance and a little surplus planting rather than control: grow enough dill to share, relocate larvae from plants you want to protect, and reserve sprays for genuine seedling threats.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on new growth and the undersides of the feathery leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
seasoned: Colonies of aphids gather on growing tips and leaf undersides; honeydew and the lodged insects contaminate a crop used fresh, and aphids can vector viruses. Dill's lacy foliage hides them, so scout closely.

beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. They can spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Several aphid species feed on dill; they reproduce rapidly and favor the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces. Dill itself, allowed to flower, is a strong insectary that recruits aphid predators.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Dill's own flowers also draw in ladybugs and lacewings that eat aphids.
seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a strong water jet or spray insecticidal soap, covering leaf undersides; repeat every few days and conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps, which dill's own umbel flowers attract.

beginner: Welcome helpful insects like ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check new growth often.
seasoned: Scout growing tips early, avoid overfeeding nitrogen, and conserve natural enemies; letting some dill flower draws in the aphid predators it is famous for hosting.

beginner: A white, powdery coating on the leaves and flower stalks, usually later in the crop and in warm, dry-day weather. Heavily coated leaves yellow and are unpleasant to eat.
seasoned: A white, talc-like fungal growth on the foliage and stems, the most commonly noted fungal disease of dill, that builds in warm days with cool humid nights, in crowded stands, and where plants are overwatered; coated leaves lose quality.

beginner: A fungal disease that coats the leaves in white powder, favored by warm days, cool nights, crowding, and overwatering.
seasoned: Powdery mildew (Erysiphe heraclei on Apiaceae), favored by warm days, cool humid nights, dense stands with poor airflow, and excess moisture. Utah State University notes dill mildews when overwatered.

beginner: Remove the worst leaves, open up the planting for airflow, and avoid crowding and overhead watering. Most home crops are picked before it does much harm.
seasoned: Improve airflow with wider spacing, remove affected leaves, avoid excess nitrogen and overhead watering; the leaf crop is usually cut before mildew matters, but a tall plant held for seed is more exposed.

beginner: Space plants for airflow, avoid crowding and overfeeding, and water at the base rather than over the leaves.
seasoned: Widen spacing for airflow, avoid heavy nitrogen and overwatering, and harvest the leaf crop promptly; remove infected foliage on plants held for seed.

beginner: Small tan to brown spots, sometimes with a yellow halo, that spread on the leaves and can merge until the leaflets wilt and die back, worst in wet weather.
seasoned: Small tan-brown leaf lesions, sometimes yellow-haloed, that expand and coalesce until leaflets blight and die; favored by wet, splashy conditions and prolonged leaf wetness. Cercospora leaf blight (Cercosporidium punctum) and Alternaria leaf spot are the documented agents on dill.

beginner: Fungal leaf diseases that spread on wet leaves and splashing water and can arrive on infected seed. Spotted, blighted leaves are not good to eat.
seasoned: Foliar fungi, chiefly Cercosporidium punctum (Cercospora blight) and Alternaria spp., spread by splash, wind, and infected seed and favored by warm, wet weather and overhead irrigation.

beginner: Remove and destroy spotted leaves, avoid wetting the foliage, improve airflow, and start with clean seed. There is no spray cure in the home garden, so prevention matters most.
seasoned: Use clean, disease-free seed, avoid overhead irrigation, space for airflow, rotate away from the carrot family, and remove infected debris; there is no effective home-garden cure once it is established.

beginner: Use clean seed, water at the soil line rather than over the leaves, space plants for airflow, rotate the bed, and clear infected debris.
seasoned: Plant clean seed, switch to drip or soil-line watering, widen spacing, rotate, and remove crop debris that carries the fungi over.

beginner: Seeds that never come up, or seedlings that flop over at the soil line with a pinched, rotted stem and then die. It strikes in cold, wet soil.
seasoned: Poor stands from seed and pre- or post-emergence collapse of seedlings with water-soaked, pinched stems at the soil line, worst in cold, wet, poorly drained soil where dill's slow germination leaves seed sitting in the danger zone.

beginner: Soil fungi attack the seeds and tiny seedlings, especially when the soil is cold and soggy and the slow-sprouting dill seed sits a long time before emerging.
seasoned: Soilborne Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Fusarium fungi attack germinating seed and seedlings; cold, saturated soil that slows dill's already slow germination favors them.

beginner: There is no cure for an affected seedling, so focus on prevention: pull and discard collapsed seedlings.
seasoned: No rescue once seedlings collapse; manage by prevention and remove affected plants.

beginner: Do not sow into cold, soggy soil, plant shallowly in well-drained ground, do not overwater, and use fresh seed so it comes up faster.
seasoned: Sow shallowly into well-drained soil under conditions that favor reasonably quick emergence, avoid overwatering, and use fresh, viable seed.

beginner: Water regularly so the soil stays evenly moist, roughly 1 inch a week, especially while the plants are young.
seasoned: About 1 inch of water per week, kept reasonably even; dill is fairly drought-tolerant once established but bolts faster and grows lank under heat and dry stress.

beginner: Aim for about 1 inch of water a week, a bit more when it is warm and dry.
seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week, more in warm, dry spells; once established dill takes some drought, but steady moisture keeps the leaves tender and slows the bolt.

beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent leaf diseases.
seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the lacy foliage dry checks powdery mildew and leaf spot on a crop used fresh.

beginner: Lower leaves yellow, seedlings rot at the base, and plants get mildewed or mushy in soggy soil.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, damping-off in seedlings, and powdery mildew or root rot in constantly wet, poorly drained ground.

beginner: Wilting leaves and a plant that bolts (flowers) sooner than you want.
seasoned: Wilting, slowed growth, and faster bolting; drought stress hurries the plant toward its flower stalk and seed.

beginner: Dill is slow to sprout, so keep the soil evenly damp until the seedlings come up.
seasoned: Dill germinates slowly, so keep the seedbed evenly moist through emergence, especially while the seedlings are young.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered as they get going.
seasoned: Grow the young plants on with steady, even moisture through the first weeks of leaf growth.

beginner: Established dill takes some drought, but even water, about an inch a week, keeps the leaves tender and slows bolting. Water at the base to keep the leaves dry.
seasoned: Dill is fairly drought-tolerant once established, but it bolts faster and grows lank under heat and dry stress, so keep a reasonably even inch a week. Even moisture keeps the leaves tender and slows the bolt; water at the soil line to keep the lacy foliage dry against powdery mildew and leaf spot.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while you cut the leaves. A hot, dry spell makes dill bolt sooner and turn coarse.
seasoned: Keep reasonably even moisture through the leaf-cutting weeks; a hot, dry check pushes the plant to flower and set seed sooner and coarsens the foliage.

beginner: As dill flowers and makes seed heads, ease off the water. If you want dill seed, a dry finish helps the heads ripen on the plant.
seasoned: As dill sends up its flower heads and sets seed, the leaf crop winds down; ease off watering, and for dill seed a drier finish helps the heads ripen and dry on the plant.

beginner: Keep the water fairly steady so the leaves stay tender and the plant does not bolt as early.
seasoned: Even moisture keeps dill growing tender and slows the bolt; hot, dry spells push it to flower and set seed sooner and coarsen the foliage.

beginner: Plant dill straight in the garden from seed, because it has a deep little root and does not like being moved. Sow the seeds about a quarter inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, since young plants handle light frost. The seeds are slow, often taking two to three weeks, so keep the soil moist. Thin the plants to about 8 to 12 inches apart, and sow again every couple of weeks for a steady supply. In hot areas plant in fall through spring instead of summer, because heat makes it bolt; a summer crop is really for the seed and pickling heads.
seasoned: Dill is almost always direct-sown, since it forms a slender taproot and resents transplanting. Sow seed about 0.25 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; young dill tolerates light frost, so Wisconsin Horticulture suggests sowing a week or two before the last hard frost, and it germinates slowly, often 10 to 21 days. Sow a little thicker than the final stand and thin to 8 to 12 inches for full plants, or 4 to 6 inches for cut leaf. Succession-sow every 2 to 3 weeks for a steady leaf supply. In hot regions, shift sowing to fall through spring, since summer heat and long days bolt the crop to seed; midsummer plantings are grown for seed and pickling heads rather than leaves.

beginner: Other carrot-family plants like carrots, parsley, cilantro, fennel, and celery, because they share the same pests and diseases.
seasoned: Other Apiaceae: carrot, parsley, cilantro, fennel, celery, parsnip, and dill itself. They share carrot-family pests and diseases (leaf blights, the carrot motley dwarf complex, and soilborne rots), so following one with another concentrates that pressure.

beginner: Try not to grow dill or other carrot-family plants (carrots, parsley, cilantro, fennel, celery) in the same spot more than about once every 3 years, since they share pests and diseases. Plant dill after peas, beans, cabbage, onions, or tomatoes instead. Dill self-sows a lot, so pull up stray seedlings that pop up where you do not want them.
seasoned: Rotate dill and its carrot-family relatives so they do not return to the same ground for about 3 years. The Apiaceae share foliar blights, the carrot motley dwarf complex, and soilborne rots, which build up where the family repeats. Follow dill with legumes, brassicas, alliums, or nightshades. Because dill self-sows heavily from bolted plants, volunteers can blur a rotation, so pull seedlings that come up out of place if you are managing the family carefully.

beginner: Dill is one of the great companion herbs, mostly because of what it does when it flowers: the yellow blooms pull in hoverflies, ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps that hunt aphids and caterpillars on nearby crops. It is a traditional companion for brassicas (cabbage, broccoli, kale), where folklore credits it with deterring cabbageworms, plausible via the beneficials it draws but not measured as a direct effect; it also interplants with cucumbers, onions, lettuce, and corn. The well-grounded cautions are its own carrot-family relatives: fennel and carrots, which can cross-pollinate dill where they flower together, and which share Apiaceae pests on rotation grounds.

Bolted plants are left for seed and pickling heads, and dill self-sows readily in this climate.

beginner: Dill gives you two things from one plant: the soft feathery leaves are dill weed, and the flower heads and seeds are what you use for pickling and as a spice. Like cilantro, and unlike warm-season herbs such as basil, dill is a cool-leaning plant. Young plants handle a light frost, but once summer heat and long days arrive it bolts, sending up a tall flower stalk that can reach 3 to 5 feet, and leaf growth slows. So the trick is to grow it for leaves in the cooler parts of the year, spring and again in late summer for fall, and to let the summer plants flower for seed heads. Sow a little every 2 to 3 weeks, since each plant bolts after a while, and plant the seeds right in the garden because dill does not like being moved. It is fast, easy, and reseeds itself, so once you grow it you often get volunteers the next year. And when it bolts, you get dill heads for pickling and dried dill seed.
seasoned: Dill (Anethum graveolens) is an annual herb in the carrot family (Apiaceae) grown for two products from one plant: the feathery leaves are the herb dill weed, and the flower heads and dried seed are used for pickling and as the spice dill seed. Like cilantro, and unlike warm-season herbs such as basil, dill is a cool-leaning crop that bolts once summer heat and long days arrive, sending up a tall flower stalk (the plant reaches 3 to 5 feet in flower) above roughly 75 to 80°F. That shapes how it is grown: the leaf crop favors the cool shoulders of the year, spring and especially a late-summer-into-fall sowing, while the heat of summer is when growers let it run to seed and pickling heads rather than leaves. Because the bolt is fast and inevitable in warmth, dill is a succession crop, sown in small batches every 2 to 3 weeks so fresh, pre-bolt plants keep coming. It is direct-sown (a slender taproot resents transplanting), young plants tolerate light frost, and it self-sows so readily that a patch often returns on its own. It is easy and largely trouble-free, with the black swallowtail caterpillar a welcome visitor as much as a pest. The grower's real skill is timing the leaf crop into the cool seasons and treating the summer bolt as the start of the seed-and-pickling harvest rather than a failure.

beginner: Start picking dill when the plants are 8 to 10 inches tall and bushy, a few weeks after sowing and before you see a tall flower stalk. Snip the feathery leaves from the outside, and pick in the cool morning for the best flavor. Pick often, because once it bolts the plant puts its energy into flowers and seed. For pickling, cut the flower heads as the blooms open. For dried dill seed, let the heads turn tan, cut and dry them, then shake out the seeds to store.
seasoned: Begin cutting dill leaves once plants are 8 to 10 inches tall and bushy, roughly 6 to 8 weeks from sowing, well before the central seedstalk rises. Snip whole feathery fronds from the outside, or shear the upper plant, taking no more than a third at a time and picking in the cool morning for the best flavor; pick often, since the leaf window closes once it bolts. For green pickling heads, cut the umbels just as the flowers open and the immature seed forms. For dried dill seed, let the plant flower and set seed and harvest the heads as they turn from green to tan but before they shatter, dry them in a paper bag, then thresh and store the seed airtight.

beginner: Rosemary likes poor, dry, gritty soil and full sun. Rich, damp soil and heavy clay make it weak and rot-prone, so the goal is fast drainage, not fertility. If your soil is heavy, plant rosemary on a mound or raised bed and mix in coarse sand or grit so water drains straight through.
seasoned: Lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun. Rosemary is a Mediterranean subshrub that grows best in poor to average, dry ground; it performs poorly in heavy, flat, poorly drained clay. Overwatering and wet soil are the biggest causes of decline and death, so drainage matters more than fertility. On clay, plant on a raised bed or mound and add coarse material rather than piling on rich compost.

beginner: Rosemary likes soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 7.0, and is not fussy within a fairly wide range. Do not worry too much about the exact number; good drainage matters much more to rosemary than pH does.
seasoned: Rosemary does best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerates a wider band from about 5.5 to 8.0. Extension herb guidance clusters around pH 6 to 7.5, and rosemary is adaptable as long as the soil drains sharply; getting drainage right matters far more than fine-tuning pH.

beginner: The trick with rosemary is to not overwater it and to give it your sunniest, best-draining spot. Water deeply but only once in a while, and skip the fertilizer. Keep it shaped by pinching and snipping the tips, but do not cut way back into the old woody stems, because those usually will not grow back. In cold-winter areas, grow it in a pot so you can bring it inside before hard frost.
seasoned: Treat rosemary lean and dry: full sun, gritty fast-draining soil, deep but infrequent water, and almost no feeding. Overwatering and soggy soil, not cold, are the top killers, though in zone 6 and colder you must also protect it from hard freezes or bring it indoors. Shape it with light tip pinching and harvest, and never cut back hard into the bare, leafless wood, which does not reliably resprout.

seasoned: Rosemary is almost always started from a nursery transplant or from stem cuttings, not from seed. Take tip cuttings a few inches long, root them with warmth (bottom heat around 70 to 75°F), and they root in a couple of weeks. To grow from seed instead, surface-sow at about 70°F since the seed needs light, starting indoors roughly 10 weeks before the last frost; germination is slow and uneven and the seedlings size up gradually, which is why most growers still choose cuttings.

seasoned: Leave some flowers for the bees. Rosemary blooms are a strong pollinator draw and, on English-clean unsprayed plants, both flowers and leaves are edible.

beginner: Rosemary is an evergreen shrubby herb with fragrant, needle-like leaves and small blue flowers. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it loves sun and hates wet feet. You grow it mostly for the leaves, which you can snip year round in mild climates. It is less cold hardy than sage or thyme: it lives outdoors year after year only in warmer areas (about zone 7 or 8 and up), and in cold-winter places most people grow it in a pot and bring it inside for the winter. Give it full sun, fast-draining soil, and go easy on the water, since too much water is the fastest way to kill it.
seasoned: Rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus, formerly Rosmarinus officinalis) is a woody evergreen Mediterranean subshrub in the mint family, grown mainly for its aromatic, needle-like culinary leaves and secondarily for its small blue flowers. It comes in upright forms that reach several feet and low trailing forms that spill over walls. Unlike hardier culinary perennials such as sage and thyme, rosemary is relatively cold tender: it is reliably perennial only in mild zones (roughly zone 7 or 8 and warmer, with the hardy cultivar Arp pushing into zone 6), and in colder regions it is grown as an annual or overwintered indoors in a pot. It wants full sun, lean sharply drained soil, and little water; overwatering and wet, poorly drained soil, not cold alone, are its most common killers.

beginner: You grow rosemary for the leaves, and in mild areas you can snip sprigs almost any time of year. For the best flavor, cut sprigs from the soft green growth in the morning, especially just before it flowers. Snip stems just above a leafy joint so the plant grows back bushy, and take no more than about a fifth of the plant at once. To dry it, cut sprigs before or during flowering, hang small bunches somewhere warm and airy, and strip the leaves off once they are dry.
seasoned: Rosemary is grown for its leaves, and in mild climates you can snip fresh sprigs almost year round. For the strongest flavor and oil, harvest sprigs from the soft green growth in the morning, just before or as the plant begins to flower. Cut individual stems above a leafy node to encourage bushy regrowth, and do not remove more than about 20 percent of the plant at any one time. For drying, cut sprigs before or at flowering, then hang them in small bundles in a warm, airy place and strip the leaves once dry.

beginner: Rosemary is less cold hardy than most herbs. It lives outdoors year after year mainly in warmer areas (about zones 8 to 10), and a few tough types like Hill Hardy and Arp can handle zone 7 or even zone 6 with shelter and good drainage. In colder places, grow rosemary in a pot and bring it inside for the winter, since it will not survive a hard freeze in the ground the way sage or thyme can.
seasoned: Rosemary is relatively cold tender for a woody herb. The species and most cultivars are reliably perennial only in about zones 8 to 10, and hardy selections such as Hill Hardy push into zone 7 while Arp is the hardiest, surviving into zone 6 with good drainage and a sheltered spot. Below that, in roughly zone 6 and colder, rosemary is grown as an annual or, better, kept in a container and moved to a bright, cool, protected place for winter. beginner: Oregano does best in poor, dry soil, so do not add fertilizer or rich compost. Give it your sunniest spot, and if your soil is heavy clay, plant on a little mound or raised bed so water drains away.
seasoned: Plant oregano lean and dry, not rich. Skip the compost-and-fertilizer routine, set it in the sunniest, best-draining spot, and on clay build a mound or raised bed. Rich, wet soil weakens flavor and rots the roots.

beginner: Oregano spreads fast, so decide up front how to contain it: a pot, or edging sunk into the soil, keeps its creeping roots from taking over the bed.
seasoned: Contain the spread from the start. Oregano creeps by rooting stems and self-sows, so plant it in a pot, a bottomless bucket sunk in the bed, or behind deep edging if you do not want it colonizing the garden.

beginner: The first year is about getting established. Water fairly often until it takes hold, then water less. Pinch the tips when it is about 6 inches tall to make it bushy, and only pick a little this year.
seasoned: Year one is about establishing, not harvesting hard. Water until the plant is settled, then taper off, pinch the tips at about 6 inches to build a bushy plant, and harvest only lightly this season.

beginner: Try not to feed it. Oregano needs very little, and too much fertilizer gives soft leaves with less flavor. The same is true for water, where more is not better.
seasoned: Resist the urge to feed. Oregano has low fertility needs, and over-fertilizing produces soft growth with weaker flavor. The same goes for water: more is not better and invites rot.

beginner: Once it is established, snip oregano often. Regular cutting keeps it bushy and slows it turning woody, and you can pick leaves anytime to cook with.
seasoned: Harvest little and often once the plant is established. Snipping sprigs regularly keeps oregano bushy and productive and slows it going woody; you can take leaves anytime for cooking.

beginner: In early spring, once new growth shows and frost is over, cut out old woody stems and pull up any pieces that have spread too far. Cut into the leafy parts, not the bare old wood.
seasoned: Cut out old, leggy wood in early spring once growth resumes and frost has passed, and pull up any shoots that have crept beyond where you want them. Cutting into leafy growth, not bare old wood, gives the best regrowth.

beginner: For the best flavor, cut oregano to dry just as the flower buds appear, before they open, when the oils are strongest. Pinch off the flowers to keep the leaves tasting their best.
seasoned: For the strongest flavor, harvest and cut for drying just as the flower buds form, before they open, when the leaf oils peak. Pinch or cut off the flowers to favor leaf growth and keep the best flavor.

beginner: Decide about the flowers. Cutting them off keeps the leaves tasting best and stops the plant spreading by seed; leaving a few for the bees is fine, but snip them before they make seed.
seasoned: Decide what to do with the flowers. Removing them keeps the leaves at peak flavor and limits self-seeding; leaving some to open feeds bees and butterflies, but deadhead before seed sets so oregano does not sow itself across the garden.

beginner: After it flowers, trim off the old flower stems and cut it back into the leafy parts for fresh new leaves, avoiding the bare woody stems. Snipping often plus this trim keeps oregano bushy, but it still gets woody, so replace or divide it every few years.
seasoned: Shear off the spent flower stems after bloom and cut the plant back into leafy growth for a fresh flush, avoiding the bare old wood. Frequent harvest plus this shear keeps oregano bushy, but it still goes woody with age, so divide or replace it every few years.

beginner: Trim off the old flowers before they make seed. Oregano drops a lot of seed and can pop up all over, so deadheading it as you cut back keeps the seedlings down.
seasoned: Deadhead as you shear to limit self-seeding. Oregano seeds readily and can sow itself across a bed, so cutting the spent flowers before seed matures keeps stray seedlings down.

beginner: In winter, do almost nothing. Stop watering and feeding, and save the trim for spring. Oregano sitting in wet winter soil rots, so do not keep watering it.
seasoned: Over winter, do almost nothing: stop watering and feeding, and leave hard cutback for spring. A plant in wet winter soil rots, so the worst thing you can do is keep it watered.

beginner: Shelter plants in very cold areas. Cover the plant with straw or evergreen branches after the ground freezes and take it off in spring, or grow less hardy types like Greek oregano in a pot you can bring under cover.
seasoned: Protect plants at the cold edge of the range. In the coldest zones, mulch over the crown with straw or evergreen boughs after the ground freezes and remove it in spring, or overwinter less hardy types like Greek oregano in a pot under cover.

beginner: A grown oregano plant gives you plenty of sprigs all season, enough to cook with fresh and to dry, especially once it is a couple of years old. The more you snip it, the more it makes.
seasoned: A mature plant yields a steady supply of sprigs through the growing season, easily enough to keep a kitchen stocked with fresh oregano plus bundles to dry; productivity is best once the plant reaches full size at about the second year, and frequent harvesting keeps it coming.

beginner: Do not expect much the first year. Picking lightly and pinching to make it bushy while the plant settles in gives you bigger harvests from year two.
seasoned: Expect only light harvests the first year; harvesting sparingly and pinching to build a bushy plant while it establishes pays off in fuller production from the second season on.
