seasoned: With oregano, yellowing and dieback almost always mean too wet, not too dry. Overwatering, poor drainage, and excess winter moisture are the number one killer, leading to root and stem rot. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.

beginner: Water much less and improve drainage. Use poor, well-draining soil in full sun, keep it on the dry side, and on heavy or humid ground plant on a mound. Never let it sit in soggy ground.
seasoned: Cut back on watering hard and fix drainage. Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, keep it on the dry side, and on clay or in humid areas use a mound or raised bed. Never let oregano sit in wet ground, especially over winter.

seasoned: Contain it: grow oregano in a pot or a sunken bottomless container, or set deep edging around it. Deadhead the flowers before seed sets, and each spring pull or dig out shoots that have crept beyond bounds.

beginner: Oregano is a low, spreading herb with pungent, fragrant leaves you cook with, famous on pizza and in tomato sauces. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor dry soil, and very little water, and it does worse if you pamper it. It grows about 1 to 2 feet tall in a bushy mound. The leaves taste best just before it flowers in mid-to-late summer, so many gardeners pinch off the flowers, and oregano is one of the few herbs that tastes even stronger dried. It is tough and rarely bothered by pests, but it spreads by creeping roots and dropped seed, so it is best grown in a pot or with edging. Watch out: Mexican oregano is a different plant, not true oregano.
seasoned: Oregano is a spreading, low, woody Mediterranean perennial in the mint family, grown for its pungent aromatic leaves that flavor pizza, tomato sauces, meats, and Mediterranean and Mexican dishes. It forms a bushy, mat-like mound about 1 to 2 feet tall and thrives on neglect in full sun and lean, well-drained soil; wet, rich, or humid conditions rot it and dull its flavor. Its flavor peaks just before its mid-to-late-summer bloom, so many growers pinch off the flowers to keep the leaves at their best, and the leaves are unusual in tasting even stronger dried. It is hardy and pest-resistant but spreads by creeping stems and self-sown seed, so it is best contained. Note that Mexican oregano is a different, unrelated plant.

beginner: You can snip oregano anytime once it is established: cut the top few inches of leafy stems. The flavor is strongest just before it flowers, so that is the best time to cut oregano to dry, in the morning after the dew dries. Pinching off the flower buds keeps the leaves tasting their best, and snipping it often keeps it bushy. Oregano is unusual in that it tastes even stronger once dried.
seasoned: Harvest oregano sprigs anytime once the plant is established: snip the top few inches of leafy growth, taking up to about three-quarters of the current season's growth at a cutting. Flavor is most concentrated just before the plant flowers, so cut for drying as the buds form, on a dry morning after the dew has lifted. Pinching or cutting off the flowers keeps the leaves pungent, and regular harvesting keeps the plant bushy. Oregano is one of the few herbs whose flavor deepens when dried.

beginner: Oregano is tough and comes back year after year in most of the country (about zones 5 to 9, and zone 4 for the hardiest common type with good drainage and a winter mulch). Greek oregano, the best for cooking, is a little less cold-hardy. In the very coldest areas (zone 3), grow it for one season or in a pot you bring inside. Just as important as cold: oregano hates wet feet and will rot in soggy soil, and it also struggles in hot, humid places.
seasoned: Oregano is a hardy perennial. Common oregano (Origanum vulgare) is the hardiest, reliably perennial to about zone 4 with sharp drainage and, at the cold edge, a winter mulch; Greek oregano (subsp. hirtum), the best culinary type, is a touch less hardy, to about zone 5. Most types are reliable in roughly zones 5 to 9, with zone 3 grown as an annual or a bring-in container plant, and tender types like Syrian oregano hardy only in the warmest zones. Good drainage matters as much as cold: oregano rots in wet winter soil before cold alone kills it, and it also struggles in hot, humid climates.

beginner: Plant sage next to other dry, sunny herbs like rosemary, thyme, and oregano, which want the same conditions. Its flowers bring in bees. seasoned: Sage pairs naturally with other sun-loving, low-water Mediterranean herbs that share its lean, well-drained conditions, such as rosemary, thyme, and oregano; group these together and run the whole bed dry. Its early-summer flowers draw bees and other pollinators. By tradition it is grown near cabbage-family crops and carrots, where growers believe its strong aroma helps confuse pests, though this is folk practice rather than a measured effect. Keep it away from thirsty, rich-soil neighbors whose watering would keep sage too wet.

beginner: Sage is a small woody herb with soft gray-green leaves that you use in cooking, fresh or dried. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor well-drained soil, and not much water. This is kitchen sage (Salvia officinalis), not the colorful flower salvias sold as annuals. It makes pretty blue-purple flower spikes in early summer that bees love, but you grow it for the leaves, so many people snip the flowers off. Sage is one of the tougher herbs and comes back year after year in much of the country, but plants get woody and leggy after a few years, so trim it each spring and plan to replace it every few years. Too much water or hot, muggy weather, not cold, is what usually rots and kills it.
seasoned: Sage (Salvia officinalis), also called common, garden, or culinary sage, is a woody Mediterranean perennial subshrub in the mint family, grown for its aromatic, pebbly-textured, gray-green leaves used fresh or dried in cooking. This is the culinary kitchen sage, not the ornamental bedding salvias (such as scarlet or mealycup sage) sold as annual flowers. It carries short spikes of blue-purple flowers in early summer that bees and butterflies love, but the leaves are the crop, and many cooks pinch the flower spikes to keep the foliage flavorful. Sage thrives on lean treatment: full sun, poor to average well-drained soil, and little water or feeding. It is one of the hardier culinary herbs, reliably perennial in much of the country, but it is short-lived and turns woody and sprawling with age, so plan to replace plants every few years and prune each spring to slow the decline. Overwatering and humid heat, not cold, are what usually kill it, through root and stem rot.

beginner: Snip sage leaves and sprigs whenever you cook once the plant is growing well. Go easy the first year, then cut more freely. The flavor is best on fresh spring and early-summer growth and just before it flowers, which is also the best time to cut some for drying. Take sprigs about 6 to 8 inches from the top, never more than about half the plant at once, and cut in mid-morning after the dew dries for the strongest flavor. In mild climates sage stays leafy, so you can pick a few leaves any time.
seasoned: Harvest sage leaves and sprigs as needed once the plant is growing well. Harvest lightly the first year while the plant establishes, then cut more freely. Flavor is strongest in new growth from spring into early summer and just before flowering, so that is the best window for drying. Cut sprigs about 6 to 8 inches from the tips, taking no more than about half the plant at once, and harvest in mid-morning after the dew dries, when leaf oils are highest. On evergreen plants in mild climates you can pick a few leaves any time of year.

beginner: Sage is one of the tougher herbs and comes back year after year in most of the country (about zones 4 to 8). Even so, plants get woody and leggy within a few years, so trim them each spring and plan to replace them every few years. The plain green kinds are the hardiest; the colorful variegated types are less cold-hardy. In the very coldest areas and in hot, muggy climates, sage is short-lived, so many people grow it for a season or in a pot they can bring inside for winter.
seasoned: Common sage (Salvia officinalis) is hardy in roughly USDA zones 4 to 8, one of the hardier culinary herbs, and reliably perennial through much of the country. It is short-lived even so, turning woody and sprawling within a few years, so plan to replace plants every three to five years and prune each spring to slow the decline. Green-leaved types are the hardiest; variegated forms (Tricolor, golden Icterina, purple Purpurascens) are progressively more tender. In the coldest zones (zone 3 and marginal zone 4) and in humid subtropical heat, sage is short-lived or best grown as an annual or a bring-in container plant.

seasoned: Sage is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer partner. It is grown for its leaves, not fruit or seed, so no cross-pollination planning is required. Its blue-purple flowers are highly attractive to bees and butterflies if left to bloom.

beginner: Trim sage back each spring when new growth appears, cutting the leggy stems but not down into the hard woody base, which will not grow back well. Keep it tidy with light trims and by snipping sprigs through the season, and cut off the old flower stems after it blooms. This keeps sage bushy and tasty, but plants still get woody after a few years and are worth replacing.
seasoned: Prune sage hard in spring as new growth breaks, cutting leggy stems back but never into the bare old wood, which resprouts poorly. Follow with light trims and sprig harvests through the season, and remove spent flower stems after bloom. This yearly renewal keeps the plant compact and flavorful and slows the woody decline, but sage is short-lived, so plan to replace plants every few years.

beginner: Eggplant likes rich, well-drained soil that warms up well in the sun, since it is a heat-loving plant that hates cold, soggy ground. Mix in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch laid down before planting warms the soil and gives eggplant the head start it wants. Aim for soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged.
seasoned: Eggplant wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam rich in organic matter, and above all a soil that warms early and stays warm. As a heat-loving crop it sulks in cold, wet ground, so a sandy loam that warms quickly in spring suits it better than a heavy, slow-warming clay. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting, and on heavy or cool soils many growers lay black plastic or fabric mulch to raise soil temperature and set transplants into warmer ground. Steady moisture in a soil that drains freely is the target, since soggy roots stall this warmth-demanding plant and invite the soilborne wilts it is prone to.

beginner: Eggplant likes slightly acidic soil, about pH 5.5 to 6.8, and a lot of garden soil is already close. The pH scale runs from acidic to alkaline, and this range is where eggplant takes up nutrients best. If your soil runs alkaline (common in the dry interior West), you may need to add sulfur before planting. An inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Eggplant grows best at a soil pH of about 5.5 to 6.8, with a sweet spot near 6.0 to 6.5 where the nutrients it needs stay most available. It tolerates a somewhat wider band, up to roughly 7.5, but uptake of iron, manganese, and other micronutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline, showing up as yellowing between the veins of younger leaves. Alkaline soils common across the interior West often need sulfur worked in before planting; most Eastern and Midwestern soils sit naturally near the target. A simple soil test from your local extension office settles it before you plant.

beginner: Eggplant grows for a long time and likes steady feeding, but the timing matters. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the soil before you plant. Then wait: once the first little eggplants have set, feed with a nitrogen fertilizer, and again a few weeks later. Going heavy on fertilizer too early gives you a big leafy plant with few flowers, so save the feeding for after the fruit starts forming.
seasoned: Eggplant is a moderately heavy feeder over a long season. Work a complete fertilizer such as 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with nitrogen once the first fruits have set and again three to four weeks later through the harvest. Hold the nitrogen back before fruit set, since too much early on drives leafy growth and few flowers; the time to push it is after the plant starts carrying fruit. Pair feeding with steady moisture, because fertilizer only helps a plant that is not also drought-stressed.

beginner: Your eggplant is setting fruit. Feed it now with a nitrogen fertilizer to keep it producing.
seasoned: Your eggplant has set its first fruit, time to side-dress with nitrogen to keep production going through the season.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then switch to a nitrogen feed once the fruit sets. Do not overdo the nitrogen early or you get all leaves and no eggplants.
seasoned: A complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 worked in at planting, then a nitrogen side-dress (for example calcium nitrate, 15.5-0-0) once fruit sets. Avoid heavy nitrogen before fruit set, which gives leaf at the expense of flowers.

beginner: Mix 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet (or a few inches of compost) into the soil before planting. Then, once fruit has set, scratch a nitrogen fertilizer into the soil a few inches out from each plant and water it in, repeating every three to four weeks.
seasoned: A common rate is 1 to 2 pounds of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet worked into the bed before transplanting, then a side-dress of about 0.5 pound of calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) per 100 square feet once the first fruits set, repeated every three to four weeks through harvest, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in.

beginner: The most useful eggplant companions help with its two biggest pests, flea beetles and Colorado potato beetles. Aromatic herbs and a ring of nasturtiums or marigolds can draw or shoo those pests away, and bush beans add a little nitrogen. The one rule that really matters is to keep eggplant away from tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes, which are all close relatives and share the same pests and soil diseases.
seasoned: Most eggplant companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested, and the ones worth acting on target its two signature problems: flea beetles and the Colorado potato beetle. Aromatic herbs and a border of nasturtium or marigold are the classic deflectors, drawing or repelling flea beetles and aphids off the crop, while bush beans both fix a little nitrogen and serve as a noted trap for the potato beetle. The single firmest rule is a rotation one: keep eggplant away from its Solanaceae relatives, tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes, which share its full pest and disease complex, including verticillium wilt and the flea beetle.

beginner: Bush beans add a little nitrogen to the soil and can lure Colorado potato beetles away from your eggplant. A good, traditional neighbor.
seasoned: Legumes fix a little nitrogen the long-feeding eggplant appreciates, and bush beans are a noted trap host for the Colorado potato beetle, helping pull it off the crop. A traditional, mechanistically plausible pairing rather than a trial-isolated one.

beginner: Nasturtiums are often grown near eggplant to lure flea beetles and aphids away from the crop. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
seasoned: Often planted around solanaceous crops as a trap and deterrent for flea beetles and aphids, drawing them off the eggplant. Trap cropping is a documented principle, but the specific nasturtium-eggplant effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

beginner: Marigolds are a classic companion flower for eggplant, traditionally grown to help keep pests down. Mostly tradition, but a cheerful, low-risk choice.
seasoned: A long-standing companion tradition near eggplant; French marigold grown as a cover crop has documented nematode-suppressive effects, though the interplanted marigold-eggplant pest benefit is traditional rather than trial-isolated.

beginner: Strong-smelling herbs like thyme, oregano, and dill are traditionally planted near eggplant to help confuse pests like flea beetles. A pleasant, low-risk companion.
seasoned: Pungent herbs such as thyme, oregano, and dill are traditionally interplanted to confuse or repel flea beetles and other pests and to draw beneficial insects. The effect is plausible and habitat-based rather than trial-isolated for eggplant.

beginner: Keep eggplant away from tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes. They are all close relatives that share the same pests and soil diseases, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
seasoned: All are Solanaceae and share eggplant's full pest and disease complex, including flea beetle, Colorado potato beetle, verticillium and bacterial wilt, and the blights. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread the nightshades out and rotate them on at least a 3 to 4 year cycle.

beginner: Many gardeners keep fennel away from eggplant and most other vegetables, since it is said to stunt their growth. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
seasoned: A widely repeated caution that fennel inhibits the growth of many garden vegetables and is best kept to its own corner. There is no strong T1 mechanism for an eggplant-fennel antagonism, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

beginner: The leaves are peppered with lots of tiny round holes, as if hit by birdshot. It hits young plants hardest and can devastate seedlings. Touch the plant and you will see tiny dark beetles jump away.
seasoned: Tiny shot-hole punctures riddle the leaves, a scatter of small round holes that is the classic flea-beetle signature on eggplant. Damage is by far most severe on seedlings and young transplants, whose small leaf area a heavy infestation can shred or kill outright; established plants tolerate considerable feeding. Brush a plant and the small dark beetles spring away like fleas.

beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas and chew tiny holes in the leaves. They are most active in spring and love eggplant, so they target young plants early in the season.
seasoned: Several Epitrix flea beetle species that feed on eggplant foliage, overwintering as adults in debris and emerging to attack the earliest, most vulnerable plants in spring. Eggplant is a strongly preferred host, and the beetles concentrate on it, which is why flea beetles are the defining early-season eggplant pest.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they are big and strong, then take it off when they flower. Setting out larger transplants helps them outgrow the damage. For heavy attacks on seedlings, an organic spray such as spinosad or a kaolin clay coating helps.
seasoned: Protect transplants with floating row cover until they are large and vigorous, removing it at flowering. Set out stout, well-hardened transplants rather than tiny seedlings so plants can outgrow the damage, and treat heavy early infestations with spinosad or kaolin clay. Mature plants rarely need treatment.

beginner: Cover plants early with row cover, set out larger transplants into warm soil so they grow quickly, and clear away weeds and old plant debris where the beetles hide over winter. A border of nasturtiums can lure them away.
seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, delay setting plants out until the soil and air are warm so they grow away fast, and clean up crop debris and weeds that harbor overwintering adults. A nasturtium or other trap planting at the bed edge can draw beetles off the crop.

beginner: Striped yellow-and-black beetles and plump red larvae with black spots eat the leaves, sometimes stripping a plant bare. Eggplant is one of their favorite foods. Check the undersides of leaves for clusters of orange-yellow eggs.
seasoned: Rounded yellow-and-black-striped adults and humpbacked, brick-red larvae with rows of black spots chew the leaves, and eggplant is a favorite host. Both stages feed voraciously and populations build fast, so an unmanaged infestation can defoliate plants and cut yield sharply. Look for clusters of orange-yellow eggs on leaf undersides.

beginner: A striped beetle whose larvae and adults both feed on eggplant and potato leaves. They overwinter in the soil, show up as plants get going, and multiply quickly through the summer.
seasoned: Leptinotarsa decemlineata, a Solanaceae specialist that prefers potato and eggplant. Adults overwinter in the soil and nearby debris and move in as plants establish; left alone they go through multiple generations a season and quickly resist many insecticides, making non-chemical control important.

beginner: Pick the beetles, larvae, and egg clusters off by hand and drop them in soapy water, checking every day or two. Squash the orange egg clusters under the leaves. For heavy infestations, an organic spray such as spinosad or Bt (the tenebrionis strain) works on the young larvae.
seasoned: In a home garden, hand-pick adults, larvae, and egg clusters daily into soapy water, which keeps small plantings clean. Crush egg masses on leaf undersides, and where pressure is high apply spinosad or Bacillus thuringiensis var. tenebrionis to young larvae. Rotating away from last year's nightshade bed cuts the overwintered population.

beginner: Do not plant eggplant where potatoes, tomatoes, or eggplant grew last year, since the beetles come up from the soil there. Cover young plants with row cover, and a thick straw mulch makes it harder for the beetles to reach them.
seasoned: Rotate eggplant well away from where potatoes, tomatoes, or eggplant grew last year, since the overwintered adults emerge near old hosts. Row cover on young plants excludes the colonizers, and a thick straw mulch hinders the adults that walk in from the soil.

beginner: Tiny soft green or black insects gather on new growth and the undersides of leaves, making them curl and yellow, often with a sticky film and black mold. They can also spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, often green peach aphid, cluster on growing tips and leaf undersides, causing leaves to curl, pucker, and yellow, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, aphids transmit mosaic and other viruses that mottle and distort the foliage.

beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that multiply quickly in warm weather, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer. The sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold.
seasoned: Several aphid species, predominantly green peach aphid, that suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on soft, over-fertilized growth. The honeydew they excrete fosters sooty mold that shades the leaves.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work instead of spraying everything.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants.

beginner: The leaves look dusty or speckled with tiny yellow dots, and in bad cases you see fine webbing underneath. The leaves can bronze and dry out. Mites love hot, dry weather.
seasoned: Fine yellow stippling speckles the leaves, which may bronze, dry, and drop, and in bad infestations fine webbing appears on leaf undersides. Two-spotted spider mites thrive in hot, dry weather, exactly the conditions eggplant is grown in, so mite pressure often peaks in midsummer.

beginner: Tiny mites, almost too small to see, that feed on the undersides of leaves and thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions. They build up fast in summer.
seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related mites that feed on the lower leaf surfaces with piercing mouthparts. Populations explode in heat and drought and on dusty, water-stressed plants, and can build quickly on eggplant in summer.

beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water every day for a week, then follow up with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if needed. Keeping plants well watered helps, since stressed plants are hit hardest.
seasoned: Spray the leaf undersides with a strong jet of water repeatedly to disrupt colonies, then apply insecticidal soap or horticultural oil to the undersides, repeating every few days. Keeping plants well watered and raising humidity discourages mites; predatory mites help under heavy pressure.

beginner: Keep plants well watered in hot weather, hose dust off the leaves now and then, and avoid spraying broad insecticides that kill the helpful bugs that eat mites.
seasoned: Keep plants well watered in hot weather, since drought-stressed plants are most vulnerable, avoid dusty conditions, and avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill the predators holding mites in check.

beginner: The tops of the leaves look pale and stippled, and underneath you find dark sticky specks and small insects with lacy-looking wings. Bad infestations brown and curl the leaves.
seasoned: Leaves develop a pale, yellow-stippled or bleached look on top, while the undersides carry dark, varnish-like specks of excrement and the small, lacy-winged adults and spiny nymphs. Heavy feeding browns and curls the foliage and can stunt the plant, and lace bugs are fairly eggplant-specific.

beginner: A small flat insect with lacy wings that feeds in groups on the undersides of eggplant leaves, sucking out the juices. It is most active in warm weather.
seasoned: The eggplant lace bug (Gargaphia solani), a true bug that feeds in colonies on leaf undersides with piercing-sucking mouthparts. It overwinters in debris and is most damaging in warm weather, with several generations a season.

beginner: Check the undersides of the leaves and spray any colonies directly with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, making sure to coat underneath. Pick off and destroy the most badly affected leaves.
seasoned: Scout leaf undersides early and treat colonies directly with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, which reach the soft nymphs, covering the undersides thoroughly and repeating as needed. Remove and destroy the worst-infested leaves.

beginner: Clear away old plants at the end of the season, move eggplant to a new spot each year, and check the undersides of the lower leaves early so you catch the bugs before they spread.
seasoned: Clean up crop debris at season's end to remove overwintering sites, rotate eggplant, and scout the undersides of lower leaves from early in the season so colonies are caught while small.

beginner: Whole leaves vanish overnight, leaving just the veins, with dark droppings on the leaves below. The cause is a large green caterpillar that hides against the stems, easier to spot by its droppings than by sight.
seasoned: Large sections of leaf, and sometimes whole shoots, are stripped down to the veins overnight, with dark pellet droppings on the leaves below. The culprits are big green tomato or tobacco hornworms, up to four inches long, that blend into the stems and are easiest to find by their frass.

beginner: Big green caterpillars, the young of large moths, that feed on eggplant and tomato leaves mostly in mid to late summer. Even a few can strip a lot of foliage.
seasoned: Tomato and tobacco hornworms, the larvae of large sphinx moths, which feed on solanaceous foliage including eggplant from midsummer on. A few caterpillars can do conspicuous damage given their size.

beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand and drop them in soapy water. If you find one covered in small white capsules, leave it, those are parasitic wasps that will do the work for you. An organic Bt spray works on the smaller caterpillars.
seasoned: Hand-pick the caterpillars, which is effective in a home garden, and apply Bacillus thuringiensis to younger larvae where numbers are high. Leave any hornworm studded with white parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the wasps will kill it and breed more.

beginner: Turn the soil at the end of the season to destroy the pupae, watch for droppings and missing leaves from midsummer, and welcome the helpful wasps that attack hornworms.
seasoned: Till the soil in fall to destroy overwintering pupae, scout for frass and stripped leaves from midsummer, and encourage the parasitic wasps and other natural enemies that keep hornworms in check.

beginner: Leaves turn yellow and wilt, often on one side of the plant first, then brown and drop while the plant stunts. Cut a wilting stem and you may see brown streaks inside. It is the most common serious eggplant disease.
seasoned: Lower and outer leaves yellow, often in a wedge or one-sided pattern, then wilt, brown, and drop, working upward as the plant stunts and fails to size its fruit. A cut through a wilting stem shows tan-to-brown streaking in the water-conducting tissue. It is the most common and damaging eggplant disease in much of the country.

beginner: A soil fungus that infects the roots and blocks the plant's water pipes, so it wilts even when watered. It lives in the soil for years and attacks many crops, especially the nightshade family.
seasoned: Verticillium dahliae, a soilborne fungus that infects the roots and clogs the vascular system, so the plant wilts despite moist soil. It persists in soil for years as resting structures, has a wide host range across the Solanaceae and many other crops, and is favored by cool-to-moderate soil temperatures.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it, so pull and destroy infected plants. The real answer is prevention: rotate your crops and choose resistant or grafted plants next time.
seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy affected plants. Management is preventive and centered on rotation and resistant or grafted plants, since the fungus cannot be eradicated from infested soil by home-garden means.

beginner: Plant eggplant in soil with no recent history of the disease, rotate away from tomatoes, peppers, and potatoes, and look for resistant or grafted plants. Keeping plants healthy with steady water and feeding helps them cope.
seasoned: Do not plant eggplant where verticillium-susceptible crops (tomato, pepper, potato, eggplant, and many others) have grown, rotate on a long cycle, choose tolerant varieties or grafted plants on resistant rootstock, and keep plants vigorous with steady water and balanced feeding. Solarizing infested beds can lower inoculum.

beginner: Pale sunken spots on the fruit spread quickly into soft, rotting patches, and the disease can also spot the leaves and rot the stem near the base. It is worst in warm, wet weather and later in the season.
seasoned: Pale, sunken spots appear on the fruit that rapidly enlarge to soft, spongy, rotting areas, sometimes shrinking the fruit into a dry mummy; the disease also causes grayish leaf spots and a collar rot that can break young stems an inch or two above the soil line. It is most damaging in warm, wet weather and toward fall.

beginner: A fungus carried on seed and in old plant debris that spreads in warm, wet weather. It can come in on infected seed, so starting clean matters.
seasoned: Phomopsis vexans, a fungus that is both soil- and seedborne and overwinters on crop debris. Warm, humid conditions and splashing water spread it, and infected seed or volunteer debris often starts an outbreak, so clean seed and rotation are central to control.

beginner: Pick off and throw away infected fruit and plants right away. Keep the leaves and fruit dry by watering at the soil, and use a labeled fungicide if it is spreading. Rotted fruit cannot be saved.
seasoned: Remove and destroy infected fruit and plants promptly to limit spread, and where the disease is active apply a labeled fungicide, keeping foliage and fruit as dry as possible. There is no rescue for badly rotted fruit.

beginner: Use clean seed and healthy transplants, do not plant eggplant in the same spot for about four years, water at the soil instead of over the leaves, and clean up old plants at the end of the season.
seasoned: Start with clean, treated, or resistant seed and disease-free transplants, rotate eggplant out of the bed for about four years, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, space for airflow, and remove crop debris at season's end.

beginner: The plant wilts and collapses suddenly even though the soil is wet, without much yellowing first. If you cut the stem near the base, the inside looks brown, and a cut stem held in a glass of water gives off milky strands. It is mainly a problem in the hot, wet South.
seasoned: Individual leaves, then whole plants, wilt and collapse suddenly even though the soil is moist, with little of the yellowing that precedes verticillium. Cut low on the stem and the pith is discolored reddish-brown; suspended in clear water, a cut stem streams milky bacterial ooze. It is most serious in hot, wet soils of the South.

beginner: A soil bacterium that gets into the roots and blocks the plant's water flow, so it wilts fast. It lives in warm, wet soil and spreads in water and on tools.
seasoned: Ralstonia solanacearum, a soilborne bacterium that invades the roots and plugs the vascular tissue. It survives in soil and infected debris, spreads in water and on tools, and is favored by high soil temperature and moisture, so it is most damaging in warm, wet regions.

beginner: There is no cure, so pull and destroy any plant that wilts from it, and clean your tools. The real fix is prevention next season.
seasoned: There is no cure; remove and destroy wilted plants promptly to limit spread, and disinfect tools. Because it persists in soil, management is preventive, through rotation, resistant or grafted plants, and improved drainage.

beginner: Do not plant eggplant where tomatoes, potatoes, or eggplant grew in the last three years, improve drainage in wet spots, and look for resistant or grafted plants if this disease is common where you live.
seasoned: Avoid planting eggplant where tomato, potato, or eggplant grew in the previous three years, choose resistant varieties or graft onto resistant rootstock in problem areas, improve drainage, and avoid moving infested soil or working among wet plants.

beginner: Dark, wet-looking patches appear on the stems, leaves, or fruit, and the plant can wilt and die quickly. The fruit can rot, sometimes with white fuzzy growth. It strikes in warm, wet, poorly drained ground.
seasoned: Dark, water-soaked lesions and streaking develop on stems, leaves, or fruit, and a plant can collapse and die rapidly once the stem is girdled. Fruit rots with a firm, sometimes white-cottony decay. It flares in warm, wet, poorly drained conditions and after heavy rain or flooding.

beginner: A mold-like disease that lives in wet soil and spreads in splashing water, attacking plants in warm, soggy conditions. It moves fast once it starts.
seasoned: Phytophthora species (such as P. capsici and P. nicotianae), water molds that thrive in saturated soil and spread in splashing and running water. They survive in soil and debris and move fast in warm, wet weather, especially on heavy or poorly drained ground.

beginner: Pull and destroy affected plants and fruit, and fix the drainage. There is no good home cure once it takes hold, so prevention is what matters.
seasoned: Remove and destroy affected plants and fruit promptly, and improve drainage immediately. There is no effective home-garden cure once plants collapse, so control is preventive and drainage-based.

beginner: Plant on raised beds or mounds so water drains away, avoid wet low spots, water at the soil, and keep fruit off soggy ground. Rotate away from peppers, tomatoes, and squash.
seasoned: Plant on raised, well-drained beds or hills, avoid low spots that stay wet, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, rotate away from solanaceous and cucurbit crops, and keep fruit up off saturated soil.

beginner: Give eggplant about 1 inch of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. Water deeply rather than a little every day. Plants in pots dry out much faster and may need checking daily in summer.
seasoned: Aim for about 1 inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. As a heat-loving plant grown through the hottest part of the year, eggplant transpires heavily in summer, and container plants dry out far faster still.

beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, soaking the soil down 6 to 8 inches so the roots grow deep. Keep it even: letting the soil go bone-dry and then flooding it stresses the plant and makes flowers drop.
seasoned: Around 1 inch per week is the working range, leaning higher during flowering and fruit set, wetting the soil to a depth of at least 6 to 8 inches so the roots follow the moisture down. Even, deep watering is what sizes well-shaped fruit; letting the soil swing from dry to soaked stresses the plant and drops blossoms.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, with a soaker hose or by holding the hose at the base. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent disease. If you must use a sprinkler, do it in the morning so the leaves dry off by evening. Mulch helps keep the soil evenly moist and warm.
seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves favor the leaf spots and fruit rots eggplant is prone to. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it in the morning so leaves dry before evening. A layer of mulch buffers soil moisture and warmth and blocks soil-borne spores from splashing onto the lower leaves.

beginner: If the lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or stems and fruit go soft and rotten, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft, rotting stems or fruit point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil starves the roots of oxygen and invites the Phytophthora and bacterial wilts eggplant is susceptible to, especially on heavy ground.

beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry, and drought while it is flowering causes dropped blossoms and small, bitter fruit.
seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is common in heat and not alarming, but leaves that stay limp and dull signal real drought. Drought stress during flowering and fruit set shows up as dropped blossoms and small, misshapen, sometimes bitter fruit.

beginner: Keep the seed tray evenly damp and warm while the seeds come up. Eggplant likes it warm and sprouts slowly, so do not let the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seed-starting mix evenly moist and warm through germination; eggplant is heat-loving and slow to sprout, and the surface must not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp, not soggy. Let the top begin to dry before watering again.
seasoned: Grow seedlings on under lights with even, moderate moisture, easing off between waterings so the mix never stays saturated.

beginner: Soak the plant in well when you set it out, then keep the soil evenly moist as it takes hold. Mulch keeps the moisture and warmth steady.
seasoned: Water in thoroughly at transplant, then hold even moisture at the base as this heat-lover establishes; mulch to buffer soil moisture and warmth.

beginner: Keep watering steady once flowers open, about 1 inch a week soaked in deep. If the soil swings from dry to soaked, the flowers drop off and you get fewer fruit.
seasoned: Eggplant wants a steady 1 inch a week soaked 6 to 8 inches deep, leaning higher through flowering and fruit set. Even moisture sets fruit and prevents blossom drop; unlike peppers, eggplant is not prone to blossom-end rot, so the failure mode of dry-wet swings here is dropped blossoms, not fruit rot.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while the fruit fill out. Letting it dry hard and then soaking it gives small, bitter, oddly shaped fruit, so keep the water steady.
seasoned: Fruit set through sizing is the water-critical stretch: steady, deep moisture sizes well-shaped fruit, while a dry-then-flooded swing gives small, bitter, misshapen fruit. Keep the ripening fruit up off wet ground and the soil evenly moist.

beginner: Keep watering evenly while you pick. Eggplant keeps making new fruit, and steady water keeps them tender instead of small and bitter.
seasoned: Keep even moisture through the picking weeks; eggplant keeps flowering and setting fruit as you harvest, and steady water keeps the later fruit from turning small and bitter.

beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for eggplant. It keeps the plant hydrated without encouraging leaf and fruit disease.
seasoned: Base watering is the most useful habit for eggplant, because the same plant that wants steady moisture is also prone to leaf spots and fruit and root rots. Keep water on the soil, air moving through the leaves, and the ripening fruit up off wet ground.

beginner: Pick eggplant while it is young and shiny, not when it is biggest. A ready eggplant has firm flesh and a bright, glossy skin, and when you press the side with your thumb the dent springs back. If the skin looks dull instead of shiny, you waited too long: the inside will be seedy, spongy, and bitter. Harvest large oval types when they are firm and glossy and slimmer Asian types at finger or hot-dog size. Cut the fruit off with scissors or a knife, leaving a little stem on, instead of pulling, because the stems are tough and sometimes prickly. Keep picking every few days, since taking the fruit young keeps the plant making more.
seasoned: Harvest eggplant YOUNG and GLOSSY, while the fruit is immature, not at full size. The single best cue is the skin: a ripe eggplant is firm and has a high, mirror-like gloss, and press the side gently with a thumbnail and the dent springs back. Once the skin turns dull or bronzed, the flesh has gone seedy, spongy, and bitter and the dent stays, the sign you waited too long. Pick large oval types from about 2 inches across up to two-thirds of their mature size, and slender Asian types at finger-to-hot-dog size. Cut the fruit with shears or a knife leaving a short piece of the stem and the green calyx attached, rather than pulling, since the stems are tough and often spiny. Harvest regularly, at least once or twice a week, because picking fruit while immature keeps the plant setting more; fruit left to over-ripen shuts down further production.

beginner: Eggplant hates the cold, so harden plants off over about a week to ten days, giving them more time outside each day, and do not set them out until nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm. Planting too early into cold ground stalls eggplant badly, so it pays to wait until it is truly warm, a couple of weeks after you would plant tomatoes.
seasoned: Eggplant transplants are especially sensitive to a cold check, so harden off carefully over 7 to 10 days, easing plants into sun and wind, and set them out only once nights stay reliably above 50°F and the soil is thoroughly warm. A transplant chilled below about 50°F sulks for weeks and yields poorly, so it is better to wait a week or two past the tomato date than to plant into cold ground.

beginner: Start eggplant seeds indoors about 8 weeks before you plan to plant out, keeping them warm (75 to 85°F) to sprout well. Eggplant needs more warmth and a longer head start than tomatoes, and it goes outside later, only once nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm. Use stocky transplants up to a foot tall, and put a stake or cage in at planting time.
seasoned: Start eggplant seeds indoors about 8 weeks before transplanting (UMD uses 8 to 10 week old transplants), with bottom heat of 75 to 85°F for fast, even germination. Eggplant needs a longer, warmer start than tomato and is set out later, once nights hold above 50°F and the soil has warmed to at least 60 to 65°F. Choose sturdy transplants up to a foot tall with stems about pencil thick, and set plant supports at planting. Direct sowing is practical only in the longest, warmest regions; everywhere else this is a transplant crop.

beginner: Do not let the pot sit in a saucer of standing water. Empty it soon after watering. A saucer is fine for keeping the pot warm, which eggplant enjoys, but the roots should never sit in pooled water.
seasoned: If you use a saucer, empty it within an hour of watering. Eggplant will not tolerate sitting in standing water, which starves the roots of oxygen and invites root rot. A saucer is useful for holding warmth, which eggplant likes, but the roots must not stay submerged.

Water consistently, since a small soil volume dries fast and moisture swings drop blossoms, feed regularly because containers leach nutrients, and cage or stake plants to carry the fruit.

beginner: Do not plant eggplant where you grew tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, or eggplant recently. They are all in the same family and share the same soil diseases and pests, which build up and carry over.
seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, and eggplant, which share verticillium and bacterial wilt, phomopsis, the flea beetle, and the Colorado potato beetle. These soilborne diseases and overwintering pests build up wherever a nightshade has grown.

beginner: Move eggplant to a different part of the garden each year, and do not return it, or its relatives tomato, pepper, and potato, to the same spot for about four years. Soil diseases like verticillium wilt and the pests that bother eggplant build up where nightshades grow, and rotation is the main tool to keep them in check. Clean up old plants at the end of the season too.
seasoned: Rotate eggplant on a long cycle, returning it to a given bed no sooner than the fourth year, to break the buildup of verticillium and bacterial wilt, phomopsis (which is also seedborne), and the flea and Colorado potato beetles. The wider Solanaceae, tomato, pepper, and potato, share that complex, so rotate as a group and avoid following any of them. Clear and remove spent plants at season's end rather than tilling them in, which removes overwintering pest and disease sites.

beginner: Eggplant does not keep well, so use it within a day or two for the best texture and flavor. At warm room temperature it goes soft and wrinkled fast, so keep it somewhere cool and out of the sun if you are not cooking it right away.
seasoned: Eggplant is a poor keeper and is best used within a day or two of picking, when its texture and mild flavor are at their best. Held at warm room temperature it softens and shrivels quickly, so a cool spot out of direct sun is better for a short hold. Unlike a winter squash, it does not cure or store, so harvest close to when you will cook it.

beginner: Eggplant does not like the cold. Keep it in the warmest part of the fridge, ideally around 45 to 50°F, loosely bagged so it does not dry out, and use it within a week. Stored too cold for too long it develops pitting and brown spots.
seasoned: Eggplant is chilling-sensitive: store it at a medium-cool 45 to 54°F with high humidity for up to about a week, not in the coldest part of the fridge. Below about 50°F for long it develops chilling injury, surface pitting, bronzing, and browning of the seeds and flesh, so a cool pantry or the warmest part of the refrigerator, loosely bagged to hold humidity, beats deep cold. Use within a week.

beginner: Do not freeze raw eggplant, as it turns mushy. Instead cook it first, by roasting or grilling, then cool it and freeze it in portions to use in cooked dishes later. It keeps a few months that way.
seasoned: Eggplant does not freeze well raw; the texture turns mushy. To freeze, slice and blanch it or, better, cook it first, for example roast or grill and puree it, then cool and freeze in portions for later dishes. Cooked or breaded-and-cooked eggplant freezes acceptably for a few months.

beginner: Eggplant is for eating fresh, not storing. Pick it shiny and young and cook it within a few days. If you need to keep it a little while, put it somewhere cool but not cold, around 45 to 50°F, loosely bagged. It bruises easily, so handle it gently, and keep it away from apples and other fruit that make it soften faster.
seasoned: Treat eggplant as a fresh-use crop, not a storage one. Pick it young and glossy and cook it within a few days. For a short hold, keep it at a medium-cool temperature (about 45 to 54°F) and high humidity, away from the coldest part of the refrigerator, since prolonged cold below 50°F causes chilling injury. Handle gently, as the skin bruises, and keep it away from ethylene-producing fruit, which hastens softening.

beginner: Pick an eggplant variety to match your space and season. For the classic big purple eggplant, grow Black Beauty, but give it a long, warm summer. Slim Asian types like Ichiban are easier, earlier, and very productive. Italian heirlooms like Rosa Bianca are beautiful and mild but slower. White types like Casper are eye-catching. If you have a short or cool season, or you are growing in a pot, choose a fast dwarf variety like Fairy Tale or Patio Baby.
seasoned: Choose by type, season, and space. The large globe types (Black Beauty and the many hybrids) give the familiar meaty slicing fruit but need a long, warm season; slender Asian types (Ichiban and kin) are earlier, more productive, tender, and less seedy; Italian heirlooms such as Rosa Bianca offer creamy, mild flesh prized for cooking but are slower. White types (Casper) are mild and striking but want sunscald protection. For containers, short seasons, or cool summers, the early dwarf hybrids Fairy Tale and Patio Baby ripen a crop fast on a compact plant, the safest choice where the warm season is short.

beginner: A healthy eggplant usually gives you several fruit over the season, around 4 to 8 for the big globe types and many more for slim Asian and baby types. Keeping it warm, evenly watered, and regularly picked makes the difference.
seasoned: A healthy full-size eggplant typically yields about 4 to 8 fruit over the season for large globe types, and many more for the slender Asian and small-fruited types, which set heavily and continuously. Steady warmth, even moisture, and regular picking are what carry a plant to the upper end; a single cold check or a flea-beetle-ravaged seedling pulls it down.

beginner: Once it gets going, eggplant keeps producing through the warm months, picking up in the heat of summer and slowing as fall cools down. Keep picking the fruit while it is young and shiny, since leaving big fruit on the plant makes it stop setting new ones.
seasoned: Eggplant bears continuously through the warm months once it starts, with production accelerating in midsummer heat (its strength relative to tomato) and slowing as nights cool in fall. Picking fruit while it is still immature and glossy keeps the plant flowering and setting; leaving fruit to over-ripen on the plant shuts down further set.

beginner: The two things that trip up first-year eggplant growers are planting too early into cold soil and letting flea beetles destroy the young plants. Wait until it is truly warm, cover the seedlings, and then just keep the plant watered, sunny, and picked.
seasoned: First-season growers most often lose eggplant to two things: setting plants out too early into cold soil, which stalls them for weeks, and flea beetles shredding unprotected seedlings. Wait for real warmth, protect young plants with row cover, and the rest is steady water, sun, and regular picking.

beginner: In warm conditions, seeds sprout in roughly one to two weeks, sending up two seed leaves first. Cool soil makes them slow or fail.
seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 7 to 14 days in warm conditions; bottom heat of 75 to 85°F is ideal, and cool soil delays or prevents germination. Two seed leaves emerge first.

beginner: Plant seeds about a quarter inch deep in a warm spot, ideally on a heat mat, and keep the soil damp until they sprout. Eggplant likes it warmer than tomatoes to come up.
seasoned: Sow about a quarter inch deep in warm flats with bottom heat (75 to 85°F), keeping the mix evenly moist, not soggy. Eggplant germinates slower and warmer than tomato, so give it heat and patience.

beginner: Pretty star-shaped purple or white flowers appear. Eggplant flowers pollinate themselves, so you do not need more than one plant. A tiny eggplant forms behind each flower that sets. Some flowers drop in very hot or cold spells, which is normal.

seasoned: Rotate to a bed with no recent nightshade history, choose tolerant varieties or grafted plants on resistant rootstock, keep plants vigorous with steady water and feeding, and consider soil solarization where the disease is established.

beginner: You plant eggplant once for the season. A single planting keeps producing all through the warm months, so there is no need to replant every few weeks. In most places a later planting would not have time to fruit before frost. Only in very warm, nearly frost-free areas, or the hot desert, can you fit a second planting, and that is really a separate season.
seasoned: Eggplant is not a succession crop. One planting produces continuously through the whole warm season, so you set plants out once rather than at intervals. In most zones a later sowing would be caught by frost before its long warm season could finish. Only in the warmest, frost-free or near-frost-free zones, and in the low desert where the planting splits around midsummer heat, is a second seasonal window viable, and that is a separate season rather than a true succession.

beginner: Eggplant is a warm-season vegetable in the same family as tomatoes and peppers, grown for its shiny, smooth fruit. The big thing to know is that eggplant loves heat: it keeps producing through hot summer weather that makes tomatoes struggle, but it really dislikes the cold and will sulk for weeks if planted out too early. It is also slower than a tomato and needs a long, warm season, so you grow it from transplants set into warm soil a week or two after you would plant tomatoes, and you usually stake the plant once it is carrying fruit. You pick eggplant while it is young and glossy, not at its biggest, because once the skin goes dull the inside turns seedy and bitter. There are many kinds: big purple globes like Black Beauty, slim Asian types like Ichiban, beautiful Italian heirlooms like Rosa Bianca, white ones like Casper, and small container types like Patio Baby and Fairy Tale. The main things to get right are warmth (never rush it into cold soil), protecting young plants from flea beetles, watering steadily, and rotating it away from where tomatoes, peppers, or potatoes grew.
seasoned: Eggplant is a warm-season fruiting vegetable (Solanum melongena) in the nightshade family, a close relative of tomato and pepper grown for its glossy, immature fruit. Where it differs from tomato is instructive: eggplant is markedly more heat-loving, thriving and setting fruit through summer heat that makes tomato sulk and drop blossoms, while it is the more cold-sensitive of the two, stalling badly if set out before the soil and nights are reliably warm. It is also slower, wanting a long, warm season (roughly 100 to 120 days from seed, about 65 to 85 from transplant), so it is grown from transplants set into warm soil a week or two after tomatoes. Plants are bushy and often need staking once loaded with fruit. The crop is harvested young and glossy and picked continuously; a dull skin signals an over-mature, seedy, bitter fruit. Types span the large purple-black globes (Black Beauty), slender Asian fruit (Ichiban), Italian heirlooms (Rosa Bianca), white-skinned (Casper), and compact container varieties (Patio Baby, Fairy Tale). The season's shape is set by three things: a long warm runway with no cold checks, the signature early pest pressure of flea beetles on seedlings (plus the Colorado potato beetle later), and the soilborne wilts (verticillium, bacterial wilt) and fruit rots (phomopsis) that rotation and warm, well-drained soil hold off.

beginner: In cold areas eggplant is a one-crop-a-summer plant and the fussiest of the warm-season vegetables. Start seeds indoors about 8 weeks early, and plant out only when nights stay above 50°F and the soil is warm, after tomato time. Pick from midsummer until frost. In the very coldest zones it is a stretch, so grow fast varieties like Fairy Tale or Ichiban and warm the soil with black plastic.
seasoned: In cold zones eggplant is a single tight summer crop and is the most demanding of the warm-season fruiting vegetables here: start transplants indoors about 8 weeks early, then set them out only once nights hold above 50°F and the soil is warm, a week or two after tomatoes. Harvest continuously from midsummer until the first frost ends the plant. In the coldest zones (3 to 4) the season is marginal for eggplant, so choose fast dwarf or Asian varieties (Fairy Tale, Patio Baby, Ichiban), use black mulch and row cover, and treat a good crop as an achievement.

seasoned: Eggplant is the marginal warm-season crop here, the weakest fit of the garden nightshades for the maritime PNW's cool, marine-tempered summer. OSU's Oregon planting table (EM9027) calls it viable only in the Willamette Valley, transplanting in May about 9 weeks after an indoor start, and flags it 'not suitable' outdoors on the immediate coast. In the valley, site it in full sun with reflected heat, warm the soil ahead of transplanting, and lean on a fast, small-fruited variety; harvest realistically runs early August into mid October, closing well before the first frost as cool, wet weather stalls fruit sizing. On the coast, delay transplanting into June, pick the single warmest microsite available, and consider a tunnel or cloche, per WSU's guidance (EM057E) that eggplant needs the most supplemental warmth of the common vegetables; treat any coastal harvest as a bonus, not a given.

beginner: Tomatillos want soil that drains well and has some compost worked in, but they are not fussy and will do fine in poorer, drier ground than tomatoes tolerate. If water pools on your bed after rain or stays soggy, fix the drainage first, because soggy roots rot. Digging in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting is plenty. Avoid piling on rich manure or heavy nitrogen, which pushes big leafy plants with little fruit.
seasoned: Tomatillos perform best in well-drained loam or sandy loam with moderate organic matter, but they are markedly less demanding than tomatoes and tolerate lean, dry soils that would stress a tomato. Good drainage is the non-negotiable: waterlogged roots invite root rot. Working 2 to 3 inches of compost in before planting is sufficient. Resist heavy nitrogen or rich manure, which drives rank vegetative growth at the expense of fruit set.

beginner: Soil pH is a measure of acidity on a scale from 1 to 14, where 7 is neutral. Tomatillos do well across a fairly wide band, from about 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerate soils a little outside that. That makes them easier to place than many crops. Soils in the interior West (Arizona, Nevada, Utah) often run alkaline (above 7); tomatillos handle the upper end better than most vegetables, but a cheap soil test from your extension office tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Tomatillos are adaptable across roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0 and tolerate the 5.5 to 7.3 margins better than tomato, one reason they succeed in the alkaline soils of the interior West. As with other Solanaceae, the slightly-acidic-to-neutral band keeps phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium available; strongly acidic soil (below 5.5) raises blossom-end-rot risk through impaired calcium uptake. Most eastern and midwestern soils sit naturally in range.

beginner: Tomatillos are light feeders compared with tomatoes. Mix a little balanced fertilizer into the bed at planting, then sprinkle a small dose around each plant about a month and two months after transplanting. Go easy on nitrogen (the first number on the bag): too much makes a giant leafy plant with few fruit. Once the plant is loaded with fruit, you can stop feeding.
seasoned: A modest feeder. Incorporate a balanced fertilizer at planting, then side-dress lightly at about 4 and 8 weeks. Utah State suggests roughly 1 tablespoon of a nitrogen source per plant at those intervals. Excess nitrogen drives rank vegetative growth and delays fruiting, so keep N moderate and lean toward potassium once flowering begins.

beginner: Time to feed your tomatillos a light dose of balanced fertilizer to keep them productive.
seasoned: Time to side-dress tomatillos lightly; keep nitrogen moderate to favor fruit over foliage.

beginner: Look for the three numbers on the bag (the NPK ratio). A balanced or slightly-higher-potassium blend such as 10-10-10 or 5-10-10 is ideal. Avoid high-nitrogen lawn-style fertilizers, which give you leaves instead of fruit.
seasoned: balanced to high-K, e.g. 10-10-10 or 5-10-10; avoid high-N

beginner: A small handful, about 1 to 2 tablespoons of balanced fertilizer scratched into the soil 6 inches out from each plant, at about 4 weeks and again at 8 weeks. Water it in and keep it off the leaves and stem. Less is more with tomatillos.
seasoned: About 1 tablespoon of a nitrogen source per plant side-dressed at 4 and 8 weeks after transplanting, per Utah State University Extension, or roughly 1 pound of 10-10-10 per 100 square feet at the same intervals. Keep granules 6 inches off the stem and water in. Tomatillos need less feed than tomatoes; over-fertilizing with nitrogen is the classic all-leaves-no-fruit mistake.

beginner: Tomatillos get along with the same companions as tomatoes. Basil, marigolds, and nasturtiums are popular neighbors and may help with pests. The most important 'companion' is simply a second tomatillo plant, since they need each other to set fruit. Keep them away from other nightshades (tomatoes, peppers, potatoes), which share their diseases.
seasoned: Tomatillo companion guidance is largely inherited from tomato tradition with little crop-specific extension testing. The marigold/nematode and basil/aromatic-deterrent pairings are the usual suggestions, honestly labeled here as traditional or mechanistic rather than proven for this crop. The one evidence-backed rule is rotational: keep tomatillos away from other Solanaceae to avoid shared disease. And remember the obligate need for a second plant for pollination.

beginner: A traditional good neighbor. Basil's strong scent may keep some pests away, and it grows happily alongside tomatillos.
seasoned: Classic Solanaceae companion; aromatic basil may deter some pests. Traditional, low-risk, not extension-documented for tomatillo specifically.

beginner: Marigolds are a favorite companion. French marigolds can help with soil pests called nematodes, and they brighten the bed and draw in helpful insects.
seasoned: French marigolds suppress root-knot nematodes when grown as a dense planting; the best-documented companion claim in the tomato family, applied here by analogy.

beginner: Fennel releases substances that hold back the growth of many plants around it, so keep it away from tomatillos.
seasoned: Fennel is broadly allelopathic and a poor neighbor for most vegetables; the tomatillo interaction is traditional but consistent with fennel's known habit.

beginner: A slender yellow beetle with three black stripes down its back, often found on tomatillos in particular. The adults and their humpbacked larvae chew ragged holes in the leaves; the larvae carry their own dark excrement on their backs as camouflage.
seasoned: Adults (yellow with three black stripes) and humpbacked larvae skeletonize and hole foliage; larvae mask themselves with frass. Tomatillo is a preferred host.

beginner: Handpick adults and larvae into soapy water, the most effective control in a home garden. Knock egg clusters off leaf undersides. Neem oil helps with heavy larval pressure.
seasoned: Handpick adults, larvae, and orange egg clusters into soapy water. Neem or spinosad for heavy larval populations. Row cover until bloom (then remove for pollinators).

beginner: Check plants early and often, especially leaf undersides, and remove the first beetles before they build up. Clearing nightshade weeds nearby removes alternate hosts.
seasoned: Scout early, destroy first arrivals and egg masses, and eliminate volunteer nightshade hosts. Rotation reduces overwintering carryover.

beginner: A striped leaf beetle that favors tomatillo and other husk-tomatoes more than it bothers tomato.
seasoned: Lema daturaphila (three-lined potato beetle), a chrysomelid leaf beetle specializing on Solanaceae, notably the husk-tomatoes.

beginner: Large green caterpillars, up to 4 inches, with a horn on the rear. They strip leaves fast and leave dark pellets of frass below; you often spot the damage before the well-camouflaged caterpillar.
seasoned: Manduca quinquemaculata/sexta larvae defoliate rapidly; large green larvae with a caudal horn, frass below feeding sites.

beginner: Handpick (a UV flashlight at night makes them glow). Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) is effective on younger larvae. Leave any hornworm covered in white cocoons, those are parasitic wasps doing your work.
seasoned: Handpick; Bt (B. thuringiensis kurstaki) on early instars; spare wasp-parasitized larvae as a biocontrol reservoir.

beginner: Till in fall to disrupt overwintering pupae. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering insectary plants. Scout for frass.
seasoned: Fall tillage destroys soil pupae; insectary plantings support Cotesia parasitoids; routine frass scouting.

beginner: The larva of a large sphinx moth; a few can defoliate a plant quickly.
seasoned: Hornworm sphinx-moth larvae, shared across Solanaceae.

beginner: Tiny black beetles that jump like fleas when disturbed and pepper the leaves with small round shot-holes. Worst on young transplants; established tomatillos shrug off the damage.
seasoned: Numerous tiny shot-holes from Epitrix/Phyllotreta adults; thresholds matter mainly at the seedling stage.

beginner: Floating row cover over young plants, kaolin clay, or spinosad if pressure is heavy. Most established plants outgrow the damage and need no treatment.
seasoned: Row cover until established, kaolin clay film, spinosad under heavy pressure.

beginner: Protect transplants with row cover early. Keep plants vigorous; clean up nightshade weeds and debris where adults overwinter.
seasoned: Early row cover, weed sanitation, and plant vigor; tomatillos tolerate moderate feeding damage.

beginner: Several small Solanaceae-feeding beetles; cosmetic on a vigorous plant but stressful to seedlings.
seasoned: Solanaceous flea beetles overwintering in debris and field margins.

beginner: Fat gray-brown caterpillars that hide in the soil by day and chew through the stems of fresh transplants at the soil line overnight, toppling them.
seasoned: Noctuid larvae (Agrotis spp.) sever transplants at the soil line during the establishment window.

beginner: Push a cardboard or foil collar an inch into the soil around each transplant. Handpick at night. Bt or diatomaceous earth around stems helps.
seasoned: Stem collars, evening handpicking, Bt, diatomaceous-earth barriers.

beginner: Clear weeds and crop debris before planting; collars on every transplant; cultivate the bed ahead of setting plants to expose larvae.
seasoned: Pre-plant weed/residue removal and shallow cultivation; collar each transplant.

beginner: Night-feeding moth larvae that sever young stems at ground level.
seasoned: Cutworm moth larvae in soil and residue.

beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or black insects on growing tips and leaf undersides, sometimes with sticky honeydew and ants. Rarely a serious problem on tomatillos.
seasoned: Colonies on new growth and leaf undersides; honeydew and sooty mold possible. Generally minor on this crop.

beginner: Blast off with a water jet; insecticidal soap or neem for stubborn colonies. Marigolds and nasturtiums nearby draw aphid-eating beneficials.
seasoned: Water jet, insecticidal soap or neem on colonies, release or conserve beneficials.

beginner: Avoid excess nitrogen, which makes the soft growth aphids prefer. Encourage ladybugs and lacewings.
seasoned: Limit nitrogen, interplant insectary flowers, support natural enemies.

beginner: Small soft-bodied insects whose numbers can build in warm weather but seldom overwhelm a healthy tomatillo.
seasoned: Multiple aphid species; populations flush in warm weather.

beginner: A white, powdery dusting on the leaves, usually late in the season and in crowded, shaded plantings. It rarely does much harm to a vigorous tomatillo.
seasoned: White powdery colonies on leaf surfaces, favored by warm days and poor air movement; generally low-impact on this crop.

beginner: Improve airflow by spacing and staking; remove the worst leaves. Potassium-bicarbonate or sulfur sprays help if it spreads.
seasoned: Improve canopy airflow, prune affected leaves, apply potassium bicarbonate or sulfur.

beginner: Give plants full sun and wide spacing, and avoid crowding. Good air movement is the main prevention.
seasoned: Full sun, wide spacing, and staking; avoid dense, shaded plantings.

beginner: A fungus that coats leaf surfaces with white powder in warm, dry conditions with poor airflow.
seasoned: Powdery mildew fungi (e.g. Leveillula/Oidium); UC notes warm sunny exposure suppresses it.

beginner: Dark brown spots with faint target-like rings on the lower, older leaves, which then yellow and drop. Less common and less damaging on tomatillos than on tomatoes.
seasoned: Concentric-ringed Alternaria lesions on older foliage first, advancing upward; lower incidence than on tomato.

beginner: Remove and discard (do not compost) affected leaves. Mulch to stop soil splash. Copper sprays preventively if pressure is high.
seasoned: Sanitation of infected leaves, mulch against splash, preventive copper under pressure.

beginner: Rotate away from nightshades for 3 years, water at the base, and stake to keep foliage off the ground.
seasoned: 3-year Solanaceae rotation, base watering, staking, airflow.

beginner: A soilborne fungus splashed up onto lower leaves in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: Alternaria solani, favored by warm wet conditions and overhead moisture.

beginner: Mottled light-and-dark green or yellow patches on leaves, sometimes with puckering or stunting. Spread by aphids and by handling.
seasoned: Mosaic mottling, leaf distortion, and stunting from mosaic and related viruses; roguing is the only response.

beginner: There is no cure: pull and discard infected plants so they do not infect others. Control aphids and wash hands and tools.
seasoned: Rogue and destroy symptomatic plants; manage aphid vectors; sanitize hands and tools.

beginner: Buy healthy plants, manage aphids, avoid handling plants when wet, and do not use tobacco products near the plants.
seasoned: Healthy transplants, vector control, tool/hand hygiene, no tobacco contact.

beginner: Plant viruses (including tobacco/tomato mosaic) carried by insects or on hands and tools.

beginner: Most tomatillos you will see are green types like Toma Verde, which are tart and perfect for salsa verde. Purple kinds (Purple De Milpa) are a bit smaller and tangier and turn purple in the husk. seasoned: Rotate on a 3-year cycle away from all Solanaceae. Note that tomatillos self-seed freely from dropped fruit, so last year's bed often sprouts volunteers, pull them if they violate your rotation.

beginner: Tomatillos keep for a week or two on the counter if you leave the papery husks on, which protect the fruit. Keep them in a single layer out of the sun, and do not peel or wash them until you are about to cook.
seasoned: Up to a week or two at cool room temperature with the husks left on. The husk is a natural wrapper that slows moisture loss. Keep them in a single layer out of direct sun. Do not husk or wash until you are ready to use them.

beginner: Pop them in a paper bag (husks on) in the fridge and they will keep 2 to 3 weeks, sometimes longer. Tomatillos, unlike tomatoes, are fine in the fridge. A cool pantry around 50 to 60°F keeps them even longer.
seasoned: Refrigerate husk-on in a paper bag for 2 to 3 weeks; some hold a month or more. Unlike tomatoes, tomatillos are not harmed by refrigeration. For long keeping, store at 50 to 60°F with about 60% humidity, where they last for months.

beginner: To keep them for months, peel off the husks, wash, and freeze the whole fruit in sealed bags. Frozen tomatillos are perfect for salsa verde and cooked sauces later, good for 8 to 12 months.
seasoned: Freeze for months: husk, wash, and freeze whole or sliced in sealed bags. They freeze well for cooked uses like salsa verde and sauces, holding 8 to 12 months.

beginner: Always store them with the husks on; the husk is what keeps them fresh. Peel and rinse off the sticky coating only when you are ready to cook.
seasoned: Store husk-on; the calyx is the fruit's natural protective wrapper. Husk and wash off the sticky resin only at use. A sticky surface under the husk is normal, not spoilage.

beginner: Indeterminate (as explained earlier in this guide) means the plant keeps growing and producing fruit all season long, rather than ripening everything at once and stopping. Almost all cherry tomato varieties work this way, which is part of why they're productive over such a long window. Because they keep growing, they need a sturdy cage or stake to stay upright. A few compact varieties like Tumbling Tom are determinate (they set fruit and stop), which makes them better choices for small containers or hanging baskets.
seasoned: Cherry tomatoes are almost always indeterminate: they grow, flower, and fruit all season until frost kills them. No stopping needed, but they need strong staking or caging. Some compact varieties (Tumbling Tom, Patio Choice) are technically determinate.
