beginner: Strawberries grow best in loose, rich soil that drains well, like a sandy loam. Their roots are shallow, so they rot if the ground stays soggy. If your soil is heavy clay or puddles after rain, build a raised bed or a mounded row about 12 inches tall and plant into that. Mixing 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting gives the roots a good start.
seasoned: Strawberries want a fertile, well-drained sandy loam or loam with steady but not excessive moisture. The roots are shallow and fibrous, so they suffocate in soil that stays waterlogged for more than a day or two, and root rots follow. On heavy or slow-draining ground, plant into a raised bed or mounded row about 12 inches high so water drains away from the crowns. Work 1 to 2 inches of compost or aged organic matter into the bed before planting to lift organic matter above 3 percent.

beginner: Strawberries prefer soil on the slightly acidic side, roughly pH 5.6 to 6.5. A cheap test kit shows where you are. Garden sulfur lowers a too-high number; garden lime raises a too-low one. Both take a few months to take effect, so test and adjust the season before you plant.
seasoned: Aim for slightly acidic soil in the range of pH 5.6 to 6.5. Test the bed a season ahead so there is time to adjust: elemental sulfur brings a high reading down, and ground dolomitic limestone raises a low one. Both amendments take months to move the soil, so apply them well before the crowns go in.

beginner: Strawberries mainly need nitrogen, and when you feed depends on the type. The first year, give a little fertilizer two or three times spread across the season rather than one big dose. After that, the rule for June-bearing plants is simple: do not feed in spring, because it grows lots of leaves but not more berries, and the thick leaves trap dampness that causes mold. Feed them once instead, right after harvest when you cut the plants back. Day-neutral and everbearing plants, which fruit all summer, get small amounts spread across the months instead. If your soil is sandy, feed smaller amounts more often.
seasoned: Strawberry feeding is nitrogen-driven and timed to the planting model. In the first year, apply a total of about 0.5 to 0.8 ounces of actual nitrogen per 10 feet of row, split across the season: a small dose one to two weeks after planting, a second about a month later, and a third roughly two months after planting. On established June-bearing beds, do not feed in spring; spring nitrogen drives leaf growth, not fruit, and a dense canopy traps moisture and promotes gray mold. Instead, fertilize once at renovation, just after harvest, to build the flower buds for next year. Established day-neutral and everbearing plants, which fruit all season, take the same total split into monthly doses through summer with an optional August feeding. On sandy soil, divide every rate into more frequent, lighter applications.

beginner: Your June-bearing strawberries are ready for their after-harvest cutback and feeding. Mow the old leaves, then give the plants a balanced fertilizer and water it in to help next year's berries.
seasoned: Time to renovate and feed your June-bearing strawberries. Mow the old leaves, narrow the row, then apply about 0.4 to 0.6 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet of row and water it in to set next year's crop.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 16-16-16 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is a good all-purpose choice. Follow the label rate for the row length you are feeding, and water it in after spreading.
seasoned: A balanced analysis such as 16-16-16 works well. Rates are given as actual nitrogen per length of row, so divide the nitrogen you need by the decimal nitrogen fraction of your product: about 0.4 to 0.6 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet at renovation works out to roughly 2.5 to 3.75 ounces of 16-16-16 per 10-foot row.

beginner: A rough guide: feed a new bed lightly two or three times the first year. Feed an established June-bearing bed once, after harvest. Feed day-neutral or everbearing plants a little each month through summer. Use the label rate on your fertilizer for the length of your row.
seasoned: First year: about 0.5 to 0.8 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet of row total, in two to three splits. Established June-bearers: about 0.4 to 0.6 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet of row, all at once at renovation. Day-neutral and everbearing: about 0.1 to 0.2 ounces of nitrogen per 10 feet each month after spring growth begins, with an optional August dose.

beginner: The most important placement rule for strawberries is about what grew there before, not what you plant beside them. Do not put strawberries where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries grew recently. Those plants can leave a soil disease called Verticillium wilt behind, and it attacks strawberries too and stays in the soil for years. Also keep weeds out, since strawberries have shallow roots and lose out to weeds easily. The companion plants listed above are nice, low-risk neighbors, but they are garden tradition rather than a proven way to grow more fruit.
seasoned: The one firm rule for strawberry placement is rotation, not companionship: do not plant strawberries where tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries have recently grown, because all of them host Verticillium wilt, a soilborne fungus that also attacks strawberries and lingers in the ground for years. Keep the same crops out of the bed for several years afterward. Beyond that, strawberries compete poorly with weeds because their roots are shallow, so the most valuable neighbor is bare, weed-free soil rather than any particular plant. The good-companion pairings above are traditional and low-risk, not documented yield boosters.

beginner: Beans are an easy, friendly neighbor for strawberries. They do not compete much and add a little nitrogen to the soil, though do not expect them to make your berries bigger.
seasoned: Bush beans bring nitrogen fixation to the strawberry bed. Working with Rhizobium bacteria on their roots, they pull atmospheric nitrogen into a plant-available form that lightly benefits strawberries as moderate feeders, and their upright, shallow habit does not compete much with low-running strawberry crowns. As with most legume pairings, the nitrogen mostly reaches neighbors as the bean roots break down, so treat it as gentle soil-building across the season rather than an immediate feed.

beginner: Lettuce fits nicely along the edge of a strawberry bed while the berries are still small, using space the strawberries are not using yet.
seasoned: Lettuce makes good use of the open space in a strawberry planting, especially in the first season before the strawberries fill in and run. It is shallow-rooted and quick, so it crops and clears before the strawberries need the room, and its low canopy helps shade soil and suppress weeds between crowns. A space-and-timing pairing rather than a pest or flavor one.

beginner: Borage is a herb with blue flowers that bees love. A few plants near your strawberries can bring in more bees, which helps the flowers turn into well-shaped berries.
seasoned: Borage is the traditional strawberry companion, and it is worth separating what it reliably does from what is folklore. Reliably: borage is a powerful bee magnet, and better pollinator visitation gives strawberries more complete fruit set and fewer misshapen berries, a real, mechanism-backed benefit. The older claim that borage directly improves strawberry flavor and yield through the soil is widely repeated but unsupported by controlled study, so lean on borage for pollination, not as a flavor additive.

beginner: Ragged holes eaten in the berries and leaves, with shiny slime trails. Worst in damp, mulchy beds and wet weather.
seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in ripe fruit and leaves, with slime trails, worst in damp, heavily mulched beds and wet weather.

beginner: Slugs, which hide in damp mulch and eat the soft ripe berries at night.
seasoned: Slugs, which shelter in deep or wet mulch and feed at night on soft ripe fruit.

beginner: Do not pile on thick straw in summer, keep the bed clean, and pick ripe berries quickly.
seasoned: Avoid deep straw mulch during the growing season, keep the bed tidy, and harvest ripe fruit promptly.

beginner: Start here: clear away damp hiding places, do not pile on thick straw mulch in summer, and keep the bed tidy so slugs have nowhere cool and wet to shelter by day. Pick ripe berries promptly so there is less soft fruit to draw them.
seasoned: Removing daytime shelter, avoiding deep summer mulch, and prompt harvest cut the slug population at its source; keep ripening fruit up off wet ground.

beginner: Hunt slugs after dark with a flashlight and pick them off, set board or beer traps for them to gather in, and ring the bed with copper strips they will not cross. Done regularly, handpicking alone can be very effective.
seasoned: Nighttime handpicking, board and beer-baited traps, and 2-inch copper barriers steadily lower numbers; empty and refresh traps every few days, and renew copper once it tarnishes.

beginner: If traps and cleanup are not enough, scatter iron phosphate slug bait on the soil, not on the plants. It is much safer around pets, kids, and wildlife than the old metaldehyde baits, though slugs take several days to die.
seasoned: Iron phosphate bait makes slugs stop feeding and is safer around pets and wildlife than metaldehyde; it works best alongside habitat removal, not alone, and takes several days to a week to kill.

beginner: Soft, sunken spots on ripening berries, with tiny maggots inside. It gets worse later in the season.
seasoned: Soft, collapsing spots on ripening and ripe fruit; tiny larvae feed inside berries. Populations build through the season, so later fruit is hit hardest.

beginner: A small fruit fly that lays eggs in the berries as they start to color, and the maggots eat the fruit from inside.
seasoned: A vinegar fly that lays eggs in coloring fruit; the larvae feed inside as the berry ripens.

beginner: Keep up with picking, never leave overripe berries on the plant, and use fine netting if the flies are bad.
seasoned: Harvest on a tight schedule, never leave overripe fruit on the plant, and exclude adults with fine netting where pressure is high.

beginner: Start here: pick all the ripe berries often and completely, and remove and destroy any overripe or damaged fruit. Overripe berries left on the plant are where this fly breeds, so tight, clean picking is your strongest everyday tool.
seasoned: Frequent, complete harvest and destroying culls removes the ripening fruit SWD breeds in; sanitation is the backbone, since populations build through the season and hit later fruit hardest.

beginner: Hang a cup of apple cider vinegar with a drop of dish soap near the berries to catch the flies. It tells you when they have arrived so you can time the other steps; it is a warning tool, not control.
seasoned: Vinegar traps checked weekly from before ripening detect adult arrival to time harvest and exclusion; monitoring, not control.

beginner: Cover the planting with very fine mesh, fine enough to stop no-see-ums, before the first berries start to color, and seal it to the ground. It physically keeps the flies off the fruit.
seasoned: Fine mesh, about 1 mm, installed before fruit colors and sealed at every edge down to the ground, excludes adult SWD; put it on too late and you trap flies inside with the fruit.

beginner: If pressure is high on a later crop, spinosad is the organic spray with the best track record on this fly, but it is hard on bees while wet, so spray at dusk and mind the days-to-harvest on the label.
seasoned: Spinosad is the most effective organic material against SWD; rotate it to slow resistance, spray at dusk to spare bees, and observe the pre-harvest interval on a crop you pick continuously.

beginner: A last resort for heavy pressure only. It kills fast but hits bees and beneficials, and on a crop you pick every few days the days-to-harvest limit really matters, so read the label.
seasoned: Rescue-only; broad-spectrum and disruptive, with a pre-harvest interval that is limiting on continuously harvested strawberries. Time it to dusk, off bloom.

beginner: Lumpy, dented berries with a pinched, seedy tip. Most common on day-neutral plants in summer.
seasoned: Catfaced fruit, dimpled and pinched at the tip with seedy, woody patches; most noticeable on day-neutrals in summer.

beginner: A small bug that feeds on the flowers and young fruit, which makes the berry tip grow lumpy.
seasoned: Lygus bugs feeding on developing flowers and fruit, which disrupts seed and berry development at the tip.

beginner: Pull broadleaf weeds near the bed, since the bugs breed on them, and keep the area tidy.
seasoned: Control broadleaf weeds that host lygus near the planting and keep the bed clean through the season.

beginner: Start here, and this is the main control: keep broadleaf weeds down in and around the bed, since that is where these bugs breed and shelter. Watch the flowers while fruiting so you catch a buildup early.
seasoned: Removing the broadleaf weeds that host lygus in and around the planting is the primary lever; scout flowers through fruiting, since the damage that catfaces fruit is done at bloom.

beginner: Minute pirate bugs, big-eyed bugs, and parasitic wasps feed on the young bugs, so avoid broad sprays that would kill them. Because lygus fly in from weeds and field edges, though, natural enemies only help so much on their own.
seasoned: Conserving natural enemies gives partial suppression, but lygus are mobile and reinvade from surrounding vegetation, so biological control is a supporting step, not a standalone fix; weed sanitation matters more.

beginner: Only if the bugs are ruining a lot of fruit and weeding has not been enough. A fast synthetic that also kills bees and beneficials, so keep it off flowers and treat it as a last resort.
seasoned: Rescue-only; broad-spectrum and disruptive to the natural enemies above, with a label pre-harvest interval. Lygus are only moderately susceptible, so it does not substitute for weed control.

beginner: Groups of tiny soft bugs on new leaves and leaf undersides, leaving a sticky film. They can also spread plant viruses.
seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new growth and leaf undersides, with sticky honeydew and sometimes sooty mold; aphids can also transmit strawberry viruses.

beginner: Aphids, tiny bugs that suck plant juices and multiply fast on new leaves.
seasoned: Aphids feeding on plant sap, building up quickly on tender new growth.

beginner: Start with clean plants, and do not over-feed, since lots of soft new growth attracts aphids.
seasoned: Start with clean, certified plants to limit virus introduction, and avoid excess nitrogen that flushes soft, aphid-prone growth.

beginner: Start here: do not overfeed. Too much nitrogen pushes out soft new growth that aphids multiply on, so feed modestly. Starting with clean, certified plants also limits the viruses aphids can spread.
seasoned: Modest nitrogen keeps growth steady and less aphid-prone; clean certified stock limits virus introduction, since aphids also vector strawberry viruses.

beginner: A strong jet of water knocks aphids off the leaves, and most cannot climb back on. Do it early in the day so the leaves dry quickly.
seasoned: A forceful spray dislodges colonies from sturdy plants; spray early so foliage dries and disease is not encouraged.

beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings, and tiny parasitic wasps eat aphids and usually keep them in check for free. Protect them by not reaching for broad sprays.
seasoned: Resident ladybugs, lacewings, syrphid larvae, and parasitic wasps hold aphids down; avoiding broad-spectrum sprays and managing the ants that tend them is what keeps them working.

beginner: For a heavy infestation, insecticidal soap kills the aphids you spray directly. It only works while wet, so coat them well, and it spares beneficials once dry.
seasoned: Contact soap smothers aphids with no residual, so coverage and repeat sprays matter; it spares dry-surface beneficials.

beginner: Neem oil is another low-residue option that coats and disrupts aphids. Do not spray it in heat above 90°F or on a drought-stressed plant, and spray at dusk to avoid wetting bees.
seasoned: Neem works by contact smothering and as an antifeedant and growth regulator; low toxicity to bees but, as a contact spray, apply at dusk. Avoid above 90°F or on stressed plants.

beginner: Rarely needed for aphids, and a last resort only. It kills fast but hits the ladybugs and other good bugs too, which can make aphids worse later, so keep it off flowers.
seasoned: Rescue-only and usually counterproductive on aphids, since it removes the natural enemies that regulate them and can trigger resurgence. Observe the label pre-harvest interval.

beginner: Leaves look speckled and bronzed, with fine webbing underneath. Worst in hot, dry, dusty weather, and bad cases weaken the plants.
seasoned: Fine stippling and bronzing of leaves with faint webbing on undersides, worst in hot, dry, dusty conditions; heavy infestations weaken plants and reduce yield.

beginner: Tiny mites under the leaves that multiply fast when it is hot and dry.
seasoned: Tiny mites that feed on the underside of leaves and multiply rapidly in hot, dry weather.

beginner: Keep plants watered in hot weather and avoid letting them get dusty and dry.
seasoned: Avoid drought stress and dusty conditions, and keep plants well watered in heat.

beginner: Start here: keep plants well watered, since spider mites flare on hot, dry, drought-stressed plants, and knock the mites back with a hard spray of water to the leaf undersides, which also raises the humidity they dislike. Keeping the bed from getting dusty helps too.
seasoned: Mites explode on drought-stressed, dusty plants, so steady watering is preventive; a forceful water spray to leaf undersides dislodges them and raises humidity. This foundation often keeps mites below the threshold that needs any spray.

beginner: Predatory mites and other tiny good bugs feed on spider mites and often control them on their own. Avoid broad sprays, including too much sulfur, that would kill these helpers.
seasoned: Predatory mites are the key natural enemy; conserve them by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays and sulfur, which set them back.

beginner: For a bad case, horticultural oil smothers the mites on contact. Cover the leaf undersides well, and do not spray in heat above 90°F or on a drought-stressed plant.
seasoned: Narrow-range oil knocks mites back by smothering; coverage of leaf undersides is everything. Avoid above 90°F, on stressed plants, or within 2 weeks of sulfur.

beginner: Neem oil is another contact option that coats and disrupts the mites. Same rules: thorough coverage, not in high heat, and spray at dusk to avoid bees.
seasoned: Neem gives partial mite control by contact and as a growth disruptor; repeat coverage is needed, and avoid high heat and stressed plants.

beginner: Sulfur is a last resort here. It does knock back spider mites, but it also harms the predatory mites that were helping you, so use it only if the softer steps have failed, and never in heat above 90°F.
seasoned: Sulfur is a protectant miticide but harms predatory mites, so it can trade a short knockdown for lost biological control; reserve it, keep a 2-week gap from any oil spray, and avoid above 90°F.

beginner: Leaf edges notched as if cut with pinking shears, and plants that wilt or collapse because grubs have eaten the roots and crown.
seasoned: Notched leaf margins from night-feeding adults, and stunted, wilting, or collapsing plants whose roots and crowns have been eaten by larvae.

beginner: Beetles whose adults chew the leaf edges at night and whose grubs eat the roots underground.
seasoned: Weevils whose adults notch leaves at night and whose larvae feed underground on roots and crowns.

beginner: Start new beds in a fresh spot, since the grubs build up in old beds, and use clean plants.
seasoned: Rotate to a fresh site when starting a new bed, since larvae build up in older plantings, and start with clean stock.

beginner: Start a new bed in a fresh spot away from old strawberry plantings, since the grubs build up in beds over the years. Begin with clean, healthy plants so you are not importing them.
seasoned: Siting a new planting away from older, infested beds starves the soil larvae, which build up over successive years; start with clean stock.

beginner: Pull and destroy badly infested plants in the fall, when the grubs are feeding on the roots and crown, so they do not carry over.
seasoned: Removing and destroying heavily infested plants in fall reduces the overwintering larval population.

beginner: On warm evenings the adult weevils come out to feed and notch the leaf edges. Go out with a flashlight and pick them off, since they cannot fly and are easy to catch by hand.
seasoned: The flightless adults feed at night; handpicking or shaking them onto a cloth after dark removes egg-laying females before the next generation of root-feeding larvae.

beginner: Beneficial nematodes are microscopic good worms you water into moist, warm soil. They hunt the grubs underground and are safe for people and pets.
seasoned: Entomopathogenic nematodes drenched into moist soil at roughly 60°F to 90°F infect the root-feeding larvae; time it to when larvae are present and keep the soil moist.

beginner: A last resort, and only against the adult beetles at night, since sprays cannot reach the grubs down in the soil. It hits bees and beneficials, so keep it off flowers and use it sparingly.
seasoned: Rescue-only and limited to adults, since foliar sprays do not reach soil larvae; broad-spectrum and disruptive, with a label pre-harvest interval. Nematodes are the better tool for the root-feeding stage.

beginner: Ripe berries pecked or half-eaten, often the best red ones taken right before you pick them.
seasoned: Pecked and partly eaten ripe berries, often the first fully colored fruit taken just before you would pick it.

beginner: Birds that go for the ripe red berries.
seasoned: Birds attracted to ripening red fruit.

beginner: Put netting on before the first berries ripen, not after the birds have already found them.
seasoned: Net the planting before the first fruit ripens rather than after birds find it.

beginner: Shiny, moving, or noisy things like reflective tape and scare-eye balloons can frighten birds off for a while, but birds get used to them fast, so move them around and swap types at least weekly. On their own they do not reliably protect the fruit.
seasoned: Visual and noise deterrents reduce pressure but birds habituate; rotate device types and do not leave one combination up more than a week. Best paired with netting, not relied on alone.

beginner: The reliable fix is bird netting draped over hoops so it sits off the berries, with the edges tucked to the ground so birds cannot get underneath. Put it on before the first berries ripen, not after the birds have found the patch.
seasoned: Netting on a hoop or PVC frame excludes birds; laid straight on the plants they still peck through it, so support it off the canopy, extend it to the ground, and tie the edges. Install before the first fruit colors.

beginner: Berries turn soft and rot, then grow a gray fuzz. It often starts where a berry touches the ground or another berry, and spreads quickly.
seasoned: A soft, tan rot of green and ripe fruit that quickly becomes a fuzzy gray mold, often starting where berries touch soil, mulch, or another berry. It spreads fast through a picked basket.

beginner: A mold that lives on old dead leaves and takes hold when it is wet while the plants are flowering and fruiting.
seasoned: The fungus Botrytis cinerea, which overwinters on dead leaves and thrives when it rains during bloom and fruit development.

beginner: Do not feed June-bearing plants in spring, since extra leaves trap dampness. Water at the soil, give plants room to breathe, and pick ripe berries often.
seasoned: Avoid spring nitrogen on June-bearers, which thickens the canopy and traps moisture. Water at the base rather than overhead, space plants for airflow, and pick fruit promptly and often.

beginner: Start here: lay straw around and between the plants so the ripening berries sit up off the wet soil. Fruit that is not touching damp ground is far less likely to rot with gray mold.
seasoned: A good straw layer keeps fruit off wet soil and cuts rain splash, lowering Botrytis pressure; a foundational cultural step, though it reduces rather than eliminates rot.

beginner: Give plants room and water at the soil rather than overhead so the canopy dries quickly. Gray mold takes hold in damp, crowded, still foliage.
seasoned: Wide spacing and base watering shorten leaf and fruit wetness, denying Botrytis the sustained moisture it needs; an open canopy dries fast after rain.

beginner: Pick off and destroy moldy berries the moment you see them, since the mold spreads fast from one berry to the next, and clear away old dead leaves where it overwinters. Go easy on spring nitrogen, especially on June-bearers, since the extra soft leaves thicken the canopy and trap the dampness the mold loves.
seasoned: Remove infected fruit immediately and clean out old leaves at renovation and early spring; avoid spring nitrogen on June-bearers, which thickens the canopy and traps moisture. There is no home spray that cures it, so these cultural steps are the whole program.

beginner: Dark, sunken round spots on the berries. The disease can also rot the crown and runners, making plants wilt and die in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: Dark, sunken, circular lesions on fruit; the fungus can also infect crowns and runners, causing wilting and plant death in warm, wet spells.

beginner: A fungus that thrives in warm, wet, humid weather and splashes around in the rain.
seasoned: Colletotrichum fungi, favored by warm, humid, rainy conditions during fruit development and spread by splashing water.

beginner: Buy clean, certified plants, water at the base, and avoid spots where this disease has been a problem before.
seasoned: Start with certified disease-free plants, avoid overhead watering, and do not plant into ground with a recent history of the disease.

beginner: Start with clean, certified disease-free plants and, where anthracnose has been a problem, choose a resistant variety. Do not plant into ground with a recent history of the disease.
seasoned: Certified clean stock and resistant cultivars are the foundation, since the fungus arrives on infected transplants and persists in old sites; avoid replanting into a recent-history bed.

beginner: Lay straw mulch to keep berries off the soil and cut down on rain splashing spores up onto the fruit, which is how this disease spreads.
seasoned: Mulch reduces the rain and irrigation splash that disperses Colletotrichum spores; water at the base rather than overhead.

beginner: Pull off and destroy diseased berries and plants promptly, and give plants room so the canopy dries. Watering at the soil instead of overhead keeps spores from splashing around.
seasoned: Prompt removal of diseased fruit and plants lowers inoculum; base watering and airflow limit the warm, wet, splashing conditions the fungus needs.

beginner: If the cultural steps are not holding in a warm, wet season, a copper spray can protect healthy fruit, but it must go on before infection and cannot cure berries already rotting. Copper is toxic to fish and builds up in the soil, so use it sparingly.
seasoned: Fixed copper is a protectant only, applied before infection during warm wet spells; it will not cure established rot. Copper accumulates in soil and harms aquatic life, so limit repeat use.

beginner: Leaf edges curl upward and turn purple, with a white dusty coating. In some varieties the berries taste bitter.
seasoned: Upward cupping and purpling of leaf edges with a white powdery film; in some cultivars infected fruit tastes bitter.

beginner: A fungus that spreads when the air is humid but the leaves are dry.
seasoned: A fungus that, unlike most strawberry diseases, spreads in dry conditions with high humidity and moderate temperatures.

beginner: Give plants room, keep them from getting crowded, and choose mildew-resistant varieties.
seasoned: Space plants well, avoid dense canopies, and select tolerant cultivars.

beginner: The easiest fix is to grow a mildew-resistant variety, especially if it keeps coming back or if it makes your berries taste bitter.
seasoned: Cultivar resistance varies widely and is the lowest-effort durable control; worth choosing where mildew recurs, since some cultivars also develop off-flavored fruit.

beginner: Give plants room and keep the canopy from getting crowded. Unlike most strawberry diseases, mildew spreads when the air is humid even if the leaves stay dry, so airflow still helps. Pick off the worst-affected leaves.
seasoned: Wide spacing and an open canopy lower the humidity mildew favors, since it spreads in dry-leaf, high-humidity conditions; remove badly affected leaves.

beginner: If mildew is heavy, sulfur is the organic spray, applied before it takes hold. Some strawberry varieties are sensitive to it, so test a few plants first, and never spray in heat above 90°F.
seasoned: Sulfur is a protectant for powdery mildew, but some strawberry cultivars are sulfur-sensitive, so spot-test first; avoid above 90°F and within 2 weeks of oil, and note it harms predatory mites.

beginner: Plants are stunted and wilt, then collapse in spring. If you cut a root open, the center is reddish-brown. It is worst in heavy, wet soil that drains poorly.
seasoned: Stunted, wilting plants that collapse in spring; roots are rotted and, when sliced lengthwise, show a reddish-brown core. Worst in heavy, wet, poorly drained soil.

beginner: A soil fungus that builds up in cold, soggy ground and stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: Soilborne Phytophthora fungi that thrive in cold, saturated soils and persist for years.

beginner: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds, buy certified plants, and pick resistant varieties if your ground stays wet.
seasoned: Plant only in well-drained soil or raised beds, start with certified plants, and choose red-stele-resistant cultivars on wet sites.

beginner: This is a soilborne rot with no home cure, so prevention is everything. On wet ground, the single most important choice is a red-stele-resistant variety, and always start with certified disease-free plants.
seasoned: Red-stele-resistant cultivars are the primary control for a soilborne Phytophthora that persists for years and cannot be cured; pair with certified clean stock.

beginner: Plant only in well-drained soil or raised beds, since this rot thrives in cold, soggy ground, and do not replant strawberries into a bed where it has struck, because the fungus lingers in the soil for years. Pull and destroy any collapsing plants.
seasoned: Improve drainage with raised beds and rotate off infested ground for years, since the pathogen is soilborne and persistent; there is no chemical rescue, so remove and destroy affected plants. Drainage, a fresh well-drained site, and resistant varieties are the whole game.

beginner: The outer leaves wilt, dry at the edges, and flop down while the middle leaves stay up. Plants are stunted and may die, often as the berries are forming.
seasoned: Outer leaves wilt, dry at the margins, and collapse while inner leaves may stay upright; plants are stunted and may die. Symptoms often appear as fruit load increases.

beginner: A soil fungus that also attacks tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, and other berries, and stays in the soil for years.
seasoned: The soilborne fungus Verticillium, which also infects tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, and brambles and persists in soil for years.

beginner: Do not plant strawberries where you recently grew tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, or other berries, and start with certified clean plants.
seasoned: Do not plant strawberries after or near tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries, and start with certified disease-free stock on a clean site.

beginner: There is no cure once a plant wilts, so it comes down to variety and site. Choose a verticillium-resistant strawberry variety and start with certified disease-free plants.
seasoned: Resistant cultivars and certified clean stock are the primary controls for a soilborne fungus with no rescue treatment; variety choice does much of the work.

beginner: Do not plant strawberries where you recently grew tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries, since verticillium builds up on all of them and lingers in the soil for years. Pick a clean site with no recent history.
seasoned: The fungus infects many hosts, including tomato, pepper, eggplant, potato, and brambles, and persists for years, so rotate onto ground clear of those crops; site choice is the main lever.

beginner: Pull and destroy plants as they wilt, so they do not add to what is in the soil, and keep the bed clean.
seasoned: Removing affected plants limits soil buildup; there is no spray, so sanitation supports the rotation and variety program rather than curing anything.

beginner: Give strawberries about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week while they are growing. Water more often in hot weather or sandy soil, and keep new plants well watered since their roots are still small.
seasoned: About 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week through the growing season, adjusted for vigor, growth stage, soil, and weather. On sandy soil and in heat, water more often and more lightly. Newly set plants have undeveloped roots and stress easily, so irrigate several times a week until established.

beginner: Water enough to wet the soil about 6 inches to a foot deep, so the roots stay moist but never soggy. Strawberry roots are shallow and rot if they sit in water, so do not overdo it.
seasoned: Wet the soil to a depth of about 6 inches to 1 foot with each irrigation, enough that the shallow root zone does not fully dry between waterings, but never so much that water stands. Standing water harms strawberries even for a day or two.

beginner: The best way to water strawberries is at the base, not over the leaves, because wet leaves and fruit lead to mold. A drip line or soaker hose along the row works well; if you water by hand, water the soil rather than the plants.
seasoned: Drip irrigation is ideal: it keeps water off the foliage and fruit, which reduces gray mold and weeds. Run a single drip line per row with half-gallon emitters spaced about every 12 inches, or use a soaker hose while monitoring soil moisture.

beginner: If the soil is wet but the plants still wilt, the leaves yellow, or the crowns turn soft and mushy, you are watering too much or the ground drains poorly. Soggy soil rots strawberry roots.
seasoned: Wilting despite wet soil, yellowing lower leaves, and soft or collapsing crowns signal waterlogging and the root and crown rots that follow. Standing water and slow-draining ground are the usual causes.

beginner: Drooping, dull leaves with dry soil, and small berries, mean the plants need more water. Strawberries especially need water while the fruit is filling out, or the berries stay small.
seasoned: Dull, wilting leaves in dry soil and small, soft berries point to drought stress. Because fruit is mostly water, under-watering during fruit development directly cuts size and yield.

beginner: Keep new plants evenly watered so they do not dry out.
seasoned: Keep new plantings evenly moist; shallow, undeveloped roots stress quickly.

beginner: Water evenly while berries are filling out, and keep the fruit off wet ground.
seasoned: Even moisture during fruit sizing drives berry size and quality; keep fruit off wet soil.

beginner: Water right after you cut the plants back and feed them, to help them regrow.
seasoned: Irrigate right after renovation to push fresh leaf and runner growth.

beginner: Dormant plants need almost no water; just do not let them sit in soggy soil.
seasoned: Dormant beds need little water; avoid waterlogged soil over winter.

beginner: Try to keep water off the berries and leaves. If you can only water from above, do it in the morning so everything dries out during the day and does not stay damp.
seasoned: Keep water off ripening fruit and foliage where possible. Overhead watering wets the canopy and raises gray mold pressure, so if you must use it, water early in the day so leaves and fruit dry quickly.

beginner: Two times are most important for watering: while the berries are forming and ripening, and again in late summer to early fall when the plant is setting up next year's crop. Keep the soil from drying out during both.
seasoned: On established beds, two periods matter most: from just after bloom through harvest, when fruit is sizing, and from late summer into early fall, when next year's flower buds form. Do not let plants stress for water in either window.

beginner: There is no hardening-off step for strawberries. You plant them either as dormant bare-root crowns, which look like a clump of roots with a small bud, or as small potted plants from a garden center. Neither one was raised soft indoors, so you can plant them straight out without the week of gradual exposure that tender seedlings need.
seasoned: Not applicable. Strawberries are set as dormant bare-root crowns (or as potted plugs), not as tender indoor-raised seedlings, so there is no hardening-off step. Dormant crowns go straight into the ground in their planting window; potted plugs from a garden center are already acclimated and can be set out the same way.

beginner: The most important thing is planting depth. A strawberry has a thick short stem called the crown. Set it so the middle of the crown sits right at soil height: roots just under the surface, the little growing bud sitting on top in the light. Plant it too deep and the bud rots; too shallow and the roots dry out. Spread the roots out without bending them, firm the soil down, and water. Bare-root crowns are usual in early spring; small potted plants are easy to set out in fall or in mild climates.
seasoned: Planting depth is the make-or-break detail: position each crown with its midpoint at soil height, roots just beneath the surface and the growing tip exposed to light. Set too deep, the bud smothers and rots; set too shallow, the roots dry out. Spread the roots in the hole without bending them, firm the soil, and water in. Bare-root crowns are the cold-region norm in early spring; potted plugs are common for fall and warm-region planting. June-bearers fill a matted row from runners over the first season, so give them room.

beginner: Use a potting mix that drains well so the plants never sit in soggy soil. An easy homemade version is two scoops of potting soil mixed with one scoop of perlite and one scoop of fine bark.
seasoned: Fast drainage is essential, because strawberry crowns rot in standing moisture. A blend that works is two parts potting or garden soil to one part perlite and one part fine bark: enough to hold some moisture while still shedding excess water quickly.

beginner: Mix a little slow-release fertilizer into the soil when you plant, and add fresh mix and fertilizer each spring if you keep the plants past the first year.
seasoned: Blend a slow-release fertilizer into the mix at planting, and refresh the top inch of mix and feed each spring for plants kept more than one season.

beginner: Strawberries in pots dry out fast, so check every day in warm weather and water when the top of the soil feels dry. Empty the saucer after watering so the roots are not sitting in water.
seasoned: Pots dry far faster than ground beds, especially in summer heat, so check daily and water whenever the top inch is dry. Do not let a pot sit in a full saucer, which keeps the lower roots waterlogged and invites crown rot.

beginner: Because watering washes food out of the pot, give container strawberries a small amount of fertilizer often instead of one large feeding. A weak liquid feed added when you water is easy.
seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients out of a pot quickly, so feed lightly and often through the growing season rather than in one big dose. A diluted soluble fertilizer applied with watering works well.

beginner: Roots in a pot get much colder in winter than roots in the ground. In cold areas, move your strawberry pots into an unheated garage or shed for the winter, or bury the pot up to its rim in the garden and cover it with mulch. Set them back out when they start growing in spring.
seasoned: A potted root ball freezes harder than the same plant in the ground, so in cold-winter regions move pots into an unheated garage, shed, or against a sheltered wall for winter, or sink the pot to its rim in a garden bed and mulch over it. Bring containers back out as growth resumes in spring.

beginner: Strawberries do great in pots, and the day-neutral kind is the best choice because it gives berries all season and does not spread much. Pick a pot at least 10 inches deep and a foot or more wide; up to four plants fit in a 12-inch pot. Snip off any runners the plants send out, since they cannot take root in a pot and just weaken the main plant. The little strawberry jars with side pockets usually only work for one year.
seasoned: Strawberries grow well in containers, and day-neutral cultivars are the best fit because they fruit all season and throw few runners. Choose a pot no less than 10 inches deep and at least a foot across; a 12-inch pot holds up to four plants. Remove any runners that form, since daughter plants cannot root over the pot edge and only drain the mother. The small pocketed strawberry jars sold at garden centers usually last just one season.

beginner: Self-watering pots are not a good match for strawberries. They keep the soil wet all the time, and wet soil rots strawberry roots and crowns. If you already have one, keep it on the drier side and use a mix that drains well.
seasoned: Self-watering containers are risky for strawberries. The constant-moisture reservoir keeps the lower root zone and crown wet, which is exactly the condition that drives crown and root rot. If you use one, run it on the dry side and make sure the mix drains freely.

beginner: One of the earliest berries of the season and very easy to grow, even where winters are cold. The fruit is bright red, firm, and a little tart, which makes it as good in a cobbler or freezer bag as it is fresh.
seasoned: A hardy, heavy-yielding early June-bearer that thrives in cold-winter matted rows. Bright, firm, slightly tart fruit; it carries little disease resistance, so keep it off poorly drained sites where red stele and verticillium take hold.

beginner: If you want the best-tasting early berry, this is the classic pick. The deep-red fruit is small to medium and the harvest is on the modest side, but the flavor is hard to beat, fresh or in jam.
seasoned: The flavor standard among early June-bearers, with good resistance to red stele and verticillium. Yields are modest and the early bloom can be caught by a late frost, so site it where cold air drains away from the planting.

beginner: A popular mid-season variety that gives you large, glossy, firm berries on a strong plant. Give it well-drained soil and it will reward you with a heavy crop for fresh eating and freezing.
seasoned: Large, firm, high-quality fruit on a vigorous mid-season plant, and a longtime home and market standard. It has little disease resistance, so avoid poorly drained sites where red stele and verticillium can set in.

beginner: A dependable choice that produces very large, sweet, light-colored berries over a long stretch of the mid to late season. It shrugs off common strawberry diseases, so it is forgiving for a first-time grower.
seasoned: A USDA release with very large, light-colored, flavorful fruit and a long mid- to late-season harvest. Resistant to both red stele and verticillium wilt, which makes it a reliable, low-worry matted-row choice, though it is a light runner producer.

beginner: A great first strawberry to try. It fruits the very first season and keeps giving you a few berries at a time into fall, and it thrives in raised beds and containers. The berries are large, firm, and sweet-tart.
seasoned: The leading day-neutral, widely adapted and productive from the planting year into fall as long as temperatures stay below 85°F. Large, conical, firm, sweet-tart fruit; it excels in raised beds and containers, though plant durability is only fair, so refresh the bed every few years.

beginner: An easygoing day-neutral that produces large, good-quality berries throughout the season. It is forgiving and does well in containers, which makes it a friendly choice for a first raised-bed or patio planting.
seasoned: A widely adapted California day-neutral with large, firm, good-flavored fruit and good plant durability across the season. Often the most productive of the common day-neutrals in trials; well suited to containers and season-long fresh picking.

beginner: A sweet, dependable day-neutral that keeps giving you a few berries at a time all season. It resists disease well and is a long-standing favorite for home gardens and containers.
seasoned: A University of Maryland day-neutral release and a long-running home-garden standard, vigorous and disease-resistant with excellent flavor. Fruit runs small to medium, so it rewards steady feeding and moisture for season-long yield.

beginner: A traditional everbearing strawberry that gives you two smaller crops, one in early summer and one later in the season. The flavor is good, though you will pick fewer berries overall than from a day-neutral.
seasoned: A classic everbearer that sets a spring and a late-summer crop with a lull between, at lower total yield than a modern day-neutral. Reliable and good-flavored, but soft-fruited and best in cooler northern gardens, since heat cuts the crop short.

beginner: An everbearing strawberry that gives you some fruit its very first year. The berries are large, soft, and sweet, best eaten fresh since they do not keep or ship well.
seasoned: A Washington State University everbearer that bears two moderate crops and can even set fruit on unrooted runners. Berries are large but very soft with only fair durability, best for fresh eating; it can overwinter without cover in milder regions.

beginner: Pick the type that matches how you want to eat your berries first: a June-bearer if you want a big batch all at once for jam or freezing, a day-neutral if you want a few fresh berries at a time over a long season. After that, choose a variety known to grow well in your area, and feel free to plant two or three to see which you like best. Buy fresh plants labeled disease-free rather than digging up runners from an old bed.
seasoned: Choose by type first, then by season and local adaptation. Match cold hardiness to your winters and pick a fruiting pattern that fits how you want to harvest: one big flush from a June-bearer for preserving, or a steady trickle from a day-neutral for fresh eating. Within a type, cultivars differ in flavor, size, firmness, and disease tolerance, so trying two or three is the fastest way to find what thrives at your site. Always start from certified disease-free stock rather than runners off an old patch.

beginner: Strawberries do not get sweeter after picking and spoil fast, so only leave them out if you will eat them that day. Otherwise, get them into the fridge soon after picking.
seasoned: Strawberries are highly perishable and do not ripen further after picking, so hold them at room temperature only if eating within a day. For anything longer, refrigerate promptly; cool freshly picked fruit as soon as possible after harvest.

beginner: Put the berries in the fridge unwashed, in their container or a loosely closed bag, and wash them only right before you eat them. Washing too early makes them mushy. Stored this way they last up to about a week, depending on how ripe they were.
seasoned: Refrigerate unwashed in the crisper drawer, kept in a closed clamshell or a partially open plastic bag to hold humidity near 90 to 95 percent. Do not wash until just before use, since surface moisture speeds spoilage. Under good conditions berries keep up to about a week, depending on ripeness at picking.

beginner: To keep strawberries for months, remove the green tops, freeze them spread out on a tray first so they do not clump, then pack them into airtight bags. In the freezer they keep for up to about a year.
seasoned: For long-term storage, hull the berries, spread them on a tray to flash-freeze, then transfer to airtight containers or bags. Held at 0 °F they keep good quality for up to about a year.

beginner: Before storing, pick out and toss any soft or moldy berries, because mold jumps quickly from one to another. Berries keep best with their green caps left on.
seasoned: Sort before storing and discard any bruised or molding fruit, since gray mold spreads quickly from one berry to the next. Pick and store fruit with the cap on for the longest shelf life.

beginner: Do not plant strawberries in a spot where you recently grew tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries. Those crops can leave behind a soil disease (Verticillium wilt) that also harms strawberries and stays in the soil for years. It is also best not to replant strawberries right where old strawberries were.
seasoned: Do not plant strawberries after tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes, raspberries, or blackberries. All host Verticillium wilt, a soilborne fungus that infects strawberries and persists in soil for years; a strawberry bed following them is at real risk. Avoid replanting strawberries into ground where strawberries recently grew, too, since soilborne pests and viruses build up.

beginner: Because a strawberry bed lasts a few years, the main thing is choosing a good spot at the start: somewhere that has not grown tomatoes, peppers, potatoes, or berries lately. When the bed slows down after three or four years, start a fresh one in a different part of the garden rather than replanting the same ground.
seasoned: Strawberries are a multi-year planting, so the rotation decision is mostly made once, at bed establishment: choose ground that has not grown a Verticillium host recently, and plan to move the next bed to fresh ground when this one declines after three to four fruiting seasons. Starting the replacement bed in a new spot during the old bed's last productive year keeps production continuous and breaks the soilborne pest cycle.

beginner: Plant your strawberry crowns or small potted plants, setting each so the middle of the crown sits right at soil height. In a wide row, leave about 15 inches between plants.
seasoned: Set dormant bare-root crowns or potted plugs in the planting window, crown midpoint level with the soil surface. In matted rows, space plants about 15 inches apart in rows 3 to 4 feet apart.

seasoned: Firm the soil around the roots and water in to settle it. Check that the crown is still at the right depth after watering and adjust if it has sunk or heaved.

beginner: On June-bearing plants, pinch off all the flowers the first year so the plant grows strong. On day-neutral or everbearing plants, only pick off flowers for the first month or so. Water often and pull weeds. The roots are shallow, so weeds crowd them out fast.
seasoned: Pinch off every flower on June-bearers through the first season so the plant invests in establishment. On day-neutral and everbearing plants, remove flowers only for the first four to six weeks, then allow fruiting. Keep the bed evenly watered and weed-free; strawberries have shallow roots and lose out to weeds quickly.

beginner: Noted that leaves are growing and, for June-bearers, that you are picking off flowers.
seasoned: Establishment: leaf-out date and, for June-bearers, that flowers are being pinched.

beginner: Through summer the plants send out long stems called runners, with baby plants on the ends. These fill in your row.
seasoned: June-bearers send out runners (stolons) bearing daughter plants from early summer. Early runners (rooted before September) are the productive ones; sweep strays back into the row so they root in the bed, not the aisle.

beginner: Let the runners root in your row to fill it in. If you are growing in a pot, snip the runners off, because they cannot root in a pot and just weaken the plant. Tuck the runners into your row so they root there, not in the path.
seasoned: Guide early runners into the row to build the matted bed. In containers or a hill system, remove runners instead, since daughter plants cannot root over a pot edge and only drain the mother. Direct early runners into the row before they root in the aisle; remove late runners that will not fruit next year.

beginner: Noted that runners are filling in the row, or that you removed them from a pot.
seasoned: Runners: that daughter plants are rooting in the row (or being removed in containers).

beginner: In the second year and after, the plants flower in mid-spring. These open flowers can be killed by a late frost.
seasoned: On an established bed (year two and later), June-bearing plants flower in mid-spring near the last-frost date. Open blossoms are frost-sensitive, so a late frost during bloom can cut the crop.

beginner: White flowers with yellow centers opening up. Each one can turn into a berry.
seasoned: White five-petaled flowers opening across the bed, with yellow centers that become the fruit.

beginner: Keep an eye on the weather while the plants flower. If frost is coming, cover the flowers in the evening with a light cloth and take it off in the morning. If you covered the plants, open them up while they flower so bees can get to them.
seasoned: Watch the forecast during bloom. Cover open flowers with row cover in the late afternoon when frost is predicted and remove it the next morning once the danger has passed. If row cover is over the bed, pull it back as bloom opens so bees can reach the flowers and set well-shaped fruit.

seasoned: Bloom: first-flower date and any frost protection used.

seasoned: Pollinated flowers form green fruit that swells and colors over roughly four weeks. Fruit is mostly water, so steady moisture through this period drives size and quality.

beginner: Plant so the crown, the spot where leaves meet roots, sits level with the soil. Bury the roots but leave that crown on top. Too deep rots it, too shallow dries it out.
seasoned: Set each crown so the midpoint sits right at the soil line: roots fully buried, the growing tip fully exposed. Plant too deep and the crown rots, too shallow and the roots dry out, and this one detail decides whether a bare-root plant takes.

beginner: Keep bare-root plants damp and in the shade until you plant them, and plant on a cool or cloudy day if possible. Dried-out roots may not survive.
seasoned: Soak bare-root crowns and keep them shaded and damp until they are in the ground, planting on a cool or overcast day if you can. Exposed strawberry roots dry out fast, and a crown that desiccates before planting often never establishes.

beginner: In the first year, pick off the flowers on June-bearing plants. Letting them fruit too early weakens the plant. Removing the blooms now gives you a much bigger crop next year.
seasoned: On a matted-row or June-bearing planting, pinch off all the first-year flowers. Letting a new plant fruit in year one starves root and runner growth, and removing those blossoms is what builds the crown that carries a full crop the next season.

beginner: Water new plants often so they stay moist while they take root. Strawberries have shallow roots and dry out fast.
seasoned: Keep new plantings consistently moist while they root in. Strawberries are shallow-rooted and dry out quickly, so even, frequent watering through establishment is what gets crowns anchored before they have to support runners or fruit.

beginner: As runners take root and make new little plants, keep the strongest and pull out crowded extras. A bed packed too tight gives small berries and more rot.
seasoned: Space the daughter plants as runners root in, keeping the strongest and removing the crowded extras to hold roughly the matted-row density your source recommends. A bed left to fill in solid yields small, hard-to-pick berries and traps the moisture that feeds fruit rot.

beginner: If you have everbearing or day-neutral strawberries, snip off the runners. These kinds fruit on the main plant, so runners just steal energy from the berries.
seasoned: On day-neutral or everbearing types, remove early runners instead of letting them root. These types fruit on the mother plant through the season, so energy spent on runners is energy taken from the berries you actually want.

beginner: Cover the plants if a late frost is coming while they are flowering. Open blooms are killed by frost, leaving a black center. A row cover or sheet protects them.
seasoned: Cover blooming plants when a late frost threatens; open strawberry flowers are killed at right around freezing, and the giveaway is a blackened center in the flower the next morning. A row cover or even a sheet over the bed saves that first set.

beginner: Water evenly and let bees visit while the plants flower. Each strawberry forms from many pollinated seeds, so poor pollination makes small, lumpy berries.
seasoned: Keep water steady and keep pollinators welcome through bloom. Each berry is built from many fertilized seeds on the flower, so poor pollination is what gives you small, lopsided, misshapen fruit even when the plant looks healthy.

beginner: Slip straw or mulch under the growing berries so they do not sit on bare dirt. Fruit touching wet soil rots, and the straw keeps it clean and dry.
seasoned: Tuck clean straw or mulch under the developing berries to keep fruit off bare soil. Berries resting on damp ground are where gray mold and rot start, and that simple barrier is where the name strawberry comes from.

beginner: Water the soil, not the berries, and do it in the morning so plants dry by night. Wet berries overnight grow gray mold.
seasoned: Water at the base and in the morning as fruit ripens, keeping the berries themselves dry. Wet fruit and wet foliage going into the night drive the gray mold that turns ripening berries fuzzy overnight.

beginner: Pick the fully red berries every couple of days, snapping the stem instead of pulling. Strawberries do not get sweeter after picking, so let them ripen on the plant.
seasoned: Pick fully red, ripe berries every two to three days, pinching the stem rather than tugging the fruit. Strawberries do not sweeten further once picked, so color-up on the plant is the whole game, and frequent picking keeps the plant setting and keeps mold from spreading off overripe fruit.

beginner: Pick in the cool morning into a shallow tray, then refrigerate soon. Wash only right before eating, since wet berries spoil fast.
seasoned: Harvest into a shallow container in the cool of the morning and chill the berries promptly; leave them unwashed until you eat them. Strawberries are fragile and short-lived, and warmth plus surface moisture is what collapses them within a day.

beginner: After the last berries on June-bearing plants, mow the leaves to about an inch above the crowns and thin the rows. This refreshes the bed for next year.
seasoned: Renovate a June-bearing matted row right after the last harvest: mow the old foliage about an inch above the crowns, then narrow and thin the rows. The planting fruits on new growth, so clearing the tired leaves now is what drives a vigorous, productive bed next year.

beginner: Right after cutting back, feed and water the bed so it grows back strong. That late-summer regrowth is what makes next year's berries.
seasoned: Feed and water right after renovating to push the regrowth that sets next year's flower buds. The new runners and leaves coming up now are forming the crowns you will harvest from, so do not let the bed coast through late summer.

beginner: Once plants are dormant and the ground begins to freeze, cover the crowns with straw. It protects them from cold and from being pushed out of the soil by freezing and thawing. Do not mulch too early.
seasoned: Mulch over the crowns with straw once plants have gone dormant and the ground starts to freeze, not before. The mulch guards against winter cold and the freeze-thaw heaving that lifts shallow crowns out of the soil, but applied too early it can smother plants still trying to grow.

beginner: In early spring, rake the winter straw off the crowns and into the paths. Leaving it on top slows new growth, and it still keeps berries clean later.
seasoned: Pull the winter mulch back off the crowns in early spring as growth resumes, raking it into the paths to keep fruit clean later. Leaving it piled on the crowns once they want to grow slows green-up and traps dampness against the plant.

beginner: Expect roughly 1 to 2 pounds of berries per plant, depending on the variety and how old the bed is.
seasoned: About 1 to 2 pounds per plant, or roughly 7 to 15 pounds per 10-foot row, varying with cultivar and planting age.

beginner: You will get the most berries the second year, the year after planting. After that the crop slowly tapers off in size and amount.
seasoned: Yield peaks the year after planting (year two). It is often similar or slightly lower in year three, and both berry size and total yield decline from years two to four.

beginner: Do not expect berries the first year. On June-bearing plants you pick the flowers off on purpose, so no first-year crop is exactly what should happen.
seasoned: Expect little or no crop in the planting year. On June-bearers the flowers are pinned off the first season by design, so a missing first-year harvest is the plan working, not a failure.

beginner: Big leafy plants and lots of runners, but hardly any berries
seasoned: Lots of runners and leaves, but little or no fruit

beginner: Too much nitrogen, or feeding a June-bearing bed in spring, pushes leaves and runners instead of berries. In the first year, no fruit is normal because you pinch the flowers off on purpose.
seasoned: Heavy leaf and runner growth at the expense of fruit usually means too much nitrogen, spring feeding on an established June-bearing bed, or, in year one, the normal result of pinching flowers to establish the plant.

beginner: Feed June-bearing plants only after harvest, not in spring, and do not overdo the fertilizer. And remember the first year is supposed to be fruitless, with the big crop the second year.
seasoned: Feed June-bearers only at renovation, not in spring, and keep total nitrogen modest. Remember that a fruitless first year on a June-bearing bed is the plan, with the real crop coming in year two.

beginner: Small, lumpy, or pinched berries
seasoned: Small, lumpy, or pinched-tip berries

beginner: Lumpy or pinched berries usually mean the flowers were not pollinated well in cold or wet weather, or a small bug fed on them and deformed the tip.
seasoned: Misshapen or grooved fruit comes from poor pollination during cold or wet bloom weather, or from tarnished plant bug feeding that pinches the berry tip (catfacing).

beginner: Cover flowers only when frost threatens and open them up for bees otherwise, and keep weeds down to reduce the bugs that deform the tips.
seasoned: Protect bloom from frost, pull row covers back so bees can work the flowers, and control broadleaf weeds that host tarnished plant bug.

beginner: Berries rotting with gray fuzz
seasoned: Berries rotting with gray fuzz

beginner: Gray fuzzy rot on the berries is a mold that takes hold when things stay wet, the plants are crowded, or berries sit on damp ground.
seasoned: Soft fruit covered in gray fuzz is gray mold (Botrytis), driven by wet conditions, a dense canopy, fruit resting on wet soil, and rain during bloom and ripening.

beginner: Give the plants more air by not feeding June-bearers in spring, water at the soil, keep berries off wet ground, clear old leaves, and pick ripe berries quickly.
seasoned: Open up the canopy by skipping spring nitrogen on June-bearers, water at the base, keep fruit off wet soil, clean out old leaves, and pick ripe fruit promptly.

beginner: No berries the first year
seasoned: No fruit at all in the first year

beginner: On June-bearing plants this is normal. You pick the flowers off the first year so the plant gets strong, and the first real crop comes the second year.
seasoned: On a June-bearing bed this is expected and correct: flowers are pinned off the first season so the plant builds roots, crown, and a matted row, with the first real crop in year two.

beginner: Keep pinching the flowers off June-bearing plants the first year and let the runners fill in. If you want berries the first year, grow a day-neutral type instead.
seasoned: Stay the course: pinch first-year flowers on June-bearers and let runners fill the row. For fruit the first year, grow a day-neutral type, which fruits in its planting season.

beginner: Plants dead or weak after winter, with dark mushy crowns
seasoned: Plants dead or stunted after winter, with blackened crowns

beginner: Winter cold killed the crowns. This happens in cold areas when there is no snow or straw cover, or when the variety is not hardy enough for your winters.
seasoned: Winter cold injury: strawberry crowns are damaged between about 10 and 20 °F at the crown, especially without snow cover or winter mulch in cold regions, or with a poorly cold-hardy cultivar.

beginner: In cold places, cover the plants with 2 to 3 inches of straw after the first hard freeze and uncover them in spring, and pick a variety hardy for your area. In mild, rainy places, skip the straw, since it makes the crowns rot.
seasoned: In cold regions, apply 2 to 3 inches of loose straw after the first hard freeze and remove it in early spring, and choose cultivars rated for your hardiness zone. Skip straw in wet-winter regions, where it causes crown rot instead.

beginner: In zone 3 your strawberry bed comes back each year, but winters are harsh, so cover the plants with a few inches of straw in late fall and pull it back when they start growing again in spring.
seasoned: Zone 3 grows strawberries as a perennial matted row, but it is the cold edge: crowns are damaged near 10 to 20°F at the crown, so without dependable snow cover apply two to three inches of straw mulch in late fall and rake it off as growth resumes in spring.

beginner: Zone 4 is a great fit for a come-back-every-year strawberry bed. Pick winter-hardy June-bearing types, mulch with straw in late fall, and uncover the plants in spring.
seasoned: Zone 4 is the reliable cold floor for perennial matted-row strawberries. Mulched June-bearing varieties such as Honeoye, Jewel, and Earliglow overwinter well here; apply straw mulch after several hard frosts in late fall and rake it off as growth resumes.

beginner: Zone 5 is a comfortable fit for a strawberry bed that returns each year. A layer of straw over winter keeps the plants safe; pull it back in spring.
seasoned: Zone 5 grows strawberries as a dependable perennial matted row. A light straw mulch over winter protects the crowns and reduces frost heaving; rake it off as growth resumes in spring.

beginner: Zone 6 strawberries come back every year and enjoy a longer growing season. A thin layer of straw over winter still helps in cold snaps.
seasoned: Zone 6 grows strawberries as a perennial matted row with a longer, milder season than the colder zones. Light winter mulch is still worthwhile to limit frost heaving and protect crowns in open winters.

beginner: Zone 7 strawberries return each year and ripen earliest in this group. Winters are mild, so you usually do not need heavy winter cover.
seasoned: Zone 7 grows strawberries as a perennial matted row with the earliest bloom and harvest in the northern tier. Winters are mild enough that heavy mulch is usually unnecessary, though a light cover helps in a hard freeze; summer heat is not yet severe enough to force an annual system here.

beginner: In the north (zones 3 to 7), strawberries are a perennial: you plant them once and the same bed comes back and fruits for several years. Plant the small brown dormant crowns in early spring, as soon as you can dig the soil, even if frost is still possible. June-bearing kinds give one big batch of berries in late spring or early summer, about a month after they bloom, then grow runners that root into new plants and fill the row. After the berries finish, cut the leaves back and thin the plants to keep the bed healthy, and start a fresh bed every three or four years. In zone 3, cover plants with straw over winter for protection; berries are most reliable from zone 4 and warmer.
seasoned: Across the northern tier (zones 3 to 7), strawberries are grown as a perennial matted-row bed, the dominant US backyard system. Set dormant bare-root crowns in early spring, about two weeks before the last frost, as soon as the soil can be worked. June-bearing types give one concentrated flush about four weeks after they flower in late spring to early summer, then send runners to fill the row. Renovate the bed within two weeks of the last harvest, mow tops two inches above the crowns, narrow the row, and fertilize, and replace the planting after three or four fruiting years. In zone 3, and in colder pockets of zone 4 without reliable snow cover, give plants extra winter protection; reliable fruiting starts at zone 4.

beginner: On the Gulf Coast, strawberries are a cool-season crop you grow over the winter and then replace, not a bed that lives for years. Plant in October or early November, pick from late fall into spring, then pull the plants out when summer arrives and start fresh next fall. Grow them on raised rows covered with plastic or pine straw so the rain drains and the berries stay clean.
seasoned: The Gulf Coast grows strawberries as a fall-planted annual, not a perennial bed. Set transplants from early October through mid November, fruit them from late fall into spring, then remove the planting in early summer because humid-summer disease pressure is severe, and replant fresh each fall. Grow on raised rows with plastic mulch or a thick pine-straw layer to keep the heavy rains drained and the fruit clean. Choose short-day varieties suited to the South.

beginner: In the warmer Gulf Coast areas, strawberries are still a winter crop you grow and then replace. Plant in October or early November, start picking as early as late fall, keep going through spring, then pull the plants before the humid summer and replant next fall. Use raised rows with plastic or pine straw for drainage.
seasoned: In the warmer Gulf Coast zone 9, strawberries are grown on the same fall-planted annual system: set transplants from early October through mid November, with production starting as early as late November from plugs and running through spring into early summer, then remove the planting before the humid summer and replant the next fall. Raised rows with plastic or pine-straw mulch handle the heavy rain and keep fruit clean.

You will pick berries from late fall through spring, into early summer. When summer arrives, pull the plants out, because the heat and humidity bring disease, and plant fresh ones the next fall. seasoned: On the Southeast and Gulf Coast (zones 8 and 9), strawberries are grown as a fall-planted annual, not a perennial bed. Set bare-root or plug transplants from early October through mid November (mid to late October is ideal in southeast Louisiana), on raised rows covered with plastic mulch or a thick layer of pine straw for drainage and clean fruit. Short-day varieties initiate flowers in the cool, short days of fall and winter; expect fruit from late fall (as early as late November from plugs) through winter and spring, running to about early June. After June the plants stop fruiting and the planting is removed, because humid-summer disease pressure is extreme; replant fresh each fall. The plants are cold-hardy to roughly 17°F, but open flowers are damaged below 32, so cover the bed with row-cover cloth on forecast freezes during bloom. Side-dress with nitrogen in January and again in mid-to-late spring, and rotate away from recent tomato, pepper, or eggplant beds.

beginner: Here in the Central Valley, strawberries are planted as an annual, meaning you replace the bed every couple of years rather than keeping the same plants going, because summer heat and soil diseases shorten their productive life. You set plants out in August. The main thing to know: your big harvest comes the following spring, from about mid-April through mid-June, not in the fall. Short-day varieties (the most common type in nurseries here, bred to flower when days get shorter in fall) may set a few berries in October or November, but if you pinch off those early blossoms, removing the flower buds before they open, the plant puts that energy into its roots and crown instead, and you get a bigger spring harvest. It feels counterintuitive to remove fruit, but it is the standard UC advice for home growers in the valley.
seasoned: The interior valley grows strawberries as a spring-cropping annual rather than a perennial bed, since summer heat and soilborne disease pressure cut productive life to one or two seasons. Short-day varieties planted in August do most of their fruiting the following spring, with harvest running from mid-April through mid-June and heaviest picking in May and June. Plants set in August may put out a small flush of blossoms the first fall, but removing those fall blossoms channels energy into crown development and produces a heavier spring crop. Replace the bed with fresh nursery stock every two to three years as heat and disease pressure accumulate. White mulch over the bed in summer keeps the soil cooler and reduces fruit burn once temperatures climb above 90°F.

seasoned: In interior arid zone 8 (the New Mexico high desert and similar areas), strawberries are grown as a perennial matted row, not a pulled annual. Late spring frosts are the main threat to the crop, so protect open blossoms, and mulch crowns with straw over winter.

seasoned: In Hawaii (zone 11), strawberries are a cool-elevation niche crop, not a warm-lowland year-round one. They are grown upcountry, on the cool slopes of Haleakala (around Kula) and at Waimea on Hawaii Island, where conditions stay mild. At a fixed upcountry site, treat the bed as a short-lived perennial: set plants in the cool fall months for a main crop through winter and spring. Year-round supply exists in Hawaii only because commercial farms move harvest up and down the mountain with the seasons, which a single home garden cannot replicate. In the warm lowlands strawberries perform poorly.

seasoned: West of the Cascades, strawberries are grown as a perennial matted-row bed, the same dominant US backyard system used farther north, and June-bearing types are the real signature here: WSU Clallam County Extension names Benton, Hood, Rainier, Puget Reliance, Puget Summer, Sweet Sunrise, Shuksan, and Tillamook as the recommended maritime cultivars. Renovate the bed within about a week of the last picking: mow the foliage, narrow the row, and fertilize. beginner: Strawberries are low, leafy plants that come back year after year. There are three kinds: June-bearing, which gives one big batch of berries in early summer; day-neutral, which gives a few berries at a time all season and does great in pots; and everbearing, which gives two smaller batches. One plant makes fruit on its own, and a strawberry patch keeps producing for about three to four years before you start a fresh one.
seasoned: The garden strawberry is a low-growing herbaceous perennial with a short, compressed stem called the crown, from which leaves, flowers, and runners arise. It is grown in three types: June-bearing (one concentrated early-summer flush, the matted-row backbone of US backyard growing), day-neutral (fruiting through the season, compact, ideal for containers), and everbearing (two lighter flushes). Plants are self-fertile, set from dormant bare-root crowns or potted plugs, and a bed stays productive for about three to four fruiting seasons before it is replaced.

beginner: A strawberry is ready when it is bright red all over, smells sweet, and comes off the plant easily. Berries taste best left to ripen on the plant. Pick every day or two, more often when it is hot, and pick before heavy rain so the berries do not get watery or moldy.
seasoned: Fruit is ready when it is fully red and fragrant and pulls free easily; flavor is best when berries ripen on the plant. Color deepens after picking, so fruit picked at about 75 percent red stores slightly longer. Pick every one to three days, more often in warm weather, and pick before forecast rain to protect flavor and limit rot.

beginner: June-bearing strawberries flower in mid-spring, around the last frost, and the berries ripen about four weeks after that. Day-neutral plants flower on and off all season as long as it is not too cold or too hot. Open flowers can be killed by a late frost, so watch the weather while they bloom.
seasoned: On established beds, June-bearing plants flower in mid-spring, near the last-frost date, and fruit ripens about four weeks later. Day-neutral plants flower and fruit through the season whenever temperatures sit between about 40 and 90 °F. Open blossoms are frost-sensitive, so bloom timing and late frosts together set the crop.
