seasoned: USU Extension places pumpkin in Group D (Very Tender), direct-sown about April 1 in St. George just after the March 30 average last frost. At a 100-day maturity the earliest fruit is ready by mid-July, and because pumpkin sets fruit through the desert's hottest months with no heat-driven pause, later-set fruit keeps finishing on the vine into late October, right up against the November 1 average first frost, which lines up well with a Halloween harvest. USU documents only this one spring sowing for pumpkin in the St. George area, no fall replanting.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo
render_evidence: referenced nowhere in either repo (PLA-255 finding)

beginner: Plum likes a deep soil that drains well, from a sandy loam to a sandy clay loam. Good drainage matters most, because plum roots do not like sitting in wet ground and can rot if they stay soggy. Of the common home fruit trees, plum is a little more forgiving of heavier ground than peach is, especially European types on a tolerant rootstock, but standing water is still the thing to avoid. If your soil is heavy clay that holds water, plant the tree on a raised mound so the roots sit above the wettest layer. A soil of average richness with some compost worked in suits it well.
seasoned: Plum wants a deep, well-drained soil ranging from a sandy loam to a sandy clay loam; drainage is the priority, since Prunus roots will not tolerate prolonged wet feet. Plum is somewhat more tolerant of heavier ground than peach, particularly European cultivars on a heavy-soil-tolerant rootstock such as Marianna or Myrobalan, but chronically saturated soil still invites crown and root rot. On heavy clay, plant on a raised berm to lift the roots above the perched water table. Moderate fertility and a modest amount of organic matter suit it well.

beginner: Plum grows best in slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and is fine up to about 7.0 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if you need to: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if the soil is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is much easier to fix before the permanent tree goes in.
seasoned: Plum does best in a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 6.5, and tolerates up to about 7.0. Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, while elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground.

beginner: Scatter the fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. On sandy soil it helps to split it, most in spring and a little after harvest. Do not overdo the nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much pushes soft, leafy growth that draws aphids and disease. Never feed late in the year, because late feeding keeps the tree growing when it should be going dormant and makes winter damage more likely.
seasoned: Broadcast the fertilizer evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, keeping it off the trunk, and water it in. Split timing (the bulk in spring, a lighter touch after harvest) suits sandy soils. Go easy on nitrogen: plums push vigorous shoots readily, and lush, succulent growth is more prone to aphids, bacterial canker, and black knot, and never feed late in the season, since late nitrogen delays dormancy and invites winter injury.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works well for backyard plums. Do not overdo nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth and more disease instead of fruit.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits backyard plums; a young tree that is not making about a foot of new growth a year can take a spring nitrogen boost, but a vigorous tree needs little. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which pushes soft, disease-prone growth at the expense of fruit.

beginner: A simple rule is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, spread in spring as the tree blooms, up to about 8 to 10 cups for a full-grown tree. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing. If the tree is already growing strongly, with lots of long new shoots, give it less, not more.
seasoned: A common home-garden rate is about 1 cup of 10-10-10 per year of tree age, applied in spring from bloom to petal fall, up to roughly 8 to 10 cups for a mature tree. Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins. Judge by shoot growth: a bearing tree making 8 to 15 inches of new wood a year is fed about right, and one growing faster than that needs less nitrogen, not more.

beginner: Whether a plum needs a companion tree is really a pollination question, and it depends on the type. European plums (like Stanley, Italian prune, and damson) are mostly self-fruitful, so one tree makes fruit on its own. Japanese plums (like Santa Rosa and Methley) usually need a second, different Japanese variety blooming nearby to set a good crop. Beyond that, the things that matter for a tree are not the usual vegetable-garden pairings but what grows around the roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, because lawn competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free area helps the tree settle in. One thing to avoid is planting a plum near other wild or neglected plums and cherries, because those spread black knot, the black warty branch disease, to your tree.
seasoned: For a plum, the key interaction is pollination, and it splits by type: European plums (Stanley, Italian prune, damson) are largely self-fruitful and fruit alone, while Japanese plums (Santa Rosa, Methley, and most others) are self-unfruitful and need a second compatible Japanese cultivar blooming at the same time. The other interactions that matter are about the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since a young tree competes poorly with grass for water and nitrogen. The site rule to respect is inoculum: do not plant near wild, ornamental, or neglected Prunus (chokecherry, wild plum, purple-leaf plum), which are reservoirs of black knot and brown rot.

beginner: On small developing plums, look for a curved, crescent-shaped scar, the mark the beetle leaves when it lays an egg. Damaged fruit often drops early, and some that stays on the tree ends up misshapen or has a grub inside. You see this soon after the petals fall, and it is the usual reason for wormy plums.
seasoned: Small developing fruit carries a distinctive crescent-shaped scar where the female cut a slit to lay an egg. Infested fruit often drops early; fruit that hangs on may be gnarled or have a grub tunneling inside. Damage appears shortly after petal fall and is one of the most common causes of wormy backyard plums.

beginner: A small beetle with a long snout called the plum curculio, which is named for this very crop. The adults show up around bloom and start damaging the little fruits right after the petals drop, laying eggs inside them. The larvae then feed within the fruit and later drop to the ground.
seasoned: The plum curculio (Conotrachelus nenuphar), a small snout beetle and a signature pest of its namesake crop. Adults emerge around bloom and attack fruit from petal fall onward, laying eggs in the developing fruit; the larvae feed inside, then drop to pupate in the soil.

beginner: Early in the morning the beetles are slow. Spread a sheet under the tree, tap the branches so the beetles fall, and destroy them. Pick up and throw away any dropped fruit promptly so the larvae inside do not mature. A kaolin clay spray (a fine white mineral coating) starting at petal fall helps keep them off.
seasoned: For a backyard tree, jarring the limbs over a sheet in the cool early morning when the beetles are sluggish, then destroying what drops, reduces the population. Promptly gather and dispose of dropped infested fruit to break the cycle. Kaolin clay applied from petal fall is an organic deterrent.

beginner: The main thing is cleanup. Pick up fallen fruit all season so the larvae inside cannot finish growing in the soil under the tree. Keeping the ground clear lowers the number of beetles the next year.
seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: remove dropped fruit through the season so larvae cannot complete development in the soil beneath the tree. A clean orchard floor and prompt fruit pickup steadily lower pressure year over year.

beginner: In spring the new leaves at the shoot tips curl up tightly, and if you unroll one you find little green or waxy-gray insects, aphids, packed inside. They leave a sticky shine (called honeydew) that turns black with sooty mold. A bad early attack curls the leaves and slows the new growth.
seasoned: In spring, new leaves at the shoot tips pucker and curl tightly around colonies of small soft-bodied aphids (leaf curl plum aphid), while the pale, wax-dusted mealy plum aphid clusters on the undersides of leaves. Both excrete honeydew that turns leaves shiny and sticky and grows black sooty mold; heavy early infestations stunt shoots and can distort young fruit.

beginner: Two kinds of aphids that live on plum: one curls the new leaves, and the other is a pale, waxy gray one. They spend the winter as eggs near the buds, then multiply fast on the tender spring growth before flying off to other summer plants.
seasoned: Two aphids specific to plum: the leaf curl plum aphid (Brachycaudus helichrysi), which curls the spring foliage, and the mealy plum aphid (Hyalopterus pruni), whitish with a mealy wax coat. Both overwinter as eggs near the buds, build up on new spring growth, then migrate to summer hosts (leaf curl plum aphid to plants in the aster family, mealy plum aphid to reeds and cattails).

beginner: Ladybugs and other helpful bugs usually clean aphids up by early summer, so avoid harsh sprays that kill those helpers too. Blast the colonies off with a hard spray of water, and for a bad case use insecticidal soap or a light horticultural oil on the curled shoots. A dormant oil spray in late winter kills the overwintering eggs.
seasoned: Natural enemies (ladybugs, lacewings, syrphid larvae, parasitic wasps) usually bring aphids under control by early summer, so protect them by not spraying broad insecticides. A strong jet of water knocks colonies off, and narrow-range horticultural oil or insecticidal soap on the affected shoots helps in a heavy infestation. A dormant or delayed-dormant oil spray targets the overwintering eggs.

beginner: Go easy on spring feeding, since lush new growth attracts aphids. Keep ants off the trunk (they protect aphids) with a sticky band, and leave the helpful bugs alone. If aphids come back every year, a dormant oil spray in late fall or winter is the best prevention.
seasoned: Avoid heavy spring nitrogen, which pushes the soft flush aphids favor. Keep ants (which farm aphids for honeydew and drive off predators) off the trunk with a sticky band, and preserve natural enemies. A late-fall or dormant oil where aphids are a chronic problem is the most effective single measure.

beginner: Look at the very bottom of the trunk where it meets the soil. The peachtree borer, which also attacks plums, leaves a sticky, gummy ooze mixed with what looks like wet sawdust (frass). You may see a small mound of gum and frass at the base. A young tree with several borers can be killed in one season, so catch this early.
seasoned: Gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass at the base of the trunk, right around the soil line, often with a mounded look where the bark meets the ground. Plums, like other stone fruit, are a host. A heavily infested young tree loses vigor as the larvae girdle the inner bark; several borers in one trunk can kill a newly planted tree in a season.

beginner: The larvae (young grub stage) of the peachtree borer, a moth whose adults look like wasps and fly by day. The adults lay eggs on the lower trunk in summer, and the larvae burrow into the bark at and below the soil line. Trees with existing wounds are hit hardest.
seasoned: Larvae of the peachtree borer (Synanthedon exitiosa), a clearwing moth whose day-flying adults are wasp-like. Eggs are laid on the lower trunk in summer; larvae tunnel in the inner bark at and just below the soil line. Trees stressed by winter injury, mechanical wounds, or bacterial canker are attacked first.

beginner: Once the larvae are tunneling inside, no spray reaches them. The backyard fix is to scrape soil away from the base in late summer or fall, find the holes marked by gum and frass, and kill the larvae with a thin, stiff wire pushed into each hole. Then smooth the soil back.
seasoned: There is no rescue spray once larvae are tunneling inside. The practical home control is to expose the crown in late summer or fall, find the entry holes by the gum and frass, and kill larvae by hand with a thin wire. Keep the trunk base free of wounds.

beginner: Keep mowers and string trimmers away from the trunk; the wounds they leave attract the egg-laying moths. Keep grass and weeds cleared from the base so you can see the soil line, and check it every late summer for fresh gummy ooze.
seasoned: Protect the lower trunk from mechanical injury (the wounds that draw egg-laying females), keep the tree vigorous, and clear weeds and tall grass from the base so the crown stays open and easy to inspect. Check the soil line each late summer for fresh gum.

beginner: Little gray, round, hard bumps crust over the bark of twigs and branches, and the fruit can get small reddish spots where the scales feed. A bad infestation makes the bark look ashy and can kill off twigs and branches, weakening the tree.
seasoned: Tiny gray, circular, hard-shelled scales encrust the bark of twigs and branches, sometimes so densely the bark looks ashy; feeding sites on fruit show as small red-purple haloed spots. Heavy infestations kill twigs and whole limbs from the top down and weaken the tree over a few seasons.

beginner: An armored scale insect called San Jose scale. After the tiny young 'crawlers' settle down, they stay put under a hard shell and suck sap, with several generations a year. Only the crawler stage moves around and can be targeted.
seasoned: San Jose scale (Diaspidiotus perniciosus), an armored scale insect. Immobile once settled, it feeds on sap under a waxy shell and passes several overlapping generations a year; crawlers (the mobile young stage) are the only vulnerable window and spread the infestation along the branches.

beginner: The main control is a thorough spray of horticultural oil in late winter while the tree is leafless, coating all the bark to smother the scales. During the season, helpful insects keep light infestations down. Prune out and destroy branches that are heavily crusted with scale.
seasoned: A thorough dormant or delayed-dormant application of horticultural oil, wetting all the bark, smothers overwintering scales and is the mainstay of home control. In-season, natural enemies (tiny parasitic wasps, predatory beetles) suppress light infestations; prune out and destroy heavily encrusted wood.

beginner: Prune for good airflow, use a dormant oil spray in areas where scale has shown up before, and check any new trees you buy, since scale often hitches in on nursery stock. Avoid harsh sprays that kill the helpful insects.
seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and well pruned so airflow is good, apply dormant oil where scale has appeared before, and inspect incoming nursery stock, since scale often arrives on new trees. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.

beginner: Hard, black, warty lumps (called knots) grow along the twigs and branches, anywhere from an inch to six inches or more long. They start as a soft olive-green swelling one year and turn coal-black and hard the next. The branch beyond a knot often wilts and dies, and a badly infected tree gets stunted and gnarled. Black knot is the classic plum disease, the one to learn to recognize.
seasoned: Hard, black, elongated, warty swellings (knots) grow along twigs and branches, from an inch to six inches or more long, girdling and eventually killing the wood beyond them. A new gall starts as an inconspicuous olive-green, corky swelling one year, then hardens and turns coal-black by the second. Leaves on knotted branches may wilt and die, and a heavily infected tree becomes stunted and misshapen. This is the signature disease of plum.

beginner: A fungus (Apiosporina morbosa) that lives in the black knots over winter, on your tree and on any wild plums or cherries nearby. In cool, wet spring weather it shoots out spores that infect the new green shoots. You will not see anything the first year; the knot swells the next year and turns black the year after.
seasoned: The fungus Apiosporina morbosa (formerly Dibotryon morbosum). It overwinters in the galls on the tree and on nearby wild or ornamental Prunus, and in cool, wet spring weather releases spores that infect the new green shoots. Infection is invisible the first season; the gall swells the following year and blackens the year after, so the disease runs on a roughly two-year cycle.

beginner: Cutting the knots out is the main fix, and when you do it matters: prune in late winter while the tree is bare, before it starts growing in spring. Cut each knot off 3 to 4 inches below the black lump, into clean wood, because the fungus reaches farther than you can see. Carry the cut pieces away and burn, bury, or bag them so they cannot re-infect the tree, and wipe your pruners with rubbing alcohol between cuts.
seasoned: Pruning is the core control, and timing is everything: in the dormant season, before growth resumes (before about April 1), cut out every knot, making the cut 3 to 4 inches below the visible gall into clean wood, since the fungus extends beyond what you can see. Remove the prunings from the area and burn, bury, or bag them, and disinfect tools between cuts. On a scaffold too valuable to remove, cut the gall out to healthy wood. A protective fungicide on the new shoots in early spring supports the pruning where pressure is high.

beginner: Check the tree every winter and cut out any knots before spring, when they spread. Just as important, clean up or remove wild plums, chokecherries, and neglected ornamental plums nearby, because they keep re-infecting your tree. Some plum varieties resist black knot better than others, so ask when you buy, but cutting the knots out each year is the habit that matters most.
seasoned: Scout and prune out knots every dormant season before they can release spores, and deal with the reservoir: remove or clean up wild plum, chokecherry, and neglected ornamental Prunus within range, which sustain the disease. Choosing a less-susceptible cultivar and keeping the tree open and vigorous both help, but annual knot removal is the non-negotiable habit.

beginner: At bloom, infected flowers go limp and brown, and small gummy dead patches can form on the nearby twigs. As the plums ripen, brown spots appear and spread quickly, sometimes rotting a whole fruit in a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan fuzz on the surface. Rotted fruit shrivels into a hard, dried mummy that hangs on the tree.
seasoned: At bloom, infected blossoms wilt and turn brown, and the infection can run back into the twig to form a small gummy canker. As fruit ripens, brown circular spots appear and spread fast, sometimes rotting a whole plum within a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan spore mass on the surface. Rotted fruit dries into a mummy that clings to the tree or drops.

beginner: A fungus called Monilinia fructicola. It survives the winter in dried mummy fruit and in dead twig patches, then releases spores at bloom that infect the flowers. Those flower infections later cause the fruit to rot. Warm, humid, wet weather makes it spread fast, and any break in the skin lets it in.
seasoned: The fungus Monilinia fructicola. It overwinters in mummified fruit (whether hanging in the canopy or fallen) and in twig cankers; spores released at bloom infect flowers, and those infections later seed the fruit rot. Warm, humid, wet conditions drive rapid spread, and any skin break (curculio scar, hail, cracking) is an entry point.

beginner: The main control is cleanup: take off and destroy every dried mummy from the tree and the ground, and prune out the gummy dead twig patches, since these hold the spores. If the weather is wet during bloom, an organic-approved spray at bloom helps protect the flowers. As soon as you see a plum rotting, pick it and throw it away, and thin the fruit so plums are not touching.
seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: remove and destroy every mummy from the tree and the ground, and prune out gummy twig cankers, because these are the spore sources. During a wet bloom, an organic-approved bloom-time fungicide reduces blossom blight. Once fruit is rotting, pick and dispose of it promptly, and thin fruit so plums do not touch, which slows spread through a cluster.

beginner: Cleanup all year prevents most of the damage: never leave dried mummies on the tree over winter, pick up dropped fruit, and prune so the tree is open and the plums dry fast after rain. Keep pests like plum curculio in check, since their wounds let rot in. Pick fruit on time, handle it gently, and chill it soon after picking.
seasoned: Year-round sanitation prevents most loss: never leave mummies on the tree over winter, remove dropped and thinned fruit, and keep the canopy open with good pruning so fruit dries quickly after rain. Control plum curculio and other pests whose wounds open the door, harvest promptly, handle fruit gently, and cool it soon after picking.

beginner: Leaves get small angular water-soaked spots that turn dark and fall out, leaving little holes, called a shot-hole look. Bad cases turn leaves yellow and thin out the tree. On the fruit, small sunken spots, pits, and cracks form. How badly a tree is hit depends a lot on the variety, and Japanese plums are often more affected than European ones.
seasoned: Small angular, water-soaked spots on leaves turn brown to purple-black and drop out, leaving a shot-hole look; heavy infection yellows and thins the canopy. On fruit, small sunken spots, pits, and cracks develop on the skin, downgrading the crop. Susceptibility varies sharply by cultivar, and Japanese plums are often hit harder than European.

beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism, not a fungus) called Xanthomonas. It spreads in warm, wet, windy weather and builds up when there are other susceptible plum or peach trees close by. The spots can look like spray damage.
seasoned: The bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It spreads in warm, wet, windy weather and builds up where susceptible plum, peach, and related trees grow nearby. Symptoms are sometimes mistaken for spray injury or nutrient problems.

beginner: There is no good home cure once it shows up. Copper sprays help a little as prevention but can hurt the tree if overused, so they are not a dependable fix. The best you can do is keep the tree healthy and the canopy open so it shrugs off the damage.
seasoned: Home options are limited once symptoms appear: copper sprays help more as prevention than cure and can injure the tree if overused, so they are not a reliable home fix. Keeping the tree vigorous and the canopy open and dry helps it tolerate the disease.

beginner: The best prevention is the variety you pick. Choosing a plum known to resist or tolerate bacterial spot avoids most of the trouble, so it is a decision to make before planting. Good airflow, going easy on nitrogen, and a healthy tree also help.
seasoned: The most effective measure is choosing a resistant or tolerant cultivar at planting; this is largely a variety decision made before the tree goes in. Good airflow, avoiding excess nitrogen, and tree vigor reduce severity.

beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Plan on about once or twice a week while a young tree is getting established, easing to about once a week for a fruiting tree in summer heat, adjusting for rain and your soil. Sandy soil dries out faster and needs watering more often; heavier soil stays wet longer. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs very little and rain usually covers it.
seasoned: Water on a deep-and-infrequent rhythm rather than a little every day: about once or twice a week while a young tree establishes, easing to roughly weekly for a bearing tree in the heat of summer, always adjusted for rain and soil type. A sandy soil dries faster and needs more frequent soaks; a heavier soil holds longer. Through winter dormancy, water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.

beginner: Each time you water, give the tree a deep soak that reaches all the way down to the roots, not just a quick splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak. An older, fruiting tree wants roughly an inch of water a week through the growing season, and more when it is hot. Deep soaks help the tree grow deep roots that handle dry spells.
seasoned: Water deeply each time so the moisture reaches the full depth of the root zone, rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing tree, that is on the order of 5 gallons per soak; for a bearing tree, aim for roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week through the growing season, more in heat. Deep, thorough soaks drive the deep rooting that carries the tree through dry spells.

beginner: Water at the ground around the roots using a drip line or a soaker hose, and keep the leaves and fruit dry. Spraying water over the top wets the leaves and fruit and helps diseases like brown rot take hold, so put the water on the soil, not on the tree. Spread it across the root area out to the edge of the branches, not just right at the trunk.
seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose, and keep the canopy and fruit dry. Overhead watering that wets the leaves and fruit prolongs leaf wetness and feeds brown rot and bacterial spot, so deliver water to the soil, not the tree. Apply it across the root area out toward the drip line rather than only at the trunk.

beginner: Too much water, or soil that drains poorly, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that slowly goes downhill. That is because waterlogged roots cannot breathe and start to rot. In plum, soil that stays wet can also bring on crown and root rot, which often kills the tree. Soil that never dries out between waterings is your warning to back off.
seasoned: Overwatering and poor drainage show as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists even in wet soil, and a generally declining tree, since waterlogged roots suffocate and rot. In stone fruit, chronically wet soil also invites crown and root rot, which is often fatal and rarely reversible once advanced. Soggy soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign to act on.

beginner: Too little water shows as wilting and dull, curling leaves, slower growth, and leaves dropping early in a long dry spell. The clearest sign is in the fruit: a tree that runs short of water while the plums are sizing up makes small, shriveled fruit, even though the tree itself lives through it. Try to catch the dry stress before the fruit suffers for it.
seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting and dull, curling leaves, slowed shoot growth, and early leaf drop in a prolonged dry spell. The most telling symptom is on the fruit: a tree short of water during the final swell sizes its plums poorly, leaving them small and prone to shriveling even though the tree itself survives. Catch the dry stress before the fruit pays for it.

beginner: While the tree is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps the tree grow the deep roots it needs.
seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the deep root system the tree relies on later.

beginner: While the plums are setting and sizing up, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch of water a week, more when it is hot, given as deep soaks. This is exactly when steady watering pays off in bigger, better plums.
seasoned: From fruit set through the final swell, do not let the tree dry out. Aim for the equivalent of about an inch of water per week, more in heat, delivered as deep soaks. Steady moisture now translates directly into larger, better-filled fruit and helps prevent the shriveling that dry stress causes.

beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during long dry stretches so the roots do not dry out. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.
seasoned: Once the tree is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only during prolonged dry spells to keep roots from desiccating. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.

beginner: Give the tree a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground (a drip line or soaker hose is ideal) instead of spraying the leaves, since wet leaves and fruit lead to disease. Young trees need steady moisture for their first couple of years to get established. Older trees can handle some dry spells, but the plums come out small if the tree gets too dry.
seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker, to encourage deep rooting; avoid wetting the canopy, which feeds brown rot and bacterial spot. Young trees need consistent moisture through their first two seasons to establish; mature trees are moderately drought-tolerant but size fruit poorly under stress.
render_status_label: B -- read, not rendered (Herb LLM grounding slice only)
render_evidence: no renderer; watering is in herb FACT_KEYS

beginner: The most important time to keep the tree watered is the last few weeks before harvest, when the plums do most of their growing. If the tree runs dry then, the fruit stays small and watering later will not fix it. The few weeks right after bloom matter too. If you ever have to cut back on water, the safest time is the middle of the season, when the pits are hardening.
seasoned: The make-or-break window is the final swell, roughly the last 3 to 5 weeks before harvest, when cell expansion adds most of the fruit's final size. Water stress then causes irreversible loss of size and can leave plums small and prone to shriveling. Early rapid growth just after bloom is also sensitive; mild stress during pit hardening (mid-season) is the most tolerable time to ease off if water is limited.
render_status_label: B -- read, not rendered (Herb LLM grounding slice only)
render_evidence: no renderer; watering is in herb FACT_KEYS

beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to outdoor conditions) does not apply to plum. You plant it bare-root and dormant, in late winter or early spring, rather than as a seedling started inside, so there is no tender young plant to ease outdoors.
seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to plum. It arrives as a dormant, bare-root tree and goes in the ground in late winter or early spring, not raised from a seedling indoors, so there is no tender transplant to acclimate to the outdoors.

beginner: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant (resting, with no leaves) in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground has thawed enough to dig. Soak the roots in a bucket of water for an hour or two first so they do not stay dried out. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots out without bending them, and set the tree so the graft union (that bumpy joint near the base, where the fruiting variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 inches above the soil. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. Refill with the same soil you removed, water it in well, and add a stake only if the spot is windy.
seasoned: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant in late winter to early spring, before bud break, once the ground has thawed enough to dig. Soak the roots in water for an hour or two beforehand to rehydrate them. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them and set the tree so the graft union (that swollen joint near the base of the trunk) sits 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line. Do not add fertilizer to the planting hole; backfill with native soil, water in well, and stake only if the site is windy.

beginner: Fill the pot with a chunky, fast-draining mix made for shrubs and trees, not a soft peat-based potting soil that stays soggy. A bark-based mix (composted bark with perlite or pumice mixed in for drainage) holds the air the roots need. Do not use soil dug from the yard in a pot, because it packs down and drains badly when you water often.
seasoned: Use a coarse, fast-draining soilless mix built for woody plants, not a peat-heavy potting soil that stays wet. Favor the low-chill Japanese plums, which are desert-adapted and fit the warm valley's limited winter chill; the high-chill European prune plums need more cold than the core banks. The dry air keeps disease low, so a late frost on the early bloom and steady summer irrigation matter more. Plant a bare-root or container tree during the dormant season.

beginner: Plum grows well in St. George if you pick the right type. The low-chill Japanese plums suit the warm valley; the European prune plums need more winter cold than the core provides. Give trees steady water through the hot summer and watch for a late frost on the early bloom.
seasoned: Plum splits along species lines here. The low-chill Japanese plums, needing only a few hundred chill hours, are a desert Southwest classic and fit the warm St. George core, where Washington County Extension lists plum among the fruits that do well at low elevation. The high-chill European prune plums need more winter cold than the valley floor banks and are a poorer fit. The dry air keeps disease low; a late frost on the early bloom and steady irrigation through the hot season, not chill or brown rot, are the defining concerns.

beginner: Apricot wants a deep soil that drains fast and lets air reach the roots. Good drainage is the one rule you cannot bend with apricot, because it has little tolerance for wet, heavy ground and the root and crown rots that follow it. A sandy loam is a great fit, and a lighter sandy soil works if you keep up with water. Heavy clay that holds water is the trouble spot; on clay, plant on a raised mound so the roots sit above the soggy soil, and choose a plum rootstock (Myrobalan or Marianna) that takes heavier ground. One apricot quirk: in the alkaline soils of the arid West it is prone to iron chlorosis, where the leaves yellow between green veins, so a near-neutral soil with some compost suits it best.
seasoned: Apricot demands a deep, well-drained loam with good aeration; drainage is the non-negotiable, since it has little tolerance for wet or heavy soils and waterlogging brings on crown and root rot. A sandy loam is well suited and a lighter sandy soil is workable with attention to water. Heavy, water-holding clay is the problem texture; on such ground, plant on a raised berm and pair the tree with a heavier-soil-tolerant plum rootstock (Myrobalan or Marianna 2624) rather than a drainage-fussy seedling stock. Note the apricot-specific weakness: on the high-pH soils of the arid West it is prone to iron chlorosis (interveinal yellowing), so a near-neutral, moderately fertile soil is ideal.

beginner: Apricot grows best in a near-neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerates from about 6.0 to 8.0 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline the soil is). It leans more tolerant of alkaline soil than most stone fruit, but on strongly alkaline western soils it often shows iron chlorosis, a yellowing between the leaf veins. Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if needed: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if it is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is far easier to fix before the permanent tree goes in.
seasoned: Apricot does best in a near-neutral soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerates about 6.0 to 8.0. It is somewhat more alkaline-tolerant than peach or cherry, but on the high-pH soils of the arid West it is notably prone to iron chlorosis (interveinal yellowing). Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground.

beginner: Feed once in early spring before the tree starts growing. Scatter the fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. Apricot does not need heavy feeding, so go light: if the tree is making plenty of new growth, it may need none at all. If the leaves yellow between the veins (common on western alkaline soils), that is an iron problem, not a nitrogen one, so use a chelated iron product instead of more fertilizer. Never feed late in the year, because soft late growth gets damaged by winter cold.
seasoned: Feed lightly in early spring before growth begins, broadcasting evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, off the trunk, and watering it in. Apricot needs modest nitrogen: judge by shoot growth and ease off if the tree is already vigorous. On the alkaline soils of the arid West, watch for iron chlorosis (interveinal yellowing) and correct it with a chelated iron rather than piling on nitrogen. Never feed late in the season, since late nitrogen pushes soft growth that winter cold injures and that canker enters.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works for backyard apricots, used sparingly. Do not overdo nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth that is more prone to disease and winter damage.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits backyard apricots, applied modestly. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which drives soft, disease-prone, overly vigorous growth at the expense of fruiting and winter hardiness.

beginner: A simple guide is a small handful of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, up to a modest amount, spread once in early spring before the buds open. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing. If the tree is already growing more than a foot of new branch each year, it probably needs little or no feeding at all.
seasoned: A common home rate is about 1/2 to 1 pound of actual nitrogen equivalent scaled to tree age, applied once in early spring before bud break, kept modest because apricot fruits on long-lived spurs and does not need the heavy nitrogen a peach does. Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins. Judge by shoot growth: a bearing tree wants roughly 12 to 18 inches of new wood a year.

beginner: Apricot is self-fruitful, which means one tree makes fruit on its own and you do not need a second tree to pollinate it. A few varieties, notably Moorpark, set a heavier crop when a second apricot blooms nearby, but even they fruit alone, so a lone tree is fine. Beyond that, what matters for a tree is the root zone, not the usual vegetable pairings: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, since lawn competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free area helps it settle in. The one site rule is replant disease: do not plant an apricot where another apricot, peach, plum, cherry, or nectarine was recently growing.
seasoned: Apricot is self-fruitful, so a single tree sets a crop on its own with no pollinizer required; a handful of cultivars (Moorpark is the classic) set more heavily with a compatible second variety, but none actually need one. Past pollination, the interactions that matter for a tree are at the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since they compete hard with a young tree, and a mulched, competition-free root area establishes it faster. The one site rule is replant disease: do not follow stone fruit with stone fruit on the same ground.

beginner: On small developing apricots, look for a curved, crescent-shaped scar, the mark the beetle leaves when it lays an egg. Damaged fruit often drops early, and some that stays on the tree ends up misshapen or has a grub inside. You see this soon after the petals fall.
seasoned: Small young fruit carries a distinctive crescent-shaped scar where the female cut a slit to lay an egg. Infested fruit often drops early; fruit that hangs on may be gnarled or have a grub tunneling inside near the pit. Damage appears shortly after petal fall and is heaviest east of the Rockies.

beginner: A small beetle with a long snout called the plum curculio. The adults show up around bloom and start damaging the little fruits right after the petals drop, laying eggs inside them. The larvae then feed within the fruit. It is mostly an eastern problem and rare in dry western climates.
seasoned: The plum curculio (Conotrachelus nenuphar), a small snout beetle native to eastern North America. Adults emerge around bloom and attack fruit from petal fall onward, laying eggs in the developing fruit; the larvae feed inside. There is little pressure in the arid West.

beginner: Early in the morning the beetles are slow. Spread a sheet under the tree, tap the branches so the beetles fall, and destroy them. Pick up and throw away any dropped fruit promptly so the larvae inside do not mature. A kaolin clay spray (a fine white mineral coating) starting at petal fall helps keep them off.
seasoned: For a backyard tree, jarring the limbs over a sheet in the early morning when the beetles are sluggish, then destroying what drops, reduces the population. Promptly gather and dispose of dropped infested fruit to break the cycle. Kaolin clay applied from petal fall is an organic deterrent.

beginner: The main thing is cleanup. Pick up fallen fruit all season so the larvae inside cannot finish growing in the soil under the tree. Keeping the ground clear lowers the number of beetles the next year.
seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: remove dropped fruit through the season so larvae cannot complete development in the soil beneath the tree. A clean orchard floor and prompt fruit pickup steadily lower pressure year over year.

beginner: Look at the very bottom of the trunk where it meets the soil. Peachtree borers leave a sticky, gummy ooze mixed with what looks like wet sawdust (called frass). You may see a small mound of gum and frass at the base. A young tree with several borers can be killed in one season, so this is one to catch early.
seasoned: Gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass at the base of the trunk, right around the soil line, often with a mounded look where the bark meets the ground. Larvae tunnel the inner bark at the crown; several borers can girdle and kill a young apricot in a single season, and the wounds also open the door to canker.

beginner: The larvae (young, grub-like stage) of the peachtree borer, a moth whose adults look like wasps and fly during the day. The adults lay eggs on the lower trunk in summer, and the larvae burrow into the bark at and below the soil line. Trees with existing wounds are hit hardest, but a healthy tree can be attacked too.
seasoned: Larvae of the peachtree borer (Synanthedon exitiosa), a clearwing moth whose adults are day-flying and wasp-like. Eggs are laid on the lower trunk in summer; the larvae tunnel the inner bark at and just below the soil line. It attacks all stone fruit, apricot included, and hits stressed or wounded trees first.

beginner: Once the larvae are inside, no spray reaches them. The backyard fix is to scrape soil away from the base in late summer or fall, find the holes marked by gum and frass, and kill the larvae with a thin, stiff wire pushed into each hole. Then smooth the soil back. Avoid nicking the trunk base with mowers or trimmers.
seasoned: There is no rescue spray once larvae are tunneling inside. The practical home control is to expose the crown in late summer or fall, find the entry holes by the gum and frass, and kill larvae by hand with a thin wire (worming). Keep the trunk base free of wounds and paint it white against sunscald cracks.

beginner: Keep mowers and string trimmers away from the trunk; the wounds they leave attract the egg-laying moths, and white trunk paint prevents the sunburn cracks they enter. Keep grass and weeds cleared from the base so you can see the soil line, and check it every late summer for fresh gummy ooze.
seasoned: Protect the lower trunk from mechanical injury and sunscald (a white trunk paint helps), keep the tree vigorous, and clear weeds and tall grass from the base so the crown stays open and easy to inspect. Check the soil line each late summer for fresh gum so an infestation is caught in its first year.

beginner: Clusters of small green or gray soft-bodied insects on the tips of new spring growth, curling and twisting the young leaves, with a sticky coating below that turns black and moldy. It is worst on young trees and mainly stunts new growth rather than ruining fruit.
seasoned: Dense colonies of green or mealy-gray aphids on the tips of new spring shoots, curling and distorting young leaves, with sticky honeydew below that blackens into sooty mold. Heaviest on vigorous young trees; it slows shoot growth but rarely harms fruit directly.

beginner: Small sap-sucking insects (green peach aphid and mealy plum aphid). Their eggs overwinter on the tree and the young hatch to feed on the soft new spring growth. The numbers usually drop on their own by midsummer as the shoots toughen and ladybugs and other helpers move in.
seasoned: Chiefly the green peach aphid and the mealy plum aphid. They overwinter as eggs on the tree and explode on the tender spring flush, feeding on sap; populations usually crash by midsummer as shoots harden and natural enemies build up.

beginner: Often you can leave it alone, since ladybugs and other helpers clear it by midsummer. On a young tree that is badly hit, blast the colonies off with a hose, or spray the curled tips with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil. Do not over-fertilize, since lush new growth is what the aphids love.
seasoned: Often no action is needed, since beneficials clean it up by midsummer. For a heavy infestation on a young tree, a strong jet of water knocks colonies off, or insecticidal soap or horticultural oil applied to the curled tips works; protect the ladybugs and lacewings that do most of the control. Avoid high-nitrogen feeding, which fuels the soft growth aphids prefer.

beginner: Avoid heavy feeding that pushes the soft growth aphids love, welcome ladybugs and lacewings, and do not panic over the spring leaf-curl, which usually does not hurt the crop. A dormant oil spray in late winter cuts down the overwintering eggs.
seasoned: Keep trees vigorous but not over-fed (high nitrogen invites aphids), encourage beneficial insects, and tolerate the early-season curl, which rarely affects the crop. A dormant oil spray reduces overwintering eggs where the pest is chronic.

beginner: Tiny gray bumps crusting the bark of twigs and branches, and small red-ringed spots on the fruit. A bad case can weaken branches and even kill them, and it spots the fruit. The scales are easy to miss because each one is barely the size of a pinhead.
seasoned: Tiny gray, cone-shaped scales encrusting bark on twigs and scaffolds, sometimes with a reddish halo, and small red-ringed spots on the fruit skin. Heavy infestations weaken and can kill branches, and the fruit blemishes downgrade the crop.

beginner: A tiny armored insect called San Jose scale that sits under a waxy cover and sucks sap from the bark. It has several rounds a year. The young, called crawlers, are the only stage that moves around and the only one a spray can hit.
seasoned: San Jose scale (Diaspidiotus perniciosus), an armored scale insect that feeds on sap under a waxy cover. It has several overlapping generations a year; the mobile crawler stage is the point at which it spreads and the only stage a spray reaches.

beginner: The main control is a good horticultural oil spray while the tree is bare and dormant, coating the twigs and branches to smother the scale. During the season, prune out and destroy any branches that are heavily crusted. Keeping the tree open and vigorous helps.
seasoned: A thorough dormant-season horticultural oil spray, applied to the leafless tree so it coats twigs and scaffolds, smothers overwintering scale and is the mainstay backyard control. In-season, time any additional oil to the crawler stage. Prune out and destroy heavily encrusted wood.

beginner: A yearly dormant oil spray in late winter keeps scale from building up. Avoid harsh insecticides so the natural enemies that eat scale can do their work, and keep the tree pruned open so any spray reaches all the bark.
seasoned: An annual dormant oil spray keeps scale from building up. Encourage the tiny parasitic wasps and predatory beetles that attack scale by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides, and prune to keep the canopy open and easy to cover thoroughly.

beginner: Ripe apricots have sunken, puckered, dimpled patches, a look growers call catfacing. It comes from insects feeding on the fruit when it was small. The fruit is still usable; the damage is mostly on the surface and does not spread.
seasoned: Mature fruit shows sunken, dimpled, corky distortions, the puckered catfaced look, where feeding occurred on young fruit. The damage is cosmetic on the surface but can run into the flesh; it does not spread or rot on its own.

beginner: A handful of insects, chiefly stink bugs and the small tarnished plant bug, that poke the young apricots to feed. The spot they feed on stops growing while the rest of the fruit swells around it, leaving a dimple. Because apricots set fruit early, the little fruit is out just as these bugs get going in spring.
seasoned: Several true bugs, mainly stink bugs and the tarnished plant bug, that puncture small apricots to feed. Tissue at each feeding point stops growing while the surrounding flesh keeps swelling, so the mature fruit is left puckered and corky. Apricot ripens early, so the vulnerable young-fruit stage overlaps the spring buildup of these bugs.

beginner: Spraying a single tree does not help much, because these bugs come in from weeds and brush nearby. The better fix is to take away their hiding spots: mow and pull the broadleaf weeds around the tree, especially in spring while the fruit is small.
seasoned: Spraying one tree does little, since these bugs commute in from nearby weeds and brush. The practical control is to deny them that harborage: mow and clear the broadleaf weeds around the tree, especially through spring when young fruit is most vulnerable.

beginner: Keep the ground around the tree mowed and clear of broadleaf weeds, which is where these bugs live and breed. A clean, grassy area around the tree means fewer of them ever reach your apricots.
seasoned: Keep the surrounding ground mowed and free of the broadleaf weeds these bugs breed in; a clean, grassy strip around the tree is the single biggest thing that lowers how many reach the fruit.

beginner: At bloom, flowers go limp and brown and small gummy dead patches form on the nearby spurs. As apricots ripen, brown spots appear and spread quickly, sometimes rotting a whole fruit in a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan fuzz on top. Rotted fruit shrivels into a hard mummy that hangs on. Apricot catches brown rot more easily than almost any other fruit.
seasoned: At bloom, infected blossoms wilt and brown and the infection runs into the spur to form a small gummy canker. As fruit ripens, firm brown spots appear and spread fast, rotting a whole apricot within a day or two in warm, wet weather, with a dusty tan spore mass on the surface. Rotted fruit dries into a clinging mummy. Apricot is among the most brown-rot-susceptible of all stone fruit.

beginner: A fungus called Monilinia. It survives winter in dried mummy fruit and dead twig patches, then releases spores at bloom that infect the flowers, which later cause the fruit to rot. Warm, wet weather makes it spread fast, which is why apricots do much better in dry-summer climates than in humid ones.
seasoned: The fungus Monilinia (M. fructicola and M. laxa). It overwinters in mummies and twig cankers; spores at bloom infect flowers, and those infections later seed the fruit rot. Warm, humid, wet weather drives it, which is a large part of why apricot is a poor risk in the humid Southeast and better in dry western summers.

beginner: Cleanup is the main control: take off and destroy every dried mummy from the tree and ground and prune out the gummy dead twig patches, which hold the spores. If bloom is wet, an organic-approved spray at bloom helps protect the flowers. Pick on time, handle gently, and throw out any rotting fruit right away.
seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: remove and destroy every mummy from the tree and ground and prune out gummy twig cankers, since these are the spore sources. In a wet bloom, an organic-approved bloom-time fungicide reduces blossom blight. Pick promptly, handle gently, and remove any rotting fruit at once; an open, fast-drying canopy is a standing defense.

beginner: Cleaning up all year prevents most of it: never leave dried mummies over winter, prune so the tree is open and dries fast after rain, and pick on time. In wet climates you will likely need an organic-approved spray at bloom and again near harvest, because apricot is so prone to this disease.
seasoned: Year-round sanitation prevents most loss: never leave mummies over winter, keep the canopy open with pruning so fruit dries fast after rain, harvest promptly, and favor a dry-summer site. In humid regions, plan on a bloom and pre-harvest fungicide program, since apricot's high susceptibility makes sanitation alone insufficient.

beginner: Sunken, dark, gummy patches (cankers) on the trunk and branches that ooze amber sap, often killing the branch above them. In spring, flowers and buds may blacken and die, and some buds never open. It is one of the worst apricot diseases and hits harder on trees grown on plum rootstocks.
seasoned: Sunken, dark, gummy cankers on trunk, scaffolds, and spurs that ooze amber gum, often girdling and killing limbs; in spring, blossoms and spurs blast (blacken and die) and dormant buds fail to open. It is one of the most serious apricot diseases and is worse on trees grown on plum rootstocks (Myrobalan, Marianna), which are especially susceptible.

beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism) called Pseudomonas syringae. It gets in through wounds, leaf scars, and frost damage during cool, wet weather, and is worse on stressed trees, those in wet soil, hit by frost, or pushed with too much nitrogen. Apricot blooms so early that its tender new growth often meets the cold, wet weather this disease loves.
seasoned: The bacterium Pseudomonas syringae. It infects through wounds, leaf scars, and frost-injured tissue in cool, wet spring and fall weather, and is worsened by anything that stresses the tree: poor drainage, ring nematodes, frost, and high-nitrogen soft growth. Apricot's very early bloom exposes fresh tissue to exactly the cold, wet spells that favor it.

beginner: There is no cure once it sets in. The approach is prevention: cut out the cankered wood well below the dead patch during dry summer weather (not in wet spring), clean your tools between cuts, and pull out a badly infected young tree. Keep the tree healthy, unstressed, and on well-drained ground; copper sprays only help a little.
seasoned: There is no cure once a tree is infected. Management is preventive: cut out cankered wood well below the canker in dry summer weather (not in wet spring), disinfecting tools between cuts, and remove badly infected young trees. Keep the tree unstressed and well drained; copper sprays give only partial protection and resistance is common.

beginner: Prevention is everything: plant where the soil drains well, pick a more resistant rootstock (a peach seedling like Lovell resists it better than plum rootstocks), avoid frosty low spots and trunk wounds, paint the trunk white to prevent sunburn cracks, prune only in dry summer weather, and do not over-feed. A healthy, unstressed tree on good ground shrugs it off best.
seasoned: Prevention is everything: plant on well-drained ground, choose a tolerant rootstock (a peach seedling such as Lovell is more canker-tolerant than the plum stocks), avoid frost-pocket sites and trunk wounds, paint the trunk white against sunscald cracks, prune only in dry summer weather, and never push soft growth with late nitrogen.

beginner: Leaves get small angular water-soaked spots that turn brown and fall out, leaving little holes, called a shot-hole look. Bad cases turn leaves yellow and thin out the tree. On the fruit, small sunken spots and skin cracks form. How badly a tree is hit depends a lot on the variety and on how humid your area is.
seasoned: Small angular, water-soaked spots on leaves turn brown and drop out, leaving a shot-hole look; heavy infection yellows and thins the canopy. On fruit, small sunken spots and cracks develop on the skin. Susceptibility varies by cultivar, and pressure is highest in warm, humid regions.

beginner: A bacterium (a microscopic organism, not a fungus) called Xanthomonas. It spreads in warm, wet weather and builds up when there are other susceptible stone-fruit trees close by. Its leaf holes can look like the fungal shot hole disease, which is a different problem.
seasoned: The bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It spreads in warm, wet weather and builds up where susceptible stone fruit grow nearby. On apricot the leaf and fruit spotting is sometimes confused with the fungal shot hole (Coryneum blight).

beginner: There is no good home cure once it shows up. Copper sprays help a little as prevention but can hurt the tree if overused, so they are not a dependable fix. The best you can do is keep the tree healthy and open so the leaves dry fast.
seasoned: Home options are limited once symptoms appear: copper sprays help more as prevention than cure and can injure the tree if overused, so they are not a reliable home fix. Keeping the tree vigorous and the canopy open and dry helps it tolerate the disease.

beginner: The best prevention is the variety and the site you pick. A tolerant variety on a spot with dry summers and good airflow avoids most of the trouble, so it is a decision to make before planting. A healthy, open tree also helps.
seasoned: The most effective measure is choosing a resistant or tolerant cultivar and a dry-summer site; this is largely a decision made before the tree goes in. Good airflow, an open canopy, and tree vigor reduce severity.

beginner: Small reddish-purple spots on the leaves whose brown centers fall out, leaving neat round holes that look like the leaf was hit with birdshot. It also spots the fruit and can kill buds. A bad case drops a lot of leaves and weakens the tree. Apricot is one of its favorite hosts.
seasoned: Small reddish-purple spots on leaves whose centers turn brown, die, and drop out, leaving clean round holes as if shot with birdshot. It also spots the fruit and can kill dormant buds and cause small twig cankers with gumming. Heavy infection defoliates and weakens the tree; apricot is a classic host.

beginner: A fungus (Coryneum blight) that spends winter in infected buds and twigs and spreads in cool, wet spring weather and wherever water splashes the leaves. Overhead sprinklers that wet the tree make it much worse.
seasoned: The fungus Wilsonomyces carpophilus (Coryneum blight). It overwinters in infected buds and twig lesions and spreads in cool, wet spring weather and by splashing water and overhead irrigation. Wet springs and sprinkler wetting of the canopy drive it.

beginner: Cut out infected twigs, rake up and destroy fallen spotted leaves, and water at the ground rather than over the top so the leaves stay dry. A copper spray on the bare, dormant tree in late winter is the main way to protect it where this disease is common.
seasoned: Prune out infected twigs and buds, rake and destroy fallen infected leaves, and switch irrigation to the root zone so the canopy stays dry. A dormant application of fixed copper on the leafless tree is the main protective spray where the disease is established.

beginner: The biggest thing is keeping the leaves dry: water at the ground, not over the tree, prune so air moves through, and clean up fallen leaves. In wet-spring areas, a copper spray on the bare tree in late winter protects it.
seasoned: Keep water off the canopy (drip or soaker, never overhead), prune for airflow, clear fallen leaves, and apply a dormant copper spray in wet-spring regions. Dry-summer irrigation discipline is the single biggest lever.

beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Plan on about once or twice a week while a young tree is getting established, easing to about once a week for a fruiting tree in summer heat, adjusting for rain and your soil. Apricot hates soggy soil, so let the surface dry out between waterings. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs very little and rain usually covers it.
seasoned: Water deep-and-infrequent rather than little-and-often: about once or twice a week while a young tree establishes, easing to roughly weekly (a deep soak) for a bearing tree in summer heat, always adjusted for rain and soil. Apricot resents constantly wet soil, so let the top of the root zone dry between soaks. Through winter dormancy water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.

beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches all the way down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 3 to 5 gallons per soak. An older, fruiting tree wants roughly an inch of water a week through the season, and more when it is hot, given as deep soaks. Steady water while the fruit is filling out makes bigger apricots.
seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root zone, not just the surface. For an establishing tree, on the order of 3 to 5 gallons per soak; for a bearing tree, roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week through the season, more in heat, delivered as deep soaks to a 3-foot depth. Steady moisture through the final swell sizes the fruit.

beginner: Water at the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, and keep the leaves and fruit dry. Spraying water over the top wets the leaves and helps diseases like brown rot and shot hole, so put the water on the soil, not the tree. Spread it across the root area out to the edge of the branches, not just right at the trunk.
seasoned: Water at the root zone by drip or soaker and keep the canopy and fruit dry. Overhead watering that wets the leaves feeds brown rot, shot hole, and bacterial canker, so deliver water to the soil, not the tree. Apply it across the root area out toward the drip line rather than only at the trunk.

beginner: Too much water, or soil that drains poorly, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that slowly goes downhill, because the roots cannot breathe. In apricot, soil that stays wet also brings on crown and root rot and the serious disease bacterial canker. Soil that never dries out between waterings is your warning to back off.
seasoned: Overwatering and poor drainage show as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists even in wet soil, and a declining tree, since apricot roots suffocate in soggy ground. Chronically wet soil also brings on crown and root rot and predisposes the trunk to bacterial canker, both often fatal. Soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign to act on.

beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, slower growth, and leaves dropping early in a long dry spell. The clearest sign is in the fruit: a tree that runs short of water while the apricots are sizing up makes small, less sweet fruit, even though the tree itself lives through it. Try to catch the dry stress before the fruit suffers for it.
seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, slowed shoot growth, and early leaf drop in a long dry spell. The most telling symptom is on the fruit: a tree short of water during the final swell sizes its apricots poorly, leaving them small and less sweet even though the tree survives. Catch the dry stress before the fruit pays for it.

beginner: While the tree is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 3 to 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps the tree grow the deep roots it needs.
seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 3 to 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the deep root system the tree relies on later.

beginner: While the apricots are sizing up and coloring, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch of water a week as deep soaks. Steady watering now is what gives you bigger, sweeter fruit.
seasoned: As the fruit sizes and colors, keep moisture steady. Aim for about an inch of water per week as deep soaks and avoid a dry-then-wet swing. Consistent soil moisture through this window is what sizes and sweetens the crop.

beginner: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant (resting, no leaves) in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground can be dug; in mild-winter areas that means December through February. Soak the roots in a bucket for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them, and set the tree so the graft union (the bumpy joint near the base, where the variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 inches above the soil. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. Refill with the same soil, water in well, and add a stake only if it is windy. Most of all, avoid low, frosty spots, because apricot blooms so early that late frosts are its biggest threat.
seasoned: Plant the bare-root tree while dormant in late winter to early spring, before bud break, once the ground can be worked; in mild-winter regions this is December through February. Do not fertilize the hole; backfill with native soil, water in well, and stake if the site is windy. Above all, choose a planting spot that is not a frost pocket, since apricot's very early bloom is its greatest vulnerability.

beginner: Pick an apricot variety first by when it blooms, because apricots flower very early and their biggest problem is losing the flowers to a late frost. Later-blooming, cold-hardy kinds (Chinese/Mormon, Goldrich, Harglow) are the safest choice if spring frosts are a worry where you live. Next, match chill hours, the amount of winter cold a variety needs: most apricots want 600 to 900 hours, and a few low-chill types like Katy need only about 350 for mild-winter areas. The famous-flavor kinds (Blenheim, Moorpark) bloom early and do best in dry-summer areas with steady springs. One tree makes fruit on its own; a second variety is just a bonus for the few that want a partner, like Moorpark.
seasoned: Choose an apricot variety first by BLOOM TIMING, because apricot's defining problem is that it blooms earlier than almost any other fruit tree and loses its crop to late frost. Later-blooming, cold-hardy cultivars (Chinese/Mormon, Goldrich, Harglow) are the safest bet wherever spring frosts are a risk. Match chill next: most apricots want 600 to 900 hours, with a few low-chill types (Katy) bearing on about 350. The famous flavor cultivars (Blenheim, Moorpark) are early-blooming and best reserved for dry-summer regions with dependable springs. beginner: Leave firm apricots on the counter, out of direct sun, to soften the rest of the way, usually 1 to 3 days, until they give to a gentle squeeze and smell sweet. Apricots you picked already soft will only keep a day or two out, so eat or refrigerate them soon.
seasoned: Hold firm-picked apricots at room temperature out of direct sun to finish softening, typically 1 to 3 days, until they yield to gentle pressure and smell fragrant. Tree-ripe fruit picked soft will only last a day or two on the counter, so plan to eat or refrigerate it promptly.

beginner: Put apricots in the fridge only after they are ripe, and eat them within about 3 to 5 days. Chilling an unripe apricot can leave it dry and grainy once you take it out, so let it soften on the counter first. For the best taste, let cold apricots warm back to room temperature before you eat them.
seasoned: Refrigerate apricots only once they are ripe, then eat within about 3 to 5 days. As with peach, refrigerating an underripe apricot risks chilling injury (dry, mealy flesh once it warms), so counter-ripen first. Bring cold apricots back to room temperature before serving for the best flavor.

beginner: Apricots freeze nicely if you halve and pit them first. Toss the halves with a little lemon juice so they do not brown, spread them on a tray to freeze, then pack them into freezer bags. They keep for several months and are best for cooking, baking, and smoothies. Apricots are also one of the best fruits for drying.
seasoned: Apricots freeze well halved and pitted. Toss the halves with a little lemon juice or an ascorbic-acid dip to limit browning, freeze them in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to freezer bags. Frozen apricots keep their quality for several months and are best used for cooking, baking, and smoothies. Apricots also dry exceptionally well.

beginner: Apricots do not keep long once ripe, so ripen firm ones on the counter, refrigerate only when ripe, and eat them within a few days. Drying or freezing is the best way to save a big harvest.
seasoned: Apricot is fragile and short-lived once ripe, so counter-ripen firm fruit, refrigerate only when ripe, and keep cold storage short. Drying and freezing are the classic ways to keep a heavy crop.

beginner: You do not rotate an apricot tree the way you rotate vegetables, because it stays in one spot for many years. What matters instead is replant disease: do not plant a new apricot where an apricot, peach, plum, cherry, or nectarine just came out. Planting a stone fruit right back where another stone fruit grew leads to weak, stunted trees, and old spots can hold pests and diseases that hurt the new tree.
seasoned: Annual crop rotation does not apply to an apricot: the tree holds its site for decades. The real concern is replant disease. Do not plant a new apricot (or other stone fruit) where an apricot, peach, plum, cherry, or nectarine was recently growing, since Prunus-after-Prunus replanting causes stunting and poor establishment, and old sites can carry ring nematodes and bacterial canker.

beginner: If you have no choice but to replant where a stone fruit was, dig out and replace a big area of soil, pick a tougher rootstock, and expect the tree to start slower. The simplest fix is to plant in a new spot instead.
seasoned: If an apricot must go where a stone fruit was removed, replace a generous volume of soil, choose a tolerant rootstock, and expect slower establishment. Best practice is simply to pick a new location.

Low chill varieties like Katy and Blenheim are the safest choice everywhere; the higher chill kinds such as Moorpark, Tilton, and Harglow do well in zone 9 and zone 8 but are a gamble at Laughlin.

Zone 8's wider band clears the whole list comfortably. At Laughlin (zone 10), only the lowest chill picks, Katy and Blenheim, are a safe bet; the 600 hour and up varieties need more cold than that warm corner reliably delivers.

beginner: An apricot is a fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and gives you fruit you can let ripen right on the branch, which is where apricots taste their best, and they ripen earlier than peaches. One tree fruits on its own, so you do not need a second one. The big thing to know is that apricots bloom earlier than almost any other fruit tree, so a late frost can kill the flowers most years unless you plant in a spot that does not get frosty and choose a late-blooming variety. Apricots also take steady work: prune the tree every winter into an open vase shape, manage diseases (brown rot most of all), thin off the extra little fruit so the rest grow big, and give the tree a cold-enough winter. With a dry-summer or frost-safe spot and that care, a backyard apricot gives you fruit far better than the store.
seasoned: Apricot is a deciduous stone-fruit tree (Prunus armeniaca) prized for fruit that ripens best tree-ripened at home, where it can hang to full flavor rather than being picked firm for shipping. It is self-fruitful, so a single tree bears, and it ripens earlier than peach. Its defining trait, and its defining challenge, is that it blooms earlier than almost any other fruit tree: the open flowers meet late frosts most springs on a frost-prone site, so variety choice and a frost-aware location matter more than anything. It also asks for real work: an annual dormant pruning to an open center, disease management (brown rot above all, plus bacterial canker and shot hole), early fruit thinning, and enough winter chill to break dormancy. Given a dry-summer or frost-safe site and that care, a backyard apricot rewards you with fruit grocery shelves cannot match.

beginner: An apricot is ripe when the whole fruit turns from green to a warm yellow or orange, gives a little when you press gently, smells sweet, and comes off the branch with a gentle twist instead of a hard pull. A pink blush alone does not mean ripe. If you need to carry, store, or dry them, pick when fully colored but still a little firm and let them soften on the counter. For eating right away, pick when they give to a gentle squeeze. The tree ripens over one to three weeks, so pick it a few times.
seasoned: An apricot is ready when the ground color shifts fully from green to a warm yellow or deep orange, the flesh gives slightly to gentle pressure, the aroma turns full and sweet, and the fruit separates from the spur with a light twist. Any pink blush is not ripeness by itself. Pick slightly firm if you need to handle, ship, or dry the fruit, and let it finish softening on the counter; pick at full give for eating that day. A tree ripens over one to three weeks, so pick in several passes.

beginner: Apricot trees flower very early, usually late winter to early spring, sometimes as early as January in warm areas and as late as March or April in cold ones, often before the leaves come out. Apricots bloom earlier than peaches, plums, or apples, and that is their weak point: a hard late frost can kill the open flowers and the tiny fruit behind them. Choosing a variety that blooms later and a spot that does not get frosty is the best way to protect the crop.
seasoned: Apricots bloom very early, typically late winter to early spring, from January in the low desert and mild coastal California to March or April in the North, usually before the leaves. Apricot opens its flowers earlier than peach, plum, or apple, and that early bloom is its chief vulnerability: the white-to-pink blossoms are killed by the hard late frosts that are still common when they open. Choosing a late-blooming cultivar and a frost-safe site is the main way to protect the crop.

beginner: Apricot trees are usually grown in zones 5 to 8, and tough varieties survive into zone 4, but living and fruiting are two different things. The problem is almost never that the tree freezes in winter; it is that apricot blooms so early that late spring frosts kill the flowers, even in places plenty warm enough to grow the tree. The most reliable apricot areas have dry summers, winters cold enough to hold bloom back a little, and springs without late frosts, like interior California and the Intermountain West. Warmer zones (9 and up) usually have too little winter cold, and the humid Southeast has too much disease. Pick a late-blooming, cold-hardy variety and a spot that does not get frosty for the best chance at a crop.
seasoned: Apricot trees are commonly grown in USDA zones 5 to 8, and the wood of hardy cultivars survives into zone 4, but surviving is not the same as fruiting. The limiting factor is almost never midwinter cold hardiness; it is the very early bloom meeting late spring frost. Because apricot flowers so early, even zones warm enough to grow it easily lose the crop in many springs, and hardy northern trees may bloom and be frozen out year after year. The most dependable apricot regions are dry-summer areas with cold-enough winters to hold bloom back and dependable, frost-free springs (interior California and the Intermountain West are classic). The warm edge (zones 9 and warmer) is limited by too little winter chill and, in the humid Southeast, by heavy disease. Match a late-blooming, cold-hardy cultivar to a frost-safe site and you give yourself the best odds.
