seasoned: Mandarins require no winter chilling to flower or fruit. They are evergreen and do not enter a chill-triggered dormancy; flowering is driven by spring warming and moisture rather than release from a prior cold period. This distinguishes citrus from deciduous fruit trees such as peaches and apples, which need hundreds of chill hours to break bud dormancy and set a normal crop.

beginner: A mandarin makes fruit on its own, with no second tree and no bees needed, and most types are seedless when grown away from other citrus. Satsuma is naturally seedless. Clementine and some others are seedless by themselves, but if pollen from another citrus nearby reaches the flowers, the fruit ends up with seeds, so keeping a seedless mandarin away from other pollen-making citrus is what keeps it seedless.
seasoned: Most mandarins set a full crop on a single tree and are seedless when grown in isolation. Satsuma is parthenocarpic and reliably seedless. Clementine and W. Murcott are self-incompatible but facultatively parthenocarpic: they set seedless fruit on their own, yet fertile pollen from another nearby citrus cross-pollinates them and puts seeds into the fruit, and citrus pollen can travel a long way, so isolation from pollen-bearing citrus is what keeps seedless types seedless. A few mandarin hybrids fruit better with a compatible pollinizer, but the common seedless mandarins need no pollinizer and no bees for a single tree to fruit.

beginner: Figs are not fussy about soil and grow in a wide range, from sandy to heavier ground, as long as it drains well and does not stay soggy. A loam with some organic matter is ideal, but figs even do fine in poor, rocky soil. The one thing to avoid is sandy soil that is full of root-knot nematodes, tiny soil pests that are the leading killer of figs. Do not make the soil too rich either: too much rich material and feeding pushes soft leafy growth and fewer figs, and that soft growth is more easily hurt by winter cold.
seasoned: Fig is adaptable across soil textures, from sandy to clay loam, provided drainage is good; it tolerates poor and rocky ground better than most fruit trees. A well-drained loam with moderate organic matter is ideal. The critical avoidance is root-knot-nematode-infested sandy soil, which is the leading cause of fig decline in warm regions, since own-rooted figs carry no resistant rootstock. Keep fertility moderate: over-rich soil and heavy feeding drive vegetative growth at the expense of fruit and produce soft wood that is more prone to winter injury.

beginner: Figs do best in slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, but they are easygoing and grow well anywhere from about 6.0 up to 7.8 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and only adjust if it is far off: garden lime raises a too-acidic pH and elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Mix any amendment in before you plant.
seasoned: Fig prefers a slightly acidic soil near pH 6.0 to 6.5 but is tolerant across roughly 6.0 to 7.8, handling near-neutral ground without trouble. Test before planting and correct only a real deficiency: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers an alkaline one. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is easiest to set before the permanent plant goes in.

beginner: Go easy on the fertilizer. Figs need much less than other fruit trees, and too much does more harm than good: lots of leaves and few figs, split fruit, and soft growth that is easily hurt by winter cold. Scatter a balanced fertilizer around the plant out to where the branches reach, keep it off the stems, and water it in. In colder areas use half as much, and stop feeding by midsummer so the plant can toughen up before winter.
seasoned: Feed lightly. Figs need far less fertilizer than most fruit trees, and over-feeding is a common mistake: excess nitrogen pushes rank leafy growth, delays and reduces fruiting, can cause fruit to split, and produces soft wood that winters poorly. Broadcast a balanced granular evenly around the root zone out toward the drip line, keep it off the stems, and water it in. Halve the rate in colder regions to favor hardiness, and never feed past midsummer, since late nitrogen keeps the plant growing when it should be hardening for winter.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 or 8-8-8 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is all a fig needs. Do not overdo the first number, nitrogen, because too much gives you leaves instead of figs.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 or 8-8-8 suits figs; they are light feeders and need no high-nitrogen program. Too much nitrogen (N) is counterproductive, driving leaves over fruit and reducing cold hardiness.

beginner: A simple guide is about 1/2 pound of 10-10-10 for a young fig and 2 to 4 pounds for a big one, spread over 2 or 3 times from early spring to early summer. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until it starts growing. In cold-winter areas, use half as much.
seasoned: A common home rate is about 1/2 pound of 10-10-10 for a young plant and 2 to 4 pounds for a mature one, split into 2 or 3 applications from early spring through early summer; UGA gives a rule of about 1/2 pound per foot of height, up to 5 pounds a year. Do not fertilize at planting; wait until growth begins. Cut these rates in half in northern gardens to keep growth firm for winter.

beginner: Figs make fruit on their own with no pollination, so you do not need any companion plants to help them fruit. What matters for a fig is what happens around its roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back and lay down mulch to hold moisture and keep weeds down, and do not plant a fig in soil full of root-knot nematodes (tiny soil pests), because figs cannot fight them off. A mulched, weed-free, pest-free root area is really all a fig asks for.
seasoned: Fig is parthenocarpic and self-fruitful, so there are no pollination companions to plant: a lone tree fruits with no bees and no fig wasp. The interactions that matter for a fig are at the root zone, not classic vegetable pairings. Keep grass and weeds cleared back and mulch the root area, which competes down weeds and holds moisture, and above all keep the plant out of soil heavily infested with root-knot nematodes, which own-rooted figs cannot resist. A well-mulched, weed-free, nematode-free root zone is the whole companion story.

beginner: The fig slowly goes downhill for no obvious reason: stunted, with thin yellow leaves, dieback, and fewer figs each year. If you dig up a root, you find small knots or swellings on it. Those knots are the damage from the pest.
seasoned: Above ground, a slow, unexplained decline: stunted growth, sparse yellowing leaves, dieback, and poor fruiting that worsens over years. Below ground, the roots carry small knots or galls, and the fine feeder roots are damaged, so the plant cannot take up water and nutrients.

beginner: Microscopic soil worms called root-knot nematodes that live in the roots and make the knots. They build up in warm, sandy soil and are the number-one killer of figs in warm areas. Because figs grow on their own roots, there is no special root you can buy to resist them and no cure once a plant is badly infested.
seasoned: Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne species), microscopic soil roundworms that feed inside the roots and form the galls. They build up in warm, sandy soils and are the leading cause of fig decline and death in the Southeast and other warm sandy regions. Own-rooted figs have no resistant rootstock, so there is no cure once a plant is heavily infested.

beginner: Once a plant is badly infested there is no fix. The best you can do is keep the fig strong with steady water and a thick mulch so it can shrug off mild damage, and, in bad sandy soil, grow it in a pot of clean potting mix instead of in the ground.
seasoned: There is no rescue treatment for an infested plant. Manage it by keeping the fig vigorous and well watered so it outgrows light damage, mulching heavily to build soil organic matter and beneficial soil life, and, in the worst sandy sites, growing in a container of clean mix instead. A thick organic mulch is the practical home tool.

beginner: The main thing is to avoid the problem: do not plant in sandy soil known to have these pests, pick well-drained ground, mulch thickly, and keep the fig healthy. Where the soil is bad, growing the fig in a pot of clean mix avoids the pest completely.
seasoned: Prevention is everything: do not plant into known nematode-heavy sandy soil, choose the best-drained ground, mulch heavily, and keep the plant vigorous. Where nematode pressure is high, container culture in clean mix sidesteps the problem entirely.

beginner: Ripe figs turn sour and mushy inside, with a fizzy or scummy ooze coming out of the little hole at the bottom (the eye) and a vinegary smell. You may see tiny beetles around the soft fruit. The affected figs are ruined.
seasoned: Ripening figs ferment and sour from the inside, oozing a scummy or bubbly liquid from the eye and smelling vinegary or yeasty. Small beetles may be seen at the eye of soft fruit. Affected figs are inedible and drop or rot on the plant.

beginner: Little beetles called dried fruit beetles are attracted to ripe figs and carry the yeasts that cause souring into the fruit through the open hole at the bottom. It is worst in humid weather and on figs with a big open eye that lets the beetles in.
seasoned: Dried fruit beetles (Carpophilus species) and other sap beetles are drawn to ripe figs and carry souring yeasts and bacteria into the fruit through the open eye. The problem is worst in humid weather and on varieties with a large, open eye, which lets the beetles and moisture in.

beginner: Pick figs as soon as they are ripe and clean up any soured or fallen fruit right away, so the beetles are not attracted and the souring cannot spread. Growing a variety with a small, tight eye like Celeste helps a lot. No spray fixes souring once it is inside the fig.
seasoned: Pick figs promptly as they ripen and remove any soured or dropped fruit right away so beetles are not drawn in and the yeasts do not build. Choosing varieties with a small or closed eye (such as Celeste) greatly reduces souring. There is no spray that reaches yeasts inside the fruit.

beginner: Keep the figs picked and throw away any soured ones, and grow a tight-eye variety like Celeste if your summers are humid. Picking often and keeping the plant open are the best defenses.
seasoned: Keep the plant picked clean during ripening, dispose of soured fruit, and favor closed-eye varieties in humid areas. Good airflow and prompt harvest are the durable controls.

beginner: Ripe figs get pecked open, half-eaten, or disappear, usually the best ones up high first. Squirrels can strip a small fig fast. It happens right as the figs start to ripen.
seasoned: Ripe and nearly ripe figs are pecked open, half-eaten, or gone entirely, often the best fruit at the top of the plant first. Squirrels strip fruit and can clear a small tree fast. Damage appears exactly as the crop begins to ripen.

beginner: Birds and squirrels love ripe figs, and because a fig's fruit is soft, sweet, and out in the open for weeks, they come back again and again. It is one of the most common fig problems.
seasoned: Birds and squirrels find ripe figs irresistible, and a fig's soft, sweet, unprotected fruit ripening over many weeks is an easy, repeated target. This is one of the most common complaints of home fig growers.

beginner: The best fix is to drape bird netting over the plant as the figs start to color, and to pick ripe figs often so fewer are left hanging. Shiny tape or scare items help for a while. A potted fig can be moved somewhere more protected.
seasoned: Netting the plant (or key branches) as fruit begins to color is the most effective home control; pick ripe figs promptly and often so less hangs waiting. Reflective tape and scare devices help briefly. A container fig can be moved to a more protected spot.

beginner: Get the netting ready before the figs ripen, not after the birds find them, and keep the plant small enough to cover and pick easily.
seasoned: Plan for netting before the crop ripens rather than after the losses start, and keep the plant a manageable size so it can be covered and picked easily.

beginner: In late summer, leaves get small yellow-orange spots that turn rusty brown, mostly underneath, and then yellow and fall early, sometimes stripping the plant before fall. That year's figs usually still ripen, but losing leaves early year after year wears the plant down.
seasoned: In mid to late summer, leaves develop small yellow-orange spots that turn rusty reddish-brown, most on the underside; heavily spotted leaves yellow and drop early, sometimes defoliating the plant well before fall. The current crop usually still ripens, but repeated early defoliation weakens the plant over years.

beginner: A fungus called Cerotelium fici. It spreads in warm, wet, humid weather and survives winter on fallen infected leaves, so it is worst in humid areas and wet summers, especially where old leaves pile up under the plant.
seasoned: The fungus Cerotelium fici. It spreads in warm, humid, wet weather and overwinters on fallen infected leaves, so it is most severe in the humid Southeast and in wet summers, building up where litter is left under the plant.

beginner: Once a leaf is spotted you cannot cure it; the aim is to slow it down and protect next year. Rake up and throw away fallen leaves, and keep the plant open so it dries fast. Where rust is bad, an organic copper spray on the new leaves through the season is the usual treatment.
seasoned: Once leaves are spotted there is no cure for that leaf; the goal is to slow the spread and protect next year. Rake up and destroy fallen leaves to remove the overwintering source, and keep the canopy open and dry. Where rust is severe, a neutral copper or Bordeaux fungicide on the new foliage through the growing season is the standard organic option.

beginner: The main prevention is cleanup: rake away fallen leaves every year, prune so air moves through the plant, and water the ground instead of the leaves. In humid areas where rust is common, an organic copper spray starting in spring keeps the leaves protected.
seasoned: Sanitation is the backbone: clear fallen leaves each year, prune for airflow, and water at the ground rather than overhead. In rust-prone humid regions, a preventive copper program from spring protects the foliage.

beginner: Leaves get a blotchy, mottled yellow pattern (called a mosaic), and sometimes the fruit is spotted or drops early. It comes and goes with the season and variety. It does not kill the plant, but it can slow it down and cut the crop.
seasoned: Leaves show scattered yellow, blotchy, or ring-like mottling (a mosaic pattern), sometimes with distorted growth; fruit may be spotted or drop early. Symptoms vary with season and variety and often come and go. The virus does not kill the plant but can reduce vigor and crop.

beginner: Fig mosaic is a virus, spread mostly by a tiny mite (the fig mite) and passed along in cuttings from infected plants. Once a plant has it, it is in the plant for good, because there is no cure for a plant virus.
seasoned: Fig mosaic is a virus complex spread mainly by the tiny fig mite (Aceria ficus) and carried in cuttings taken from infected plants. Once a plant has it, it is systemic and permanent, since there is no cure for a virus in a plant.

beginner: There is no cure for a plant virus. Just keep the fig healthy and well cared for, since many infected plants still fruit alright. Do not take cuttings from a mottled plant to start new ones, and pull out a plant that is badly stunted and barely fruiting.
seasoned: There is no treatment for a virus in a plant. Manage it by keeping the plant otherwise healthy and vigorous; many infected figs still crop acceptably. Do not propagate cuttings from a mottled plant, and remove a severely stunted, poor-cropping plant.

beginner: The best prevention is starting with a healthy plant and controlling the tiny fig mites that spread it. Buy or take cuttings from plants with clean, un-mottled leaves. There is no way to cure a plant once it is infected.
seasoned: Prevention is about clean stock and mite control: start with cuttings or plants from healthy, unmottled sources, and keep fig mites in check since they spread the virus. There is no way to cure an infected plant.

beginner: Figs rot from the inside near the little hole at the bottom, going brown and mushy inside even when the outside still looks okay, then souring and dropping. It goes hand in hand with the souring that beetles cause, and is worst in humid weather on figs with a big open eye.
seasoned: Ripening fruit rots from the inside near the eye, turning brown and mushy internally while the outside may still look sound; affected figs sour, ooze, and drop. It overlaps with beetle-spread souring and is worst in humid weather on open-eye varieties.

beginner: A rot inside the fruit caused by fungi that get in through the open hole at the bottom, often carried by the same little beetles that cause souring. Humid weather and big-eye varieties make it worse.
seasoned: An internal fruit rot caused by fungi (including Fusarium) carried into the fruit through the open eye, often by the same sap beetles that spread souring. Humid conditions and large-eye varieties make it worse.

beginner: You cannot cure it inside the fruit. Handle it like souring: pick figs promptly, throw away rotten and dropped ones, and grow a tight-eye variety like Celeste if your area is humid.
seasoned: There is no in-fruit cure. Control it the same way as souring: pick promptly, remove affected and dropped fruit, and favor small or closed-eye varieties (such as Celeste) in humid areas.

beginner: Grow a tight-eye variety in humid areas, keep the figs picked and the ground clean, and control the little beetles that carry it.
seasoned: Choose closed-eye varieties in humid regions, keep fruit picked and the ground clean, and manage the sap beetles that carry the fungi.

beginner: Water deeply now and then instead of a little every day. Aim for about 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week from rain or the hose during the growing season, more when it is hot or the soil is sandy. A new fig needs steady water while it gets its roots going. An older fig can take some dry spells, but the figs come out small and less sweet if it gets too dry.
seasoned: Water deeply and regularly rather than lightly and often: figure roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water per week from rain or irrigation through the growing season, more in heat and sandy soil, easing off as fruit finishes and through winter dormancy. A newly planted fig needs the most attention while it roots in; an established fig is fairly drought-tolerant but sizes and sweetens fruit poorly when it runs dry.

beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches the roots, not just a splash on top. A new fig wants about 10 gallons per soak, two or three times a week its first summer. An older, fruiting fig wants roughly 1 to 1.5 inches of water a week, and more when it is hot.
seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root zone rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing fig, UF/IFAS suggests around 10 gallons per soak two to three times a week in the first season; for a bearing plant, aim for the equivalent of about 1 to 1.5 inches per week through the growing season, more in heat.

beginner: Water at the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, and try to keep the leaves and fruit dry, since wet leaves invite disease. Keep the watering steady while the figs are filling out and ripening, because going from dry to very wet, or a hard rain on ripe figs, makes them split and spoil.
seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose out toward the drip line, keeping the canopy dry to limit fig rust and fruit souring. Keep moisture especially steady as the fruit sizes and ripens, since a swing from dry to soaked (or heavy rain on ripening figs) causes fruit to split and sour.

beginner: Too much water, or soil that stays soggy, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and a plant slowly going downhill, because the roots cannot breathe. Figs handle moisture better than a peach but still cannot sit in waterlogged soil. Figs that split and sour after a lot of water or rain are another sign near harvest.
seasoned: Chronically wet, poorly drained soil shows as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists in wet soil, and general decline as waterlogged roots suffocate. Figs tolerate more moisture than stone fruit but still fail in standing water. Fruit that splits and sours after heavy watering or rain is the other overwatering signal near harvest.

beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull yellow leaves, leaves dropping early, and, most clearly, small figs falling off or ripening tiny and less sweet. A fig that gets too dry in summer drops some of its fruit, so try to catch the dryness before the figs suffer.
seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull and yellowing leaves, early leaf drop, and, most tellingly, fruit that drops while small or ripens undersized and less sweet. A fig short of water during the summer swell aborts part of its crop, so catch the dry stress before the fruit pays for it.

beginner: While the fig is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 10 gallons two or three times a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps it grow strong roots.
seasoned: Through the first season keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never waterlogged. Deep soaks of roughly 10 gallons two to three times a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the root system the plant relies on later.

beginner: While the figs are filling out, keep the water steady, about 1 to 1.5 inches a week as deep soaks. Even watering now means bigger, sweeter figs, and it keeps the fruit from splitting.
seasoned: As the main crop sizes, keep moisture steady, about 1 to 1.5 inches per week as deep soaks. This is the window where even watering translates directly into fuller, sweeter figs and where a dry-then-wet swing causes fruit to split and sour.

beginner: After the leaves drop and the fig is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during long dry stretches. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.
seasoned: Once the fig is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only in prolonged dry spells so roots do not desiccate. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.

beginner: Give the fig a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground instead of over the top, since wet leaves and fruit invite disease. Young figs need steady water the first season. Older figs handle dry spells, but they drop figs when too dry and split them when a dry spell ends in a big soak or rain.
seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker, keeping the canopy dry to limit fig rust and souring. Young figs need consistent moisture through the first season to establish; mature figs are moderately drought-tolerant but drop and undersize fruit under stress, and split when a dry spell breaks in heavy water or rain.

beginner: Fill the pot with a good-quality potting mix that drains well. A bark-based mix, or a general potting soil with some extra perlite stirred in, works nicely. Figs are not picky, but avoid a heavy soil dug from the yard, which packs down and drains poorly in a pot.
seasoned: Use a quality bark-based or peat-based potting mix amended for drainage, not native garden soil, which compacts under container irrigation. Figs tolerate a more moisture-retentive mix than stone fruit but still perform best with free drainage and an air-filled root zone.

beginner: Keep it simple. Mix in a little compost for fertility and some perlite if the mix seems to hold too much water. Figs take richer mixes better than a peach does, but you still want the pot to drain freely rather than stay wet.
seasoned: Blend in modest compost for fertility and extra perlite or pumice if the base mix is water-retentive. Figs accept richer container media than most fruit trees, but keep drainage the priority; a top-dress of compost each spring covers most of the plant's needs.

beginner: A fig in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground. In summer heat, check it daily and water when the top inch or two is dry, until water runs out the bottom. Water more often than a ground fig, but do not leave the pot standing in a saucer of water. In winter, when the plant is resting, give it just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
seasoned: A potted fig dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to draw on, so check moisture daily in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes. Water more often, but never leave the pot standing in a full saucer. Through dormancy the plant needs only enough water to keep the root ball from drying out.

Do not feed at planting, and stop once it drops its leaves for winter.
seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so feed lightly and often: a dilute balanced liquid feed every few weeks through the spring-to-midsummer flush, then stop by late summer so no soft growth is pushed into fall. Do not feed at planting, and ease off entirely once the plant goes dormant.

beginner: Growing a fig in a pot is the easiest way to keep one where winters are too cold for it in the ground, because you can move it somewhere protected. Before hard freezes come, move the pot into an unheated but sheltered spot like an attached garage, shed, or basement that stays cold but does not deep-freeze. The fig is leafless and resting, so it does not need light in there. Water it just once in a while so the roots do not dry out, and bring it back outside when hard frosts are past in spring.
seasoned: A container is the standard way to carry a fig through winters colder than its in-ground range. Once the plant is dormant and leafless, move the pot to an unheated but protected space (attached garage, shed, or cool basement) that holds above roughly the mid teens but stays cold enough to keep it dormant. It needs no light while leafless; water sparingly to keep the root ball from drying out. Return it outdoors after hard frosts pass. A container fig still needs its short winter chill, so do not overwinter it in a heated room.

beginner: Figs are one of the best fruit trees for a pot, and a pot is the way to grow one if your winters are too cold for a fig in the ground. Use a large container that drains well, keep it watered more often than a ground plant, and move it to a protected spot for winter. A potted fig stays smaller and still gives you a good crop.
seasoned: Fig is exceptionally well suited to container culture, and a pot is the practical route to fruit in regions colder than its in-ground range, since the plant can be moved to shelter for winter. Use at least a 15-gallon container (20 or more is better) with excellent drainage, water more frequently than an in-ground plant, and overwinter the dormant pot in a protected, unheated space. Expect a smaller plant and a lighter but dependable crop.

beginner: A self-watering pot (one with a water tank in the bottom) is not the best choice for a fig. Figs do best when the soil dries out a bit between waterings, and a tank keeps the roots wet all the time, which can cause root trouble and split fruit. Figs handle moisture better than a peach, so it can work if that is what you have, but a regular pot that drains well and that you water yourself grows better figs.
seasoned: A self-watering or sub-irrigated planter is not the best choice for fig. Figs fruit and firm up best on a wet-then-dry cycle and dislike a root zone held constantly moist by a reservoir, which can invite root problems and, near harvest, split fruit. Figs are more forgiving of moisture than stone fruit, so a self-watering pot is workable in a pinch, but a freely draining pot you water yourself gives better fruit.

beginner: Protecting a potted fig in winter mostly means moving it somewhere sheltered, because the roots in a pot get much colder than roots in the ground. Put the resting, leafless plant in an unheated garage or shed for the coldest months. If it has to stay outside, push the pots together against a wall, wrap them, and pile mulch around them to keep the roots from freezing.
seasoned: Cold protection for a potted fig is mostly about moving it: the exposed pot lets roots freeze several zones colder than in the ground, so shelter the dormant plant in an unheated garage or shed through the coldest months. If it must stay outside in a marginal zone, cluster pots against a wall, wrap them, and bank mulch around them. The goal is a cold, stable dormancy without the deep freezes that kill exposed roots and top growth.

beginner: Figs are very perishable and do not ripen after you pick them, so pick them ripe and eat them quickly. On the counter ripe figs last only about a day or two before they go bad, so eat, cook, or refrigerate them the same day you pick.
seasoned: Figs are highly perishable and do not ripen further once picked, so pick them fully ripe and eat them fast. At room temperature ripe figs hold only about a day, sometimes two, before they begin to spoil, so plan to eat, cook, or refrigerate them the day you pick.

beginner: Put ripe figs in the fridge unwashed, in a single layer so they do not crush, and eat them within about 2 to 3 days. Let them warm up to room temperature before eating for the best taste.
seasoned: Refrigerate ripe figs unwashed in a single layer and use them within about 2 to 3 days. Cold slows the spoilage but figs are fragile; keep them shallow so they do not crush, and bring them to room temperature before eating for the best flavor.

beginner: Figs freeze nicely whole or cut in half. Rinse and dry them, freeze them on a tray, then pack them into freezer bags. They keep for several months and are great for cooking and jam. Figs also dry very well, which is the traditional way to save a big crop.
seasoned: Figs freeze well whole or halved. Rinse, dry, and freeze them in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to freezer bags; they keep several months and are best for cooking, baking, and preserves. Figs also dry excellently, the classic way to keep a big crop.

beginner: The main thing to remember is that figs do not ripen after picking and spoil in a day or two, so pick them ripe and use them fast, or refrigerate, freeze, or dry them right away.
seasoned: The key with figs is that they do not ripen off the plant and spoil within a day or two, so ripeness at picking and speed to the table (or fridge, freezer, or drying rack) is everything.

beginner: All common figs need about the same small amount of winter cold, so you do not pick a fig by chill hours the way you would a peach. Instead, choose by how cold-hardy it is and how well it handles your weather. In cold areas, pick a hardy type like Chicago Hardy or Celeste. In humid areas, pick a small, tight-eye type like Celeste or a rust-tolerant one like LSU Purple to avoid souring and rust. Where it is mild and dry, almost any fig does well, so pick by taste. All of these are common figs that fruit on their own with no pollination.
seasoned: Because all common figs need only about 100 chill hours, choose a variety not by chill (as you would a peach) but by cold-hardiness, disease tolerance, and eye type for your climate. In cold-winter areas favor the hardiest types (Chicago Hardy, Celeste, Marseilles). In humid areas favor a small, closed-eye variety (Celeste) or a rust-tolerant one (LSU Purple) to limit souring and rust. In mild, dry regions almost anything thrives, so pick by flavor and use. All the recommended types are common (parthenocarpic) figs that fruit alone with no pollination.

beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to the outdoors) does not apply to fig. You plant it as a dormant bare-root or potted plant, so there is no tender young seedling to ease outside.
seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to fig. It is planted as a dormant, own-rooted bare-root or container plant, not raised from a seedling indoors, so there is no tender transplant to acclimate.

beginner: Plant a dormant bare-root or potted fig in late winter or early spring after the worst cold, or in fall to early winter where winters are mild. Figs grow on their own roots, so unlike a peach there is no graft joint to keep above the soil; you can even plant it a little deeper to help it grow into a sturdy, multi-stem bush, which bounces back best if winter kills the top. Dig a hole wide enough for the roots, fill it back with the same soil, water it in well, and spread mulch, keeping it off the stems. Do not put fertilizer in the hole.
seasoned: Plant a dormant, own-rooted bare-root or container fig in late winter to early spring, once the hardest cold has passed, or in fall to early winter in mild regions. Because figs are grown on their own roots there is no graft union to keep above grade; you can even set the plant an inch or two deeper than it grew to encourage a well-anchored, multi-stem bush, the form that best recovers from winter dieback. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots, backfill with native soil, water in well, and mulch, keeping mulch off the stems. Do not fertilize in the hole.

beginner: You do not rotate a fig the way you rotate vegetables, since it stays put for many years. What matters is root-knot nematode, a tiny soil pest that is the main killer of figs. Do not plant a fig in sandy soil that is known to be full of these pests, or right where a sick fig just came out, unless you dig out and replace a big area of soil first.
seasoned: Annual crop rotation does not apply to a fig, which holds its site for decades. The real site concern is root-knot nematode. Because own-rooted figs have no resistant rootstock, do not plant a fig into sandy ground known to be heavily infested with root-knot nematodes, or where a nematode-declined fig was just removed, without replacing a generous volume of soil.

beginner: If you have to plant where nematodes might be a problem, pick the best-drained, least sandy spot, dig out and replace a big area of soil, and keep the fig healthy and mulched. Remember there is no special root you can buy to protect a fig from these pests.
seasoned: If a fig must go where nematodes are a concern, choose a site with the least sandy, best-drained soil available, replace a generous volume of soil, keep the plant vigorous and mulched, and accept that own-rooted figs cannot be rootstock-protected the way stone fruit can.

seasoned: Late winter to early spring after the hardest cold, or fall to early winter in mild regions.

Common home varieties such as Celeste, Brown Turkey, and Black Mission are parthenocarpic, so a single tree crops alone with no visible bloom: an early breba crop, then a heavier main crop from summer into early fall. Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant, and keep summer irrigation deep and consistent; that, not chill, is the real constraint.

beginner: A fig (Ficus carica) is a fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and gives you soft, very sweet fruit that has to ripen on the plant and does not keep, which is why a homegrown fig is so much better than a store one. Where winters are mild, figs are one of the easiest fruit trees to grow: one plant makes fruit all by itself with no pollination needed, it needs very little winter cold, and it loves heat, so warm areas suit it perfectly. The one real limit is cold: the stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F. So figs grow in the ground in zones 7 to 10, need heavy winter protection in zone 6, and are best grown in a pot you bring into shelter for winter where it is colder. Many figs give two crops: a few early figs in summer on last year's stems, and a bigger crop in late summer and fall on the new growth.
seasoned: Fig (Ficus carica) is a deciduous, Mediterranean fruit tree grown on its own roots from cuttings, prized for soft, honey-sweet fruit that must ripen on the plant and does not survive shipping, so a backyard fig gives you something no store can match. It is one of the easiest fruit trees to grow where winters are mild: it is self-fruitful and parthenocarpic (it sets fruit with no pollination at all), needs very little winter chill (about 100 hours), and thrives on heat, which makes warm regions its home, the opposite of a high-chill tree like cherry. The one real limit is cold. Fully dormant wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, so fig is grown in the ground in zones 7 to 10, given heavy winter protection in zone 6, and kept in a container that overwinters indoors where winters are colder. Many figs carry two crops: a light early-summer breba crop on last year's wood and a larger late-summer to fall main crop on the new growth.

beginner: A fig is ripe when it turns soft, droops down instead of sticking straight out (the neck bends), colors up fully, and maybe shows a drop of syrup at the bottom. A ripe fig gives easily to a gentle squeeze and comes off with the lightest pull. Color by itself does not mean ripe; a fig can be fully colored but still hard and not ready. Since figs do not ripen after you pick them, wait for them to go soft and droop, and pick every day or two, because a plant ripens just a few at a time over many weeks.
seasoned: A fig is ripe when it softens fully, its neck bends so the fruit droops rather than standing out from the stem, it colors up to its full variety color, and a drop of nectar may appear at the eye. Ripe figs feel soft to a gentle squeeze and detach with the barest tug. Color alone is not ripeness; a fig can be fully colored and still firm and unready. Because figs do not ripen after picking, wait for full softness and droop, and pick every day or two, since a plant ripens a few at a time over many weeks.

beginner: A fig never shows flowers, because they are hidden inside the fruit (the fig you eat is really a bundle of flowers turned inside out). Instead of a bloom, you watch for the leaves opening in early spring and the small early figs (the breba crop) swelling on last year's stems. Common figs make that fruit on their own, with no pollination. The main crop then forms on the new shoots as they grow through late spring and summer.
seasoned: A fig has no showy bloom. Its flowers are tiny and hidden inside the young fruit (the fig you eat is essentially an inside-out cluster of flowers), so there is nothing to see the way a peach or apple flowers. What you watch for instead is leaf-out in early spring and the swelling of the small breba figs on last year's wood. Because common figs are parthenocarpic, that fruit forms and ripens with no pollination at all. The main crop then sets on the new shoots as they extend through late spring and summer.

beginner: Cold is the one thing a fig cannot handle, so plan around it first. The stems are hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F, and sustained cold below that kills the top of the plant, though the roots are tougher and usually grow back. That gives a simple map: figs grow in the ground easily in zones 7 to 10, need heavy winter protection to fruit in zone 6, and are best grown in a pot you move into an unheated garage or shed where it is colder. Even a fig killed to the ground usually grows back from the roots and can ripen a late crop on the new stems, so a hard winter rarely kills the whole plant. Pick a cold-hardy variety like Chicago Hardy or Celeste at the cold edge. Winter chill is never the problem, since figs need so little.
seasoned: Cold is the one thing a fig cannot shrug off, so lead your planning with it. Fully dormant wood is hardy only to about 15°F to 20°F; sustained lows below that injure or kill the above-ground stems, though the roots are hardier and usually resprout. That sets a clear map: figs grow in the ground with little fuss in zones 7 to 10, need heavy winter protection (wrapping, or cutting back and burying under mulch and leaves) to fruit in zone 6, and are best grown in a container that winters in an unheated garage or shed where winters are colder still. A top-killed fig usually regrows from the base and can ripen a late main crop on the new wood, so a hard winter is rarely the end of the plant, just the end of that year's early fruit. Choose a cold-hardy variety (Chicago Hardy, Celeste, Marseilles) at the cold edge of the range. Winter chill is never the limiter, since a fig's small chill need is met almost everywhere.

beginner: Figs need only a little winter cold, about 100 hours below 45°F, which almost any area that can grow them gets easily. So chill is hardly ever the problem for a fig, and figs do great in mild, warm-winter places that are too warm for high-chill trees like cherry. What actually limits a fig is the other extreme: not too little cold, but too much. Hard freezes below about 15°F to 20°F kill the top of the plant, so the number to match to your area is cold-hardiness, not chill.
seasoned: Figs need very little winter cold, only about 100 hours below 45°F, which nearly every region that can grow them meets easily. That is why chill is almost never the limiting factor for a fig, and why figs do so well in mild, warm-winter areas that are too warm for high-chill trees like cherry. What actually limits a fig is the opposite end of the thermometer: not too little cold, but too much. Hard winter freezes below about 15°F to 20°F kill the top growth, so cold hardiness, not chill, is the number to match to your area.

beginner: Common figs make and ripen fruit with no pollination at all, so one plant is all you need, with no second tree, no bees, and no special wasp. The flowers are inside the fruit, which is why a fig never shows a bloom. A few unusual types (Smyrna and San Pedro) do need a special fig wasp, and that wasp is not around in most of the country, so they just drop their fruit and are not worth planting. Choose a common type like Celeste, Brown Turkey, or Chicago Hardy and you never have to think about pollination.
seasoned: Common home figs are parthenocarpic: they set and ripen fruit with no pollination whatsoever, so a single plant fruits alone with no partner, no bees, and no fig wasp. The flowers are hidden inside the fruit, which is why a fig never shows a visible bloom. The Smyrna and San Pedro types sold in some catalogs are the exception, needing a specific fig wasp (Blastophaga psenes) that is absent across most of the country, so they drop their fruit and are not recommended for home gardens. Stick to the common types (Celeste, Brown Turkey, Chicago Hardy, Black Mission, Kadota) and pollination is simply a non-issue.

beginner: The first year is about helping the plant get established and through winter, not about fruit. Plant a dormant fig in late winter or early spring after the worst cold, in full sun in well-drained soil, and against a warm wall in cold areas. Water it steadily the first season, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around it, and protect it especially well its first winter, since a young fig is more easily hurt by cold than an older one. Wait to fertilize until it starts growing, and go easy. A few figs may form, which is a nice bonus, but do not count on a crop yet.
seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment and winter survival over fruit. Plant a dormant own-rooted fig in late winter or early spring after the hardest cold, in full sun on well-drained ground, and against a warm wall at the cold edge of the range. Water consistently through the first season, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the plant, and protect it especially well its first winter, since a young fig is the most cold-tender it will ever be. Hold fertilizer until growth begins and keep it light. A few figs may form; enjoy them, but do not count on a crop yet.

beginner: Figs grow on their own roots from cuttings, so there is no rootstock to pick the way there is for a peach or apple. You control the size by how you prune it, by the variety, and by growing it in a pot. Because there is no special root to resist soil pests, the main thing is to plant it in well-drained ground that is free of root-knot nematodes.
seasoned: Figs are propagated from dormant hardwood cuttings and grown on their own roots, so unlike stone and pome fruit there is no rootstock system: no grafting, no graft union, and no rootstock-driven size control or disease resistance to select. Size is managed by pruning, by variety, and by growing in a container. The one soil-pest caveat is root-knot nematode, which own-rooted figs have no resistant rootstock to fall back on, so a nematode-free, well-drained site is the real substitute for rootstock choice.

beginner: Pomegranate is famously easy about soil. It grows best in a deep loam but will handle sandy soils and even heavy clay, as long as water drains away and does not sit around the roots. It also shrugs off alkaline (high-pH) and mildly salty soils that bother most fruit. The one thing it will not take is soggy ground: constantly wet roots bring on root rot. If your soil is heavy or drainage is poor, plant on a raised mound or bed so the roots stay above the wet.
seasoned: Pomegranate is one of the most soil-adaptable fruits: it prefers a deep loam but tolerates sandy soils, heavy clay, alkaline pH, and mild salinity that would stunt most fruit trees. Drainage is the one firm requirement, since waterlogged soil invites root rot (including Armillaria on wet, heavy ground). On clay or low sites, plant on a raised berm or bed to lift the crown above standing water. It needs little organic matter and thrives on lean ground.

beginner: Pomegranate grows well in a wide pH range, about 5.5 to 7.0, and tolerates up to around 7.2 (pH just measures how acidic or alkaline the soil is). It is unusually easygoing about alkaline soil, so most gardeners never need to adjust pH for it. Test your soil before planting, and only correct if it is far outside that range.
seasoned: Pomegranate does well across a broad pH band, roughly 5.5 to 7.0, and tolerates up to about 7.2. It is notably alkaline-tolerant, so pH is seldom a limiting factor and rarely needs amending. Test before planting and correct only if the soil is well outside the tolerated range.

beginner: Pomegranate does not need much feeding. In late winter or early spring, scatter a small amount of balanced fertilizer around the plant and water it in. Do not overdo nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much grows leaves and base shoots instead of fruit. On poor or sandy soil, a light second feeding in late spring helps a young plant, but an established one usually needs very little.
seasoned: Pomegranate is a light feeder. Broadcast a modest amount of balanced fertilizer around the root zone in late winter to early spring as growth begins, and water it in. Avoid heavy nitrogen: excess N drives vegetative growth and suckering at the expense of flowers and fruit, and can worsen soft, split-prone fruit. On lean or sandy soils a light second feeding in late spring helps young plants; established plants often need little or none.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is plenty for a pomegranate. Go light, and especially do not overdo the first number, nitrogen, which grows leaves and shoots instead of fruit.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits pomegranate; it is a light feeder and draws modestly on all three nutrients. Keep nitrogen restrained, since excess pushes suckers and soft growth over flowering and fruit set.

beginner: Feed lightly. A simple approach is a small handful of 10-10-10 for each foot of the plant's height, spread around the plant in late winter, and no more than that for a full-grown one. Do not fertilize right when you plant; wait until it starts growing. If the plant is already growing strongly with deep green leaves, feed less or skip it.
seasoned: A light hand is the rule. A common home approach is about 1 to 2 ounces of actual nitrogen per year of plant age in the early years (for example, a modest handful of 10-10-10 per foot of height), capped for a mature plant, applied in late winter. Skip feeding at planting; wait until growth begins. If growth is already vigorous and green, feed less or not at all.

beginner: Pomegranate is self-fruitful, so one plant makes fruit on its own and you do not need a second plant to pollinate it (though a second pomegranate nearby can improve fruit set a little). For a shrub like this, the things that help are not the usual vegetable-garden pairings but the space around it: keep grass and weeds pulled back from the base so they do not compete with a young plant, and give it an open, sunny, breezy spot, because crowded, still, humid air at bloom makes flowers drop instead of setting fruit. Flowering plants nearby that draw bees can help set, and they bring in helpful insects that keep aphids and whiteflies down.
seasoned: Pomegranate is self-fruitful, so a single plant sets a crop on its own (a second plant nearby can modestly improve set). The interactions that matter for this shrub are about air, light, and the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared from the base so they do not compete with a young plant, and site it in open, sunny, breezy ground, since crowded, humid, still air at bloom causes flowers to abort. Nearby pollinator plantings aid set and recruit the beneficials that hold aphids, whiteflies, and mealybugs in check.

beginner: Usually you see nothing wrong on the outside of the fruit, because the damage is inside. If you cut a fruit open, you find brown spots on the inner skin and seeds (arils) that have gone dark, shriveled, or corky. It is worst late in the season as the fruit ripens, and it can let rot start inside.
seasoned: Often no external mark on the fruit at all; the damage is inside. Cut a fed-on fruit and you find brown spots on the inner rind where the insect's needlelike mouthpart pierced, and arils that have darkened, withered, or turned corky. Late-season feeding as fruit ripens is the worst, and it opens the door to internal fungal rots.

beginner: A big brown bug called the leaf-footed bug, named for the little leaf-shaped flares on its back legs. It and its young pierce the fruit to feed, and that can carry in yeasts and fungi that discolor and rot the seeds inside. The adults spend winter hidden in sheltered groups, then move onto the fruit as it forms.
seasoned: The leaf-footed bug (Leptoglossus species), a large brown true bug with flattened, leaf-like flares on its hind legs. Adults and nymphs pierce fruit to feed; on pomegranate their feeding can introduce yeasts and fungal spores that discolor and rot the arils. They overwinter as adults in sheltered aggregations and move onto fruit as it develops.

beginner: For a backyard plant, the best fixes are hands-on: in the cool early morning, knock the bugs into a bucket of soapy water, and clean up the weedy, sheltered places where they spend the winter and gather. Where you can, cover fruit clusters with fine mesh bags. Flowers nearby that bring in helpful insects also keep numbers down.
seasoned: There is no easy rescue spray for a backyard plant. The practical controls are physical: hand-pick or knock adults and nymphs into soapy water in the cool early morning when they are sluggish, clear the weedy and sheltered spots where they overwinter and aggregate, and bag developing fruit clusters in mesh where feasible. Encourage the natural egg parasites and general predators by keeping insectary flowers nearby.

beginner: Keep an eye out from the time fruit forms, because you cannot see the damage from outside until you cut a fruit open. Keep weeds cleared to take away the places the bugs hide and breed, and look for the adults gathering in spring. Catching and removing them early, before there are many, works best.
seasoned: Monitor from fruit set onward, since the internal damage is invisible until you cut the fruit. Keep the area weed-free to remove overwintering and breeding habitat, and watch for the adults congregating in spring. Early detection and hand-removal before populations build is the most effective home strategy.

beginner: Groups of tiny soft insects on new shoots and the undersides of leaves, leaving a sticky coating (honeydew) that turns into black sooty mold, plus curled new leaves and ants running up and down the plant.
seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new shoots, leaf undersides, and flower stems, with sticky honeydew, sooty black mold on leaves and fruit, curled or distorted new growth, and attending ants.

beginner: Aphids, tiny sap-sucking insects that build up on soft new growth in spring. They multiply quickly, and the sticky honeydew they leave grows black mold and attracts ants that guard them.
seasoned: Several aphid species colonize tender pomegranate growth in spring, multiplying fast in warm weather. Their honeydew supports sooty mold and draws ants, which protect the aphids from predators.

beginner: Spraying the plant with a strong stream of water knocks most aphids off and is often all an established plant needs. Let the good bugs (ladybugs, lacewings) do their job by avoiding harsh sprays; insecticidal soap helps if there are a lot. Keeping ants off the plant lets the helpful insects control them.
seasoned: A strong jet of water knocks aphids off and is often enough on an established plant. Preserve natural enemies (ladybugs, lacewings, syrphid larvae) by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays; insecticidal soap or horticultural oil handles heavier infestations. Control ants, which farm aphids, to let predators work.

beginner: Do not overfeed with nitrogen, because all that soft new growth attracts aphids. Grow flowers nearby to bring in helpful insects, and keep ants away so those helpers can do their work.
seasoned: Keep nitrogen feeding moderate, since lush growth pushed by excess nitrogen draws aphids. Support beneficial insects with nearby flowers, and manage ants so predators are not chased off.

beginner: Tiny white insects like little moths that flutter up when you brush the plant, sitting under the leaves along with their flat, pale young. They leave sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, and a lot of them yellow the leaves.
seasoned: Tiny white moth-like insects that fly up in clouds when the plant is disturbed, gathered on leaf undersides with their pale nymphs; honeydew and sooty mold follow, and heavy infestations yellow and weaken leaves.

beginner: Whiteflies, small sap-sucking insects that live under the leaves and multiply fast in warm weather. Like aphids, they leave honeydew that grows sooty mold.
seasoned: Whiteflies, small sap-feeding insects that colonize leaf undersides and reproduce rapidly in warm weather. Like aphids, they excrete honeydew that fosters sooty mold.

beginner: Spray the leaves with water and let helpful insects do most of the work; they usually keep whiteflies under control outdoors. Insecticidal soap sprayed under the leaves helps if there are many, and yellow sticky cards catch the adults.
seasoned: Hose off foliage and rely on natural enemies (lacewings, ladybugs, parasitic wasps), which usually keep whiteflies in check on an outdoor plant. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on leaf undersides helps in heavy cases; yellow sticky traps monitor and reduce adults.

beginner: Keep the plant healthy, avoid overfeeding with nitrogen, and do not let it get dusty and stressed, which whiteflies like. Avoid harsh sprays so the helpful insects survive.
seasoned: Keep plants healthy and avoid excess nitrogen and dusty, stressed conditions that favor whitefly buildup. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides.

beginner: Fuzzy white cottony spots (mealybugs) tucked into branch joints and inside the crown of the fruit, or small hard brown bumps (scale) stuck to stems and leaves. Both leave sticky honeydew and black mold, and mealybugs hiding in the fruit crown can get inside the fruit.
seasoned: Cottony white tufts (mealybugs) in leaf axils, branch crotches, and inside the fruit calyx (crown), or small immobile brown or waxy bumps (scale) on stems and leaves; both produce honeydew and sooty mold, and mealybugs hidden in the crown can contaminate the fruit interior.

beginner: Mealybugs and scale insects, sap-sucking pests that hide in sheltered spots, including the crown of the fruit. Ants move them around and protect them, and their honeydew grows black mold.
seasoned: Mealybugs and various scale insects, slow-moving or immobile sap feeders that shelter in protected spots including the fruit's crown. Ants tend and spread them, and their honeydew fuels sooty mold.

beginner: Wipe visible mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, spray with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, and cut out badly infested branches. Keep ants off so the helpful insects can work, and throw away any fruit with bugs packed into the crown.
seasoned: Spot-treat with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, dab visible mealybug colonies with an alcohol-dipped swab, and prune out heavily infested wood. Control ants to let natural enemies (including mealybug destroyers and parasitic wasps) suppress them. Remove fruit with infested crowns.

beginner: Keep ants away, do not overfeed, and check the fruit crowns and branch joints where these pests hide. An open, airy plant with good light bothers them.
seasoned: Keep ants under control, avoid excess nitrogen, and inspect the fruit crown and branch crotches where these pests hide. Good airflow and light through the canopy discourage them.

beginner: From the outside the fruit looks almost fine, maybe a bit light or a paler red, but inside it is rotting: the seeds turn brown and mushy with black mold. There is usually no sign on the outside, so you only find it when you cut the fruit open.
seasoned: The fruit looks nearly normal outside, perhaps a little light in weight or slightly off-color (a paler red), while the interior rots: arils turn brown and mushy and a black mold sporulates inside. There is often no external cue, so the rot is discovered only on cutting.

beginner: A fungus called Alternaria gets into the fruit through the open flower in damp, rainy bloom weather and grows quietly inside. Wounds from insects (like the leaf-footed bug) or birds let it in too. Wet weather around bloom is the main cause, so it is worse in humid areas.
seasoned: The fungus Alternaria (and related molds) infects through the open flower during rainy or humid bloom weather and grows silently inside the developing fruit. Insect and bird punctures (notably leaf-footed bug feeding) give it a second way in. Wet weather at and after bloom is the main driver, which is why it is a bigger problem in humid climates.

beginner: Once a fruit is rotting inside, it cannot be saved. The way to fight it is to prevent it: it is much less of a problem in hot, dry weather, so keep the leaf-footed bug and other fruit-piercing pests under control, keep the plant open and airy, and pick off and throw away any rotted or old dried fruit so the mold does not spread to next year.
seasoned: There is no cure once the inside is rotting; the fruit is lost. Control is preventive: it is far less of a problem in hot, dry climates, so the main levers are managing leaf-footed bug and other fruit-piercing pests, keeping the canopy open and airy, and removing and destroying infected and mummified fruit so spores do not carry over.

beginner: Grow it where summers are hot and dry if you can, keep the plant open, and water at the ground rather than over the top. Keep fruit-piercing bugs in check, clean up rotted and old dried fruit, and know that in humid, rainy areas this disease may limit your crop, so pick the most open, breezy spot.
seasoned: Favor dry-climate siting, open canopies, and drip (not overhead) watering to keep bloom and fruit dry. Control fruit-piercing insects, sanitize by removing mummies and rotted fruit, and, in humid regions, expect this to be a limiting disease and choose the most open, breezy sites.

beginner: Fuzzy gray-brown mold on the flowers and fruit, often starting at the crown end or a wound, with soft brown rot that spreads in cool, damp weather and in storage. It can spread from one fruit to another where they touch.
seasoned: Fuzzy gray-brown mold on flowers, on fruit (often starting at the crown or a wound), and on stored fruit; soft brown rot spreads in cool, wet, or humid conditions and in storage, and can move between touching fruit.

beginner: A fungus called Botrytis, or gray mold, that infects flowers and damaged or overripe fruit in cool, damp weather. It survives on old fruit and plant litter and is a common cause of rot in stored fruit.
seasoned: The fungus Botrytis cinerea (gray mold), which infects flowers and wounded or overripe fruit in cool, wet, humid conditions. It overwinters on plant debris and old fruit and is a common cause of post-harvest rot.

beginner: Pick off and throw away moldy flowers, fruit, and litter right away. Keep the plant open and dry, pick before the rains, handle fruit gently so it does not bruise, and refrigerate good fruit soon, since cold slows the mold. Once a fruit is rotting there is no home spray that fixes it.
seasoned: Remove and destroy moldy flowers, fruit, and debris promptly. Keep the canopy open and dry, harvest before rains, handle fruit gently to avoid wounds, and refrigerate sound fruit quickly, since cold storage slows the mold. There is no home spray cure once fruit is rotting.

beginner: Keep the plant open and the leaves dry: prune for airflow, water at the ground, clean up old fruit and litter, and handle and chill fruit carefully at harvest. Remove split or damaged fruit, which is where the mold gets in.
seasoned: Prioritize air circulation and dry foliage: open pruning, root-zone watering, prompt sanitation of old fruit and debris, and gentle handling with quick cooling at harvest. Cull split and wounded fruit, which are entry points.

beginner: Small dark spots on the fruit and leaves that grow and run together; badly spotted fruit looks rough and russeted, and heavy leaf spotting yellows the leaves and drops them. It is worst in warm, humid, rainy areas.
seasoned: Small dark spots and blotches on fruit and leaves that enlarge and merge; heavily spotted fruit is russeted and downgraded, and severe leaf infection causes yellowing and drop. Most common and damaging in warm, humid, rainy climates.

beginner: A fungus (Cercospora punicae, along with related fungi in the same wet climates) that spreads when leaves and fruit stay wet for a long time. It is a big reason pomegranate does poorly in the humid Southeast and other rainy places.
seasoned: The fungus Cercospora punicae (with related fungi such as Colletotrichum and Botryosphaeria in the same wet climates). It thrives on prolonged leaf and fruit wetness, so it is a leading reason pomegranate fruits poorly in the humid Southeast and other rainy regions.

beginner: There is no easy home cure, so prevention matters: plant in an open, sunny, breezy spot so the leaves dry quickly, prune to open the plant, water at the ground, and clean up fallen leaves and spotted fruit. In damp, rainy climates this disease will likely limit your fruit quality no matter what.
seasoned: Home control is limited and preventive: choose an open, sunny, breezy site so foliage dries fast, prune for airflow, water at the ground, and remove fallen leaves and infected fruit. In consistently humid, rainy climates, expect this disease to cap fruit quality regardless of care.

beginner: The best defense is where and how you plant it: an open, breezy, sloped spot with good air movement, wide spacing, an open plant, watering at the ground, and cleaning up fallen leaves and fruit. In hot, dry climates it is barely a problem.
seasoned: Site selection is the main defense: open, sloped, breezy ground with strong air movement, especially at bloom. Wide spacing, open canopies, ground-level irrigation, and sanitation of fallen debris reduce pressure. In hot, dry climates it is a minor issue.

beginner: Water deeply and regularly through spring and summer, then cut back in winter. A young plant needs steady water to get established. An older plant can take drought but makes much better fruit with regular deep watering, about once a week in summer heat, more or less depending on your soil and the weather. The most important thing is to keep the water STEADY once the fruit is forming: letting it go dry and then soaking it (or the first fall rains) is what makes pomegranates split. In winter, when the plant is resting, it needs very little.
seasoned: Water deeply and regularly through the growing season, then ease off. Young plants need steady moisture to establish; bearing plants are drought-tolerant but crop far better with regular deep watering, roughly weekly in summer heat, adjusted for soil and weather. The critical discipline is CONSISTENCY from fruit set through ripening: a dry spell followed by heavy water (or the first fall rains) is what splits the fruit. In winter dormancy, water need drops sharply and rainfall usually suffices.

beginner: Each watering should soak the soil deeply down to the roots, not just wet the top. During the fruiting season, aim for about an inch of water a week, more when it is very hot, given as deep, even soaks. beginner: Water a young pomegranate deeply and often through its first summer so the roots get going. It only becomes drought-tough after it is established.

beginner: Pomegranate makes fruit on older wood and on the tips of new shoots, so prune to shape and open it up rather than cutting it back hard all over, which cuts off the fruiting wood.
seasoned: Pomegranate fruits on spurs on older wood and on shoot tips, so prune to shape and open the plant rather than heading it back hard, which removes fruiting wood.

beginner: Prune in late winter: thin the plant so light and air get in, cut out dead and crossing branches, and remove the base shoots. Keep it light and make clean cuts.
seasoned: Prune in late dormancy: thin for light and air, remove dead and crossing wood, and clear base suckers. Keep it light, and make clean cuts.

beginner: Pomegranate makes fruit on its own and blooms late over several weeks, so it usually avoids spring frost. Damp, still air during bloom, not frost, is the main thing that hurts fruit set.
seasoned: Pomegranate is self-fruitful and blooms late over several weeks, so it largely dodges spring frost. Humid, still air at bloom, not frost, is the main threat to fruit set.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist from the time fruit forms until harvest. Going dry and then soaking (or a big rain) is what splits pomegranates, the most common problem there is.
seasoned: Keep soil moisture EVEN from fruit set to harvest. A dry spell followed by heavy water or rain is what splits pomegranates, the single most common failure.

beginner: Watch for the leaf-footed bug once fruit forms. Its feeding leaves no mark outside but darkens and shrivels the seeds inside and lets rot start in the fruit.
seasoned: Scout for leaf-footed bug from fruit set on. Its feeding leaves no external mark but darkens and withers the arils inside and opens the fruit to internal rot.

beginner: Ripe or nearly ripe fruit cracked open, sometimes showing the seeds. This is the number-one pomegranate problem, and it is about water, not disease: the skin splits when the seeds soak up water faster than the skin can stretch, which happens when the watering swings from dry to wet, after a big watering or the first fall rains following a dry stretch. It is easy to blame the variety, but the fix is how you water and when you pick: keep the soil evenly moist from the time fruit forms until harvest, and pick before big rains instead of leaving fruit out.
seasoned: Ripening or ripe fruit cracked, often exposing the arils. It is tempting to blame the variety, but the fix is watering and timing: keep soil moisture EVEN from fruit set through harvest, and pick ahead of significant rain rather than leaving fruit on the plant.

This is Alternaria heart rot, or black heart: a fungus gets in through the flower in damp bloom weather, or through insect holes (especially from the leaf-footed bug), and rots the inside with little sign outside. There is no cure once it is inside. It is much less of a problem in hot, dry weather, so the fixes are climate, pest control, and cleanup, not a spray.

beginner: A pomegranate is a leafy shrub, easily trained into a small tree, that loves hot, dry summers, the kind of weather that gives most fruit trouble. One plant makes fruit on its own, so you do not need a second one. It is one of the easiest fruits to grow in a warm climate: once it is established it handles drought, poor and salty soils (as long as they drain), and it needs only a little winter cold. The main thing is where you live. Pomegranate needs a long, hot, dry summer to ripen sweet, richly colored fruit, so it is wonderful in hot inland and desert gardens and only so-so in cool foggy coastal spots or humid, rainy areas, where the fruit sets poorly and gets diseases. Its big weak spot is splitting: the fruit cracks open when the watering swings from dry to wet near ripening, so keep the water steady and pick before the fall rains.
seasoned: Pomegranate (Punica granatum) is a deciduous, multi-stemmed fruiting shrub, easily trained to a small tree, that thrives on exactly the hot, dry summers most fruit dreads. It is self-fruitful, so a single plant bears, and it is one of the most forgiving fruits a warm-climate gardener can grow: drought-tolerant once established, tolerant of alkaline and heavy soils given drainage, and needing only a short winter chill. The catch is climate fit. Pomegranate wants a long, hot, dry season to ripen sweet, well-colored fruit, so it is superb in California's interior valleys and the low deserts and merely marginal in cool-summer coastal or humid southeastern gardens, where poor set and fruit disease follow the humidity. Its signature failure is splitting: fruit cracks when water swings from dry to wet near ripening, so steady moisture and picking ahead of the fall rains are the two habits that make or break a crop.

beginner: A pomegranate is ripe when the skin turns its full color (deep red for 'Wonderful'), goes from shiny to a little dull, and the round fruit flattens into more of a six-sided shape as the seeds inside swell. A ripe one feels heavy and makes a light metallic, tinny sound when you tap it. Pomegranates do not get sweeter after you pick them, so wait for full color, but do not leave them too long, because fruit left on the tree once the fall rains start will crack open. Cut the fruit off with clippers instead of pulling, and leave a little stem so you do not tear the skin.
seasoned: A pomegranate is ready when the rind takes on full varietal color (deep red for 'Wonderful'), shifts from glossy to a slightly matte finish, and the fruit's round shape flattens to a faintly hexagonal, ridged profile as the arils swell and press outward. A ripe fruit feels heavy for its size and makes a metallic, tinny sound when tapped. Pomegranate does not ripen further once picked, so pick at full color; but pick a touch early rather than late, because fruit left on the tree into the fall rains splits. Cut, do not pull, the fruit, leaving a short stem so you do not tear the rind.

That low requirement is met almost everywhere it is grown, including the low deserts, so chill is rarely the limiter; the frost-free tropics are the only places that may fall short. The real climate driver for pomegranate is the opposite end of the season: it needs a long stretch of summer heat to ripen sweet, well-colored fruit, which is why hot interior and desert sites outperform cool coastal ones regardless of chill.

If a pomegranate flowers but sets little fruit, the cause is usually the weather (damp, still, or cool weather at bloom makes the flowers drop) rather than a missing partner plant.
seasoned: Pomegranate is self-fruitful: a single plant sets a crop on its own, with no pollinizer partner required. Because self-pollination works, a lone plant fruits, but planting a second pomegranate nearby, or simply supporting bee activity at bloom, can improve fruit set. Poor set is far more often a weather problem (humid, still, or cool bloom conditions cause flowers to abort) than a pollination-partner problem.
