beginner: A persimmon is a good-looking fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and gives you one of the easiest crops you can grow, with brilliant fall color and bright orange fruit that hangs on after the leaves fall. There are two main kinds. The Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki) is the popular one for backyards: it fruits on its own, needs little winter cold, and handles down to about zone 7, with firm types eaten crisp like an apple (Fuyu) and soft types ripened until sweet and jelly-like (Hachiya). The American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) is much hardier, down to about zone 4, but usually needs separate male and female trees, unless you plant a self-fruitful kind like Meader. Persimmon blooms late, in May or June, so it usually escapes the spring frosts that hurt earlier fruit trees, and it hardly ever has pest or disease trouble. It just needs full sun, well-drained soil, a little pruning, and a few years of patience.
seasoned: Persimmon (Diospyros) is a handsome, low-maintenance deciduous fruit tree that yields some of the easiest home fruit there is, plus fiery orange-to-scarlet fall color and bright fruit that clings decoratively after the leaves drop. It comes in two very different forms. The Asian or Oriental persimmon (D. kaki) is the dooryard favorite: self-fruitful, low-chill, hardy to about USDA zone 7, with large fruit in non-astringent types eaten crisp like an apple (Fuyu) or astringent types ripened to a sweet, jelly-soft pulp (Hachiya). The American persimmon (D. virginiana) is far more cold-hardy, to roughly zone 4, but is usually dioecious, so a female needs a male tree nearby unless you plant a self-fruitful selection like Meader. Persimmon blooms late, in May or June, so it largely dodges the spring frosts that plague earlier fruit, and it is famously untroubled by pests and diseases. It asks little: full sun, well-drained soil, light pruning, and patience for the first three to five years.

beginner: A persimmon is ready when the fruit turns fully deep orange. For firm types like Fuyu, orange plus a firm feel means you can pick and eat it crisp. For astringent types like Hachiya and most American persimmons, orange means ready to pick but not yet to eat: let them sit until completely soft and jelly-like, when the pucker is gone. Clip or gently twist the fruit off with the leafy cap on instead of pulling. The fruit hangs on well into cool fall weather, so you do not have to rush.
seasoned: Persimmon is ready when the fruit reaches full, deep orange color. For non-astringent types (Fuyu), that plus a firm feel means ready to pick and eat crisp. For astringent types (Hachiya and most American persimmons), full color means ready to harvest, but not yet to eat: they must then ripen to a jelly-soft, nearly translucent stage before the astringency clears. Clip or twist fruit free with the calyx (the leafy cap) attached rather than pulling. The fruit holds on the tree well into cool fall weather, so harvest can be unhurried.

beginner: Pollination is the biggest difference between the two persimmon types, and it decides whether you need one tree or two. Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki), including Fuyu and Hachiya, fruits on its own: a single tree makes a full crop by itself, and the main kinds make seedless fruit with no pollen at all. American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) is the opposite: it usually has separate male and female trees, so a female needs a male American persimmon nearby to fruit. The exceptions are self-fruitful American kinds like Meader, which make seedless fruit with no male. The two species do not pollinate each other. For most gardeners the easy choice is one self-fruitful Asian tree; go with American (a female plus a male, or a self-fruitful kind like Meader) where winters are too cold for the Asian type.
seasoned: Pollination is the headline difference between the two persimmon types, and it decides whether you need one tree or two. American persimmon (D. virginiana) is the opposite: it is typically dioecious, carrying male and female flowers on separate trees, so a female needs a male American persimmon within roughly 50 to 200 feet to fruit. The exceptions are self-fruitful American cultivars such as Meader, bred to set seedless fruit with no male present. The two species do not cross-pollinate each other, and even among self-fruitful types, planting a pollinizer often gives heavier, seedier crops. For most home gardeners the simple path is one self-fruitful Asian tree; choose the American route (a hardy female plus a male, or a self-fruitful selection like Meader) where winters are too cold for Asian persimmon.

beginner: Mulberry is about as easygoing as a fruit tree gets when it comes to soil. It does best in a deep, rich, well-drained loam, but it also grows in sandy soil and even heavy clay, and it puts up with poor, dry ground once it is established. The one thing it does not want is soil that stays wet: constant waterlogging can rot the roots. Full sun and any soil that drains is really all it asks, and a little compost worked in at planting gives a young tree a good start.
seasoned: Mulberry is broadly soil-tolerant. It grows best in a deep, moist, well-drained loam but performs across sandy loams, sands, and clays, and tolerates infertile, dry, and even mildly alkaline ground once established (white mulberry in particular takes a wide pH span). The only real limit is drainage: chronically waterlogged soil invites root rot. Site it in full sun on any freely draining ground; a modest amount of organic matter at planting speeds establishment, but rich soil is not required and heavy feeding is unnecessary.

beginner: Mulberry grows well across a wide range of soil pH and is not fussy (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). It is happiest around pH 6.0 to 7.0 but tolerates soil from about 5.5 up to 8.0, including the mildly alkaline soils that trouble many fruit trees. For most gardens you do not need to adjust the pH at all; just make sure the soil drains.
seasoned: Mulberry is pH-adaptable, doing best around pH 6.0 to 7.0 but tolerating roughly 5.5 to 8.0. White mulberry in particular handles alkaline ground that stresses many stone fruits, so pH correction is rarely needed. Test before planting if in doubt, but in most soils the practical limits are drainage and sun, not pH.

beginner: Mulberry hardly ever needs feeding. It is a fast, vigorous tree that does fine on its own in most soils. If a young tree looks weak or the leaves are pale, scatter a little balanced fertilizer around the root zone in early spring and water it in. Do not overdo it, especially with nitrogen (the first number on the bag), because too much just makes leafy growth instead of fruit. Do not feed late in the year.
seasoned: Mulberry is a vigorous, undemanding tree that rarely needs feeding once established; on decent soil it grows fast on its own. If a young tree is weak or the leaves pale, apply a light broadcast of balanced fertilizer around the root zone in early spring and water it in. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which pushes rank, soft growth at the expense of fruit and can worsen bird-magnet leafiness. Never feed late in the season.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) covers the rare time a mulberry needs feeding. Most mature trees need none at all. When in doubt, feed less, because too much nitrogen means leaves instead of fruit.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 is more than enough for the rare occasion a mulberry needs feeding. Mature trees typically need nothing; err on the side of underfeeding, since excess nitrogen (N) drives vegetative growth over fruit.

seasoned: If feeding a young or weak tree, roughly 1/2 to 1 cup of 10-10-10 per year of tree age in early spring is ample, broadcast around the root zone and watered in, up to a few cups for a larger tree. Established trees on reasonable soil generally need no fertilizer at all. Do not fertilize in the planting hole; wait until growth begins.

beginner: Mulberry is self-fruitful, which means one named tree makes fruit on its own with no second tree needed (a few wild seedlings are single-sex, so buy a named fruiting variety and this never comes up). Because it is a big, fast tree, the things that matter are not vegetable-garden pairings but where you put it: keep grass and weeds pulled back from a young trunk so it establishes faster, and above all keep it away from paths, patios, driveways, and parked cars, because the dropped fruit stains everything it lands on. Under the dense canopy, lawn and most plants struggle from shade and shallow roots, so plan for mulch or shade-tolerant groundcover there.
seasoned: Mulberry is self-fruitful, so a single named tree fruits on its own without a pollinizer (a few wild seedlings are dioecious, but named cultivars sidestep that). The interactions that matter are about siting a large, vigorous tree, not classic vegetable companions: clear turf back from a young trunk to speed establishment, and site the tree well away from walkways, patios, driveways, and parking, since the abundant dropped fruit stains hard surfaces and gets tracked indoors. The dense canopy and shallow feeder roots make the ground beneath it a tough spot for lawn or bedding plants, so mulch it or use a shade-tolerant groundcover.

beginner: Birds strip the ripe berries fast. You will see missing fruit, half-eaten berries, and purple bird droppings under and around the tree. Big flocks can show up daily while the fruit ripens.
seasoned: Ripe and near-ripe berries disappear, half-eaten fruit and purple droppings appear on the ground and on nearby surfaces, and flocks work the tree through the ripening weeks. On a large tree the loss is simply shared; on a small or netted tree it can be nearly total if not managed.

beginner: Lots of birds love sweet, soft mulberries and eat them as they ripen. This is the main reason people lose fruit to the tree, though it is also why a mulberry is such a great tree for attracting birds.
seasoned: Many birds, especially catbirds, mockingbirds, robins, and waxwings, are drawn to sweet, soft mulberries and feed heavily as they ripen. This is the number-one reason home growers lose fruit, and it is a feature as much as a pest, since a mulberry is one of the best wildlife trees you can plant.

beginner: For a small tree, cover it with bird netting when the first berries start to color, and pick ripe fruit every day so there is less left for the birds. A big tree is too large to net, so the usual approach is to accept that you are sharing, or even to let the mulberry act as a decoy that keeps birds off your other fruit.
seasoned: For a small tree, drape bird netting over it as the first berries color, and harvest ripe fruit promptly each day so less hangs available. For a large tree, netting is impractical; the traditional answer is to plant enough that there is plenty to share, and some growers deliberately keep a mulberry as a decoy to lure birds away from cherries and other prized fruit.

beginner: You cannot really keep birds off a big mulberry, so plan on sharing; luckily the tree makes far more fruit than you can eat. Only bother netting small or dwarf trees, and pick ripe fruit quickly.
seasoned: There is no way to keep birds off a large mulberry, so plan the siting and the crop around sharing: a big tree yields far more than a household can use. Net only small or dwarf trees, and pick promptly.

beginner: Tiny white flies rise up off the undersides of the leaves when you brush the branches, sometimes leaving a sticky film and black sooty mold below. They rarely bother an established tree much.
seasoned: Tiny white flying insects lift off the undersides of leaves when disturbed, sometimes with sticky honeydew and sooty mold on lower foliage in a heavy infestation. Vigor is rarely affected on an established tree.

beginner: Whiteflies are small sap-sucking insects that gather under the leaves. They show up on mulberry fairly often but rarely do real harm.
seasoned: Whiteflies (including the mulberry whitefly) are sap-feeders that colonize leaf undersides. They are a common but minor mulberry pest and mostly a cosmetic nuisance.

beginner: A healthy tree does not need treatment. On a small tree with a lot of them, spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water or insecticidal soap, and welcome the ladybugs and lacewings that eat them.
seasoned: A healthy tree needs no treatment. If numbers are high on a small tree, a strong water spray to the leaf undersides or an insecticidal-soap application knocks them back; encourage the lacewings and ladybugs that prey on them.

beginner: Keep the tree healthy and go easy on nitrogen feeding, which draws whiteflies. Natural predators usually keep them under control outside.
seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and avoid heavy nitrogen feeding, which encourages the soft growth whiteflies favor. Natural predators usually keep them in balance outdoors.

beginner: Small holes, sawdust-like frass, or oozing on the trunk or big branches, mostly on trees that are already stressed or damaged. A healthy tree is rarely bothered.
seasoned: Small entry holes, frass, or oozing on the trunk and larger limbs, usually on trees already stressed by drought, injury, or decline. Healthy, vigorous mulberries are seldom attacked.

beginner: A few kinds of borer (beetle and moth larvae) can get into mulberry, but usually only when the tree is already weak from drought, wounds, or old age. They tend to follow trouble rather than start it.
seasoned: Several wood-boring beetle and moth larvae can attack mulberry, but almost always as a secondary problem on trees weakened by drought stress, mechanical wounds, or age. Borers follow decline rather than cause it in a healthy tree.

beginner: The best fix is a healthy tree: water it in droughts, keep mowers and trimmers off the trunk, and cut out and destroy any dead or infested branches. Once larvae are inside the wood, no spray reaches them.
seasoned: The durable control is tree health: water through droughts, avoid trunk wounds from mowers and trimmers, and prune out and destroy any dead or infested wood. There is no practical rescue spray for larvae already tunneling inside.

beginner: Keep the tree healthy and avoid wounding the trunk. A well-placed, watered mulberry rarely has borer trouble.
seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous and unwounded. A well-sited, adequately watered mulberry rarely gives borers an opening.

beginner: Some berries grow oddly, with the little segments puffing up hard and greenish so the fruit looks like tiny popcorn instead of a soft berry. Those berries never ripen right and hang on the tree.
seasoned: Some berries on the tree swell up abnormally, with individual segments (carpels) enlarging and staying hard and greenish, so the fruit looks like a little cluster of popcorn kernels instead of a normal soft berry. Affected fruit does not ripen properly and clings to the tree.

beginner: Popcorn disease is a fungus (Ciboria carunculoides) that gets into the developing fruit and makes it swell into hard, popcorn-like lumps. It mostly shows up in the South, and white mulberries and hybrids catch it most. It is usually minor but can cost you fruit on a tree you grow for eating.
seasoned: Popcorn disease is caused by the fungus Ciboria carunculoides, which infects the developing fruit and turns the carpels into hard sclerotia. It is largely a southern problem, and white mulberries and their hybrids are the most susceptible; it is usually of minor importance but can cause real fruit loss on trees grown for eating.

beginner: No home spray fixes it. The control is cleanup: pick off and throw away the affected berries, and rake up and bury or bin the fallen fruit under the tree, because that is where the fungus waits out the winter to come back next year.
seasoned: There is no home spray that cures it. Control is sanitation: as the disease appears, remove and destroy the affected fruit on the tree and rake up and bury or discard fallen fruit and debris beneath it, since that is where the fungus overwinters to reinfect next year.

beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen fruit each year so the fungus cannot overwinter. If popcorn disease is common in your area, choose a red mulberry or a tougher hybrid rather than the most susceptible white types.
seasoned: Year-round sanitation is the prevention: clear fallen and mummified fruit each season so the fungus has nowhere to overwinter. Where popcorn disease is a known local problem, favor red mulberry or a more resistant hybrid over the most susceptible white types.

beginner: Leaves get angular, water-soaked spots that turn dark, and new shoots can have black streaks; bad cases kill the shoot tips. It usually just looks bad rather than harming an established tree, and it is worst in wet weather.
seasoned: Angular, water-soaked spots appear on the leaves and turn dark, and young shoots can show black streaks or stripes; badly hit shoot tips may die back. Damage is usually cosmetic on an established tree and worst in wet springs.

beginner: Bacterial blight is a bacterium (Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori) that spreads in cool, wet spring weather and infects new growth. It is a minor disease that shows up in wet years and rarely hurts a healthy tree.
seasoned: Bacterial blight is caused by the bacterium Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori, which spreads in cool, wet spring weather and enters young tissue. It is a minor mulberry disease that flares in wet seasons and rarely threatens a healthy tree.

beginner: Cut out and throw away the blackened, blighted shoots in dry weather, and avoid watering over the top of the tree so the leaves stay drier. On a backyard tree, that cleanup is all that is needed.
seasoned: Prune out and destroy blackened, blighted shoots during dry weather to remove the bacterial source, and avoid overhead watering that keeps foliage wet. No spray is warranted on a home tree beyond this sanitation.

beginner: Keep the tree open so air moves through it, prune only when it is dry, and remove any infected shoots. A healthy, well-spaced tree easily shrugs this off most years.
seasoned: Keep the canopy open and the foliage dry, prune only in dry weather, and remove infected wood promptly. A vigorous, well-spaced tree shrugs off the disease in most years.

beginner: Spots on the leaves, or whitish patches underneath them in late summer, sometimes with a few leaves dropping in a wet year. It rarely affects how the tree grows or fruits.
seasoned: Scattered fungal leaf spots, or whitish patches (false mildew and powdery mildew) on leaf undersides in mid to late summer, sometimes with modest leaf drop on older trees in a wet season. Vigor and cropping are rarely affected.

beginner: A few minor leaf fungi (leaf spots and mildews) can mark mulberry leaves, mostly late in the season and in wet weather. On mulberry they are just cosmetic and rarely worth doing anything about.
seasoned: A group of minor leaf fungi (Cercospora and Cercosporella leaf spots, false mildew, and powdery mildews) can spot or coat mulberry foliage, mostly late in the season and mostly in wet weather. On mulberry these are cosmetic and seldom worth treating.

beginner: A healthy tree needs no treatment. Rake up and remove fallen leaves in fall to cut down on next year's spores, and keep the tree open so air flows through. Sprays are only for special trees with a bad, repeated problem.
seasoned: No treatment is needed on a healthy tree. Rake and remove fallen leaves in autumn to reduce carryover, and keep the canopy open for airflow. Fungicides are reserved for prized specimens with a serious recurring problem.

beginner: Keeping the tree open, cleaning up fallen leaves in fall, and letting air move through are all you need. A well-grown mulberry carries these without real harm.
seasoned: Open-canopy pruning, autumn leaf cleanup, and good air movement are the whole prevention program. Well-grown mulberries carry these diseases without meaningful harm.

beginner: Water a new mulberry regularly for its first year or two, about once a week when it does not rain, so the roots get going. After that it is very drought-tolerant and an older tree seldom needs watering, though a good soak while the berries are filling makes them bigger and sweeter. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs almost none.
seasoned: Water regularly through the first one to two seasons to establish the roots, roughly weekly in the absence of rain. After that, mulberry is notably drought-tolerant and an established tree rarely needs irrigation, though watering through the final weeks of fruit sizing improves size and sweetness. Cut back sharply in winter dormancy.

beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak. An older tree needs little, but a deep weekly soak while the fruit is filling, if the weather is dry, pays off in better berries. Deep soaks grow deep, drought-proof roots.
seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root depth rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing tree, on the order of 5 gallons per soak; a bearing tree that is watered at all wants the rough equivalent of an inch per week during fruit fill in dry spells. Deep, infrequent soaks build the deep roots that carry mulberry through drought.

beginner: Water the ground around the roots with a drip line, soaker hose, or a slow trickle from a hose, spreading it out toward the edge of the branches. The main thing is that the soil drains between waterings; mulberry hates sitting in water much more than it minds being dry.
seasoned: Water at the root zone by drip, soaker, or a slow hose out toward the drip line, keeping the trunk base itself uncrowded. Overhead watering is not the concern it is with stone fruit, but soil that drains freely between waterings matters most, since mulberry dislikes standing water far more than dryness.

beginner: Too much water, or soil that stays soggy, shows up as yellow leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree that just sits there or goes downhill. Since mulberry handles dry soil so well, staying too wet is the bigger risk. Soil that never dries out is your cue to back off.
seasoned: Overwatering or poor drainage shows as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists in wet soil, and a stalled or declining tree, since waterlogged roots suffocate. Because mulberry is so drought-adapted, chronic wet feet is a far more common cause of trouble than dryness; soil that never dries between waterings is the warning sign.

beginner: Too little water shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, and some early leaf drop in a long dry spell, and smaller berries if it runs dry while the fruit is filling. An established mulberry shrugs off dry spells and usually bounces back; the tree itself is rarely killed by drought.
seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting, dull curling leaves, and early leaf drop in a prolonged drought, and on the fruit as poor sizing during the fill period. An established mulberry tolerates real dry stress and usually recovers, but berries sized under drought stay small; the tree itself is rarely lost to dryness.

beginner: While the tree is settling in, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps it grow the deep roots that make it so drought-tough later.
seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil evenly moist, never waterlogged. A deep soak of about 5 gallons weekly, adjusted for rain and heat, builds the deep root system mulberry relies on to shrug off later droughts.

beginner: While the berries are filling, an older tree in a dry spell does better with about an inch of water a week as deep soaks. Steady water now means bigger, sweeter fruit. If it is raining regularly, you do not need to add any.
seasoned: During fruit fill, a bearing tree in a dry spell benefits from the equivalent of about an inch of water per week as deep soaks. Steady moisture now translates into larger, sweeter berries; an established tree with regular rain needs nothing extra.

beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs almost no water. Let rain do the work and water only during a long dry winter stretch. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.
seasoned: Once the tree is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely on rainfall and water only in a prolonged dry winter. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.

beginner: Give a deep soak now and then at the ground rather than a little every day, and make sure the soil drains between waterings. Mulberry handles dry soil far better than wet. Young trees need steady water for the first year or two to get established; after that, an older tree can often go without watering entirely.
seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone to encourage deep rooting; free drainage between waterings matters more than frequency, since mulberry is drought-adapted but intolerant of standing water. Young trees need consistent moisture through their first season or two to establish; mature trees are strongly drought-tolerant and often need no irrigation at all.

seasoned: The one window where watering clearly pays off is fruit fill, the couple of weeks as berries size and sweeten; a bearing tree kept watered then, in a dry spell, sizes better fruit. Establishment (the first season or two) is the other sensitive period. Outside those, an established mulberry is remarkably self-sufficient.

beginner: Mulberries do not keep on the counter. Ripe fruit gets soft and starts to spoil within a day, so eat them the day you pick them or put them in the fridge right away. They stain everything, so work over a bowl.
seasoned: Mulberries are extremely perishable and do not hold at room temperature; ripe fruit begins to soften and ferment within a day. Eat them the day they are picked, or refrigerate immediately. They also stain hands, cloth, and counters, so handle over a bowl.

beginner: Keep ripe mulberries in the fridge, unwashed, in a shallow open container, and eat them within 2 to 3 days (wash them only right before eating). They spoil fast and bruise easily, which is why you almost never see them in a grocery store; a mulberry is a fruit you grow or pick yourself.
seasoned: Refrigerate ripe mulberries unwashed in a shallow, breathable container and use within 2 to 3 days; washing before storage hastens breakdown. Their very short shelf life (and how poorly they pack and ship) is exactly why mulberries are a home-grown and farmers-market fruit, rarely a grocery one.

beginner: Mulberries freeze really well, which is the best way to deal with a big crop. Rinse them gently, drain and pat dry, spread them on a tray to freeze, then pack them into freezer bags. They keep for months and are great for baking, jam, syrup, and smoothies.
seasoned: Mulberries freeze very well. Rinse gently, drain and pat dry, freeze in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to freezer bags. Frozen berries keep for many months and are excellent for baking, jam, syrup, and smoothies. Freezing is the practical way to handle a heavy crop that ripens faster than you can eat it fresh.

beginner: Ripe mulberries only last a couple of days and stain easily, so have a plan for them: pick into shallow containers, chill or freeze them right away, and turn a big pick into jam, syrup, or frozen bags instead of letting them drop and stain the ground.
seasoned: Because tree-ripe mulberries last only days and stain readily, plan for the crop: pick into shallow containers, refrigerate or freeze promptly, and turn a heavy flush into jam, syrup, or the freezer rather than letting it drop and stain the ground.

beginner: Pick a mulberry first by your climate and how big a tree you want, then by the fruit. For cold winters, choose a hardy hybrid like Illinois Everbearing or Silk Hope; for warm areas, low-chill types like Pakistan, Black Beauty, or Oscar do great. For a small yard or a pot, choose a real dwarf like Dwarf Everbearing. Almost all named fruiting varieties fruit on their own, so one tree is enough. The one rule is to buy a NAMED fruiting variety, not an unnamed seedling, because a few wild seedlings turn out to be male and never fruit.
seasoned: Choose a mulberry first by climate and size, then by fruit. For cold winters, pick a hardy hybrid such as Illinois Everbearing or Silk Hope (zones 4 to 5 and up); for mild and warm regions, low-chill types like Pakistan, Black Beauty, and Oscar shine. For a small space or a container, choose a genuine dwarf such as Dwarf Everbearing. Nearly all named fruiting cultivars are self-fruitful and often parthenocarpic, so a single tree bears; the caveat is to buy a NAMED fruiting cultivar rather than an unnamed seedling, since a few wild seedlings are single-sex.

beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to outdoors) does not apply to mulberry. You plant it as a dormant bare-root tree in late winter or early spring, or from a pot, so there is no tender young plant to ease outdoors.
seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to mulberry. It is planted as a dormant bare-root tree in late winter to early spring, or as a container tree, not raised from a tender indoor seedling, so there is no soft transplant to acclimate.

beginner: Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground can be dug; a potted tree can go in during the growing season if you keep it watered. Soak bare roots in water for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots out, and set the tree at the same depth it grew before (if it is a grafted tree, keep the graft bump above the soil). Fill in with the soil you dug out, water it in well, and keep the area around it weed-free and mulched. Give it plenty of space, because a standard mulberry gets big.
seasoned: Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter to early spring before bud break, once the ground can be worked; container trees can go in through the growing season with attentive watering. Soak bare roots for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them and set the tree at the depth it grew in the nursery; if it is grafted, keep the graft union above the soil line. Backfill with native soil, water in well, and keep the surrounding area weed-free and mulched. Give it room: a standard mulberry is a large, spreading tree.

beginner: If you grow a dwarf mulberry in a pot, use a chunky, free-draining mix made for shrubs and trees, not a soft peaty potting soil that stays soggy. A bark-based mix with perlite or pumice drains well. Do not use soil dug from the yard in a pot, because it packs down and drains poorly when watered often.
seasoned: For a dwarf or weeping mulberry in a container, use a coarse, free-draining soilless mix built for woody plants, not a peat-heavy potting soil. A bark-based mix (composted pine bark with perlite or pumice) gives the air-filled porosity roots need; skip native garden soil, which compacts under frequent irrigation.

seasoned: Keep amendments drainage-first: blend in extra perlite or pumice if the base mix is water-retentive, and top-dress with a thin compost layer rather than mixing heavy organics throughout. Avoid moisture-retentive additives, which work against the freely draining root zone mulberry wants.

beginner: A potted mulberry dries out much faster than one in the ground, so check it often in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until water runs out the bottom. It still hates sitting in water, so never leave the pot in a full saucer. In winter, when the tree is resting, give just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
seasoned: A potted mulberry dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to draw on, so check moisture often in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes. It still resents standing water, so never leave the pot in a full saucer. Through dormancy it needs only enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.

beginner: Frequent watering washes food out of a pot, so feed lightly with a diluted balanced liquid fertilizer every few weeks from spring into midsummer, then stop by late summer so the tree does not push tender growth into fall. Do not feed at planting, and stop once the tree drops its leaves.
seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so feed lightly and often rather than in one heavy dose: a dilute balanced liquid feed every few weeks through the spring-to-midsummer flush, then stop by late summer so no soft growth is pushed into frost. Do not feed at planting, and ease off once the tree goes dormant.

beginner: Roots in a pot get much colder than roots in the ground, because cold reaches the soil from every side. A mulberry that is hardy in your yard can still have its roots freeze in a pot. Before hard freezes, either sink the pot to its rim in a garden bed or move it into an unheated but sheltered spot like a garage or shed that stays cold but not deep-freezing. It still needs the cold to rest, so do not bring it into a warm room.
seasoned: Roots in a container sit several zones colder than roots in the ground, so a mulberry hardy in your soil may still freeze its roots in a pot. Before hard freezes, sink the pot to its rim in a bed or move it to an unheated but sheltered space (garage or shed) that holds dormancy without the deep lows that kill exposed roots. It still needs its winter chill, so do not overwinter it in a heated room.

beginner: A standard mulberry is far too large and vigorous for a pot, so container growing means choosing a naturally dwarf or weeping variety like Dwarf Everbearing, which is bred for it and even fruits young in a pot. In a big, well-draining container it can be a productive patio tree, but plan on regular watering, occasional root pruning, and winter protection of the pot. For the everyday full-size mulberry, plant it in the ground.
seasoned: A standard mulberry is far too large and vigorous for containers, so container culture means starting with a genetic-dwarf or weeping cultivar (Dwarf Everbearing and similar), which are bred for pots and bear young. Given the largest practical, freely draining pot, such a tree makes a productive patio specimen, but expect regular watering, periodic root pruning to hold size, and winter root protection. For the ordinary full-size mulberry, in-ground is the only sensible choice.

beginner: A self-watering pot (one with a water tank in the bottom) is not a good choice for mulberry. The tank keeps the lower roots wet all the time, and wet roots are the one thing mulberry really dislikes. Use a pot that drains freely and let the soil dry out a bit between waterings.
seasoned: A self-watering or sub-irrigated planter is a poor match for mulberry. Its reservoir keeps the lower root zone continuously moist, and mulberry's one real intolerance is standing water at the roots. Use a pot that drains freely and let the mix dry between waterings, rather than a constant water table held against the roots.

beginner: Protecting a potted mulberry in winter is about more than the roots. The bare trunk, and the graft bump on a grafted tree, can also be hurt by freezing. In exposed spots wrap or shade the lower trunk, and pile mulch around a sunk pot to insulate the roots. You want a cold, steady rest without the deep freezes that kill exposed roots, and be careful that a too-warm spot can wake the tree early.
seasoned: Cold protection in a pot covers more than the roots: an exposed trunk and, on a grafted tree, the graft union are also vulnerable to freeze. Wrap or shade the lower trunk in exposed sites and bank mulch or sink the pot to insulate the roots. Aim for a cold, stable dormancy without the deep lows that kill exposed roots; a too-warm shelter that breaks dormancy early is its own hazard.

beginner: You do not rotate a mulberry the way you rotate vegetables, because it stays put for decades. Unlike peaches, mulberry has no special replant problem, so it can follow most things. The main thing is to pick the right spot from the start, away from paths and patios, because a big tree is hard to move.
seasoned: Annual crop rotation does not apply to a mulberry: it is a permanent tree that holds its site for decades. Mulberry has no notable replant-disease problem the way stone fruit does, so it can follow most previous plantings, but choose the site carefully for the long term, since a mature tree is hard to move and the fruit drop dictates placement.

beginner: For a mulberry, choosing the spot matters far more than rotation. Give it full sun, soil that drains, lots of room, and keep it away from anything the fruit could stain. There is no rotation schedule to follow.
seasoned: Site selection, not rotation, is the real decision for a mulberry: full sun, free drainage, plenty of room for a large spreading tree, and well clear of hard surfaces the fruit would stain. There is no rotation interval to observe.

seasoned: A dormant bare-root whip with firm buds and healthy roots, or a leafy container tree. If it is grafted, find the graft union low on the trunk and keep it above the soil.

beginner: A mulberry is a fast, very easy fruit tree that gives you sweet, blackberry-like berries over several weeks in early summer. You pick them dead ripe off the tree, which is why you almost never see them in a store. Almost all named mulberries fruit on their own (many even set fruit without any pollination), so one tree is all you need. It is tough and adaptable, handling poor soil, drought, heat, and most pests, and birds are really its only serious competition. The catch is that a standard tree gets big and drops a lot of staining fruit, so the main decision is where to put it (well away from paths, patios, and driveways) or to choose a small dwarf or weeping type. Give it sun, soil that drains, and room, and it asks for little more than a light winter pruning and keeps bearing for decades.
seasoned: Mulberry (Morus) is a fast-growing, exceptionally easy deciduous fruit tree that ripens sweet, blackberry-like berries over a long early-summer window, picked dead ripe off the tree, which is why they are almost never sold in stores. Nearly all named cultivars are self-fruitful, and many set fruit parthenocarpically (without pollination), so a single tree bears heavily on its own. It is vigorous and broadly adaptable, tolerating poor soil, drought, heat, and a wide pH range, with few serious pests (birds are the main competitor). The trade-offs are size and mess: a standard tree grows large and drops abundant staining fruit, so siting well away from paths, patios, and drives, or choosing a dwarf or weeping cultivar, is the key decision. Given a sunny, well-drained spot with room, a mulberry needs little more than light winter pruning and rewards you for decades.

beginner: A mulberry is ripe when the berry turns fully dark purple-black (or the ripe color of your variety, some are white or pink), goes soft, tastes sweet, and comes off at the lightest touch. Ripe fruit almost falls into your hand or drops when you shake the branch. There is no picking firm and ripening later like a peach: you pick mulberries dead ripe, and they spoil fast, so pick into shallow containers and chill or freeze them the same day.
seasoned: A mulberry is ready when the berry reaches full deep purple-black (or the ripe color of its cultivar, some are white or pink), turns soft, tastes sweet, and detaches at the gentlest touch. Ripe fruit will practically fall into your hand or drop when the branch is shaken. Unlike stone fruit, there is no firm-pick-and-ripen stage: a mulberry is picked dead ripe and is extremely perishable, so harvest into shallow containers and refrigerate or freeze the same day.

beginner: Mulberry flowers in spring as its leaves come out, earlier in warm areas and later in cold ones. The flowers are small greenish catkins, not showy blooms, and the wind does the pollinating. Because named mulberries fruit on their own (often without any pollination at all), there is really nothing to do at bloom. Unlike a peach, early flowers are not a big frost worry, since mulberry leafs out later and bounces back easily.
seasoned: Mulberry blooms in spring as it leafs out, the timing shifting by region from late winter in the warm South and mild California to spring in the North. The flowers are inconspicuous greenish catkins rather than showy blossoms, and pollination is by wind. Because named cultivars are self-fruitful and often parthenocarpic, bloom is largely uneventful for the grower; unlike stone fruit, early bloom is not a major frost liability, since mulberry leafs out later and recovers readily.

beginner: Mulberry as a whole grows across a huge range of climates, because there are several kinds. The hardy white mulberry and hybrids (like Illinois Everbearing) take cold winters down to about zones 4 to 5, the native red mulberry covers roughly zones 4 to 9, and the tender black and low-chill types are warm-climate trees for about zones 7 to 10 and warmer. So almost everyone can grow some kind of mulberry: pick a hardy hybrid for cold winters and a low-chill or black type for warm areas. Only the very coldest spots (zone 3) are too cold, and in the warmest areas you just need a low-chill variety so it gets enough winter cool to fruit.
seasoned: Mulberry as a group spans a very wide climate range because three species and their hybrids cover it: white mulberry (Morus alba) and the hardy hybrids (Illinois Everbearing, Silk Hope) are cold-hardy to about zones 4 to 5 and up; red mulberry (Morus rubra), the native, runs roughly zones 4 to 9; and black mulberry (Morus nigra) and low-chill types are tender, warm-climate trees for about zones 7 to 10 and into the subtropics. The practical result is that some mulberry fruits well across nearly the whole country: choose a hardy hybrid for cold winters and a low-chill or black type for mild and warm regions. Zone 3 is the cold limit for reliable survival; the warm and tropical edge is limited less by heat than by whether enough winter chill accrues for the chosen cultivar, which is why low-chill types are used there.

beginner: Mulberry needs only a modest amount of winter cold, much less than a peach, which is why it fruits in so many places, including mild and even subtropical areas. Different varieties need different amounts, from very little (dwarf and Pakistan types) up to a few hundred hours for the hardy northern kinds. For most gardeners, winter chill is never a problem; only in the very warmest, nearly frost-free areas does it matter, and there you just pick a low-chill variety. (Exact chill-hour numbers for mulberry are hard to find in extension sources, so these are best estimates.)
seasoned: Mulberry has a modest winter-chill requirement, low compared with stone fruit, which is why it fruits across so wide a range including mild-winter and subtropical areas. Requirements are cultivar-driven and roughly span about 100 chill hours (low-chill dwarf and Pakistan types) to around 400 to 500 (the hardy northern hybrids). In most of the country chill is never the limiting factor; only in the warmest, nearly chill-free zones does it matter, and there a low-chill cultivar solves it. Note: extension literature rarely publishes numeric mulberry chill figures, so the values here are a horticultural-consensus estimate rather than a single sourced number (see the notes).

beginner: The wind does the pollinating for mulberries, so you do not need bees or, usually, a second tree. The one thing to know: mulberry trees vary, and some kinds have separate male and female trees. A wild, unnamed seedling might turn out to be a male that never fruits, so buy a named fruiting variety instead, which usually makes a full crop on its own. This is the reverse of many apples, which need a second variety nearby to make fruit.
seasoned: Mulberries are wind-pollinated, not insect-pollinated, so pollinators are not needed for fruit set. At the species level they are variable: an individual tree is either monoecious, with male and female flowers together, or dioecious, with the sexes on separate trees, and wild red mulberry is usually dioecious, so an unnamed seedling can turn out to be a non-fruiting male. The practical rule is to buy a named fruiting cultivar, which is typically female and bears a full crop on its own, with many reported to set fruit with little or no pollination. This is the opposite situation from many apples, which require a second, compatible variety to cross-pollinate.

beginner: The wind pollinates mulberries, so you do not need bees. Mulberry trees vary: some have both male and female flowers on one tree, and some have separate male and female trees. The safe bet is to buy a named fruiting variety, which usually makes fruit on its own. An unnamed seedling can turn out to be a male that never fruits, or need a male tree nearby.
seasoned: Mulberries are wind-pollinated, so no bees or insects are needed for fruit. Trees are variable: some are monoecious, with both flower sexes on one tree, and some are dioecious, with separate male and female trees, and wild red mulberry is usually dioecious. For a home garden the reliable choice is a named fruiting cultivar, which is typically female and bears a good crop on its own; an unnamed or dioecious seedling can turn out to be a non-fruiting male or need a male tree nearby. This is the opposite of many apples, which require a second, compatible variety to cross-pollinate.

seasoned: Most common form for mulberry. The tree grows on its own roots, propagated from a hardwood cutting, so there is no graft union to worry about and any suckers are true to type. Full-size and vigorous; choose the cultivar for the size you want.

beginner: The first year is about helping the tree settle in, not getting fruit. Plant a bare-root tree in late winter (or a potted one during the growing season), water it steadily through the first season while the roots get going, and keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk. Do only the lightest shaping, and shorten the tree early if you want it easy to pick. Mulberry is easy: skip fertilizer unless it looks weak, and never feed late in the year. A little fruit the first year on an everbearing type is a nice bonus, not the point.
seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment over fruit. Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter (or a container tree in the growing season), water consistently through the first season while the roots establish, and keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk. Begin only the lightest formative shaping, and reduce height early if you want an easy-to-pick tree. Mulberry is undemanding: hold off on fertilizer unless growth is weak, and never feed late in the season. Any light first-year fruit on an everbearing cultivar is a bonus, not the goal.

beginner: Pawpaw wants a deep, rich, moist soil that still drains well, on the slightly acid side (around pH 5.5 to 7.0). In the wild it grows in bottomland woods with fertile, damp ground, so it likes steady moisture and plenty of organic matter, yet it will not tolerate soil that stays waterlogged. A deep loam with compost worked in is ideal. Heavy clay that holds water is the trouble spot and can rot the roots, so if your soil is heavy, plant on a raised mound and mix in compost to open it up. The one rule you cannot bend is drainage: moist is good, soggy is not.
seasoned: Pawpaw wants a deep, fertile, moisture-retentive loam that still drains freely, slightly acid at roughly pH 5.5 to 7.0. Its native haunts are bottomland woods with rich, damp soil, so it favors consistent moisture and high organic matter but will not thrive in heavy or waterlogged ground. Work in generous compost before planting. On heavy clay, plant on a raised berm to lift the roots above standing water and amend for aeration. Moisture with drainage is the balance to strike: pawpaw likes it damp but never soggy.

beginner: Pawpaw grows best in slightly acidic soil, about pH 5.5 to 7.0 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting and adjust slowly if you need to: garden lime raises the pH if the soil is too acidic, and elemental sulfur lowers it if the soil is too alkaline. Mix any of this in before you plant, because pH changes slowly and is much easier to fix before a permanent tree goes in. Pawpaw dislikes very alkaline, chalky soils.
seasoned: Pawpaw does best in a slightly acidic soil, roughly pH 5.5 to 7.0. Test the soil before planting and adjust gradually if needed: lime raises a too-acidic pH, while elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting, since pH shifts slowly and is far easier to correct before the permanent tree is in the ground. Pawpaw performs poorly on high-pH, calcareous soils.

beginner: Pawpaw does not need heavy feeding. Scatter a balanced fertilizer evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. Young trees do best with a little food given often, so feed lightly every few weeks through the first half of the season while the tree is getting going. An older tree needs just one spring feeding, or none at all if the soil is good. Stop by midsummer so the tree is not pushed into soft growth that winter can damage. A layer of mulch does a lot of the work.
seasoned: Pawpaw is a light feeder. Spread a balanced fertilizer evenly around the root zone out to the drip line, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. Young trees respond well to a little fed often, so a light balanced feeding every few weeks through the first half of the season speeds establishment; an established tree needs only a single spring application, if any, on decent soil. Stop feeding by midsummer so no soft late growth is pushed into fall. A ring of organic mulch supplies much of what the tree needs.

beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) works well for pawpaw, and on rich soil it may need none. For young trees, a balanced feed given lightly every few weeks in the first half of the season helps them settle in. Do not overdo the nitrogen, the first number, because too much pushes leafy growth instead of a strong frame.
seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits pawpaw; on fertile, organic-rich ground it may need no feeding at all. Kentucky State recommends a balanced feed (a 20-20-20 is often cited) applied lightly and often to young trees during the first half of the season. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which pushes soft growth at the expense of a sturdy framework.

beginner: For a young tree, a light balanced feeding (a weak liquid feed, or about a handful of 10-10-10 spread over the roots) every few weeks from when growth starts until midsummer helps it establish. For an older, fruiting tree, about 1 cup of 10-10-10 for each inch of trunk thickness, given once in spring, is plenty. Do not put fertilizer in the planting hole or feed right at planting; wait until the tree starts growing, and stop feeding after midsummer.
seasoned: For a young tree, a light balanced feed (for example a dilute 20-20-20, or about a handful of 10-10-10 scattered over the root zone) every few weeks from bud break through midsummer supports establishment. For a bearing tree, roughly 1 cup of 10-10-10 per inch of trunk diameter, applied once in spring, is ample. Do not fertilize at planting or place fertilizer in the hole; wait until growth begins, and do not feed after midsummer.

beginner: The most important companion for a pawpaw is another pawpaw. Pawpaw cannot pollinate itself, so a single tree, or a group of trees that are all the same variety or all suckers from one plant, will flower but set little or no fruit. Plant at least two genetically different pawpaws (two different named varieties, or two or more seedlings) close together so their flowers can cross-pollinate. Beyond that second tree, what matters most is the root zone: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under a young tree, since lawn competes hard for water, and remember pawpaw is a woodland tree that wants shade over its roots and its young leaves for the first year or two.
seasoned: The companion that decides whether a pawpaw fruits is a second, genetically distinct pawpaw. The species is self-incompatible, so a lone tree, or a block of one clone (a named variety and its own root suckers are genetically identical), blooms but sets almost nothing. Plant two or more different cultivars or seedlings within a short distance so the fly and beetle pollinators can move pollen between distinct trees. Past that, pawpaw's interactions are about the root zone, not classic vegetable pairings: clear turf from under a young tree, which competes for moisture, and honor its woodland nature by shading the roots and the sun-sensitive young foliage through establishment.

beginner: Flowers wilt, turn black, and fall off right when they should be turning into fruit. If you open a fallen flower you may find a tiny pale caterpillar tunneling inside the flower stalk. In a bad year it can ruin most of the flowers, so a tree that bloomed heavily still gives you very few pawpaws.
seasoned: Open flowers wilt, blacken, and drop just as they should be setting fruit. Splitting a dropped flower reveals a small pale caterpillar tunneling in the fleshy flower stalk (the peduncle) and floral tissue. In a bad year the borer can destroy the majority of a tree's blossoms, so a heavy bloom yields almost no fruit.

beginner: The caterpillar of a small moth called the pawpaw peduncle borer. It burrows into the soft tissue of the flower, which makes the flower die and fall. How bad it is changes a lot from one year to the next.
seasoned: Larvae of the pawpaw peduncle borer (Talponia plummeriana), a small moth. At roughly 5 millimeters the larva is easy to miss, and the feeding happens out of sight inside the flower itself, so the first sign is a bloom that dies back and drops instead of setting fruit. How much of the bloom you lose swings widely from one season to the next.

beginner: There is no easy spray for this on a home tree once the caterpillars are inside the flowers. The best thing you can do is pick up and throw away the fallen, damaged flowers to lower their numbers, and hand-pollinate the healthy flowers so you still get fruit. It does not hurt the tree itself, and it is usually less of a problem the next year.
seasoned: There is no practical spray for a backyard tree once larvae are inside the flowers. The workable response is sanitation: gather and destroy dropped, infested flowers to reduce the local population, and lean on hand pollination of the healthy flowers to secure a crop despite the losses. Damage is rarely fatal to the tree and often eases the following year.

beginner: Rake up and remove fallen flowers so the borer cannot keep its cycle going under the tree. Because pawpaw already sets fruit unreliably, the best insurance is to hand-pollinate the good flowers so you get fruit from the ones the borer does not reach.
seasoned: Keep the ground under the tree clear of fallen flowers and debris where the borer can complete its cycle. A tree with two genetic partners and hand pollination will still set a crop from the flowers the borer misses, so protecting fruit set is more about pollination insurance than eradication.

beginner: A few young leaves chewed here and there, with a striped green-and-black caterpillar on them. The damage is minor and just cosmetic; there are never enough of them to strip a tree.
seasoned: Chewed young leaves, usually only a few at a time, with a green-and-black banded caterpillar feeding on the foliage. Damage is almost always light and cosmetic; the caterpillars never appear in numbers large enough to defoliate a tree.

beginner: The caterpillar of the zebra swallowtail butterfly, which can only grow on pawpaw leaves. It feeds on the young leaves but never in big numbers. This is really a bonus, not a pest problem: the beautiful butterfly needs pawpaw to survive.
seasoned: Larvae of the zebra swallowtail butterfly (Protographium marcellus), for which pawpaw is the sole larval host plant. The caterpillars feed only on young pawpaw foliage and never in great numbers, so they are far more a delight than a threat: the striking adult butterfly depends entirely on pawpaw.

beginner: Do nothing. The leaf nibbling is harmless, and these are the caterpillars of a lovely native butterfly that has nowhere else to live. Just enjoy them.
seasoned: No treatment is warranted. The feeding is negligible, and controlling it would remove the caterpillars of a native butterfly that has no other host. Simply leave them be.

beginner: None needed. A healthy pawpaw is not bothered by them, and the butterfly is one of the nicest reasons to grow the tree.
seasoned: None needed or advised. A healthy pawpaw shrugs off the light feeding, and the butterfly is a welcome part of having the tree.

beginner: Ripe or almost-ripe fruit vanishes from the tree or turns up chewed on the ground, usually overnight, just as it gets soft. The strong ripe smell draws animals, and they often get to the fruit before you do.
seasoned: Ripe and nearly ripe fruit disappears from the tree or is found half-eaten on the ground, often overnight, right as it softens. Because pawpaw ripens over a short window and soft fruit is highly aromatic, animals frequently harvest it before the gardener does.

beginner: Raccoons, opossums, squirrels, and other animals love the strong smell of ripening pawpaw and will help themselves. Deer are the exception: they avoid pawpaw leaves and fruit, so it is the fruit-eaters you are competing with.
seasoned: Raccoons, opossums, squirrels, and other wildlife are strongly attracted to the intense aroma of ripening pawpaw. Deer, by contrast, avoid the foliage and fruit, so the competition here is from fruit-eating mammals, not browsers.

beginner: Get to the fruit first. Pick pawpaws when they are full-sized and just beginning to soften, then let them finish ripening indoors instead of leaving soft fruit on the tree overnight. Check the tree every day while it is ripening. Netting or a baffle on the trunk can help if animals are a big problem.
seasoned: Beat the animals to the fruit: pick pawpaws firm but full-sized as they begin to soften and finish ripening indoors, rather than leaving tree-ripe fruit hanging overnight. Check the tree daily through the harvest window. Netting or trunk baffles help where pressure is heavy.

beginner: Pick fruit promptly and do not let ripe pawpaws pile up on the tree or the ground. Since the fruit does not keep long anyway, picking it as soon as it starts to soften and ripening it indoors both saves it from animals and lets you manage it better.
seasoned: Harvest promptly and do not let ripe fruit accumulate on the tree or ground. Since pawpaw is so perishable anyway, picking at the first give and ripening indoors both protects the crop from wildlife and gives you better control over the fruit.

beginner: Small tan or brown spots on the leaves, and sometimes dark surface blotches on the fruit skin. It looks worse than it is: the spots are just on the surface, do not harm the tree, and the fruit inside is fine. It shows up most in warm, wet, muggy summers.
seasoned: Small tan-to-brown spots on the leaves and, at times, superficial dark blotches on the fruit skin. The spotting is cosmetic: it does not defoliate a healthy tree or spoil the flesh, and the fruit inside remains sound. Worst in warm, wet, humid summers with crowded, poorly ventilated foliage.

beginner: A leaf-spot fungus that spreads in warm, damp weather, especially where leaves stay wet and crowded. Apart from this minor spotting, pawpaw has very few disease problems.
seasoned: Fungi in the Phyllosticta group (and similar leaf-spot fungi). Spores spread in warm, humid, wet weather, and infection is favored by dense canopies that stay wet. Pawpaw is otherwise notably free of serious disease.

beginner: No spray is needed for what is only a cosmetic problem. Give trees room for air to move, rake up and remove the spotted fallen leaves in autumn, and keep the tree healthy. The fruit itself is fine to eat.
seasoned: No fungicide is warranted for what is a cosmetic issue. Improve airflow by not crowding trees, rake and remove fallen spotted leaves at season's end to reduce carryover, and keep the tree vigorous. The fruit is unaffected inside and fully edible.

beginner: Give trees enough space for air to move, avoid wetting the leaves when you water, and clean up fallen leaves in fall. That keeps the minor spotting down. Pawpaw does not need a regular spray schedule.
seasoned: Space and site trees for good air movement, avoid overhead wetting of the foliage, and clear fallen leaves in autumn. These reduce the minor spotting; no routine spray program is needed for pawpaw.

beginner: Pawpaw likes steady moisture, so water deeply and regularly, and never let a young tree go dry. For the first two years, plan on a deep soak once or twice a week, easing to about once a week for an older tree in summer heat, adjusting for rain and your soil. It likes more water than most fruit trees, but it still cannot sit in soggy soil, so aim for damp, not waterlogged. In winter, when the tree is resting, it needs much less and rain usually covers it.
seasoned: Pawpaw wants consistent soil moisture, so water deeply and regularly rather than sparingly, and never let a young tree dry out. Plan on a deep soak once or twice a week through the first two seasons while roots establish, easing toward weekly for a bearing tree in summer heat, always adjusted for rain and soil. It is more moisture-loving than most fruit trees, but it still will not tolerate standing water, so keep the soil damp, not soggy. Through winter dormancy the need drops and rainfall usually suffices.

beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches all the way down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak. An older, fruiting tree wants roughly an inch of water a week through the growing season, and more when it is hot. A thick layer of mulch over the roots really helps pawpaw, holding in the steady moisture it likes and keeping the roots cool.
seasoned: Water deeply each time so moisture reaches the full root depth rather than wetting only the surface. For an establishing tree, that is on the order of 5 gallons per soak; for a bearing tree, aim for roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week through the growing season, more in heat. A thick organic mulch over the root zone is especially valuable on pawpaw, holding the even moisture it prefers and keeping the shallow feeder roots cool.

beginner: Water at the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, spreading it out to the edge of the branches rather than just at the trunk. Try not to spray water over the leaves, since wet foliage can bring on minor leaf spots; put the water on the soil. The feeder roots run shallow, so a wide, mulched, evenly damp area around the tree suits it better than soaking only right at the trunk.
seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose, out toward the drip line rather than only at the trunk. Overhead watering that wets the foliage is best avoided, since it favors the minor leaf spotting pawpaw can get; deliver water to the soil. Because the young feeder roots run shallow under the natural leaf litter, a wide, mulched, evenly moist root area serves the tree better than a narrow deep well at the trunk.

beginner: Soil that stays too wet, or drains poorly, shows up as yellowing leaves, wilting that does not go away even when the soil is wet, and a tree slowly going downhill, because the roots cannot breathe and start to rot. Soil that never dries out between waterings is your warning. Pawpaw likes steady moisture, but not water sitting around the roots.
seasoned: Waterlogged, poorly drained soil shows as yellowing leaves, wilting that persists even in wet ground, and a generally declining tree, since pawpaw roots suffocate and rot when the soil stays saturated. Soggy soil that never dries between waterings is the warning to act on: pawpaw wants steady moisture, but not standing water.

beginner: Too little water shows as wilting and drooping, dull leaves, brown or scorched leaf edges (worse in sun and wind), and leaves dropping early in a dry stretch. A young pawpaw is very sensitive to drying out, and the fruit stays small if the tree gets too dry while the pawpaws are filling out. Catch it early, because a dried-out young tree can die.
seasoned: Underwatering shows as wilting and drooping, dull leaves, browning or scorched leaf margins (worse in sun and wind), and early leaf drop in a dry spell. A young pawpaw is especially unforgiving of drought, and the fruit sizes poorly if the tree runs short of water while the crop is filling. Catch the dry stress early, since a stressed young tree can be lost outright.

beginner: For the first two years, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist, never bone dry and never soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, plus a thick mulch, helps a young pawpaw through the time it is most easily lost. Do not let it dry out.
seasoned: Through the first two seasons, keep the root ball and surrounding soil consistently moist, never dry and never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, plus a thick mulch, carry a young pawpaw through its most vulnerable period. Do not let it dry out.

beginner: While the pawpaws are sizing up over summer, keep the water steady. Aim for about an inch of water a week, more when it is hot, given as deep soaks. Steady watering now means bigger, better fruit and keeps the tree from dropping fruit under stress.
seasoned: While the fruit sizes through summer, keep moisture steady. Aim for the equivalent of about an inch of water per week, more in heat, as deep soaks. Even moisture now translates directly into larger, better-filled fruit and prevents the drop that dry stress can trigger.

beginner: After the leaves drop and the tree is resting for winter, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water during a long dry stretch so the roots do not dry out. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.
seasoned: Once the tree is dormant and leafless, water need drops sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only during a prolonged dry spell to keep roots from desiccating. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated.

beginner: Give the tree a deep soak now and then rather than a little every day, water at the ground (a drip line or soaker hose under a thick mulch is ideal) instead of spraying the leaves, and keep the soil evenly moist. Young trees are sensitive to drying out and need steady water for at least their first two years. An older tree can handle a short dry spell, but the fruit comes out small if it gets too dry, and pawpaw is thirstier than most fruit trees.
seasoned: Water deeply and regularly at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker under a generous mulch, to hold the even moisture pawpaw prefers; avoid wetting the canopy. Young trees are drought-sensitive and need consistent moisture through at least their first two seasons to establish; a mature tree tolerates short dry spells but sizes fruit poorly under stress and is less drought-hardy than a peach or apple.

Named grafted varieties, like the well-known Peterson types (Shenandoah, Susquehanna, Allegheny, Potomac) and older favorites like Sunflower and Overleese, give bigger fruit with fewer seeds and better flavor than plain seedlings, and they fruit sooner. USU Washington County Extension lists pawpaw on neither its low-elevation nor its higher-elevation fruit list. Chill is close to adequate on paper, since the area banks roughly 250 to 450 hours against pawpaw's 400 to 1,000 hour need, near or just under it, but aridity, heat, and alkaline soil, not chill, are what rule it out.

seasoned: St. George's low-elevation Dixie banks roughly 250 to 450 chill hours, near or just under pawpaw's 400 to 1,000 hour requirement. Even where the chill number would nearly pencil out, it is not what matters: the arid heat and alkaline soil, not winter cold, rule pawpaw out here.
