seasoned: Artichoke will grow on this ground and it will not crop on it, and the reason is narrow rather than general. The part you eat is an immature flower bud, and bud initiation needs a run of hours below 50°F that this climate never banks. UF/IFAS ran that experiment in Florida and reported both halves of it: plants sprayed with gibberellic acid formed buds, while the untreated ones stayed leafy right through to the end of the season and never bolted at all. Those plants did not struggle or die, they simply never flowered. Spraying a growth regulator on a schedule is a commercial operation rather than a garden one, so plan on the plant and not on the crop. What the plant gives you is genuinely worth having: UF/IFAS describes the rosette as arching, deeply toothed, silvery, woolly leaves 20 to 32 inches long. This is UF/IFAS's own ground, so the evidence here is direct rather than borrowed. The planting is a single cool season rather than a standing one, because the recommended October to May cycle exists specifically to dodge a summer whose heat and wet drive disease and pests. Artichoke is also absent entirely from the Florida vegetable gardening guide, whose alphabetical planting table runs straight past where it would sit, and a UF/IFAS county guide footnotes that globe artichokes, asparagus and rhubarb are not well adapted to Florida. That is a verdict on the crop, and it is correct; it is not a verdict on whether the plant will grow, and the same service's trial answers that question the other way.

beginner: An artichoke is a flower bud you pick before it opens, growing on a plant that looks like a five-foot silver thistle. That one fact drives everything: to get artichokes, the plant first has to be convinced to make flowers, and it does that after a stretch of cool weather. In mild-winter places like coastal California you plant once and pick from the same plants for years. Anywhere with a real winter you grow it as a yearly crop instead: start seed indoors, give the young plants a few weeks in the cold on purpose, plant them out, pick in late summer, and start over next spring. Neither way is harder than the other, they are just different, and your winter decides which one you are doing.
seasoned: Globe artichoke is a big herbaceous perennial thistle grown for an immature flower bud, which is the single fact that explains everything else about it. Because the crop is a flower, the plant has to be persuaded to flower, and it does that after a run of cool weather: roughly 500 hours between 35°F and 50°F is the figure the peer-reviewed trial work converges on, though published requirements span 205 to 1356 hours and the spread is driven by cultivar rather than by measurement error. The requirement is quantitative, not absolute. Rutgers recorded 74 percent of Imperial Star and 57 percent of Green Globe Improved setting buds with no cold treatment at all, rising to 98 and 86 percent with it, so cold advances and synchronizes budding rather than permitting it. That is why artichoke runs two completely different careers. Where winters stay above roughly 15°F it is a permanent bed cropping for years from crown divisions, the Castroville model; everywhere colder it is an annual, started indoors, chilled deliberately as a seedling, set out, cropped in its first season and lost to winter. Both are real, both are extension documented, and which one applies to you is a question about your winter, not about your skill.

beginner: Squeeze the bud. If it is firm and the scales are still shut tight against each other, cut it. If the scales have started to loosen and open out, you waited too long, and it will be woody and bitter no matter how you cook it. Size is not the signal, tightness is. Cut the big bud at the top of the stalk first, taking 2 to 3 inches of stem with it, and the smaller ones lower down will come along afterward. In hot weather check every day, because heat makes buds open fast.
seasoned: Cut on bract tightness, not on size. A bud is ready once it has reached full size for its position on the stalk and while its bracts are still closed flat against each other; the moment they loosen and begin to spread, the bud turns woody and bitter and is finished as food. University of California is explicit that on seeded varieties a mature bud stops enlarging, so waiting past that point buys nothing and costs the bud. Take the terminal bud first, since it matures well ahead of the two or three secondaries below it, and cut with 2 to 3 inches of stem attached. Heat compresses this window sharply: above 86°F buds open quickly and the heart loses tenderness and compactness, so in a hot spell check daily rather than every few days.

beginner: Think about it as two separate questions: will the buds get damaged, and will the plant survive the winter. Buds start taking frost damage around 30°F, which mostly just blisters the outside and still tastes fine, and gets serious in the mid 20s. Cover plants when a night below 25°F is coming. The roots are much hardier and only die around 15°F, even under mulch, which is the real dividing line between a plant that comes back next year and one that does not. You may see artichoke listed as hardy to zone 7, or zone 6, or zone 5. Those numbers disagree with each other and with the measured temperatures, so we do not publish one. Go by your actual winter lows.
seasoned: Four different temperatures matter here and they are commonly confused with one another. Bud tissue starts to freeze at about 29.9°F, which blisters and bronzes the outer bracts without harming eating quality, and the damage turns serious below about 24.8°F. Texas A&M sets 25°F as the practical management floor, the point at which you cover plants with straw or a frost blanket. The crown itself is far tougher and is the thing that decides whether a planting persists: Oregon State reports severe crown loss below 15°F even under mulch, and a peer-reviewed study independently puts the perennial limit at about 14°F. There is no published foliage-damage temperature for this crop, so beware anyone quoting one. Deliberately absent from this guide: a USDA hardiness zone. Three extension sources give three incompatible answers, from zone 7 and warmer to zone 6 with mulch to occasional zone 5, and all three are warmer-tolerant than the measured crown-kill temperature allows. Picking one would mean preferring a source over two others with no basis, so the temperatures do the work instead.

beginner: There is one step in the first year that decides whether you get artichokes at all, and it is easy to skip because it sounds strange: you have to make the young plants cold on purpose. Start seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before you plan to plant out. Once each seedling has four to six real leaves, put the tray somewhere between 35°F and 50°F for about three weeks. A spare refrigerator, an unheated garage, or a cold frame all work, and a bit of light during those weeks helps. In trials, plants given about three weeks of cold flowered at up to 100 percent, while plants given only half that flowered as little as 3 percent. Same seed, same year, and the only difference was the cold. After that, keep them under 80°F until they go outside, because heat undoes the cold treatment. Even done right, one plant in five may never make a bud, so plant a couple more than you think you need.
seasoned: The first year is where this crop is won or lost, and the step people skip is the cold treatment. Sow 6 to 8 weeks ahead of the intended set-out date, germinate at 70°F to 80°F, then grow the seedlings at about 75°F day and 65°F night. Once they reach four to six true leaves, chill them for roughly three weeks at 35°F to 50°F. That duration is not folklore: a three-year replicated University of Maine trial measured 3 to 33 percent of plants flowering after 303 hours and 68 to 100 percent after 550 hours, and its conclusion is that duration is the key driver above 35°F. Supplemental light during chilling accompanied the higher figure, so give them light rather than a dark refrigerator if you can. Afterwards keep them under 80°F, because heat reverses accumulated chilling; Connecticut measured bare-soil temperatures of 84°F to 102°F devernalizing plants outright and leaving them barren. Virginia runs the inverse system, setting transplants out at or just before last frost so the seedlings take their 190 to 240 hours at 50°F or below in the ground. Either route works, but do not blend them, and expect 15 to 25 percent of plants to stay barren even when chilling was adequate.

beginner: Give artichoke more room than you think. A mature plant is about four feet wide, so allow at least a foot and a half between plants and two to three feet between rows. It wants full sun, deep soil that drains well, and plenty of compost dug in. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.5. Get the perennial weeds out before you plant: water the bed, wait a couple of weeks for the weed seeds to sprout, then hoe them off and plant into clean ground. If the plants are going to stay put for years, it is worth digging the bed properly now.
seasoned: Site this crop the way you would site a small shrub, because that is the footprint. Plants reach four feet across and want deep, fertile, well-drained ground in full sun with a generous amount of organic matter worked in; University of California puts the target pH at 6.0 to 6.5 and suggests lime or gypsum where calcium is low. Clear perennial weeds before planting rather than after, and UC's pre-plant trick is worth the fortnight it costs: irrigate the cleared bed deeply, let a flush of weed seed germinate, then work the ground again to kill the seedlings. Space plants 18 to 36 inches apart depending on whose spacing you follow, with 2 to 4 feet between rows; crowded plants make smaller buds and are miserable to harvest from. Where the bed is permanent, take the time to loosen it deeply, because you will not get another chance for years.

beginner: Pick each artichoke while it is still tight. Run a thumb over it: if the scales are shut flat against each other, cut it now. If they have started to loosen and spread apart, that one is past its best and will be tough and bitter however you cook it. Do not wait for a bud to get bigger, because once it is fully grown it stops growing and only opens. In hot weather check every day, since heat makes them open fast. Unlike some crops there is no point where you have to stop picking to protect the plant, so keep going until frost or until the plant runs out of buds.
seasoned: Artichoke's stop rule governs the individual bud, not the season, and that is a real difference from the other crop on this archetype rather than a wording choice. Cut each bud while its bracts are still closed flat against one another. Once they loosen and begin to spread, the bud has passed: University of California notes that on seeded varieties a mature bud neither enlarges further nor re-tightens, and that buds left past their prime turn woody and bitter. Size is not the trigger, since a small secondary bud is perfectly good eating and a large one that has begun to open is not. Heat compresses the window, because above 86°F buds open quickly and the heart loses tenderness and compactness, so switch to daily checks in hot weather. There is no reserve-protection stop for this crop of the kind asparagus has; harvesting does not draw down a storage organ, so you pick until frost or until the flush ends rather than stopping to spare the plant.

Either way, what to expect from a season is under yields.
seasoned: No bed-age harvest ramp is published for artichoke, so this guide does not carry one. Two things are true at once. Where artichoke perennializes, on the California coast and the warm maritime Northwest, the crown does get more productive with age, and University of California describes a first-year planting as giving a light pick about a year after planting; but no source turns that into a picking duration by bed year, and inventing one would put a manufactured number where a real one is missing. Everywhere else the question does not arise at all, because artichoke is grown as an annual and every planting is a year-one planting with no crown carried into a second season. What can be said about duration is said where it is actually sourced: the concentrated six to eight week flush of annual culture, in yield_expectations, and the two regional durations carried on the cells that have them.
render_status_label: C -- never referenced in either app repo

beginner: Turnips like loose, fertile, well-drained soil with no hard layer underneath. Loosen the bed about 8 to 10 inches down and rake out rocks and clods, because the root grows rounder and smoother in loose soil and comes out forked or lumpy in packed, stony ground. Mix in some compost or well-rotted (never fresh) manure, since fresh manure can make the roots branch and grow hairy. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8. If clubroot, a disease that swells and deforms the roots, has been a problem in your garden, adding lime to raise the pH closer to 7.0 to 7.2 helps hold it back.
seasoned: Turnips do best in deep, loose, fertile, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, ideally a sandy loam or loam. They are quick and shallow-rooted compared with carrots, but stones, clods, and compaction still cause forking and misshapen roots, so a friable seedbed matters. Work in well-finished compost or well-rotted manure rather than fresh manure, which drives leafy top growth and can cause hairy, branched roots. Keep pH in the slightly acidic to neutral range, about 6.0 to 6.8. The brassica-specific soil caution is clubroot: the soilborne pathogen Plasmodiophora brassicae thrives in wet, poorly drained, acidic ground, so on a clubroot-prone bed improve drainage and lime toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.0 to 7.2, which suppresses it.

beginner: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Turnips like it slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 6.8, though they grow across a fairly wide range. A cheap soil test from your local extension office tells you your number and whether to add lime. One turnip-specific point: a root disease called clubroot is worse in acidic soil, so if your turnips have come out swollen and deformed, raising the pH toward 7.0 to 7.2 with lime helps hold the disease back.
seasoned: Turnips grow best at a slightly acidic to neutral pH of about 6.0 to 6.8; Clemson recommends maintaining roughly 6.0 to 6.5, and Minnesota gives a workable range of about 6.0 to 7.5. The brassica-specific reason to watch pH is clubroot: the pathogen is favored by acidic soil, and the standard cultural control is to lime the bed toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.2 to 7.5 where the disease is established. There is thus a mild tension between the ideal growing pH and the clubroot-suppressing pH, resolved by liming only on a clubroot-prone bed. A standard soil test from your local extension office removes the guesswork before sowing.

beginner: Turnips do not need heavy feeding. Mix a balanced fertilizer and some compost into the bed before planting, and give one light feeding later only if the plants look weak and pale. Go easy on nitrogen if you want good roots, because too much grows big leafy tops and small roots. If you are growing turnips mainly for the greens, a little extra nitrogen is fine, since the leaves are what you are after. Do not use fresh manure, which makes the roots hairy and forked.
seasoned: Turnips are light to moderate feeders. Work well-finished compost and a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing, then side-dress lightly once the tops are established if growth is weak. The key brassica-root caution is nitrogen: excess nitrogen grows lush tops at the expense of the root and can leave roots small and poorly formed, so go easy where you want good roots. A crop grown mainly for greens tolerates and even rewards more nitrogen, since the leaves are the harvest. Avoid fresh manure, which both over-supplies nitrogen and causes hairy, branched roots.

beginner: The three numbers on a fertilizer bag are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (N-P-K). Turnips do well with a balanced blend where the numbers are about even, like a 10-10-10, mixed into the soil before planting along with compost. Do not pile on high-nitrogen fertilizer if you want roots, since it grows leaves instead. If you are after the greens, a bit more nitrogen is okay.
seasoned: Turnips want steady phosphorus and potassium for root development plus modest nitrogen, so a balanced blend such as a 10-10-10 worked into the bed before sowing suits a root crop, with most of the feeding coming from incorporated compost. Hold back on nitrogen for roots, since it pushes leafy tops over the root; a greens crop can take more. Skip fresh manure, which over-supplies nitrogen and branches the roots.

beginner: Turnips are easygoing neighbors. They share a bed nicely with leafy greens like lettuce, with onions and other alliums, which grow upright and shallow and do not crowd the roots, and they do well following beans or peas that added nitrogen to the soil. The main plants to keep away from turnips are their own cabbage-family relatives: cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, and mustard. These cousins share the turnip's pests, the flea beetle and the cabbage maggot, plus the soil disease clubroot, so growing them together lets those problems build up. As always, do not trust every companion chart online, since many of their claims have never been tested.
seasoned: Turnips fit easily into mixed beds, and their clearest companion rule is the brassica avoid: keep them away from the other cabbage-family crops (cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard), which share the turnip's flea beetles, cabbage maggot, and the soilborne clubroot pathogen, so clustering the family concentrates that pressure. On the positive side, leafy greens like lettuce and shallow-rooted alliums share the surface layer while the turnip swells just below, and a legume grown the season before leaves nitrogen behind. Treat the good pairings as sensible defaults rather than proven effects: as University of Minnesota's research review stresses, most companion-planting claims are tradition rather than tested science, so use them as a starting point and watch your own results.

beginner: Lettuce and other quick, shallow-rooted greens grow near the surface and finish fast, while the turnip root swells just below them, so they share a bed without fighting for the same space. Both like the same cool weather, a handy way to fit more into a small garden.
seasoned: Lettuce and turnips interplant well on root structure and timing: lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick, the turnip swells just under the surface and takes a little longer, so they draw on different layers and share the cool-season window. This is a space-and-soil benefit rather than a pest one, and one of the more dependable interplants for that reason.

beginner: Onions, leeks, and garlic grow tall and narrow with shallow roots, so they tuck between turnip rows without crowding the roots, and their strong smell is widely used to help confuse some leaf-eating pests. A popular, space-saving pairing.
seasoned: Alliums are a classic interplant for root crops: shallow-rooted and upright, they share the bed without competing for the turnip's space, and their sulfur volatiles are widely credited with masking the crop from some leaf-feeding pests. The space-use benefit is solid; the pest deterrence is plausible but not proven for turnips specifically.

beginner: Beans and peas pull nitrogen from the air and leave some in the soil, so turnips planted after a legume crop get a gentle nutrient boost. They are better as the crop you grow before turnips than right alongside, since bushy legumes can shade the low turnips.
seasoned: Legumes earn their place in the turnip rotation more than the turnip bed: beans and peas fix nitrogen and leave residual fertility, so a turnip crop following a legume benefits, which is why extension rotation guides list legumes among good preceding crops for brassicas. Grown concurrently the value is mostly space-sharing, and tall climbing legumes shade the low turnip, so the cleaner use is in sequence.

beginner: Cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard, and other cabbage-family plants are turnip's close relatives and share its pests, the flea beetle and the cabbage maggot, plus the soil disease clubroot. Growing them right next to turnips lets those problems build up, so give them separate spots and rotate where each goes each year.
seasoned: Turnips are brassicas, so the other cabbage-family crops, cabbage, broccoli, kale, radish, mustard, share their exact pest and disease spectrum: flea beetles, the cabbage maggot, and the soilborne clubroot pathogen. Clustering the family in one bed sustains and concentrates that pressure, the same reason extension sources advise rotating among brassicas rather than planting them together year after year.

beginner: Lots of tiny round holes peppering the leaves, like buckshot, worst on young seedlings in spring. The beetles are very small, dark, and shiny, with big back legs, and they hop away like fleas the moment you get close. If you are growing turnips for the greens this really matters, since the chewed leaves are what you eat; for the root, fast-growing plants usually shrug it off, but tiny seedlings can be set back.
seasoned: Tiny, round shot-hole punctures riddling the leaves, the classic flea-beetle signature, heaviest on young spring seedlings and along bed edges. The beetles themselves are minute, shiny black or bronze, with enlarged hind legs, and they spring away like fleas when disturbed. On a turnip grown for greens the damage is more than cosmetic, since riddled leaves are the harvest; on a root crop a vigorous stand outgrows light feeding, but a seedling losing much of its leaf area slows down.

beginner: Small beetles that spend the winter in leaf litter and weeds and come out in early spring hungry for cabbage-family leaves. Turnips and their relatives (radish, mustard) are among their favorite foods. They do the most damage in spring and early summer and ease off as it gets hotter, so fall turnips usually face fewer of them.
seasoned: Adult flea beetles, chiefly the crucifer flea beetle (Phyllotreta cruciferae) and striped flea beetle (Phyllotreta striolata), which overwinter in leaf litter and field edges and emerge in early spring to feed on brassica foliage. Turnip, radish, mustard, and other crucifers are highly preferred hosts. Pressure is heaviest in spring and early summer and tapers as the season warms, which is one reason fall turnip crops face less of it.

beginner: A healthy, well-watered turnip patch usually grows right through light damage. If the little seedlings are getting hammered, cover the row with a floating row cover (a light fabric) right after planting and tuck in the edges so the beetles cannot get under it. Dusting with kaolin clay helps, and sprays like spinosad or pyrethrin are options if seedlings are losing a lot of leaf. Check in the cool morning, when the beetles are slow.
seasoned: On a vigorous stand a well-watered turnip usually outgrows light feeding. Where pressure is heavy on seedlings, a floating row cover set at sowing and sealed at the edges excludes the beetles entirely, the most reliable home defense. Kaolin clay reduces feeding, and spinosad or pyrethrin products are labeled options if a seedling stand is losing more than roughly a quarter to a third of its leaf area; scout in the cool morning when the beetles are sluggish.

beginner: Clear away old plants and weeds at the end of the season so fewer beetles survive the winter nearby. Covering the seedbed with a row cover is the surest fix for early spring turnips. Leaning on fall plantings, which get hit less, and keeping the turnips growing fast with steady water also help.
seasoned: Clean up crop debris and weeds at the end of the season to cut overwintering sites. A row cover over the seedbed is the most reliable defense for early spring sowings. Favoring fall plantings, which see lighter pressure, and keeping the stand growing fast with even moisture both reduce impact.

beginner: The trouble is underground. Small white legless maggots tunnel into the turnip, leaving winding brown trails that spoil the root and let rot set in. Aboveground the plant may look pale, wilted, or stunted. It shows up most in cool, wet springs and in soil full of un-rotted material. A tunneled turnip is ruined, but pulling and tossing it right away gets the maggots out before they become the next generation of flies.
seasoned: The damage is underground: small, white, legless maggots tunnel and score the surface and interior of the root, leaving winding brown trails that ruin the turnip and open the door to rot. Aboveground, infested plants may look off-color, wilted, or stunted. It is most common in cool, wet springs and in soil rich in undecomposed organic matter. A scored root is unsalable but a useful sentinel, since pulling and destroying it removes maggots before they pupate.

beginner: The maggots (young) of the cabbage maggot fly, a small gray fly. It spends the winter as pupae in the soil, and in spring the females lay tiny white eggs at the base of cabbage-family plants. The eggs hatch in about a week and the maggots burrow into the roots for three to four weeks. It goes after the whole cabbage family, turnips, radishes, cabbage, broccoli, and is worst in cool, damp spring weather.
seasoned: Larvae of the cabbage maggot (Delia radicum), a small gray fly that overwinters as pupae in the soil. In spring the adults emerge and females lay white eggs at the base of crucifer stems and in nearby soil cracks; the eggs hatch within about a week and the maggots feed on roots for three to four weeks before pupating. It attacks the whole cabbage family, including turnip, radish, cabbage, and broccoli, with several generations a year and the worst damage in cool, moist spring weather.

beginner: You cannot save a turnip that is already tunneled. Pull up and throw away (do not compost) the affected ones so the maggots cannot grow into more flies. There is no good home spray for this, and sprays do nothing once the maggots have already left the root, so prevention is the real fix.
seasoned: There is no rescue for a root already tunneled. Pull and destroy infested turnips (do not compost them) to keep maggots from completing their cycle. Insecticide drenches are difficult and rarely worthwhile in a home garden, and are pointless once the maggots have left the root to pupate, so the lever is prevention.

beginner: The best home defense is a row cover laid over the bed right after sowing and tucked in at the edges, so the flies cannot reach the plants to lay eggs, just make sure the soil is not already carrying them from an earlier crop. Move turnips away from spots that grew cabbage-family crops recently, avoid fresh manure, and lean toward fall planting, which usually has fewer maggots than cool wet spring.
seasoned: A floating row cover sealed at the edges at sowing is the most effective home defense, since it blocks the egg-laying flies; be sure no flies are already in the soil from a previous crop. Rotate turnips and other crucifers away from beds that grew them recently, avoid fresh manure and freshly turned-under residue that attract the flies, and favor fall plantings, which see less pressure than cool wet spring.

beginner: Little soft insects, often gray-green and sometimes dusty-looking, gather in clusters on the undersides of leaves and on new growth. Leaves curl and yellow and turn sticky from the sugary honeydew the aphids leave behind, which can grow a black sooty mold. On turnips these are usually the turnip aphid and cabbage aphid. They can also spread plant viruses, so knock them back early, especially if you are eating the greens.
seasoned: Clusters of small, soft-bodied insects, often grayish-green and sometimes coated with a waxy bloom, collect on the undersides of leaves and on new growth, leaving leaves curled, yellowed, and sticky with honeydew that can blacken with sooty mold. On turnips the culprits are typically the turnip aphid (Lipaphis erysimi) and the cabbage aphid (Brevicoryne brassicae). Beyond direct feeding they can transmit virus, so colonies on the greens are worth removing early.

beginner: Sap-sucking turnip and cabbage aphids that feed only on cabbage-family plants. They multiply fast in mild weather, especially on soft, over-fertilized growth, and fly in from weeds and other cabbage-family crops. They can be a real pest on fall turnip greens.
seasoned: The turnip aphid and cabbage aphid, sap-feeding insects specific to the cabbage family. Populations build fastest in mild weather and on lush, over-fertilized growth, and winged forms move them in from cruciferous weeds and other brassica crops. They can be a particular nuisance on fall greens crops.

beginner: Spray the colonies off with a strong stream of water, which often does the trick. Ladybugs and other helpers usually take care of the rest; if not, insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on the undersides of the leaves works well. Do not over-feed with nitrogen, which just grows more aphids.
seasoned: A strong jet of water knocks colonies off the leaves and is often enough in a home garden. Natural enemies (ladybugs, lacewings, parasitic wasps) usually bring numbers down; where needed, insecticidal soap or horticultural oil sprayed on the undersides of leaves is effective, taking care to reach the protected cabbage-aphid colonies. Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen, which fuels buildup.

beginner: Let helpful bugs like ladybugs live in your garden by not spraying broadly, go easy on nitrogen fertilizer, and pull cabbage-family weeds nearby. Check the undersides of leaves now and then so you catch aphids while there are only a few, and clean up old plants at the end of the season.
seasoned: Encourage beneficial insects by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays, keep plants from being pushed with excess nitrogen, and control nearby cruciferous weeds that host the aphids. Inspect new growth and the undersides of leaves so colonies are caught small, and clear crop debris at season end.

beginner: Showy black-and-orange (or black-and-red) shield-shaped bugs on the leaves, leaving pale, blotchy, stippled spots where they have sucked the juices out. A lot of them can yellow and kill leaves and even kill small plants. It is mainly a warm-weather pest, worst on fall and winter turnips and greens in the South.
seasoned: Striking black-and-orange (or black-and-red) shield-shaped stink bugs feeding on the foliage, leaving pale, blotchy, stippled or wilted patches where they have sucked sap; heavy feeding can yellow and kill leaves and stunt or kill young plants. It is chiefly a warm-region pest, most damaging on fall and overwintering brassicas in the South, and it readily attacks turnip and its greens.

beginner: The harlequin bug, a stink bug that feeds almost only on cabbage-family plants. The adults spend winter in garden trash in warm areas and get active as it warms up, with several generations a year. Look for its odd barrel-shaped, striped eggs lined up in two neat rows under the leaves.
seasoned: The harlequin bug (Murgantia histrionica), a stink bug that feeds almost exclusively on cabbage-family plants. Adults overwinter in garden debris in warmer regions and become active as the weather warms, with several generations a year; the barrel-shaped, black-and-white striped eggs are laid in neat double rows on the undersides of leaves.

beginner: Pick off the adults, the young, and the striped egg rows by hand and drop them in soapy water, which works well if you start early. Pull and destroy badly infested plants and clean up cabbage-family debris. Insecticidal soap helps on the young bugs, and a patch of mustard planted as bait can draw them together so they are easy to remove.
seasoned: Handpick adults, nymphs, and the distinctive egg rows into soapy water, which is effective in a home garden caught early. Remove and destroy heavily infested plants and brassica debris that harbor them. Insecticidal soap helps on nymphs; a trap crop of mustard or another preferred crucifer can concentrate the bugs for removal.

beginner: Clean up old cabbage-family plants and weeds at the end of the season, which is the biggest help since that is where the bugs spend winter. Rotate where you plant brassicas, check under the leaves for the striped eggs, and plant a little mustard as bait if the bug keeps coming back.
seasoned: Clear cabbage-family crop debris and weeds at season end to remove overwintering sites, the single most useful step. Rotate brassicas, scout the undersides of leaves for the egg rows, and use a trap crop where the bug is a recurring problem.

beginner: Aboveground the plant looks stunted and yellow and wilts in the afternoon sun, then perks up at night. Underground is the giveaway: instead of a clean turnip, the roots swell into lumpy, club-shaped galls that eventually rot. It lives in the soil and builds up when you grow cabbage-family crops in the same spot over and over, especially in wet, acidic soil.
seasoned: Aboveground, plants are stunted and yellowish and wilt in the heat of the day even in moist soil, recovering overnight. The diagnostic sign is below ground: the roots are swollen, distorted, and clubbed into gnarled, spindle-shaped galls rather than forming a clean turnip, and they later rot. It is a soilborne disease that builds up where crucifers are grown repeatedly and is favored by wet, poorly drained, acidic soil.

beginner: A soil organism (Plasmodiophora brassicae) that attacks the roots of cabbage-family plants and survives in the soil for years. Wet, poorly drained, acidic soil makes it worse, and it spreads on dirty tools and on soil moved from an infected bed.
seasoned: Plasmodiophora brassicae, a soilborne pathogen that infects the roots of cabbage-family plants and persists in soil as resting spores for many years. Wet, poorly drained, acidic soils favor infection, and the disease spreads on contaminated soil, tools, and transplants.

beginner: There is no way to cure a plant that has it, so pull and throw away (do not compost) the affected ones. The fix is for next time: improve drainage, add lime to raise the soil pH toward 7.2 to 7.5, which holds the disease back, and keep cabbage-family crops out of that spot for a few years.
seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected; remove and destroy affected plants and do not compost them. Management is preventive across seasons: improve drainage and lime the soil toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.2 to 7.5, which suppresses the pathogen, and rotate crucifers out of the bed for several years.

beginner: Do not grow turnips or other cabbage-family crops in the same bed year after year; move them on a multi-year cycle. Keep the soil well drained and add lime to raise the pH toward neutral, and avoid carrying soil from an infected bed on your tools. A raised bed with clean soil avoids it where it is a known problem.
seasoned: Rotate turnips and other crucifers on a multi-year cycle (a long rotation of several years is advised where it is established), since the pathogen builds in soil grown to the family. Keep soil well drained and limed toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH, start with clean soil and tools, and avoid moving soil from an infested bed. Raised beds with clean mix sidestep the problem where it is entrenched.

beginner: Raised white or cream blister-like spots on the undersides of the leaves, with a faint yellow patch on the top of the leaf opposite each blister. A bad case can twist the leaves. It mostly affects the leaves, so it matters most when you are growing turnips for greens, and it likes cool, damp weather.
seasoned: Raised, white to cream, blister-like pustules form on the undersides of leaves, with a faint yellow spot on the upper surface opposite each lesion. Heavy infection can distort leaves and, less commonly, the growing point. It is chiefly a foliar disease, most damaging on turnips grown for greens, and is favored by cool, moist weather.

beginner: A fungus-like water mold (Albugo candida) that lives on cabbage-family plants, survives on old plant debris, and spreads in cool, wet weather by spores carried on wind and splashing water. There is no home spray for it, so the fix is in how you grow the crop.
seasoned: Albugo candida, a water mold (formerly classed as a fungus) specific to crucifers that survives as thick-walled resting spores on crop debris and in soil and spreads by airborne and splash-borne spores in cool, wet conditions. No fungicides are registered for it in the home garden, so control is cultural.

beginner: There is no spray for the home garden, so pick off and throw away infected leaves and the worst plants, and help the plants dry out by giving them room. Water at the soil instead of overhead, and clear away cabbage-family weeds and old debris that carry it.
seasoned: There is no home chemical control; remove and destroy infected leaves and badly affected plants to reduce spread, and improve airflow and drying. Cultural control carries the load: water at the base, space for airflow, and clear cruciferous weeds and debris that carry it.

beginner: Do not grow cabbage-family crops in the same spot repeatedly, clear away old plant debris and weeds, and water at the base instead of overhead. Give plants room so the leaves dry fast, and choose a tolerant variety if it keeps coming back.
seasoned: Rotate crucifers, clear and destroy crop debris and cruciferous weeds that harbor the spores, and avoid overhead watering. Space and thin for airflow so foliage dries quickly, and use tolerant varieties where the disease recurs.

beginner: Pale green to yellow angular patches on top of the leaves, with a grayish or white fuzzy growth underneath in damp weather; the spots later turn tan and papery. It mainly hurts the leaves and is worst in cool, wet weather, like a rainy fall, which is also when turnip greens are growing.
seasoned: Small, angular, pale green to yellow lesions on the upper leaf surface, bounded by the veins, with a grayish to white downy growth of spores on the corresponding undersides in damp weather. Affected areas later turn tan and papery. It chiefly disfigures the foliage and is most damaging in cool, moist conditions such as a wet fall.

beginner: A fungus-like water mold (Peronospora parasitica) that infects cabbage-family plants in cool, wet weather, best around 50 to 60°F. It survives on old plant debris and spreads in damp air and splashing water.
seasoned: Peronospora parasitica (also called Hyaloperonospora parasitica), a water mold that infects crucifers in cool, moist conditions, with infection favored around 50 to 60°F. It survives on crop debris and related hosts and spreads in moist air and splashing water.

beginner: You cannot cure infected leaves, so pick off and throw away the worst ones and help the plants dry out by giving them room. Keeping the leaves dry does most of the work; a copper fungicide is a last resort in a very wet stretch.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue; remove and destroy affected leaves to reduce spread, and improve airflow and drying. Cultural control is the mainstay for a home crop, with copper fungicides a last resort in a persistently wet season.

beginner: Water at the soil instead of overhead, give plants room so air moves through, and stay out of the bed when the leaves are wet. Move turnips away from where you grew cabbage-family crops, clean up old debris, and pick a tolerant variety if it keeps showing up.
seasoned: Water at the base rather than overhead, space and thin for airflow, and avoid working among wet plants. Rotate away from crucifers, clear crop debris, and where it recurs choose tolerant varieties.

beginner: Small, round, dark spots on the leaves, each with a yellow ring around it and faint target-like circles inside, that grow and run together in wet weather and turn sooty in the center. It mostly affects the leaves, so it matters most for turnip greens, and a bad case can slow the plant down.
seasoned: Small, circular, dark spots on the leaves, each with a yellow halo and characteristic concentric rings, that darken to a sooty center as spores build up and enlarge and merge in wet weather. It is primarily a foliar disease, most important on turnips grown for greens, and severe infection can reduce vigor and quality.

beginner: Alternaria fungi that can travel on seed and survive on old plant debris, spreading in splashing water and needing wet leaves to take hold. Warm, humid weather with wet foliage brings it on.
seasoned: Alternaria fungi (chiefly Alternaria brassicae), which are seedborne and survive on crop debris, spreading in splashing water and needing leaf wetness to infect. Warm, wet weather and prolonged wet foliage drive it.

beginner: Pick off the worst leaves, water at the soil in the morning so leaves dry quickly, and clean up debris. Using clean seed and giving plants room for airflow handle most of it; a copper fungicide can help in a very wet spell if you start early.
seasoned: Remove badly spotted leaves, water at the base in the morning so foliage dries, and clear debris. Clean seed and airflow are the main home levers; a copper fungicide can help in a persistently wet season if started early.

beginner: Use clean seed, water at the base instead of overhead, give plants room so the leaves dry, and clear away old plant material between plantings.
seasoned: Use clean seed, avoid overhead watering, space for airflow, and rotate crucifers and clear debris that carry the fungi between seasons.

beginner: Yellow, V-shaped patches creeping in from the edges of the leaves, with the point of the V aimed at the center vein, and the veins in those patches turning black. The leaves yellow and die, and a bad case can rot the plant. It is a bacterial disease that hits the whole cabbage family in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: Yellow, V-shaped lesions advancing inward from the leaf margins, with the V pointing toward the midrib and the veins in the affected area turning black. Infected leaves yellow and die, and severe infection can rot the plant and move into the root. It is a bacterial disease of the whole cabbage family, spread in warm, wet conditions.

beginner: A bacterium (Xanthomonas campestris) that can travel on seed and splashing water and gets into the leaves through their edges and any wounds. Warm, humid, wet weather brings it on, and it spreads on infected seed, water, tools, and old plant debris among cabbage-family plants.
seasoned: Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris, a seedborne and splash-spread bacterium that enters through leaf margins (water pores) and wounds. It is favored by warm, humid, wet conditions and spreads on contaminated seed, water, tools, and crop debris across cabbage-family crops.

beginner: You cannot cure leaves that are already infected. Pull and throw away affected plants, stay out of the bed when the leaves are wet, and clean up old plant material. Clean seed and rotating where you plant cabbage-family crops handle most of it.
seasoned: There is no cure for infected tissue. Remove and destroy affected plants, avoid working among plants when the foliage is wet, and clear crop debris. Starting with clean seed and rotating crucifers do most of the work in a home garden.

beginner: Use clean, disease-free seed, do not grow cabbage-family crops in the same spot repeatedly, and clear away old plant debris. Water at the soil instead of overhead, do not handle wet plants, and give them room so the leaves dry fast.
seasoned: Start with clean, disease-free seed, rotate crucifers out of the bed for at least a year or more, and clear debris that harbors the bacterium. Water at the base rather than overhead, avoid handling wet plants, and space for airflow so foliage dries quickly.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp, and pay closest attention while the seeds are sprouting and later while the roots are bulking up. From planting until the sprouts appear (about 7 to 10 days), keep the surface moist so it does not dry into a hard crust. After that, give about 1 inch of water a week, counting rain, in fewer but deeper waterings, and a bit more in hot or sandy conditions.
seasoned: Even, consistent moisture is the rule, and it matters most during germination and again as the roots size up. Turnip seed and seedlings need a moist, uncrusted surface for the roughly 7 to 10 days to emergence. Once established, turnips want steady moisture rather than a wet-dry swing: aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, up to 1 to 2 inches in heat or sandy soil, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings.

beginner: About 1 inch of water a week, including rain, once the plants are growing, up to about 2 inches in hot, dry weather or sandy soil. While the seeds are sprouting, just keep the top of the soil damp, not soggy.
seasoned: Roughly 1 inch per week including rainfall once established, rising toward 1 to 2 inches in heat or on sandy soil and easing in cool or clay soil. During germination the seedbed needs only enough to stay evenly moist near the surface, not soaked.

beginner: Water gently at soil level, using a soft spray, soaker hose, or drip line. A hard blast from the hose can wash out the shallow seeds or pack the soil into a crust the sprouts cannot push through, so keep it gentle. Watering at the soil also keeps the leaves dry, which helps prevent the leaf diseases turnips get in wet weather.
seasoned: Water at the base with a gentle setting, soaker hose, or drip line to keep the surface evenly moist without crusting the bed or washing out the shallow-sown seed. Base watering also keeps the foliage dry, which limits the leaf diseases (downy mildew, white rust, leaf spot) turnips are prone to in wet weather.

beginner: If the soil stays soaking wet, turnips can rot, seedlings can damp off, and the clubroot disease gets worse. Watch for yellow leaves, soft roots, and a constantly wet, sour-smelling bed. If you see these, water less and make sure the soil drains well.
seasoned: Constantly saturated soil invites damping-off, root rots, and clubroot and can yellow the tops; soft roots and a sour, waterlogged bed are signs to back off. Poor drainage is the usual cause, which is why loose, well-draining soil matters for this crop.

beginner: Dry, cracked soil on top, droopy or dull leaves, and slow growth mean the turnips need more water. Letting them go dry is the main thing that makes the roots bitter, woody, and pithy, and swinging from bone dry to soaked can crack them. Keep the watering steady.
seasoned: Dry, cracked surface soil, dull or wilting tops, and slow growth signal too little water. Drought is the classic cause of poor turnip quality: it drives bitter, woody, strong-flavored, and pithy roots, and an irregular dry-then-wet cycle can crack them.

beginner: Turnip seeds come up in about 7 to 10 days. Keep the top of the soil damp and uncrusted until then, watering gently at the base.
seasoned: Turnip emerges in roughly 7 to 10 days, and the shallow-sown seed needs a moist, uncrusted surface the whole time or the stand fails. Water at the base with a gentle setting to avoid crusting.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp and try to water the ground, not the leaves. Dry leaves get fewer diseases.
seasoned: Settle into even moisture and water at the base. Keeping the leaves dry limits the downy mildew, white rust, and leaf spot turnips are prone to in wet weather.

seasoned: Hold even moisture and harvest young; turnips left oversized and drought-stressed turn woody and strong flavored.

beginner: You do not need to harden off turnips. They are sown straight into the garden from seed, not started indoors and transplanted.

Plant turnip seeds right in the garden where they will grow, since turnips do not like being moved. Sow them about 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep once the soil is no longer frozen or soggy (about 40 to 45°F), roughly 2 to 3 weeks before your last spring frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop, which is usually the best crop. seasoned: Direct-sow turnips into the garden; they grow fast from seed in place and, like most root crops, do not transplant well. Seeds germinate best at about 60 to 85°F and emerge in roughly 7 to 10 days. Sow a little thick and plan to thin: the thinnings are edible baby greens. Keep the surface moist and uncrusted until the seedlings emerge.

Make sure it has drainage holes and use loose potting mix. Width helps too, since you want room to thin the turnips to about 3 to 4 inches apart.
seasoned: Turnips suit containers well and need less depth than carrots because the root is round and sits near the surface. Width matters as much as depth, since you want several roots thinned to 3 to 4 inches apart. Provide drainage holes and a loose potting mix.

beginner: There are turnips for different uses. Purple Top White Globe is the dependable classic for both roots and greens, ready in about 50 to 55 days. For sweet, mild turnips you can eat raw, look for fast salad types like Hakurei or Tokyo, ready in about 35 to 40 days. If you mainly want the leafy greens, grow Shogoin or Seven Top (which makes greens but no real root). Golden Ball has sweet yellow flesh and Scarlet Queen has red skin. Plant salad and greens kinds a bit thicker and pick them young; let regular turnips grow to about 2 to 3 inches across.
seasoned: Turnip variety choice splits by purpose and speed. Purple Top White Globe is the dependable all-rounder for roots and greens, maturing in about 50 to 55 days; for a sweet, mild root eaten raw, the fast white salad types (Hakurei, Tokyo Cross) are ready in roughly 35 to 40 days. Greens growers choose leafy types such as Shogoin or the rootless Seven Top, which put their energy into abundant tops. For color and flavor, Golden Ball offers sweet yellow flesh and Scarlet Queen a red skin. Sow salad and greens types thicker and harvest young; let main-crop and storage types size to about 2 to 3 inches. Full-size storage roots can take 60 to 80 days.

beginner: Do not grow turnips where you grew turnips, radish, cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, collards, or mustard in recent years. These are all in the same cabbage family and share the same soil pests (cabbage maggot, flea beetle) and a root disease called clubroot, which build up over time. Minnesota suggests waiting four years before any of them go back in the same bed, and longer where clubroot is a known problem. Also avoid beds that got a lot of manure for the last crop, since the extra nitrogen grows leafy tops and makes the roots branch.
seasoned: Do not plant turnips where another cabbage-family crop (Brassicaceae) grew the previous seasons, including turnip, rutabaga, radish, cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, collards, Brussels sprouts, kohlrabi, and mustard, since they share soilborne clubroot and root pests (cabbage maggot, flea beetle) that build up where the family is grown repeatedly. University of Minnesota advises against following any of these crops for the past four years, and longer rotations are recommended where clubroot is established. Avoid beds heavily manured for the previous crop, because the readily available nitrogen drives leafy top growth and branches the roots.

beginner: Move your turnips to a different spot each year, and do not put them, or their relatives like cabbage, broccoli, radish, and kale, back in the same bed for several years (Minnesota says about four). This keeps the cabbage maggot, flea beetle, and clubroot disease from piling up. Turnips do well following beans or peas, which add nitrogen, but not right after a bed that got heavy manure, since leftover nitrogen grows leaves instead of roots.
seasoned: Rotate turnips on a multi-year cycle, keeping them and all other cabbage-family crops out of a bed for several seasons after they are grown there; Minnesota recommends a four-year gap, and a longer one where clubroot is present. This breaks the buildup of the soilborne clubroot pathogen and the root pests the family shares. Following a legume that has added nitrogen, or another nitrogen-depleting crop, suits turnips well; avoid following a heavily manured crop, whose residual nitrogen pushes tops over roots and branches them.

beginner: Not good for more than a few days. Left out, turnip roots go soft and the leaves wilt fast. Cut the tops off, keep out only what you will eat soon, and refrigerate the rest.
seasoned: Poor for more than a few days. At room temperature turnip roots lose moisture and soften quickly, and the greens wilt within a day; cut the tops from the roots and refrigerate both. Counter storage is only for what you will use within a couple of days.

beginner: This is the best way for everyday storage. First cut off the leafy tops, because the leaves draw water out of the root. Keep the greens in a separate bag and eat them within a few days. Put the unwashed roots in a loosely closed or vented plastic bag in the crisper drawer, where they stay firm for one to several weeks. Little salad turnips do not keep as long as bigger main-crop ones.
seasoned: The best everyday option. Cut off the green tops first, since the leaves pull moisture from the root; store the greens separately in a bag and use them within a few days. Keep the unwashed roots in a perforated or loosely closed plastic bag in the crisper drawer, where high humidity and cold hold them for one to several weeks. Small salad turnips are most perishable; main-crop roots keep best.

beginner: You can freeze turnips, but cook them first. Peel, dice, and boil or steam them until just tender, cool, and freeze, or freeze them mashed. The greens freeze like spinach after a quick dip in boiling water. They keep well for about 8 to 12 months.
seasoned: Workable after cooking. Turnip roots are best frozen cooked rather than raw: peel, dice, boil or steam until just tender, cool, and freeze, or freeze as a mash. The greens freeze like spinach after a brief blanch. Quality holds for roughly 8 to 12 months.

beginner: If you grow a lot, regular turnips store for a while. In cold areas you can cover the row with thick straw and dig them until the ground freezes solid, or pack unwashed roots in damp sand in a box kept somewhere cold like an unheated garage, around 32 to 40°F, where they last two to four months. Store just the roots; eat the leafy greens fresh.
seasoned: For larger harvests, main-crop turnips are fair keepers. In cold climates they can be left in the ground under a thick straw mulch and pulled until the soil freezes hard, or packed unwashed in damp sand in a box in a root cellar or unheated garage held near 32 to 40°F at high humidity, where they hold for two to four months. beginner: Turnips are planted a bit thick, so you need to thin them, or the crowded roots stay small and lumpy. Thin them to about 2 to 4 inches apart once they are 2 to 4 inches tall, closer together if you just want greens or small salad turnips, snipping the extra ones off at the soil line with scissors instead of pulling. Thin to a final 2 to 4 inches apart once seedlings reach 2 to 4 inches tall, closer for salad turnips and greens and wider (3 to 4 inches) for full-size roots, snipping the extras at the soil line rather than pulling so you do not disturb the ones you keep. Do not waste the thinnings: the young leaves are tender baby turnip greens, so thinning is also a first small harvest.

beginner: Do not forget the leaves: pick a few young outer ones as you go and cook the rest like spinach or collards. There is no rush to dig mature turnips in cool weather, since they get sweeter after a light frost and keep in the ground under a layer of straw.
seasoned: Do not forget the greens: pick a few young outer leaves through the season and cook the rest like spinach or collards at harvest. Mature roots are in no rush in cool weather, since flavor sweetens after light frost and roots hold in the ground under a straw mulch.

beginner: Each plant gives you one turnip root, plus leaves you can eat as it grows. It helps to think by row length: a 10-foot row gives roughly 5 to 10 pounds of turnips depending on size, plus greens picked as outer leaves and thinnings.
seasoned: One root per plant, plus a flush of edible leaves along the way. Yield is best thought of by row length: at a 2 to 4 inch final spacing, a 10-foot row yields roughly 5 to 10 pounds of roots depending on size at harvest, alongside greens taken as outer leaves and thinnings. A greens-only crop yields more leaf per foot of row.

beginner: Turnips do not regrow a new root after you pull them, since each plant makes one root. A planting is ready about 50 to 60 days after sowing and you harvest it over a couple of weeks, while the leaves give a longer, light harvest. For a steady supply, plant a new short row every 3 to 4 weeks.
seasoned: There is no repeat root harvest; a sowing matures over a short window roughly 50 to 60 days after planting and is pulled over a couple of weeks. The greens give a longer, light pick-as-you-go harvest. Continuous supply comes from succession sowing every 3 to 4 weeks through the cool-season window.

beginner: Turnips are grown fresh from seed each year, so your very first planting can do just as well as any later one. The main things that decide your results are loose soil, thinning the seedlings, and keeping the bed evenly damp.
seasoned: Turnips are an annual grown fresh from seed every season, so there is no first-year-versus-later distinction as with perennials; the first sowing performs as well as any, provided the soil is loose, the stand is thinned, and moisture stays even.

beginner: Turnips flower instead of making roots
seasoned: Plants bolt (run to seed)

beginner: The turnip sent up a tall flower stalk instead of growing a good root. This usually happens with heat and long days, or when young plants get a cold snap followed by the long days of late spring. Once it flowers, the root stays small and tough.
seasoned: The plant sent up a flower stalk instead of sizing a root. Turnip bolting is driven by heat and lengthening days, and by a cold spell on young plants (vernalization) followed by long spring days. Once it bolts, the root stays small, woody, and strong, so spring crops sown too late or carried into early summer heat are most at risk.

beginner: Plant the spring crop early enough to finish before the summer heat and long days, and rely on the fall crop, which avoids the long days that cause flowering. Do not plant too late in spring, keep the watering steady, and pick bolt-resistant varieties for spring.
seasoned: Sow the spring crop early enough to mature before summer heat and long days, and lean on the fall crop, which dodges the long-day trigger. Avoid sowing too late in spring, keep moisture even, and choose bolt-resistant varieties for spring sowings.

beginner: Tough, spongy, strong turnips
seasoned: Woody, pithy, strong-flavored roots

beginner: The turnips came out tough, spongy in the middle, and strong-tasting. This usually comes from growing in heat above about 75°F, leaving them in the ground too long, or letting them get too dry.
seasoned: Roots grew coarse, fibrous, spongy in the center (pithy), and sharp-tasting. The usual causes are maturing in sustained heat above about 75°F, over-maturity from being left in the ground too long, or drought and uneven moisture. Pithiness and strong flavor are the classic signs of turnips grown or held through hot, dry weather.

beginner: Plan the crop so the turnips finish in cool weather: rely on the fall planting and sow spring crops early. Harvest them at 2 to 3 inches instead of letting them get big, and keep the watering steady. Turnips that finish after a frost are the sweetest.
seasoned: Time the crop so roots mature in cool weather, leaning on the fall crop and sowing spring crops early; harvest at 2 to 3 inches rather than letting roots oversize, and keep moisture even. Frost-finished turnips are the sweetest and mildest.

beginner: Lumpy, club-shaped roots
seasoned: Swollen, clubbed, distorted roots

beginner: Instead of clean turnips, the roots came out swollen, lumpy, and club-shaped, and the plants looked stunted and yellow and wilted in the afternoon. This is clubroot, a soil disease of the cabbage family that gets worse in wet, acidic soil and in beds where you grow cabbage-family crops over and over.
seasoned: Instead of clean turnips, the roots are swollen, distorted, and clubbed, with the plants stunted and yellow and wilting by day. This is clubroot, a soilborne disease of the cabbage family favored by wet, poorly drained, acidic soil that builds up where crucifers are grown repeatedly.

beginner: Keep cabbage-family crops out of that bed for a few years, improve drainage, and add lime to raise the pH toward 7.2 to 7.5, which holds the disease back. Pull and throw away affected plants (do not compost), and do not carry soil from that bed on your tools.
seasoned: Rotate crucifers out of the bed for several years, improve drainage, and lime toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.2 to 7.5, which suppresses the pathogen. Remove and destroy affected plants (do not compost), and avoid moving soil from the infested bed on tools.

beginner: Forked or hairy turnips
seasoned: Forked, hairy, or misshapen roots

beginner: The turnips came out forked, twisted, hairy, or lumpy because they hit something hard as they grew, like a rock or packed soil, because they were too crowded, or because of fresh manure or too much nitrogen, which makes roots branch and grow hairy.
seasoned: Roots grew forked, twisted, hairy, or lumpy because they met an obstruction, a stone, clod, or compacted layer, because the stand was left unthinned and crowded, or because of fresh manure or excess nitrogen, which causes branching and hairy roots.

beginner: Loosen the bed and pull out rocks before planting, thin the turnips to 2 to 4 inches so they are not crowded, and skip fresh manure and heavy nitrogen feeding. On rocky or heavy soil, use a raised bed or a deep, loose container.
seasoned: Work the bed loose and remove stones before sowing, thin to 2 to 4 inches so roots are not crowded, and avoid fresh manure and heavy nitrogen. On heavy or rocky ground, use a raised bed or a deep, loose container.

beginner: Leaves full of tiny holes
seasoned: Leaves riddled with shot-holes

beginner: The leaves are covered in tiny round holes, worst on young spring plants. This is flea beetle damage. If you are growing turnips for greens it spoils the leaves; for the root it mostly just slows down the young plants.
seasoned: The leaves are peppered with tiny round shot-holes, heaviest on young spring seedlings, the work of flea beetles. On a turnip grown for greens this ruins the harvest; on a root crop it mostly slows seedlings, but a heavily fed-on stand sizes up poorly.

beginner: Cover the seedbed with a row cover when you plant to keep the beetles off, clean up old plant debris where they spend winter, and lean on fall crops, which get hit less. Keep seedlings growing fast with steady water so they outgrow light damage.
seasoned: Cover the seedbed with a floating row cover at sowing to exclude the beetles, clean up debris where they overwinter, and favor fall crops, which face less pressure. Keep seedlings growing fast with even moisture so they outgrow light feeding.

beginner: Seeds did not come up well
seasoned: Poor or patchy germination

beginner: Few seedlings came up, or they came up patchy. Turnip seed usually sprouts fast, so most failures come from the soil surface drying out or crusting while sprouting, old seed, planting too deep, or cold soggy soil.
seasoned: Few or uneven seedlings emerged. Turnip seed normally germinates fast, so most failures trace to a seedbed that dried or crusted during the roughly week-long germination, old seed, sowing too deep, or cold wet soil that slows emergence and invites damping-off.

beginner: Keep the soil surface damp from sowing until the seedlings appear, plant shallow (about 1/4 to 1/2 inch) with fresh seed, and wait until the soil warms to at least 40 to 45°F before planting.
seasoned: Keep the surface evenly moist from sowing to emergence, sow shallowly (about 1/4 to 1/2 inch) with fresh seed, and wait for the soil to warm to at least 40 to 45°F before sowing.

beginner: Instead of planting all your turnips at once, sow a short row every 3 to 4 weeks. That way they are ready a few at a time over several weeks. In places with cool summers, start in spring and keep going into early summer, then sow again in late summer for the main fall crop. In hot-summer places, grow them in fall, winter, and early spring and skip the summer heat. The fall crop is usually the best one.
seasoned: Turnips succession well: sow a short row every 3 to 4 weeks through the cool-season window rather than one large planting, so roots mature in sequence. In cold-summer climates that means spring through early summer, then a late-summer sowing for the main fall crop; in hot-summer climates it means fall through early spring, skipping the heat. Stop spring sowings before sustained heat, since turnips maturing in hot soil turn woody, pithy, and strong and tend to bolt. The fall crop is the prime one in most regions.

beginner: In the coldest zones, sow turnips in late spring once the soil reaches about 40 to 45°F and harvest summer into fall; a late-July sowing gives the prime fall crop before the ground freezes.
seasoned: In the coldest zones, sow turnips in late spring once the soil reaches about 40 to 45°F and harvest summer into fall; a late-July sowing gives the prime fall crop before the ground freezes.

beginner: In the Rio Grande Valley, grow turnips in the cool season, not summer. Plant Oct 15 through Dec 15 and harvest from Dec 4 into spring; it rarely if ever frosts here, so the challenge is heat, not cold. Turnips go straight into the ground mid-October through mid-December, the same window TAMU gives for beets and carrots, for roots and greens through the cool season. Skip planting turnips from spring through summer: the Valley heat keeps them from growing well here.
seasoned: Turnips in the RGV run on the winter-garden calendar: direct-sow Oct 15 through Dec 15, with harvest running Dec 4 through Feb 23. Direct-sown mid-October through mid-December (TAMU RGV Homeowner Guide); 50 to 70 days to harvest (Bilingual LRGV table). Frost is essentially absent here, so timing is heat-bounded rather than cold-bounded. Windows are authored identically for zones 9 and 10: the TAMU AgriLife sources describe a single Valley-wide planting calendar, not a zone-9/zone-10 split.

beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, direct-sow turnips in late winter through spring, from about mid-February to the end of March, for a late-spring harvest. Once daytime highs push past 90°F, roots left in the ground turn woody and sharp, so pull them promptly. Sow again from about mid-August to mid-September; the fall crop is usually the better one here, finishing in cooler, milder weather.
seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley (Mojave high desert) grows turnips on two direct-sown cycles, per the UNLV/UNR Cooperative Extension Master Gardener planting chart. Spring sowing runs roughly mid-February to the end of March, with harvest beginning about 50 days later. University of Nevada, Reno Extension's home-vegetable guidance (Fact Sheet FS-02-61) notes plants generally stop growing well once daytime highs run past 90°F, and turnip roots held in hot soil turn woody and sharp, so the chart splits into a real spring cycle and a distinct late-summer fall cycle. The fall sowing (about mid-August to mid-September) goes in as the heat breaks and finishes close to the valley's first fall frost, the more reliable of the two windows here. Zone 8's cooler pockets reach frost sooner, tightening the fall finish; zone 10 at Laughlin has the most room to spare.

seasoned: St. George's Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) grows turnips on two direct-sown cycles, per Utah State University Extension's suggested vegetable planting dates for Utah. The spring sowing runs February 15 to March 1, the Group A (Hardy) date for St. George, with roots ready in about 50 days and the crop pulled by late April before the heat builds. beginner: Turnips are a fast cool-weather crop in the cabbage family that you grow for two foods at once: the round root and the leafy greens, which you cook like collards or spinach. You plant the seeds right in the garden, and they are quick: they sprout in about a week to ten days, and most are ready in roughly 40 to 60 days, with fast salad kinds ready in about 35 days and greens sooner. Roots taste best pulled small, about 2 to 3 inches across; in heat above about 75°F they turn woody and strong-tasting, and hot, long days make the plant flower (bolt), so the fall crop is usually the best one. Turnips handle frost and get sweeter in cool weather. Because turnips are a cabbage-family plant, their bugs and diseases are the cabbage-family ones (flea beetle, cabbage maggot, aphids, harlequin bug, plus clubroot and some leaf diseases), so you rotate and group them with cabbage and kale, not with carrots. When you plant depends on your climate: spring and fall where summers are cool, and fall through early spring where summers are hot.
seasoned: Turnip (Brassica rapa) is a fast, cool-season, dual-purpose crop in the cabbage family (Brassicaceae), grown for both its swollen root and its edible leaves, the turnip greens cooked like collards or spinach. It is direct-sown and quick: seed germinates in about 7 to 10 days, and most varieties size a usable root in roughly 40 to 60 days, with fast salad types ready in about 35 days and greens harvestable sooner. Roots are sweetest, mildest, and most tender pulled at about 2 to 3 inches across; sustained heat above about 75°F turns them woody, pithy, and sharp, and long days plus heat push the plant to bolt, so the fall crop is the prime one in most climates. Turnips tolerate frost and sweeten in cool weather. As a brassica, turnip's pests and diseases are the cabbage-family set, flea beetle, cabbage maggot, aphids, and harlequin bug, with clubroot, white rust, downy mildew, Alternaria leaf spot, and black rot, so it is rotated and grouped with the cole crops, not with carrots. The planting season inverts by climate: spring and fall where summers are cool, and fall through early spring where summers are hot.

beginner: Turnips give you two harvests. You can pick the leaves young all along, taking a few outer ones per plant so the root keeps growing, and the seedlings you thin out are your first baby greens. The roots are ready by size, not a set date: brush the soil off a shoulder and pull when the turnip is about 2 to 3 inches across, the sweet, tender stage, usually around 50 to 60 days, sooner for salad kinds. Do not let them get too big or sit through hot weather, which makes them woody and strong. There is no rush in cool weather: they get sweeter after a light frost and hold in the ground. In cold areas, pile straw over the row and dig them into early winter until the ground freezes. Pull by hand, or loosen with a fork in heavy soil, and cut off the tops, keeping the greens to cook and storing the roots separately.
seasoned: Turnips are a dual harvest. The leaves can be picked young throughout, taking a few outer leaves per plant so the root keeps sizing; the thinnings at the seedling stage are the first baby greens, and greens-type varieties are cut and allowed to regrow. The roots are ready by size rather than the calendar: brush soil from a shoulder and pull when it is about 2 to 3 inches across, the sweet, tender, mild stage, which for most main-crop varieties lands near 50 to 60 days and for salad types sooner. Do not let roots oversize or sit in heat, which turns them woody, pithy, and strong. There is no rush in cool weather: flavor sweetens after light frost, and roots hold in the ground. In cold regions a heavy straw mulch lets you dig through early winter until the ground freezes hard. Lift by hand, or loosen with a fork in heavier soil, and cut off the tops, keeping the greens for the kitchen and storing the roots separately.

beginner: Turnips do best in loose, rich, well-drained soil raked smooth before you plant. Loosen the bed about 8 to 10 inches down, a bit less than carrots need since turnip roots sit near the surface, and pull out rocks and hard clumps that make roots fork. Rake the top fine and smooth for the small seeds, and mix in compost or well-rotted (never fresh) manure, since fresh manure makes the roots hairy and branched. Aim for a soil pH around 6.0 to 6.8. One cabbage-family note: a root disease called clubroot is worse in wet, acidic soil, so if it has been a problem, improve drainage and add lime to raise the pH toward 7.2 to 7.5. If your soil is heavy clay, mix in compost or use a raised bed for the loose, well-drained soil turnips like.
seasoned: Turnips reward a loose, fertile, well-drained seedbed worked fine before sowing. Loosen the bed about 8 to 10 inches deep, less than carrots need since the root swells near the surface, and remove stones and clods that fork the roots. Rake the surface smooth and fine for the small seed, and work in well-finished compost or well-rotted (not fresh) manure, since fresh manure branches the roots and over-supplies nitrogen. Aim for a slightly acidic to neutral pH of about 6.0 to 6.8. The brassica-specific concern is clubroot: it thrives in wet, poorly drained, acidic soil, so on a clubroot-prone bed improve drainage and lime toward a neutral to slightly alkaline pH of about 7.2 to 7.5, which suppresses it. On heavy clay, work in compost or use a raised bed for the drainage and loose texture turnips prefer.

beginner: Leeks like deep, loose, rich soil with lots of compost worked in. Loose soil matters because you grow the long white part of a leek by pulling soil up around the stem, and that is much easier in soft, crumbly ground than in heavy clay. Keep the soil evenly moist all season.
seasoned: Work in generous compost or rotted manure before planting and aim for a deep, loose, fertile, well-drained bed. Leeks are long-season, moderately heavy feeders with a shallow root system, so the soil must hold both moisture and nutrients near the surface across many months; loose ground also makes the repeated earthing-up that blanches the shank far easier.

beginner: Leeks grow best in soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about 6.0 to 7.0. A simple soil test takes out the guesswork. If your test comes back below about 6.0, adding garden lime brings it up.
seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0 (UMN gives 6.0 to 7.0; UF/IFAS lists 6.5 to 7.0 for Florida). Leeks tolerate a wider 5.5 to 7.5 band but dislike strongly acid ground; below about 6.0 a liming amendment helps. Confirm with a soil test before adjusting.

beginner: Leeks grow for a long time and are fairly hungry plants. Mix a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting, then feed once or twice with a nitrogen fertilizer through the summer while the stems are growing. Steady feeding builds thick stems. Do not pile on a lot of fertilizer late in the season, since soft, crowded, well-fed plants get rust more easily.
seasoned: Leeks are long-season, moderately heavy feeders. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (UMN suggests about one cup per 10 feet of row mid-season), then side-dress with nitrogen once or twice while the shafts are lengthening. USU gives a quarter pound of ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) per 100 square feet in the middle of May and again in late June. Keep nitrogen steady through summer for thick shanks, but avoid heavy late feeding, which together with crowding and wet leaves worsens leek rust.

beginner: Feed your leeks some nitrogen now to grow thicker stems.
seasoned: Time to side-dress your leeks with nitrogen to push shaft growth.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 at planting, then feed with a nitrogen fertilizer once or twice during summer.
seasoned: A balanced base such as 10-10-10 at planting, then nitrogen side-dressings (for example ammonium sulfate, 21-0-0) through summer to build long, thick shanks.

beginner: About a quarter pound of a nitrogen fertilizer such as ammonium sulfate for every 100 square feet each time you feed, or follow the package directions.
seasoned: About a quarter pound of ammonium sulfate (21-0-0) per 100 square feet at each side-dressing (USU), or roughly one cup of 10-10-10 per 10 feet of row mid-season (UMN), or the label rate of a balanced fertilizer.
