beginner: A shallot is a small, mild onion relative that grows in a cluster. Here is the fun part: you plant one little bulb (called a set) and it splits underground into a bunch of 6 to 12 bulbs, so you dig up a whole clump from each one you planted. Shallots taste sweeter and gentler than regular onions, with a hint of garlic, and they keep for many months once dried. They are the same species as the onion, so like onions they start making bulbs based on how long the days are, not on the calendar. The traditional kinds grown from sets are easygoing about this, but it still helps to pick a type suited to where you live. Give them rich, loose soil and full sun, water them steadily, and they are one of the easiest alliums to grow.
seasoned: Shallot (Allium cepa, Aggregatum group) is a cool-season allium grown for the small, fine-grained bulbs prized for their mild, sweet, faintly garlicky flavor. Its signature is multiplication: plant one set and it divides underground into a cluster of 6 to 12 bulbs, so you lift a whole clump where an onion gives a single bulb. Like the bulb onion it shares a species with, shallot is photoperiodic, a cluster sizes up only once day length crosses a cultivar threshold, which is why the right type tracks your latitude. Traditional set-grown shallots are more forgiving about day length than seed onions, but matching the type to your region still pays off. Grow it like an onion otherwise: a heavy-feeding, shallow-rooted plant in loose, fertile soil, kept evenly moist while the clump fills, then eased off water as the tops fall to begin curing. Well-cured shallots store for months, often longer than onions.

beginner: Your shallots are ready to dig when most of the leafy tops have flopped over and turned yellow and the necks feel soft, usually about 3 to 4 months after planting sets in spring. Dig up the whole clump on a dry day, then dry (cure) the bulbs before storing. If you want fresh green shallots sooner, you can pull a few young plants at around 50 to 60 days and use them like green onions.
seasoned: A shallot clump is ready when most of the tops have yellowed and fallen over on their own and the necks have started to soften and dry, usually 90 to 120 days from a spring set. Lift the whole cluster on a dry day, brush off loose soil, and cure before storing. You can also pull green shallots early, at 50 to 60 days, for fresh use like scallions.

beginner: Shallots are the same species as onions, so like onions they decide to start making bulbs based on how long the days are, not on a date. The types are sorted the same way: long-day kinds suit the North, short-day kinds suit the South (where they are planted in fall or winter), and intermediate kinds suit the middle of the country. One nice thing: the traditional shallots grown from sets are more easygoing about day length than seed onions, so they are forgiving for beginners. Still, picking a type that matches where you live gives you the fullest clumps. Day length decides when the bulbs form, but it does not change when you plant, which still depends on frost and soil temperature.
seasoned: Shallot is the same species as the bulb onion (Allium cepa), so it is photoperiodic: the clump stops adding leaves and starts dividing into bulbs only once day length crosses a cultivar threshold. Types fall into the same classes by latitude, long-day at 14 to 16 hours, intermediate-day at 12 to 14 hours, and short-day at 10 to 12 hours. Long-day types fit northern latitudes, short-day types fit the South where they are fall or winter planted, and intermediate types span the middle. One important nuance: traditional set-grown shallots are widely reported as more day-length forgiving, closer to day-neutral, than seed onions, while modern seed-grown hybrids behave like day-length-typed onions. Matching the type to your latitude still gives the fullest clumps. Day length triggers bulbing only; it never moves your planting date, which stays anchored to frost and soil temperature.

beginner: Give lemongrass rich, moist soil that has been improved with plenty of compost. It is a hungry, thirsty grass, so the better the soil, the bigger the clump. Make sure the spot still drains, because soil that stays soggy can rot the roots.
seasoned: Lemongrass grows best in a moist, rich, well-drained loam with high organic content. As a fast-growing grass it is a heavy user of both nutrients and water, so a fertile soil amended generously with compost supports the vigorous clump growth that produces thick, harvestable stalks. Good drainage matters despite the high water demand: soils that stay waterlogged invite root rot. The plant tolerates a range of soil types, so the practical goal is a soil that holds moisture and feeds well while still draining freely.

beginner: Lemongrass is easygoing about soil pH. Aim for roughly 6.0 to 7.5, which is ordinary garden soil, and you will not need to make any special adjustment.
seasoned: Lemongrass is not fussy about pH and tolerates a wide range of soils. A preferred range of 6.0 to 7.5 keeps the full spectrum of nutrients available to this fast-growing, nutrient-hungry grass, and it will grow acceptably in mildly acidic through mildly alkaline ground. No specific pH figure is published in the Tier-1 extension guides consulted, so this range is modeled from the plant's documented tolerance of varied soils and from general practice for culinary grasses.

beginner: Lemongrass is a hungry grass and grows fastest when fed often. Use a liquid fertilizer at about half strength every week or two through the summer. If it is in a pot, feed a bit more often, since watering washes nutrients out. Stop feeding as fall nears.
seasoned: Like other grasses, lemongrass is a heavy nitrogen feeder, and steady feeding drives the vigorous leaf and stalk growth that makes a productive clump. Utah State Extension recommends feeding weekly with a half-strength solution of a balanced soluble fertilizer from June through September; a nitrogen-forward all-purpose liquid every one to two weeks works similarly. Container plants need more frequent feeding than in-ground clumps because nutrients leach with each watering. Taper feeding as fall approaches so growth is not pushed into cold weather.

beginner: Your lemongrass could use a feed. Mix a liquid fertilizer to about half the label strength and water it in at the base. Do this every week or two through summer, a bit more often for pots.
seasoned: Time to feed your lemongrass. Grasses are heavy nitrogen users; apply a balanced soluble fertilizer at half strength, or a nitrogen-forward all-purpose liquid, every one to two weeks through the summer growing season. Feed container plants a little more often.

beginner: Use a general-purpose feed higher in the first number (nitrogen)
seasoned: Nitrogen-forward; a balanced soluble at half strength or a higher-first-number all-purpose liquid keeps this fast-growing grass in vigorous leaf

beginner: Half the label strength, every week or two through summer
seasoned: Half-strength soluble fertilizer weekly through summer; more frequent for containers as nutrients leach

beginner: Lemongrass is one of the least pest-troubled herbs you can grow. Its own lemony oils keep most bugs away, so outdoor plants usually look clean.
seasoned: Healthy in-ground lemongrass rarely shows insect damage. Extension guides describe it as essentially free of pest problems when grown well, an effect attributed to the citral-rich essential oils in its foliage that repel many insects. Scattered chewing or a few sap-feeders may appear on stressed or crowded plants but seldom rise to a real infestation outdoors.

beginner: Lemongrass makes lemony oils that many insects dislike, so it is naturally left alone. Keeping it healthy and unstressed keeps it that way.
seasoned: The plant's aromatic oils (notably citral) are used in insect-repellent products. Robust, well-watered clumps in full sun are the least attractive to pests; stress and crowding are what invite occasional trouble.

beginner: You will seldom need to treat lemongrass. If you do see a few bugs, blast them off with water or use an insecticidal soap. Trim off any damaged leaves.
seasoned: Rarely needed outdoors. For the occasional sap-feeder, a strong jet of water or an insecticidal soap spray is sufficient. Remove and destroy badly damaged outer leaves. Improving airflow and vigor usually resolves minor issues without any product.

beginner: Keep lemongrass healthy with sun, rich soil, and plenty of water, and divide it when it gets crowded. A strong plant rarely has pest trouble.
seasoned: Grow in full sun with rich soil and steady water to keep clumps vigorous, and divide crowded clumps so air moves through them. Vigorous plants are the best defense.

beginner: Tiny specks and a faded, dusty look on the leaves, sometimes with fine webbing. This shows up mostly on plants kept indoors over winter.
seasoned: Fine stippling or a dusty, faded look on the leaf blades, sometimes with delicate webbing where the leaf meets the stem, most often on plants overwintered indoors or grown in hot, dry, stagnant air. Heavy feeding bronzes and dries the foliage.

beginner: Spider mites are tiny pests that love warm, dry indoor air. They tend to appear on lemongrass that is overwintering inside.
seasoned: Spider mites (Tetranychidae) thrive in the warm, dry, low-airflow conditions of a heated indoor room, which is exactly where potted lemongrass spends the winter. They are far less of a problem on well-watered outdoor clumps.

beginner: Spray the leaves with water to knock mites off and raise the humidity around indoor plants. For stubborn cases, use insecticidal soap. Cutting the plant back before bringing it inside helps a lot.
seasoned: Rinse the foliage with a strong spray of water, raise humidity around indoor plants, and treat persistent infestations with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, covering the leaf undersides. Cutting the plant back hard before bringing it indoors reduces the mite population it carries in.

beginner: Before bringing lemongrass indoors, trim it back and check it over. Keep the indoor air from getting too hot and dry by misting now and then.
seasoned: Before overwintering, cut the plant back and inspect it, and keep indoor humidity up with misting or a nearby water tray. Avoid hot, dry, stagnant spots for indoor pots.

beginner: Yellow flecks that turn into reddish streaks, plus orange-brown powdery spots on the undersides of the leaves. Bad cases dry the leaves out. It shows up most in warm, humid, crowded conditions.
seasoned: Small chlorotic (yellow) flecks appear on both leaf surfaces and enlarge into reddish to crimson streaks; on the leaf underside these rupture into powdery orange-brown pustules. Severe infection produces large patches of tan to purplish dead tissue and dries the leaves, cutting yield and quality. It is favored by warm, humid weather and crowded, poorly ventilated plantings.

beginner: A fungus called rust, spread by wind and splashing water. It is most common where it is warm, humid, and the plants are packed close together.
seasoned: Rust caused by the fungus Puccinia nakanishikii, the most notable disease of lemongrass in humid tropical and subtropical areas; the University of Hawaii CTAHR documents it, and it has been reported on Florida lemongrass. Spores spread on wind and splashing water, and dense, wet, still canopies favor infection.

beginner: Cut off and throw away badly spotted leaves, and thin or divide crowded clumps so air moves through. Water at the base, not over the leaves. A copper fungicide can help if rust is a recurring problem.
seasoned: Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves to reduce spore load, and open the clump up by dividing and thinning to improve airflow. Water at the base rather than overhead so leaves dry quickly. Copper-based fungicides can be used preventively where rust pressure is high; culture is the primary control.

beginner: Give plants room, divide crowded clumps, and water at the base so the leaves stay dry. Good airflow and full sun are the best prevention.
seasoned: Space and divide clumps for good air movement, water at the soil line to keep foliage dry, and avoid overhead irrigation in humid weather. Vigorous, uncrowded plants in full sun resist rust best.

beginner: Brown streaks and dead patches on the leaves during warm, wet spells. In crowded plants it can spread fast.
seasoned: Brown, elongated lesions develop along the leaf blades in warm, wet weather and can spread quickly through dense plantings, browning and drying the foliage from the tips and margins inward.

beginner: A leaf fungus that thrives when leaves stay wet and plants are packed together in warm, humid weather.
seasoned: A foliar leaf-blight fungus that is favored by prolonged leaf wetness, high humidity, and crowding. As with rust, still, wet canopies drive it, and it is the second disease of note for lemongrass grown in humid regions.

beginner: Trim off the blighted leaves, thin crowded clumps, and water at the base instead of over the top. A copper spray can help in bad cases.
seasoned: Remove affected leaves, thin or divide crowded clumps, and switch to base watering to shorten leaf-wetness periods. Copper-based products can be used preventively under heavy pressure.

beginner: Keep plants spaced and divided so air moves through, and water at the base so leaves dry fast. Try not to handle the plants while they are wet.
seasoned: Prioritize airflow (wide spacing, regular division) and dry foliage (base watering, morning irrigation). Avoid working in or harvesting from wet plants, which spreads spores.

beginner: The plant yellows, wilts, and rots at the base even though the soil is wet. The roots turn soft and dark. This comes from soil that stays soggy.
seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, and collapse of stalks despite wet soil, with soft, dark, decayed roots and stalk bases. It appears when a thirsty plant is grown in soil that stays waterlogged, especially in containers with poor drainage.

beginner: Lemongrass loves water but hates sitting in it. If the soil or pot does not drain, the roots rot.
seasoned: Although lemongrass demands abundant water, its roots rot in soil that is chronically waterlogged. Soil-borne rot organisms take hold when drainage is poor or a pot sits in standing water, so drainage is as important as watering volume.

beginner: You cannot save a badly rotted plant, so remove it. Fix the drainage, repot into fresh mix if it is in a container, and never let the pot sit in standing water.
seasoned: There is no cure once roots are extensively rotted; remove affected plants. Improve drainage, repot into a free-draining mix, empty saucers after watering, and water generously but allow excess to drain freely.

beginner: Grow lemongrass in soil or a pot that drains well. Water it a lot, but make sure the extra water can run out and the pot never sits in a full saucer.
seasoned: Plant in well-drained, organically rich soil; in containers use a free-draining mix and pots with ample holes, and empty the saucer after each watering. Water deeply and often, but let the excess escape.

beginner: Water often. In the ground, water deeply a few times a week in hot weather; in a pot, check daily and do not let it dry out.
seasoned: Frequently through the warm season; in-ground clumps deeply 2-3 times per week in heat, containers often daily

beginner: Keep the soil consistently moist, never bone dry. Lemongrass drinks a lot.
seasoned: Keep the root zone consistently moist; this is a high-water-demand grass, so err toward generous, deep watering while ensuring drainage

beginner: Water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves, to help prevent leaf diseases. In a pot, water until it runs out the bottom, then empty the saucer.
seasoned: Water at the base by hand or flood irrigation rather than overhead sprinklers; keeping the foliage dry limits rust and leaf blight, and base watering suits this thirsty grass. In containers, water until it drains from the bottom and empty the saucer.

beginner: Yellow, wilting leaves and a soft, dark base even though the soil is wet mean the roots are sitting in water. Improve the drainage.
seasoned: Yellowing and wilting despite wet soil, soft dark stalk bases, and a soured, waterlogged root zone signal root rot from poor drainage rather than too little water.

beginner: Browning, curling leaf tips and slow growth mean it is thirsty. Lemongrass wilts and browns quickly when it runs short of water.
seasoned: Leaf tips and margins browning and curling, slowed clump expansion, and thin, slow-forming stalks indicate the plant is not getting enough water, especially during hot, dry spells.

beginner: Keep a new plant's soil moist while it settles in. Do not let it dry out.
seasoned: A newly set-out division or rooted start needs consistently moist soil to establish its roots; do not let it dry out during the first few weeks.

beginner: During the hot growing months, water deeply and often. This is when the clump bulks up.
seasoned: This is the main growth phase, when heat and water drive rapid clump expansion. Water deeply and often, ensuring drainage.

beginner: Keep watering well as the stalks fatten up. Dry spells make thin stalks.
seasoned: Maintain generous, consistent moisture as stalks thicken to harvestable size; water stress thins the stalks.

beginner: Keep watering as you harvest so the clump keeps making new stalks.
seasoned: Keep moisture steady through the harvest period to sustain continued stalk production from the clump.

beginner: Lemongrass drinks more than most herbs but hates soggy roots. Water it deeply and often, at the base, and make sure the extra water drains away.
seasoned: Lemongrass has an unusually high water demand for an herb, yet it still needs sharp drainage. The reconciling rule is to water deeply and frequently while never letting the root zone stagnate. Watering at the base or by flood irrigation, rather than overhead, both suits the plant and keeps foliage dry to limit rust and leaf blight.

beginner: The easiest way to start lemongrass is from a division or a nursery plant, or by standing a fresh grocery-store stalk in a glass of water until it grows roots (about two to three weeks), then potting it up. Get it going indoors about 8 weeks before your last frost, then set it outside once frost is past and the soil is warm. Ease it into the outdoors over a few days first. It stays small until summer heat kicks in, then takes off.
seasoned: Lemongrass is almost always started from a division of an existing clump, from a nursery transplant, or by rooting a fresh grocery-store stalk (leaves and roots removed) in a glass of water, where roots form in about two to three weeks. Seed is possible but slow and rarely used. Start or pot up divisions indoors roughly 8 weeks before the last frost to have a well-rooted plant ready to set out. Transplant outdoors only after all frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed, and harden plants off over several days first. It grows slowly until summer heat arrives, then bulks up dramatically.

beginner: Fresh stalks last a few days to a week on the counter. For longer storage, use the fridge or freezer.
seasoned: Whole fresh stalks keep for several days to about a week at cool room temperature. For anything longer, refrigerate or freeze. The tough stalks are far more durable than tender leafy herbs.

beginner: Lemongrass keeps well in the fridge, about 2 to 3 weeks, wrapped or in a bag. Cold does not hurt it the way it does basil.
seasoned: Wrapped loosely or sealed in a bag, fresh stalks keep 2 to 3 weeks in the refrigerator. Unlike basil, lemongrass has no chilling-injury problem and refrigerates well.

beginner: Lemongrass freezes very well. Freeze whole stalks or chop the tender part and freeze it in bags. It keeps its flavor for months. Dry the leaves for tea.
seasoned: Lemongrass freezes excellently and is the best way to keep a large harvest. Freeze whole trimmed stalks, or slice or mince the tender bases and freeze in bags or portioned in ice cube trays; frozen stalks keep their flavor for many months. Leaves can be dried for tea.

beginner: Lemongrass is easy to store. Keep stalks in the fridge for a couple of weeks or freeze them for months. Trim the tops and peel the tough outer layers off the part you cook with. Dry the leaves for tea.
seasoned: Lemongrass stores far more easily than delicate leafy herbs: the stalks are fibrous and sturdy, refrigerate for weeks, and freeze for months with little flavor loss. Trim the leafy tops and peel tough outer layers before storing the tender stalk base you cook with. The cut leaves dry well for tea.

beginner: For cooking, choose West Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus), the kind sold in grocery stores with the thick, tender stalks. There is also East Indian lemongrass (C. flexuosus), which is edible too and used for oil. Watch out for citronella grass, a lookalike relative grown to make citronella oil and to repel bugs, not for eating. If you want to cook with it, make sure you are getting C. citratus.
seasoned: For cooking, grow West Indian lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus), the species with the plump, tender stalk bases used in kitchens and the one usually sold fresh in stores. East Indian lemongrass (C. flexuosus) is also edible and is the main oil-crop species, with more slender stalks. The genus Cymbopogon holds dozens of species, and it is worth knowing that citronella grass (C. nardus and C. winterianus), the source of citronella oil, is a close relative that looks similar but is grown for repellent oil and ornament, not for eating. When buying a plant or a rooting stalk for the kitchen, confirm it is C. citratus.

beginner: Lemongrass and tomatoes both want heat, sun, and regular water, so they make easy neighbors. Lemongrass's strong lemony scent is a traditional way to help keep some insects away. Just give the grass its own space, because it grows into a big clump.
seasoned: Lemongrass shares tomatoes' love of heat, full sun, and steady water, and its strong citrus oils are a traditional insect deterrent, so gardeners often tuck a clump at the corner of a warm-season bed. Give it room, since a mature clump is large.

beginner: Peppers love the same heat and sun as lemongrass, so they grow well side by side. The grass's lemony scent may help keep some bugs off. Give the clump room to spread out.
seasoned: Peppers want the same heat, sun, and moisture as lemongrass and mature on a similar warm-season schedule, so they share a bed comfortably. The grass's aromatic oils are a traditional pest deterrent for the planting.

beginner: Herbs like rosemary, sage, and thyme want dry, lean soil, which is the opposite of what thirsty lemongrass needs. If you plant them together, one will always be unhappy. Give the dry-loving herbs their own spot and let lemongrass have the rich, well-watered ground it likes.
seasoned: Mediterranean herbs want lean, dry, sharply drained soil, while lemongrass wants rich ground and constant moisture, so the two pull a shared bed in opposite directions. Keep the drought-tolerant herbs in their own drier spot.

beginner: Lemongrass grows happily next to other sun-and-water lovers like tomatoes and peppers, and its lemony scent is a traditional way to discourage some insects. Keep it away from dry-soil herbs like rosemary and sage, which want the opposite conditions. Remember that lemongrass becomes a big clump, so give it plenty of space.
seasoned: Lemongrass has little formal companion-planting research behind it, but two practical points hold up. First, its essential oils (rich in citral) are documented insect repellents, which is the basis for the tradition of planting it near warm-season vegetables such as tomatoes and peppers; treat the pest-deterrent benefit as traditional rather than proven at garden scale. Second, its cultural needs are the deciding factor in placement: it demands rich soil, heavy feeding, full sun, and abundant water, so it pairs naturally with other heat-loving, well-watered crops and conflicts with lean, dry-soil Mediterranean herbs. Give a mature clump ample room, since it reaches 3 to 6 feet.

beginner: After watering, empty the saucer under the pot. Lemongrass drinks a lot but its roots rot if left standing in water.
seasoned: Empty the saucer after each watering; despite its thirst, lemongrass rots if its roots sit in standing water.

seasoned: A rich, moisture-retentive but free-draining potting mix, ideally amended with compost for fertility

seasoned: Feed container plants more often than in-ground clumps, since frequent watering leaches nutrients; a half-strength soluble feed every week through active growth suits them.

beginner: To keep lemongrass over winter, grow it in a pot. Before the first frost, cut it back to a few inches and move the pot to your sunniest indoor window. Water it less and do not feed it through winter. When frost is past in spring, put it back outside. This lets you keep the same plant year after year.
seasoned: In any zone that frosts, a container is the standard way to carry lemongrass over winter. Before the first fall frost, cut the plant back hard (to roughly 4 to 6 inches, which also sheds pests) and bring the pot to the brightest indoor spot available; a large clump can be divided down to a smaller pot first. Kept in bright light, watered less, and unfed through winter, it holds until spring, when it can go back outside after frost. This is also how gardeners in cold zones keep a favorite plant going year to year rather than buying new each spring.

beginner: Lemongrass grows very well in a big pot, which is the easiest way to grow it in cold areas since you can bring it inside for winter. Use a large pot (5 gallons is great) with good drainage and rich mix. Water and feed pots more often than ground plants. Divide the clump in spring when it fills the pot.
seasoned: Lemongrass is an excellent container plant, and in cold regions a pot is the practical way to grow it, because it can be moved indoors before frost. Use a large pot (at least 3 gallons, ideally 5 or more) to support the vigorous clump, with ample drainage holes and a rich, free-draining mix. The main tradeoffs of container culture are water and feeding: pots dry and leach faster than ground soil, so both must be more frequent. A potted clump outgrows its container within a season or two and benefits from spring division.

beginner: Self-watering pots work well for thirsty lemongrass. Just let the water reservoir run low now and then so the roots do not stay soaked.
seasoned: Self-watering containers suit this high-water-demand grass well, keeping the reservoir topped up during hot weather. Ensure the mix wicks moisture without becoming waterlogged, and let the reservoir draw down periodically to keep the roots healthy.

beginner: Lemongrass is a perennial that stays in one place for years, so you do not rotate it like an annual vegetable. Just give a new clump a sunny, rich, well-drained spot.
seasoned: As a long-lived perennial clump, lemongrass is not part of an annual rotation; it holds its spot for years and is renewed by division rather than replanted each season. If starting a new clump, simply choose a sunny, rich, well-drained site.

beginner: Lemongrass is a grass that lives for years in one spot, so you do not move it around each season like a vegetable. Plant it in a sunny, rich, well-drained place and divide the clump every few years to keep it strong.
seasoned: Lemongrass belongs to the true grass family, Poaceae, unrelated to the mints, carrots, or nightshades of a typical vegetable rotation. Because it is a perennial clump held for several years and divided to renew, it sits outside the annual crop-rotation cycle. The practical placement rule is simply full sun, rich soil, and good drainage; every few years, lift and divide the clump to keep the center vigorous.

beginner: Your new plant getting established. It may look a little limp at first, then start sending up fresh green blades from the middle once its roots catch on.
seasoned: A newly set-out division or rooted start settling in: leaves may look tired for a week or two, then new green blades begin pushing from the center as roots take hold. Growth is slow in cool weather and accelerates as the soil warms.

beginner: Keep it watered and in full sun while it settles in. Hold off on heavy feeding for now, and make sure cold nights are behind you.
seasoned: Keep the soil consistently moist while roots establish, and site the plant in full sun. Do not feed heavily yet. Protect from any late chill; do not set out until frost is safely past and soil is warm.

beginner: Seeing fresh blades?
seasoned: New growth appearing?

beginner: Fast growth once it gets hot. The clump fills out with lots of new shoots and gets bigger every week.
seasoned: Rapid clump expansion once summer heat arrives: many new tillers (shoots) fan out from the base, and the clump widens and thickens noticeably week to week. This is the heavy feeding and watering phase.

beginner: Water a lot and feed often through the summer to grow a big clump. Make sure it gets full sun, or it will make only a few thin stalks.
seasoned: Water deeply and often and feed regularly with a nitrogen-forward soluble fertilizer to drive clump growth. Ensure full sun; shaded plants make few, thin stalks.

beginner: Clump filling out?
seasoned: Clump expanding?

beginner: Stalks getting about half an inch thick at the bottom, which means they are ready to cut. The plant is now a tall, full clump.
seasoned: Individual stalks swelling to about half an inch thick at the base, the signal that they are ready to harvest. The clump stands 3 to 6 feet tall in good conditions, with dense, aromatic foliage.

beginner: Start cutting the thickest outer stalks. Keep watering and feeding so more keep coming. If you get frost, plan to dig it up or harvest it all before then.
seasoned: Begin harvesting the thickest outer stalks while keeping moisture and feeding steady so the clump keeps producing. In cold zones, plan the pre-frost lift or final harvest.

beginner: Stalks thick enough to cut?

beginner: Lemongrass is a tall, lemon-scented grass that loves heat, sun, rich soil, and plenty of water. It grows as a tidy clump, not a spreader like mint, so it will not take over your bed. It cannot survive frost, so in most of the country you plant it after your last frost and grow it through the warm months, then either dig it up and bring it indoors in a pot for winter or start fresh next spring. In the warmest, frost-free areas it can live outdoors year round. It is one of the easiest herbs to grow and is rarely bothered by insects, since its own lemony oils keep many pests away. To harvest, cut a whole stalk off at the base once it is about as thick as a pencil or thicker; the tender white bottom flavors cooking and the leaves make a lovely tea.
seasoned: Lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus) is a tender tropical grass, a member of the true grass family (Poaceae), grown for the aromatic swollen white bases of its stalks and its lemon-scented leaves. Everything about its care follows from two facts: it is a warm-season grass that thrives on heat, full sun, rich soil, and abundant water, and it is frost-tender, damaged when temperatures drop toward 40 °F and killed outright by frost. It grows as a dense, non-running clump 3 to 6 feet tall, not a spreading runner like mint, so it stays where you put it and is increased by dividing the clump or by rooting a fresh stalk in water. In the tropics and frost-free zones it is a true perennial that can be harvested year round; across most of the country it is grown as a warm-season annual set out after the last frost, then either lifted and potted indoors before fall frost or replaced each spring. Because its own essential oils repel many insects, it is notably free of pest problems; rust and leaf blight are the diseases to watch in warm, humid, crowded plantings. Harvest by cutting whole stalks at ground level once they thicken to about half an inch; the tender inner stalk base flavors soups and curries, and the leaves make a fragrant tea.

beginner: You can start harvesting once a stalk is about half an inch thick at the bottom, roughly a few months after planting. Pick a stalk from the outside of the clump: bend it to the side and twist and pull it off at the base, or cut it right at ground level. Cut off the grassy top and peel away the tough outer layers to get to the tender white part for cooking. You can snip leaves anytime to dry for tea.
seasoned: Begin harvesting once individual stalks have swelled to about half an inch thick at the base, which in a warm season is usually 75 to 120 days after planting a division or rooted start. Harvest a whole stalk rather than picking leaves: grasp an outer stalk, push it to the side, and twist and pull it free at the base, or cut it at ground level with a knife. Take the outermost stalks first and leave the clump intact to keep producing. Trim off the leafy top and peel away the tough outer layers to reach the tender inner base used in cooking; the fragrant leaves can be cut anytime for tea.

beginner: Lemongrass only survives winter outdoors in the warmest, nearly frost-free areas (roughly zones 8b to 11). There it comes back year after year. Anywhere colder, frost kills it, so you either grow it as a one-season plant or keep it in a pot and bring it indoors for winter. Temperatures below about 40 °F start to hurt it, and a frost kills the leaves.
seasoned: Lemongrass is a tender tropical grass, reliably perennial only in essentially frost-free climates, roughly USDA zones 8b through 11, where established clumps persist and can be cut year round; foliage may redden and growth slows in the coolest winters of that range. Below about 40 °F the plant is damaged, and frost kills the top growth outright. In colder zones it is grown as a warm-season annual or, more often, kept in a pot that is moved indoors before frost and back out in spring, which lets the same clump live for years despite the cold.

beginner: Marigolds are easy, cheerful flowers and the classic companion plant, grown for blooms rather than food. They love heat and full sun, handle poor soil and dry spells, and bloom from summer until the first fall frost. There are three main kinds: small bushy French marigolds, tall big-flowered African (or American) marigolds, and tiny lacy Signet marigolds with edible petals. Plant the seeds outside after your last frost once the soil is warm, and you get flowers in about two months. Keep snipping off faded blooms to get more. Their most proven garden trick is fighting soil nematodes: grow a thick patch of French marigolds and dig them in before planting vegetables that nematodes attack.
seasoned: Marigold (Tagetes species) is a warm-season, frost-tender annual in the Asteraceae family, native to Mexico and Central America. It is grown for showy blooms and as the classic companion plant, in three main types: compact French marigolds (Tagetes patula), tall large-pompon African or American marigolds (Tagetes erecta), and petite, lacy, edible-flowered Signet marigolds (Tagetes tenuifolia). Sown into warm soil after frost, it reaches first bloom in roughly 7 to 9 weeks and flowers continuously from summer until the first fall frost. It thrives in heat, full sun, and even poor soil, and is notably drought-tolerant once established. Its best-supported pest function is nematode suppression: French marigolds grown as a dense cover stand and incorporated lower root-knot nematode populations for the following crop.

beginner: Marigolds are not fussy and grow in most ordinary garden soil as long as water drains away and does not pool. Soil that is moderately fertile and well drained is ideal; very rich soil grows lots of leaves and fewer flowers. Avoid soggy ground, which rots the roots. If your soil is very acidic, the leaves can speckle bronze, so a normal garden range works best.
seasoned: Marigolds want moderately fertile, well-drained soil and tolerate a wide range of textures, including poorer ground; the consistent failure is wet, poorly drained soil that rots roots and crowns. They are light feeders, so over-rich soil pushes foliage at the expense of bloom. On strongly acidic soil (below about pH 5.5), foliage can show a bronze speckling from manganese or iron toxicity, so a near-neutral range is preferred.

beginner: Marigolds are not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range around 6.0 to 7.0 is ideal, and you usually do not need to change anything. Only very acidic soil, below about 5.5, can cause speckled, bronze-looking leaves.
seasoned: Marigolds perform best across roughly 6.0 to 7.0 and tolerate a little outside that. No pH adjustment is typically warranted, but strongly acidic soil (below about 5.5) can trigger manganese or iron toxicity that bronze-speckles the foliage, so favor a near-neutral bed.

beginner: Wait until the soil is warm (about 65 to 70 °F) before planting marigold seeds outside; they sprout in under a week in warm soil. Go easy on fertilizer and do not overwater, since both give you lots of leaves but fewer flowers. Snip off faded blooms (deadheading) to keep more coming. If you have a nematode problem in a vegetable bed, the trick that actually works is to plant a thick patch of French marigolds there for a couple of months first, then dig them in, not just dotting a few among your vegetables.
seasoned: Soil warmth, not the calendar, is the real germination trigger: direct-sow into soil near 65 to 70 °F after frost and seedlings break ground in 5 to 8 days. Go light on nitrogen and avoid overwatering, both of which give leaves at the expense of bloom; deadhead or cut for the vase to sustain flowering to frost. For root-knot nematode pressure, grow French types (Tagetes patula) as a dense, solid cover stand for two months before the susceptible crop, then turn them under, rather than scattering a few among the vegetables.

beginner: If lower leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base looks soft and mushy, you are likely overwatering or the soil drains poorly. Wet flowers also turn moldy.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and soft, rotting stems or crowns signal overwatering or poor drainage; persistently wet, dense blooms also raise gray-mold pressure. Dwarf French types rot readily if kept saturated.

beginner: Marigolds that are too dry wilt in the afternoon heat, look dull, and make smaller flowers. They are thirstiest right after planting and when the first buds form, but established plants bounce back from short dry spells.
seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day that recovers by evening, dulling leaf color, and reduced flower size at bud point indicate underwatering, most critically during establishment and at first bloom; established plants are forgiving of short dry spells.

seasoned: Keep the seedbed evenly moist through germination and establishment, marigold's one critical moisture window.

beginner: Established marigolds handle dry spells well. About an inch a week, deep and less often, letting the soil dry a bit between waterings. Frequent shallow watering causes rot, and the little French types especially rot in soggy soil.
seasoned: Established marigolds are notably drought-tolerant: about an inch a week applied deeply and less often, letting the soil dry somewhat between waterings. Over-frequent shallow watering invites root rot and foliar disease, and dwarf French types rot readily if kept saturated.

beginner: Marigolds are flowers for the garden and the vase, not food to store, so there is nothing to refrigerate or freeze. To make cut flowers last, trim the stems, pull off the smelly lower leaves that would sit underwater, and use a clean vase with fresh water. They usually stay nice for several days to a week. The small Signet marigolds have edible petals with a spicy, tarragon-like flavor, used fresh.
seasoned: Marigold is grown for bloom and companion value, not as a stored edible, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply. For cut flowers, recut stems and strip the strongly scented lower leaves below the waterline (they foul vase water fast), use clean water with floral preservative, and keep blooms out of direct sun. Vase life is several days to about a week. The Signet types have edible, spicy-tarragon petals used fresh as a garnish.

beginner: Pick the type for your spot. French marigolds are small, bushy, and bloom for a long time, perfect for beds, pots, and edging, and they are the type that suppresses soil nematodes when planted thickly. African marigolds are the tall ones with big round pompon flowers, good at the back of a bed and for cutting. Signet marigolds are tiny, lacy plants covered in small flowers, very tough in heat and drought, with petals you can eat. Open, single flowers are best for bees and butterflies.
seasoned: Choose by type and purpose. French marigolds (Tagetes patula) are the compact, bushy, long-blooming bedding and edging workhorses and the type to use for root-knot nematode cover plantings (cultivars such as 'Single Gold' and 'Tangerine' are the trialed performers). African or American marigolds (Tagetes erecta) are the tall, large-pompon types for the back of the border and for cutting; they benefit most from deadheading and staking. Signet marigolds (Tagetes tenuifolia) are the petite, lacy, heat- and drought-tough edgers, smothered in small single flowers whose petals are edible. Single, open-faced flowers serve pollinators better than the densest doubles.

beginner: Marigolds are the classic companion plant, grown to help the rest of the garden more than for themselves. The one pest benefit that research actually supports is against root-knot nematodes (tiny soil worms that damage roots): if you grow a thick, solid patch of French marigolds in a problem bed for about two months and then dig them in, before planting a crop that nematodes attack, they can lower the nematode numbers. Just dotting a few marigolds among your vegetables has not been shown to do this. The old idea that their strong smell drives away insects, rabbits, and deer is traditional belief, sometimes helpful but not reliable. What marigolds clearly do is bring in bees and helpful insects, so they are a cheerful, useful edge or border plant almost anywhere. There is no plant you must keep them away from; just give them room and sun.
seasoned: Marigold inverts the usual companion framing: it is the plant you place to benefit others. Its one research-supported pest function is nematode suppression, and only in a specific form: French marigolds (Tagetes patula) grown as a dense, weed-free solid stand for about two months in the target bed and then incorporated, ahead of a susceptible crop, can reduce root-knot and lesion nematode populations via root-released alpha-terthienyl. UF/IFAS is explicit that simply interplanting a few marigolds among vegetables has not been shown to reduce nematodes, and the African types are less effective than French for this. The broader reputation, that marigold scent repels insects, rabbits, and deer, is traditional companion lore: sometimes borne out, not reliably documented. What is solid is that marigold is a strong pollinator and beneficial-insect draw, so it earns its place as an insectary edge or border. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; site for sun and airflow.

beginner: If a bed has root-knot nematodes, grow a thick patch of French marigolds there for about two months, then dig them in, before planting vegetables that nematodes attack. This is the marigold trick that research actually backs.
seasoned: This is marigold's evidence-based pest function. French marigolds planted as a dense, weed-free solid stand for about two months and then incorporated, ahead of the susceptible crop, reduce root-knot and lesion nematode populations through root-released alpha-terthienyl. It is a sequential, whole-bed treatment, not a concurrent interplant: keep the stand free of grass and weeds (so nematodes cannot feed on other roots) and follow with the vegetable crop the next season. African types are less effective than French.

beginner: Marigolds are traditionally planted with tomatoes and peppers, and they do draw in bees and helpful predator insects. The idea that their smell repels pests is folklore, so enjoy the flowers and beneficial bugs and do not count on them as bug spray.
seasoned: A traditional pairing whose real, defensible benefit is beneficial-insect habitat rather than pest repellence. Marigold nectar and pollen draw hoverflies, lacewings, ladybugs, and parasitic wasps whose larvae prey on aphids and other soft-bodied pests of tomatoes and peppers. Note the honest limits: the popular claims that marigold scent repels pests, and that interplanting a few marigolds controls the nematodes that bother tomatoes, are not supported by extension trials. Plant them as an insectary edge for predator support and color, not as a substitute for pest control.

beginner: Squash, melons, and cucumbers need insects to move pollen to set fruit. Marigolds bloom a long time and bring in the bees that do that job.
seasoned: A well-grounded pollinator pairing. Cucurbits depend on insect pollination, with several bee visits needed per flower for proper fruit set, and marigold is a reliable, long-blooming pollinator magnet across the cucurbit fruiting window. More pollinator traffic plausibly means better set and fewer aborted fruits. Plant marigolds in nearby rows so the pollinators they draw spill onto the crop; this is a visitation benefit, not a pest-control one.

beginner: Marigolds add color and bring in helpful bugs alongside cabbage-family crops and beans without crowding them for food. Traditionally they are also planted to deter pests, though that part is folklore.
seasoned: A habitat-level pairing. Marigold adds beneficial-insect and pollinator habitat alongside cabbage-family crops and beans with low nutrient competition, and the flowers support parasitic wasps and predators that help manage aphids and caterpillars. The traditional claim that marigold scent deters cabbage pests and bean beetles is not extension-verified; treat it as a loose, garden-ecosystem pairing, kept to the edges so it does not shade lower crops.

beginner: Nasturtiums are some of the easiest flowers to grow, and the whole plant is edible with a peppery, watercress-like taste: the round leaves, the bright flowers, and even the green seed pods, which you can pickle like capers. They come in two styles: trailing kinds that spill from baskets and climb low supports, and bushy kinds that stay about a foot tall. The big surprise with nasturtiums is that they flower best in poor soil. Rich soil or fertilizer gives you lots of leaves but few flowers, so do not feed them. They also make a famous companion plant: aphids love nasturtiums, so gardeners use them as a sacrificial trap to pull aphids away from beans, cabbage-family crops, and squash. Sow the big seeds right where they will grow, since nasturtiums do not like being moved. They love cool weather, slow down in extreme summer heat, and die at the first frost.
seasoned: Nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) is an easy, fast-growing, frost-tender annual in the Tropaeolaceae family, native to the Andes of South America. It comes in two habits: trailing or climbing types that scramble several feet across the ground, up low trellises, or out of hanging baskets, and compact bush or mounding types that hold to about a foot. It is grown for three things at once: cheerful long-spurred flowers in warm yellows, oranges, and reds; an entirely edible plant with a peppery, watercress-like bite in its leaves, flowers, and seed pods; and a well-known companion role as an aphid trap crop. A counterintuitive key to flowering: nasturtium blooms best in lean, poor soil, and rich soil or extra fertilizer drives lush leaves at the expense of flowers. It is a cool-preference plant that flowers most freely in spring and fall, slows or stops in extreme summer heat, and is killed by the first frost.

beginner: Nasturtiums are happiest in poor, lean, well-drained soil. This is the opposite of most flowers: rich, fertile soil or added fertilizer makes them grow lots of leaves and very few flowers. Ordinary or even sandy, sandy-loam soil that drains well is ideal, and you do not need to add compost or feed. Just make sure water drains away and does not pool, since soggy soil rots the roots.
seasoned: Nasturtium wants lean, well-drained soil and is one of the few garden plants that flowers better in poor ground: high fertility and nitrogen push vigorous foliage and delay or suppress bloom. Sandy to sandy-loam soils are ideal, and the plant tolerates a wide pH and even neglect, but the consistent failure is wet, poorly drained soil that rots the roots. Skip compost and fertilizer at planting; reserve any feeding for genuinely impoverished soil, and even then keep it light and low-nitrogen.

beginner: Nasturtiums are not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range, roughly 6.0 to 7.5, is fine, and they tolerate a bit outside it. You usually do not need to change anything.
seasoned: Nasturtium performs across a broad pH band and is essentially unfussy; roughly 6.0 to 7.5 is ideal, and it tolerates mildly acidic to mildly alkaline soil. No pH adjustment is typically warranted. Soil fertility and drainage matter far more to flowering than pH does.

beginner: The most important nasturtium tip is surprising: do not fertilize them. Poor soil gives you lots of flowers, while rich soil or feeding gives you lots of leaves and hardly any flowers. Plant the big seeds right where you want them to grow, about half an inch deep, after your last frost, because nasturtiums do not like having their roots disturbed. Soaking the seeds overnight helps them sprout. If you want to use them against aphids, plant a patch a few feet away from your beans, cabbage, or squash as a trap, and pull it out once it is covered in aphids. Pick the peppery leaves, flowers, and young green seed pods to eat.
seasoned: The single most useful nasturtium rule is counterintuitive: do not feed them. Lean, poor soil gives the most flowers, while rich soil or nitrogen gives all leaves and few blooms. Direct-sow the large seeds where they are to grow, about 1/2 in deep, after frost once soil is near 55 to 65 °F; they resent transplanting, so if you must start indoors use biodegradable pots. Soak seeds overnight to speed germination. As an aphid trap crop, plant a sacrificial stand a few feet away from beans, brassicas, or squash, then pull and destroy it once aphids load up. Pick leaves, flowers, and young green seed pods for the kitchen as they come.

seasoned: Nasturtium is the rare flower that should not be fed: it blooms best in lean soil, and added nitrogen or fertilizer drives leafy growth at the expense of flowers. On genuinely poor or sandy soil, at most one light, low-nitrogen feeding can help, but in average soil skip fertilizer entirely. Over-feeding is the most common reason a healthy-looking nasturtium refuses to bloom.

beginner: A reminder that nasturtiums do best with no fertilizer. Feeding them usually means more leaves and fewer flowers, so you can skip it unless your soil is very poor.
seasoned: Reminder: nasturtiums usually need no feeding at all. Skip fertilizer unless the soil is genuinely impoverished, and even then keep it light and low-nitrogen, since feeding favors foliage over flowers.

beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For nasturtiums the best choice is usually none at all. A high first number (nitrogen) is the worst thing for them, giving leaves instead of flowers.
seasoned: Nasturtium generally wants no supplemental feeding; if soil is genuinely impoverished, a single light, low-nitrogen application is the most it needs. High-nitrogen feeds favor foliage over bloom.

beginner: Usually none. If your soil is very poor, you can give one small, light feeding, but otherwise do not feed them at all.
seasoned: Typically zero. Reserve feeding for genuinely poor soil, and then use a single light, low-nitrogen application at roughly half the label rate for annual flowers; do not feed routinely.

seasoned: Roughly one inch of water per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, applied deeply; let the surface dry slightly between waterings. Raise frequency during hot, dry spells, when consistent moisture sustains bloom and keeps the edible parts tender rather than bitter.

beginner: Water the soil around the plant, not the leaves. A watering can or soaker hose at the base works best. If the leaves get wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday.
seasoned: Water at the base with a can, drip, or soaker hose and keep water off the foliage where practical; the dense trailing mat of a vigorous plant stays wet and invites slugs and leaf problems. Morning watering lets any wet foliage dry quickly.

beginner: If lower leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base looks soft and mushy, you are overwatering or the soil drains poorly. A big leafy plant with no flowers usually means the soil is too rich, not too wet.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting despite wet soil, and soft, rotting stems signal overwatering or poor drainage; nasturtium rots readily in saturated soil. Lush, dark, flowerless foliage usually points to over-rich soil rather than water.

beginner: Nasturtiums that are too dry wilt in the afternoon, look dull, and make fewer, smaller flowers, and the leaves can taste sharp and tough. A good deep watering usually perks them up.
seasoned: Wilting in the heat of the day, dulling leaf color, and smaller, sparser flowers indicate underwatering; bitter, tough leaves and a flowering pause in heat are also relieved by deeper, more frequent watering.

seasoned: Established nasturtiums tolerate some drought and even neglect, so water moderately, about an inch a week applied deeply, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. beginner: Use nasturtium leaves and flowers the same day you pick them, since they wilt fast. Pick them in the morning and use them soon. Green seed pods for pickling can wait a little while before you process them.
seasoned: Nasturtium leaves and flowers are best used the day they are picked; they wilt quickly at room temperature. Harvest in the cool of the morning and use promptly. Green seed pods for pickling can sit briefly at room temperature before processing.

beginner: Keep nasturtium leaves and flowers in the fridge in a loose bag or on a damp paper towel, and use them within a day or two. The flowers are delicate, so handle them gently.
seasoned: Refrigerate flowers and leaves gently: wash, pat dry, and store in a loose bag or a container lined with damp paper towel, ideally using within a day or two. The delicate flowers bruise easily, so handle minimally and refrigerate only briefly.

beginner: You cannot really freeze the fresh leaves or flowers to use later, but you can freeze flowers in ice cubes to look pretty in drinks. To keep nasturtiums long-term, pickle the green seed pods.
seasoned: Fresh leaves and flowers do not freeze well for later use, though flowers can be frozen into ice cubes for decoration. The durable storage form is the pickled green seed pods, which keep for months refrigerated.

beginner: You can eat the whole nasturtium plant, and it tastes peppery like watercress. Use the leaves and flowers fresh in salads or as a garnish; younger leaves are milder. The best part to store is the green seed pod: pick it young and pickle it in vinegar to make poor man's capers, which keep for months. When eating the flowers, pull out the inner parts and the white base of the petals, which can taste bitter.
seasoned: The whole plant is edible with a peppery, watercress-like bite. Use leaves and flowers fresh in salads, as a garnish, or stuffed; younger leaves are milder, while stressed or older leaves and hot-weather growth turn sharper. The standout keeper is the green, immature seed pod: harvested young and pickled in spiced vinegar, it becomes poor man's capers and stores for months. Remove interior flower parts and the bitter white petal base before eating the flowers.

beginner: Pick the type for your spot. Bushy types like Jewel and Tip Top stay about a foot tall and are great in pots, beds, and edging, with flowers that sit up where you can pick them. Trailing or climbing types grow several feet and are perfect for hanging baskets, fences, and trellises, and they make the biggest patches for trapping aphids. Some types, like Alaska with its variegated leaves, look good even without flowers. Every kind is edible.
seasoned: Choose by habit and use. Bush or mounding types (Jewel, Tip Top, Whirlybird, Alaska) stay near a foot and suit beds, edging, containers, and the kitchen, with flowers often held up above the foliage for easy picking. Trailing and climbing types (Tall Trailing / Climbing mixes) run 6 to 10 ft and are the choice for trellises, fences, spilling baskets, and quick screening, and they make the most generous trap-crop stands. Foliage-feature types such as Alaska (variegated) and Empress of India (dark leaves) earn their place even between flushes of bloom. All parts of all types are edible.

beginner: Nasturtiums are a famous companion plant, mostly because aphids love them. The trick that actually works is to use nasturtium as a trap crop: plant a patch a few feet away from beans, cabbage-family crops, or squash, let the aphids gather on the nasturtiums instead of your vegetables, then pull and destroy the patch once it is covered in them. Plant the trap a little distance off, not right next to your crops, or the pests just hop over. Nasturtiums also bring in hoverflies and ladybugs that eat aphids. The old idea that their smell drives squash bugs and cucumber beetles away from squash and cucumbers is traditional garden lore, sometimes helpful but not proven. There is no plant you must keep nasturtiums away from, but remember that as a trap they draw pests, so site the trap stand thoughtfully.
seasoned: Nasturtium's companion value rests on one well-supported function and several traditional ones. The supported function is as an aphid trap crop: aphids strongly prefer nasturtium, and extension sources report it reduces pest pressure when planted near brassicas, beans, and cucurbits, so it is used as a sacrificial decoy that is monitored and destroyed once loaded. Effective use is sequential and spatial, a stand set a few feet off from the protected crop, not a casual interplant right among it, because a trap concentrates pests (and aphid-borne viruses) where it sits. Nasturtium also recruits aphid predators (hoverflies, lacewings, ladybugs) as an insectary plant. The broader reputation, that nasturtium scent repels squash bugs and cucumber beetles from cucurbits, is traditional companion lore: occasionally borne out, not reliably documented. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; the main caution is trap placement.

beginner: Aphids love nasturtiums more than they love your vegetables. Plant a patch of nasturtiums a few feet away from cabbage-family crops or squash so the aphids gather there instead, then pull and destroy the patch once it is loaded. This is the nasturtium trick that research actually supports.
seasoned: This is nasturtium's evidence-based pest function. Aphids strongly prefer nasturtium, so a stand grown as a sacrificial trap a few feet from brassicas or cucurbits pulls aphids off the protected crop; extension sources report reduced pest pressure with this use. It is a monitored, sequential treatment: site the trap at a distance (too close and pests simply move onto the crop), scout it, and pull and destroy the planting once it is heavily infested so it does not become a pest and virus reservoir.

beginner: Nasturtium flowers bring in hoverflies, ladybugs, and lacewings, whose young eat aphids, plus bees. So even beyond the trap-crop trick, a few nasturtiums help the good bugs in your garden.
seasoned: Beyond the trap function, nasturtium acts as an insectary plant: its open, nectar-rich flowers recruit hoverflies, lacewings, and ladybugs whose larvae prey on aphids, alongside bees. Interplanted at the garden edge, it supports the beneficial community that helps manage soft-bodied pests on neighboring crops. A habitat benefit, well-grounded but inferred rather than directly measured for nasturtium.

beginner: Gardeners have long planted nasturtiums with squash and cucumbers in the hope of keeping squash bugs and cucumber beetles away. This is traditional advice and not proven, so enjoy the flowers and the beneficial bugs, but do not rely on nasturtiums as a bug repellent.
seasoned: A traditional cucurbit pairing whose repellent claim is not extension-verified. Nasturtium is widely interplanted with squash and cucumbers on the belief that its scent deters squash bugs and cucumber beetles; this is companion lore, occasionally reported, not documented in trials. The honest, defensible benefits in a cucurbit bed are aphid trap-cropping and beneficial-insect habitat, not repellence. Treat the deterrent reputation as a bonus, not a control method.

beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week before planting them out, and move them in their biodegradable pots so you do not disturb the roots.

beginner: Lavender likes poor, dry, gritty soil and full sun. That sounds backward, but it comes from the dry Mediterranean hills, so rich, damp soil actually makes it weak and rot-prone. If your soil is heavy clay, mix in coarse material so water drains fast, and skip the compost.
seasoned: Lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun. Lavender is a Mediterranean sub-shrub that does best in poor, dry ground with very little organic matter; rich, moist soil produces soft, floppy growth and invites root rot. Amend heavy clay for drainage before planting rather than adding fertility.

beginner: Lavender likes soil that is neutral to a little bit chalky (about pH 6.5 to 7.5, and it copes up to around 8.0). If your soil is on the acidic side, a small amount of garden lime nudges it where lavender wants it.
seasoned: Lavender prefers a near-neutral to slightly alkaline soil, roughly pH 6.5 to 7.5, and tolerates alkaline ground up to about 8.0. In acidic soils a light addition of garden lime brings the pH up. This alkaline tolerance is part of why it suits dry-climate and high-pH gardens.

beginner: The trick with lavender is to not fuss over it. Give it the sunniest, driest, best-draining spot you have, water it deeply but only once in a while, and do not feed it much. After it finishes blooming, trim about a third off the leafy green growth (never down into the hard woody stems) so it stays bushy instead of going leggy.
seasoned: Treat lavender mean: full sun, lean fast-draining soil, deep but infrequent water, and almost no feeding. Overwatering and rich soil are the top killers, not cold. Shear it back by about a third after bloom every year, cutting into green growth only and never into the bare woody base.

beginner: Lavender barely needs feeding, and too much fertilizer actually hurts it. A little compost mixed in when you plant is enough. Feed it heavily and you get a big leafy plant with few flowers that is more likely to get sick or die back in winter.
seasoned: Lavender has very low fertility needs and is one of the few plants you can harm by feeding. A single inch of compost worked in at planting, or one application of a slow-release fertilizer for the season, is plenty. Over-fertilized plants put on lush foliage at the expense of flowers and fragrance and become more prone to disease and winter injury.

beginner: A little compost at planting, and usually nothing after that.

beginner: Plant lavender next to other plants that also like full sun and dry soil, such as drought-tolerant perennials. Keep it away from plants that need a lot of water, because the wet soil those plants want will rot your lavender.
seasoned: Lavender pairs naturally with other sun-loving, low-water plants that share its lean, dry, sharply drained conditions; group it with drought-tolerant perennials rather than thirsty, rich-soil neighbors. As a strong pollinator draw it also supports nearby flowering plants. Avoid siting it among plants that need frequent water, which forces conditions that rot lavender.

beginner: Likes the same sunny, dry spot and brings in pollinators.
seasoned: Echinacea is one of the most reliable lavender partners because it asks for the same things: full sun, lean soil, and not much water. That shared appetite is the real reason it works, you can run the whole bed on a waterwise schedule without the overwatering that rots lavender at the crown. The broad, flat coneflower heads also play off lavender's narrow spikes, and the two bloom together as a pollinator draw. Site them in the same free-draining ground and resist the urge to pamper either.

beginner: Another sun-and-dry-soil plant that grows happily next to lavender.
seasoned: Salvia and lavender are natural bedfellows, many ornamental salvias are cousins of culinary sage and want the identical conditions: full sun, sharp drainage, low water. Growing them together means one easy, dry-loving border rather than a watering compromise. The salvia's flower spikes echo lavender's shape while often blooming longer into the season, and both keep the bees busy. Plant in the same lean, well-drained soil and water sparingly once established.

beginner: Tough and drought-tolerant, so it shares lavender's conditions.
seasoned: Rudbeckia is a tough prairie native that thrives on the same neglect lavender does, full sun, poor-to-average soil, and minimal water once it is going. That makes it an easy companion that will not pull the bed toward the rich, damp conditions lavender hates. Its golden, dark-eyed daisies are a bold contrast to lavender's purple haze, and both feed pollinators through summer. Keep the soil lean and well-drained for both.

beginner: Easygoing and handles dry soil well alongside lavender.
seasoned: Daylilies are nearly indestructible and add bold strappy foliage and big blooms next to lavender's fine texture, which is why the pairing is popular. One honest caveat for the seasoned eye: daylilies are happy in richer, moister soil than lavender's lean, dry, sharply-drained ideal, so site them at the edge of the dry border rather than in the heart of it, and water to the lavender's tune (sparingly) so you do not push the lavender toward crown rot. A handsome combination as long as you manage to lavender's drier standard.

beginner: Blobs of white froth that look like spit on the stems in late spring, with a tiny bug hidden inside. It looks worse than it is.
seasoned: Frothy white spit-like foam on stems in late spring, with the small nymph hidden inside. It looks alarming but rarely harms an established lavender plant.

beginner: Young spittlebugs hiding in the foam while they feed. There are usually only a few, and they do little real harm.
seasoned: Spittlebug nymphs, which shelter inside their own foam while feeding on plant sap. Numbers are usually low and the damage is mostly cosmetic.

beginner: If the froth bothers you, spray it off with a hose. You usually do not need to do anything else.
seasoned: Knock them off with a strong spray of water if you find them unsightly. No treatment is needed for plant health in most cases.

beginner: Nothing special is needed. Giving plants room and not overwatering keeps lavender healthy enough to handle small pests.
seasoned: No specific prevention is warranted. Keeping plants spaced for airflow and not overwatering keeps lavender vigorous enough to shrug off minor pests.

seasoned: Occasional clusters of tiny white flies or soft aphids on new growth, most likely on stressed or overcrowded plants in poor conditions rather than on healthy lavender.

seasoned: Sap-feeding insects that occasionally find lavender. Lavender has few pests overall and is typically grown with little or no pesticide.

beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap if there are a lot. Giving the plant more air and removing stress usually fixes it.
seasoned: Rinse them off with water or use insecticidal soap if numbers climb. Removing nearby stressors and improving airflow usually resolves it.

beginner: Keep lavender in full sun with room around it, dry lean soil, and not too much water. Healthy plants rarely get these bugs.
seasoned: Give plants full sun, lean soil, and good spacing, and avoid overwatering. Vigorous, unstressed lavender rarely attracts these pests.

beginner: Leaves yellow and the plant wilts and dies back even though the soil is wet, often with a dark, rotted spot where the stems meet the ground. This is the main disease that kills lavender, and it comes from staying too wet.
seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, and dieback that does not recover with watering, often with a darkened, decayed crown at the soil line. It is the disease of concern for lavender and is tied to wet conditions and poor drainage.

beginner: A rot that takes hold when soil stays soggy and drains badly, attacking the roots and base. The real cause is wet soil, not cold weather.
seasoned: Water mold pathogens that thrive in saturated, poorly drained soil and attack the roots and crown. Wet feet, not cold, is the underlying cause.

beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fix, so pull out and throw away affected plants. The answer is preventing it with good drainage, not curing it.
seasoned: There is no cure once the crown is rotting; remove and discard affected plants. Focus everything on prevention through drainage rather than rescue.

beginner: Plant in well-draining soil in full sun, water deeply but rarely, and never let lavender sit in soggy ground. On heavy clay, plant on a mound or raised bed and give plants room.
seasoned: Plant in sharply drained soil in full sun, water deeply but infrequently, and never let lavender sit in wet ground. On clay, use a mound or raised bed, and space plants for airflow.

beginner: Small spots on the leaves, more likely in damp weather or on crowded plants. It is a minor problem next to root rot.
seasoned: Small spots or blotches on the foliage, more likely in humid weather or on crowded, poorly ventilated plants. It is a minor issue compared with root and crown rot.

beginner: Leaf fungi that like damp, still air around the plant. Crowding and watering from above make it worse.
seasoned: Foliar fungi favored by damp, still air around the plant. Crowding and overhead watering raise the risk.

beginner: Pick off the spotted leaves, give the plant more air, and water at the soil instead of over the top. The yearly trim helps too.
seasoned: Remove affected foliage, improve airflow, and water at the base rather than overhead. The annual cut-back also helps clear and renew the canopy.

beginner: Leave 2 to 3 feet between plants for airflow, plant in full sun, and avoid watering over the leaves. Good air movement is the main thing.
seasoned: Space plants at least 2 to 3 feet apart for air circulation, site in full sun, and avoid overhead watering. Good airflow is the main defense.

beginner: Water deeply but not often. A new plant wants about a soak a week until it settles in; an established lavender needs only a little water every couple of weeks, with a bit more while it is flowering.
seasoned: Deep and infrequent. After planting, water about once a week until established; mature plants need roughly half a gallon every two weeks until flower buds form, then once or twice a week through bloom and harvest.

beginner: Roughly a gallon a week for a new plant, then much less once it is established.
seasoned: About 1 gallon per plant per week while establishing; roughly 1/2 gallon every two weeks once mature, until bud formation.

beginner: Pour water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves, and let it dry out before watering again. Wet leaves and a soggy crown are what make lavender rot.
seasoned: Water at the base and let the soil dry between waterings. Avoid wetting the foliage and crown, which invites root and crown rot.

beginner: If leaves yellow and shoots wilt or die back even though you are watering, the problem is almost always too much water, not too little. Soggy roots rot.
seasoned: Yellowing leaves, wilting or dieback of whole shoots, and a plant that fails despite regular watering signal too-wet roots and likely Phytophthora root or crown rot, not drought.

beginner: Lavender almost never gets too little water once established. A little droop on a very hot afternoon that bounces back by morning is fine.
seasoned: Established lavender rarely shows true drought stress; brief wilting in extreme heat that recovers overnight is normal and not a reason to increase watering.

beginner: Water a new lavender about a soak a week until it settles in, roughly a gallon a plant. Water at the base and let the soil dry between waterings, keeping the crown dry.
seasoned: The first season after planting is the only time regular watering matters: water a new lavender about once a week, roughly a gallon per plant, until it is established. Water at the base and let the soil dry between waterings, keeping the foliage and crown dry against Phytophthora root and crown rot.

beginner: Once established, cut way back: a mature lavender needs only a little water every couple of weeks, with a bit more while it is flowering. More lavender dies from too much water than too little, so when in doubt, water less.
seasoned: Once established, taper off sharply: a mature lavender needs only about half a gallon every two weeks until flower buds form, then once or twice a week through bloom and harvest. beginner: In winter an established lavender needs almost no water. Soggy winter soil rots the crown, so make sure it drains well and never sits wet.
seasoned: Through dormancy an established lavender wants next to no water; wet winter soil around the crown is the classic killer, so ensure sharp drainage and do not let a dormant plant sit wet.

beginner: Remember: more lavender dies from too much water than too little.
seasoned: The single most common way to kill lavender is overwatering. When in doubt, water less.

beginner: The easy and reliable way to grow lavender is to buy a small plant, or take a cutting from an existing one. Growing it from seed is slow and unpredictable, and seed-grown plants often do not match the parent, so most gardeners skip it. If you do want to grow it from seed, chill the seed in the refrigerator for a few weeks first, then surface-sow it and do not cover it, since it needs light to sprout; keep it around 70°F, start indoors about 10 weeks before your last frost, and be patient, because it comes up slowly and unevenly.

To raise it from seed anyway, cold-stratify the seed for three to six weeks (moist, in the refrigerator) to improve and even germination, then surface-sow at about 70°F since light aids germination, starting indoors roughly 10 weeks before the last frost; expect slow, erratic emergence.

beginner: There are a few kinds of lavender. English lavender (like Munstead or Hidcote) is the toughest and the one you cook with, so it is the best all-rounder. The big hybrid types (lavandins like Grosso) are great for drying and scent. The frilly Spanish and French types are pretty but not cold-hardy and are mainly for looks, grown in pots in cold areas. If you want just one plant, choose an English lavender.
seasoned: Lavender reaches the grower as four practical groups on one plant page. English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia, e.g. Munstead and Hidcote) is the hardiest and the type used in cooking. Lavandins (L. x intermedia, e.g. Grosso and Phenomenal) are larger, vigorous hybrids best for drying and oil and nearly as hardy. Spanish (L. stoechas) and French (L. dentata) lavenders are tender, showy, ornamental-only types grown in pots and overwintered indoors where winters are cold. Pick English if you want one hardy plant for both the garden and the kitchen.

It is the toughest kind and comes back year after year in zones 5, 6, and 7, where it lives in the ground, flowers in early summer, and gets trimmed back after it blooms. beginner: Lavender is a small woody shrub with silvery leaves and fragrant purple flower spikes in summer. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor dry soil, and very little water, and it actually does worse if you pamper it. The one job that matters is trimming it back every year after it flowers so it stays bushy instead of turning into bare woody sticks. English lavender is the hardy, cook-with-it kind; the frillier Spanish and French types are mainly for looks and are not cold-hardy.
seasoned: Lavender is a woody Mediterranean perennial sub-shrub in the mint family, grown for its fragrant summer flower spikes and silvery, aromatic foliage. It thrives on neglect in full sun and lean, sharply drained soil, and its defining care act is an annual hard cut-back after bloom that keeps it compact and prevents it from going woody and splitting open. English lavender is both the hardiest type and the one used in cooking, while the showy Spanish and French types are tender and ornamental.

beginner: For a fresh vase, cut the stems when about half the little buds on the spike have opened. For drying or cooking, cut a bit sooner, when just the first couple of buds have opened. Cut in the morning once the dew has dried, when lavender smells strongest.
seasoned: Cut for fresh bouquets when about half the buds on a spike have opened; cut for drying or culinary use a little earlier, when only the first one or two buds on the spike have opened, so the buds hold their color and oils. Harvest in the morning after the dew dries but before the heat, when the fragrance is most concentrated.

beginner: English lavender is the toughest and comes back year after year in most of the country (about zones 5 to 9, and zone 4 if you protect it). The showy Spanish and French types are not cold-hardy, so in cold areas grow them in pots you bring inside for winter. Just as important as cold: lavender hates wet feet in winter and will rot in soggy soil.
seasoned: English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) is the hardiest type, reliably perennial in roughly zones 5 to 9 and surviving zone 4 with good drainage and winter protection. Lavandins are nearly as hardy. Spanish and French lavenders are tender (about zone 7 to 8 and warmer) and are grown as container plants brought in for winter in colder regions. Good drainage matters as much as cold: lavender rots in wet winter soil before cold alone kills it.
