beginner: Sunflowers are easy, fast, cheerful flowers grown both for their blooms and for edible seeds that people and birds love. They come in a huge range: towering giants over 10 feet tall with one big head, bushy branching types with lots of smaller flowers, and little dwarf kinds under 2 feet for pots. Plant the large seeds straight into warm soil after your last frost, because sunflowers have a deep taproot and do not like being moved. They love heat and full sun and handle dry spells well. Young plants turn to follow the sun across the sky, and the open flowers bring in bees and butterflies. Watch out: birds and squirrels will raid the ripening seed heads, so cover them if you want to save the seeds. One thing to know is that sunflowers can hold back a few nearby plants with natural chemicals from their roots and old stalks, so it is smart to plant them along an edge.
seasoned: Sunflower (Helianthus annuus) is a fast, warm-season, frost-tender annual in the Asteraceae family, native to North America and grown both as an ornamental and for its edible, wildlife-valuable seed. Cultivars range enormously: from single-stem giants that top 10 feet with one massive head, to multi-branching types that carry many smaller blooms, to dwarf forms under 2 feet for pots and edging, in oilseed, confection, and pollen-free cut-flower classes. It is direct-sown into warm soil after frost (the big taproot resents transplanting), thrives in heat, full sun, and even lean soil, and is notably drought-tolerant once established. Young plants are heliotropic, tracking the sun east to west by day, while mature heads settle facing east. The flowers are a major pollinator and beneficial-insect draw, and the ripening seed heads are a magnet for birds and squirrels. Note its mild allelopathy: roots and decomposing residue release compounds that can suppress some neighboring plants, so it is best sited at a bed edge.

beginner: Sunflowers are not fussy and grow in most ordinary garden soil as long as water drains away and does not pool. A deep, loose, well-drained soil suits their long taproot best. They tolerate sandy, clay loam, and silty soils, but soggy, heavy clay that stays wet can rot the roots. Mixing in some compost helps, especially for the big branching and large-flowered types, which are hungrier feeders.
seasoned: Sunflowers do best in deep, loose, well-drained soil that lets the taproot run, and they tolerate a wide range of textures including clay loam, silty clay loam, and sandy loam; the consistent failure is wet, poorly drained ground that rots roots and invites stalk rot. They are moderate to heavy feeders, especially the multi-branching and large single-flowered types, so soil enriched with composted organic matter plus a slow-release fertilizer supports the biggest plants and heads. Excess nitrogen, however, gives soft, leafy, weak-stalked growth prone to lodging, so favor balanced fertility over a high-nitrogen push.

beginner: Sunflowers are easygoing about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A range around 6.0 to 7.5 is ideal, and most garden soil is already fine, so you usually do not need to change anything. They even tolerate slightly alkaline soil.
seasoned: Sunflowers perform best across roughly 6.0 to 7.5 and are tolerant of soils a little outside that, including mildly alkaline ground up to about 8.0. pH adjustment is rarely warranted; focus instead on drainage and depth for the taproot rather than on fine-tuning acidity.

beginner: Wait until the soil is warm before planting sunflower seeds outside, about a week after your last frost; plant them an inch deep and they sprout in 7 to 10 days. Plant the seeds right where they will grow, because sunflowers have a deep root and do not like being moved. Space small types about 6 inches apart, medium ones about a foot, and the big branching or giant ones 18 to 24 inches apart. Tie tall sunflowers to a stake so wind does not topple them. When the seed heads start to ripen, cover them with a paper bag or cheesecloth if you want to keep the seeds, or the birds will get them first.
seasoned: Soil warmth, not the calendar, is the germination trigger: direct-sow about 1 inch deep once soil is past 50 °F and warming (ideally 70 to 85 °F) after frost, and seedlings emerge in 7 to 10 days. Direct sowing is strongly preferred because the taproot resents disturbance; if you must start indoors, use biodegradable pots and transplant young, before the taproot develops. Match spacing to type: roughly 6 inches for small cut-flower singles, 12 inches for mid-size, and 18 to 24 inches for branching and giant types. Stake tall single-stem giants against wind, and as seed heads ripen, bag them in paper or cheesecloth to beat the birds if you want the seed.

beginner: Sunflowers, especially the big branching and large-flowered kinds, are fairly hungry plants. beginner: Water the ground around the plant, not the leaves, using a soaker hose or watering can at the base. Dry leaves get less disease. Water deeply so it soaks down to the deep root. If leaves do get wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday.

beginner: Sunflower seeds are something you can actually store, unlike most cut flowers. After you dry the heads until the backs are brown and the seeds come off easily, keep the dried seeds in an airtight jar somewhere cool and dark. They last several months at room temperature. Check now and then that they are still dry and not mouldy. Flowers cut for a vase are just enjoyed fresh.
seasoned: Sunflower seed is a real, storable harvest, unlike a pure cut flower. Once heads are cured until the backs are brown and dry and the seeds part easily, thoroughly dried seed keeps for several months at cool room temperature in an airtight container, away from light and humidity; check periodically for any sign of moisture, mold, or insects. Heads cut for the vase are enjoyed fresh, not stored.

beginner: To keep sunflower seeds longer, put the well-dried seeds in a sealed container in the fridge, where they stay good for up to a year. The cold keeps the oils in the seed from going stale. This works for seeds to eat and seeds to plant next year.
seasoned: For longer keeping, hold thoroughly dried seed (in-hull or hulled) in a sealed container in the refrigerator, where it stays fresh for up to a year; the cold slows the seed oils from going rancid. This suits both eating seed and seed saved for next year.

beginner: For the longest storage, freeze well-dried sunflower seeds in a sealed container, where they keep for a year or more, whether you are saving them to plant or to eat. Let them warm up still sealed so water does not collect on them.
seasoned: Fully dried sunflower seed freezes well in an airtight container for long-term storage of a year or more, useful for saved planting seed or eating seed; thaw it still sealed so condensation does not form on the seed.

beginner: Sunflowers give you both flowers and edible seeds, so unlike most cut flowers there is a harvest to store. The main thing is to dry the seeds completely: hang cut heads in a warm, dry, airy place safe from mice until the seeds come off easily, then store them dry. For flowers in a vase, cut when the bloom is just opening, trim the stem, pull off the lower leaves, and use clean water; they last about a week. If you want the seeds, cover the ripening heads so birds and squirrels do not eat them first.
seasoned: Sunflower is grown both for ornament and for an edible, wildlife-valuable seed crop, so it does have a harvest to store. The key to good storage is full drying: cure cut heads in a warm, dry, airy, rodent-free spot until the seeds rattle loose, then store dry as above. For cut flowers, cut when the bloom is just opening, recut the stem, strip lower leaves below the waterline, and use clean water; vase life is roughly a week, longer for pollen-free types. If you are growing for seed, protect ripening heads from birds and squirrels, which strip them fast.

beginner: Pick the type for your goal. For big edible or bird seeds, grow the giant kinds like 'Mammoth', which make one huge head but need a stake and lots of room. For cutting flowers for a vase, pollen-free single-stem types like the ProCut series are clean and tidy, while branching types like 'Autumn Beauty' and 'Lemon Queen' make lots of smaller flowers over a long time and are best for bees. For pots and small spaces, dwarf types like 'Teddy Bear' stay short. Open, single flowers with pollen are the best ones for bees and butterflies.
seasoned: Choose by purpose and size. For edible or bird seed, the giant single-stem types ('Mammoth', 'Sunzilla', 'American Giant') deliver one large head of plump seed but need staking and 18 to 24 inches of space. For cutting, single-stem pollen-free types (ProCut series, 'Italian White') give clean, uniform, mess-free stems and succession-sow well, while branching types ('Autumn Beauty', 'Lemon Queen') carry many smaller blooms over a long window and are the best pollinator and color choice. For pots, edging, and small spaces, dwarf types ('Teddy Bear', 'Sunspot', 'Music Box') stay under 2 to 3 feet. Open, single, pollen-bearing flowers feed pollinators best; pollen-free cut-flower types trade that for vase tidiness.

beginner: Sunflowers are mainly grown for their own flowers and seeds, but they are a strong pollinator and beneficial-insect plant, so they help the wider garden too. Their open heads, made of hundreds of tiny flowers, bring in bees, butterflies, and helpful predator insects, and the ripening seeds feed birds. Tall, sturdy types can act as a natural trellis or windbreak for vining crops like cucumbers, squash, and melons, which also benefit from the extra pollinators. The honest catch is allelopathy: sunflower roots and old stalks release natural chemicals that can hold back some plants, especially potatoes and pole beans, and the hulls can stop seeds from sprouting. So plant sunflowers along an edge rather than in the middle of sensitive crops, and clean up the stalks and dropped hulls at season end.
seasoned: Sunflower is grown chiefly for itself, but it earns a place in the wider garden as a pollinator and beneficial-insect powerhouse: the composite heads supply abundant nectar and pollen to bees (including specialist sunflower bees), butterflies, and predatory and parasitic insects, and the seed heads are a documented wildlife and bird food. Sturdy tall types double as a living trellis or windbreak for cucurbits, which tolerate sunflower's allelopathy and gain from the pollinator traffic. The load-bearing honest caveat is that allelopathy: Helianthus annuus is a recognized allelopathic species (roots, residue, and seed hulls release growth-inhibiting compounds), best documented as a weed-suppressing cover-crop trait but also capable of stunting sensitive neighbors. Site sunflowers at a bed edge, not amid sensitive crops, keep potatoes and pole beans clear, and remove residue and spilled hulls at season end. There is no concurrent pairing that is broadly antagonistic to the sunflower itself; the antagonism runs the other way, from sunflower to certain neighbors.

beginner: A sunflower head is hundreds of tiny flowers, so it brings in lots of bees and butterflies, plus helpful bugs that eat pests. Planting sunflowers along the edge of a vegetable garden is a great way to support pollinators.
seasoned: Sunflower's best-supported companion function. The composite head offers abundant, accessible nectar and pollen across a long bloom, drawing honey bees, native and specialist sunflower bees, butterflies (a noted late-season nectar source for monarchs), and predatory and parasitic insects that help manage aphids and caterpillars elsewhere in the garden. Single, pollen-bearing types serve pollinators far better than pollen-free cut-flower selections. Plant as an insectary edge or border near the vegetable garden.

beginner: Tall, strong sunflowers can act like a living pole for vining cucumbers, squash, and melons to climb, and they pull in the bees these crops need to set fruit. These vine crops handle sunflowers nearby better than most.
seasoned: A well-grounded structural and pollinator pairing. Cucurbits need many bee visits per flower for proper set, and sunflower is a reliable, long-blooming pollinator magnet; the sturdy stalks of tall single-stem types also serve as a living trellis or windbreak. Cucurbits, corn, and squash are noted to tolerate sunflower allelopathy comparatively well, unlike potatoes and pole beans. Site sunflowers on the windward or northern edge so they support rather than shade the crop, a visitation-and-structure benefit, not a pest-control one.

beginner: Left to ripen and dry on the plant, sunflower heads become a natural bird feeder that finches and other birds love through fall and winter. This is wonderful for wildlife, but it is the opposite of what you want if you are trying to save the seeds for yourself.
seasoned: A deliberate wildlife-gardening use rather than a crop interaction. Standing heads left to ripen are a documented food source for finches, jays, and other seed-eating birds (and small mammals) into fall and winter, so dead heads left on the plant function as natural bird feeders. The tension is direct: this is mutually exclusive with saving seed for yourself, which requires bagging the heads. Choose the use per planting.

beginner: Sunflowers can hold back potatoes growing right next to them, because of natural chemicals from the sunflower's roots and old stalks. Keep potatoes out of the sunflower bed, and plant sunflowers along an edge instead.
seasoned: Sunflower allelopathy in action. Helianthus annuus releases growth-inhibiting compounds from roots and decomposing residue, and potatoes are among the crops commonly reported as sensitive, showing stunting near sunflowers or in soil where they grew. The species-level allelopathy is documented by extension sources; the potato-specific call is well-reported tradition rather than a single trial, so keep potatoes out of the sunflower bed, avoid following sunflower with potatoes in the same soil, and clear residue and hulls.

beginner: Pole beans are another crop that sunflowers can slow down when planted close, so do not use a sunflower as a bean pole. Grow beans elsewhere and use cucumbers or squash near sunflowers instead.
seasoned: A hedged allelopathy caution. Pole and runner beans are traditionally listed among crops sensitive to sunflower's allelochemicals, so despite the tempting idea of using a sunflower stalk as a bean trellis, the pairing is commonly discouraged. Note the honest uncertainty: reports conflict, and some sources hold that beans tolerate sunflower better than potatoes do. Treat it as a cautious, traditional avoidance, favor cucurbits for the living-trellis role, and keep beans in a separate bed.

beginner: The hulls that drop from sunflower seeds (including under bird feeders) carry chemicals that can stop other seeds from sprouting and stunt small plants. Do not start a seedbed right under sunflowers or a feeder, and rake up fallen hulls.
seasoned: The residue side of sunflower allelopathy. Seed hulls are the most-cited source of the inhibitory compounds, the reason a bare, weed-free patch often forms under a sunflower-seed bird feeder. Avoid sowing a fresh seedbed directly beneath sunflowers or a feeder, rake up accumulated hulls, and do not mulch sensitive beds with sunflower residue. This is a residue-management caution rather than a living-plant antagonism, and it is part of why sunflower works as a weed-suppressing cover crop.

beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they get used to sun and wind before planting them out, and be gentle with the roots.
seasoned: Any indoor-started transplants need 7 to 10 days of hardening off, increasing outdoor exposure gradually, before setting out after all frost danger has passed; handle the rootball gently, since sunflowers resent root disturbance.

beginner: The best way is to sow sunflower seeds straight into warm garden soil (about 1 inch deep) after your last frost; they sprout in 7 to 10 days. Sunflowers have a deep root and do not like being moved, so plant them where they will grow. If your season is short, you can start a few indoors 2 to 3 weeks before the last frost in biodegradable pots and move them out gently, pot and all. Put a stake in for tall types early, before the big flower makes them top-heavy.
seasoned: Direct sowing is the strongly preferred method: sunflowers form a deep taproot early and resent transplanting, so sow seed about 1 inch deep into warmed soil (past 50 °F, ideally 70 to 85 °F) after frost, and they germinate in 7 to 10 days. To gain a couple of weeks in short seasons, start indoors only 2 to 3 weeks before last frost in biodegradable pots and transplant before the taproot circles, disturbing roots minimally. Thin to type-appropriate spacing once seedlings are up. Stake tall single-stem giants early so the support is in place before the head gets top-heavy.

beginner: Sunflowers are in the daisy family (Asteraceae). Do not plant sunflowers, or other daisy-family plants, in the same spot the next year, especially if there was any stalk or head rot, since that fungus stays in the soil. Because sunflowers leave behind chemicals that can slow some plants, also avoid planting potatoes right where sunflowers grew, and rake up old stalks and hulls first.
seasoned: As an aster-family (Asteraceae) annual, avoid following sunflower immediately with itself or other susceptible asters where soilborne disease has built up, especially Sclerotinia (white mold), which persists in soil for years; rotate to an unrelated family for a season or more. beginner: Rotating sunflowers helps more than it does for many flowers, because their main diseases live in the soil. On the useful side, sunflowers are sometimes grown on purpose as a cover crop to hold down weeds, using the same natural chemicals that mean you should not follow them with touchy crops like potatoes.
seasoned: Rotation matters more for sunflower than for many ornamentals because its key diseases are soilborne and persistent. Avoid planting sunflower on the same ground in back-to-back years, particularly where Sclerotinia, downy mildew, or rust appeared, and clear infected debris at season end. Used deliberately, sunflower is also a recognized weed-suppressing cover crop thanks to the same allelopathy that cautions against following it with sensitive vegetables.

beginner: Plant the seeds about an inch deep. Keep an eye out for birds and cutworms, which like to eat the big sprouting seeds.

beginner: Cutworms can cut down young sunflowers at night. Put a little collar of cardboard or foil around the stem of a new seedling, and clear weeds before planting. Bigger plants are not bothered.

beginner: Put a stake in for tall sunflowers early, before the heavy flower forms, so wind does not topple them. Branching types hold themselves up. Go easy on high-nitrogen fertilizer so the stems stay strong.

beginner: Young sunflowers turn to follow the sun across the sky during the day, then face east again by morning. As they get older, the flowers settle facing east for good. This is normal and even helps bring in bees.
seasoned: Young plants and buds are heliotropic, tracking the sun east to west by day and resetting east overnight; as heads mature and stems stiffen they settle facing east, which warms them at sunrise and draws more morning pollinators. This is normal, not a problem.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist as the bud forms. The weeks just before and after flowering are the most important time to water, or you get a smaller flower and fewer seeds. Water deeply, but do not make the soil soggy.
seasoned: Keep moisture even as the head forms; the roughly 20 days before and after flowering are the critical water window, when shortage cuts head size and seed fill. Water deeply to the taproot, never to saturation.

beginner: As the flower opens, check for head pests: sunflower moth caterpillars web and tunnel the head, and the head-clipping weevil chops the stalk just below the flower. The best fixes are cleaning up old stalks and not planting sunflowers in the same spot each year.
seasoned: Scout opening heads for sunflower moth (webbing and tunneled seeds) and the head-clipping weevil (a girdle 1 to 2 inches below the head that drops it). Garden management is sanitation and rotation, not routine spraying.

beginner: For a vase, cut sunflowers just as they open, trim the stem, and pull off the lower leaves; pollen-free kinds stay neatest. Snip faded flowers off branching types for more blooms. Leave the flowers on the plant if you want seeds instead.

beginner: Open sunflowers with pollen are great for bees and butterflies, and the visiting bees also help the plant make more seeds. The pollen-free types meant for vases do not feed bees, so grow some regular ones too if you want to help pollinators.
seasoned: Open, pollen-bearing flowers are a major nectar and pollen source for honey bees, native and specialist sunflower bees, and butterflies; pollinator visitation also improves the plant's own seed set. Pollen-free cut-flower types trade this away for vase tidiness.

beginner: If you want the seeds, cover the heads with a paper bag or cheesecloth once the petals turn brown, or birds and squirrels will get them first. If you would rather feed the birds, just leave the heads standing as a natural bird feeder.
seasoned: To save seed, bag ripening heads in paper sacks or cheesecloth once petals brown; birds and squirrels otherwise strip a head fast. The same standing heads make excellent natural bird feeders if you would rather feed wildlife.

beginner: How much you get depends on the type. A giant sunflower makes one big head full of seeds, sometimes over a foot wide. A single-stem giant produces one large head (often 8 to 14 inches or more across) yielding a substantial crop of seed; branching types produce many smaller heads over a longer window, ideal for cut flowers and pollinators but smaller individual seed heads; dwarf types give modest blooms for color. A well-grown large head can hold many hundreds to over a thousand seeds.

beginner: Sunflowers give you two harvests. For a vase, cut the flowers just as they open, in the morning, into clean water, and pull off the lower leaves; pollen-free types stay neatest. For seeds, leave the heads on the plant until the back turns brown and the seeds are plump and firm, about a month after the flower opens. Cover the ripening heads with a paper bag or cheesecloth so birds and squirrels do not get them, then cut the head and dry it somewhere warm and airy until the seeds come loose.

For seed, let heads ripen on the plant until the back turns from yellow to brown, the florets dry, and the seeds plump and firm (about 30 to 45 days after bloom); bag ripening heads in paper or cheesecloth to beat birds and squirrels, then cut and cure the head in a warm, dry, airy, rodent-free spot until the seeds release.

beginner: Borage is a big, easy, bushy herb with fuzzy leaves and beautiful blue, star-shaped flowers. Bees absolutely love it, which is why gardeners plant it near vegetables like tomatoes, squash, and strawberries. The young leaves taste like cucumber, and both the leaves and the blue flowers are edible, though you should eat them only in small amounts. Borage grows fast, sprawls out, so give it room, and it drops seed and comes back on its own year after year. It likes the warm part of the year in most gardens and is killed by frost; in hot, humid places it is grown in the cooler months instead.
seasoned: Borage (Borago officinalis), also called starflower, is a large, fast-growing, frost-tender annual herb in the borage family (Boraginaceae), native to the Mediterranean. It builds a bushy, sprawling plant about 2 to 3 ft tall and 1 to 2 ft wide, clothed in coarse, bristly, gray-green leaves, and carries loose clusters of nodding, star-shaped, sky-blue flowers from late spring into fall. Borage is one of the best bee and pollinator plants a garden can grow, a traditional companion set near tomatoes, squash, and strawberries, and a vigorous self-seeder that naturalizes readily once established. Both the cucumber-flavored young leaves and the blue flowers are edible, used fresh as a garnish and in drinks and salads, though borage is best eaten in moderation. It grows through the warm months in cool and temperate regions and is killed by hard frost; in hot, humid climates it is grown instead as a cool-season plant.

beginner: Borage is not fussy about soil and grows well even in poor ground, as long as water drains away and does not pool. Ordinary, well-drained garden soil is perfect. Very rich soil just makes big floppy plants, and soggy soil rots the roots, so pick a spot that drains well and go easy on the compost.
seasoned: Borage is highly adaptable and grows in almost any soil, including poor and sandy ground, provided drainage is adequate; extension descriptions list it as tolerating clay, loam, and sand and even nutritionally poor soil. It is a light feeder, so overly rich soil pushes soft, floppy, leafy growth at the expense of sturdiness and bloom, and constantly wet, poorly drained soil rots its roots. Well-drained soil of moderate to low fertility gives the best-structured plants.

beginner: Borage is not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range of about 6.0 to 7.0 is ideal, and it tolerates soil well outside that, so you usually do not need to change anything.
seasoned: Borage performs best across roughly 6.0 to 7.0 and is broadly adaptable to soil chemistry; extension descriptions record it growing in acid, neutral, and alkaline soils alike (tolerating roughly 5.5 to 8.0). pH adjustment is rarely warranted, so focus on drainage and modest fertility instead.

beginner: Plant borage seeds right where you want it to grow, since it does not like being moved. Sow after your last frost in most gardens, or in the cool season where summers are hot. Cover the seeds about half an inch deep; they sprout in a week or two and flower in about eight weeks. Give each plant plenty of room because it gets big and sprawly, keep it in sun, and do not over-fertilize. Snip off faded flowers for more blooms, let a few go to seed so it comes back, and wear gloves because the stems are prickly.
seasoned: Grow borage like a big, easygoing warm-season herb: direct-sow it where it is to grow, because it has a taproot and does not transplant well. Sow after the last spring frost in cool and temperate regions, or in fall and the cool season in hot, humid ones, covering the seed about 1/2 in. It germinates in 1 to 2 weeks and reaches first bloom in roughly 8 weeks. Give it room (12 to 24 in), full sun, and lean soil, go very light on fertilizer, and deadhead or cut flowers to prolong bloom. Leave a few late flowers to drop seed and it returns on its own; wear gloves, since the stems are prickly.

Those pest-fighting claims are garden tradition rather than proven fact, so enjoy borage mainly as a pollinator plant. Those neighbor-benefit and pest-repellent effects are traditional practice rather than trialed results, so they are framed as tradition. beginner: Calendula, also called pot marigold, is an easy, cheerful flower for cool weather. It is not the same plant as the marigolds you may know (those are a different plant called Tagetes). Calendula handles light frost, blooms in the cool parts of the year, spring and fall, and right through winter in mild-winter areas, but it fades and stops flowering in hot summer weather. The gold and orange petals are edible and add color to food, and the flowers have long been used in skin creams and salves. seasoned: Calendula (Calendula officinalis), commonly called pot marigold, is a cool-season, frost-tolerant annual in the Asteraceae family, native to the Mediterranean. Despite the name, it is not a true marigold (those are Tagetes); it is a separate genus grown for single to double daisy-form blooms in gold, orange, yellow, and apricot. It thrives in the cool shoulders of the year, blooming almost continuously from spring or fall sowings, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones, but it languishes and stops flowering once sustained summer heat above roughly 85°F sets in. Plants tolerate frost to about 25°F, self-seed readily, and rebloom well with deadheading. The petals are edible, lending a saffron-like color to food, and calendula has a long traditional use in skin salves.

beginner: Calendula is easygoing and grows in most ordinary garden soil as long as water drains away and does not pool. Moderately fertile, well-drained soil is ideal. seasoned: Calendula wants well-drained, moderately fertile loam but is highly adaptable to a wide range of soil textures, from sand to clay, provided drainage is adequate. The consistent failure is wet, poorly drained soil, which rots roots and crowns, especially in the cool, damp conditions calendula otherwise favors. It is a light feeder, so very rich soil pushes soft foliage at the expense of bloom and invites disease.

beginner: Plant calendula in cool weather, not summer heat. Sow the seeds in early spring and again in late summer or fall (and through winter where winters are mild). They sprout in a week or two and flower in about 6 to 8 weeks. Go easy on fertilizer, snip off faded flowers to keep more coming, and know that hot summer weather will slow or stop the blooms. seasoned: Treat calendula like a cool-season crop, the way you would spinach or lettuce: direct-sow into cool soil near 60°F, in early spring and again in late summer or fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones. It germinates in 1 to 2 weeks and reaches first bloom in about 6 to 8 weeks. Go light on nitrogen, deadhead or cut for the vase to sustain bloom, and expect it to fade once sustained heat above about 85°F arrives. Leave a few heads to drop seed and it returns on its own.

seasoned: Zinnia is a cut flower, not a stored edible, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply. For vase life, recut stems on arrival, strip leaves below the waterline, use clean water with floral preservative, and keep blooms out of direct sun and away from ripening fruit. beginner: If powdery mildew (a white coating on leaves) is common where you garden, the most important choice is the variety: Profusion and Zahara types resist it and stay healthy in heat and humidity. For tall flowers to cut and put in a vase, pick double-flowered types like Benary's Giant or State Fair. For pots and small spaces, the compact Profusion and Zahara types are easiest. Flat, open, single flowers with an obvious center are the best for feeding bees and butterflies.
seasoned: Variety choice is the highest-leverage disease decision: the interspecific hybrid series Profusion and Zahara (Zinnia x marylandica) are bred for powdery-mildew and leaf-spot resistance and hold up in hot, humid conditions where tall Zinnia elegans types mildew. For cutting, the tall fully double elegans types (Benary's Giant, State Fair, Queen, Oklahoma) give the best stems and vase performance; for beds, borders, and containers, the compact resistant hybrids are the low-maintenance pick. Single and semi-double, wide-faced blooms with prominent centers serve pollinators best.

beginner: Zinnias are mostly planted to help other crops. They are one of the best flowers for attracting bees and butterflies, so gardeners plant them next to or around vegetables (like tomatoes, squash, and beans) to bring in pollinators and helpful bugs that eat pests. Open, flat, single flowers feed pollinators best. There is no plant you need to keep zinnias away from. The only thing to watch is crowding: packing them tightly against bushy, disease-prone plants traps damp air and makes powdery mildew (a white coating on leaves) more likely, so give them room for air to move.
seasoned: Zinnia's companion role inverts the usual framing: it is the crop you place to benefit others. As one of the best annual pollinator magnets, especially for butterflies, it is interplanted between vegetable rows or as a border to pull bees, hoverflies, and predatory insects toward fruiting and cucurbit crops, and it doubles as a trap crop that can draw Japanese beetles and aphids off more delicate plants. Tall, single, wide-faced blooms with prominent disc florets serve pollinators better than dense doubles. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; the only caution is spacing. Crowding zinnias against dense, disease-prone neighbors traps humidity and raises shared powdery-mildew pressure, so site for airflow rather than avoiding any particular plant.

beginner: Zinnias draw bees and helpful predator insects that improve tomato pollination and pest control when planted nearby.
seasoned: With tomatoes, zinnia's contribution is mostly beneficial insects rather than pollination, since tomatoes self-pollinate. Zinnia's nectar draws hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps whose larvae prey on aphids and other soft-bodied pests that bother tomatoes, and the bold blooms can pull some pests onto the zinnias instead. Site them at the bed edge as an insectary strip; expect predator support and color, not a direct pollination boost.

beginner: Squash, melons, and cucumbers need insects to move pollen to make fruit. Zinnias bring in the bees that do that job.

More pollinator traffic means better fruit set and fewer aborted or misshapen fruits. As a bonus, zinnias can also draw cucumber beetles and aphids onto themselves. Plant them in nearby rows so the pollinators they pull in spill over onto the crop.

beginner: Zinnias bring in bees and helpful bugs without crowding beans for food, since beans make their own nitrogen.
seasoned: Beans gain mostly from the beneficial insects zinnia brings in. The nectar supports parasitic wasps and predators that help manage bean beetles and aphids, and the flowers add pollinator traffic and structural diversity to the planting. beginner: Zinnias are easy, cheerful flowers you grow for blooms, not for eating. They love heat and full sun, so summer is their best season. You plant the seeds outside after your last frost, once the soil is warm, and you get your first flowers in about two months. They keep blooming until the first frost in fall. The more you cut the flowers, the more the plant makes, so cutting and removing faded blooms (called deadheading, snipping off spent flowers) keeps them going. Give plants room to breathe so the leaves stay dry and healthy.
seasoned: Zinnia (Zinnia elegans and related species) is a warm-season, frost-tender annual in the Asteraceae family, native to Mexico. It is grown for showy blooms, not food, across a wide size range from dwarf bedding types near 6 in to cut-flower types reaching 3 to 4 ft. Sown into warm soil after frost, it reaches first bloom in roughly 60 to 70 days and flowers continuously from summer until the first fall frost. It loves heat and full sun, so summer is its peak rather than a stress period. The defining care moves are cutting and deadheading, which drive cut-and-come-again bloom, and spacing for airflow to limit powdery mildew.

beginner: Cut zinnias for a vase when the flower is almost fully open. Test the stem first: hold it and give a gentle shake. If it stands up straight and stiff, it is ready to cut. If the flower flops over, wait a day or two. Cut in the morning and put the stems straight into clean water. Cut flowers usually last a week or longer indoors.
seasoned: Harvest for the vase when the bloom is nearly but not fully open and the stem is firm from the cut point to just below the flower head; a stem that stays rigid when gently shaken is ready, a floppy one is not. For longest vase life, cut before the small true flowers (the disc florets) emerge at the center. Cut in the cool of morning into clean water. Typical vase life is one week or more.

beginner: Deadheading means snipping off flowers once they fade. Do it regularly: cut the old bloom back to the next set of leaves, and the plant will make more flowers instead of going to seed. Cutting fresh flowers for a vase does the same job. When plants are young, pinch out the top above the fourth set of leaves to make them branch out bushier with more stems.
seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms back to the next leaf node throughout the season to redirect energy from seed set into new flower production and sustain cut-and-come-again bloom. Cutting for the vase serves the same function, so a working cutting garden is effectively self-deadheading. Pinch young plants at about four true-leaf sets to force basal branching and longer, more numerous stems.

beginner: Cosmos grows in almost any soil that drains well, and it actually flowers best in poor, un-fed soil. You do not need to add compost or fertilizer. The main thing to avoid is rich, soggy ground: too much richness gives leaves instead of flowers, and wet soil can rot the roots.
seasoned: Cosmos wants well-drained soil that is on the lean side; low fertility is a feature, not a problem. It tolerates a wide range of textures, from sand to clay, and a wide pH range. The one thing to avoid is rich, heavily amended, or wet ground: excess fertility, especially nitrogen, drives tall leafy growth with few flowers, and soggy soil invites root and stem rots.

beginner: Cosmos is not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). A normal garden range around 6.0 to 7.0 is fine, and it tolerates soils quite a bit more acidic or alkaline, so you usually do not need to change anything.
seasoned: Cosmos is not pH-fussy and performs across roughly 6.0 to 7.0, tolerating both mildly acidic and alkaline soils well outside that band. No pH adjustment is normally warranted.

beginner: Cosmos likes to be left alone. Give it full sun and poor soil, and do not fertilize; rich soil and feeding give you tall leafy plants with hardly any flowers. Plant the seeds outside after your last frost once the soil is warm, keep cutting the flowers to get more, and give the tall types something to lean on. A few dropped seeds will come back on their own next year.
seasoned: Grow cosmos hard: full sun and lean, unimproved soil are the whole trick. Rich ground and fertilizer push soft, tall, floppy foliage with few flowers, so skip the feed and go easy on water. Direct sow after the last frost once the soil reaches about 65 °F, deadhead or cut for continuous bloom, stake or plant the tall types close together, and let a few heads drop seed to renew the stand.

beginner: Do not feed cosmos. It flowers best in poor soil, and fertilizer, especially the high-nitrogen kind, gives you lots of leaves and few flowers, plus tall floppy plants. Only if your soil is very poor sand should you give one small dose of a low-nitrogen flower fertilizer when you plant.
seasoned: Do not fertilize cosmos. It flowers best in lean soil, and feeding, especially nitrogen, pushes soft foliage and stem elongation at the expense of bloom and makes tall types flop. If the soil is truly impoverished sand, a single light dose of a low-nitrogen, bloom-leaning fertilizer at planting is the most you should give.

beginner: Good news: cosmos usually needs no fertilizer at all. Only feed if your soil is very poor, and then just a little of a low-nitrogen flower food. Too much feeding means fewer flowers.
seasoned: Cosmos rarely needs feeding. Skip fertilizer unless your soil is very poor; if you feed at all, use a small dose of a low-nitrogen, bloom-oriented blend, since extra nitrogen costs you flowers.

beginner: The three numbers on fertilizer (N-P-K) are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. If you feed cosmos at all, pick one low in the first number (nitrogen), like 5-10-10, not a high-nitrogen lawn feed.
seasoned: If you feed at all, a low-nitrogen, phosphorus-leaning ratio such as 5-10-10 suits cosmos; avoid balanced or high-nitrogen lawn-type feeds, which drive foliage over bloom.

beginner: For most gardens, none. At most, one small feeding of a low-nitrogen fertilizer when you plant, and only if the soil is very poor. More than that gives you leaves instead of flowers.
seasoned: None is the right amount for most soils. At most, one light application of a low-nitrogen fertilizer at planting on very poor ground; never feed repeatedly, which favors foliage and lodging over bloom.

seasoned: Keep soil evenly moist through germination and establishment, then water sparingly; established cosmos is markedly drought-tolerant and resents wet feet. Overwatering, like overfeeding, favors foliage over flower.

beginner: Cosmos needs only a moderate amount of water, about half an inch to an inch a week counting rain, and less once it is established. Water deeply now and then rather than a little every day.
seasoned: A modest amount of water is plenty; roughly half an inch to an inch per week from rain plus irrigation during active growth, less once established. Deep, infrequent watering suits its drought-adapted roots; constant moisture reduces bloom and raises disease risk.

beginner: Water the ground around the plant, not the leaves. If you do get the leaves wet, water in the morning so they dry by midday, which helps prevent disease.
seasoned: Water at the base and avoid keeping foliage wet; if overhead watering is unavoidable, do it early so leaves dry fast. Dry foliage limits powdery mildew and gray mold.

beginner: If lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base gets soft and mushy, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly. Lots of leaves but few flowers is another sign of too much water and food.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting in wet soil, soft stems, and root or stem rot signal overwatering or poor drainage; lush, dark, flowerless growth also points to too much water and fertility.

beginner: Cosmos that is too dry wilts in the afternoon heat and looks dull. It is thirstiest right after planting and when the first buds form; once established it handles dry spells well.
seasoned: Afternoon wilting that recovers by evening and dulling foliage indicate underwatering, most critically during establishment and at first bud; established plants tolerate real drought.

beginner: Keep the soil evenly damp until the seedlings come up. Do not sow into cold, wet soil, which rots the seed.
seasoned: Keep the seedbed evenly moist through germination and establishment, cosmos's one critical moisture window; avoid cold, wet soil at sowing, which rots seed.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly watered while they get going. After that, cosmos needs much less.
seasoned: Grow seedlings on with steady moisture while they establish; after this, cosmos wants far less.

beginner: Once established, cosmos is very drought-tolerant and hates soggy soil. Half to one inch a week, deep and not too often, is plenty. Too much water gives you leaves instead of flowers.
seasoned: Established cosmos is markedly drought-tolerant and resents wet feet: half an inch to an inch a week is plenty, deep and infrequent, letting the soil dry between waterings. Overwatering, like overfeeding, favors foliage over flower.

beginner: As buds form, ease off the water. Cosmos blooms best when kept a bit lean and dry; too much water gives leafy growth and few flowers.
seasoned: As buds form, ease off: cosmos flowers best kept lean and on the dry side, and a plant that is too well watered runs to lush, dark, flowerless growth.

beginner: Keep cosmos on the dry side while it blooms, watering only when the soil dries out. Lean plants flower the most.
seasoned: Keep it lean through bloom, watering only when the soil dries; the drought-adapted plant flowers most freely on modest water and stays healthier with dry foliage.

beginner: As cosmos goes to seed, it needs little or no water and reseeds itself.
seasoned: As cosmos sets seed, little to no water is needed; it self-sows readily from a dry finish.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, and let the soil dry between waterings. Cosmos likes it on the dry side once established, and dry leaves help prevent disease.
seasoned: Water at the base and keep foliage dry; dry leaves are the main cultural lever against powdery mildew and gray mold. Water only when the soil dries, since cosmos is drought-adapted and overwatering reduces bloom.

beginner: Cosmos are flowers for a vase, not food to store, so there is nothing to refrigerate or freeze. To keep cut cosmos fresh, cut when the buds are just opening, trim the stem ends, remove any leaves that would sit under water, and use a clean vase. They usually last about 4 to 6 days.
seasoned: Cosmos is a cut flower, not a stored edible, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply. For vase life, cut when buds are just opening, recut stems, strip leaves below the waterline, use clean water, and keep blooms out of direct sun. Expect a fairly short vase life of about 4 to 6 days.

beginner: There are two kinds of cosmos. Garden cosmos is tall with feathery leaves and pink, white, or lavender flowers, and it is the best for cutting (look for Sensation, Purity, or Versailles). Orange cosmos is shorter with orange, gold, and red flowers and handles heat and humidity better, so choose it in hot, humid areas (Cosmic, Bright Lights). For pots and edges pick a dwarf like Sonata or Cosmic. Flat, open, single flowers feed bees and butterflies best.
seasoned: The most important choice is species. Garden cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus) is the tall, airy, feathery-foliage plant with pastel pink, white, and lavender daisies, and it supplies the premier cut-flower series (Sensation, Versailles, Purity, Seashells). Sulphur or orange cosmos (Cosmos sulphureus) is usually shorter and coarser, in hot orange, gold, and red, and takes heat and humidity notably better, so it is the stronger pick for the Deep South and low desert (Cosmic, Bright Lights, Sunny). Dwarf series such as Sonata and Cosmic suit beds and containers; tall types want support and are the best for cutting. Single, open-faced blooms serve pollinators better than dense doubles.

beginner: Cosmos is mostly grown to help the rest of the garden. It is one of the best flowers for bringing in bees, butterflies, and helpful bugs that eat pests, so plant it near vegetables like tomatoes, squash, and beans. One important tip: cosmos blooms best in poor soil, so do not plant it in a rich, well-fed vegetable bed, or you will get tall leafy plants with few flowers. Put it along a leaner edge instead. It also drops seed and comes back on its own, so pull extra seedlings if you do not want more. There is no plant you need to keep it away from.
seasoned: Cosmos, like other insectary annuals, is planted to benefit its neighbors rather than the other way around. Both species are strong nectar sources that draw bees, butterflies, and other beneficial insects, and birds feed on the seed heads; sulphur cosmos is an especially noted beneficial-insect plant. Interplant it as a border or insectary strip near fruiting and cucurbit crops to lift pollinator visitation and natural pest control. One cosmos-specific caution: it flowers best in lean soil, so do not plant it inside a richly fertilized vegetable bed, where the extra nitrogen makes it tall, leafy, and flowerless; site it at the drier, leaner edge. It also self-seeds freely, so deadhead or thin volunteers where you do not want a stand. No plant is biologically antagonistic to it.

beginner: Cosmos draws bees and helpful predator insects that improve pest control near tomatoes.
seasoned: With tomatoes, cosmos's contribution is beneficial insects rather than pollination, since tomatoes self-pollinate. Its nectar draws hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitic wasps whose larvae prey on aphids and hornworm eggs. Site it at the bed edge as an insectary strip, in leaner soil, and expect predator support and color rather than a direct pollination boost.

beginner: Squash, melons, and cucumbers need insects to move pollen to set fruit, and cosmos brings in the bees that do it.
seasoned: This is cosmos's strongest vegetable pairing: cucurbits depend on insect pollination, their flowers need several bee visits to set well, and cosmos is a reliable, long-blooming pollinator magnet through the fruiting window. More pollinator traffic means better fruit set. Plant it in nearby rows so the bees it pulls in spill onto the crop.

beginner: Cosmos brings in bees and helpful bugs without competing for food, since beans make their own nitrogen.
seasoned: Beans gain mostly from the beneficial insects cosmos brings in. Its nectar supports predators and parasitoids that help manage bean beetles and aphids, and it adds pollinator traffic and habitat with little nutrient competition, since legumes fix their own nitrogen. Keep cosmos to the edges so tall plants do not shade low bush beans.

beginner: A traditional pairing: cosmos near corn draws in pollinators and helpful insects.
seasoned: Corn benefits the least directly, since it is wind-pollinated and gains nothing from added bee traffic. What cosmos offers is general garden-ecosystem support, drawing predators and parasitoids that prey on aphids and caterpillars, plus height and color at the field edge. Treat this as a loose, habitat-level pairing.

beginner: If you started plants indoors, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week before planting them out.
seasoned: Indoor-started transplants need 7 to 10 days of hardening off, with gradually increasing outdoor exposure, before setting out after all frost danger has passed.

beginner: The easiest way is to sow cosmos seeds straight into warm garden soil (about 65 °F) after your last frost, about a quarter inch deep. If your season is short, you can start them indoors about 4 weeks before the last frost and move them outside afterward. Remember to use poor soil, not rich, and pinch the young tops to make them branch.
seasoned: Cosmos direct-sows readily into warm soil (about 65 °F) at roughly 1/4 in depth and is very successful sown straight into the garden, so direct sowing is the simplest, strongest method. To gain time in short seasons, start indoors about 4 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost. Sow into lean soil in full sun, and pinch young plants at three to four leaf sets to encourage branching.

beginner: Cosmos are easy, airy flowers you grow for blooms, not for eating. There are two kinds: tall garden cosmos with feathery leaves and pink, white, or lavender flowers, and shorter orange cosmos in bright orange, gold, and red that handle heat better. They love full sun and, unusually, they bloom best in poor soil with no fertilizer. Plant the seeds outside after your last frost, once the soil is warm, and you get flowers in about two months that keep coming until the first fall frost. Bees and butterflies love them, they make good cut flowers, and they drop seed and come back on their own.
seasoned: Cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus and Cosmos sulphureus, Asteraceae) is a warm-season, frost-tender annual grown for airy, daisy-like blooms on tall, branching, fine-foliage plants, not for food. Garden cosmos (C. bipinnatus) reaches roughly 3 to 6 ft with pink, white, rose, and lavender flowers; sulphur or orange cosmos (C. sulphureus) is usually shorter, 1 to 3 ft, in hot orange, gold, and red, and takes heat and humidity better. Sown into warm soil after frost, cosmos reaches first bloom in about 60 to 70 days and flowers from summer to the first fall frost. Its defining trait is that it thrives on neglect: lean, low-fertility soil and full sun give the most flowers, while rich soil and fertilizer give lush leaves and few blooms. It is a top pollinator and beneficial-insect plant, a good cut flower, and it self-seeds freely.

beginner: Cut cosmos flowers when the buds are just starting to open and show their color; they keep opening in the vase. Cut in the morning, put the stems straight into clean water, and pull off the lower leaves. Cosmos does not last as long as some cut flowers, about 4 to 6 days, so cut them often.
seasoned: Cut cosmos for the vase when the buds are just cracking open and showing color, since the flowers continue to open in water. Cut in the cool of the morning into clean water and strip the lower leaves. Cosmos has a fairly short vase life, roughly 4 to 6 days, so cut often and keep the plants deadheaded to drive fresh stems.

beginner: Deadheading means snipping off flowers once they fade. Do it regularly, cutting the old bloom back to the next set of leaves, and the plant makes more flowers instead of going to seed. Cutting flowers for a vase does the same thing. If plants get tall and floppy with few flowers, cut them back to about 12 to 18 inches and they will bush out and rebloom in about a month.
seasoned: Deadhead spent blooms back to the next leaf or side bud through the season to redirect energy from seed set into new flowers and sustain bloom to frost. Cutting for the vase does the same job. When plants grow tall and leggy, cut them back to about 12 to 18 in to force a fresh flush of branching and rebloom in roughly a month. Pinch young plants at three to four leaf sets to encourage bushier, better-branched growth.

beginner: Chamomile is an easy, cheerful herb grown for the little white daisy flowers you dry to make a soft, apple-scented tea. The common garden kind, called German chamomile, is a fast annual that grows about 2 ft tall with feathery leaves, flowers in early to midsummer, and drops seed so it often comes back on its own. It likes cool weather and well-drained soil, does not need rich soil or much fertilizer, and its flowers bring in bees and helpful insects. There is a second, different plant also called chamomile: Roman chamomile, a low, spreading perennial used as a fragrant ground cover or lawn. For tea flowers, grow German chamomile; for a carpet you can walk on, grow Roman chamomile.
seasoned: Chamomile most often means German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla, also sold as Matricaria recutita), an easy, quick-growing annual in the Asteraceae family grown for the small white-and-gold daisy flowers used to make a mild, apple-scented tea. It forms erect, branching stems to about 2 ft with fine, ferny foliage, blooms from early to midsummer, and self-seeds so freely that it often returns on its own. It prefers cool conditions and well-drained soil, tolerates poor ground and light frost, and asks for little fertilizer; the open flowers draw bees, hoverflies, and other beneficial insects. A distinct plant, Roman chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile), is a low, mat-forming perennial groundcover used for aromatic chamomile lawns rather than as an upright cutting herb, so choose German chamomile for tea flowers and Roman chamomile for a perennial carpet.

beginner: Chamomile is easygoing and grows in most ordinary garden soil as long as water drains away and does not pool. Light, well-drained soil is ideal, and it even does well in poor, sandy ground. Heavy, soggy clay is the one thing to avoid, since wet soil rots the roots, so pick a spot that drains well and only add a little compost if your soil is very thin.
seasoned: German chamomile wants well-drained soil and actually thrives in poor, light ground, so it is one of the few flowers that flowers better lean than rich. It grows in sandy to loamy soils and even tolerates clay if drainage is good, but heavy, wet, poorly drained soil is the consistent failure, rotting shallow roots and feeding botrytis and damping-off. Because it is a light feeder that thrives on minimal fertility, skip heavy amendment; the priority is drainage, not richness.

beginner: Chamomile is not picky about soil pH (how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Anywhere from about 6.0 to 7.5 is fine, and it even takes slightly alkaline soil, so you usually do not need to change anything.
seasoned: Chamomile is broadly adaptable to soil chemistry and performs well across roughly 6.0 to 7.5, leaning if anything toward the neutral-to-slightly-alkaline end (UC Master Gardeners note a slightly alkaline soil is preferred). pH adjustment is rarely warranted; focus on drainage and lean fertility instead.

beginner: Plant chamomile in cool weather. Scatter the tiny seeds on top of the soil and just press them in without covering, because they need light to sprout, in early spring (or fall where winters are mild). They come up in one to two weeks and flower in about eight to ten weeks. Go easy on fertilizer and water, and pick the little daisy flowers every few days when they are fully open to dry for tea. Leave a few flowers at the end to drop seed and it usually comes back on its own.
seasoned: Grow chamomile like an easy cool-season herb: surface-sow the tiny seed and press it in without covering, because light aids germination, into soil around 55°F in early spring (or in fall, and through winter in mild and Mediterranean zones). It sprouts in about 1 to 2 weeks and reaches first bloom in roughly 8 to 10 weeks. Keep fertilizer minimal, water only moderately, and pick the flowers every few days at full open for the best tea. Leave a few late heads to drop seed and it reseeds itself readily.

beginner: Chamomile hardly needs feeding and actually does better in poor soil. Mix a little compost in before planting only if your soil is very thin, and otherwise leave it alone. seasoned: Chamomile is a light feeder that thrives in poor soil and needs little or no supplemental fertilizer. If the ground is very thin, a modest amount of compost at planting is plenty. Excess nitrogen pushes soft, floppy foliage at the expense of flowers and invites aphids and mildew, so favor lean conditions and skip routine feeding.

beginner: You can usually skip feeding chamomile. Only if the plants look pale and hungry in poor soil, give one small dose of a balanced fertilizer. Lean soil actually gives you more flowers.
seasoned: Optional: chamomile rarely needs feeding. Only if plants look pale and starved in genuinely poor soil, give one light dose of a balanced fertilizer; otherwise skip it, since lean soil gives the best flowers.

beginner: Chamomile is a flower you dry for tea, not a vegetable to store. Pick the little daisy flowers when they are fully open, best on a dry morning, taking just the flower heads. Spread them out in a single layer on a screen or tray in an airy, shaded spot and let them air-dry for a few days, then keep the dried flowers in a sealed jar out of the light. Only use flowers that have not been sprayed. One safety note: chamomile is a daisy-family plant, and people who are allergic to ragweed or daisies can react to it, so be careful with chamomile tea if you have those allergies.
seasoned: Chamomile is grown for tea flowers, a pollinator draw, and a traditional companion, so the refrigerate and freeze fields do not apply as for produce. Pick the flowers when they are just fully open, ideally on a dry morning, snipping or stripping only the heads. Dry them promptly, spread in a single layer on a screen out of direct sun with good airflow, and handle gently so they do not discolor or heat; a few days of air-drying is usual. Store the dried flowers airtight, away from light, for tea. Use only unsprayed flowers. A safety note: chamomile is in the daisy (Asteraceae) family, and NC State cautions it can cause allergic skin reactions or oral swelling in people who are allergic to ragweed and related plants, so anyone with a ragweed or daisy allergy should be cautious with chamomile.

beginner: First decide which chamomile you want. For tea, grow German chamomile, the tall annual with lots of little daisy flowers; 'Bodegold' is a popular type that flowers early and heavily and is easy to pick. Roman chamomile is a different, low, spreading perennial used as a scented ground cover or lawn, not for cutting: 'Treneague' makes a no-mow chamomile lawn because it barely flowers, and 'Flore Pleno' has pretty double cream flowers. German chamomile grows easily from seed and reseeds itself; the Roman kinds are usually bought as small plants.
seasoned: The most important variety choice is which species you want. For tea flowers, grow German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla), the erect, self-seeding annual; named strains such as 'Bodegold' (upright, earlier and heavier bloom, easy to pick) and 'Bona' (bred for oil content) are selections of it. Roman chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile) is a separate low-growing perennial used as a fragrant groundcover or lawn, not as a cutting herb: 'Treneague' is a non-flowering clone grown for chamomile lawns, and 'Flore Pleno' bears double cream flowers. German chamomile comes readily from seed and self-sows; Roman selections are usually set from plants or divisions.

beginner: Chamomile is a classic, easygoing companion flower. Its open flowers bring in bees, hoverflies, and other helpful insects, and gardeners have long planted it near cabbage-family crops, onions, and herbs, where tradition says it improves their vigor and flavor (a nice old belief, though not something studies have proven). It asks for little, self-sows, and there is no plant you must keep it away from; just give it sun and room, and pair it with other cool-season crops. Do not let it reseed into beds where you do not want volunteers.
seasoned: Chamomile's best-grounded companion value is pollinator and beneficial-insect support: its open, apple-scented flowers draw bees, hoverflies, and other predators of aphids, so it earns a place as an insectary planting. It also carries a deep well of traditional companion lore, especially as a good neighbor to brassicas, onions, and other herbs and as a general garden tonic (the old name 'the plant's physician'); that tradition is worth passing along but is not formally trialed. As an easy, self-seeding annual it slots naturally among cool-season vegetables and herbs. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; the main caution is its prolific self-seeding, so site it where volunteers are welcome.

beginner: Chamomile flowers a long time and brings in bees and helpful bugs like hoverflies and ladybugs. Their young eat aphids, so a patch or border of chamomile helps the whole garden.
seasoned: Chamomile's best-grounded companion function. Its open, apple-scented flowers recruit bees and aphid predators (hoverflies, lacewings, ladybugs), supporting biological control nearby. Plant it as an insectary edge or interplant; this is a habitat benefit, not a documented pest-repellent effect.

beginner: Gardeners have long planted chamomile next to cabbage-family crops, onions, and other herbs, saying it helps them grow better and taste better. It is a lovely old tradition, not something proven, but chamomile is a harmless, pretty neighbor that also feeds pollinators.
seasoned: A traditional companion pairing. Folk practice places chamomile beside brassicas, onions, and herbs as a vigor-and-flavor tonic (the 'plant's physician' lore). The defensible part is the pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat it adds; the direct vigor claim is traditional, not trialed, so grow it for habitat and color rather than a promised yield effect.

beginner: Chamomile grows in the same cool weather as many vegetables and herbs, so it makes an easy, colorful companion that adds flowers and pollinators without crowding them. Keep it to edges so its reseeding does not take over.
seasoned: A cool-season habitat pairing. Chamomile occupies the same mild-weather window as many vegetables and herbs, adding pollinator and beneficial-insect habitat and color with low nutrient competition on lean soil. Keep it to edges and manage its self-seeding so volunteers do not crowd the crop.

seasoned: Indoor-started transplants need about a week of hardening off before setting out. Move chamomile out young: it resents transplanting once it is more than a couple of inches tall, so set out small plants. Seedlings tolerate light frost, so they can go out around the last spring frost.

beginner: The easiest way is to scatter chamomile seeds right on top of cool garden soil (about 55°F) and just press them in, without covering, because the seeds need light to sprout. seasoned: Chamomile is easiest direct-sown: scatter the fine seed on the surface of cool soil (around 55°F) and press it in without covering, since light aids germination. It sprouts in about 1 to 2 weeks and self-thins little, so thin to 8 to 12 in. To gain time in short-season areas, start indoors about 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant while seedlings are small, because larger plants transplant poorly. Sowing in fall lets it overwinter and reseed in mild zones.

beginner: Scatter the tiny seeds on top of the soil and press them in, but do not cover them, because chamomile needs light to sprout. In cool soil they come up in one to two weeks.
seasoned: Surface-sow chamomile and press the fine seed in without covering; light aids germination, so do not bury it. In cool soil near 55°F seedlings emerge in about 1 to 2 weeks.

beginner: Plant chamomile in cool weather, in early spring (or fall where winters are mild). It does not need warm soil. Just keep the surface damp until the little seeds sprout.
seasoned: Sow into cool soil in early spring (or fall in mild zones); chamomile prefers cool conditions and does not need warm soil to start. Keep the surface evenly moist while the fine seed germinates.

beginner: Once seedlings have a few real leaves, thin them to about 8 to 12 inches apart. Room for air to move helps prevent mildew and mold.
seasoned: Thin seedlings to 8 to 12 in once they have a few true leaves; spacing for airflow is the main defense against powdery mildew, botrytis, and damping-off on a stand of fine-seeded chamomile.

beginner: Keep young chamomile from drying out, but not soggy, since cold wet soil rots seedlings. Water the soil, not the leaves, and thin crowded ones.
seasoned: Do not let surface-sown seedlings dry out, but avoid keeping them soggy; cold, wet, crowded soil causes damping-off. Water at the base and thin promptly.

beginner: Go easy on food and water. Chamomile actually does better in poor soil, and too much fertilizer gives you floppy leaves and more bugs instead of flowers.
seasoned: Keep chamomile lean: it thrives in poor soil and flowers best with little or no fertilizer, while rich soil and excess nitrogen make soft, floppy, aphid- and mildew-prone growth.

beginner: Pinch off the top once when the plant is young to make it branch out with more flowering stems.
seasoned: Pinch the growing tip once on young plants to encourage branching and more flowering stems; it also makes the airy, upright plant a little sturdier.

beginner: As buds form, keep chamomile in sun with room around it and water the soil, not the leaves. Dry, airy plants resist mildew and mold.
seasoned: As buds form, keep plants in full sun with airflow and water at the base; dry, well-spaced foliage is what keeps powdery mildew and botrytis in check as the weather warms and humidifies.

beginner: As buds form, check the tips for aphids and for any white mildew in warm, damp weather. Catching crowding and wet leaves early keeps both down.
seasoned: Scout buds and tips for aphids and, in warm humid weather, for early powdery mildew; addressing crowding and overhead wetness early limits both on an otherwise trouble-free herb.

beginner: Pick the flowers when they are fully open, before the petals start to droop and dry, best on a dry morning. Take just the flower heads, and pick every few days to keep more coming.
seasoned: Pick heads when just fully open, before the white rays reflex and dry, ideally on a dry morning, snipping only the flower. Picking every few days sustains bloom and, by removing heads, holds down self-seeding.

beginner: Dry the flowers right after picking: spread them in one layer on a screen or tray in an airy, shaded spot for a few days, then keep them in a sealed jar out of the light. Only use flowers you have not sprayed.
seasoned: Dry picked flowers promptly in a single layer on a screen, out of direct sun with good airflow, handling gently to avoid discoloration or heating; store airtight, away from light, for tea. Use only unsprayed flowers.

beginner: To get chamomile back next year, leave a few flowers on the plant to dry and drop seed. It reseeds itself easily, so pick all the flowers if you do not want it spreading.
seasoned: To let chamomile return, leave some late heads to dry and shed seed; it self-sows freely and can become weedy. To prevent volunteers, pick or remove all heads before they mature.

beginner: One chamomile plant makes lots of little flowers over several weeks, and you pick a handful every few days. A short row gives you plenty of flowers to dry for tea, and it keeps blooming the more you pick.
seasoned: A single chamomile plant carries a long, prolific flush of small daisy flowers from early to midsummer, yielding a steady, repeated harvest of tea heads picked every few days. A short row supplies plenty of flowers for home tea; picking often extends the bloom and self-seeding keeps the patch going.

beginner: Chamomile flowers the same season you plant it, about eight to ten weeks after sowing. There is no waiting year, and it usually drops seed and comes back on its own.
seasoned: Chamomile blooms the first season from seed, roughly 8 to 10 weeks after sowing, so there is no establishment year; a cool-season sowing flowers through the season and self-sows for the next.

beginner: Sweet alyssum is not fussy about soil as long as it drains well. Average garden soil is fine, and it even tolerates poor, sandy, or gritty ground. What it cannot take is heavy, soggy soil that stays wet, which leads to the stem and root rots that are the main way this plant is lost. seasoned: Sweet alyssum grows in average, well-drained soil and tolerates poor, sandy, or rocky ground, a nod to its Mediterranean coastal origins. Sharp drainage is the priority: poorly drained, consistently wet soil drives the stem and crown rots that are its chief weakness, and plants decline outright in soggy beds. Avoid over-enriching, since overly fertile soil promotes foliage at the expense of flowers.

beginner: Sweet alyssum grows across a wide range of soil pH and does not need special adjustment. A near-neutral soil, roughly 6.0 to 7.0 on the pH scale (a measure of how acidic or alkaline soil is), suits it well, and it tolerates soil somewhat more acidic or more alkaline than that. Getting the drainage right matters far more than the exact pH.
seasoned: Sweet alyssum is adaptable on pH, growing in acid, neutral, or mildly alkaline soils; a near-neutral 6.0 to 7.0 is a safe target, with tolerance to either side. No narrow optimum is published for it, so drainage and moderate fertility are the levers that matter, not pH correction.

beginner: Sweet alyssum is quick and easy. Scatter the seed on the surface and barely cover it, because it needs light to sprout, or plant small transplants around your last frost. It blooms in about 6 to 8 weeks and flowers best in cool spring and fall weather, slowing down when it gets hot. Do not feed it much, because too much fertilizer gives you leaves instead of flowers, and plant it in soil that drains well so it does not rot. If it gets scraggly in summer, cut it back by about a third and it will flower again once it cools off. Plant some right in your vegetable bed to bring in the good bugs that eat aphids.
seasoned: Treat sweet alyssum as a fast, cool-season carpet: surface-sow the seed and barely cover it, since it needs light to germinate, or set out transplants around your last frost. It flowers in 6 to 8 weeks and blooms hardest in the cool of spring and fall, stalling in summer heat. Do not over-fertilize, since rich soil pushes leaves at the expense of flowers, and give it well-drained soil to head off the stem and root rots that are its main weakness. When it looks ragged in the heat, shear it back by a third to a half and it reflushes as the weather cools. Interplant it among vegetables to draw in the hoverflies and parasitic wasps that prey on aphids.

The honey-scented sprigs are short-stemmed and suit tiny nosegays; cut in the cool of the morning into clean water, keep them cool and out of direct sun, and expect only a few days of vase life. beginner: The main differences between types are color and how well they handle heat. Seed-grown kinds like Carpet of Snow (white) and Royal Carpet (purple) give a low, spreading carpet and reseed themselves, but they slow down in summer heat. If you want flowers all summer long, look for a sterile hybrid like Snow Princess, which is bred to keep blooming in heat and cold. Because it makes no seed, it flowers nonstop but will not come back on its own from dropped seed.
seasoned: Variety choice mostly trades flower color and heat tolerance. Seed-grown types (Carpet of Snow, Royal Carpet, Rosie O'Day, Easter Bonnet, Clear Crystal) give a low spreading carpet and reseed, but bloom declines in summer heat. The tetraploid Snow Crystals is more vigorous and somewhat more heat- and drought-tolerant. For unbroken bloom through summer, choose sterile vegetative hybrids such as Snow Princess, which are bred for heat and cold tolerance and, being sterile, put all their energy into flowers rather than seed and do not self-sow.

beginner: Sweet alyssum is one of the best companion flowers for a vegetable garden. Its sweet, honey-scented flowers pull in helpful insects, hoverflies (also called flower flies), tiny parasitic wasps, ladybugs, and lacewings, whose young feed on aphids and other pests. Planting it as an edging or in strips right among your vegetables, especially aphid-prone crops like lettuce, brassicas, and peppers, gives those good bugs food and a home base so they stick around. It is also a magnet for bees. One thing to know: sweet alyssum is in the cabbage (mustard) family, so it can share a few pests with cabbage-family crops, like flea beetles and cabbage caterpillars; usually its benefits far outweigh that. There is no plant you must keep it away from. Just do not crowd it into soggy soil, where it tends to rot.
seasoned: Sweet alyssum's headline role is as an insectary, or companion, plant. Its honey-scented, easily accessible flowers supply nectar and pollen to natural enemies of aphids, syrphid (hover) flies, parasitic wasps, ladybugs, and lacewings, over a long bloom period, and their larvae or broods then prey on pest aphids. This is well documented in commercial agriculture: sweet alyssum is planted in insectary strips in California organic lettuce and broccoli fields to draw syrphid flies for aphid control, and extension and university trials report increased hoverfly and parasitoid abundance and reduced aphid numbers where it is interplanted (the field-level effect is real but context-dependent, so it is best framed as habitat support rather than a guaranteed control). Interplant it as edging or strips among aphid-prone crops. A caveat: as a Brassicaceae member it can host some brassica pests (flea beetles, cabbage caterpillars, aphids), so monitor when interplanting near cole crops. There is no biologically antagonistic companion to avoid; the meaningful caution is siting, since wet, poorly drained beds raise its rot pressure.

seasoned: Interplanting sweet alyssum among aphid-prone vegetables provides nectar and pollen that sustain syrphid flies and parasitic wasps whose offspring prey on aphids. beginner: If you started or bought plants grown under cover, harden them off first: set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week. Sweet alyssum handles cool weather and light frost, so this is mostly to get it used to wind and full sun.

beginner: The easiest way is to sow sweet alyssum right where you want it: scatter the seed on cool, moist soil and barely cover it, because it needs light to sprout, around your last frost. It flowers in about 6 to 8 weeks. To get a jump on the season, start seed indoors about 5 to 6 weeks early, pressing it onto the surface so light reaches it, and plant out around the last frost. In mild areas, sow in fall for winter and spring flowers. Do not bury the seed, and leave a few plants to drop seed for next year.
seasoned: Sweet alyssum is easily direct-sown and is often the simplest path: surface-sow and barely cover the seed, since it needs light to germinate, on cool, moist soil around the last frost, and it flowers in roughly 6 to 8 weeks. For a head start, sow indoors about 5 to 6 weeks before set-out, pressing seed onto the surface under light, and transplant around the last frost. In mild-winter regions, sow in fall for winter and spring bloom. Do not bury the seed. Deadhead or shear rather than pinch, and leave a few plants to self-sow.
